MIDDLEBURG

Pages 66-67

one of the Friendly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was first discovered by Tasman, a Dutch navigator, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1742-3; and is called by the natives Ea-Oo-weh: it is about 16 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and in the widest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> about 8 miles from east to west. The skirts are chiefly laid out in plantations, the south-west and north-west sides especially. The interior parts are but little cultivated, though very capable of it: but this neglect adds greatly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the island; for here are agreeably dispersed groves of cocoa-nuts and other trees, lawns covered with thick grass, here and there plantations and paths leading to every part of the island, in such beautiful disorder, as greatly to enliven the prospect. The hills are low; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is delightful; but unfortunately <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is denied to this charming spot. Yams, with other roots, bananas, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit, are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of food; but the latter appeared to be scarce. Here is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>-tree, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVA">ava</a>-ava, with which they make an intoxicating liquor, in the same disgusting manner as is practised in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> islands. Here are several odoriferous trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, particularly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the lemon tribe; and the botanical gentlemen met with various new species of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Here also are a few hogs and fowls. There are no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> or villages; most of the houses are built in plantations, which are laid out in different parts, with no other order than what convenience requires. They are neatly constructed, but are less roomy and convenient than those in the Society islands. The floors are a little raised, and covered with thick strong mats. The same sort of matting serves to enclose them on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> side, the others being open. They have little areas before most of them, which are planted round with trees or ornamental shrubs, whose fragrance perfumes the air. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture consists of a few wooden platters, cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a> shells, and pillows made of wood, and shaped like four-legged stools or forms: their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> clothing, with the addition of a mat, serves them for bedding. The natives are of a clear mahogany or chestnut <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, in short frizzled curls, which seems to be burnt at the tips; their beards are cut or shaven. The general stature of the men is equal to our middle size, from five feet three to five feet ten inches; the proportions of the body are very fine, and the contours of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> extremely elegant, though something more muscular than at Otaheite, which may be owing to a greater and more constant exertion of strength in their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy. Their features are extremely mild and pleasing; and differ from the old Otaheitan faces in being more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> than round, the nose sharper, and the lips rather thinner. The women are, in general, a few inches shorter than the men, but not so small as the lower class of women at the Society islands. The practice of puncturing the skin, and blacking it, which is called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TATTOOING">tattooing</a>, is in full force among the men here, for their belly and loins are very strongly marked in configurations more compounded than those at Otaheite. The tenderest parts of the body were not free from these punctures; the application of which, besides being very painful, must be extremely dangerous on glandulous extremities. The men in general go almost naked, having only a small piece of cloth round the loins, but some wrap it in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance round them from their waist: this cloth is manufactured much like that at Otaheite, but overspread with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, which makes it stiff, and fit to resist the wet. The women are likewise covered from the waist downwards: they often have loose necklaces, consisting of several strings of small shells, seeds, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of fishes; and in the middle of all, the round operculum, or cover of a shell as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>-piece. The men frequently wear a string round their necks, from which a mother-of-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a> shell hangs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; both the ears of the women were perforated with two holes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> cut out of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORTOISE_SHELL">tortoise-shell</a> or bone was stuck through both the holes. The most remarkable circumstance observed of this people was, that most of them wanted the little finger on one, and sometimes on both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> did not exempt them from this amputation; for even among the few children that were seen running about naked, the greater part had already suffered such loss. This circumstance was observed by Tasman. Another singularity which was observed to be very general among these people, was a round spot on each cheek-bone, which appeared to have been burnt or blistered. On some it seemed to have been recently made, on others it was covered with scurf, and many had only a slight mark of its former existence: how, or for what purpose it was made, could not be learnt. The women here, in general, were reserved; and turned, with disgust, from the immodest behaviour of ungovernable females: there were not, however, wanting some who appeared to be of easy virtue, and invited their lovers with lascivious gestures. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> spoken here is soft, and not unpleasing; and whatever they said was spoken in a kind of singing tone. Omai and Mahine, who were both passengers on board the ship, at first declared that the language was totally new and unintelligible to them; however, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> of several words being pointed out, they soon caught the particular modification of this dialect, and conversed much better with the natives than any on board the ships could have done, after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> intercourse. They have the neat- eft ornaments imaginable, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little flat sticks, about five inches long, of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> wood like box, firmly and elegantly connected together at the bottom by a tissue of the fibres of cocoanut, some of which were of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and others dyed black; the same fibres were likewise used in the making of baskets, the taff of which was highly elegant, and varied into different forms and patterns. Their clubs are of a great variety of shapes, and many of them so ponderous as scarcely to be managed with one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The most common form was quadrangular, so as to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RHOMBOID">rhomboid</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> end, and gradually tapering into a round triangle at the other. Far the greater part were carved all over in many chequered patterns, which seemed to have required a long space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and incredible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> up; as a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or a piece of coral, are the only tools made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of: the whole surface of the plain clubs was as highly polished as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> an European workman had made them with the best instruments. Besides clubs, they have spears of the same wood, which were sometimes plain sharp-pointed sticks, and sometimes barbed with a flint-ray's tail. They have likewise bows and arrows of a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>: the bow, which is six feet long, is about the thickness of a little finger, and when slack forms a slight curve; its convex part is channelled with a single deep <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a>, in which the bow-string is lodged. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> is made of reed, near six feet long, and pointed with hard wood: when the bow is to be bent, instead of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it so as to increase the natural curvature, they draw it the contrary way, make it perfectly straight, and then form the curve on the other side. Most of their canoes have outriggers, made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>; and their workmanship is very admirable: two of these canoes are joined together with a surprising exactness, and the whole surface receives a very curious polish. Their paddles have short broad blades, something like those at Otaheite, but more neatly wrought and of better wood. They keep their dead above ground, after the manner of the Society islands; as a corpse was seen deposited on a low hut. Here were seen several men and women afflicted with leprous diseases, in some of whom the disorder had risen to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of virulence: one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in particular had his back and shoulders covered with a large cancerous ulcer, which was perfectly livid within, and of a bright yellow all round the edges. A woman was likewise unfortunate enough to have her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> destroyed by it in the most shocking manner; there was only a hole left in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of her nose; her cheek was swollen up, and continually oozing out a purulent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and her eyes seemed ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> out of her head, being bloody and sore. Though these were some of the most miserable objects that could possibly be seen, yet they seemed to be quite unconcerned about their misfortunes, and traded as briskly as any of the rest.

MIDDLEHAM

Pages 67-67

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, situated on the river Ure, 255 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It had once a castle, where was born Edward <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, only son of Richard III.; and is noted for a woollen manufactory and frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races. Its market is on Monday; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> Nov. 6. and 7. The town stands on a rising ground; and the castle, which was on the south side, was formerly mounted round by the help of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> conveyed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> from the higher grounds.

MIDDLESEX

Pages 67-67

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, which derives its name from its situation amidst the three kingdoms of the East, West, and South Saxons. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>; on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>; on the west by the river Colne, which separates it from Buckinghamshire; and on the east by the river Lea, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. It extends about 23 miles in length, but hardly 14 in breadth, and is not more than 115 in circumference; but it comprehends the two vast cities of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Westminster, which are situated in the south-east <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, it is by far the wealthiest and most populous county in England. It is divided into 602 liberties, containing 220 parishes, besides a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of chapels of ease, and 5 market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, exclusive of the cities of London and Westminster. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very pleasant and healthy, to which a fine gravelly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> does not a little contribute. The soil produces plenty of corn, and the county abounds with fertile meadows and gardeners grounds. In a word, the greater part of the county is so prodigiously afflited by the rich compost from London, that the whole of the cultivated part may be considered as a garden. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions are cattle, corn, and fruit; but its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are too many to be enumerated here, there being hardly a single manufacture practised in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> but what is also established in this county.—Though London is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRENTFORD">Brentford</a> is the county town where the members of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> are elected. It contains 77,712 houses, inhabited by 130,742 families, containing 349,958 males, and 294,371 females, so that the whole amount of its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is 635,329 persons. Middlesex is also the name of four different counties in the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; one of them is in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSACHUSETTS">Massachusetts</a>, another in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONNECTICUT">Connecticut</a>, a third in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEW_JERSEY">New <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERSEY">Jersey</a>, and the fourth in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>.

MIDDLETON

Pages 67-68

Dr Conyers, a very celebrated English divine, the son of a clergyman in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a> in 1683. He distinguished himself, while fellow of Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, by his controversy with Dr Bentley his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, relating to some mercenary conduct of the latter in that station. He afterwards had a controversy with the whole body of physicians, on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the medical profession; concerning which he published De medicorum apud veteres Romanos degentium conditio et differentia; qua, contra viros celeberrimos Jacobum Sponium et Richardum Medium, servilum aequo ignobilium eam juvfe offenditur; and in the course of this dispute much resentment and many pamphlets appeared. Hitherto he had stood well with his clerical brethren; but he drew the resentment of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> on him in 1729, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> "A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> from Rome, showing an exact conformity between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> and Paganism," &c.; as this letter, though politely written, yet attacked Popish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> with a gaiety that appeared dangerous to the cause of miracles in general. Nor were his Objections to Dr. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERLAND">Waterland</a>'s manner of vindicating Scripture against Tindal's "Christianity as old as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">Creation</a>," looked on in a more favourable point of view. In 1741, came out his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, "The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of M. Tullius Cicero." Cicero," 2 vols 4to: which is indeed a fine performance, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably be read as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as false and polite literature subsist among us: the author has nevertheless fallen into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of biographers, who often give panegyrics instead of history. In 1748, he published, "A free inquiry into the miraculous powers which are supposed to have subsisted in the Christian church from the earliest ages, through several successive centuries." He was now attacked from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; but before he took any notice of his antagonists, he supplied them with another subject, in "An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>'s discourses concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of prophecy," &c. Thus Dr Middleton <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to display talents and learning, which are highly esteemed by men of a free turn of mind, but by no means in a method calculated to invite promotion in the clerical line. He was in 1723 chosen <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> librarian of the public library at Cambridge; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he rose not to dignities in the church, he was in easy circumstances, which permitted him to assert a dignity of mind often forgotten in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of preferment. He died in 1753, at Hildersham in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, an estate of his own purchasing; and in 1752, all his works, except the life of Cicero, were collected in 4 vols. 4to.

MIDDLEWICH

Pages 68-68

a town of Cheshire, 167 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It stands near the confluence of the Croke and Dan, where are two <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, from which are made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities of salt, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> being laid to be so strong as to produce a full fourth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> salt. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> borough, governed by burgesses; and its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> extends into many adjacent townships. It has a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. By means of inland <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Ribble, Ouse, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, Darwent, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, Humber, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Avon, &c.; which navigation, including its windings, extends above 500 miles, in the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, &c. The river Wheeock, after a course of about 12 miles from Mowcop-hill, runs into the Dan a little above this town.

MIDHURST

Pages 68-68

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, 52 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, has been represented in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> ever since the 4th of Edward II. It is a neat small town, on a hill surrounded with others, having the river Arun at the bottom; and is a borough by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, chosen annually by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-leet of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>.

MIDIAN

Pages 68-68
or MADIAN, in Ancient Geography, a town on the south side of Arabia Petraea, so called from one of the sons of Abraham by Keturah.—Another Midian, near the Arnon and Jezreel, in ruins in Jerome's time. With the daughters of these Midianites the Israelites committed fornication, and were guilty of idolatry. A branch of the Midianites dwelt on the Arabian gulf, and were called Kenites: some of whom turned profanists, and dwelt with the Israelites in the land of Canaan. MID-LOTHIAN. See Lothian and Edinburghshire.

MIDSHIP-FRAME

Pages 68-68

a name given to that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of pieces formed into one timber, which determines the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> breadth of the ship, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> of all the inferior timbers. In the article SHIP-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a full explanation of what is meant by a frame of timbers. He will also perceive the outlines of all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> frames, with their gradual dimensions, from the midship-frame, delineated in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of projection annexed to that article.

MIDSHIPMAN

Pages 68-69

a sort of naval <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADET">cadet</a>, appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the orders of the superior officers, and assist in the necessary business of the vessel, either abroad <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at home. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of midshipmen, like that of several other officers, is always in proportion to the size of the ship to which they belong. Thus a first-rate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of war has 24, and the inferior <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> a suitable number in proportion. No person can be appointed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> without having previously served two years in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> in this capacity, or in that of mate, besides having been at least four years in actual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, either in merchant ships or in the royal navy. Midshipman is accordingly the station in which a young volunteer is trained in the several exercises necessary to attain a sufficient knowledge of the machinery, movements, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations of a ship, to qualify him for a sea officer. On his first entrance in a ship of war, every midshipman has several disadvantageous circumstances to encounter. These are partly occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the sea service; and partly by the mistaken prejudices of people in general respecting naval <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and the genius of sailors and their officers. No character, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, is more excellent than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sailor, whom they generally suppose to be treated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> severity by his officers, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between them not very advantageous to the latter. The midshipman usually comes aboard tainted with these prejudices, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> has been amongst the higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of people; and if the officers happen to answer his opinion, he conceives an early distrust to the service, from a very partial and incompetent view of its operations. Blinded by these prepossessions, he is thrown off his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and very soon surprised to find, amongst those honest fellows, a crew of abandoned miscreants, ripe for any mischief or villainy. Perhaps, after a little observation, many of them <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> appear to him equally destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, shame, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and only deterred from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of any crimes by the terror of severe <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. He will discover, that the pernicious example of a few of the vilest in a ship of war is too often apt to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> the principles of the greatest number, especially if the reins of discipline are too much relaxed, so as to foster that idleness and dissipation, which engender sloth, diseases, and an utter profligacy of manners. If the midshipman on many occasions is obliged to mix with these, particularly in the exercises of extending or reducing the sails in the tops, he ought resolutely to guard against this contagion, with which the morals of his inferiors may be infected. He should, however, avail himself of their knowledge, and acquire their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in managing and fixing the sails and rigging, and never suffer himself to be excelled by an inferior. He will probably find a virtue in almost every every private sailor, which is entirely unknown to many of his officers: that virtue is emulation, which is not indeed mentioned amongst their qualities by the gentlemen of terra firma, by whom their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are often copiously described with very little judgment. There is hardly a common tar who is not envious of superior skill in his fellows, and jealous on all occasions to be outdone in what he considers as a branch of his duty: nor is he more afraid of the dreadful consequences of whittling in a storm, than of being flattered with the opprobrious epithet of lubber. Fortified against this scandal, by a thorough knowledge of his business, the sailor will sometimes sneer in private at the execution of orders which to him appear awkward, improper, or unlike a seaman. Nay, he will perhaps be malicious enough to suppress his own judgment, and, by a punctual obedience to command, execute whatever is to be performed in a manner which he knows to be improper, in order to expose the person commanding to disgrace and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>. Little skilled in the method of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, he considers the officer who cons his lesson by rote as very ill qualified for his station, because particular situations might render it necessary for the said officer to assist at putting his own orders in practice. An <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> in this practical knowledge will therefore necessarily be thought an unpardonable deficiency by those who are to follow his directions. Hence the midshipman who associates with these sailors in the tops, till he has acquired a competent skill in the service of extending or reducing the sails, &c. will be often entertained with a number of scurrilous jests, at the expense of his superiors. Hence also he will learn, that a timely application to those exercises can only prevent him from appearing in the same despicable point of view, which must certainly be a cruel mortification to a man of the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. If the midshipman is not employed in these services, which are undoubtedly necessary to give him a clearer idea of the different parts of his occupation, a variety of other objects present themselves to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Without presuming to dictate the studies which are most essential to his improvement, we could wish to recommend such as are most suitable to the bent of his inclination. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, which are in the first rank of science, are the materials which form the skilful pilot and the superior mariner. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> is entirely derived from the two former, and all the machinery and movements of a ship are founded upon the latter. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> upon the sails, and the resistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> at the stern, naturally dictate an inquiry into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of solids and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>; and the state of the ship, floating on the water, seems to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his application to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">hydrostatics</a>, and the effects of gravity. A proficiency in these branches of science will equally enlarge his views, with regard to the operations of naval war, as directed by the efforts of powder and the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>. The most effectual method to excite his application to those studies, is, perhaps, by looking round the navy, to observe the characters of individuals. By this inquiry he will probably discover, that the officer who is eminently skilled in the sciences, will command universal respect and approbation; and that whoever is satisfied with the despicable ambition of shining the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, will be the object of universal contempt. The attention of the former will be engaged in those studies which are highly useful to himself in particular, and to the service in general. The employment of the latter is to acquire those superficial accomplishments that unbind the mind from every useful science, emasculate the judgment, and render the hero infinitely more dexterous at falling into his station in the dance than in the line of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Unless the midshipman has an unconquerable aversion to the acquisition of those qualifications which are so essential to his improvement, he will very rarely want opportunities of making a progress therein. Every step he advances in those meritorious employments will facilitate his accession to the next in order. If the dunces, who are his officers or messmates, are rattling the dice, roaring bad verses, hissing on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>, or scraping <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> from the fiddle, his attention to more noble studies will sweeten the hours of relaxation. He should recollect, that no example from fools ought to influence his conduct, or seduce him from that laudable ambition which his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and advantage are equally concerned to pursue.

MIDWIFE

Pages 69-98

one whose profession is to deliver women in labour. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">MIDWIFERY</a>. **MIDWIFERY** 1. **<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">Definition</a>.** The art of assisting women in labour. In a more extended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, it is understood to comprehend also the treatment of the diseases of women and children. In this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> we shall consider it in the former limited sense, viz. as relating to the birth of the offspring of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. 2. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Midwifery.** It must be very obvious that this art must have been almost coeval with mankind; but in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a very rude state till the 17th century; and even after physic and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> had become distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, it remained almost totally uncultivated. It is a curious fact, that in the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> the very reverse of this has taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In that empire, according to the latest accounts, both physic and surgery are still in a state of utmost <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>, even more so than among the savages of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; but for some hundred years, the art of midwifery has been practised by a set of men destined to the purpose by order of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. These men, who hold in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> which lithotomists did in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about the beginning of last century, are called in whenever a woman has been above a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hours in labour, and employ a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> contrivance for History. for completing the delivery without injury to the infant. A certain number of such individuals is allotted to each district of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>. It is said, that the Chinese government was led to make this provision for alleviating the sufferings of child-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> women, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a representation, that annually many women died undelivered, and that in the majority of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the cause of obstruction might have been removed by very simple mechanical expedients. Both Sir George Staunton and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a> were ignorant of this fact; and the latter in particular expressly mentions, that there are no men-midwives in China. But the writer of this article had his information from a more authentic source than the works of gentlemen who were only a few months in that country, and were in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> treated as state prisoners. He has it, through the medium of a friend, from a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who resided upwards of twenty years as surgeon to the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a>, and who had both the ability and the inclination to learn, during the course of so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> a residence, all the customs and prejudices of the natives relating to the preservation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Towards the end of the 17th century, the same causes which had so long before led to the cultivation of midwifery in China produced the same effect in Europe. The dangers to which women are sometimes exposed during labour excited the compassion of the benevolent; so that a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> which was established for the reception of the indigent sick, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">Hotel</a> Dieu of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> was appropriated to lying-in women. The opportunities of practice which that hospital afforded, directed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of medical men to the numerous accidents which happen during labour, and to the various diseases which occur after delivery. Public teaching followed, and soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of employing men in the practice of midwifery began. From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the art became rapidly improved; and it is now in many parts of Europe, and particularly in Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, in as great a state of perfection as physic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> surgery. In the year 1725, a professorship of midwifery was established in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; and the town <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ordained, that no woman should be allowed to practise midwifery within the liberties of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, without having previously obtained a certificate from the professor of her being properly qualified. This salutary regulation has fallen into desuetude. There can be no doubt that the improvement of the art of midwifery was chiefly in consequence of medical men directing their attention to the subject; but the propriety of men being employed in such a profession is much questioned by many individuals of considerable reputeability. Dr John Gregory, in his Comparative View, p. 22, says, "every other animal brings forth its young without any assistance, but we think a midwife understands it better." Had this eminent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> said, "other animals content themselves with the clothing which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> has bestowed, but we think it necessary to cover our bodies with the workmanship of weavers," very few in this northern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> would have attended to the sneer. His son, the present professor, has improved upon the idea. He seems to suppose that women without any instruction, and of course without any knowledge of the subject, are capable of afflicting one another while in labour; and in the sportiveness of his lively imagination, he compares men-midwives to that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of frog, in which, according to the allegation of Reaumur, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> draws out the ova from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, or, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the naturalist's words, "accouche la femelle." It appears to us that this question, on which much <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECLAMATION">declamation</a> has been employed by the parties who have agitated it, may be brought within a very narrow compass. It may be assumed as a fact established beyond the reach of controversy, that sometimes dangers and difficulties occur during labour (from causes to be explained in a subsequent part of this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a>), which can be lessened or removed by those only who have an intimate knowledge of the structure of the human body and of the practice of physic. On such occasions, it must be admitted, medical men alone can be useful. But as such labours occur only in proportion of two or three in the hundred, the general practice might be confined to midwives, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they could be taught to manage ordinary cases, and to foresee and distinguish difficulties or dangers, so as to procure in sufficient time additional assistance. It is on this point that the decision of the question must depend. It conflicts with the knowledge of the writer of this article, that women may be taught all this. But there are many who allege, that a little knowledge being a dangerous thing, midwives acquire a self-sufficiency which renders them averse from calling in superior assistance, and that, in consequence, they often occasion the most deplorable accidents both to mother and child. In England this is the popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, so that there women are almost entirely excluded from the practice of midwifery. A similar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> against midwives has, it is believed, begun in some parts of Scotland; but it is presumed this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> gradually cease, when it is considered that, in general, the Scotch midwives are regularly instructed, and are at the same time both virtuous and industrious. If they attend strictly to their duty, and invariably prefer their patients safety to their own feelings or supposed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, they will deservedly retain the public confidence. But if in cases of difficulty or danger they trust to their own exertions, or from interested motives decline the assistance of able practitioners, and if they interfere in the treatment of the diseases of women and children, they will in a few years be excluded from practice. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">Division</a> of the subject. In order to exhibit an accurate view of what relates to the birth of man, we shall consider, in the first place, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>; secondly, the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a>; thirdly, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of childbearing; and lastly, the deviations from the ordinary course which sometimes happen. These topics will form the subjects of the following chapters. Chap. I. Of Conception. Three circumstances are required for conception in the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, viz. puberty; a healthy, vigorous, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state of the parts subservient to the operation in both sexes; and successful sexual intercourse. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of puberty in women differs considerably in different climates. In Europe it takes place <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> between the fourteenth and sixteenth year. This important era is marked by certain changes both in the mind and body. The girl feels sensations to which she had been formerly unaccustomed. She loses a relish for her former amusements, and even for her youthful companions. She seeks solitude, indulges in the depressing passions, and these are excited by the most apparently trifling causes. She feels occasionally certain desires which modestly repel; and it is by degrees only that she regains her former tranquillity. The changes in her body are even more strongly marked than those in her mind. Her breasts assume that form which adds to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of her person, and renders them fit for nourishing her infant; and every part of the genital system is enlarged. A periodical discharge from the uterus renders the woman perfect. In young men the same causes produce very different effects. The lad, about fifteen or sixteen, feels a great increase of strength; his features expand, his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> becomes rough, his step firm, his body athletic; and he engages voluntarily in exercises which require an exertion of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. The changes in his mind are as strongly marked as those in his body. He loses that restless peculiarly which had distinguished his early years, and becomes capable of attending steadily to one object. His behaviour to the fair <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> is suddenly altered. He no longer shows that contempt for women, which he had formerly betrayed. He is softened, approaches them with deference, and experiences a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, for which he can scarcely account. In him too there is an important change in the condition of the genital organs. 2. Unless the parts which constitute peculiarity of sex be in a healthy, vigorous, and natural state, conception cannot take place. In women, conception is prevented if the organs be too much relaxed; if there be obstruction between the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and internal parts; if any premature discharge take place from the internal parts; if the menstrual evacuation be not natural in every respect; and if the appendages of the uterus, called fallopian tubes, and ovaria, be not of the natural structure. In men, the same circumstance happens if the organs be too much relaxed; if the orifice of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a> be in an improper situation; if the urethra be diseased; if the testes be not in a natural healthy state; and if there be any defect in the erections <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a>; which prevents the proper erection of that organ. 3. The sexual intercourse cannot be successful unless somewhat necessary for conception be furnished by both sexes. This consists in the male of a fluid secreted by the testes; and in the female, of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of a substance, supposed to resemble a very minute vesicle situated in the ovarium, and called by physiologists ovum. Each ovarium contains a number of these vesicles. After every conception, certain marks of the detachment of the ovum remain in the respective ovarium. When the circumstances required for conception concur, a being is produced which generally resembles both parents. This resemblance is most strikingly marked in the human subject, when one of the parents is an European, and the other an African. What is called a mulatto is produced. The human race possesses the power of propagation in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with all the other species of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and also, it has been said, with the vegetable kingdom. As <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> then, as it has been styled, is common to two of the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, it has been imagined by ingenious men, that this wonderful operation is regulated in both by a certain general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. But they have differed much in their account of this law. The question at issue between the two parties is whether the embryos of animals be prepared by the sexual intercourse out of inorganic materials, or whether they pre-exist in the bodies of animals, and are only developed as it were by that intercourse. The former of these opinions is called the doctrine of epigenesis, the latter that of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a>. Both doctrines have been maintained with much ingenuity by equally respectable authorities. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGATIVE">Negative</a> arguments have been adduced in favour of the one, positive in support of the other, and it must be confessed that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> between them seems nearly equal. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRE_EXISTENCE">pre-existence</a> of ova in the oviparous animals appears a positive argument in favour of evolution; but the satirical remark of a late witty author, * that, were *Rhumus* this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> true, every individual of the human race *bach* must have been lodged in the ovaria of our first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, by affording a negative argument in favour of epigenesis, restores the balance. The various arguments advanced on each side by the opposite parties in this dispute are so very numerous, that we cannot attempt to detail them in this work; and on a subject which has divided the opinions of so many able physiologists, it would be presumption to decide prematurely. If generation be regarded as an animal operation, one is led to inquire whether the product be the result of the combined influence of both sexes, or whether it be produced by either sex alone. The first opinion was generally adopted by physiologists, till about the end of the 17th century, when an accidental discovery convinced many that the embryo was produced by the male parent alone; and another discovery some years afterwards again overturned that opinion, and rendered it believed by not a few that the embryo is furnished exclusively by the female parent. Several circumstances concurred to render the first opinion probable; the structure of the organs which constitute peculiarity of sex in both parents, the circumstances necessary for successful impregnation, and the similitude of children to both parents, appear very strong arguments in its favour. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> theory, although first brought into vogue about the end of the 17th century by the discoveries of Leeuwenhoek, had been formerly propounded by the followers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>. Their argument was <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>: the seed, said they, is sown in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, nourished and evolved there; so the male semen is sown in the uterus, and in the same manner nourished and evolved. Leeuwenhoek's discovery seemed a more conclusive argument in favour of the theory than vague analogy. He observed innumerable animalcula in the seminal fluid of the males of many animals. These he imagined to be embryos. But as animalcula of apparently the same nature have been observed in many animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> besides the semen masculinum, the opinion of Leeuwenhoek and the theory itself are overturned. It was owing principally to the labours, industry, and ingenuity of Baron Haller, that the third theory, that of the pre-existing germ, became fashionable. His observations seem to contain a demonstration of the fact. Those who have adopted this theory, imagine that the semen masculinum possesses the power of stimulating the various parts of the pre-existing embryo. And hence they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the filimitude to both parents, and particularly the appearance of the hybrid productions, to that fluid nourishing certain parts, and new-arranging others. But if this were true, then the semen masculinum of all animals should possess the power of stimulating the germs of all female animals; and besides, in each class of animals it should possess certain specific powers of giving a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to the growth of parts. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a>, however, has not proved this to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, for the hybrid productions are very limited; and we may be permitted perhaps, without the imputation of arrogance in pretending to search into the intentions of the Author of nature, to observe, that had the semen masculinum been possessed of such powers, the whole species of animals would have been soon confounded, and the whole animal kingdom would soon have returned to that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a> from which it has been allegorically said it originated. Yet we are reduced to the alternative of either rejecting the theory, or of believing that the semen does possess the powers alluded to. If we examine attentively the anatomical discovery on which this theory is built, we shall perhaps be inclined to believe that the foundation of the whole is very insufficient; and hence to conclude that the great superstructure is in a very tottering condition. If it be possible that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of the chick to the yolk of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> should be in consequence of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a>, the theory must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to the ground. Haller has endeavoured to obviate this objection, but not with his usual judgment. Two circumstances, however, seem to show that the attachment is really by inoculation: 1. That vessels are seen in the membrane of the yolk evidently containing blood before the heart of the chick begins to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>; yet these vessels afterwards appear to depend on the vascular system of the chick. And, 2. That in many animals, as in the human subject, the umbilical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> seems to be attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> by inoculation; for there is a circle round the root of the cord which resembles a cicatrix, and within a few days after birth, the cord uniformly drops off at that very circle, whatever portion may have been retained after delivery. There is one objection equally applicable to all the three theories, viz. the difficulty of explaining the steps of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. A variety of explanations have been offered by ingenious men. Spallanzani and Mr John Hunter lately, Haller and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONNET">Bonnet</a> formerly, have rendered themselves conspicuous on this subject. Spallanzani, in particular, appears to many to have produced, by his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> impregnation, the most convincing proofs of the pre-existence of the germ. But to what do his celebrated experiments amount? They show, that in all animals it is necessary that the semen masculinum should be applied to the somewhat expelled by the female during the coitus, otherwise impregnation cannot take place. But was not this universally acknowledged before the abbeé was born? In the unfortunate frogs who were the subjects of his experiments, the whole operation of generation was completed except the application of the male semen to the substances expelled by the female. Nature, by establishing that the substances should be carried on in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, shows that the semen must be diluted, otherwise it cannot fecundate. The abbeé only imitated nature. He left the question in the state in which he found it. His experiment on the bitch may appear more conclusive; but alas! it has never succeeded with any person but himself. On the whole, since the process of generation is so obscure that no rational explanation of it has yet been offered, are we not entitled to conclude that the general theory which accounts most satisfactorily for the various phenomena which impregnation exhibits is the best; and consequently, that the product of generation cannot pre-exist in the body of either parent exclusively? **Chap. II. Effects of Impregnation.** In consequence of impregnation, certain important changes take place in the uterine system of the human subject. We shall consider the natural changes only. On some occasions, there are morbid changes; but we shall not notice them, except in so far as some of them serve to illustrate the nature of the usual ones. The first visible change is on the ovarium. One of those organs swells out at one point like a small papilla, then bursts, and somewhat is discharged. A substance is found in the ovarium after this, which is called corpus luteum. Roederer has described very accurately its appearance a few hours after delivery. He says "corpus luteum locatur in rotundo apice. Totam ovarii crassitatem occupat, immediate pone ovarii membranam illa fede tenuiorem locatum; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> ovario cum quo celluloae ope coheret separari sine laetione potest; nulli peculiari ovarii rimae respondet; neque canalis in illo excavatus, sed totum folidum est. Luteus color est, subfinitia acinoa, acinis admodum compactis et <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> se preffis <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBITUS">ambitus</a> rotundus. Potest aliquo modo, velut in glandulis suprarenalibus, duplex substantia distingui, corticalis et medullaris; quarum illa inaequalis cellulae 1—2 lin. lutea comprehendit hanc medullarem <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUM">album</a>, quae tenuis et membrana quasi callofa, alium nucleum flavum includit cafforem *." It is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> soon after conception, and then gradually becomes smaller; but never totally disappears. Roederer observes, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> puerperium eo magis contrahi et induari illa corpora videntur, quo remotor fit partes illa qualia videbatur observantur in feminis que nuper partum non ediderunt." "Lutea corpora quo serius a partu observantur cuncta glandulis suprarenalibus familiae ehe videntur, duplici nempe substantia, exteriore corticali, solida seu flava lutea et nucleo fusco: velut etiam illae glandulae com-+Ibid. pressa sunt +." In cases where there is a plurality of offspring, children, Effects of children, there is evidently a corpus luteum to each impregnated child. In some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, as in the bitch or cat, the number of young in the uterus may be generally known by the corresponding corpora lutea in the ovaria. The next change in the human uterine system which deserves notice is that in the fallopian tubes. They swell out towards the fimbriated extremity, and form a cavity which has been called antrum. Köderer was the first who observed and accurately delineated this change. He says, p. 14, loco citato, "In hoc etiam utero antrum tubae dextrae appareat, c.f. tab. i. not. 5, ubi quidem in utraque tuba adeunt, in hujus iconis utero ad forum tubam dextram antrum pertinet. Ad uterum feminam oviduum puerperae non longe a fimbria in illiusmodi antrum tuba sinistra prominet: dextra quidem sine antro est, sed versus fimbriam ita flectitur ut ultima flexura dimidium pollicem ultra reliquam tubam effaretur. Tubae feminae qua max a maturo parte mortua est, et alterius tres dies puerperae antris quidem carent, sed multum versus fimbrias dilatantur. An est facta conceptione illa antra nascuntur?" "In uteri, tab. iv. ovario dextro luteum corpus latet in uteri feminae oviduum puerperae ovario sinistro; in uteri, tab. i. ovario sinistro." He adds, "ulteriores indagines illa antra non indigna esse mihi videntur. Licet forsan conjectare aliquod liquor ex vesicula graeciana in tubam lapillum et ad introitum morans illam dilatam." But the most astonishing changes are those produced in the uterus itself. Its parietes separate, a cavity is formed which becomes filled with a fluid, and the os uteri is closed up. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> contained within the cavity soon assumes an organized form. It is said that some time after conception, a small vesicle is observed attached at one point to the internal surface of the uterus; that the rest of the parietes is covered with a gelatinous fluid; and that the whole internal surface assumes a flocculent appearance. By degrees the vesicle, which is in fact the ovum containing the embryo, increases so much in size that it nearly fills the whole cavity in which it is contained, and then its structure becomes the object of our senses. The increase of size in the uterus is very gradual. It is at first confined almost entirely to the fundus, and it proceeds so slowly that it does not leave the cavity of the pelvis till nearly the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> change in the cervix for the first five months is the complete closure of the orifice, which is effected by a gelatinous fluid: afterwards the cervix is gradually extended, and at last its form is obliterated, the whole uterus becoming like an oval pouch. After the fifth month the increase of size in the uterus is very rapid. The fundus can be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> felt above the pubes about the fifth month, but at the end of the ninth month it extends to the scrobiculus cordis. Some authors have alleged that the changes in the cervix and in the situation of the fundus are so uniformly regular in every case, that by attending to them it is possible to ascertain the exact period of impregnation. But in this respect they are much mistaken; the changes being not only different in different women, but also in the same woman in different pregnancies. The texture of the parietes of the uterus seems much altered after impregnation. It becomes spongy and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a>. The fibres run in very different directions, and from their power and appearance are certainly muscular. The blood-vessels become much enlarged, but are still in a tortuous direction. They are particularly large at one part of the uterus. The lymphatic vessels, which in the unimpregnated uterus cannot be demonstrated by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANASTOMOSIS">anastomosis</a>, become, as well as the blood-vessels, remarkably large. The ovum is not often expelled entire till after the eighth or twelfth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> after conception. It is shaped somewhat like an egg, and is about the latter period about four inches in length. When cut into, it is found to consist of four layers or membranes, and to contain a fetus surrounded by a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water and connected to one part of the parietes (which is considerably thicker than the rest) by a vascular cord. The external membrane covers the whole ovum. It is thick, spongy, and very vascular, the vessels evidently deriving their blood from the uterus; it has three perforations which correspond with the openings of the os tineae and fallopian tubes. It has been called decidua, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNICA">tunica</a> filamento, &c., but its most ordinary appellation is spongy chorion. The second membrane proceeds from the edges of that part into which the vascular rope which connects the fetus is attached. It was first pointed out to anatomists by Dr William Hunter, and called by him decidua reflexa. The name unfortunately records to posterity the absurd idea respecting its origin which was entertained by Dr Hunter. It is not so thick and spongy as the former membrane, nor so vascular. It lies loyally between the external membrane and that to be next described; but it appears only for a short time, as it soon becomes blended with the others. The third membrane is thin and transparent, but strong. It is lined with the fourth membrane, and lies in the same situation with it. It contains no vessels at this period of impregnation conveying <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> blood in the human subject, but in the cow the vessels are very distinct at every period. This membrane however in the early period of impregnation is very vascular, and its vessels are derived from the fetus. The history of a case of morbid impregnation, where the fetus was extra-uterine, detailed by Dr Clarke in the "Transactions of a Society for the Improvement of Medical and Chirurgical Knowledge," proves this circumstance very clearly. He says, p. 220, "a laceration was found to be in the fallopian tube about an inch and a half in length, each extremity of which was about an equal distance from the respective termination of the tube in the fimbriae and in the uterus. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the tube at this part was nearly of the size of a large walnut, forming a kind of pouch. More of the coagulated blood being removed from the lacerated part, the flabby vessels of the chorion immediately appeared, interposed with small coagula, and lying in contact with the internal surface of the pouch formed by the fallopian tube; these being separated, and the chorion divided, the amnios showed itself, containing a fetus perfectly formed of above six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> weeks growth," &c. This membrane is called the true chorion. The fourth membrane is even thinner and more transparent... It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> the whole internal surface of the ovum, and together with the chorion is continued along the vascular cord which connects the ovum and fetus. Between this membrane and the chorion, near the insertion of the vascular cord, a small <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> vesicle appears very distinct at this period; it was first described and delineated by Dr W. Hunter, and was called by him vesicula umbilicalis. At the full period of utero-gestation it is no longer visible, being then quite transparent. The fetus at this period is between two and three inches in length, and its external conformation is nearly complete. The fluid contained in the ovum is in such quantity as to prevent the fetus from touching the parietes of the covering in which it is included. It is a clear watery fluid, of greater specific gravity than water, and of a saltish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. When examined chemically it is found not coagulable by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>, and to contain a proportion of ammoniacal and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. This fluid is called liquor amnii. The connection of the parts thus enumerated with the uterus cannot be explained, unless the appearance of the ovum at the full period of gestation be described. The ovum then consists of three membranes; a spongy vascular substance called placenta, to which the fetus is connected by a vascular rope, and the liquor amnii. The three membranes consist of the spongy chorion, the true chorion, and the amnios. The spongy chorion covers the whole. Its vessels are numerous, and they can be filled by throwing hot wax into the vessels of the uterus. The true chorion and amnios are in the same situation as in the early months, being continued along the navel-string. They are quite transparent, and contain no visible vessels of any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. The placenta is a large vascular spongy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, of various forms in different cases, most generally approaching to a round one, placed on the outside of the true chorion, between it and the spongy chorion. Its external surface is lobulated; its internal or that towards the fetus is smooth, except from the rising of the blood-vessels. It is not attached to the uterus at any regular place, being sometimes at the cervix or side, but most generally about the fundus. On the one side it receives blood from the mother, and on the other from the child. Mr John Hunter was the first who clearly traced the insertion of the blood-vessels in the uterus into the placenta. He describes it thus (d): "The late indefatigable Dr McKenzie, about the month of May 1754, when assistant to Dr Smellie, having procured the body of a pregnant woman who had died undelivered at the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, had injected both the veins and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> with particular success; the veins being filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, the arteries with red." Having opened the abdomen, and exposed the uterus, he made an incision into the fore part, quite through its substance, and came to somewhat having the appearance of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> mass of injected matter, which afterwards proved to be the placenta. This appearance being new, he flopped, and greatly obliged me by desiring my attendance to examine the parts, in which there appeared something so uncommon. "I first raised, with great care, part of the uterus from the irregular mass above mentioned; in doing which, I observed regular pieces of wax, passing obliquely between it and the uterus, which broke off, leaving part upon this mass; and when they were attentively examined, towards the uterus, plainly appeared to be a continuation of the veins passing from it to this substance or placenta. "I likewise perceived other vessels, about the size of a crow quill, passing in the same manner, although not so obliquely: these also broke upon separating the placenta and uterus, leaving a small portion on the surface of the placenta; and, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, they were discovered to be continuations of the arteries of the uterus. My next step was to trace these vessels into the substance of what appeared placenta, which I first attempted in a vein; but that soon lost the regularity of a vessel, by terminating at once upon the surface of the placenta, in a very fine spongy substance, the interstices of which were filled with the yellow injected matter. This termination being new, I repeated the same kind of examination on other veins, which always led me to the same terminations, never entering the substance of the placenta in the form of a vessel. I next examined the arteries, and, tracing them in the same manner toward the placenta, found that they made a twist, or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> spiral turn upon themselves, and then were lost on its surface. On a more attentive view, I perceived that they terminated in the same way as the veins; for opposite to the mouth of the artery, the spongy substance of the placenta was readily observed, and was intermixed with the red <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJECTION">injection</a>. "Upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> into the placenta, I discovered, in many places of its substance, yellow injection; in others red, and in many others these two colours mixed. This substance of the placenta, now filled with injection, had nothing of the vascular appearance, nor that of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRAVASATION">extravasation</a>, but had a regularity in its form, which shewed it to be a natural cellular structure fitted for a reservoir for blood. "In some of the vessels leading from the placenta to the uterus, I perceived that the red injection of the arteries (which had been first injected) had passed into them out of the substance of the placenta, mixing itself with the yellow injection. I also observed, that the spongy chorion, called the decidua by Dr Hunter, was very vascular, its vessels coming from, and returning to, the uterus, being filled with the different coloured injections." It appears then that the placenta has a cellular structure, which receives blood from the arteries of the mother, and that there are veins by which that blood is returned, so that not a drop passes into the fetus. Of this practitioners of midwifery have a very familiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. When the placenta is retained attached to the uterus, after the birth of the child, not a drop of blood passes from the umbilical cord, except what was contained in the ramifications of the foetal vessels when the child. (d) Observations on certain parts of the Animal Oeconomy, by John Hunter, p. 127. child was separated. Yet, if a small portion of the edge of the placenta be detached, such a quantity of blood escapes from the uterine vessels of the mother, as sometimes proves fatal to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: a circumstance which clearly shews that the blood is still conveyed into the cellular part of the placenta. It has been said, that the placenta on one side receives blood from the fetus. In fact, the greatest part of the placenta seems to be made up of ramifications of the fetal vessels. The internal iliacs of the fetus are conveyed through the vascular rope which connects the placenta and child, into the placenta: they then ramify into as many minute branches as the pulmonary arteries do in the lungs of the adult; they then terminate in various branches, which, uniting, form one large <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> that is conveyed along the vascular rope, and returns all the blood which had been distributed by the arteries.
