But if there be any doubt on the subject, the practitioner has it in his power to ascertain the point by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. When there is no second child in the uterus, the further the fingers are carried up within the passages, the more contracted do they feel; whereas, if there be a second child, the more open are they found. When it is ascertained that another infant remains, the woman's belly should be immediately compressed by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, in order to prevent faintness from the sudden relaxation of the parietes abdominis, and the portion of the navel-string remaining attached to the after-birth of the first born should be carefully secured, lest the vessels of the placenta anasto- mose. In regard to the subsequent treatment, there has been much variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among practitioners. Some have proposed waiting till the action of the uterus expel the second as it had done the first infant. Others urge strongly the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for immediate delivery. Against the former of these practices it is to be objected; firstly, that in some cases, days or even weeks have been known to intervene between the birth of one child and the action of the uterus which expelled the second. Secondly, that if this happen, the passages must become contracted and their subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> may be productive of inflammatory symptoms. Thirdly, that during the time the uterine action is suspended, internal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAEMORRHAGE">haemorrhage</a> may take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and may destroy the patient. And, fourthly, the second child may be suddenly forced down in such a position, as may endanger its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and at the same time occasion <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pain to the mother. For these reasons it is now an established rule among judicious practitioners, to examine the situation of the second infant, as soon as the patient shall have recovered from the shock of the birth of the first child; and, if its position be natural and the patient have not been exhausted by the previous labour, and pains come on, to rupture the membranes, and allow the natural powers to complete the delivery. But if the infant present any other part than the head, or though the head do present, if the woman be exhausted, or if there be no appearance of the return of pains within an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after the birth of the first, then the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is to be passed up to bring down the feet of the second child, and the delivery is to be expedited. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of the placenta is to be conducted with great care, and every possible precaution is to be adopted against the occurrence of flooding, which is always to be dreaded as the consequence of plurality of children. The same principles apply to the management of triplets, &c. d. Umbilical <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a>, to which women are perhaps more subject than to any other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of rupture, may influence the labour materially. If it be reducible, it disappears after the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of pregnancy; but immediately after the expulsion of the child it returns, and occasions frightful faintings and floodings. This may be prevented by the simple expedient of having the belly compressed by a roller in such a manner, that in proportion as the infant advances, the compression may be increased. Should it be irreducible, if the hernia be affected by the continuance of labour, as may be known by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, &c. the operation of turning must be had recourse to. e. Convulsions sometimes happen during labour, and occasion great danger both to the mother and the child. The woman is quite insensible during the fit, which consists of violent convulsions of the muscles which move the body, and of those of the eyes, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and the lower jaw; it lasts in some cases only a few seconds, and Opening the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> jugular might answer both purposes, but the difficulties of the patient in many cases makes the surgeon or attendants dread this operation. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of blood, therefore, adapted to the exigency of the case, is to be drawn from the arm, and either a branch of the temporal artery is to be divided, or several leeches are to be applied to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>. After the bleeding, a powerful laxative glyther ought to be exhibited. And if there be any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of disordered prime vae, an emetic must, if possible, be given. The state of the os uteri is then to be ascertained; and if labour have not commenced, no attempts whatever are to be made to promote that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. In some rare cases, however, where the bulk of the gravid uterus is enormous, it may be necessary to remove a part of its contents; but such cases cannot happen once in a thousand instances of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. Should the fits still continue, the head must be shaved, and covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> blister; and if the oppression or fulness, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, be not removed, the blood-letting is to be repeated. As soon as the patient becomes capable of swallowing, the camphor, in doses of ten grains, ought to be given every three or four hours. The most efficacious and palatable form in which this medicine can be prescribed, is by suspending it in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, through the medium of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>. Its use must be persevered in for several days, gradually lessening the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of doses. Where the eclampsia has been preceded by oedema, the digitalis may be employed with much success. Convulsions during labour are to be treated upon the same principles, with these additional precautions, that delivery is to be accomplished by the most expeditious possible means, and that if the delivery be followed by uterine haemorrhage, the discharge is for some time to be rather encouraged than checked. I knew two instances of the fits, which had been suspended for some hours, recurring, in consequence of the flooding being stopped, and in both cases the convulsions were removed, by allowing the discharge to return. When the symptoms that precede eclampsia, take place in the latter months of pregnancy, the most certain method of guarding against the threatening accident is, having recourse to immediate blood-letting, and afterwards prescribing camphor, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the state of the bowels, and a spare diet. When the same symptoms occur during labour, a copious bleeding should be instantly ordered, and the appropriate means of terminating the delivery should be adopted with as much expedition as may be consistent with the safety both of mother and child. In these concise practical suggestions, practitioners will observe circumstances omitted, which have been recommended by gentlemen of deserved professional eminence, and novelties of practice proposed, which I believe have not hitherto been explicitly advised. Some explanation, therefore, of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> above recommended may perhaps be expected. The most obvious remedy apparently omitted is opium. This powerful medicine was not prescribed, as far as we have reason to know, by the practitioners who lived at the end of the 17th and beginning of the 18th centuries. The first author who, in strong terms, affirms the efficacy of opium in such cases, appears to be the translator. translator of Astruc's Midwifery (A); and his opinion has been adopted by Dr Denman (B), and by Dr Bland (C). But in every case of true eclampsia, during pregnancy or labour, opiates do irreparable mischief, where a copious bleeding has not been prevented; and even where that precaution has been attended to, they have been found useless, if not hurtful. Melancholy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has completely established in my mind this practical precept; and I consider it to be a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of very great moment, that it should be universally known; for general practitioners, who are often first called to those cases where the fits happen during pregnancy, are extremely apt to prescribe opium. I can solemnly declare, that no patient to whose assistance I have been called, who had taken a dose of opium previous to my arrival, has recovered, and I have known that medicine given in almost every variety of dose. My father, Dr A. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, of whose judgment and practical knowledge it does not become me to speak in the terms they so justly merit, prevented my ever employing opium under such circumstances. "A second remedy extolled by Dr Denman, and now, after a fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, rejected in my practice, is vomiting. This seems to have been a very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a> in the time of Mauriceau, as he takes great pains to point out its hurtfulness in several parts of his works (D). Where there are unequivocal marks of disordered stomach, an emetic may be prescribed with advantage after blood-letting, but it should be avoided under all other circumstances. "With regard to the warm-bath, which is a favorite remedy among foreign practitioners, and has been advised by several British authors, I have never had an opportunity of trying its effects. Upon theoretical principles I should reject it; but my <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> reason for never having directed its use, has been the imposibility, in ordinary cases of practice, of commanding a warm-bath into which a woman in such a situation could be put. "Dashing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water by surprise upon the face is a practice suggested by Dr Denman, and on which he had much dependence at one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. Experience lessened his hopes, and, many years ago, prevented my ever indulging any. I gave it several fair trials, (once or twice in public in the lying-in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Infirmary), and had even reason to be convinced, that it rather aggravated than diminished the violence of the paroxysms." In addition to these observations it may be proper to remark, that a much larger quantity of blood should be drawn in those cases than has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> been done. Dr H. advises forty ounces to be taken at this first bleeding, and the same quantity to be again drawn within an hour, if the symptoms be not mitigated; and he talks with the utmost confidence of the utility of this practice. f. Although the woman be delivered safely both of the child and afterbirth, she may sink very soon after parturition in consequence of internal flooding. This is to be suspected if the patient suddenly complain of giddiness or sickness, or ringing in the ears, or impaired vision; or if she become delirious, with a pallid face and cold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. The state of the pulse at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a> too should <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a judicious practitioner to suspect the existence of internal flooding. Positive certainty of this accident may be obtained by feeling through the belly the condition of the uterus; or, more certainly still, by feeling the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a>, for if its parietes approach, there is not much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of there being any considerable internal hemorrhage; whereas, if it be found filled with coagulated blood, there is a certainty, that the womb too is distended from the same cause. This accident is entirely owing to the womb not having contracted with sufficient energy. It very often proves the cause of sudden and unexpected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The boldest and apparently most violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> are required to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the patient in many of those cases. The womb and vagina must be immediately emptied, and such pressure must be made on the inside of the uterus with the hand, as shall force it into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a>. In some cases cold water in great quantity must be dashed from a height on the naked belly at the same time; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> while the strength of the patient must be supported with large doses of opium. If there be vomiting, which is a frequent symptom in such cases, five grains of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> opium should be given at first, and afterwards three grains every three or four hours, till the pulse becomes steady and the strength recruited, when the opiates are to be withdrawn and lessened by degrees. The writer of this article cannot avoid this opportunity of paying a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> tribute of respect to the practical discernment of the able editor of the New <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> Medical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, who seems the first author who has mentioned this practice of giving large doses of opium; a practice by which many valuable lives have been saved. Conclusion.—In the preceding account of the deviations, which sometimes happen in the process of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> parturition, although we have endeavoured to give a full view of the subject, we have not pursued the beaten track. But as this article may rather be consulted by many as a dictionary, than pursued regularly as a treatise, we shall add the ordinary arrangement of labours, with the reference to the numerical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, under which the several varieties may be found. Labours are divided into four classes; viz. natural, laborious, preternatural, and complex. Natural labour comprehends all cases where the head of the infant is forced foremost; and the whole process is completed with safety, both to mother and child, within twenty-four hours from the commencement. It is described under articles 48. to 60. (A) The Art of Midwifery, &c. 8vo. London, printed for J. Nourse 1767. Appendix, p. 295. (B) Vol. ii. p. 418. (C) Loco citato, page 136. (D) Particularly in Aphorism 232. "L'émeticque est pernicieux aux femmes grosses, ou nouvellement accouchées, qui sont surprisées des convulsions." And Levret, page 451. of his L'Art des Accouchemens, says, in reference to that aphorism, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CETTE">Cette</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> est des mieux fondées, et elle doit être rigoureusement observée dans tous ses <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>." Laborious labour is that where, although the head of the infant be forced foremost, the process is protracted beyond twenty-four hours from the commencement. It is divided into three orders: First, where the natural powers at last, after much suffering on the part of the mother, complete the delivery. See article 64. Secondly, Where, although the action of the uterus be inadequate to the expulsion of the infant, it is practicable to extract the child through the natural passages, without injury either to it or to the mother. See articles 66. to 74. 82 and 84. Thirdly, Where it is impossible to extract the child alive through the natural passages. See articles 80. and 99. to 133. Preternatural labours comprehend all cases where any other part of the child than the head is forced foremost; and consist of two orders: First, Presentations of the lower extremities, viz. footling cases, article 87. Breech cases, article 91. Cases where one foot presents, article 89. and knee-cases, article 95. Secondly, Presentations of the superior extremities or other parts than the head or lower extremities, articles 192. to 196. Complex labours include all cases where any other circumstances than those enumerated under the former three classes take place, viz. Cases where the pelvis is too large, articles 110. and 111. Cases where haemorrhagy occurs at the beginning of labour, article 76. or at the conclusion of that process, articles 152. and 153. Cases where there is more than one child, articles 143. 144. 145. Cases where the patient had previously been affected with umbilical hernia, article 146. Cases where convulsions happen, articles 147. 148. Cases where the navel-string is twisted round the neck of the infant, article 149. or where it is forced down along with some part of the child, article 141. And cases of rupture of the uterus, article 65.

MIEDNIKI

Pages 114-114
or Mednik, or Warmic, a town of Samogitia, and the residence of the bishop. It is 28 miles N.E. from Konigsberg, and 60 miles S.S.W. from Mittau.

MIEKOW

Pages 114-114

a town of Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRACOW">Cracow</a>. The founder of this town is said to have been Gripfus Jana, who built it after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, when he returned from a pilgrimage to that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. It is 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from Cracow.

MIERIS

Pages 114-116

Francis, the Old, a justly celebrated painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1635; and was at first placed under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Toorne Vliet, one of the best designers of the Low Countries, and afterwards entered himself as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> with Gerard Douw. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he far surpassed all his companions, and was by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of his disciples. His manner of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> silks, velvets, stuffs, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> carpets, was so singular, that the different kinds and fabric of any of them might easily be distinguished. His pictures are rarely to be seen, and as rarely to be sold; and when they are, the purchase is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, their intrinsic value being so incalculably <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. Besides portraits, his general subjects were conversations, persons performing on musical instruments, patients attended by the apothecary or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, chemists at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, mercers shops, and such like; and the usual valuation he set on his pictures was estimated at the rate of a ducat an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The finest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of this master's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is that which he painted for the wife of Cornelius Plaats, which is said to be still preserved in the family, although very great sums have been offered for it. In the possession of the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> was another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Mieris, representing a lady fainting, and a physician applying the remedies to relieve her. For that performance he was paid (at his usual rate of a ducat an hour) so much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> as amounted to fifteen hundred florins when the picture was finished. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> wished to purchase it, and offered three thousand florins for it; but the offer was not accepted. However, that prince procured several of his pictures, and they are at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> an ornament to the Florentine collection. One of the most curious of them is a girl holding a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> in her hand, and it is accounted ineffable. This painter died in 1681. Mieris, William, called the Young Mieris, was son of the former, and born at Leyden in 1662. During the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of his father, he made a remarkable progress; but, by being deprived of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> when he was only arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of nineteen, he had recourse to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, as the most instructive guide; and by studying with diligence and judgment to imitate her, he approached near to the merit of his father. At first he took his subjects from private life, in the manner of Francis; such as tradesmen in their shops, or a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> selling vegetables and fruit, and sometimes a woman looking out at a window; all which he copied minutely after nature, nor did he paint a single object without his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>. As Mieris had observed the compositions of Gerard Laireffe, and other great historical painters, with singular delight, he attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> subjects in that style; and began with the story of Rinaldo sleeping on the lap of Armida, surrounded with the Loves and Graces, the foreground being enriched with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; a work which added greatly to his fame, and was sold for a very high price. This master also painted landscapes and animals with equal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and neatness; and modelled in clay and wax, in so sharp and accurate a manner, that he might justly be be ranked among the most eminent sculptors. In the delicate finishing of his works, he imitated his father; as he likewise did in the liveliness, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>, and truth, of his paintings, which makes them to be almost as highly prized; but they are not equal in respect of design, or of the striking effect, nor is his touch so very exquisite as that of the father. The works of the old Mieris are better composed, the figures are better grouped, and they have less confusion; yet the younger Mieris is acknowledged to be an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> of extraordinary merit, although inferior to him, who had scarcely his equal. He died in 1747. Mieris, Francis, called the Young Francis, was the son of William, and the grandson of the celebrated Francis Mieris; and was born at Leyden in 1689. He learned the art of painting from his father, whose manner and style he always imitated; he chose the same subjects, and endeavoured to resemble him in his colouring and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>. But with all his industry he proved far inferior to him: and most of those pictures which at the public sales are said to be of the young Mieris, and many also in private collections ascribed to the elder Francis, or William, are perhaps originally painted by this master, who was far inferior to both; or are only his copies after the works of those excellent painters, as he spent abundance of his time in copying their performances. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIEZA">Mieza</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, which was anciently called Strymonium, situated near Stagira. Here, Plutarch informs us, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> seats and shady walks of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> were thrown. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was Peucestas, one of Alexander's generals, and therefore surnamed Miezeus, (Arrian). <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGDOL">Migdol</a>, or Magdol, in Ancient Geography, a place in the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on this side Pihahiroth, or between it and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, towards its extremity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denotes a tower or fortress. It is probably the Magdolum of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, seeing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> render it by the same name. Mignard, Nicholas, an ingenious French painter born at <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-TROYES">Troyes</a> in 1628; but, settling at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>, is generally distinguished from his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> by the appellation of Mignard of Avignon. He was afterwards employed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he became rector of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of painting. There is a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his historical pieces and portraits in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the Thuireries. He died in 1695. Mignard, Peter, the brother of Nicholas, was born at Troyes in 1610; and acquired to much of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the Italian school, as to be known by the name of the Roman. He was generally allowed to have a superior genius to his brother Nicholas; and had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of painting the popes Alexander VII. and Urban VIII., besides many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> at Rome, and several of the Italian princes; his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>, ten times to him for his portrait, and respected his talents so much as to ennoble him, make him his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> painter after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Le Brun, and appointed him director of the manufactories. He died in 1695, and many of his pieces are to be seen at St Cloud. Mignon, or Minjon, Abraham, a celebrated painter of flowers and still life, was born at Frankfort in 1639; and his father having been deprived of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his substance by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of losses in trade, left him in very necessitous circumstances when he was only <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of age. From that melancholy situation he was rescued by the friendship of James Murel, a flower painter in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; who took Mignon into his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and instructed him in the art, till he was 17 years old. Murel had often observed an uncommon genius in Mignon; he therefore took him along with him to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he placed him as a disciple with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> de Heem; and while he was under the direction of that master he laboured with incessant application to imitate the manner of De Heem, and ever afterwards adhered to it; only adding daily to his improvement, by studying nature with a most exact and curious observation. "When we consider the paintings of Mignon, one is at a loss (Mr <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PILKINGTON">Pilkington</a> observes) whether more to admire the freshness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of his colouring, the truth in every part, the bloom on his objects, or the perfect resemblance of nature visible in all his performances. He always shows a beautiful choice in those flowers and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> from which his subjects are composed; and he groups them with uncommon elegance. His touch is exquisitely neat, though apparently easy and unlaboured; and he was fond of introducing insects among the fruits and flowers, wonderfully finished, so that even the drops of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> appear as round and as translucent as nature itself." He had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to be highly paid for his works in his lifetime; and he certainly would have been accounted the best in his profession even to this day, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> John Van Huyfum had not appeared. Weyerman, who had seen many admired pictures of Mignon, mentions one of a most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> kind. The subject of it is a cat, which had thrown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a pot of flowers, and they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> scattered on a marble <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. That picture is in every respect so wonderfully <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, that the spectator can scarce persuade himself that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which is spilled from the vessel is not really running down from the marble. This picture is distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Mignon's Cat. This painter died in 1679, aged only 40. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">Migration</a>, the passage or a removal of a thing out of one place into another. Migration of Birds.—It has been generally believed, that many different kinds of birds annually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> generally from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to another, and spend the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> or believe the winter where it is most agreeable to them; and that even the birds of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> seek the most distant southern regions of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, when directed by a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> to leave their own country. It has <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> pretty generally received, that swallows reside during the winter season in the warm southern regions; and Mr Adanson particularly relates his having seen them at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a> when they were obliged to leave this country. But besides the swallow, Mr Pennant enumerates many other birds which migrate from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> at different times of the year, and are then to be found in other countries; after which they again leave these countries, and return to Britain. The reason of these migrations he supposes to be a defect of food at certain seasons of the year, or the want of a secure <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> during the time of courtship, incubation, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a>. The following is his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the migrating <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. 1. Crows. Of this genus, the hooded crow migrates regularly with the woodcock. It inhabits <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Britain the whole year; a few are said annually to breed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, breeding in one part of this island, and remove with their young to others. All finches feed on the seeds of plants. 13. Larks, fly-catchers, wagtails, and warblers. All of these feed on insects and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>; yet only part of them quit these kingdoms; though the reason of migration is the same to all. The nightingale, blackcap, fly-catcher, willow-wren, wheat-eat, and whitethroat, leave us before winter, while the small and delicate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a>-crested wren braves our severest frosts. The migrants of this genus continue longest in Great Britain in the southern counties, the winter in those parts being later than in those of the north; Mr Stillingfleet having observed several wheat-eats in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Purbeck on the 18th of November. As these birds are incapable of very distant flights, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, or the south of France, is probably their winter asylum. 14. Swallows and goatsucker. Every species disappears at the approach of winter.

MILBORN-PORT

Pages 129-129

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> in England, feated on a branch of the river Parret, 115 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Though represented in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, it is no market town nor corporation; but it appears in Domesday book to have had a market once, and 36 burgesses. It is in a manner surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>. Here are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, who yearly choose two bailiffs, that have the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the borough under them, and jointly return the members to parliament with the two stewards, who are chosen yearly out of nine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a> stewards, and have the custody of the corporation-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. These two stewards also distribute the profits of the lands given to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> here, of which the said commonalty stewards are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a>. The inhabitants in 1801 were nearly about 1000, the houses not much above 200. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 37. N. Lat. 50. 50.

MILBROOK

Pages 129-129

a town of Cornwall, on the west side of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> haven. It has a good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> trade, and has formerly furnished our fleet with many able <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>.

MILDENHALL

Pages 129-129

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from Newmarket, 12 from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">Bury</a>, and 70 from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> populous town on the river Lark, a branch of the Ouse, with a harbour for boats. It has a well frequented market on Fridays, especially for fish and wild fowl. Its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has a tower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> steeple 120 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 33. N. Lat. 52. 24.

MILDEW

Pages 129-129

is said to be a kind of thick, clammy, sweet juice, exhaled from, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> falling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon, the leaves and blossoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. By its thickness and clamminess it prevents perspiration, and hinders the growth of the plant. It sometimes rests on the leaves of trees in form of a fatty juice, and sometimes on the ears of corn. It is naturally very tough and viscous, and becomes still more so by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> exhaling its more fluid parts; by which means the young ears of corn are so daubed over, that they can never arrive at their full growth. Bearded wheat is less subject to the mildew than the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> sort; and it is observed that newly dugged lands are more liable to mildew than others. The best remedy is a smart shower of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and immediately afterwards a brisk <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the mildew is seen before the sun has much power, it has been recommended to fend two men into the field with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, each holding one end; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> this along the field through the ears, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be dislodged from them, before the heat of the sun is able to dry it to that viscous state in which it does the mischief. Some also say, that lands which have for many years been subject to mildews, have been cured of it by sowing foot along with the corn, or immediately after it. Mr J. S. Segar, the author of a treatise upon this subject, observes, that the mildew is of such a sharp corrosive <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, that it raises blisters on the feet of the shepherds who go barefoot, and even consumes the hoofs of the cattle. He suspects that it possesses some arsenical qualities, though he does not pretend to affirm this positively. Its pernicious influence, according to him, is rendered still more powerful by a variety of circumstances; such as sending the cattle into the fields too early in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; their drinking <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> mixed with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, or but lately thawed; their being kept in stables that are too <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and filthy, and which are not sufficiently aired. The same author considers the mildew as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of epidemical distempers among the cattle. The mildew producing these diseases, he says, is that which dries and burns the grass and leaves. It falls usually in the morning, particularly after a thunderstorm. Its poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> (which does not continue above 24 hours) never operates but when it has been swallowed immediately after its falling. The disorder attacks the stomach, is accompanied with pimples on the tongue, loss of appetite, a defecation of the aliments in the stomach, a cough, and difficulty of respiration. As a preservative, the author prescribes purging in spring and in winter. The medicine he advises is composed of 30 grains of sulphur of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, and 60 grains of resin of jalap. He is against vomiting, and every thing that is of a heating nature.

MILE

Pages 129-129

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distance, containing eight furlongs. The English statute mile is 80 chains, or 1760 yards; that is, 5280 feet. We shall here give a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the miles in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> nations of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in geometrical places, 60,000 of which make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the equator. | Mile of Russia | 750 | | Mile of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> | 1000 | | Mile of England | 1200 | | Mile of Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> | 1500 | | Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of France | 1500 | | Small league, ibid. | 2000 | | <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> league, ibid. | 2500 | | <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> league, ibid. | 3000 | | Mile of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> | 3000 | | Mile of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> | 3428 | | Mile of Germany | 4000 | | Mile of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> | 5000 | | Mile of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> | 5000 | | Mile of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> | 6000 |

MILETUS

Pages 129-130

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>; but where situated does not appear. It is said to be the mother town of Miletus in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, whether a colony was led by Sarpedon, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, (Ephorus, quoted by Strabo). Mileti, the people, (Ovid). Miletus, in Ancient Geography, a celebrated town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a> and Caria. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of all Ionia, and famous both for the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and peace. It was situated about 10 stadia south of the mouth of the river Maeander, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. It was founded by a Cretan colony under Miletus, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> (according to others) by Neleus the son of Codrus; or by Sarpedon a son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. It has successively been called Leleges, Pithyusa, and Anaetoria. The inhabitants, called Mileti, were very powerful, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> maintained an obstinate war against the kings of Lydia. They early applied themselves to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; and planted no less than 80 colonies, or (according to Seneca) 380, in different parts of the world. It was the only town that made head against Alexander, and was with much difficulty taken. It gave birth to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THALES">Thales</a>. Thales, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wise men, and the first who applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. It was also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAXIMANDER">Anaximander</a>, the scholar and successor of Thales, the inventor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> dials and the gnomon, and the first that published a geographical map; of Anaximenes, scholar and successor to the foregoing; and of other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. It was noted for its excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>; and was also celebrated for a temple and oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> Didymus. This famous people, from being powerful, becoming afterwards opulent and abandoned to pleasures, lost both their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and their power.—At present it is called by the Turks Melas, and not far distant from it runs the river Maeander. St Paul going from Corinth to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> passed by Miletus, and as he went by sea, and could not take Ephesus in his way, he caused the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and priests of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Ephesus to come to Miletus (Acts xx. 15. &c.), which was about 12 leagues from them.

MILFORD

Pages 130-130

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> state, is situated at the source of a small river, 15 miles from Delaware <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and 150 southward of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>. This town, which contains about 80 houses, has been built, except one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, since the revolution. It is laid out with much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and is by no means disagreeable. The inhabitants are Episcopalians, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILFORD_HAVEN">Milford Haven</a>, one of the finest harbours in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and indubitably the best in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is situated in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a> in South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> channel. It is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, safe, and deep; there is no danger of going in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> out with the tide, or almost with any <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a ship comes in without a cable or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> she may run <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> on the ooze, and there <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> safe till she is refitted; and in an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> she may get out of the harbour into the open <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It lies extremely convenient for ships bound from the English or Bristol channels to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, or farther west, and from thence to the channels. It is said, that 1000 sail of any size may ride secure in this haven. It has 16 deep and safe creeks, five bays, and 13 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, all distinguished by their several names. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> tide rises 36 feet, so that ships may at any time be laid aground. Dale harbour is a ready outlet for small vessels, where they may ride in two or three fathoms at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.—In the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, before the Spanish invasion, two forts were begun at the entrance of Milford Haven, one on each side, called Nangle and Dale blockhouses; but they were not then finished.—The Stack rock rises here above water, lying near the middle of the entrance between Nangle and Dale. Pencroft is the opening of that branch of the haven on which the town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> is seated, and where the customhouse of Milford is kept. The breadth of the entrance between rock and rock is but 200 yards at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water, and 112 at low water. There is a ridge of rocky ground that has the name of Carrs, which runs almost across Milford Haven, from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> towards Llandaffwell, where it renders the landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> difficult to strangers, from its not appearing at low water. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> convenience of this harbour is, that in a hour's time a ship may be in or out of it, and in the way between the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>'s End and Ireland. As it lies near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, a ship in eight or ten hours may be over on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Ireland, or off the Land's End in the English Channel; and a vessel may get out hence to the west much sooner than from either <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>. This harbour has been greatly improved by new works, at the expense of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> on April 14, 1759 granted £10,000 for fortifying the harbour of Milford, all of which was expended on the fort at Neyland, which, however, still remains unfinished.

MILIO

Pages 145-147

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol2.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> of Crotona in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. His father's name was Diotimus. He early accustomed himself to carry the greatest burdens, and by degrees became a prodigy of strength. It is said that he carried on his shoulders a young bullock, four years old, for above forty yards; and afterwards killed it with one blow of his fist, and ate it up in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times crowned at the Pythian games, and six at the Olympian. He presented himself a seventh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but no one had the courage <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> boldness to enter the lists again. Milo against him. He was one of the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>; and to his uncommon strength, it is said, the learned preceptor and his pupils owed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: The pillar which supported the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the school suddenly gave way; but Milo supported the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and gave the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and his auditors time to escape. In his old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Milo attempted to pull up a tree by the roots, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> it. He partly effected it; but his strength being gradually exhausted, the tree when half clefled re-united, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> remained pinched in the body of the tree. He was then alone; and, being unable to disentangle himself, he was devoured by the wild beasts of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, about 500 years before the Christian era. Milo, T. Aurinius, a native of Lanuvium, who attempted to obtain the consulship at Rome by intrigue and seditions tumults. Clodius the tribune opposed his views; yet Milo would have succeeded but for the following event: As he was going into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, attended by his wife and a numerous retinue of gladiators and servants, he met on the Appian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> his enemy Clodius, who was returning to Rome with three of his friends and some domestics completely armed.—A quarrel arose between the servants. Milo supported his attendants, and the dispute became general.—Clodius received many severe wounds, and was obliged to retire to a neighbouring cottage. Milo pursued his enemy in his retreat, and ordered his servants to despatch him. The body of the murdered tribune was carried to Rome, and exposed to public view. The enemies of Milo inveighed bitterly against the violence and barbarity with which the sacred person of a tribune had been treated. Cicero undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Milo; but the continual clamours of the friends of Clodius, and the sight of an armed soldiery, which surrounded the seat of judgment, so terrified the orator, that he forgot the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his arguments, and the defence he made was weak and injudicious.—Milo was condemned, and banished to Massilia. Cicero soon after sent his exiled friend a copy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> which he had prepared for his defence, in the form in which we have it now; and Milo, after he had read it, exclaimed, O Cicero, hadst thou spoken before my accusers in these terms, Milo would not be now eating figs at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>. The friendship and cordiality of Cicero and Milo were the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> intimacy and familiar intercourse. It was to the successful labours of Milo that the orator was recalled from banishment, and restored to his friends. Milo, (anciently <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELOS">Melos</a>), an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, about 50 miles in circumference, with a harbour, which is one of the largest in the Mediterranean. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is of the same name as the island, and was prettily built, but abominably nasty: the houses are two stories <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with flat roofs; and are built with a fort of pumice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which is hard, blackish, and yet very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. This island was formerly rich and populous. From the earliest times of antiquity it enjoyed pure <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. The Athenians, not being able to persuade the Melians to declare in their favour in the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon the island, and attacked them vigorously. In two different expeditions they failed of their purpose: but returning with more numerous forces, they laid siege to Melos; and obliging the besieged to surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> all the men who were able to bear arms. They spared only the women and children, and these they carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of cruelty puts <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to the blush, and disgraces the Athenian name. But war was then carried on with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of wild rage, unexampled in the present times. Republics know not how to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and always carry their vengeance to an extravagant height. When Lygander, the Macedonian general, came to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the Athenians, he expelled the colony which they had sent to Melos, and re-established the unfortunate remains of its original inhabitants. This island lost its liberty when Rome, aspiring to the empire of the world, conquered all the isles of the Archipelago. In the partition of the empire, it fell to the share of the eastern emperors, was governed by particular dukes, and was at last conquered by Soliman II. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, it has groaned under the yoke of Turkish despotism, and has lost its opulence and splendour. At the commencement of the present century, it boasted of 17 churches and 11 chapels, and contained more than 20,000 inhabitants. It was very fertile in corn, wine, and fruits; and the whole space from the town to the harbour, which is nearly two miles, was laid out in beautiful gardens. M. Tournefort, who visited it in the year 1700, gives a fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. "The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, being constantly warmed by subterraneous fires, produced almost without interruption plenteous crops of corn, barley, cotton, exquisite wines, and delicious melons. St Elias, the finest <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in the island, and situated on the most elevated spot, is inclosed with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, and fig trees. Its gardens are watered by a copious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Olive trees, of which there are but few in the other parts of the island, grow in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers around this monastery. The adjacent vineyards afford excellent wine. In a word, all the productions of the island are the very best of their kinds; its partridges, quails, kids, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, are highly valued, and yet may be bought at a very cheap price." Were M. Tournefort to return to Milo, M. Savary assures us, he would no longer see the fine island which he has described. "He might still see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, in the form of feathers, and fringed with silver thread, hanging from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of the caverns; pieces of pure sulphur filling the cliffs of the rocks; a variety of mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> (though these are now only a set of small dirty caves); the same subterraneous fires which in his days warmed the bosom of the earth, and were the cause of its extraordinary fertility; but instead of 5000 Greeks, all paying the capitation tax (A), he would now find no more than about 700 inhabitants. (A) Grown-up men are the only persons who pay the capitation tax. Therefore, by adding to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 5000 who paid the tax, the women, boys, and girls, we find that Melos, in the days of Tournefort, contained at least 20,000 souls. inhabitants on an island 18 leagues in circumference. He would figh to behold the finest lands lying uncultivated, and the most fertile valleys converted into marshes; of the gardens scarcely a vestige is left; three-fourths of the town in ruins, and the inhabitants daily decreasing. In short, during the last 50 years, Melos has assumed a quite different appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, which the Turks propagate everywhere, has cut off one part of its inhabitants; the injudicious administration of the Porte, and the oppressive extortions of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> pacha, have destroyed the rest. At present, for want of hands, they cannot cut out a free channel for their waters, which stagnate in the valleys, corrupt, and infect the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> with their putrid exhalations. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> marshes, of which there are numbers in the island, being equally neglected, produce the same effects. Add to these inconveniences, those fulvous exhalations which arise all over the island, and by which the inhabitants of Melos are afflicted with dangerous fevers during three-fourths of the year. Perhaps they may be obliged to forfeit their country. Every countenance is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and livid; and none bears any marks of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The prudent traveller <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be careful to spend but a very short time in this unwholesome country, unless he chooses to expose himself to the danger of catching a fever. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> over night, or to spend but one day in the island, is often enough to occasion his being attacked with that distemper. "Yet (continues our author) a judicious and enlightened <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> might expel those evils which ravage Melos. Its first care would be to establish a lazaret, and to prohibit vessels whose crews or cargoes are infected with the plague from landing. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">Canals</a> might next be cut, to drain the marshes, whose exhalations are so pernicious. The island would then be repeopled. The sulphurous vapours are not the most noxious. These prevailed equally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, yet the island was then very populous. M. Tournefort, who travelled through it at a time less distant from the period when it was conquered by the Turks, and when they had not yet had time to lay it waste, reckons the number of its inhabitants (as we have said) at about 20,000. The depopulation of Melos is therefore to be ascribed to the despotism of the Porte, and its defective <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>." The women of Milo, once so celebrated for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, are now fallow, unhealthy, and disgustingly ugly; and render themselves still more hideous by their drabs, which is a kind of loose jacket, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> coat and petticoat, that scarcely covers two-thirds of their thighs, barely meeting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> above the knee. Their hind <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hangs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the back in a number of plaits; that on the fore part of the head is combed down each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and terminated by a small stiff curl, which is even with the lower part of the cheek. All the inhabitants are Greeks, for the Turks are not fond of trifling themselves in the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> the captain bawhaw goes round with a squadron to keep them in subjection, and to collect the revenue. When the Russians made themselves masters of the Archipelago, many of the islands declared in their favour; but being abandoned by the peace, they were so severely mulcted by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior, that they have professed a determination to remain perfectly quiet in future. As the Turks, however, do not think them worth a garrison, and will not trust them with arms and ammunition, all those which the Russians may choose to invade will be obliged to submit. The two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which form the entrance of the harbour, crossing each other, render it imperceptible until you are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it. Thus, while you are perfectly secure within it, you find great difficulty in getting out, particularly in a northerly <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and as no trade is carried on except a little in corn and salt, Milo would scarcely ever be visited, were it not that, being the first island which one makes in the Archipelago, the pilots have chosen it for their residence. They live in a little town on the top of a high rock, which, from its situation and appearance, is called the Castle.—Partridges still abound in this island; and are so cheap, that you may buy one for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of powder only. The peasants get them by standing behind a portable screen, with a small aperture in the centre, in which they place the muzzle of their piece, and then draw the partridges by a call. When a sufficient number are collected, they fire among them, and generally kill from four to seven at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>; but even this method of getting them is so expensive, from the scarcity of ammunition, that the people can never afford to shoot them, except when there are gentlemen in the island, from whom they can beg a little powder and shot. Milo is 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Candia; and the town is situated in E. Long. 25° 15', N. Lat. 36° 27'. MILSTONE. See MILLSTONE.

MILITANT

Pages 130-130
or Church-militant, denotes the body of Christians while here on earth.

MILITARY

Pages 130-133

something belonging to the soldiery <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. MILITARY <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">Discipline</a>, the training of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and the due enforcement of the laws and regulations instituted by authority for their conduct. Next to the forming of troops, military discipline is the first object that presents itself to our notice; it is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of all armies; and unless it be established amongst them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and supported with unflinching <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, they are no better than so many contemptible heaps of rabble, which are more dangerous to the very state that maintains them than even its declared enemies. MILITARY Execution, the ravaging or destroying of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or town, that refuses to pay the contribution inflicted upon them. MILITARY <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">Exercise</a>. See Exercise and Words of Command. MILITARY State, in British polity, one of the three divisions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>. See Laity. This state includes the whole of the soldiery, or such persons as are peculiarly appointed among the rest of the people for the safeguard and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the realm. In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, it is extremely dangerous to make a distinct order of the profession of arms. In <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarchies, this is necessary for the safety of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and arises from the main principle of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, which is that of governing by fear; but, in free states, the profession of a soldier, taken singly and merely as a profession, is justly an object of jealousy. In these no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should take up arms but with a view to defend his country and its laws; he puts not off the citizen when he enters the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; but it is because he is a citizen, and would wish to continue so, that he makes himself for a while a soldier. The laws therefore, and constitution of these kingdoms, know no such state as that of a perpetual standing soldiery, bred up to no other profession than that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and it was not till the reign of Henry VII. that the kings of England had so much as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> about their persons. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Anglo-Saxons, as appears from Edward the Confessor's laws, the military force of England was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the dukes or heretochs, who were constituted through every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; being taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and such as were most remarkable for being... Military ing sapientes, fideles, et animosi. Their duty was to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and regulate the English armies with a very unlimited power; prout eis visum fuerit, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> honorem coronae et utilitatem regni. And because of this great power they were elected by the people in their full <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, or folkmote, in the same manner as sheriffs were elected: following still that old <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> maxim of the Saxon constitution, that where any officer was entrusted with such power, as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> abused, might tend to the oppression of the people, that power was delegated to him by the vote of the people themselves. So too, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of our Saxon forefathers, they had their dukes, as well as kings, with an independent power over the military, as the kings had over the civil state. The dukes were <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>, the kings <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>: for so only can be confidently underlaid that passage of Tacitus, Reges ex nobilitate, duces ex virtute sumunt. In constituting their kings, the family or blood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> was regarded; in choosing their dukes or leaders, warlike merit: <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as Caesar relates of their ancestors in his time, that whenever they went to war, by way either of attack or defence, they elected leaders to command them. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of power, thus conferred by the people, though intended to preserve the liberty of the subject, was perhaps unreasonably detrimental to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>: and accordingly we find a very ill <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> made of it by Edric <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Mercia, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edmund Ironside; who, by his office of duke or heretoch, was entitled to a large command in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and by his repeated treacheries at last transferred the crown to Canute the Dane. It seems universally agreed by all historians, that King Alfred first settled a national militia in this kingdom, and by his prudent discipline made all the subjects of his dominions soldiers: but we are unfortunately left in the dark as to the particulars of this his so celebrated regulation; though, from what was last observed, the dukes seem to have been left in possession of too large and independent a power: which enabled Duke Harold, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Edward the Confessor, though a stranger to the royal blood, to mount for a short space the throne of this kingdom, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of Edgar Etheling the rightful heir. Upon the Norman conquest, the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal <a </a>class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> was introduced here in all its rigour, the whole of which is built on a military <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> thereof, all the lands in the kingdom were divided into what were called <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s fees, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> above 60,000; and for every knight's fee, a knight or folder, miles, was bound to attend the king in his wars, for 40 days in a year; in which space of time, before war was reduced to a science, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> was generally finished, and a kingdom either conquered or victorious. By this means the king had, without any expense, an army of 60,000 men always ready at his command. And accordingly we find one, among the laws of William the Conqueror, which in the king's name commands and firmly enjoins the personal attendance of all knights and others; quod habeant et teneant se semper in armis et equis, ut decet et oportet: et quod semper sint prompti et parati ad servitium suum integrum nobis explendum et peragendum, cum opus adferatur, secundum quod debent de feudis et tenementis suis de jure nobis facere. This personal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time degenerated into pecuniary commutations or aids; and at last the military <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the feudal system was abolished at the Restoration, by stat. 12 Car. II. c. 24. See Feudal System. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, we are not to imagine that the kingdom was left wholly without defence in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> insurrections, or the prospect of foreign invasions. Besides those who by their military tenures were bound to perform 40 days service in the field, with the assize of arms, enacted 27 Hen.
