And the water-mill at Manchester was fixed immediately below the Castlefield and the town, and on the channel of the Medlock. There, a little above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ford, the fluence of it was accidentally discovered about 30 years ago. On the margin of Dyer's croft, and opposite to some new constructions, the current of the river, acci- dentally swelled with the rains, and obstructed by a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>, broke down the northern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, swept away a large oak upon the edge of it, and disclosed a long <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TUN">tun</a>- nel in the rock blow. This has been since laid open in part with a spade. It appeared entirely uncovered at the top, was about a yard in width, and another in depth, but gradually narrowed to the bottom. The sides showed everywhere the marks of the tool on the rock, and the course of it was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with the channel. It was barred by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> about 25 yards only in length, but was evidently continued for several further; hav- ing originally begun, as the nature of the ground evin- ces, just above the large curve in the channel of the Medlock. For the first five or six centuries of the Roman state, there were no public bread <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> in the city of Rome. They were first introduced into it from the east, at the conclusion of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Perseus, and about the year 167 before Christ. And, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the first century, the Roman families were supplied by them every morning with fresh loaves for breakfast.— But the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, which prevailed originally among the Romans and many other nations, has continued nearly to the present time among the Mancunians. The providing of bread for every family was left entirely to the attention of the women in it; and it was baked upon stones, which the Welsh denominate grei- dials and we griddles. It appears, however, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KILN">kiln</a>-burnt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a> which has been discovered in the British sepulchres, and from the British appellation of an odyn or oven remaining among us at present, that furnaces for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a> were generally known among the original Britons. An odyn would, therefore, be erect- ed at the mansion of each Britith baron, for the use of himself and his retainers. And, when he and they removed into the vicinity of a Roman station, the oven would be rebuilt with the mansion, and the public bakehouses of our <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> commence at the first founda- tion of them. One bakehouse would be constructed, as we have previously shown one mill to have been set up, for the public service of all the Mancunian families. One oven and one mill appear to have been equally established in the town. And the inhabitants of it ap- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a> immemorially accustomed to bake at the one and grind at the other. Both, therefore, were in all proba- bility constructed at the first introduction of water- mills and ovens into the country. The great similarity of the appointments refers the consideration directly to one and the same origin for them. And the gene- ral nature of all such institutions <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> immediately to the first and actual introduction of both. And, as the same establishments prevailed equally in other parts of the north, and pretty certainly obtained over all the ex- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> of Roman <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the same erections were as certainly made at every stationary town in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>- dom.

MILL

Pages 141-141

John, a very learned divine, was born at Shap in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, about the year 1645; and be- came a servitor of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. On his entering into orders he became an eminent preacher, and was made prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. In 1681, he was created <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he was made chaplain in ordinary to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and in 1685 he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of St Edmund's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in Oxford. His edition of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever render his name memorable, was pub- lished about a fortnight before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which hap- pened in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1727. Dr <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">Mills</a> was employed 30 years in preparing this edition.

MILLARIUM AUREUM

Pages 145-145

was a gilded pillar in the forum of Rome, at which all the highways of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> met, as one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre. From this pillar the miles were counted, and at the end of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was put <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The milliary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> was erected by Augustus Caesar, and, as we are informed by travellers, is still to be seen. MILLING OF CLOTH. See Fulling.

MILLE PASSUS

Pages 142-142
or Millia Passuum**; a very common expression among the ancient Romans for a measure of distance, commonly called a mile. *Milliarium*, rarely used. Which Hesychius made to consist of seven stadia; Plutarch, little short of eight; but many others, as Strabo and Polybius, make it just eight stadia. The reason of this difference seems to be, that the former had a regard to the Grecian foot, which is greater than the Roman or Italico. This distance is oftentimes called *lapis*, which see. Each passus consisted of five feet (Columella).

MILLENER

Pages 142-142
or Milliner**, one who sells ribbons and dresses, particularly head dresses for women; and who makes up those dresses. Of this word different etymologies have been given. It is not derived from the French. The French cannot express the notion of milliner, otherwise than by the circumlocution *marchand* or *marchande des modes*. Neither is it derived from the Low Dutch language, the great, but neglected, magazine of the Anglo-Saxon. For Sewell, in his Dictionary English and Dutch, 1758, describes millener to be "en kraamer van lint en andere optonifelen, Fransche kraamer;" that is, "a pedlar who sells ribbons and other trimmings or ornaments; a French pedlar." Littleton, in his English and Latin dictionary, published 1677, defines millener, "a jack of all trades;" q.d. *millenarius*, or *mille mercurium venditor*; that is, "one who sells a thousand different sorts of things." This etymology seems fanciful: But, if he rightly understood the vulgar meaning of the word millener in his time, we must hold that it then implied what is now termed "a haberdasher of small wares," one who dealt in various articles of petty merchandise, and who did, not make up the goods which he sold. Before Littleton's time, however, a somewhat nicer characteristic than seems compatible with his notion, appears to have belonged to them; for Shakespeare, in his Henry IV., makes Hotspur, when complaining of the dainties of a courtier, say, "He was perfumed like a milliner." The fact seems to be, that there were milliners of several kinds: as, horse milliners, (for so those persons were called who make ornaments of coloured worsted for horses); haberdashers of small wares, the milleners of Littleton; and milleners such as those now peculiarly known by that name, whether male or female, and to whom Shakespeare's allusion seems most appropriate. Lastly, Dr Johnson, in his dictionary, derives the word from *milaner*, an inhabitant of Milan, from whence people of this profession first came, as a Lombard is a banker.

MILLENIARIES

Pages 142-142
or Chiliiasts**, a name given to those in the primitive ages, who believed that the saints will reign on earth with Christ 1000 years. See **Millennium**.

MILLENNIUM

Pages 142-144

"a thousand years;" generally employed to denote the thousand years, during which, according to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, grounded on some doubtful texts in the Apocalypse and other Scriptures, our blessed Saviour shall reign with the faithful upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> after the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> completion of beatitude. Though there has been no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the church in which the millennium was not admitted by individual divines of the first eminence, it is yet evident from the writings of Eusebius, Irenaeus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, and others among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as well as from the histories of Dupin, Molheim, and all the moderns, that it was never adopted by the whole church, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> made an article of the established creed in any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. About the middle of the fourth century the Millenniumians held the following tenets: 1stly, That the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> should be rebuilt, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Judea should be the habitation of those who were to reign on earth 1000 years. 2ndly, That the first resurrection was not to be confined to the martyrs; but that after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of Antichrist all the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> were to rise, and all that were on the earth were to continue for that space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. 3rdly, That Christ shall then come <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven, and be seen on earth, and reign there with his servants. 4thly, That the saints during this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> shall enjoy all the delights of a terrestrial paradise. These opinions were founded upon several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture, which the Millenniumians among the fathers understood in no other than a literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, but which the moderns, who hold that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, consider as partly literal and partly metaphorical. Of these passages, that upon which the greatest stress has been laid, we believe to be the following:— "And I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> an angel come down from heaven, having the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the bottomless pit, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chain in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. And he laid hold on the dragon, that old <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and Satan, and bound him a thousand years, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> him into the bottomless pit, and shut him up, and set a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> upon him, that he should deceive the nations no more till the thousand years should be fulfilled; and after that he must be loosed a little season. And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them: and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years. But the rest of the dead lived not again till the thousand years were finished. This is the first resurrection." This passage all the ancient *Rom.xx.*, Millenniumians took in a sense grossly literal; and taught, that during the millennium the saints on earth were to enjoy every bodily delight. The moderns, on the other hand, consider the power and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> as wholly spiritual; and they represent them as not to commence till after the consummation of the present earth. But that this last supposition is a mistake, the very next <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> except one assures us: for we are there told, that "when the thousand years are expired, Satan shall be loosed out of his prison, and shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the earth;" and we have no reason to believe believe that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have such power or such <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in "the new heavens and the new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness." For this and other reasons, which our limits will not permit us to enumerate, the most judicious critics contend, that the prophecies of the millennium point, not to a resurrection of martyrs and other just men to reign with Christ a thousand years in a visible kingdom upon earth, but to that state of the Christian church, which, for a thousand years before the general judgment, will be so pure and so widely extended, that, when compared with the state of the world in the ages preceding, it may, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Scripture, be called a resurrection from the dead. In support of this interpretation they quote two passages from St. Paul, in which a conversion from Paganism to Christianity, and a reformation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, is called a resurrection from the dead: "Neither yield ye your members as instruments of unrighteousness unto sin; but yield yourselves unto God as those that are alive from the dead."* And again, "Therefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>."† It is likewise to be observed, that in all the descriptions of the resurrection and future judgment which are given us at such length in the gospels and epistles, there is no mention made of a first and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> resurrection at the distance of a thousand years from each other. There is indeed an order in the resurrection: for we are told‡, that "every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall rise in his own order; Christ the first <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, afterwards they that are Christ's at his coming," &c. But were the millenarian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> well founded, the words should rather have run thus: "Christ the first fruits, then the martyrs at his coming, and a thousand years afterwards the residue of mankind. Then cometh the end," &c. These arguments strongly incline us to believe, that by the reign of Christ and the saints for a thousand years upon earth, nothing more is meant, than that before the general judgment the Jews should be converted, genuine Christianity be diffused through all nations, and mankind enjoy that peace and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and precepts of the gospel are calculated to confer on all by whom they are sincerely embraced. Our Saviour's own account of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is, that from a small beginning it will increase to the full <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. The millennium therefore is to be considered as the full effect of the Christian principles in the hearts of men, and over the whole world; and the divines who have treated of this subject endeavour to prove, that this is to be expected from the facts which have already existed, and from the importance of the Christian doctrine. 1. The gradual progress of Christianity is no objection to this fact. This is similar to the progress and advancement from less to greater perfection in everything which possesses vegetable or animal life. The same thing is observed in the arts, in civilization, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, and in individuals—and why should it not be admitted to have <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in religion? There is, indeed, a general principle on which a gradual progression, both in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and moral world, is founded. The Almighty never employs supernatural means where the thing can be accomplished by those which are natural. This idea is of the most general <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> through the whole of the present system of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The possibility of another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> could easily be admitted; but in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> there would be a total <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the works of God or of man that we are acquainted with. In the same manner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the religion of Christ had been irresistible, it would have totally altered its natural consequences. It was necessary, therefore, from the present condition of man, as an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, intelligent, and accountable being, that means should be employed; and wherever means are employed, the effects produced must be gradual, and not instantaneous. 2. Though the progress of a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> be gradual, yet it is to be expected, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and compassion of God, that it will still be advancing in the hearts of men, and over the world. In the first age of the church, the word of God, supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, and by the animated zeal of men who spoke what they saw and heard, grew and prevailed. In this case supernatural means were necessary, because the prejudices of the world could not be subdued without them. It was the first watering of a plant which you afterwards leave to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> of heaven. Miracles at the same time were employed only as the means of conviction; and they were not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, because in this case they would have become a constant and irresistible principle, incompatible with the condition of man as a reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>. After this power was withdrawn, there were many ages of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> in the Christian church. But what is necessary to be established on this subject is, not that the progress of Christianity has never been interrupted, but that on the whole it has been advancing. The effects of this religion on mankind, in proportion as it was received, were immediate and visible: it destroyed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> superstition of idol worship; it abolished the practice, which was general in the heathen world, of reducing to the lowest state of servitude the greatest part of our brethren; it softened the horrors of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; even when the vices of mankind made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> necessary; it entered into social and private life, and taught men benevolence, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and mercy. It is in these blessed effects that we can observe the progress of Christianity even to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Superstition and idolatry were soon engrafted on the stem which our Saviour planted in the world; but the simplicity of the gospel has been gradually undermining the fabric of superstition; and the men who are most nearly interested in the deceit are now almost ashamed to show their faces in the cause. The practice of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> has, generally speaking, been extinguished in the Christian world; yet the remains of it have been a disgrace to the Christian name, and the professors of that religion have now begun to see the inconsistency. War is not only carried on with less animosity, and less havoc of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; but men begin to cultivate more generally, and to delight in, the arts of peace. The increasing spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> and benevolence, of which it were easy to give unexampled instances in the present age, is a decided <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the increasing influence of Christianity. At the same time, if instead of these general principles, we were to descend to private examples of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>, or of wickedness, it would be easy to bring proofs in support of an opposite opinion: but the reasoning would by no means be equally conclusive; for if the general principles by which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> is regulated be more liberal and merciful, it it is evident that there is more goodness in a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Society is nothing more than a collection of individuals; and the general tone, especially when it is on the side of virtue, which almost in every instance opposes the designs of leading and interested men, is a certain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the private spirit. To show that this reformation is connected with Christianity, it is unnecessary to state any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the influence of heathen, and the influence of Christian principles: between civilization as depending on the powers of the human understanding, and on the efficacy of the word of God. The whole of this controversy may be appealed to an obvious fact, viz. that as any nation has come nearer to the simplicity of the gospel in the standard of its worship, it has been more possessed of those national virtues which we have ascribed to the influence of Christianity. This fact is worth a thousand volumes of speculation on this subject. 3. A revelation sanctioned by God, for a benevolent purpose, will be expected to produce effects corresponding to the wisdom which gave it, and to the purpose for which it is employed. It may be gradual; but it will be increasing, and it must increase, to the full harvest. He that has begun the good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> will also finish it. It is reasonable to expect this illustrious success of the gospel, both from the nature of the thing, and from the prophecies contained in the sacred scriptures. The precepts of the gospel, in their genuine sense, are admirably calculated for the peace and welfare both of individuals and society. The greatest liberality of mind, the greatest generosity of temper, the most unbounded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and the greatest indifference to the accumulation of this world's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, if they flowed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to breast, and operated with equal force on all men, would be productive of equal good and happiness to all. We are scarcely able to perceive the force of this at first view, because the deceit and imposition which yet exist in the world, prevent the operation of the best principles even in the best hearts. But in proportion to the improvement of mankind, what is their real <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and what are the real objects of happiness, will gradually unfold. The contempt of vice will be greater in proportion to the scarcity of it: for one villain gives countenance and support to another, just as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> sharpeneth iron. This opens to our view another fact connected with the practice of Christianity, namely, that the nearer it arrives to its perfect state, it will be the more rapid in its progress. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> will be more visible; and, in the strong language of the prophet, "the earth shall bring forth in one day, and a nation shall be born at once."* This future perfection of the gospel is consistent with its nature and importance.—We can scarcely believe that means so admirably adapted to the reformation of mankind should be without their effect; and if the most difficult part be already accomplished, we have no reason to apprehend that the scheme will not be completed. This fact is also clearly the subject of ancient prophecy. For "thus faith the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the Gentiles like a flowing stream. And it shall come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, from one Sabbath to another, and from one new <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to another, shall all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> come to worship before me, saith the Lord."† "Violence shall be no more heard in thy land, wasting nor destruction within thy border; but thou shalt call thy walls <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a>, and thy gates praise." (Isaiah 60:18.) Without entering more minutely on the prophecy already quoted from chap. xx. of the book of the Revelation, it is sufficient to observe, that Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITBY">Whitby</a>, in his treatise on the millennium at the end of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, proves, in the clearest manner, from the spirit of the passage and the similarity of the expressions with those of other prophets, that it refers to a state of the church for a thousand years, which shall be like life from the dead. The commencement of this period is connected with two events: the fall of antichrist, and the conversion of the Jews. The latter of these events must be considered as a key to all the prophecies concerning the millennium. As the Jews were the ancient people of God, and as their conversion is to be the previous step to the general knowledge of Christianity, the prophecies of the millennium have a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> relation to this important event. We have already observed, that God never interposes with miraculous power to produce what can be effected by natural means; and from what we know of human nature, we cannot but perceive that the conversion of the Jews will powerfully operate to the general conversion of mankind. Freed from those prejudices which now make them the objects of hatred in all nations, and fired with that zeal by which new converts are always actuated, they will preach the gospel with a fervour of which we, who have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been blest with its rays, can hardly form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>; and, by their present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> over the whole earth, they will be enabled to adapt their instructions to every individual of the human race in the language of his fathers. Indeed, if they are not at some future period to be employed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> for this purpose, it is difficult, if not impossible, to give any reason for their dispersed state and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> existence. Just now it must be confessed that they are the most implacable enemies of the Christian name; but their conversion is not on that account more unlikely or improbable than were events which have taken place of nearly equal importance a very few years ago. On the whole, the perfection of Christianity is a doctrine of reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> to the church; and it is impossible for the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for natural religion to deny, that unlimited obedience to its precepts is consistent with the purest state of liberty and of happiness. This is the only millennium which the prophets and apostles, as we understand them, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to the saints; but as men figuring in the very first ranks of learning have thought otherwise, we would not be too confident that our interpretation is just.—Such of our readers as wish for further information, will find it in the works of Mr Mede, Bishop Newton, Dr Whitby and Dr Gill; and to those masterly writers we refer them for that satisfaction which in such an article as this cannot be given.

MILLEPORA

Pages 144-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name by which Linnaeus distinguishes that genus of lithophytes, of a hard structure and full of holes, which are not fluted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> radiated, and whose animal is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRA">hydra</a>, in which it differs from the madrepora, and comprehending 14 different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. In the millepora, the animal which forms and inhabits it occupies the substance; and it is observed that MILLEPORA. The millepora grow upon one another; their little animals produce their spawn; which attaching itself either to the extremity of the body already formed, or underneath it, gives a different form to this production. Hence the various shapes of the millepora, which is composed of an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the cells of those little insects, which all together exhibit different figures, though every particular cellula has its essential form, and the same dimensions, according to its own species. MILLET. See Millium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MILLIARE

Pages 145-145
or MILLARIUM, a Roman mile, which consisted of 1000 paces, mille passus, whence the name.

MILLION

Pages 145-145

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, the sum of ten hundred thousand, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a thousand times a thousand. See Arithmetic.

MILLO

Pages 145-145

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZION">Zion</a> at its extremity; and therefore called Millo of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> (2 Chron. xxiii.), taken in with the wall that encompassed Mount Zion. Uncertain whether Beth Millo, (Judges ix. 20.) denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it did, it lay near Sechem.

MILLOT

Pages 145-145
CLAUDE FRANCIS XAVIER, of the French academy, was born at Béziers, March 1726, and was for some time a Jesuit. He was consecrated for the pulpit, and continued to preach after he left the society: But the weakness of his voice, his timidity, and the awkwardness of his manner, not permitting him to continue in this profession, he relinquished it, although he had preached Advent sermons at Versailles, and Lent sermons at Luneville. The marquis de Feline, minister of Parma, instituted an historical class for the benefit of the young nobility; and, at the desire of M. le Duc de Nivernois, he gave the charge of it to the abbé Millot. The minister having occasioned a kind of rebellion among the people by some innovations which he had made in the state, the abbé continued attached to the interests of his patron, and would not desert him till the storm was blown over. When he was told that he would lose his place by this conduct, he replied, "My place is with a virtuous persecuted man who has been my benefactor; and that I shall never lose." At length, having filled the historical chair with great approbation, he returned to France, and was appointed preceptor to M. le Duc d'Enghien. In this situation he died, A.D. 1785, aged 59. The abbé Millot did not shine in company; he was cold and reserved in his manner; but everything he said was judicious, and exactly in point.—D'Alembert said, that of all his acquaintance the abbé Millot had the fewest prejudices and the least pretension. He composed several works, which are digested with great care, and written in a pure, simple, and natural style. The principal are, 1. Éléments de l'Histoire de France, depuis Clovis jusqu'à Louis XIV. 3 vols. in 12mo. The author, selecting the most curious and important facts, has suppressed every thing foreign to the subject; and has not only arranged the materials in their proper order, but chosen them with the greatest judgment. Querlon thought this the best abridgement which we have of the history of France, and preferred it to that of the president Renaut. 2. Éléments de l'Histoire d'Angleterre depuis son origine jusqu'aux Romains, jusqu'à George II. 3 vols. 12mo. In this valuable abridgement, the author satisfies, without tiring, his readers. It is all that is necessary for those who wish to gain a general knowledge of the English history, without entering minutely into its particular parts.—3. Éléments de l'Histoire Universelle, 9 vols. 12mo. A certain critic maintains, that this work is merely a counterfeit of Voltaire's general history. But this censure is altogether unjust. The ancient history in this work is wholly composed by the abbé Millot; and, no less than the modern part, discovers his abilities in the choice of facts, in divesting them of useless circumstances, in relating them without prejudice, and in adorning them with judicious reflections. 4. L'Histoire des Troubadours, 3 vols. 12mo, compiled from the manuscripts of M. de Saint-Palace. This work appears rather tedious, because it treats of men almost unknown, and most of them deserving to be so. What is there quoted from the Provengal poets is not at all interesting; and, according to the observation of a man of wit, "it serves no purpose to search curiously into a heap of old ruins while we have modern palaces to engage our attention." 5. Mémoires Politiques et Militaires pour servir à l'Histoire de Louis XIV. et de Louis XV., composed from original papers collected by Adrian Maurice duc de Noailles, marshal of France, in 6 vols. 12mo. 6. The abbé Millot published also several Discourses, in which he discusses a variety of philosophical questions, with more ingenuity of argument than fire of expression; and a translation of the most select harangues in the Latin historians; of which it has been remarked, as well as of the orations of the abbé d'Olivet, that they are coldly correct, and elegantly insipid. The character of the author, more prudent and circumspect than lively and animated, seldom elevated his imagination above a noble simplicity without warmth, and a pure style without affectation. Some of the critics, however, have accused him of declamation in some parts of his histories, particularly in those parts which concern the clergy. But, in our opinion, the word declamation is totally inapplicable to the writings of the abbé Millot. He flatters, it is true, neither priests nor statesmen; and he relates more instances of vicious than virtuous actions, because the one are infinitely more common than the other: But he relates them coldly; and he appears to be guided more by sincerity and a love of truth, than by that partial philosophy which blames the Christian religion for those evils which it condemns.

MILLSTONE

Pages 141-142

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> by which corn is ground. —The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a> which we find preserved from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times are all small, and very different from those in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> at present. Thoresby mentions two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three such found in England, among other Roman antiquities, which were but 20 inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and there is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reason to believe that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, as well as the Egyptians of old, and the ancient Jews, did not em- ploy horses, or <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as we do, to turn their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, but made their slaves and captives of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> do this laborious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; they were in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> placed behind these millstones, and pushed them on with all their force. Sampson, when a prisoner to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILISTINES">Philistines</a>, was treated no better, but was con- demned to the millstone in his prison. The runner or loose millstone, in this sort of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>, was usually very heavy for its size, being as thick as broad. This is the millstone which is expressly prohibited in Scrip- ture to take in pledge, as lying loose it was more easily removed. The Talmudists have a story, that the Chaldeans made the young men of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> carry millstones with them to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, where there seems to have been a scarcity at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and hence, probably, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> renders the text "have borne the mills or millstones;" which might thus be true in a literal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. They have also a proverbial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with a millstone about his neck; which they use to express a man under the severest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. weight of affliction. This also plainly refers to this small fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. **Rhombus** MILSTONE, a stone which has been clasped among volcanic products, on account of its appearance, which is a blackish gray, porous, and very much resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>.

MILT

Pages 147-147
or Melt, in href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural History, the soft roe in fishes; thus called from its yielding, by expression, a whitish juice resembling milk. See ROE. The melt is properly the feed or spermatic part of the male fish. The melt of a carp is reckoned a choice bit. It consists of two long whitish irregular bodies, each included in a very thin fine membrane. M. Petit considers them as the testicles of the fish wherein the feed is preserved; the lower part next the anus, he supposes to be the vesiculae feminales.

MILTHORP

Pages 147-147

a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a>, at the mouth of the Can, eight miles south from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENDAL">Kendal</a>. It is the only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and goods are brought hither in small vessels from Grange in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>. Here are two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>. It has a market on Friday, and a fair on Old May <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and there is a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river Betha, which runs through the town.

MILTIADES

Pages 147-150

an Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, son of Cypselus. He obtained a victory in a chariot <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> at the Olympic games. He led a colony of Athenians to the Chersonesus. The causes of this appointment are striking and singular. The Thracian Dolonci, harried by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Ablynthians, were directed by the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> to take for their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> they met in their return home, who invited them to come under his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> and partake his entertainments. This was Miltiades, whom the appearance of the Dolonci, with their strange arms and garments, had struck. He invited them to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and was made acquainted with the commands of the oracle. He obeyed; and when the oracle of Delphi had approved a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the choice of the Dolonci, Miltiades, Ionici, he departed for the Chersonesus, and was invested by the inhabitants with sovereign power. The first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> he took were to stop the further incursions of the Abysynthians, by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a strong wall across the isthmus. When he had established himself at home, and fortified his dominions against foreign invasion, he turned his arms against <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LAMPSACUS">Lampsacus</a>. His expedition was unsuccessful; he was taken in an ambuscade, and made prisoner. His friend Croesus king of Lydia was informed of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and procured his release. He lived few years after he had recovered his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. As he had no issue, he left his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> and possessions to Stefagoras the son of Cimon, who was his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> by the same mother. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Miltiades was greatly honoured by the Dolonci, and they regularly celebrated festivals and exhibited shows in commemoration of a man to whom they owed their greatness and preservation. Miltiades, the son of Cimon, and brother of Stefagoras mentioned in the preceding article, was some time after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the latter, who died without issue, sent by the Athenians with one ship to take possession of the Chersonesus. At his arrival Miltiades appeared mournful, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> lamenting the recent death of his brother. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> visited the new governor to console with him; but their confidence in his sincerity proved fatal to them. Miltiades seized their persons, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> in Chersonesus. To strengthen himself, he married Hegesipyla, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Olorus the king of the Thracians. His triumph was short. In the third year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, his dominions were threatened by an invasion of the Scythian Nomades, whom <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> had some time before irritated by entering their country. He fled before them; but as their hostilities were of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, he was soon restored to his kingdom. Three years after, he left Chersonesus; and set sail for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, where he was received with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. He was present at the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARATHON">Marathon</a>; in which all the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officers ceded their power to him, and left the event of the battle to depend upon his superior abilities. He obtained an important victory over the more numerous forces of his adversaries. Some time after, Miltiades was intrusted with a fleet of 70 ships, and ordered to punish those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> which had revolted to the Persians. He was successful at first, but a sudden report that the Persian fleet was coming to attack him, changed his operations as he was besieging Paros. He raised the siege, and returned to Athens. He was accused of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, and particularly of holding correspondence with the enemy. The falsity of these accusations might have appeared, if Miltiades had been able to come into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. But a wound which he had received before Paros detained him at home; and his enemies, taking advantage of his absence, became more eager in their accusations, and louder in their clamours. He was condemned to death; but the rigour of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> was retracted on the recollection of his great services to the Athenians, and he was put into prison till he had paid a fine of 50 talents to the state. His inability to discharge so great a sum detained him in confinement; and his wounds becoming incurable, he died a prisoner about 489 years before the Christian era. His body was ransomed by his son Cimon; who was obliged to borrow and pay the 50 talents, to give his father a decent <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>.—The accusations against Miltiades were probably the more readily believed by his countrymen, when they remembered how he made himself absolute in Chersonesus; and in condemning the barbarity of the Athenians towards a general, who was the source of their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> prosperity, we must remember the jealousy which ever reigns among a free and independent people, and how watchful they are in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> which they see wrested from others by violence. Cornelius Nepos has written the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Miltiades the son of Cimon; but his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is incongruous and unintelligible, from his confounding the actions of the son of Cimon with those of the son of Cypselus. Greater reliance is to be placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, whose veracity is confirmed, and who was indubitably better informed and more capable of giving an account of the life and exploits of men who flourished in his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and of which he could see the living monuments. Herodotus was born about six years after the famous battle of Marathon; and C. Nepos, as a writer of the Augustan age, flourished about 450 years after the age of the father of history. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, John, the most illustrious of the English poets, was descended of a genteel family, seated at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their own name, viz. Milton, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. He was born <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 9, 1608, and received his first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under the care of his parents, assisted by a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. He afterwards passed some time at St Paul's school, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> his father had settled, being engaged in the business of a scrivener. At the age of 17, he was sent to Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; where he made great progress in all parts of academical learning; but his chief delight was in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. In 1623, he proceeded bachelor of arts, having performed his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> for it with great applause. His father designed him for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but the young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> was so strong, that it became impossible to engage him in any other pursuits. In 1632, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; and having now spent as much time in the university as became a person who determined not to engage in any of the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, he left the college, greatly regretted by his acquaintance, but highly displeased with the usual method of training up youth there for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and being much out of humour with the public administration of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs, he grew dissatisfied with the established form of church government, and disliked the whole <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of education practised in the university. His parents, who now dwelt at Horton, near Colnbrook, in Buckinghamshire, received him with unabated affection, notwithstanding he had thwarted their views of providing for him in the church, and they amply indulged him in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of retirement; wherein he enriched his mind with the choicest stores of Grecian and Roman literature; and his poems of Comus, l'Allegro, Il Penseroso, and Lycidas, all wrote at this time, would have been sufficient, had he never produced anything more considerable, to have transmitted his fame to the latest posterity. However, he was not so absorbed in his studies as not to make frequent excursions to London; neither did so much excellence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> Milton was unnoticed among his neighbours in the country, with the most distinguished of whom he sometimes chose to relax his mind, and improve his acquaintance with the world as well as with books. After five years spent in this manner, he obtained his father's permission to travel for farther improvement. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> he became acquainted with the celebrated Hugo Grotius; and from thence travelling into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he was everywhere cared for by persons of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and learning. Upon his return home, he set up a genteel academy in Aldergate street. In 1641, he began to draw his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> in defense of the Presbyterian party; and the next year he married the daughter of Richard Powell, Esq., of Forest Hill in Oxfordshire. This lady, however, whether from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> on account of party, her father being a zealous royalist, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other cause, soon thought proper to return to her relations; which so incensed her husband, that he resolved never to take her again, and wrote and published several tracts in defense of the doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of divorce. He even made his addresses to another lady; but this incident proved the means of a reconciliation with Mrs Milton. In 1644, he wrote his Tract upon Education; and the restraint on the liberty of the press being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he wrote boldly and nobly against that restraint. In 1645, he published his juvenile poems; and about two years after, on the death of his father, he took a smaller house in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Holborn, the back of which opened into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn Fields. Here he quietly prosecuted his studies, till the fatal catastrophe and death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.; on which occasion he published his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">Tenure</a> of Kings and Magistrates, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> of the fact. He was now taken into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the commonwealth, and made Latin secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state, who resolved neither to write to others abroad, nor to receive any answers, except in the Latin tongue, which was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to them all. The famous Exon Basilicon coming out about the same time, our author, by command, wrote and published his Iconoclastes the same year. It was also by order of his masters, backed by the reward of 100l. that in 1651 he published his celebrated piece, entitled Pro Populo Anglicano Defensio; "A Defence of the people of England, in answer to Salmasius's Defence of the King;" which performance spread his fame over all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He now dwelt in a pleasant house with a garden in Petty France, Westminster, opening into St James's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a>. In 1652 he buried his wife, who died not long after the delivery of her fourth child; and about the same time he also lost his eye-sight, by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUTTA">gutta</a> serena, which had been growing upon him many years. Cromwell took the reins of government into his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the year 1653; but Milton still held his office. His leisure hours he employed in prosecuting his studies; wherein he was so far from being discouraged by the loss of his sight, that he even conceived hopes this misfortune would add new vigour to his genius; which in fact seems to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>.—Thus animated, he again ventured upon matrimony: his second lady was the daughter of Captain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HACKNEY">Hackney</a>: she died in childbirth about a year after. On the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of the protector, Richard Cromwell, and on the return of the long parliament, Milton being still continued secretary, he appeared again in print; pleading for a farther reformation of the laws relating to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and, during the anarchy that ensued, he drew up several schemes for re-establishing the commonwealth, exerting all his faculties to prevent the return of Charles II. England's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>, however, and Charles's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> prevailing, our author chose to confine his safety, and retired to a friend's house in Bartholomew Clove. A particular prosecution was intended against him; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> esteem to which his admirable genius and extraordinary accomplishments entitled him, had raised him so many friends, even among those of the opposite party, that he was included in the general amnesty. This storm being over, he married a third wife, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, daughter of Mr Minshall a-Cheshire gentleman; and not long after he took a house in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a> Walk, leading to Bunhill Fields. This was his last stage: here he fat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for a longer continuance than he had been able to do anywhere; and though he had lost his fortune (for every thing belonging to him went to wreck at the Restoration), he did not lose his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature, but continued his studies with almost as much ardour as ever; and applied himself particularly to the finishing his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the Paradise Lost; one of the noblest poems that ever was produced by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> genius.—It was published in 1667, and his Paradise Regained came out in 1670.—This latter work fell short of the excellence of the former production; although, were it not for the transcendent merit of Paradise Lost, the second <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> would doubtless have stood foremost in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of English epic poems. After this he published many pieces in prose; for which we refer our readers to the edition of his Historical, Poetical, and Miscellaneous Works, printed by Millar, in 2 vols. 4to, in 1753. In 1674, this great man paid the last debt to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> at his house in Bunhill Fields, in the 66th year of his age; and was interred on the 12th of November, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of St Giles's, Cripplegate.—A decent monument was erected to his memory, in 1737, in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, by Mr Benson, one of the auditors of the impress.—Milton was remarkably handsome in his person; but his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was tender, and by no means equal to his incessant application to his studies.—Though greatly reduced in his circumstances, yet he died worth 1500l. in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, besides his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods.—He had no son: but left behind him three daughters, whom he had by his first wife. Milton, the name of several places in England; particularly, Milton, or Middleton, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANDFORD">Blandford</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>, 114 miles from London. It is chiefly noted for its abbey, built by King Athelstan. The church stands near the south side of the abbey. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and magnificent pile of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and contains several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments. Here is an almshouse for six people, who have 12s. a-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and three yards of cloth for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of shoes and stockings, and 10s. each on St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> yearly. Here is a free school, and a market on Tuesdays. Milton, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, near Sittingbourne and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Sheppey, 6 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Faversham, and 40 from London. It is also called Middleton from its situation near the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, i.e., from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>. The kings of Kent had a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> here, which was cattellated, and stood below the church; but was burnt down in Edward the Confessor's time by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Goodwin, &c. Its church stands near a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> off. On approaching the town up the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, by the Earl Swale, it seems hid among the creeks; yet it is a large town; and has a considerable market on Saturdays, and a fair on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 24. The officers taken here are the most famous of any in Kent. This town is governed by a portreeve, chosen yearly on St James's day, who supervises the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and measures</a> all over the hundred of Milton. Milton, in Kent, a mile on the east side of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVESEND">Gravesend</a>, was incorporated with it in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Elizabeth, by the name of the portreeve, jurats, and inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Gravesend and Milton. King Henry VIII. raised a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> or blockhouse here, for the defence both of this town and Gravesend, and the command of the river. It has a fair <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 25.

MILTON

Pages 119-123

but scout and hurry along in little detached parties of six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and sweeping low, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> over the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> their course to the opposite continent at the narrowest passage they can find. They usually slope across the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> to the south-west, and so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TANGIER">Tangier</a>, which it seems is the narrowest space. "In former letters we have considered whether it was probable that woodcocks in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>-shiny nights <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the German ocean from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>. As a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that birds of less speed may pass that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, considerate as it is, I shall relate the following incident, which, though mentioned to have happened so many years ago, was strictly <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact:—As some people were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Trotton, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, they killed a duck in that dreadful winter 1789, with a silver collar about its neck (I have read a like anecdote of a swan), on which were engraven the arms of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. This anecdote the rector of Trotton at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> has often told to a near relation of mine; and, to the best of my <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>, the collar was in the possession of the rector. "At present I do not know any body near the sea side that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> take the trouble to remark at what time of the moon woodcocks first come. One thing I used to observe when I was a sportsman, that there were times in which woodcocks were so sluggish and sleepy that they would drop again when flushed just before the firearms, nay just at the muzzle of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> that had been fired at them: whether this strange laziness was the effect of a recent fatiguing journey, I shall not presume to say. "Nightingales not only never reach <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> and Scotland, but also, as I have been always told, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> and Cornwall. In those two last counties we cannot <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the failure of them to the want of warmth: the defect in the west is rather a presumptive argument that these birds come over to us from the continent at the narrowest passage, and do not stroll so far westward." Upon the subject of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> of the swallow there are three opinions. Some say that it migrates to a warmer <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>; some, that it retires to hollow trees and caverns, where it lies in a torpid state; and others have affirmed, that it lies in the same state in the bottom of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is supported by Marigny, Ray, Willoughby, Catesby, Reaumur, Adanson, Buffon, &c. The first and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> opinion are both adopted by Pennant and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a>. The third is sanctioned by Scheffer, Hevelius, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a>, Klein, Ellis, Linnæus, Kalm: and the second and third have been strongly defended by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Migration Daines Barrington. Though we cannot help giving a preference to that opinion which appears the most probable, yet we do not think that any one of them is established upon such <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> as so curious a subject requires, and as the advanced state of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> would <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to expect. We shall therefore state the arguments upon which each opinion is founded as fairly and distinctly as we can, and as often as possible in the very words of their respective <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>. By doing so, we shall <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the whole subject before the eyes of our readers, who will thus have an opportunity of examining it attentively, and of making such observations and experiments as may lead to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Those who assert that the swallow migrates to a warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in winter, argue in this manner: That many birds migrate, is a fact fully proved by the observations of various natural historians. Is it not more probable, therefore, that swallows, which disappear regularly every season, retire to some other country, than that they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a state of torpor in caverns or lakes? But this opinion does not rest on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, it is founded on facts. We often see them collected in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flocks on churches, rocks, and trees, about the time when they annually disappear. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of their flight has been observed to be southward. Mr White, the ingenious natural historian of Selborne, travelling near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the British Channel one morning early, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a flock of swallows take their departure. At the beginning of his journey he was environed with a thick fog; but on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> wild heath the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIST">mist</a> began to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, and discovered to him numberless swallows, cluttered on the standing bushes, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had roosted there: as soon as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> burst out, they were instantly on wing, and with an easy and placid flight proceeded towards the sea. After this he saw no more flocks, only now and then a straggler. Mr Lafkey of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> observed attentively the direction which a flock of swallows took in the autumn of 1793. On the 22nd of Sept., about seven o'clock in the morning, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> being easterly, accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> drizzling <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, Mr Lafkey's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was entirely covered with house-swallows. At intervals large flocks arrived and joined the main body, and at their arrival an unusual chirping commenced. The appearance of the whole company was so lethargic, that he found it an easy matter to catch a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them, which he kept in a room all that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. By four o'clock heating the room they all revived: he opened four of them, and found their stomachs quite full. The main body occupied the house top all day, except for two hours. About half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> after <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the morning of the 23rd, there was a great commotion, with very loud chirping, and within a few minutes after, the whole multitude took their flight, in a direct south-east direction, having ascended to a great height in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. He let go the birds which he had caught, at certain intervals till four o'clock, and they all flew toward the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. Not only has the direction of their flight been observed, but they have also been found on their passage at a great distance from land. Mr Adanson informs us, that about 50 leagues from the coast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a> four swallows settled upon the ship on the 6th of October; Migration. that these birds were taken; and that he knew them to be European swallows, which, he conjectures, were returning to the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Wager's authority may also be appealed to: "Returning home (says he) in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the year, as I came into foundings in our channel, a great flock of swallows came and settled on all my rigging; every rope was covered, they hung on one another like a swarm of bees; the decks and carving were filled with them. They seemed almost famished and spent, and were only feathers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; but, being recruited with a night's rest, took their flight in the morning." This vast fatigue proves that their journey must have been very great, considering the amazing swiftness of these birds: in all probability they had crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, and were returning from the shores of Senegal, or other parts of Africa; so that this account from that most able and honest seaman, confirms the later information of Mr. Adanson. Mr. Kalm, who is an advocate for the opinion that swallows lie immersed in lakes during winter, acknowledges that in crossing the Atlantic from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> a swallow lighted on the ship on the 2d September, when it had passed only two-thirds of the ocean. Since, therefore, swallows have been seen assembled in great flocks in autumn <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> off in company towards southern climes, since they have been found both in their passage from Europe and returning again, can there be any doubt of their annual migration?—Mr. Barrington's objections to this opinion have been noticed above in No. 5. The second notion (says Mr Pennant) has great antiquity on its side. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and Pliny give it as their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, that swallows do not remove very far from their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> habitation, but winter in the hollows of rocks, and during that time lose their feathers. The former <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their opinion has been adopted by several ingenious men; and of late several proofs have been brought of some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, at least, having been discovered in a torpid state. Mr Collinson favoured us with the evidence of three gentlemen, eye-witnesses to numbers of sand martins being drawn out of a cliff on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1762. And the honourable Daines Barrington communicated to us the following fact, on the authority of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Belhaven, That numbers of swallows have been found in old dry walls and in sand-hills near his Lordship's seat in East <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a>; put once only, but from year to year; and that when they were exposed to the warmth of a fire, they revived.
