You must likewise accustom yourself to put white in your colours only in proportion as you work lighter or darker; for the colour you use the second time muft be always a little stronger and deeper than the first, unless it be for softening. Different colourings are easily made, by putting more or less of red, or blue, or yellow, or bitfre, whether for the dead-colouring, or for the finishing.—That for women ought to be bluish; that for children a little red; and both fresh and florid. That for men ought to be yellower; especially when they are old. To make a colouring of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, there muft be a first lay of white and orpiment, or a very pale ochre; dead-colour with vermilion, and lake, instead of carmine, and a good deal of white; and afterwards work over it with a green mixture, in which there is more blue than any other colour, to the end the flesh may be livid and of a purple colour. The tints are done the same way as in another colouring; but there muft be a great many more blue than yellow ones, especially upon the parts which fly from the sight, and about the eyes; and the last are only to be upon the parts which rise and come nearer the eye. They are made to die away in one another, according to the ordinary manner; sometimes with very pale blue, and sometimes with ochre and white, and a little vermilion; softening the whole together. The parts and contours muft be rounded with the same colours. The mouth is to be, in a manner, of a quite violet. It is dead-coloured, however, with a little vermilion, ochre, and white; but finished with lake and blue; and to give it the deep strokes, they take bitfre and lake, with which they likewise do the same to the eyes, the nose, and the ears. If it be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a>, or some <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>, upon whom blood is to be seen, after the finishing the carnation, form it with vermilion, and finish it with carmine, making in the drops of blood a little bright reflecting spark, to round them. For the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of thorns, make a lay of sea-green and masticot; shadow it with bitfre and green; and heighten the clear and light parts with masticot. Iron is formed, or first laid, with indigo, a little black and white; and finished with pure indigo, heightening it with white. For painting fire and flames, the lights are done with masticot and orpiment; and for the shades, they mix vermilion and carmine. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> is done with black, indigo, and white, and sometimes with bitfre; one may likewise add vermilion or ochre, according to the colour it is to be of. Pearls are painted by putting a lay of white, and a little blue; they are shadowed and rounded with the same colour, deeper; a small white dot is made almost in the middle on the side of the light; and on the other side, between the shadow and the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">pearl</a>, they give a touch with masticot, to make the reflection; and under the pearls is made a little shadow of the colour of the ground they are upon. Diamonds are made with pure black; then they heighten them with little touches of white on the side of the light. It is the same thing for any other jewels you have a mind to paint: there is nothing to be done but to change the colour. For making a figure of gold, put a lay of shell-gold, and shadow it with gallstone. Silver is done the same way; excepting that it must be shadowed with indigo.

MINIMS

Pages 314-314

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, founded by St Francis de Paula, towards the end of the 15th century. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> is a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> woollen stuff, with a woollen girdle, of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, tied in five knots. They are not permitted to quit their habit and girdle night nor <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Formerly they went barefooted, but are now allowed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of shoes.

MINIMUM

Pages 314-314

in the higher <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> attainable in a given <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>.

MINISTER

Pages 314-314

a person who preaches, performs <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship in public, administers the sacraments, &c. MINISTER of State, a person to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> intrusts the administration of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a>. Foreign MINISTER, is a person sent into a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to manage the affairs of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the state to which he belongs. Of these there are two kinds: those of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are ambassadors and envoys extraordinary, who represent the persons of their sovereigns; the ministers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> rank are the ordinary residents.

MINNIN

Pages 314-314

a stringed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hebrews, having three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four chords to it, although there is reason to question the antiquity of this instrument; both because it requires a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> bow, which was a kind of plectrum not known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and because it so much resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> viol. Kircher took the figures of this, the machul, chinnor, and psaltery, from an old book in the Vatican library.

MINOR

Pages 314-315

MINOR, a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, literally denoting less; used in opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, greater. Minor, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes a person under <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who, by the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, is not yet arrived at the power of administering his own affairs, or the possession of his estate. Among us, a person is a minor till the age of twenty-one, before which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his acts are invalid. See Age, and Infant. It is a maxim in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, that in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> there is no minority, and therefore he hath no legal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> grants and attests to acts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> are good, though he has not in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> capacity attained the legal age of twenty-one. It is also provided by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> and law of parliament, that no one shall sit or vote in either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, unless he be twenty-one years of age. This is likewise expressly declared by stat. 7. and 8 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">Will</a>. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 25, with regard to the house of commons. Minor, in Logic, is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> proposition of a formal or regular syllogism, called also the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a>. Minor, in Music, is applied to certain concords, which differ from or are lower than others of the same denomination by a lesser semitone or four commas. Thus we say, a third minor, or lesser third, or a sixth major and minor. Concords that admit of major and minor, i.e. greater and lesser, are said to be imperfect concords.

MINORCA

Pages 315-318

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Mediterranean, situated between 39 and 40 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and near four degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is about 33 miles in length from north-west to south-east, in breadth from eight to twelve, but in general about ten miles; so that in size it may nearly equal the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Huntingdon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>. The form is very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; and the coasts are much indented by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which forms a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little creeks and inlets, some of which might be very advantageous. This island is one of those called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Baleares, which arose from the dexterity of the inhabitants in using the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLING">sling</a>. It fell under the power of the Romans, afterwards of the northern barbarians, who destroyed that empire. From them it was taken by the Arabs; who were subdued by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, and he by the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The English subdued it in 1708; it was afterwards retaken by the French in 1756, but restored to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1763. The Spaniards took it in 1782; and in 1798, it again became subject to Great Britain. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of this island is much more clear and pure than in Britain; being seldom darkened with thick fogs; yet the low valleys are not free from mists and unwholesome vapors; and in windy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> the spray of the sea is driven over the whole island. Hence it happens that utensils of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> are extremely susceptible of rust, in spite of all endeavours to preserve them; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> furniture becomes mouldy. The summers are dry, clear, calm, and excessively hot; the autumns moist, warm, and unequal; at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> perfectly serene, at another cloudy and tempestuous. During the winter there are sometimes violent storms, though neither frequent nor of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance; and whenever they cease, the weather returns to its usual serenity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is always variable, but resembles the winter more than the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The changes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> are neither so great nor so sudden in this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> as in many others. In the compass of a year, the thermometer seldom rises much above the 80th, or falls below the 48th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. In summer there is scarcely ever a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of four or five degrees between the heat of the air at noon and at night; and in winter the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> is still less considerable. But this must be understood of a thermometer shaded from the influence of the solar beams: for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> exposed to them it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> often rise 12, 14, or 16 degrees higher than what we have mentioned; and in other seasons the difference between the heat of the air in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> is much greater. Yet even in the dog-days, the heat of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, at least in open places, seldom surpasses that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood. The winds are very boisterous about the equinoxes, and sometimes during the winter. At other times they are generally moderate, and, according to the observations of seamen, they rarely blow in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> adjacent to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Lyons as in the open sea. During the summer there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a perfect calm in the mornings and evenings; but the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> is cooled by refreshing breezes which come from the east, and, following the course of the sun, increase gradually till two or three in the afternoon, after which they insensibly die away as night approaches. This renders the heat of the sun less dangerous and inconvenient; and if these breezes intermit for a day or two, the natives grow languid and inactive from the heat. The northerly winds in general are clear and healthy, dispel the mists, and make a clear blue sky; whilst those which blow from the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, render the air warm, moist, and unhealthy. The north <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is superior in power to all the rest; which appears from hence, that the tops of all the trees incline to the south, and the branches on the north side are bare and blasted. The next to it in force is the north-west. Both are frequent towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of winter and in the spring; and, being dry and cold, they shrivel up the leaves of the vegetables, destroy their tender shoots, and are often excessively detrimental to the vineyards and rising corn. The piercing blasts at that season from the north-east, as they are more moist, and more frequently attended with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, are less prejudicial. The south and south-east winds are by much the most unhealthy. In whatever seasons they blow, the air is foggy, and affects the breathing; but in the summer season they are sultry and suffocating. An excessive dejection of spirits is then a universal complaint; and on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> the thermometer to the rays of the sun, the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> has frequently risen above the 100th degree. The west wind is usually drier than the south; the east is cold and blustering in the spring, and sultry in the summer. The weather in Minorca is generally fair and dry; but when it rains, the showers are heavy, though of short continuance, and they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> most commonly in the night. The sky in summer is clear, and of a beautiful azure, without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> or rain; but moderate dews descend regularly after sunset. In autumn the weather becomes less serene; whirlwinds and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> become frequent; and in the night time <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and those meteors called fulminations, are very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> spouts also are often seen at that season, and frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> upon the shore. A sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the weather takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> about the autumnal equinox; the skies are are darkened with clouds, and the rains fall in such quantities, that the torrents thereby occasioned, pouring <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the hills, tear up trees by the root, carry away cattle, break down fences, and do considerable mischief to the gardens and vineyards. But these anniversary rains are much more violent than lasting; always falling in sudden and heavy showers, with intervals of fair weather. They are accompanied with thunder, lightning, and squalls of wind, most commonly from the north. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">Hail</a> and snow are often intermixed with the rains which fall in winter and in spring; but the snow, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, dissolves immediately; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> is here an uncommon appearance. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Minorca lies low; and there are only a few hills near the centre, of which the most considerable, named Toro by the inhabitants, may be seen at the distance of 12 or 14 leagues from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The surface of the island is rough and unequal; and in many places divided by long narrow vales of a considerable depth, called barracones by the natives. They begin towards the middle of the island, and after several windings terminate at the sea. The south-west side is more plain and regular than towards the north-east; where the hills are higher, with low marshy valleys between them, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> less fruitful, and the whole tract unhealthy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. Near the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages the fields are well cultivated, and enclosed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> walls; but the rest for the most part are rocky, or covered with woods and thickets. There are some pools of standing water, but very few rivulets, which is the greatest defect about the island, as the inhabitants have scarcely any wholesome water excepting what is saved from the clouds. The soil is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, thin, and very stony, with a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of sea <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and, in some places, of calcareous nitre intermixed. In most places there is so little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, that the island appears to be but one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> irregular rock, covered here and there with mould, and an infinite variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Notwithstanding this, however, it is not only extremely proper for vineyards, but produces more wheat and barley than could at first sight be imagined; and if the peasants may be credited, it would always yield a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn and wine sufficient for the natives, did not the violence of the winds, and the excessive drought of the weather, frequently spoil their crops. The fields commonly <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> fallow for two years, and are sown the third. About the latter end of winter, or the beginning of spring, they are first broke up; and next autumn, as soon as the rains fall, they are again ploughed and prepared for receiving the proper seeds. The tillage is very easily performed; for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> so light as to be transported from place to place on the ploughman's shoulder, and to be drawn by a heifer, or an ass sometimes assisted by an ox, is sufficient for opening to thin a soil. The later the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> happens, the more plentiful it proves. The barley is usually cut down about the 20th of May and the wheat is reaped in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, so that the whole harvest is commonly got in by Midsummer day. The grain is not thrashed with flails as in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but trodden out on a smooth piece of rock by oxen and asses, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the eastern nations. The natives of Minorca are commonly lean, thin, and well-built, of a middle stature, and olive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>; but their character is by no means agreeable. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> impetuosity of their temper, that the slightest cause provokes them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, and they seem to be incapable of forgiving or forgetting an injury. Hence quarrels break out daily, even among neighbours and relations; and family disputes are transmitted from father to son; and thus, though lawyers and pettyfoggers are very numerous in this country, there are still too few for the clients. Both sexes are, by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, extremely amorous: they are often betrothed to each other while children, and marry at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 14. The women have easy labours, and commonly return in a few days to their usual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> business; but, lest the family should become too numerous for their income, it is a practice among the poorer sort to keep their children at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> for two or three years, that by this means the mothers may be hindered from breeding. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a> of the finest wheat flour, well fermented and well baked, is more than half the diet of people of all ranks. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">Rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, vermicelli, herbs and roots from the garden, summer <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, pickled olives and pods of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, make up almost all the other half, so that scarce a fifth of their whole food is furnished from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and of this fish makes by much the most considerable portion. On Fridays, and other fast days, they abstain entirely from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; and during <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> they live altogether on vegetables and fish, excepting Sundays, when they are permitted the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of eggs, cheese, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. Most of their dishes are highly-seasoned with pepper, cloves, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, and other spices; and garlic, onions, or leeks, are almost constant ingredients. They eat a great deal of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and that none of the sweetest or best flavoured; using it not only with salads, but also with boiled and fried fish, greens, pulse, &c. instead of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>. A slice of bread soaked in boiled water, with a little oil and salt, is the common breakfast of the peasants, well known by the name of oleagno. Their ordinary meals are very frugal, and consist of very little variety; but on festivals and other solemn occasions their entertainments are to the last degree profuse and extravagant, inasmuch that the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of fare of a country <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>'s wedding dinner would scarce be credited. With regard to other matters, the Minorquins are accused of prodigious indolence in the way of business, and neglect of the natural advantages they possess. In the bowels of the earth are iron, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ores, of none of which any use hath been made except the last. A lead mine was worked to advantage some time ago, and the ore sent into France and Spain for the use of the potteries in those countries. The proprietor discontinued his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on some small discouragement; and indeed it is said, that these people are of all mankind the most easily put out of conceit with an undertaking that does not bring them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of present <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, or that admits of the slightest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of disappointing their most languid expectations: nor will their purse admit of many disappointments; and thus their poverty co-operating with their natural despondency and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of ease, is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of their backwardness to engage in projects, though ever so promising, for the improvement of their private fortune, and the advantage of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of their country. Minorca country. This lead ore went under the name of vernis among the natives, as it was wholly used by the potters in varnishing and glazing their earthen vessels. There are few exports of any account, and they are obliged to their neighbours for near one-third of their corn, all their oil, and such a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of less consideration, that nothing could preserve them from a total bankruptcy, but the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> circulated by the troops, which is exchanged for the daily supplies of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, increased by the multiplication of vineyards, the breeding of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, and the production of vegetables, in a proportion of at least five to one since the island has been in our possession. It will not require many words to enumerate their exports: they make a sort of cheese, little liked by the English, which sells in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> at a very great price; this, perhaps, to the amount of 800l. per annum.—The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> they send abroad may produce 900l. more.—Some wine is exported; and, if we add to its value that of the home consumption, which has every merit of an export, being <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> parts in ten taken off by the troops for ready money, it may well be estimated at 16,000l. a-year. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, and salt, their yearly exports may be about 400l. and this comes pretty near the sum of their exports, which we estimate together at 18,000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> per annum. A vast <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> lies against them, if we consider the variety and importance of the articles they fetch from other countries, for which they must pay ready cash. Here it may be necessary to withdraw some things from the heap, such as their cattle, sheep, and fowls, on which they get a profit; for the country does not produce them in a sufficient abundance to supply them, especially when we have a fleet of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> stationed there. Their imports are, corn, cattle, sheep, fowls, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, oil, rice, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, spices, hardware, and tools of all kinds; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; chocolate, or cocoa to make it; tobacco, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, plank, boards, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>, tobacco <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, playing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, turnery <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, seeds, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, faddles; all manner of cabinetmakers work, iron spikes, nails, fine earthen ware, glass lamps, braffery; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> wares; copperas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, dye stuffs, painters brushes and colours; musical instruments, music, and strings; watches, wine, fruit, all manner of fine and printed linens, mullins, cambrics, and laces; bottles, corks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, fans, trinkets, toys, ribbands, tape, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, pins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, mohair, lanthorns, cordage, tar, pitch, rosin, drugs, gloves, fire-arms, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, and lead; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, caps, velvet, cotton stuffs, woollen cloths, stockings, capes, medals, vestments, lustrous pictures, images, agnus dei's, books, pardons, bulls, relics, and indulgences. The island is divided into what they style terminos, of which there were anciently five, now reduced to four, and resemble our counties. The termino of Ciutadella, at the north-western extremity of the island, is so styled from this place, which was once a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Minorca. It makes a venerable and majestic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, even in its present state of decay, having in it a large Gothic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, some other churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the governor's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, which is no contemptible pile.—There are in it 600 houses, which before the seat of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> were removed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a>, were fully inhabited; and Minorca there are still more gentlemen's families here than in all the rest of the island. It hath a port commodious enough for the vessels employed in the trade of this country, which, though in the possession of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> power, is less than it formerly was. It is still, in the style of our officers, the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> (and there are none bad) in the country; and if there was a civil government, and the place made a free port, the best judges are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> it would very soon become a flourishing place again; and the fortifications, if it should be found necessary, might then also be easily restored and improved. The termino of Tererias is the next, a narrow lip reaching across from sea to sea, and the country little cultivated; it is therefore united to Mereandall. In this last termino stands Mont-toro in the very centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a>, and the highest ground, some say the only mountain in it; on the summit of which there is a convent, where even in the hottest months the monks enjoy a cool air, and at all times a most delightful prospect. About six miles north from Mont-toro stands the castle that covers Port Formelles, which is a very spacious harbour on the east side of the island. There are in it shoals and foul ground, which, to those who are unacquainted with them, render it difficult and dangerous; yet the packets bound from Mahon to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a> frequently take shelter therein; and while the Spaniards were in possession of the isle, large ships and men of war frequented it. At a small distance from this lies another harbour called Ada, which runs far into the land; but being reputed unsafe, and being so near Formelles, is at present useless. The country about it is, however, said to be the pleasantest and wholesomest spot in the island, and almost the only one plentifully supplied with excellent spring water; so that the gardens are well laid out, and the richest and finest fruits grow here in the highest perfection. Alaior is the next termino, in which there is nothing remarkable but the capital of the same name, well situated on an eminence, in a pleasant and tolerably cultivated country. The termino of Mahon, at the south-east end of the island, is at present the most considerable of them all, containing about 60,000 English acres, and nearly one-half of the inhabitants in Minorca. The town of Mahon derives its name from the Carthaginian general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGO">Mago</a>, who is universally allowed to be its founder.—It stands on an eminence on the west side of the harbour, the ascent pretty steep. There are in it a large <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, three convents, the governor's palace, and some other public edifices. It is large, but the streets are winding, narrow and ill paved. The fortress of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> stands near the entrance of the harbour, which it covers, is very spacious, of great strength, with subterranean works to protect the garrison from bombs, large magazines, and whatever else is necessary to render it a complete fortification, and hath a numerous and well disposed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. Port Mahon is allowed to be the finest harbour in the Mediterranean, about 90 fathoms wide at its entrance, but within very large and safe, stretching a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> or more into the land. Beneath the town of Mahon there is a very fine quay, one end of which is reserved for the ships of war, and furnished with all the accommodations necessary for careening and refitting them; the other serves for merchantmen. On the other side of the harbour is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLA">Mola</a>, where it is generally agreed a fortres might be constructed which would be impregnable, as the castle of St Philip was deemed before we took it, and bestowed so much money upon it, that, though some works were erected at Cape Mola, it was not judged proper to proceed in the fortifications there at a fresh expense; at least this is the only reason that hath been assigned. Minorca was taken by the Spaniards during the American war, and is now in their possession.

MINORS

Pages 318-318
or FRIERS MINOR, an appellation which the Franciscans assume, out of show of humility; calling themselves fratres minoris, i.e. lesser brothers, and sometimes minorites. There is also an order of regular minors at Naples, which was established in the year 1583, and confirmed by Sixtus V.

MINOS

Pages 318-318

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>. He flourished about 1432 years before the Christian era. He gave laws to his subjects, which still remained in full force in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, about 1000 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and moderation procured him the appellation of the favourite of the gods, the confidant of Jupiter, and the wife legislator, in every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and, according to the poets, he was rewarded for his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> after death with the office of supreme and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> judge in the infernal regions. In this capacity he is represented sitting in the middle of the shades, and holding a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The dead plead their different causes before him; and the impartial judge shakes the fatal urn, which is filled with the destinies of mankind. He married Ithona, by whom he had Lycastes, who was the father of Minos II. MINOS II. was a son of Lycastes, the son of Minos I. and king of Crete. He married Pasiphae, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sol and Perseis, and by her he had many children. He increased his paternal dominions by the conquest of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but showed himself cruel in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> which he carried on against the Athenians, who had put to death his son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDROGEUS">Androgeus</a>. He took <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a> by the treachery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCYLLA">Scylla</a>; and not satisfied with victory, he obliged the vanquished to bring him yearly to Crete <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> chosen boys and the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of virgins to be devoured by the Minotaur. This bloody tribute was at last abolished when <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> had destroyed the monster. When Daedalus, whose industry and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> had fabricated the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>, and whose imprudence in afflicting Pasiphae in the gratification of her unnatural desires, had offended Minos, fled from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his confinement with wings, and arrived safe in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; the incensed monarch pursued the offender, resolved to punish his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>. Cocalus, king of Sicily, who had hospitably received Daedalus, entertained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> guest with dissembled friendship; and, that he might not deliver to him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whose ingenuity and abilities he so well knew, he put Minos to death. Minos died about 35 years before the Trojan war. He was father of Androgeus, Glaucon, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>; and two daughters, Phaedra, and Ariadne. Many authors have confounded the two Minoes, the grandfather and the grandson; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, Plutarch, and Diodorus, prove plainly that they were two different persons.

MINOTAUR

Pages 318-318

in Fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a celebrated monster, half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and half a bull, according to this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of Ovid, Semibovemque virum, semivirumque bovem. It was the fruit of Pasiphae's amours with a bull. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> refused to sacrifice a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> bull to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, an animal which he had received from the god for that purpose. This offended Neptune, and he made Pasiphae the wife of Minos enamoured of this fine bull, which had been refused to his altars. Daedalus prostituted his talents in being subservient to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s unnatural desires; and by his means, Pasiphae's horrible passions were gratified, and the Minotaur came into the world. Minos confined in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a> this monster, which convinced the world of his wife's lasciviousness, and reflected disgrace upon his family. The Minotaur usually devoured the choicest young men and maidens which the tyranny of Minos yearly exacted from the Athenians. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a> delivered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from this tribute, when it had fallen to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> to be sacrificed to the voracity of the Minotaur; and by means of Ariadne, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, he destroyed the monster, and made his escape from the windings of the labyrinth.—The fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the Minotaur, and of the infamous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Pasiphae with a favourite bull, has been often explained. Some suppose that Pasiphae was enamoured of one of her husband's courtiers called Taurus; and that Daedalus favoured the passions of the queen, by suffering his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> to become the retreat of the two lovers. Pasiphae some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after brought twins into the world, one of whom greatly resembled Minos and the other Taurus; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> resemblance of their countenance with that of their supposed fathers, originated their name, and consequently the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the Minotaur.

MINSTER

Pages 318-318

(Saxon, Mynster <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mynstre), anciently signified the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> or convent.

MINSTREL

Pages 318-320

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for a singer and instrumental performer. The word minstrel is derived from the French menestrier, and was not in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> here before the Norman conquest. It is remarkable, that our old monkish historians do not use the words citharodus, cantator, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, to express a minstrel in Latin; but either minus, histrion, joculator, or some other word that implies glee. Hence it should seem that the minstrels set off their singing by mimicry or <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; or, according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, united the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>, poem, and dance. The Saxons as well as the ancient Danes, had been accustomed to hold men of this profession in the highest reverence. Their skill was considered as something divine, their persons were deemed sacred, their attendance was solicited by kings, and they were everywhere loaded with honours and rewards. In short, poets and their art were held among them in that rude admiration which is ever shown by an ignorant people to such as excel them in intellectual accomplishments. When the Saxons were converted to Christianity, in proportion as letters prevailed among them this rude admiration began to abate, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was no longer a peculiar profession. The poet and the minstrel became came two persons. Poetry was cultivated by men of letters indiscriminately, and many of the most popular rhymes were composed amidst the leisure and retirement of monasteries. But the minstrels <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a distinct order of men, and got their livelihood by singing verses to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> at the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. There they were still hospitably and respectfully received, and retained many of the honours shown to their predecessors the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BARDS">Bards</a> and Scalds. And indeed, though some of them only recited the compositions of others, many of them still composed songs themselves; and all of them could probably invent a few stanzas on occasion. There is no doubt but most of the old heroic ballads were produced by this order of men. For although some of the larger metrical romances might come from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of the monks or others, yet the smaller narratives were probably composed by the minstrels who sang them. From the amazing variations which occur in different copies of these old pieces, it is evident they made no scruple to alter each other's productions, and the reciter added or omitted whole stanzas according to his own fancy or convenience. In the early ages, as is hinted above, this profession was held in great reverence among the Saxon tribes, as well as among their Danish brethren. This appears from two remarkable facts in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which show that the same arts of music and song were equally admired among both nations, and that the privileges and honours conferred upon the professors of them were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both; as it is well known their customs, manners, and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, were not in those times very dissimilar. When <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred the Great was desirous to learn the true situation of the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, which had invaded his realm, he assumed the dress and character of a minstrel; and taking his harp, and only one attendant (for in the earliest times it was not unusual for a minstrel to have a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to carry his harp), he went with the utmost security into the Danish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. And though he could not but be known to be a Saxon, the character he had assumed procured him an hospitable reception; he was admitted to entertain the king at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and stand among them <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to contrive that assault which afterwards destroyed them. This was in the year 878. About 65 years after, a Danish king made use of the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> to explore the camp of King Athelstan. With his harp in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and dressed like a minstrel, Anlaf, king of the Danes went among the Saxon tents, and taking his stand near the king's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>, began to play, and was immediately admitted. There he entertained Athelstan and his lords with his singing and his music; and was at length dismissed with an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> reward, though his songs must have discovered him to have been a Dane. Athelstan was saved from the consequences of this stratagem by a soldier, who had observed Anlaf <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> which had been given him, from some scruple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. This occasioned a discovery. From the uniform procedure of both these kings, it is plain that the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of entertainment prevailed among both peoples, and that the minstrel was a privileged character among both. Even as late as the reign of Edward II, the minstrels were easily admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> presence, as appears from a passage in Stow, which also shows the splendour of their appearance. "In the year 1316, Edward II did solemnize his feast of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a> at Westminster, in the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; where sitting royally at the table with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> about him, there entered a woman adorned like a minstrel, fitting on a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> trapped, as minstrels then used, who rode round about the tables, showing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>; and at length came up to the king's table and laid before him a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and forthwith <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> her horse, saluted every one, and departed."—The subject of this letter was a remonstrance to the king on the favours heaped by him on his minions, to the neglect of his knights and faithful servants. The messenger was fain in a minstrel's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, as what would <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> an easy admission; and was a woman concealed under that habit, probably to disarm the king's resentment; for we do not find that any of the real minstrels were of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; and therefore conclude this was only an artful contrivance peculiar to that occasion. In the 4th year of Richard II, John of Gaunt erected at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TETBURY">Tetbury</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of minstrels, with a full power to receive <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> from the men of that profession within five neighbouring counties, to enact laws, and determine their controversies; and to apprehend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> such of them as should refuse to appear at the said court, annually held on the 16th of August. For this they had a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, by which they were empowered to appoint a king of the minstrels with four officers to preside over them. These were every year elected with great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; the whole form of which is described by Dr Plott; in whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, they seem to have become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> musicians. Even so late as the reign of King Henry VIII, the reciters of verses or moral speeches learnt by heart, intruded without ceremony into all companies; not only in taverns, but in the houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> themselves. This we learn from Erasmus, whose argument led him only to describe a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of these men who did not sing their compositions; but the others that did, enjoyed without doubt the same privileges. We find that the minstrels continued <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; in whose time they had lost much of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and were sinking into contempt and neglect. Yet still they sustained a character far superior to anything we can conceive at present of the singers of old ballads. When <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Elizabeth was entertained at Killingworth castle by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> in 1575, among the many devices and pageants which were exhibited for her entertainment, one of the personages introduced was that of an ancient minstrel, whose appearance and dress are so minutely described by a writer there present, and gives us so distinct an idea of the character, that we shall quote the passage at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. "A person very meet seemed he for the purpose, of a xlv. years old, appareled partly as he would himself. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> off: his head seemingly rounded toisterwife: fair kembed, that, with a sponge daintly diet in a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPON">capon</a>'s grease, was finely smoothed, to make it shine like a mallard's wing. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> snugly. Minstrel, shaven: and yet his thirst after the new trink, with ruffs fair starched, flecked, and glittering like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of new shoes, marhalled in good order with a setting stick, and strut, 'that every ruff stood up like a wafer. A side [i.e. long] <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> of Kendale green, after the freshness of the year now, gathered at the neck with a narrow gorget, fastened afore with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> clasp and a keeper <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> up to the chin; but easily, for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, to undo when he lift. Seemingly begun in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> caddis girdle: from that a pair of capped <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a> knives hanging a' two sides. Out of his bosom drawn from a lappet of his napkin edged with a blue <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, and marked with a D for Damian; for he was but a bachelor yet. "His gown had side [i.e. long] sleeves down to midlegs, slit from the shoulder to the hand, and lined with white cotton. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLET">doublet</a> sleeves of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> worsted: upon them a pair of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of tawny chamlet laced along the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a> with blue threaden pointes. A wealt towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>-a-napes. A pair of red neather stocks. A pair of pumps on his feet, with a crofs cut at his toes for corns; not new indeed, yet cleanly blackt with foot, and shining as a foaming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>. "About his neck a red ribband suitable to his girdle. His harp in good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> dependent before him. His wrest tied to a green lace and hanging by: under the gorget of his gown a fair flaggon chain (<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> for) silver, as a Squire Minstrel of Middlefex, that travelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, unto fair and worshipful men's houses. From his chain hung a festcheon, with metal and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, resplendent upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, of the ancient arms of Illington." —This minstrel is described as belonging to that village. We suppose such as were retained by noble families wore their arms hanging down by a silver chain as a kind of badge. From the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of Squire Minstrel above, we may conclude there were other inferior orders, as Yeomen Minstrels or the like. This minstrel, the author tells us a little below, "after three lowly courtesses, cleared his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> with a hem... and wiped his lips with the hollow of his hand for 'filing his napkin; tempered a string or two with his wrist'; and, after a little warbling on his harp for a prelude, came forth with a solemn song, warranted for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> out of King <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>'s acts, &c." Towards the end of the 16th century, this class of men had lost all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, and were sunk so low in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that in the 39th year of Elizabeth a statute was passed by which "minstrels," wandering abroad, were included among "rogues, vagabonds, and sturdy beggars," and were adjudged to be punished as such. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> seems to have put an end to the profession, for after this time they are no longer mentioned.

MINT

Pages 320-321

the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is coined. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COINAGE">COINAGE</a>. There were anciently mints in almost every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in England; but the only mint at present in the British dominions is that in the Tower of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The officers of the mint are, 1. The warden of the mint, who is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; he oversees the other officers, and receives the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULLION">bullion</a>. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> worker, who receives bullion from the wardens, causes it to be melted, delivers it to the moneyers, and, when it is coined, receives it again. 3. The comptroller, who is the overseer of all the inferior officers, and sees that all the money is made to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> assize. 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSAY">assay</a> master, who weighs the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, and fees that it is according to the standard. 5. The two auditors who take the accounts. 6. The surveyor of the melting; who, after the assay master has made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of the bullion, fees that it is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out, and not altered after it is delivered to the melter. 7. The engraver; who engravés the stamps and dies for the coining of the money. 8. The clerk of the irons; who fees that the irons are clean and fit to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> with. 9. The melter, who melts the bullion before it be coined. 10. The provost of the mint; who provides for and oversees all the moneyers. 11. The blanchers, who anneal and cleanse the money. 12. The moneyers; some of whom forge the money, some share it, some round and mill it, and some stamp and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> it. 13. The porters who keep the gate of the mint. Mint was also a pretended place of privilege, in Southwark, near the King's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, put <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by statute. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any persons, within the limits of the mint, shall obstruct any officer in the serving of any writ <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, &c. or assault any person therein, so as he receive any bodily hurt, the offender shall be guilty of felony, and be transported to the plantations, &c. Stat. 9 Geo. I. MINT MARKS. It hath been usual, from old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, to oblige the masters and workers of the mint, in the indentures made with them, "to make a privy mark in all the money that they make, as well of gold as of silver, so that another time they might know, if need were, and witte which moneys of gold and silver among other of the same moneys, were of their own making, and which not." And whereas, after every trial of the pix at Westminster, the masters and workers of the mint, having there proved their moneys to be lawful and good, were immediately entitled to receive their quietus under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, and to be discharged from all suits or actions concerning those moneys, it was then usual for the said masters and workers to change the privy mark before used for another, that so the moneys from which they were not yet discharged might be distinguished from those for which they had already received their quietus: which new mark they then <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to stamp upon all their moneys, until another trial of the pix gave them also their quietus concerning those. The pix is a strong box with three locks, whose keys are respectively kept by the warden, master, and comptroller of the mint; and in which are deposited, sealed up in several parcels, certain pieces taken at random out of every journey as it is called; that is, out of every 15 pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of gold, or 60 pounds weight of silver, before the same is delivered to the proprietors. And this pix is, from time to time, by the king's command, opened at Westminster, in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, the lords commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, the justices of the several benches, and the barons of the exchequer; before whom a trial is made, by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> of goldsmiths impannelled and sworn for that purpose, of the collective weights of certain parcels of the several pieces of gold and silver taken at random from those contained in the pix; after which those parcels being severally melted, assays are then made of the bullion. bullion of gold and silver so produced, by the melting certain small quantities of the same against equal weights taken from the respective trial pieces of gold and silver that are deposited and kept in the exchequer for that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. This is called the trial of the pix; the report made by the jury upon that trial is called the verdict of the pix for that time; and the indented trial pieces just above mentioned, are certain plates of standard gold and standard silver, made with the greatest care, and delivered in upon oath, from time to time as there is occasion, by a jury of the most able and experienced goldsmiths, summoned by virtue of a warrant from the lords of the treasury to the wardens of the mystery of goldsmiths of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London for that purpose; and which plates being so delivered in, are divided each, at this time, into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> parts by indentures, one of which parts is kept in his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of exchequer at Westminster, another by the said <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of goldsmiths, and two more by the officers of his majesty's mint in the Tower; the remaining three being for the use of the mint, &c., in Scotland. The pix has sometimes been tried every year, or even oftener, but sometimes not more than once in several years: and from hence is understood how it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, that, among the pieces that are dated as well as marked, three or more different dates are sometimes found upon pieces impressed with the same mark: and again, that different marks are found upon pieces <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>. These marks are first observable upon the coins of King Edward III.; the words above quoted concerning those marks are from the indentures made with the lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HASTINGS">Hastings</a>, master and worker to King Edward IV.; and the marks themselves continued to be stamped very conspicuously upon the moneys, till the coinage by the mill and screw was introduced and settled after the Restoration, in the year 1662; since which time, the moneys being made with far greater regularity and exactness than before, these marks have either been totally laid aside, or such only have been used as are of a more secret <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and only known to the officers and engravers concerned in the coinage: and indeed the constant practice that has ever since prevailed, of dating all the several pieces, has rendered all such marks of much less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> than before. MINT. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTHA">MENTHA</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">MATERIA MEDICA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MINTURNÆ, a town of Campania, between Sineuella and Formiae. It was in the marshes in this neighbourhood that Marius concealed himself in the mud to avoid the partizans of Sylla. The people condemned him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but when his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> alone had terrified the executioner, they showed themselves compassionate and favoured his escape.

MINUET

Pages 321-321

a very graceful kind of dance, consisting of a coupee, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> step, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>: it begins with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is triple. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the minuet seems generally to be ascribed to the French, and particularly to the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Poitou. The word is said by Menage and Furetiere to be derived from the French menue <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> menu, "small or little;" and in strictness signifies a small space. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> of this dance consists of two strains, which, as being repeated, are called reprises, each having eight or more bars, but never an odd <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> is three crotchetts in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and is thus marked $\frac{3}{4}$, though it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> performed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> $\frac{4}{4}$. Walther speaks of a minuet in Lully's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> of Roland, each strain of which contains ten bars, the sectional number being 5; which renders it very difficult to dance.

MINUTE

Pages 321-321

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, usually denotes the 60th, sometimes the 30th, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a module. See ARCHITECTURE. Minute is also used for a short memoir, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sketch of a thing taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. MINUTUS FELIX. See Felix. MINYÆ, a name given to the inhabitants of Orchomenos in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, from Minyas <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Orchomenos the son of Minyas gave his name to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the country; and the inhabitants still retained their original appellation, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the Orchomenians of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. A colony of Orchomenians passed into Thessaly and settled in Iolchos; from which circumstance the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and particularly the Argonauts, were called Minyæ. This name they received, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some, not because a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Orchomenians had fettled among them, but because the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and noblest of them were descended from the daughters of Minyas. Part of the Orchomenians accompanied the sons of Codrus when they migrated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>. The descendants of the Argonauts, as well as the Argonauts themselves, received the name of Minyæ. They first inhabited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a>, where they had been born from the Lemnian women who had murdered their husbands. They were driven from Lemnos by the Pelagi, about 1160 before the Christian era, and came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, from whence they passed into Calliste with a colony of Lacedaemonians.

MIRACLE

Pages 321-326

in its original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is a word of the same import with wonder; but in its usual and more appropriate signification, it denotes "an effect contrary to the established <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and course of things, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a sensible deviation from the known laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>." That the visible world is governed by stated general rules, or that there is an order of causes and effects established in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the system of nature which falls under our observation, is a fact which cannot be controverted. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the Supreme Being, as some have supposed, be the only real <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in the universe, we have the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that, in the particular system to which we belong, he acts by stated rules. If he employs inferior agents to conduct the various motions from which the phenomena result, we have the same evidence that he has subjected ed those agents to certain fixed laws, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the laws of nature. On either <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, effects which are produced by the regular operation of these laws, or which are conformable to the established course of events, are properly called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; and every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to this constitution of the natural system, and the correspondent course of events in it, is called a miracle. If this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a miracle be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, no event can be deemed miraculous merely because it is strange, or even to us unaccountable; since it may be nothing more than a regular effect of some unknown <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nature. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> earthquakes are rare; and for monstrous births perhaps no particular and satisfactory account can be given: yet an earthquake is as regular an effect of the established laws of nature as any of those with which we are most intimately acquainted; and under circumstances in which there would always be the same kind of production, the monster is nature's genuine illuse. It is therefore necessary, before we can pronounce any effect to be a true miracle, that the circumstances under which it is produced be known, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> course of nature be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> understood; for in all those <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which we are totally ignorant of nature, it is impossible to determine what is, or what is not, a deviation from its course. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>, therefore, are not, as some have represented them, appeals to our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. They suppose some antecedent knowledge of the course of nature, without which no proper judgment can be formed concerning them; though with it their reality may be so apparent as to prevent all possibility of a dispute. Thus, were a physician to cure a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a cataract, by anointing his eyes with a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> which we had never before seen, and to the nature and effects of which we are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> strangers, the cure would undoubtedly be wonderful; but we could not pronounce it miraculous, because, for anything known to us, it might be the natural effect of the operation of the unguent on the eye. But were he to recover his patient merely by commanding him to see, or by anointing his eyes with spittle, we should with the utmost confidence pronounce the cure to be a miracle; because we know perfectly that neither the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> nor human spittle have, by the established constitution of things, any such power over the diseases of the eye. No one is now ignorant, that persons apparently dead are often restored to their families and friends, by being treated in the manner recommended by the Humane <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. To the vulgar, and sometimes even to men of science, these effects appear very wonderful; but as they are known to be produced by physical agency, they can never be considered as miraculous deviations from the laws of nature. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, no one could doubt of his having witnessed a real miracle who had seen a person that had been four days dead come alive out of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> at the call of another, or who had even beheld a person exhibiting all the symptoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> instantly resuscitated merely by being desired to live. Thus easy is it, in all cases in which the course of nature is understood, to determine whether any particular event be really a miracle; whilst in circumstances where we know nothing of nature and its course, even a true miracle, were it performed, could not be admitted as such, or carry any conviction to the mind of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. If miracles be effects contrary to the established constitution of things, we are certain that they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be performed on trivial occasions.
