But as all the candidates for initiation might not aspire to the rank of heroes and demigods, a more easy and a more attainable mode of conduct, in order to arrive at the palace of happiness, behoved to be opened. Private virtues were inculcated, and these too were to meet a condign reward. But alas! this present life is too often a chequered scene, where virtue is depressed and trodden under foot, and vice lifts up its head and rides triumphant. It is a dictate of common sense, that virtue should sooner or later emerge, and vice sink into contempt and misery. Here then the conductors of the mysteries, properly and naturally, adopted the doctrine of a future state of rewards and punishments. The dogma of the immortality of the human soul was elucidated, and carefully and pathetically inculcated. This doctrine was likewise imported from Egypt; for Herodotus informs us, "that the Egyptians were the first people who maintained the immortality of the human soul." The Egyptian immortality, however, according to him, was only the metempsychosis or transmigration of souls. This was not the system of the ancient Egyptians, nor indeed of the teletæ. In these, a metempsychosis was admitted; but that was carried forward to a very distant period, to wit, to the grand Egyptian period of 36,000 years. As the mystagogues well knew that the human mind is more powerfully affected by objects presented to the eyes than by the most engaging instructions conveyed by the ear, they made the emblems of Elysium and Tartarus pass in review before the eyes of their novices. There the Elysian scenes, so nobly described by the Roman poet, appeared in mimic splendour; and, on the other hand, the gloom of Tartarus, Charon's boat, the dog of hell, the Furies with tresses of snakes, the tribunal of Minos and Rhadamanthus, &c., were displayed in all their terrific state. Tantalus, Ixion, Sisyphus, the daughters of Danaus, &c., were represented in pageants before their eyes. These exhibitions were accompanied with most horrible cries and howlings, thunders, lightnings, and other objects of terror which we shall mention in their proper place. No contrivance could be better accommodated to animate the pupils to the practice of virtue on the one hand, or to deter them from indulging vicious passions on the other. It resembled opening heaven and hell to a hardened sinner. The practices inculcated in celebrating the mysteries are too numerous to be detailed in this imperfect sketch. The worship of the gods was strictly enjoined, as has been shown above. The three laws generally ascribed to Triptolemus were inculcated, 1. To honour their parents; 2. To honour the gods with the first fruits of the earth; 3. Not to treat brute animals with cruelty. These laws were imported from Egypt, and were communicated to the Eleusinians by the original missionaries. Cicero makes the civilization of mankind one of the most beneficial effects of the Eleusinian institutions: "Nullum mihi, cum multo eximia divinaque videtur Athenae tuae perifisse; tum nihil melius illis mysteriis, quibus ex agresti immanique vita, exculti ad humanitatem, et mitigati fumus; initiaque, ut appellantur, ita revera principia vitae cognovimus; neque folum cum leetitia vivendi rationem accipimus, fed etiam cum spe meliore moriendi." Hence it is evident that the precepts of humanity and morality were warmly recommended in these institutions. The virtue of humanity was extended, one may say, even to the brute creation, as appears from the last of Triptolemus's laws above quoted. Some articles were enjoined in the teletæ which may appear to us of less importance, which, however, in the symbolical style of the Egyptians, were abundantly significant. The initiated were commanded to abstain from the flesh of certain birds and fishes; from beans, from pomegranates and apples, which were deemed equally polluting. It was taught, that to touch the plant of asparagus was as dangerous as the most deadly poison. Now, says Porphyry, whoever is versed in the history of the visions, knows for what reason they were commanded to abstain from the flesh of birds." The initiated then bound themselves by dreadful oaths to observe most conscientiously and to practise every tied bond precept tendered to them in the course of the teletæ; by oaths and at the same time never to divulge one article of observe the all that had been heard or seen by them upon that occasion. In this they were exceedingly jealous, that the mysteries of Æschylus the tragedian was in danger of capital punishment, for having only alluded to one of the Eleusinian arcana in a tragedy of his; and one of the articles of indictment against Diagoras the Melian was, his having spoken disrespectfully of the mysteries, and diffused people from partaking of them. It must then be allowed, that the institution of the mysteries was of infinite advantage to the Pagan world. They were indeed a kind of sacraments, by which the initiated bound themselves by a solemn vow to practise piety towards the gods, justice and humanity towards their fellow men, and gentleness and tenderness towards the inoffensive part of the brute creation. The Pagans themselves were so thoroughly convinced of this fact, that in their disputes with the apologists for Christianity, they often appealed to the teletæ, and contrasted their maxims with the most sublime doctrines of that heavenly institution. In order to impress these maxims the more deeply upon the minds of the novices, and to fix their attention more steadfastly upon the lectures which were delivered them by the mystagogue or the sacred herald, a mechanical operation was played off at proper intervals during the course of the celebration. "Towards the end of the celebration (says Stobaeus), the whole scene is terrible; all is trembling, shuddering, sweat, and astonishment. Many horrible spectres are seen, horrible and strange cries and howlings uttered. Light succeeds darkness; and again the blackest darkness most glaring light. Now appear open plains, flowery meadows, and waving groves; where are seen dances and bated choruses; and various holy phantasies enchant the flight. Melodious notes are heard from far, with all the sublime symphony of the sacred hymns. The pupil now is completely perfect, is initiated, becomes free, released, and walks about with a crown on his head, and is admitted to bear a part in the sacred rites." Arriades de Myt. Eleus. calls Eleusis "a kind of temple of the whole earth, and of all that man beholds done in the most dreadful and the most exhilarating manner. In what other place have the records of fable sung of things more marvellous? or in what region upon earth have the objects presented to the eye borne a more exact resemblance to the sounds which strike the ear? What object of sight have the numberless generations of men and women beheld comparable to these exhibited in the ineffable mysteries?" To the same purpose, Pletho, in the oracles of Zoroasteres, informs us, "that frightful and shocking apparitions, in a variety of forms, used to be displayed to the mystae in the course of their initiation." And a little after, he adds, "that thunder and lightning and fire, and every thing terrible which might be held symbolical of the divine presence, were introduced." Claudian, in his poem *De Raptu Proserpina*, gives an elegant, though brief, description of this phenomenon, which throws some light on the passages above quoted. *Jam mihi cernuntur trepidis delubra moveri* *Satibus et clarum dis pergere culmina lucem,* *Adventum teftata Dea, jam magnus ab imis* *Auditur fremitus terris, templumque renuit* *Cecropidum.* The sight of those appearances was called the *Antopia*, or "the real presence:" hence those rites were sometimes called *Epoptica*. The *Epoptae* were actually initiated, and were admitted into the *Sanctum Sanctorum*, and bore a part in the ceremonial; whereas the *mylæ*, who had only been initiated in the lesser mysteries at Agrae, were obliged to take their station in the porch of the temple. The candidates for initiation bathed themselves in holy water, and put on new clothes, all of linen, which they continued to wear till they were quite torn, and then they were consecrated to Ceres and Proserpine. From the ceremony of bathing they were denominated *Hydræ*; and this again was a kind of baptismal ablution. Whether the phrases of *washing away sin, putting on the Lord Jesus Christ, putting off the old man with his deeds, putting on a robe of righteousness, being buried in baptism*, the words *mystery, perfect, perfection*, which occur so frequently in the New Testament, especially in the writings of the apostle St Paul, are borrowed from the Pagan mysteries, or from usages current among the Jews, we leave to our more learned readers to determine. The *Epoptae* having sustained all those fiery trials, heard and seen every thing requisite, taken upon them the vows and engagements above narrated, and, in a word, having shown themselves good soldiers of Ceres and Proserpine, were now declared *perfect men*. They might, like Cebes's *virtuous man*, travel wherever they chose; those wild beasts (the human passions) which tyrannise over the rest of mankind, and often destroy them, had no longer dominion over them. They were now not only *perfect* but *regenerated* men. They were now crowned with laurel, as was said above, and dismissed with two barbarous words, *κορυφαίους, κορυφαῖοι*, of which perhaps the hierophants themselves did not comprehend the import. They had been introduced by the first Egyptian missionaries, and retained in the sacra after their signification was lost. This was a common practice among the Greeks. In the administration of their religious ceremonies, they retained many names of persons, places, things, customs, &c. which had been introduced by the Phoenicians and Egyptians, from whom they borrowed their system of idolatry. These terms constituted the language of the gods, so often mentioned by the prince of poets. To us the words in question appear to be Syriac, and to signify, *Be vigilant, be innocent*. Numerous and important were the advantages supposed to redound to the initiated, from their being admitted to partake of the mysteries, both in this life and that which is to come. Firstly, They were highly honoured, and even revered by their contemporaries. Indeed, they were looked up to as a kind of sacred persons: they were, in reality, consecrated to Ceres and Proserpine. Secondly, They were obliged by their oath to practise every virtue, religious, moral, political, public, and private. Thirdly, They imagined, that found advice and happy measures of conduct were suggested to the initiated by the Eleusinian goddesses. Accordingly, says Pericles the celebrated Athenian statesman, "I am convinced, that the deities of Eleusis inspired me with this sentiment, and that this stratagem was suggested by the principle of the mystic rites." There is a beautiful passage in Aristophanes's *comedy of the Aetæ*, Ranæ to the very same purpose, of which we shall subjoin the following periphrasis. It is sung by the chorus of the initiated. Let us to flow'ry meads repair, With deathless roses blooming, Whose balmy sweets impregn the air, Both hills and dales perfuming. Since fate benign our choir has join'd, We'll trip in mystic measure; In sweetest harmony combin'd We'll quaff full draughts of pleasure. For us alone the pow'r of day A milder light dispenses; And theds benign a mellow'd ray To cheer our ravish'd senses: For we beheld the mystic show, And brav'd Eleusis' dangers. We do and know the deeds we owe To neighbours, friends, and strangers. Euripides, in his *Bacchæ* (E), introduces the chorus extolling the happiness of those who had been acquainted with God, by participating in the holy mysteries, and whose minds had been enlightened by the mystical rites. They boast, "that they had led a holy and unblemished life, from the time that they had been initiated in the sacred rites of Jupiter Ideus, and from the time that they had relinquished celebrating the nocturnal rites of Bacchus, and the banquets of raw flesh torn off living animals." To this sanctity of life they had no doubt engaged themselves, when they were initiated in the mysteries of that god. The Eleusinian *Epoptae* derived the same advantages from their sacramental engagements. Fourthly, The initiated were imagined to be the peculiar wards of the Eleusinian goddesses. These deities were supposed to watch over them, and often to avert impending danger, and to rescue them when beset with troubles.—Our readers will not imagine that the initiated reaped much benefit from the protection of his Eleusinian tutelary deities; but it was sufficient that they believed...

MITHRIDATE

Pages 333-333

an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>; an antidote, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in form of an electuary, supposed to serve either as a remedy or a preferative against poisons. It takes its name from the inventor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pontus, who is said to have fortified his body against poisons with antidotes and preferatives, that when he had a mind to dispatch himself, he could not find any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> that would take effect.

MITHRIDATES VII

Pages 333-335

surnamed Eupator and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, succeeded to the throne at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 11 years, about 123 years before the Christian era. The beginning of his reign was marked by ambition, cruelty, and artifice. He murdered his own mother, who had been left by his father co-heirless of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and he fortified his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> by drinking antidotes against the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> with which his enemies at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> attempted to destroy him. He early incurred his body to hardship, and employed himself in the most manly exercises, often remaining whole months in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and making frozen snow and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his repose. Naturally ambitious and cruel, he spared no pains to acquire himself power and dominion. He murdered the two sons whom his father Laodice had had by Ariarathes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Cappadocia, and placed one of his own children, only eight years old, on the vacant throne. These violent proceedings alarmed Nicomedes king of Bithynia, who had married Laodice the widow of Ariarathes. He suborned a youth to be king of Cappadocia, as the third son of Ariarathes; and Laodice was sent to Rome to implore upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and assure them that her third son was now alive, and that his pretensions to the kingdom of Cappadocia were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and well grounded. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, on his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, sent to Rome Gordius the governor of his son; who solemnly declared before the Roman people, that the youth who sat on the throne of Cappadocia was the third son and lawful heir of Ariarathes, and that he was supported as such by Mithridates. This intricate affair displeased the Roman senate; and finally to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the dispute they took away the kingdom of Cappadocia from Mithridates, and Paphlagonia from Nicomedes. These two kingdoms being thus separated from their original possessors, were presented with their freedom and independence; but the Cappadocians refused it, and received Ariobarzanes for king. Such were the first seeds of enmity between Rome and the king of Pontus. Mithridates never lost an opportunity by which he might lessen the influence of his adversaries; and the more effectually to destroy their power in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, he ordered all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> that were in his dominions to be massacred. This was done in one night, and no less than 150,000, according to Plutarch, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 80,000 Romans, as Appian mentions, were made the victims of his cruelty. This called aloud for vengeance. Aulicus, and soon after Sylla, marched against Mithridates with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The former was made prisoner; but Sylla obtained a victory over the king's generals; and another decisive engagement rendered him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. This ill fortune was aggravated by the loss of about 200,000 men, who were killed in the several engagements that had been fought; and Mithridates, weakened by repeated ill success by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, sued for peace from the conqueror, which he obtained on condition of defraying the expenses which the Romans had incurred by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and of remaining satisfied with the possessions which he had received from his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. While these negotiations of peace were carried on, Mithridates was not unmindful of his real <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. His poverty, and not his inclinations, obliged him to wish for peace. He immediately took the field with an army of 140,000 infantry, and 16,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, which consisted of his own forces and those of his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> Tigranes king of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>. With such a numerous army he soon made himself master of the Roman provinces in Asia; none dared to oppose his conquests; and the Romans, relying on his fidelity, had withdrawn the greatest part of their armies from the country. The news of his warlike preparations were no sooner heard, than Lucullus the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> marched into Asia; and without delay he blocked up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of Mithridates who was then besieging Cyzicus. The Asiatic monarch escaped from him, and fled into the heart of his kingdom. Lucullus pursued him with the utmost celerity; and would have taken him prisoner after a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, had not the avidity of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> preferred the plundering of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to the taking of a monarch who had exercised such cruelties against their countrymen, and shown himself so faithless to the most solemn engagements. After this escape Mithridates was more careful about the safety of his person; and he even ordered his wives and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> to destroy themselves, fearful of their falling into the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The appointment of Gaius to the command of the Roman forces, instead of Lucullus, was favourable to Mithridates, who recovered the greatest part of his dominions. The sudden arrival of Pompey, however, soon put an end to his victories. A battle in the night was fought near the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, in which the troops of Pontus laboured under every disadvantage. The engagement was by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and as the moon then shone in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the enemy, the lengthened shadows of the arms of the Romans having induced Mithridates to believe that the two armies were <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together, the arrows of his soldiers were darted from a great distance, and their efforts rendered ineffectual. An universal overthrow ensued, and Mithridates, bold in his misfortunes, rushed through the thick ranks of the enemy at the head of 800 horsemen, 500 of whom perished in the attempt to follow him. He fled to Tigranes; but that monarch refused an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to his father-in-law, whom he had before supported with all the collected forces of his kingdom. Mithridates found a safe retreat among the Scythians; and though destitute of power, friends, and resources, yet he meditated the overthrow of the Roman empire, by penetrating into the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by land. These wild projects were rejected by his followers, and he sued for peace. It was denied to his ambassadors; and the victorious Pompey declared, that, to obtain it, Mithridates must ask it in person. He scorned to trust himself in the hands of his enemy, and resolved to conquer or to die. His subjects refused to follow him any longer; and revolting from him, made his son Pharnaces king. The son showed himself ungrateful to his father; and even, according to some writers, he ordered him to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This unnatural treatment broke the heart of Mithridates; he obliged his wife to poison herself, and attempted to do the same himself. It was in vain; the frequent antidotes he had taken in the early part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, strengthened his constitution against the poison; and when this was unavailing, he attempted to stab himself. The blow was not mortal; and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> who was then present, at his own request, gave him the fatal stroke, about 64 years before the Christian era. Such were the misfortunes, abilities, and miserable end, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who supported himself so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> against the power of Rome, and who, according to the declarations of the Roman authors, proved a more powerful and indefatigable adversary to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Italy than the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, Pyrrhus, Perseus, or Antiochus. Mithridates has been commended for his eminent virtues, and censured for his vices. As a commander he deserves the most unbounded applause; and it may create admiration to see him waging war with such success, during so many years, against the most powerful people on earth, led to the field by a Sylla, a Lucullus, and a Pompey. He was the greatest monarch that ever sat on a throne, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Cicero; and indeed no greater <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> character can be brought, than the mention of the great rejoicings which happened in the Roman armies and in the capital at the news of his death. No less than 12 weeks were appointed for public thanksgivings to the immortal gods; and Pompey, who had sent the first intelligence of his death to Rome, and who had partly hastened his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, was rewarded with the most uncommon honours. It is said that Mithridates conquered 24 nations, whose different languages he knew and spoke with the same ease and fluency as his own. As a man of letters he also deserves <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He was acquainted with the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and even wrote in that dialect a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. His skill in physic is well known; and even now there is a celebrated antitode which bears his name, and is called mithridate. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a> as well as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> nature had united to render him great; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we rely upon the authority of Justin, his birth was accompanied by the appearance of two large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a>, which were seen for 70 days successively, and whose splendour eclipsed the mid-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and covered the fourth part of the heavens.

MITHRIDATICUM BELLUM

Pages 335-335

the *Mithridatic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>*, one of the longest and most celebrated wars ever carried on by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> against a foreign power. See *Pontus*.

MITRA

Pages 335-335

was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covering for the head, worn by the Roman ladies, and sometimes by the men; but it was looked upon as a mark of effeminacy in the laft, especially when it was tied upon their heads.

MITRE

Pages 335-335

in *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>*, is the workmen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> that is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> 45 degrees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> one. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the angle be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a right angle, they call it a *half mitre*. To describe such <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, they have an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called the *mitre <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>*; with this they strike mitre <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> or battens; and for dispatch, they have a *mitre box*, as they call it, which is made of two pieces of wood, each about an inch thick, one nailed upright on the edge of the other; the upper piece hath the mitre lines struck upon it on both sides, and a kerf to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the mitre <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> readily, by only applying the piece into this box. **MITRE** is used by the writers of the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for a fort of base <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which was very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> there about the year 1270, and for 30 years before and as many after. There were besides the mitre several other pieces, called, according to the figures impressed upon them, rofaries, lionades, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, and by the like names. They were imported from France and other countries, and were so much below the proper currency of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, that they were not worth so much as a halfpenny each. They were at length decried in the year 1300, and good coins struck in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. There were the first Irish coins in which the sceptre was left out. They were struck in the reign of Edward, the son of our Henry III, and are still found among the other antiquities of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They have the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s head in a triangle full faced. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, when well preserved, weighs 22 grains; the halfpenny 10½ grains.

MITTAU

Pages 335-335

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>. It is strongly fortified; but was taken by the Swedes in 1701, and by the Muscovites in 1706. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° 51'. N. Lat. 56° 44'.

MITTIMUS

Pages 335-335

as generally used, hath two significations. 1. It signifies a writ for removing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transferring of records from one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to another. 2. It signifies a precept, or command in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, directed to the gaoler or keeper of some prison, for the receiving and safe keeping of an offender <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with any crime, until he be delivered by due course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

MITYLENE

Pages 335-335
or **MYTELENE**, in *Ancient Geography*, a celebrated, powerful, and affluent city, capital of the island of Lesbos. It received its name from Mitylene, the daughter of Macareus, a king of the country. It is greatly commended by the ancients for the flatnesses of its buildings and the fruitfulness of its soil, but more particularly for the great men it produced: Pithecus, Alcaeus, Sappho, Terpander, Theophanes, Hellenicus, &c. were all natives of Mitylene. It was long a seat of learning; and, with Rhodes and Athens, it had the honour of having educated many of the great men of Rome and Greece. In the Peloponnesian war, the Mitylenians suffered greatly for their revolt from the power of Athens; and in the Mithridatic wars, they had the boldness to resist the Romans, and disdain the treaties which had been made between Mithridates and Sylla. See *Metelin*.

MIXTURE

Pages 335-335

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblage of several different bodies in the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. Chemical mixture is attended with many phenomena which are never observed in simple mixtures; such as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, effervescence, &c. To chemical mixture belong the union of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, the amalgamation of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, solution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, &c. and upon it depend many of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> operations of *<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>*. See that article, *puifum*. **Mixture**, in *<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>*, a medicine which differs from a julep in this respect, that it receives into its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> not only salts, extracts, and other substances dissoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but also earths, powders, and such substances as cannot be dissolved.

MIZEN

Pages 335-335

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is a particular mast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sail. The mizen mast stands in the sternmost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship. In some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ships there are two of these; when that next the mainmast is called the *main-mizen*, and that next the poop the *bonaventure mizen*.

MIZRAIM

Pages 335-335
or **MISRAIM**, the dual name of Egypt, used in Scripture to denote the Higher and Lower Egypt, which see. It sometimes occurs singular, *Mazor*: 2 Kings xix. Isaiah xix. Micah vii.

MNEMOSYNE

Pages 335-335

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Coelus and Terra. She married <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, by whom she had the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>. The word *mnemosyne* signifies "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>;" and therefore the poets have rightly called Memory the mother of the Muses, because it is to that mental endowment that mankind are indebted for their progress in science.

MNIUM

Pages 335-335

*Marshmoss*; a genus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of musci, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See *<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*.

MOAB

Pages 335-336

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea; so called from Moab the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, to whose posterity this country was allotted by divine appointment, Deut. xi. 9. It was originally occupied by the Emim, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of giants extirpated by the Moabites, *ibid*. Moab anciently lay to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, before Sihon the Amorite stripped both nations of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their territory, afterwards occupied by the Israelites, Numb. xxi.; and then Moab was bounded by the river Arnon to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the Lacus <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a> to the west, the brook Zared to the south, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> Abarim to the east.

MOAT

Pages 336-336
or DITCH, in Fortification, a deep trench dug round the rampart of a fortified place, to prevent surprieses. The brink of the moat, next the rampart, is called the carpe; and the opposite one, the counter-carpe. A dry moat round a large place, with a strong garrison, is preferable to one full of water; because the pallage may be disputed inch by inch, and the besiegers, when lodged in it, are continually exposed to the bombs, grenades, and other fire works, which are thrown incessantly from the rampart into their works. In the middle of dry moats, there is sometimes another small one, called cunette; which is generally dug so deep till they find water to fill it. The deepest and broadest moats are accounted the best; but a deep one is preferable to a broad one: the ordinary breadth is about 20 fathoms, and the depth about 16. To drain a moat that is full of water, they dig a trench deeper than the level of the water, to let it run off; and then throw hurdles upon the mud and slime, covering them with earth or bundles of rushes, to make a sure and firm pallage.

MOATAZALITES

Pages 336-336
or Separatists, a religious sect among the Turks, who deny all forms and qualities in the Divine Being; or who divest God of his attributes. There are two opinions among the Turkish divines concerning God. The first admits metaphysical forms or attributes; as, that God has wisdom, by which he is wise; power, by which he is powerful; eternity, by which he is eternal, &c. The second allows God to be wise, powerful, eternal; but will not allow any form or quality in God, for fear of admitting a multiplicity. Those who follow this latter opinion are called Moatazalites; they who follow the former, Sephaties. The Moatazalites also believed that the word of God was created in subjecto, as the schoolmen term it, and to consist of letters and sound; copies thereof being written in books to express or imitate the original: they denied absolute predestination, and affirmed that man is a free agent. This sect is said to have first invented the scholastic divinity, and is subdivided into no less than 20 inferior sects, which mutually brand one another with infidelity.

MOBILE

Pages 336-336

Moveable, anything susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is disposed to be moved either by itself or by some other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> mobile or mover. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMUM_MOBILE">Primum Mobile</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, was a ninth heaven or sphere, imagined above those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> and fixed stars. This was supposed to be the first mover, and to carry all the lower spheres round along with it; by its rapidity communicating to them a motion whereby they revolved in 24 hours. But the diurnal revolution of the planets is now accounted for without the affiance of any such primum mobile. Perpetuum Mobile. See Perpetual Motion.

MOCHO

Pages 336-336

Moco, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mocha; by some supposed to be the Mufa or Muza of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, is a port and town on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, of considerable trade; contains about 10,000 inhabitants, Jews, Armenians, and Mohammedans; and it gives name to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> extending along the most southern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; of which that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which lies next the sea is a dry barren <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, in some places 10 or 12 leagues over; but bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which being well watered, enjoy an almost perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and besides coffee, the peculiar produce of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, yields corn, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, frankincense, caffia, balm, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> of several sorts, mangos, dates, pomegranates, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> here is so hot and sultry in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, especially when the south <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, that it would be insupportable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was not mitigated by the cool breezes that generally blow from the mountains on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, or the Red and Arabic seas on the west and east. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in winter is equal to that of our warmest summers; and it is very seldom that either <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> are seen. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mocha is now the emporium for the trade of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> to the Red sea. The trade was removed hither from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the prophecy of a thick, much revered by the people, who foretold that it would soon become a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of extensive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> notwithstanding its disadvantageous situation. The buildings here are lofty, and tolerably regular, having a pleasant aspect from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. The steeples of several mosques are very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, presenting themselves to view at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. Their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are well stored with beef, mutton, lamb, kid, camels, and antelopes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fowls, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> hens, partridges, and pigeons. The sea affords plenty of fish, but not savoury; which some think proceeds from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> saltness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their aliment. The markets are also stocked with fruit, such as grapes, peaches, apricots, quinces, and nectarines; although neither shrub nor tree is to be seen near the town, except a few <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> trees. Frequently no rain falls here in two or three years, and seldom more than a shower or two in a year; but in the mountains, at the distance of about 20 miles from Mocha, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is watered with a gentle shower every morning, which makes the valleys fertile in corn and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The Arab inhabitants, though remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and superstitious, are said to be extremely covetous and hypocritical; robbing, thieving, and committing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>, without the least scruple or remorse. The English and Dutch companies have handsome houses here, and carry on a great trade in coffee, olibanum, myrrh, aloes, liquid storax, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> arenic, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, mummy, balm of Gilead, and other drugs. One inconvenience, however, they sustain from the violence and exactions of the Arabian princes; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s customs are easy, being fixed at three per cent. to Europeans. Of the coins at Mocha, the most current is the camafiee, which rises and falls in value at the banker's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>: they are from 50 to 80 for a current dollar, which is but an imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, being always reckoned one and a half per cent. lower than Spanish dollars. MOCKING <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">BIRD</a>. See Turdus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MOCOCO. See Lemur, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index.

MODE

Pages 336-337

which is a word of the same general import with manner, is used as a technical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>, and music. For its import in Grammar, see that article, No 80. Mode, in Metaphysics, seems properly to denote the manner of a thing's existence; but Locke, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> language in that science is generally adopted, uses the word in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> somewhat different from its ordinary and proper signification. "Such complex <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, which, however compounded, contain not in them the supposition of subsisting by themselves, but are considered as dependencies on, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> affections of, substances," he calls modes. Of these modes, there are, according to him, two sorts, which deserve distinct consideration. First, there are some "which are only variations, or different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of the same simple idea, without the mixture of any other, as a dozen or a score; which are nothing but the ideas of so many distinct units added together;" and these he calls simple modes. Secondly, "There are others compounded of simple ideas of several kinds put together to make one complex one; v.g. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, consisting of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, causing delight in the beholder; theft, which being the concealed change of the possession of anything without the consent of the proprietor, contains, as is visible, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of several ideas of several kinds;" and these he calls mixed modes. For the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> distinction between ideas and notions, as well as between ideas and the qualities of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> objects, which in this account of modes are all confounded together, see Metaphysics. Mode, in Music, a regular disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and accompaniments, relative to certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sounds upon which a piece of music is formed, and which are called the essential sounds of the mode. Our modes are not, like those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, characterized by any sentiment which they tend to excite, but result from our system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> alone. The sounds essential to the mode are in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> three, and form together one perfect chord. 1. The tonic or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> both of the tone and of the mode. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a>, which is a fifth from the tonic. 3. The mediant, which properly constitutes the mode, and which is a third from the same tonic. As this third may be of two kinds, there are of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> two different modes. When the mediant forms a greater third with the tonic, the mode is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>; when the third is lesser, it is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>. See Music.

MODEL

Pages 337-339

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, an original pattern, proposed for any one to copy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> imitate. This word is particularly used, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> pattern made in wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, or other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, with all its parts and proportions, in order for the better conducting and executing some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and to give an idea of the effect it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. In all great buildings, it is much the surest way to make a model in relievo, and not to trust to a bare <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or draught. There are also models for the building of ships, &c. and for extraordinary staircases, &c. They also <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> models in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>; whence, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, they give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> model to a naked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or women, disposed in several postures, to afford an opportunity to the scholars to design them in various views and attitudes. Models in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or artificial substance, are most usually made by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> composed of plaster of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. For the purpose of making these moulds, this kind of plaster is much more fit than any other substance, on account of the power it has of absorbing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and soon condensing into a hard substance, even after it has been rendered so thin as to be of the consistence of cream. This happens in a shorter or longer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as the plaster is of a better or worse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and its good or bad properties depend very much upon its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to which, therefore, particular regard ought to be had. It is sold in the shops at very different prices; the finest being made use of for casts, and the middling sort for moulds. It may be very easily coloured by means of almost any kind of powder excepting what contains an alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; for this would chemically decompose the substance of it, and render it unfit for use. A very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of chalk would also render it soft and useless, but lime hardens it to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The addition of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size will likewise render it much harder than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> water is made use of. In making either moulds or models, however, we must be careful not to make the mixture too thick at first; for if this is done, and more water added to thin it, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> must always prove brittle and of a bad quality. The particular manner of making models (or casts, as they are also called) depends on the form of the subject to be taken. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is easy, where the parts are elevated only in a slight degree, or where they form only a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> surface from which they project; but where the parts project in smaller <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, or form curves inclined towards the principal surface, the work is more difficult. This observation, however, holds good only with regard to hard and inflexible bodies; for such as are soft may often be freed from the mould, even though they have the shape last mentioned. But though this be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the soft original substance, it is not so with the inflexible model when once it is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. The moulds are to be made of various degrees of thickness, according to the size of the model to be cast; and may be from half an inch to an inch, or, if very large, an inch and a half. Where a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of models are to be taken from one mould, it will likewise be necessary to have it of a stronger contexture than where only a few are required, for very obvious reasons. It is much more easy to make a mould for any soft substance than a rigid one, as in any of the viscera of animals; for the fluidity of the mixture makes it easily accommodate itself to the projecting parts of the substance; and as it is necessary to inflate these substances, they may be very readily extracted again by letting out the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> which distended them. When a model is to be taken, the surface of the original is first to be greased, in order to prevent the plaster from sticking to it; but if the substance itself is slippery, as is the case with the internal parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, this need not be done: when necessary, it may be laid over with linseed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> by means of a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. The original is then to be laid on a smooth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, previously greased or covered with a cloth, to prevent the plaster sticking to it; then surround the original with a frame or ridge of glaziers' putty, at such a distance from it as will admit the plaster to rest upon the table on all sides of the subject for about an inch, or as much as is sufficient to give the proper degree of strength to the mould. A sufficient cipient quantity of plaster is then to be poured as uniformly as possible over the whole substance, until it be everywhere covered to such a thickness as to give a proper substance to the mould, which may vary in proportion to the size. The whole must then be suffered to remain in this condition till the plaster has attained its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>; when the frame is taken away, the mould may be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, and the subject removed from it; and when the plaster is thoroughly dry let it be well seasoned. Having formed and seasoned the moulds, they must next be prepared for the casts by greasing the inside of them with a mixture of olive oil and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> in equal parts, and then filled with fine fluid plaster, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the mould formed by its resting on the surface of the table covered to a sufficient thickness with coarse plaster, to form a strong basis or support for the cast where this support is requisite, as is particularly the case where the thin and membranous parts of the body are to be represented. After the plaster is poured into the mould, it must be suffered to stand until it has acquired the greatest degree of hardness it will receive; after which the mould must be removed; but this will be attended with some difficulty when the shape of the subject is unfavourable; and in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the mould must be separated by means of a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a> and chisel. If by these instruments any parts of the model should be broken off, they may be cemented by making the two surfaces to be applied to each other quite wet; then interposing between them a little liquid plaster; and lastly, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> smoothed after being thoroughly dry. Any small holes that may be made in the mould can be filled up with liquid plaster, after the sides of them have been thoroughly wetted, and smoothed over with the edge of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. In many cases it is altogether impracticable to prepare a mould of one piece for a whole subject; and therefore it must be considered how this can be done in such a manner as to divide the mould into the fewest pieces. This may be effected by making every piece cover as much of the pattern as possible, without surrounding such projecting parts, or running into such hollows as would not admit a separation of the mould. It is impossible, however, to give any particular directions in this matter which can hold good in every instance, the number of pieces of which the mould is to consist being always determined from the shape of the pattern. Thus the mould of the human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a> will require no more than three pieces, but that of an os femoris could scarce have fewer than ten or twelve.—Where any internal pieces are required, they are first to be made, and then the outer pieces after the former have become hard. To make a mould upon a hard and dry substance, we must, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, rub the surface of it smoothly over with the mixture of oil and lard above mentioned. Such hollows as require internal pieces are then to be filled up with fluid plaster; and while it continues in this state, a wire loop must be introduced into it, by which, when hardened, it can be pulled off. The plaster should be somewhat raised in a pyramidal form around this wire, and afterwards cut smooth with a knife while yet in its soft state; preserving two or three angular ridges from the loop to the outer edge, that it may fix the more steadily in the outer piece of the mould to be afterwards made upon it. Let the outer piece then be well greased, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> piece from adhering; the loop being enclosed with some glaziers putty, both to prevent the second piece from adhering and to preserve a hollow place for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. To form the second or outside piece, mix a quantity of plaster proportioned to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of surface it is to cover and the intended thickness of the mould; when it is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> beginning to thicken, or assumes such a consistency as not to run off very easily, spread it over the internal piece or pieces as well as the pattern, taking care at the same time not to go too far lest it should not deliver safely; and as the plaster becomes more tenacious, add more upon the pattern until it has become sufficiently thick, keeping the edges <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and smooth like the edge of a board. The plaster should be spread equally upon all parts, which is best done by a painter's pallet knife or apothecary's bolus knife; but for this the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> should be somewhat less pliable than it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made. When the outside piece is hardened, the edges are to be pared smooth, and nearly made square with a small pointed knife. Little holes of a conical shape are to be made with the point of a knife about an inch distant from one another, according to the size of the piece. These are designed to receive the fluid plaster in forming the adjacent parts of the mould, and occasion <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> corresponding to the hollows; and are intended to preserve the edges of the different pieces steadily in their proper relative situations. The third piece is then to be formed in a manner similar to the second; greasing the edges of the former plentifully with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s lard and oil, to prevent the pieces from adhering to each other. Thus the pattern is to be wholly enclosed, only leaving a proper orifice for pouring in the plaster to form the model; small holes being also bored in the mould opposite to the wire-loops fixed in the inside pieces, through which a cord is to be conveyed from the loop to confine such pieces during the time of casting. In some cases, however, it is not necessary that the mould should totally enclose the pattern; for instance, where a model is to be made of a pedestal, or a butt of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the human body. The bottom of such moulds being left open, there is accordingly ample room for pouring in the plaster. After the mould is completely formed, it is next to be dried either naturally or by a gentle artificial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and then seasoned in the following manner:—Having been made thoroughly dry, which, if the mould is large, will require two or three weeks, it is to be brushed over plentifully with linseed oil boiled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, finely levigated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>, or oil of vitriol. The inside and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the mould should be particularly well supplied with it. If the mould be large, it is needless to attend to the outside; but when the moulds are small, it will not be improper to boil them in the oil; by which means their pores are more exactly filled than could otherwise be done. After the moulds have undergone this operation, they are again set by dry, when, being greased with olive oil and hog's lard, they are fit for use. If linseed oil be used for greasing the moulds, it will in a short time impart a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the casts. The mould being properly prepared and seasoned, nothing more is requisite to form the model than to pour the fine liquid plaster of Paris into it. After a layer of this, about half an inch in thickness, has been formed all round the mould, we may use the coarser kind to fill it up entirely, or to give to the model what thickness we please. Besides the models which are taken from inanimate bodies, it has been frequently attempted to take the exact resemblance of people while living, by using their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> as the original of a model, from whence to take a mould; and the operation, however disagreeable, has been submitted to by persons of the highest ranks in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. A considerable difficulty occurs in this, however, by reason of the person's being apt to shrink and distort his features when the liquid is poured upon him; neither is he altogether without danger of suffocation, unless the operator well understands his business. To avoid the former inconvenience, it will be proper to mix the plaster with warm instead of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, by which means the person will be under no temptation to shrink; and to prevent any danger of a fatal accident, the following method is to be practised: Having laid the person horizontally on his back, the head must first be raised by means of a pillow to the exact position in which it is naturally carried when the body is erect; then the parts to be represented must be very thinly covered over with fine oil of almonds by means of a painter's brush; the face is then to be first covered with fine fluid plaster, beginning at the upper part of the forehead, and spreading it over the eyes, which are to be kept <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, that the plaster may not come in contact with the globe; yet not closed so strongly as to cause any unnatural wrinkles. Cover then the nose and ears, plugging first up the meatus auditorii, with cotton, and the nostrils with a small quantity of tow rolled up, of a proper size, to exclude the plaster. During the time that the nose is thus stopped, the person is to breathe through the mouth; in this state the fluid plaster is to be brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> low enough to cover the upper lip, observing to leave the rolls of tow projecting out of the plaster. When the operation is thus far carried on, the plaster must be suffered to harden; after which the tow may be withdrawn, and the nostrils left free and open for breathing. The mouth is then to be closed in its natural position, and the plaster brought down to the extremity of the chin. Begin then to cover that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> which is to be represented, and spread the plaster to the outsides of the arms and upwards, in such a manner as to meet and join that which is previously laid on the face: when the whole of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> has acquired its due hardness, it is to be cautiously lifted, without breaking, or giving pain to the person. After the mould is constructed, it must be seasoned in the manner already directed; and when the mould is cast, it is to be separated from the mould by means of a small mallet and chisel. The eyes, which are necessarily shown closed, are to be carved, so that the eyelids may be represented in an elevated posture; the nostrils hollowed out, and the back part of the head, from which, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, no mould can be taken, must be finished according to the skill of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. The edges of the model are then to be neatly smoothed off, and the bust fixed on its pedestal. The method of making models in the plaster of Paris is undoubtedly the most easy way of obtaining topical models. When models, however, are made of wood, etc., for large objects that the model itself must be of considerable size, it is vain to attempt making it in the way above described. Such models must be constructed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> with some lost substance, as wax, clay, putty, etc., and it being necessary to keep all the proportions with mathematical exactness, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of a single model of this kind must be a work of great labour and expense as well as of time. Of all those which have been undertaken by human industry, however, perhaps the most remarkable is that constructed by General Pfister, to represent the mountainous parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It is composed of 142 compartments, of different sizes and forms, respectively numbered, and so artfully put together, that they can be separated and replaced with the greatest ease. The model itself is 20 feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and formed on a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> which represents two English miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> by an English foot: comprehending part of the cantons of Zug, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, Schwyz, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNTERWALDEN">Unterwalden</a>, Lucerne, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, and a small part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Glarus; in all, an extent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of 18 leagues in length and 12 in breadth. The highest point of the model, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the centre (which is the lake of Lucerne), is about ten inches; and as the most elevated mountain represented therein rises 1475 toises or 9440 feet above the lake of Lucerne, at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> calculation, the height of an inch in the model is about 900 feet. The whole is painted of different colours, in such a manner as to represent objects as they exist in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and so exactly is this done, that not only the woods of oak, beech, pine, and other trees, are distinguished, but even the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of the several rocks are marked, each being shaped upon the spot, and formed of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, gravel, or such other substances as compose the natural mountain. So minute also is the accuracy of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, that it comprises not only all the mountains, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, villages, and forests, but every cottage, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and even every path is distinctly marked. The principal material employed in the construction of this extraordinary model, is a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, lime, clay, a little pitch, with a thin coat of wax; and is so hard that it may be trod upon without any damage. It was begun in the year 1766, at which time the general was about 50 years of age, and it employed him till the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August 1785; during all which long space of time he was employed in the most laborious and even dangerous tasks.—He raised the plans with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on the spot, took the elevation of mountains, and laid them down in their several proportions. In the prosecution of this laborious employment, he was twice arrested for a spy; and in the popular cantons was frequently forced to work by moonlight, in order to avoid the jealousy of the peasants, who imagined that their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> would be endangered should a plan of their country be taken with such minute exactness. Being obliged frequently to remain on the tops of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, where no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> could be procured, he

MODENA

Pages 340-340

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, in Latin Mutina, which gives name to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and is its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. It stands 28 miles east of Parma, 44 almost south of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and 20 west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; and is a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous, but not a handsome city. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is said to amount to about 40,000. It is much celebrated by Roman authors for its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and opulence; but was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sufferer by the siege it underwent during the troubles of the triumvirate. It hath <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> been the usual residence of the dukes; and is also the see of a bishop, who is suffragan to the archbishop of Bologna. Mr Keyfeler says, that when Decius Brutus was besieged here by Mark Antony, Hirtius the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRIER">carrier</a> pigeons; and that, even at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, pigeons are trained up at Modena to carry letters and bring back answers. This city hath given birth to several celebrated persons, particularly Tasso the poet, Corregio the great painter, Sigonius the civilian and historian, Da Vignola the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, and Montecuculi the imperial general. The tutelary saint of it is named Geminianus. The ducal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is a very noble edifice, in which, among the other fine pictures, the birth of Christ by Corregio, called la Notte Felice, is much celebrated. The only manufacture for which this city is noted, is that of snuffs, of which great numbers are exported. The churches of the Jesuits, of the Theatines, and of St Dominic, are well worth viewing. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of St Carlo Borromeo between 70 and 80 young noblemen are continually maintained, and instructed both in the sciences and genteel exercises. St Beatrix, who was of the family of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>, is said to knock always at the gate of the palace three days before any of the family dies. Before most of the houses are covered walks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> porticoes, as at Bologna. The city is fortified, and on its south side stands the citadel. E. Long. 11° O. N. Lat. 44° 34'.

MODERATION

Pages 340-340

in Ethics, is a virtue consisting in the proper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of our appetites, passions, and pursuits, with respect to honours, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and pleasures; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>: it is also often used to denote candour.

MODERATOR

Pages 340-340

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, the person who presides at a dispute, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in a public <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>: thus the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the annual assembly of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland is styled moderator.

MODERN

Pages 340-340

something new, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; in opposition to what is antique or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>. MODERN Authors, according to Naude, are all those who have wrote since <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>. The modern <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> commences with Galileo; the modern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> with Copernicus.

MODESTY

Pages 340-341

in fact brings it nearer. The veil of shame only makes the desires more attractive. Modesty kindles that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> which it endeavours to suppress: its fears, its evasions, its caution, its timid avowals, its pleasing and affecting finesses, speak more plainly what it wishes to conceal, than <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> can do without it: it is MODESTY, in short, which enhances the value of a favour, and mitigates the pain of a refusal. Since modesty is the secret fear of ignominy; and since all nations, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, have confessed the obligation of its laws; it must be absurd to violate them in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of crimes, which should always have for its object the re-establishment of order. Was it the intention of those oriental nations, who exposed women to elephants, trained for an abominable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of punishment, to violate one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> by the observance of another? By an ancient practice among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> a girl could not be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> before she was marriageable. Tiberius found means to evade this law, by ordering them to be violated by the executioner previous to the infliction of punishment; the refinement of a cruel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, who sacrificed the morals to the customs of his people!
