When the legislature of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> caused women to be exposed naked in the market places, and obliged them to walk on all fours like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, modesty was shocked: but when it wanted to force a mother—when it wanted to compel a son—<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> received an outrage. Such is the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in other countries, that the physical <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> possesses an almost irresistible force. The resistance is feeble; the attack is accompanied with a certainty of success. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> at Patana, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANTAM">Bantam</a>, and in the small kingdoms on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>. When the women in these countries (says Mr Smith) meet with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, they lay hold of him and threaten to inform their husbands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he despises their favours. But here the sexes seem to have abolished the laws peculiar to each. It is fortunate to live in a temperate climate like ours, where that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> which possesses the most powerful charms exerts them to embellish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and where modest women, while they reserve themselves for the pleasures of one, contribute to the amusement of all.

MODIFICATION

Pages 341-341

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, that which modifies a thing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gives it this or that manner of being. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">Quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> are accidents which modify all bodies. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">Decree</a> of Modification, in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a decree ascertaining the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a minister's stipend, without proportioning it among the persons liable in payment.

MODILLIONS

Pages 341-341

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, ornaments in the corniche of the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite columns.

MODIUS

Pages 341-341

a Roman dry <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for all sorts of grain, containing 32 heminae, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 16 sextarii, or one-third of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHORA">amphora</a>; amounting to an English peck. See MEASURE.

MODULATION

Pages 341-341

in Music, derived from the Latin modulari. This word, in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is susceptible of several different significations. It frequently means no more than an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of musical sounds properly connected and arranged. Thus it answers to what Mr Malcolm understands by the word tune, when he does not expressly treat concerning the tuning of instruments. Thus likewise it expresses the French word chant; for which reason, in the article MUSIC, we have frequently expressed the one word by the other. But the precise and technical acceptation to which it ought to be confined, is the art of composing <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> agreeably to the laws prescribed by any particular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, that of changing the key, or of regularly and legitimately passing from one key to another. See MUSIC.

MODULE

Pages 341-341

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a certain <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bigness, taken at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, for regulating the proportions of columns, and the symmetry or disposition of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Architects generally choose the femidiameter of the bottom of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> for their module, and this they subdivide into parts or minutes.

MOESIA

Pages 341-341
or MYSIA, in Ancient Geography, a country of Europe, extending from the confluence of the Sava and the Danube to the shores of the Euxine. It was divided into Upper and Lower Moesia. Lower Moesia was on the borders of the Euxine, and comprehended that tract of country which received the name of Pontus from its vicinity to the sea. Upper Moesia lay beyond the other in the inland country.

MOFFAT

Pages 341-341

a village of Scotland, in Annandale, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUMFRIES">Dumfries</a>, 50 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>; famous for its sulphurous well, which has been in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> estimation for near 150 years as a remedy in all cutaneous and scrofulous complaints; and for its chalybeate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, called Hartfell Spaw, which was discovered above 50 years ago, and is of a very bracing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is chiefly supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> who <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> thither for the benefit of its waters and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; but it has also a manufacture of coarse woollen stuffs. It is a well-built clean village; and contains many good and even elegant lodgings, a tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> room, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a> green and walks, and a good inn. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1801 amounted to 1619. MOFFETTA. See AMPSANCTI.

MOGODORE

Pages 341-342
or MAGADORE, a large, uniform, and well built town in the kingdom of Morocco, situated about 350 miles from Tangier on the Atlantic ocean, and surrounded on the land side by deep and heavy sands. The European factory here consists of about a dozen mercantile houses of different nations, whose owners, from the protection granted them by the emperor, live in full security from the Moors, whom indeed they keep at a rigid distance. They export, to America, mules; to Europe, Morocco leather, hides, gum arabic, gum sandarac, ostrich feathers, copper, wax, wool, elephant's teeth, fine mats, beautiful carpeting, dates, figs, raisins, olives, almonds, oil, &c. In return, they import timber, artillery of all kinds, gunpowder, woollen cloths, linens, lead, iron in bars, all kinds of hardware and trinkets, such as looking glasses, snuff boxes, watches, small knives, &c., tea, sugar, spices, and most of the useful articles which are not otherwise to be procured in this empire. The town is regularly fortified on the sea Mogul, sea side; and on the land, batteries are so placed as to prevent any incursion from the southern Arabs, who are of a turbulent disposition, and who, from the great wealth which is known to be always in Mogodore, would gladly avail themselves of any opportunity that offered to pillage the town. The entrance, both by sea and land, consists of elegant stone arch-ways, with double gates. The market place is handsomely built, with piazzas of the same materials; and at the water port there is a customhouse and powder magazine, both of which are neat stone buildings. Besides these public edifices, the emperor has a small but handsome palace for his occasional residence. The streets of the town, though very narrow, are all in straight lines; and the houses, contrary to what we meet with in the other towns of the empire, are lofty and regular. The bay, which is little better than a road, and is very much exposed when the wind is at north-west, is formed by a curve in the land, and a small island about a quarter of a mile from the shore. Its entrance is defended by a fort well furnished with guns.

MOGUE

Pages 490-491

a temple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship among the Mahometans. All mosques are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings, generally constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> gate there is a square <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> paved with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble; and low galleries round it, whose <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is supported by marble pillars. In these galleries the Turks wash themselves before they go into the mosque. In each mosque there is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lamps; and between these hang many crystal rings, ostriches eggs, and other curiosities, which, when the lamps are lighted, make a fine show. As it is not lawful to enter the mosque with stockings or shoes on, the pavements are covered with pieces of stuff sewed together, each being wide enough to hold a row of men kneeling, sitting, or prostrate. The women are not not allowed to enter the mosque, but stay in the porches without. About every mosque there are six <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers, called minarets, each of which has three little open galleries, one above another; these towers, as well as the mosques, are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and adorned with gilding and other ornaments; and from thence, instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, the people are called to prayers by certain officers appointed for that purpose. Most of the mosques have a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> belonging to them, in which travellers of what <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> soever, are entertained three days. Each mosque has also a place called tarbe, which is the burying-place of its founders; within which is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, covered with green velvet or satin; at the ends of which are two tapers, and round it several seats for those who read the Koran and pray for the souls of the deceased.

MOGULS

Pages 342-346

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, whose conquests formerly were the most rapid and extensive of any people recorded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. They themselves deduce their origin from Japhet, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as they call him, Japhis, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>. His son Turk, they say, was the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, or khan, of those nations who are now known by the separate names of Turks, Tartars, and Moguls; and the Tartars especially assert, that their proper designation is Turks. To this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> is attributed many of those inventions which barbarous nations <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> ascribe to their first sovereigns. He was succeeded by Taumak; in whose reign the whole posterity of Turk were divided into four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tribes, denominated the order's of Erlat, Gialair, Kaugin, Berlas or Perlas; of which last came the famous Timur Beg, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>.—From this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to that of Alanza Khan, we meet with nothing remarkable. In his reign the Turks being immersed in all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, universally apostatized into idolatry. Having two sons, Tartar and Mogul, he divided his dominions among them, and thus gave rise to the two empires of the Tartars and Moguls. The two nations had not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> existed before they began to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon each other; and after long contention, the event at last was, that Il Khan, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Moguls, was totally overthrown by Siuntz Khan, emperor of the Tartars; and so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> was the defeat, that the Mogul nation seems to have been almost exterminated. Only two of Il Khan's family survived this disaster. These were Kajan his youngest son, and Nagos his nephew, who were both of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and had both been married the same year. These two princes, with their wives, had been taken prisoners by Siuntz Khan, but found means to make their escape to their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Here they seized upon all the cattle which had not been carried off by the Tartars; which was easily done, as having none to dispute the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> with them; then stripping some of the slain, they took their clothes, and retired into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. They passed several mountains without much difficulty; but at last advanced to the foot of one exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, which had no way over it but a very small path made by certain animals, called in the Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> ar- chara. This path they found themselves obliged to make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, though it was so strait, that only one could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> at a time, and he was in the most imminent danger of breaking his neck at the least false step. Having ascended the mountain on one side by this path, they descended by the same on the other side; and were agreeably surprised to find themselves in a delightful tract, interspersed with rivulets and charming meadows, abounding with a vast variety of delicious <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and enclosed on all sides by inaccessible mountains, in such a manner as to shelter them from all future pursuits of the Tartars. Here they lived some time, and gave this beautiful country the name of Ir-gana-kon, in allusion to its situation; Ir-gana signifying, in the old language of the Moguls, a "valley," and Kon a "steep height." In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time these two families very much increased. Kajan, whose posterity was the most numerous, called his descendants Kajath; but the people springing from Nagos were divided into two tribes; one of which received the appellation of Nagoster, and the other that of Durlagan. These two Mogul princes and their descendants lived in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for more than 400 years; but the latter then finding it too narrow for them, meditated a return to the country from which their forefathers had been driven. For some time, however, they found this impracticable, as the path that conducted their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had been long since destroyed. At last they discovered, that one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the high mountain above mentioned was not very thick in a certain place; and also, that it consisted entirely of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore. To this, having before set fire to a layer of wood, and another of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, laid along the foot of the mountain, they applied 70 large bellows, and at last melted the mountain in such a manner, that an opening was made large enough for a loaded camel to pass; and through this passage they all marched out with great joy. The Moguls having thus issued as it were from a new world, overthrew the Tartars in their turn; and whence <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be a very considerable nation till the time of their great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Temujin, afterwards called Jenghiz Khan, whom they extol in the most extravagant manner. It is difficult, however, to say, at the time Temujin made his appearance, how far the dominions of the Moguls extended, or in what estimation they were held by their neighbours. It seems to be pretty certain that great part of the vast region, now known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, was then in a state of considerable civilization, and likewise extremely populous, as we find mention made of many cities which the Moguls destroyed; and the incredible multitudes whom they slaughtered, abundantly show the populousness of the country. On the east, the country of the Moguls and Tartars had the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> which divides Tartary from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; on the west, it had the empire of Karazm, State of A- founded by Mahmand Gazni; and on the south were the countries now known by the name of Indistan, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, Tonguin, and Cochlin China. Thus it comprehended the eastern part of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Tartary, and all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. This whole region was divided among a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Aymacks, or tribes; who had each one or more khans, according as it was more or less numerous, or divided into branches. Among these that of the Kara-its was the most powerful: their prince... prince assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Khan, and among the rest the Moguls were tributary to him; but, according to the Chinese historians, both the one and the other were tributary to the emperor of Kitay or Katay. China was divided into two parts: the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> southern provinces were in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Chinese emperors of the Song dynasty, who kept their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> at Hang-chew, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Chek-yang; the five northern provinces, excepting part of Shenfu, were possessed by the Kin, a people of Eastern Tartary, from whom are descended the Manchew Tartars, at present masters of China. This vast dominion was named Kitay or Katay, and was divided into two parts: that which belonged to China, was properly called Kitay; and the part which belonged to Tartary was called Karakitay, in which some even include the territories of the Moguls, Karaites, and other tribes which are the subject of the present history. The western part of the empire of Kitay was possessed by a Turkish prince, who had lately founded a new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> there called Hya; whose capital <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was Hyachew, now Ninghia in Shenfu, from whence the kingdom took its name. To the west of Hya lay Tangu; a country of great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and formerly very powerful; but at that time reduced to a low state, and divided among many princes; some of whom were subject to the emperor of Hya, and others to the emperor of China. All Tartary to the westward as far as the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, with the greater part of Little Bucharia, which then passed under the general name of Turkestan, was subject to Ghurkhan, Karakhan, or Kaver Khan; to whom even the Gazni monarchs are said to have been tributary. This Ghurkhan had been prince of the Western Kitay or Lyau; who, driven out of Kitay by the king, settled in Little Bucharia, and the country to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, where they founded a powerful state about the year 1124. Thus the Moguls, properly so called, had but a very small extent of empire which could be called their own, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> indeed they had any, when Temujin made his appearance. This hero is said by the Tartars to have been of divine origin, since his family could be traced no farther back than ten generations, the mother of whom was got with child by a spirit. The names and transactions of his predecessors are equally uncertain and unimportant: he himself, however, was born in the year 1163, and is said to have come into the world with concealed blood in his hands; from whence it was prognosticated that he would be a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, and obtain the victory over all his enemies. This prediction, if any such there was, Temujin most literally fulfilled. At the time of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his subjects amounted to between 30,000 and 40,000 families; but of these two-thirds quickly deserted, and Temujin was left almost without subjects. When only 13 years of age, he fought a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> against these revolters; but either was defeated, or gained an indecisive victory; so that he remained in obscurity for 27 years longer. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> at last he owed to the friendship of Vang Khan, who ruled over a great number of Tartar tribes to the north of Kitay, and has been heard of under the name of Prefect John among the Europeans. This prince took Temujin under his protection; and a rebellion being afterwards raised against himself, Temujin was made his general, and the khan was kept in possession of his throne: soon after which Temujin subdued the tribes which had revolted from himself, treating them at the same time with the utmost barbarity. This happened in the year 1201; but Vang Khan, who became jealous of continuing the friend of Temujin, now became jealous, and resolved to destroy him by treachery. With this view he proposed a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> between Temujin's son Juji and his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and another between Temujin's daughter and his own son. Temujin was invited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of Vang Khan, in order to celebrate this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> marriage; but receiving intelligence of some evil intention against him, he excused himself to Vang Khan's messengers, and desired that the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> might be put off to some other time. A few days after the departure of these messengers, Badu and Kithlik, two brothers, who kept the horses of one of Vang Khan's <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> domestics, came and informed Temujin, that the grand Khan finding he had missed his aim, was resolved to set out instantly, and surprize him next morning, before he could suspect any danger. Temujin, alarmed at this intelligence, quitted his camp, in the night time, and retired with all his people to some distance. He was scarce gone when Vang Khan's troops arrived, and discharged an incredible number of arrows among the empty tents; but finding nobody there, they pursued Temujin in such haste that they fell into great disorder. In this condition they were suddenly attacked and routed by Temujin; after which an open war with Vang Khan took place. By this quarrel almost all the princes of Tartary were put in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, some siding with Temujin, and overcomes others with Vang Khan. But at last fortune declared all his enemies in favour of the former: Vang Khan was overthrown in a battle, where he lost 40,000 men, and obliged to fly for refuge to a prince named Tayyan Khan, who was Temujin's father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and his own enemy, and by whom he was ungenerously put to death. Temujin immediately began to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> on his dominions, great part of which voluntarily submitted: but a confederacy was formed against him by a number of Vang Khan's tributaries, at the head of whom was Jamuka, a prince who had already distinguished himself by his enmity to Temujin; and even Tayyan Khan himself was drawn into the plot, through jealousy of his son-in-law's good fortune. But Temujin was well prepared; and in the year 1204 attacked Tayyan Khan, entirely routed his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, killed himself, and took Jemuka prisoner, whose head he caused instantly to be struck off; after which he marched against the other tribes who had conspired against him. Them he quickly reduced; took a city called Kajbin, where he put all to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> who had borne arms against him; and reduced all the Mogul tribes in 1205. Temujin now, having none to oppose him, called a general diet, which he appointed to be held on the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> 1206; that is, on the day in which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> entered Aries. To this diet were summoned all the great lords both Moguls and Tartars; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, to establish good order in the army, he divided his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> into bodies of 10,000, 1000, 100, and 10 men, with their respective officers, all subordinate to the generals, or those who commanded the bodies of 10,000; and these were to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> under his owne. own sons. On the day of holding the diet, the princes of the blood and great lords appeared dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. Temujin dressed in the same manner, with his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> on his head, sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on his throne, and was complimented by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, who wished him the continuance of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and prosperity. After this they confirmed the Mogul empire to him and his successors, adding all those kingdoms which he had subdued, the descendants of whose vanquished kings were deprived of all <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or title to them; and after this he was proclaimed emperor with much ceremony. During this inauguration, a pretended prophet declared that he came from God to tell the assembly, that from thenceforth Temujin should assume the name of Jenghiz Khan, or the most Great Khan of khans; prophesying also, that all his posterity should be khans from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation. This prophecy, which was no doubt owing to Temujin himself, had a surprising effect on his subjects, who from that time concluded that all the world belonged of right to them, and even thought it a crime against heaven for any body to pretend to resist them. Jenghiz Khan having now reduced under his subjection all the wandering tribes of Moguls and Tartars, began to think of reducing those countries to the south and south-west of his own, where the inhabitants were much more civilized than his own subjects; and the countries being full of fortified cities, he must of course expect to meet with more resistance. He began with the emperor of Hya, whose dominions he invaded in 1209, who at last submitted to become his tributary. But in the mean time Jenghiz Khan himself was supposed to be tributary to the emperor of Kitay: who, in 1210, sent him an officer, demanding the customary tribute. This was refused with the utmost indignation, and a war commenced, which ended not but with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the empire of Kitay, as mentioned under the article China. In the year 1216, Jenghiz Khan resolved to carry his arms westward, and therefore left his general Mochuli to pursue his conquests in Kitay. In his journey westward he overthrew an army of 300,000 Tartars who had revolted against him; and, in 1218, sent ambassadors declaring an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Mohammed Karazm Shah, emperor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAZNA">Gazna</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> was haughtily treated; however, the alliance was concluded; but soon after broken, through the treachery, as it is said, of the Karazmian monarch's subjects. This brought on a war attended with the most dreadful devastations, and which ended with the entire destruction of the empire of Karazm or Gazna, as related under the article Gazna. After the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Karazm, part of the Moguls broke into Iran or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, where also they made large conquests, while others of their armies invaded <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> and the countries to the west; all this time committing such enormities, that the Chinese historians say both men and spirits burnt with indignation. In 1225, Jenghiz Khan returned to Hya, where he made war on the emperor for having sheltered some of his enemies. The event was, that the emperor was slain, and his kingdom conquered, or rather destroyed; which, however, was the last exploit of this most cruel conqueror, who died in 1227, as he marched to complete the destruction of the Chinese. The Mogul empire, at the death of Jenghiz Khan, extended over a prodigious tract of country; being more than 1800 leagues in length from east to west, and upwards of 1000 in breadth from north to south. Its extent was vast, and its princes, however, were still infatuated, and pushed on pire, their conquests on all sides. Oktay was acknowledged emperor after Jenghiz Khan; and had under his immediate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> Mogulestan (the country of the Moguls properly so called), Kitay, and the countries eastward to the Tartarian sea. Jagaty his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> governed under him a great part of the western conquests. The country of the Kipjacks, and others to the east, and north-east, north, and north-west, were governed by Batu or Patu the son of Juji, who had been killed in the wars; while Tuli or Toley, another son of Jenghiz Khan, had Khorasan, Peria, and what part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> was conquered. On the east side the Mogul arms were still attended with success; not only the empire of Kitay, but the southern part of China, was conquered, as already related under that article, No 24—42. On the west side matters continued much in the same way till the year 1254, when Magu, or Menkho, the fourth khan of the Moguls, (the same who was afterwards killed at the siege in China), raised a great army, which he gave to his brother Hulaku or Hulagu, to extend his dominions westward. In 1255, he entered Iran, where he suppressed the Hmactians or Affains, of whom an account is given under the article Assassins, and two years afterwards he advanced to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, which he took, and cruelly put the caliph to death, treating the city with no more lenity than the Moguls usually treated those which fell into their hands. Every Bagdad resisting was put to fire and sword; and in the city and its neighbourhood the number of slain, it is said, amounted to 1,600,000. The next year he invaded <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>; the city of Damacus was delivered up, and, as it made no resistance, the inhabitants were spared; but <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a> being taken by storm, a greater slaughter ensued there than had taken place at Bagdad, not even the children in their cradles being spared. Some cities of this country revolted the next year, or the year after; but falling again into the hands of the Moguls, they were plundered, and the inhabitants butchered without mercy, or carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. Hulaku died in 1264, and at his death we may fix the greatest extent of the Mogul empire. It now comprehended the whole of the continent of Asia, excepting part of Indostan, Siam, Pegu, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHIN_CHINA">Cochin China</a>, and a few of the countries of Lesser Asia, which had not been attacked by them; and during all these vast conquests no Mogul army had ever been conquered, except one by Jalaloddin, as mentioned under the article Gazna.—From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, however, the empire began to decline. The ambition of the khans having prompted them to invade the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> and Cochin China, they were miserably disappointed in their attempts, and lost a great number of men. The same bad success attended them in Indostan; and in a short time this mighty empire broke into several smaller ones. The governors of Persia being of the family of Jenghiz Khan, owned no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to any superior; those of Tartary did the same. The Chinese threw off the yoke; and thus the continent of Asia wore much the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> that it had done before Jenghiz Khan began his conquests. The successors of Hulaku reigned in Persia till the year 1335; but that year Abulaid Khan, the eighth from Hulaku, dying, the affairs of that country fell into confusion for want of a prince of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of Jenghiz Khan to succeed to the throne. The empire, therefore, was divided among a great number of petty princes who fought against each other almost without intermission, till in the year 1360 Timur Bek, or Tamerlane, one of these princes, having conquered a number of others, was crowned at Balkh, with the pompous title of Saheb Karan; that is, "the emperor of the age, and the conqueror of the world." As he had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> before taken that city, and destroyed one of his most formidable rivals who had shut himself up in it, the new emperor began his reign with beheading some of the inhabitants, imprisoning others, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> their houses, and killing the women and children for slaves. In 1370 he crossed the Silim, made war on the Getes, and attacked Karazim. Next year he granted a peace to his enemies; but two years after, he again invaded the country of the Getes, and by the year 1379 had fully conquered that country as well as Korazan; and from that time he continued to extend his conquests in much the same manner as Jenghiz Khan had done, though with less cruelty.—In 1387 he had reduced <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, Georgia, and all Persia; the conquest of which last was completed by the reduction of Isfahan, 72,000 of the inhabitants of which were slaughtered on account of a sedition raised by some ruffians or evil disposed persons. After the reduction of Persia, Timur turned his arms northward and westward, subduing all the countries to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. He took the city of Bagdad; subdued Syria; and having ravaged great part of Russia, returned to Persia in 1396, where he splendidly invades and feasted his whole army. In 1398 he invaded Indofstan, crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> on the 17th of September, reduced several fortresses, and made a vast number of captives. However, as he was afraid that, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any emergency, these prisoners might take part with the enemy, he gave orders to his soldiers to put all their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> slaves to death; and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this inhuman order, more than 100,000 of these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> wretches were slaughtered in less than an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. In the beginning of the year 1399 Timur was met by the Indian army; whom, after a desperate battle, he defeated with great slaughter, and soon after took the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a> the capital of the country. Here he seated himself on the throne of the Indian emperors, and here the sharifs, kadis, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inhabitants of the city, came to make their submission, and begged for mercy. The tame elephants and rhinoceroses likewise were brought to kneel before him as they had been accustomed to do to the Indian emperors, and made a great cry as if they implored his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>. These war elephants, 120 in number, were, at his return, sent to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARCAND">Samarcand</a>, and to the province where his sons resided. After this, at the request of the lords of the court, Timur made a great feast; at which he distributed presents to the princes and principal officers. Delhi at this time consisted of three cities, called Seyri, Old Delhi, and Jehan Penah. Seyri was surrounded with a wall in form of a circle. Old Delhi was the same, but much larger, lying south-west of the other. These two parts were joined on each side by a wall; and the third, lying between them, was called Moguls, Jehan Penah, which was larger than Old Delhi. Penah had ten gates; Seyri had <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, three of which looked towards Jehan Penah; this last had 13 gates, six to the north-west, and seven to the south-east. Everything seemed to be in a quiet posture; when, on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1399, the soldiers of Timur being assembled at one of the gates of Delhi, inflicted the inhabitants of the suburbs. The great emirs were ordered to put a stop to these disorders; but their endeavours were not effectual. The sultans, having a curiosity to see the rarities of Delhi, and particularly a famous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> adorned with 1000 pillars, built by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> king of India, went with all the court; and the gate being on that occasion left open for everybody, above 15,000 soldiers got in unperceived. But there was a far greater number of troops in a large place between Delhi, Seyri, and Jehan Penah, who committed great disorders in the two last cities. This made the inhabitants in despair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on them; and many, setting fire to their houses, burnt their wives and children. The soldiers seeing this confusion, did nothing but pillage the houses; while the disorder was increased by the admission of more troops, who seized the inhabitants of the neighbouring places who had fled thither for shelter. The emirs, to put a stop to this mischief, caused the gates to be shut; but they were quickly opened by the soldiers within, who rose in arms against their officers; so that by the morning of the 13th the whole army was entered, and this great city was totally destroyed. Some soldiers carried out 150 slaves, men, women, and children; nay, some of their boys had 20 slaves a piece to their share. The other spoils, in jewels, plate, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, were immense; for the Indian women and girls were adorned with precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and had bracelets and rings on their hands, feet, and even toes, so that the soldiers were loaded with them. On the 15th, in Old Delhi, the Indians retired into the great mosque to defend themselves; but being attacked by the Tartars, they were all slaughtered, and towers erected with their heads. A dreadful carnage now ensued throughout the whole city, and several days were employed before the inhabitants could be made to quit it entirely; and as they went, the emirs took a number of them for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The artisans were also distributed among the princes and commanders; all but the masons, who were reserved for the emperor, in order to build him a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> mosque at Samarcand. After this terrible devastation, Timur marched into the different provinces of Indofstan, everywhere defeating the Indians who opposed him, and slaughtering the Ghebrs or worshippers of fire. On the 25th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> he set out on his return, and on the 9th of May arrived at Samarcand. In a few months after his arrival, he was obliged to undertake an expedition into Persia, where affairs were in the utmost disorder on account of the misconduct of his son, whom he had appointed sovereign of that empire. Here Timur soon settled matters; after which he again set out on an expedition westward, reduced many places in Georgia which had not submitted before, and invaded and conquered Sy-Timurria. At the same time he quarrelled with Bajazet the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, then buried in an enterprise against Constantinople, in which he would probably have succeeded had not Timur interfered. The cause of this quarrel... quarrel at first was, that Bajazet had demanded tribute from a prince who was under Timur's protection, and is said to have returned an insulting answer to the Tartar ambassadors who were sent to him on that account. Timur, however, who was an enthusiast in the cause of Mahometanism, and considered Bajazet as engaged in the cause of heaven when besieging a Christian city, was very unwilling to disturb him in so pious a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and therefore undertook several expeditions against the princes of Syria and Georgia, in order to give the Turkish monarch time to cool and return to reason. Among other places, he again invested the city of Bagdad, which had <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off its allegiance to him; and having taken it by storm, made such a dreadful massacre of the inhabitants, that 120 towers were erected with the heads of the slain. In the mean time Bajazet continued to give fresh provocation, by protecting one Kara Yufet a robber, who had even insulted the caravan of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>; so that Timur at length resolved to make war upon him. The sultan, however, foreseeing the danger of bringing such a formidable enemy against himself, thought proper to ask <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, for what was past, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> obedience to Timur's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> for the future. This embassy was graciously received; and Timur returned for answer, that he would forbear hostilities, provided Bajazet would either put Kara Yufet to death, send him to the Tartar camp, or expel him out of his dominions. Along with the Turkish ambassadors he sent one of his own; telling Bajazet that he would march into the confines of Anatolia, and there wait his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> answer. Though Bajazet had seemed at first willing to come to an agreement with Timur, and to dread his superior power; yet he now behaved in such an unsatisfactory manner, that the Tartar monarch desired him to prepare for war; upon which he raised the siege of Constantinople, and having met Timur with an army greatly inferior to the Tartars, was utterly defeated and taken prisoner. According to some accounts, he was treated with great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; while others inform us, that he was shut up in an iron cage, against which he dashed out his brains the following year. At any rate, it is certain that he was not restored to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but died in confinement. This victory was followed by the submission of many places of the Lesser Asia to Timur; the Greek emperor owning himself his tributary, as did also the sultan of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. After this Timur once more returned to Georgia, which he cruelly ravaged; after which he marched to Samarqand, where he arrived in the year 1405. Here, being now an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, this mighty conqueror began to look forward to that state which at one time or other is the dread of all living creatures; and Timur, in order to quiet the remorse of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, came to the following curious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, which he communicated to his intimate friends; namely, that "as the vast conquests he had made were not obtained without some violence, which had occasioned the destruction of a great number of God's creatures, he was resolved, by way of atonement for his past crimes, to perform some good <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; namely, to make war on the infidels, and exterminate the idolaters of China." This atonement, however, he did not live to accomplish; for he died the same year of a burning fever, in the 71st year of his age and 36th of his reign. On the death of Timur, his empire fell immediately into great disorder, and the civil wars continued for five or six years; but at last peace was restored, by the settlement of Shah Rukh, Timur's son, on the throne. He did not, however, enjoy the empire in its full extent, or indeed much above one half of it; having only Karazm, Khorassan, Kandahar, Persia, and part of Hindostan. Neither was he able, though a brave and warlike prince, to extend his dominions, though he transmitted them to his son Ulug Beg. He proved a wise and learned monarch; and is famous for the astronomical tables which he caused to be composed, and which are well known at this day. He was killed in 1448 by his son Abdallatiff, who six months after was put to death by his own soldiers. After the death of Abdallatiff, Abdallah, a grandson of Shah Rukh, seized the throne; but, after reigning one year, was expelled by Abuafud Mirza, the grandchild of Miran Shah the son of Timur. His reign was one continued <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of wars and tumults; till at last he was defeated and taken prisoner by one Haffan Beg, who put him to death in 1468. From this time we may look upon the empire of Timur as entirely dissolved, though his descendants still reigned in Persia and Hindostan, the latter of which is still known by the name of the Mogul's empire. On the death of the above-mentioned monarch, his History of son Babr or Babor succeeded him, but was soon driven Hindostan out by the Ulbeck Tartars; after which he retired some time in Gazna, whence he made incursions into Hindostan, and at length became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole empire, excepting the kingdoms of Dukan, Guzerat, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>.—For the transactions subsequent to this period, see Hindostan and India.

MOHAIR

Pages 346-346

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> of a kind of goat frequent about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGORA">Angora</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; the inhabitants of which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> are all employed in the manufacture of camlets made of this hair. Some give the name mohair to the camlets <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stuffs made of this hair; of these there are two kinds; the one smooth and plain, the other watered like tabbies: the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two only consists in this, that the latter is callendered, the other not. There are also mohairs both plain and watered, whose woof is of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, cotton, or thread. MOHAIR Shell, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a>, a name given to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of voluta, which seems of a clothy and finely reticulated texture, and resembles on the surface a piece of mohair or a very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>-worm's web. MOHAWKS. See Muck. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOHAWK">MOHAWK</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">Country</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, inhabited by one of the five nations of the Iroquois, situated between the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, and the lake <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a> or Frontignac.

MOHILA

Pages 346-346
or MOELIA, one of the Comora islands in the Indian sea, between the north end of Madagascar and the continent of Africa. The inland parts are mountainous and woody; but the lands adjoining to the sea are watered by several fine streams. The island abounds with provisions of all kinds; and the East India ships of different nations sometimes touch here for refreshment.

MOHILOF

Pages 346-347

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of Mecislau. It is well built, populous, and has a considerable trade. Near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the Swedes obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victory over the Russians in 1707.

MOIRA

Pages 347-347

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">Down</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, 69 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; noted for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> manufacture. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Rawdon. MOISTURE. See Humidity. The moisture of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> has considerable effects on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. For the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the food, and the proportion of the meat to the drink, being given, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of a human body is less, and consequently its discharges greater in dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> than in wet weather; which may be thus accounted for: the moisture of the air moistens the fibres of the skin and lessens perspiration by lessening their vibratory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. When perspiration is thus lessened by the moisture of the air, urine indeed is by degrees increased, but not equally. Hence, according to Dr Bryan Robinson, we learn, that to keep a body of the same weight in wet weather as in dry, either the quantity of food must be lessened, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the proportion of the meat to the drink increased; and both these may be done by lessening the drink without making any change in the meat. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used for determining the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of moisture in the air, is called an hygrometer. See Hygrometer.

MOIVRE

Pages 347-347
Abraham, a learned mathematician, was born at Vitri in Champagne, in France, 1667, where his father was a surgeon. At the revocation of the edict of Nantes, he came to England. Before he left France, he had begun the study of mathematics; and having perfected himself in that science in London, he was obliged, by necessity, to teach it. Newton's Principia, which accidentally fell into his hands, showed him how little progress he had made in a science of which he thought himself master. From this work he acquired a knowledge of the geometry of infinitesimals with as great facility as he had learned the elementary geometry; and in a short time he was fit to be ranked with the most celebrated mathematicians. His success in these studies procured him a seat in the Royal Society of London and in the Academy of Sciences at Paris. His merit was so well understood in the former, that he was thought capable of deciding in the famous dispute between Leibnitz and Newton concerning the differential calculus.—He published a Treatise on Chances in 1738, and another on Annuities in 1752; both extremely accurate. The Philosophical Transactions contain many interesting memoirs of his composition.—Some of them treat of the method of fluxions; others are on the lunula of Hippocrates; others on physical astronomy, in which he resolved many important problems; and others, in short, on the analysis of the games of chance, in which he followed a different course from that of Montmort. Towards the close of his life he lost his sight and hearing; and the demand for sleep became so great that he required 20 hours of it in a day. He died at London, 1754, aged 87. His knowledge was not confined to mathematics; but he retained to the last a taste for polite literature. He was intimately acquainted with the best authors of antiquity; and he was frequently consulted about difficult passages in their works. Rabelais and Molière were his favourite French authors: he had them by heart; and he once observed to one of his acquaintances, "that he would rather have been Molière than Newton." He recited whole scenes of the Misanthrope, with that delicacy and force with which he remembered to have heard them recited at Paris 70 years before, by Molière's own company. The character indeed was somewhat similar to his own. He judged severely of mankind; and could never conceal his disgust at the conversation of a fool, or his aversion to cunning and dissimulation. He was free from the affectation of science, and no one could know him to be a mathematician but from the accuracy of his thoughts. His conversation was general and instructive. Whatever he said was well digested and clearly expressed. His style possessed more strength and solidity than ornament and animation; but he was always correct, and he bestowed as much pains on his sentences as on his calculations. He could never endure any bold affections or indecent witticisms against religion.

MOLA

Pages 347-347

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Terra di Lavoro, where they pretend to show the ruins of Cicero's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 50' N. Lat. 41° 5'. MOLA Salfa (<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> Cake), in antiquity, was barley parched, and afterwards ground to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flour, then mixed with salt and frankincense, with the addition of a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Thus prepared, it was sprinkled between the horns of the victim before it was killed in sacrifice. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> was called immolatio, and was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the Greeks as well as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the mola of the Romans was of wheat. The Greeks called it ἀλάς or ἀλάσιν.

MOLARES

Pages 347-347
or Dentes Molares, in Anatomy, the large teeth, called in English the grinders. See Anatomy Index.

MOLDAVIA

Pages 347-347

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east by the river Nisiter, which divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>; on the east, by Bessarabia; on the south by the Danube, which parts it from Bulgaria; and on the west, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a> and Transylvania. It is 240 miles in length and 150 in breadth. It lies in a good <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> and fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, producing corn, wine, rich pastures, a good breed of horses, oxen, sheep, plenty of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, fish, fowl, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, and all European <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Danube, Nisiter, Pruth, Bardalach, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERET">Ceret</a>. The inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JASSY">Jassy</a> is the principal town. It has been tributary to the Turks since the year 1574; who appoint a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who is a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but have no regard to his being of the principal families. The province pays a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> yearly tribute to the Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; besides raising a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> at its own expense.

MOLE

Pages 347-349

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of flabby <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, of a spherical Mole, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mark. See Nævus. Mole, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> formed of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> laid in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by means of coffer dams, extended either in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line or an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of a circle, before a port, which it serves to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>; to defend the vessels in it from the impetuosity of the waves, and to prevent the passage of ships without leave. Thus we say the mole of the harbour of Messina, &c. Mole is sometimes alluded to signify the harbour itself. Mole, (moles), among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was also used for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>, built in manner of a round tower on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> base, insulated, encompassed with columns, and covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOME">dome</a>.—The mole of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, now the castle of St. Angelo, was the greatest and most stately of all the moles. It was crowned with a brazen pine apple, wherein was a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> urn containing the ashes of the emperor. Mole Cricket. See Gryllotalpa, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Mole Hills. These little hillocks of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> are a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> to the pasture lands, not only in wasting so much of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> as they cover, but in obstructing the scythe in mowing. In the west of England they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for the breaking up of these; it is a flat board, very thick, and of about eight inches in diameter, into which there is fastened a perpendicular handle of three or four feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. It has four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and sharp <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, which readily cut through the hill, and spread the earth it consists of; and behind there is a large knob proper for breaking the clods with, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there are any. Some use a spade, or other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> instrument, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of this, but not so well. There is, however, a much better instrument even than this, for destroying these hills, where they are in very great numbers. This is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> machine; it has a sharp iron about three feet over, and with a strong back.—It is about four or five inches broad, and has two long handles for a horse to be harnessed to, and a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of iron to strengthen it at the bottom of the handles, reaching from the one handle to the other. The middle of this cross bar is furnished with one, two, or more sharp pieces of iron like small ploughshares, to cut the mole hills into two, three, or more parts. The iron behind is of a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. A single horse is harnessed to this machine, and a boy must be employed to drive it, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to hold and guide it; the sharp irons or shares are the first things that meet the hill, they run through it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> its texture, and cut it into several parts; and the circular iron following immediately behind them, cuts up the whole by the roots, and leaves the land <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. This instrument <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> destroy as many mole hills in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> as a common labourer can do in eight, and would be of very great advantage to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> if brought into general use. Molière, John Baptist, a celebrated French comedian and dramatic writer, whose true name was Poquelin, which for some reason he changed to that of Molière. He was the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">valet</a> de chambre, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> about the year 1620. He went through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the classics under the Jesuits in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Clermont, and was designed for the bar; but at his quitting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, he made choice of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>'s profession. From a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the drama, Molière's whole study and application were directed to the stage, and he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to exhibit plays, which were greatly applauded. It is said the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of his going upon the stage was to enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of an actress for whom he had contracted a violent fondness. His comedies are highly esteemed. And it is no wonder he so justly represented <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> feuds, and the torments of jealous husbands, or of those who have reason to be so; for it is alleged that no man ever experienced this more than Molière. His last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> was Le Malade Imaginaire, which was brought on the stage in 1673; and Molière died on the fourth night of its representation; some say in acting the very <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the pretended dead man, which gave some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> for the wits of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but according to others he died in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> that night, from the bursting of a vein in his lungs by coughing. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, as a last mark of his favour, prevailed with the archbishop of Paris to suffer him to be buried in consecrated ground; though he had irritated the clergy by his Tartuffe. The most esteemed editions of his works are that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, 5 vols. 12mo, 1699; and that of Paris, 6 vols. 4to, 1734. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLINISTS">Molinists</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who follow the doctrine and sentiments of the Jesuit Molina, relating to sufficient and efficacious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. He taught that the operations of divine grace were entirely consistent with the freedom of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> will; and he introduced a new kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> to remove the difficulties attending the doctrines of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREDESTINATION">predestination</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and to reconcile the jarring opinions of Augustines, Thomists, Semi-Pelagians, and other contentious divines. He affirmed, that the decrees of predestination to eternal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> was founded upon a previous knowledge and consideration of the merits of the elect; that the grace, from whose operation these merits are derived, is not efficacious by its own intrinsic power only, but also by the consent of our own will, and because it is administered in those circumstances, in which the Deity, by that branch of his knowledge which is called scientia media, foresees that it will be efficacious. The kind of proficiency, denominated in the schools scientia media, is that foreknowledge of future contingents that arises from an acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and faculties of rational beings, of the circumstances in which they shall be placed, of the objects that shall be presented to them, and of the influence which their circumstances and objects must have on their actions. Molinists, a sect among the Romanists, who adhere to the doctrine of Molinos. These are the same with what are otherwise called Quietists, whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> principle was, that men ought to annihilate themselves in order to be united to God, and afterwards remain in quietness of mind, without being troubled for what shall happen to the body. Molinos, the author of those opinions, was a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and was born in 1627. His 68 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> were examined in 1687 by the pope and inquisitors, who decreed that his doctrine was false and pernicious, and that his books should be burned. He was forced to recant his errors publicly in the Dominican church, and was condemned to perpetual imprisonment. He was then 60 years old, and had been spreading his doctrine 22 years before. He died in prison in 1692. Mollugo, African Chickweed; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. plants belonging to the triandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 22d order, Caryophyllae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

MOLLUSCA

Pages 349-349

in the Linnean system, one of the orders of vermes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. These are simple naked animals, not included in a shell, but furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOLOCH

Pages 349-349

a false god of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, who dedicated their children to him, by making them "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the fire," as the Scriptures express it. There are various opinions concerning this method of consecration. Some think, the children leaped over a fire sacred to Moloch; others, that they passed between two fires; and others, that they were really burnt in the fire, by way of sacrifice to this god. There is foundation for each of these opinions. For, first, it was usual among the pagans to lustrate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> purify with fire; and, in the next <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it is expressly said, that the inhabitants of Sepharvaim burnt their children in the fire to Anamchel and Adramelech; much such deities as Moloch of the Ammonites. Moses, in several places, forbids the Israelites to dedicate their children to this god as the Ammonites did, and threatens <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> and utter extirpation to such persons as were guilty of this abominable idolatry. And there is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> that the Hebrews were much addicted to the worship of this deity: since <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a>, and after him St Stephen, reproaches them with having carried along with them into the wilderness the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> of their god Moloch. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> built a temple to Moloch upon the mount of Olives; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, imitated his impiety, by making his son pass through the fire in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Moloch. It was chiefly in the valley of Tophet and Hinnom, to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, that the Israelites paid their idolatrous worship to this false god of the Ammonites. There are various sentiments concerning the relation which Moloch had to the other pagan divinities. Some believe he was the same with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, to whom it is well known that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sacrifices were offered. Others suppose him to be <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; others, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>; others, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRAS">Mithras</a>; and others, Venus. Lastly, Others take Moloch to be the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of heaven. Moloch was likewise called Milcom; as appears from what is said of Solomon, that he went after Astarteoth the abomination of the Zidonians, and Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.

MOLOSSES

Pages 349-349

Molasses, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Melasses, that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> fluid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> remaining of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> after refining, and which no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring to a consistence more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> than that of syrup; hence also called syrup of sugar. Properly, molasses are only the sediment of one kind of sugar called chypre, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> sugar, which is the refuse of other sugars not to be whitened or reduced into loaves. Molasses are much used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and also among <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people instead of sugar. There is a kind of brandy or spirit made of molasses; but by some held exceedingly unwholesome. See below. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Molosses. There has been found a method of making molasses from apples without the addition of sugar. The apple that succeeds best in this operation is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> sweeting of a middle size, pleasant to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and so full of juice that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> bushels will yield a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of cider. The manner of making it is this: the apples are to be ground and pressed, then the juice is to be boiled in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, till three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of it be evaporated; this will be done with a moderate fire in about six hours, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of juice above mentioned; by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it will be of the consistence and taste as well as of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of molasses. This new molasses serves all the purposes of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> kind, and is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in preserving cider.
