The warlike animals on which the Spanish officers were mounted, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> with which they were armed, the wooden castles on which they had crossed the ocean, the armour with which they were covered, the victories which they gained wherever they went; all these circumstances, added to that foolish disposition to wonder which always characterizes a simple people, so operated upon the minds of the Mexicans, that when Cortez arrived at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mexico, he was received by Montezuma as his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and by the inhabitants as a god. At first they fell <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the streets when a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">valet</a> passed by; but by degrees the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Montezuma grew familiar with the strangers, and ventured to treat them as men. Montezuma, unable to expel them by force, endeavoured to inspire them with confidence at Mexico by expressions of friendship, while he employed secret means to weaken their power in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. With this view, one of his generals, who had private orders to that purpose, attacked a party of the Spaniards who were stationed at Vera Cruz; and, although his troops were unsuccessful, yet three or four of the Spaniards were killed. The head of one of them was carried to Montezuma. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, Cortez did what has been reckoned one of the boldest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> strokes that ever was performed. He ran to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, followed by fifty of his troops; and, by persuasion and threats, carried the emperor prisoner into the Spanish quarters. He afterwards obliged him to deliver up those who had attacked his troops at Vera Cruz; and, like a general who punishes a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> folder, he loaded Montezuma with chains. He next obliged him to acknowledge himself in public the vassal of Charles V.; and, in name of tribute for this homage, Cortez received 600,000 merks of pure <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. Montezuma soon afterwards felt a sacrifice to his submission to the Spaniards. He and Alvaro, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of Cortez, were besieged in the palace by 200,000 Mexicans. The emperor proposed to show himself to his subjects, that he might persuade them to desist from the attack; but the Mexicans no longer considered him in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> but as the slave of foreign conquerors. In the midst of his speech, he received a blow with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> which wounded him mortally; and he expired soon after, A.D. 1520.—See Cortez. This unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> left two sons and three daughters, who embraced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. The eldest received <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, and obtained from Charles V. lands, revenues, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Montezuma. He died in 1608; and his family is one of the most powerful in Spain. Montferrat, a province of Italy, with the title of a duchy; bounded on the east by the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and part of the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>; on the north, by the Vercellese and Canavese; on the west, by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a> properly so called; and on the south by the territory of Genoa, from whence it is separated by the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It contains 200 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages; and is very fertile and well cultivated, abounding in corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. It belongs to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, and Caffal is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>, a town of France, in Upper Bretagne, seated on the River Men, 12 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RENNES">Rennes</a>. W. Long. 1. 38. N. Lat. 48. 8. Montfort, a handsome and strong town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the United Provinces, with an ancient castle; seated on the river Yssel, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>. E. Long. 5. 0. N. Lat. 52. 4. Montfort, a town of Germany, in the circle of Suckia, on the confines of Tirol, 16 miles south of Lindow, and the lake <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>. It is capital of a country of the same name, which has been almost all purchased by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. E. Long. 9. 51. N. Lat. 47. 22. Montfort-de-Lemos, an ancient town of Spain, in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, with a magnificent castle, where the Comarca of Lemos resides. It is seated in a fertile country, 25 miles north-east of Orensa, and 55 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSTELLA">Compostella</a>. W. Long. 7. 9. N. Lat. 42. 28. Montfort-l'Amuly, a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, with the title of a duchy, 25 miles from Paris. E. Long. 2. 50. N. Lat. 48. 45. Montgatiz, a town of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Poreczas, with a strong fortress. It is encompassed with a great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>, and art and nature have rendered it almost impregnable. It was defended by the princess Ragotkay, wife of Count Tekeli, when besieged by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the imperialists, who were obliged to raise the siege in 1688. E. Long. 21. 55. N. Lat. 46. 26. Montgeron, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>-Basile-Carre de, was born at Paris in 1686; his father was master of requests. He was scarcely 25 years of age when he purchased the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of counsellor in parliament, where by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> qualifications he gained considerable reputation. Deeply engaged in all the vices which flow from irreligion, he was converted by an extraordinary circumstance. He went on the 7th of September 1731 to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Deacon Paris, with an intention to examine, with the rigour of the severest critic, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> which were reported to be performed there. But, according to his own account, he felt himself suddenly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> by innumerable flashes of light with which he was surrounded. His incredulity was converted into flaming zeal, and he became the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of the saint whom he formerly ridiculed. From that moment he devoted himself to the fanaticism of convulsions, with the same impetuosity of character with which he had run into the most shameful excesses. He had not long been the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Janiferina when he suffered <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. When the chamber of inquests was banished in 1732, he was sent into the mountains of Auvergne; which, instead Montgeron stead of cooling, tended rather to inflame his zeal. During his exile, he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of collecting the proofs of the miracles wrought at the tomb of the abbé Paris, and of composing what he called a Demonstration of them. On his return to Paris, he prepared to execute this plan; and on the 29th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1737, he actually presented to the king at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> a volume in quarto superbly bound. This work he accompanied with a speech, which is a mixture of zeal and argument in a tolerable style. In consequence of this work, which some consider as a masterpiece of eloquence, and others as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of absurdities, he was committed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BASTILLE">Bastille</a>. After a few months confinement, he was sent to an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Benedictine monks in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIGNON">Avignon</a>; whence he was in a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> carried to Viviers. He was afterwards confined in the citadel of Valence, where he died, A.D. 1574, aged 68. The work which he presented to the king was entitled La vérité des Miracles opérés par l'intercession de M. Paris, &c., &c.—The critics, even to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, seem to be guided in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> concerning this book either by hatred or by enthusiasm. "It would be extremely rash (says the abbé de St Pierre, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> volume of his Annales, p. 593.) to maintain with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLINISTS">Molinists</a>, that no miraculous cure was ever performed at the tomb of the abbé Paris; and to say with the Janissaries, that these cures were performed by a supernatural power, would be the height of fanaticism. The truth is, (adds the same author), that no miracle appears ever to have been performed at this tomb except in the cure of the human body; in all other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, there would have been the want of that imagination on which the whole miracle depended." Thus, although Montgeron ventured to compare these prodigies with the miracles of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ and his apostles, yet we find no person raised from the dead, no multiplication of loaves, no command obeyed by the elements, and no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> or deaf restored to their sight or hearing. It belongs to the Author of nature alone, or to those who have derived power from him, to work such miracles as are recorded by the evangelists, or in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the apostles. Montgeron added a second and third volume on the same subject: he left also in manuscript a work which he composed in prison <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRE">contre</a> les Incrédules. Religion, it must be confessed, has had much more powerful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>. Fortunately Pascal and Buffet are among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: and it could well have wanted both Paris and Montgeron, whatever virtues they might possess in other respects.

MONTGOMERY

Pages 390-390

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, 158 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, took its name from Roger de Montgomery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Shrewsbury, who built the castle. It is called by the Welsh Tra Valdwin, that is, Baldwin's town; having been built by Baldwin, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of the marches of Wales, in the reign of William I. The Welsh, after having put the garrison to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, demolished it in 1295; but Henry III. rebuilt it, and granted it the privileges of a free borough, with other liberties. It is a tolerably well built town, in a healthy situation and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, with 947 inhabitants in 1801.

MONTGOMERYSHERE

Pages 390-390

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, 40 miles in length and 37 in breadth; bounded on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a> and Denbighshire, on the north-east and east by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a> and Cardiganshire, and on the west by the last-mentioned county and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Merionethshire. It is divided into six <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>; and contains five market <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 47 parishes, and 47,978 inhabitants. It lies in the three several dioceses of St Asaph, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>; but sends only two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, one for the county, and one for the town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is pleasant and salubrious; but this county, being extremely mountainous, is not very fertile, except in the valleys, which afford some corn and plenty of pasture; but the south, south-east, and north-east parts, being more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, are extremely fruitful, especially a pleasant vale, watered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>.

MONTH

Pages 390-392

the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a year. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">CHRONOLOGY</a>, No. 17. Month, in its proper acceptation, is that space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> takes up in passing from any certain point to the same again, which is called a periodical month; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is the space of time between two conjunctions of the moon with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which is called a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> month. That space of time which the sun takes up in passing through one sign or 12th part of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, is also called (but improperly) a month. So that there are two sorts of months; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a>, which are measured by the moon; and solar, which are measured by the sun. The lunar periodical month consists of 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes 5 seconds: The lunar synodical month is 29 days 12 hours 44 minutes 3 seconds and 11 thirds. A solar month contains, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> calculation, 30 days 10 hours 29 minutes 5 seconds. The Jews, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of lunar synodical months; but, to avoid fractions, they confessed alternately of 29 and 30 days. The former, the Romans called calends, and the Greeks <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a>; the latter were termed plenilunia and angustae. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> months were ranged differently in their sacred and in their civil year. Order of the Sacred Year. | 1 Nisan | <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. | | 2 Sivan | April. | | 3 Tammuz | May. | | 4 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">Ab</a> | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. | | 5 Elul | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. | | 6 Tishri | August. | | 7 Cheshvan | September. | | 8 Kislev | October. | | 9 Tebeth | November. | | 10 Shebat | <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. | | 11 Adar | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>. | | 12 Adar | February. | Order of the Civil Year. | 1 Tishri | September. | | 2 Cheshvan | October. | | 3 Kislev | November. | | 4 Tebeth | December. | | 5 Shevat | January. | | 6 Adar | February. | | 7 Nisan | March. | | 8 Iyar | April. | | 9 Sivan | May. | | 10 Tammuz | June. | | 11 Ab | July. | | 12 Elul | August. | These months being lunar cannot exactly answer to our solar months; but every Jewish month must be conceived to answer to two of ours, and partake of both. As these 12 lunar months consist only of 354 days, the Jews, in order to bring it nearer to the true year, took care every three years to intercalate a 13th month into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, which they called Ve-adar, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Adar. The new moon was always the beginning of the month; and it is said the Jews had people posted on elevated places, to give notice to the Sanhedrim as soon as the moon appeared. After this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, and "the feast of the new moon, the feast of the new moon," resounded amongst the people. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hebrew months were of 30 days each, excepting the last, which consisted of 35; so that the year contained 365 days, with an intercalary month at the end of 120 years, which, by affording the odd hours which remained at the conclusion of each year, brought it back nearly to its proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. This regulation of the year was borrowed from the Egyptians. 2. The months of the Athenian year, as we have before observed, consisted alternately of 29 and 30 days. The first month, according to Meton's reformation of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, began with the first new moon after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice, and was called Hecatombaion, answering to the latter half of June, and the former half of July. The order of the months, with the number of days in each, are as follow: | Month | Days | |------------------------|------| | Hecatombaion | 30 | | Melagettion | 29 | | <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEDROMION">Boedromion</a> | 30 | | Maimakterion | 29 | | Panephiion | 30 | | Anthesterion | 29 | | Poseidon | 30 | | <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMELION">Gamelion</a> | 29 | | Elaphebolion | 30 | | Munichion | 29 | | Thargelion | 30 | | Scirrophorion | 29 | Each month was divided into three decades of days called ἑξήκοντα. The first was called ἡμέραις ἀρχαίαις or ἐπαρχίαις, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECADE">decade</a> of the beginning of the month; the second was ἡμέραις μεσαῖαις or the decade of the middle; and the third was ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς or ἐπιφανεῖς, the decade of the expiring month. The first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the first decade was termed ἡμέραις ἀρχαίαις, because the first month began with the new moon; the second day was ἡμέραις ἐπαρχίαις; the third ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς, &c. The first day of the second decade was ἡμέραις μεσαῖαις, the second ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς, &c.—the days of this decade were also called ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς, ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς, &c. The first day of the third decade was ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς; the second was ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς, &c. i.e., the first, second, &c., after 20, because the last decade began on the 20th day. This decade was also counted by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> thus; ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς the 21st, ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς the 22d, ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς the 23d, and so of the rest to the last day of the month, which was called ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς, the old and the new, because one part, of that day belonged to the old and the other to the new moon; but after the time of Demetrius, the last day of the month was called from him Ἀναστάσις; it sometimes was named ἡμέραις ἐπιφανεῖς. The Grecian months, thus consisting of 29 and 30 days alternately, fell short of the solar year 11 days 6 hours. To remedy this defect, the cycle of four years, called ἐπιστροφῆς, was invented.—In this cycle, after the first two years, they added an intercalated month called ἐπιστροφῆς, consisting of 22 days; and again, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of two years more, they inserted another month of 23 days, the fourth part of a day having in the space of four years amounted to a whole day. See Year. 3. The Roman year under <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> consisted of 10 months only, and began with March, which contained 31 days; then followed April which had 30, May 31, June 30, Quintilis 31, Sextilis 30, September 30, October 31, November 30, December 30. These 10 months containing no more than 304 days, this account was in a short time found to be deficient. Numa Pompilius, therefore, took away one day from each of these five months, April, June, Sextilis, September, November, December; and to the six days thus obtained he added 51, which was the number that Romulus's year, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, wanted to make it perfect. Numa had now 57 days to dispose of; he therefore divided them, and constituted two other months, January and February; the former consisting of 29 and the latter of 28 days. The month of January, which he placed at the winter solstice, he made instead of March to begin the year. Thus Numa's year consisted of 355 days: but this being found 10 days 6 hours short of the solar year, he made use of the intercalation of 90 days at the expiration of eight years perpetually; which number, being made up of the 11 days and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, kept the year pretty well to its place. The beginning of the year in Julius Caesar's time had anticipated its true place 67 whole days: these he intercalated betwixt November and December: so that the year consisted, for this one time, of 15 months or 445 days. This reformation was called the Julian correction, and this year the year of confutum. At the end of 12 years, by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of priests, who did not understand intercalation, 12 days had been intercalated for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. This was observed by Augustus Caesar, and rectified, by ordering 12 years to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without any intercalary days. The order and succession of months was the same as that of Numa: But January, March, May, Quintilis, Sextilis, October, and December, had each 31 days; April, June, September 30, and February, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> years, 28; but every fourth year or bissextile 29. This, with a very little <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, is the account observed at present. Quintilis, in compliment to Julius Caesar was called July, because in this month he was born; and Sextilis, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Augustus, was called August; both which names are still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>.—See Year. Each month by the Romans was divided into kalends, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONES">nones</a>, and ides, all of which were reckoned backwards. The kalends were the first day of the month. The nones fell on the seventh, and the ides on the 15th, of March, May, July, October—but in all other months the nones were on the fifth, and the ides on the 13th. For the more easy comprehension of the Roman manner of dating, according to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the months, here follows a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. | Month | March | April | May | June | July | August | September | October | |-------|-------|-------|-----|------|------|--------|-----------|---------| | Kalendæ | Kalendæ | Kalendæ | Kalendæ | Kalendæ | | 2 | 6 | 4 | 4 | 4 | | 3 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 3 | | 4 | Prid. Non. | Prid. Non. | Prid. Non. | Prid. Non. | | 5 | None | None | None | None | | 6 | Prid. Non. | 8 | 8 | 8 | | 7 | None | 7 | 7 | 7 | | 8 | 8 | 6 | 6 | 6 | | 9 | 7 | 5 | 5 | 5 | | 10 | 6 | 4 | 4 | 4 | | 11 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 3 | | 12 | 4 | Prid. Idus | Prid. Idus | Prid. Idus | | 13 | 3 | Idus | Idus | Idus | | 14 | Prid. Idus | 19 | 18 | 16 | | 15 | Idus | 18 | 17 | 15 | | 16 | 17 | 17 | 16 | 14 | | 17 | 16 | 16 | 15 | 13 | | 18 | 15 | 15 | 14 | 12 | | 19 | 14 | 14 | 13 | 11 | | 20 | 13 | 13 | 12 | 10 | | 21 | 12 | 12 | 11 | 9 | | 22 | 11 | 11 | 10 | 8 | | 23 | 10 | 10 | 9 | 7 | | 24 | 9 | 9 | 8 | 6 | | 25 | 8 | 8 | 7 | 5 | | 26 | 7 | 7 | 6 | 4 | | 27 | 6 | 6 | 5 | 3 | | 28 | 5 | 5 | 4 | Prid. Kal. | | 29 | 4 | 4 | 3 | | | 30 | 3 | 3 | Prid. Kal. | | | 31 | Prid. Kal. | Prid. Kal. | | | N. B. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> year, February consisting of 29 days, the 24th and 25th of that month are written Sexto Kal. Mart.; hence leap year is called Biflexitilis.

MONTIA

Pages 392-392

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MONTINIA

Pages 392-392

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MONTMEDI

Pages 392-392

a small but strong town of France, in Luxemburg, seated on the river Chire, which divides it into the upper and lower <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. It is 22 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>, 27 south-west of Luxemburg, and 135 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 23. N. Lat. 49. 32.

MONTMORENCY

Pages 392-392

a town of France, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>, remarkable for the tombs of the dukes of this name. It is seated on a hill, near a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> valley, fertile in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, especially excellent cherries. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 24. N. Lat. 48. 59.

MONTPELIER

Pages 392-392

one of the finest <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of France, and the most considerable in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERAULT">Herault</a>, excepting Thoulouse, is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 58. N. Lat. 43. 37. This town has been long famous for its salubrious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and on this account has been the frequent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of invalids. But the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, according to some travellers, is considerably changed, having at times continual rains for three months together, and often very thick fogs. Its situation, though on an eminence, never could be healthy; for between it and the Mediterranean (which is about three leagues distant) it is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> marsh, covered with noxious vapours, which, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> breeze sits in, blows directly on the town and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> adjacent; of the sad effects of which, its unhealthy inhabitants, with their meagre looks, are the most convincing proofs. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> stands upon a rising ground fronting the Mediterranean; on the other side is an agreeable plain, extending about the same distance towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the Cevennes. It is reckoned well built, yet the streets are in general narrow and the houses dark. The inhabitants, many of whom are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, are supposed to amount to 40,000, are sociable, gay, and good tempered. The trade of Montpelier is very extensive in wine, cordials, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, verdigris, and faltpetre; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and woollen goods are considerable. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are well supplied with fish, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s meat, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, at reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>. The wine of the country is strong and harsh; <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> is dear, and so is sweet wine of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONTIGNAN">Frontignan</a>, though made in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CETTE">Cette</a>. Liquors of various sorts are compounded and distilled at Montpelier. The environs are extremely pleasant, having on one side La <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> de Peyrou, which forms a fine terrace. From thence on a clear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, may be seen to the eastward the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, which form the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; to the south-west, the Pyrenean mountains, which form those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, both at about 50 leagues distant; and to the southward a most extensive view of the Mediterranean. Not far from thence is a noble aqueduct, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> tier of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>; by this, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is brought from a mountain at three leagues distance, into two balcons in a small elegant temple at the west end of the town. Here also is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> garden, where on certain days public lectures were formerly held on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. On the other side of the town is the esplanade, a beautiful walk, bordered on each side by olive trees, from whence there is a pleasing prospect of the sea and the country adjacent to the town. Previous to the revolution, Montpelier had a university, an academy of sciences, and it was the see of a bishop.

MONTREAL

Pages 392-394

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the river St Lawrence, ten leagues in length, and four leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and about 60 miles above Quebec. It was taken from the French by generals <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a> and Murray on the 8th of September 1760. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the island is exceedingly rich and good, producing all kinds of European <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and vegetables in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance, with variety of garden fruits. The south side is the most inhabited, and of course best cultivated; and besides the settlements, which are numerous, the island is adorned with villas, for the retirement of the more wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season. Since this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has been in the possession of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, it has suffered much by fires, the houses being mostly built of wood. The town of Montreal, situated on this island; and formerly called Ville Marie, is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> place in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, buildings and strength; and besides possessing the advantage of a less rigorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, for delightfulness. Montreal delightfulness of situation is infinitely preferable to Quebec. It stands on the side of a hill, sloping to the south, with many agreeable villas upon it, which, with the island of St Helen, and the river (which is here about two miles broad), form a most charming landscape. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is not very broad from north to south, it covers a great length of ground from east to west, and is nearly as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous as Quebec. The streets are regular, forming an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; the houses well built, and in particular the public edifices, which far exceed those of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and commodiousness; the residence of the knights hospitaliers being extremely magnificent.—There are several gardens within the walls, in which, however, the proprietors have consulted more than elegance, particularly those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">Sisters</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">Congregation</a>, the Nunnery <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, the Recollets, Jesuit Seminary, and Governor. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is said to be between 5000 and 6000. By the situation of the place, the inhabitants are well supplied with all kinds of river fish, some of which are unknown to Europeans, being peculiar to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They have likewise plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, horses, hogs, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. The neighbouring shores supply them with a great variety of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> in the different seasons; and the island abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and numerous rivulets. The trade in furs is considerable, and vessels of 200 tons can come up to the town. Montreal, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, with a castle, seated on the river Xiloea, 25 miles north-west of Tervilla, and 40 south-east of Calataud. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 2. N. Lat. 41. 9. Montreal, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and in the valley of Mazara, with an archbishop's see; seated on a rivulet, five miles west of Palermo, and 50 north-east of Mazara. E. Long. 13. 31. N. Lat. 38. 14. Montreal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, a fortress of Germany, in the circle of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRIER">Trier</a>; seated on the river Moselle, 22 miles north-east of Trier. E. Long. 7. 6. N. Lat. 49. 59. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>, a handsome town of North Britain, in the thire of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, situated at the mouth of the river Esk, on the German ocean, 46 miles north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The houses are neat, and many of them in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The most remarkable public buildings are, the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and an elegant episcopal chapel.—Montrose is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> town, and a dukedom in the family of Graham. It stands between two rivers, the south and north Esk, over the latter of which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and over the former there is one of wood. The salmon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> on these rivers are very extensive, and form a considerable branch of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The harbour is a fine circular basin defended by a handsome stone pier. A great number of trading vessels belong to this port. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Montrose in 1801 amounted to nearly 8000. W. Long. 2. 32. N. Lat. 36. 40. Montrose, Marquis of. See Graham; and Britain, No. 137, 138, 143, 265. Montserrat, a mountain of Spain, in Catalonia, one of the most singular in the world for situation, shape, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. It stands single, towering over a hilly country like a pile of grotto <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> or Gothic spires; and its height so great, that to a beholder on the top the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> appear to be sunk to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the plain. It is composed of steep rocks, which at a distance seem indented; whence it is said to have received the name Montserrat from the Latin word ferrra, a "faw." It is impossible to describe the beauty, richness, and variety, of the landscapes discovered from the most elevated point; but the extensiveness of the prospect may be conceived by the reader, upon being told that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, which are at the distance of 60 leagues, are discovered from this elevation. Montserrat is particularly famous for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> that is paid to an image of the Virgin, which according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> was found in a cave in this mountain by some shepherds in the year 880. Over this image, Guthred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a> caused a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> and chapel to be erected; but after remaining in this receptacle upwards of 700 years, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. and Philip III. built a magnificent church for its reception. Innumerable and astonishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> are ascribed to this holy image. The convent or monastery is situated in a nook of the mountain; it seems as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> vast torrents of water, or some violent convulsion of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, had split the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of Montserrat, and formed in the cleft a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> to build the monastery upon. The river Llobregat roars at the bottom, and perpendicular walls of rock of prodigious height, rise from the water edge near half way up the mountain. Upon these masses of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> stone rests the small piece of level ground which the monks inhabit. Closer behind the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, and in some parts impending over it, huge cliffs shoot up in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> to a stupendous elevation: their summits are split into sharp cones, pillars, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, and other odd shapes, blanched and bare; but the interstices are filled up with forests of evergreen and deciduous trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Fifteen hermitages are placed among the woods; nay, some of them on the very pinnacles of the rocks, and in cavities hewn out of the loftiest of these pyramids. The monastery is one of the 45 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses of the Spanish congregation of the order of St Benedict; their general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> is held every fourth year at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VALLADOLID">Valladolid</a>, where the deputies choose abbots and other dignitaries for the ensuing quadrennium. In this monastery, they elect for <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> a Catalan and a Castilian alternately. Their possessions are great, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> villages lying to the south of the mountain; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> has lately curtailed their income about 6000 livres a-year, by appropriating to his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the best house in each village, some of which, with their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, are worth 200 dollars per annum. Their original foundation, in 866, gave them nothing but the mountain; and to donations and economy they owe the great increase of their landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. They are bound to feed and harbour for three days all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> pilgrims that come up and pay their homage to the Virgin; and the allowance is a luncheon of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> in the morning, as much more, with broth at noon, and bread again at night. Sometimes, on particular festivals, 7000 persons arrive in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but people of condition pay a reasonable price for what they eat.—The number of professed monks, according to Mr Swinburne, is 76 (according to M. Bourgoanne 60); of lay brothers, 28; and of singing boys 25; besides physician, surgeon, and servants. The church is a gloomy edifice; and the gilding is much filled with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of 85 lamps of silver, of various forms and sizes, that hang round the cornice of the sanctuary. Funds have been bequeathed by different devotees for furnishing them with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The choir above stairs is decorated with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Christ, in good wooden carving. A gallery runs on each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a>, for the convenience of the monks. A large <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> grate divides the church from the chapel of the Virgin, where the image stands in a niche over the altar, before which burn four tapers in large silver candlesticks, the present of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Medina Celi. In the sacrifice, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> leading to it, are presses and cupboards full of relics and ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; they point out, as the most remarkable, two crowns for the virgin and her son, of ineffable value; some large <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> rings; an excellent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CAMEO">cameo</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>'s head; the Roman emperors in alabaster; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of St Ignatius. But as no offerings to this miraculous statue can be rejected or otherwise disposed of, the shelves are crowded with most whimsical ex voto, viz. silver legs, fingers, breasts, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings, watches, two wheeled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, boats, carts, and such like trumpery. On different parts of the mountain, as already noticed, are a number of hermitages. Each of these solitary retreats, which at a distance seem destitute of every thing, has a chapel, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, a well in the rock, and a little garden. The inhabitant of one of them, which is dedicated to St Beneto, has the privilege of making an annual entertainment on a certain day; on which day all the other hermits are invited, when they receive the sacrament from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the mountain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, and after divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> dine together. They meet also at this hermitage, on the days of the saints to which their several hermitages are dedicated, to say <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> and commune with each other. But at other times they live in a very solitary and recluse manner, perform various penances, and adhere to very rigid rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>; nor do they ever eat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; nor are they allowed to keep within their walls either dog, cat, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, or any living thing, lest their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> should be withdrawn from heavenly to earthly affections. Most of these hermits are said to be persons of fortune and family, disquieted with the world, who have retired thither to devote themselves to meditation, self-denial, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRITION">contrition</a>. Montserrat, one of the Caribbee isles, belonging to Great Britain. It is a very small, but very pleasant island, so called by Columbus from its resemblance to the famous mountain near Barcelona in Catalonia. It lies in W. Long. 61°. c. N. Lat. 16°. 50'. having Antigua to the north-east, St Christopher's and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a> to the north-west, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a> lying south-east at the distance of about nine leagues. It is about nine miles in diameter, and is supposed to contain about 40,000 or 50,000 acres. The climate is warm, but less so than Antigua, and is esteemed very healthy. The surface is mountainous, but with pleasant, rich, and fertile valleys; the hills are covered with cedars and other fine trees. Here are all the animals as well as vegetables and fruits that are to be found in the other islands. The inhabitants raised formerly a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>. The produce now is chiefly cotton, rum, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. There is no good harbour, but three tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, Old Harbour, and Ker's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>.

MONUMENT

Pages 394-394

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> destined Monument to preserve the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, &c. of the person who raised it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the person for whom it was raised; such are a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>, a triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, &c.

MOON

Pages 394-398

Influence of, on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">Atmosphere</a>.—It has has been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the vulgar in almost all ages and countries, that the changes which take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the state of our atmosphere, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the changes of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, depend in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> on certain situations of the moon. This particular opinion is alluded to by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> (A), and is applied in the Shepherd of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANBURY">Banbury</a>'s rules for judging of the weather (v). We have, under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>, No 90 to 92, given the result of some observations on the connection between the changes of the moon and those of the weather. It can scarcely be doubted that an opinion so generally received must be founded on something more than fancy or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>; and indeed the observations of several eminent meteorologists within the last thirty years have contributed materially to favour this opinion. Independent of actual observation, it appears reasonable to infer, that a body so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and so near the earth, as the moon, whose gravitating influence on the earth's surface in producing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and reflux of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, cannot be altogether inactive with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, a fluid much more susceptible of changes than the sea. We have already noticed (Meteorology, No 14) the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of Mr Luke Howard, on the moon's influence on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>, and we are now to give a short account of what has been advanced on her general influence by the philosophers of the continent. Among these, Signor Toaldo may be said to have led the way. From observations made at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, during fifty years, on the state of the weather that corresponded to certain changes of the moon, he found that these changes were always accompanied by good or bad weather; and at length became enabled to foretell with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of certainty what would be the state of the atmosphere that should follow any situation of the moon. There are ten situations of the moon, which, according to Toaldo, are capable of producing a sensible effect on the earth's atmosphere. These are the syzygies* or new and full moon; the quadratures; the apsides, or apogee and perigee; the lunifices, or those <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> when the moon is nearest to our zenith and at the greatest distance from it; and the moon's equinoxes. There are three different relations of the moon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> producing a corresponding <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of revolutions, each having a certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, and each corresponding to some of the above ten situations, as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen by the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. | Revolutions | Situations | |-------------|------------| | 1. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">Synodical</a>, in regard to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; continues 29 days 12 hours 44 minutes. | New moon. First <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. Full moon. Last quarter. | | 2. Anomalistic, in regard to the moon's course; continues 27 days 13 hours 43 minutes. | Apogee. Perigee. | That a change will take place at - New moon - First quarter - Full moon - Last quarter - Perigee - Apogee - Ascending equinox - Northern lunifices - Descending equinox - Southern lunifices is - 6:1 - 5:2 - 5:2 - 5:4 - 7:1 - 4:1 - 13:4 - 11:4 - 11:4 - 3:1 In general, each of the ten situations changes the weather that prevailed under the preceding situation, and it seldom happens that a change of weather takes place without a corresponding change in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> situations. From the inequality of their revolutions, these situations are often combined, and by this union their effect in producing changes of the atmosphere is greatly increased, especially when a union takes place between the syzygies and apsides. Thus, That a change will follow - New moon with perigee - <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DITTO">Ditto</a> with apogee - Full moon with perigee - Ditto with apogee is - 33:1 - 7:1 - 10:1 - 8:1 These combined situations are generally accompanied or followed by storms and tempests, especially when they take place near the moon's passage over the equator. This is more particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and September, and we find that at the new and full moon in these months, the weather takes a certain character, by which it is distinguished for the succeeding three or six months. The same takes place at the lunifices, especially at the winter solstice. The new moon does not always, however, produce a change of weather; and this want of effect is most likely to happen at those new moons which are most distant from the apsides. Though Toaldo considers it as perfectly ascertained that each succeeding situation of the moon alters that state of the atmosphere which had been produced by the preceding situation; it must, however, be observed that some situations of the moon favour good and others bad weather. Thus the perigee, the new and full moon, the passage over the equator, and the northern lunifices are favourable to bad weather, while the apo- --- (A) "lunaeque sequentes Ordine respiciens; nunquam te crassina fallet Hora, neque insidiis noctis capire serenae." Georg. I. 424. (B) 1. Horns of the moon obscure—<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a>. 2. When the moon is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>—<a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>. 3. On the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the new moon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> bright, with sharp horns—No wind nor rain till the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> be finished. gee, quadratures, and southern lunifices, are more favourable to good weather. The changes produced by the influence of the lunar situations, seldom take place on the exact days on which these situations happen, but either precede or follow them; and Toaldo has found that, in the six winter months, the changes of weather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> precede the lunar situations, whereas in the six <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months they more commonly follow them. There are certain days before and after new and full moon, which deserve particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> in forming our judgments of the weather, especially the octants or the fourth day before new and full moon, as at these times the weather is inclined to change, and it may be pretty certainly predicted, that a change will follow at the next lunar situation. Virgil has particularly noticed this fourth day as a sure mark of the succeeding weather (c). If the weather continues unchanged on the fourth, fifth, and sixth day of the moon, it proves that the lunar influence is at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> very weak, and we are to expect no change till the full moon, or perhaps till the next new moon. Sig. Toaldo compared a diary which he had kept for many years of the state of the barometer with the ten situations of the moon, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> deduced the following conclusions, viz: 1. That at the time of the moon's apogee, the mercury rises higher by the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a line than at the perigee. 2. That at the time of the quadratures it is higher by the tenth of a line than at the time of the fyzigies. 3. That it is higher by a fourth of a line at the southern than at the northern lunifice. This correspondence of the lunar situations with the ascent of the mercury in the barometer does not hold at the time of the moon's passage through her equinoctial points. The mercury is then higher, especially when the is passing in Libra; and as such situations of the moon generally indicate bad weather, this circumstance is not conformable to meteorological observations. In this case Toaldo thinks that we must be guided, in our judgment of the weather, rather by the moon than by the barometer. The case is similar during the coincidence of the equinoctial points with the perigee, at which time the mercury is unusually <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; but this coincidence is a sign of great irregularity. According to Toaldo, the rising and setting of the moon, as well as its superior and inferior passage of the meridian, all which situations he calls the moon's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, may serve for foretelling rain. The fountains most exposed to rain, are the rising and setting of the moon; while its passage over the meridian is most favourable to good weather. It has ever been observed that during rainy days, the sky always clears a little while the moon is passing the meridian. An exception to this rule must, however, be made when the moon's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> does not coincide with that of the sun. Bad years take place when the apsides of the moon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the four <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> points of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>. Their intervals, therefore, are as four to five, eight to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, &c., or as the intervals of the passage of the apsides through the four cardinal points of the zodiac. Thus the year 1777 was, in general, a bad year; and in that year the apsides of the moon were in the equinoctial signs; and it is probable that the years in which the apsides fall in the signs Taurus, Leo, Virgo and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUARIUS">Aquarius</a>, will be good and moderate years, as the year 1776 really was; and in that year the apsides of the moon were in Taurus and Virgo. Every 18th year must be similar. We, however, cannot depend upon a return altogether the same, on account of the three different revolutions of the moon; and therefore it may happen, that the epoch of this extraordinary year may be retarded a year or perhaps two. Though approximations only are here given, this does not prevent their being useful to farmers, if they only pay attention to circumstances. Besides, various exceptions must be made for different parts of the earth; and it is difficult to determine these beforehand, as what regards this system is applicable to the whole globe; but when the result of the system has been improved by local observations, the conjectures for each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> will be attended with more certainty. The 54th year must have a greater similarity to the first than to all the rest; because, at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the situations of the moon, in regard to the sun and the earth, are again found in the same points. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the rain which falls in nine successive years, is almost equal to that which falls in the next following nine. But this is not the case when we compare in like manner the quantity of rain which falls in six, eight, or ten years.* *See Phil. The observations of M. Lamarck, though they confirm the opinion of the moon's general influence on the atmosphere, do not agree with those of Toaldo, as to the situations of that luminary which correspond to the changes of the weather. He could not find that agreement between the fyzigies and quadratures of the moon and a change of weather, which has been so much dwelt on by Toaldo; but he is of opinion; that we are to consider the declination of the moon as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of her influence on the atmosphere. Lalande had conceived the idea that when the moon entered the northern hemisphere, or had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> declination, the weather was most likely to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and dry, and that when she passed to the south of the equator, it was likely to be rainy. The observations of Lamarck, however, tend to establish the contrary opinion. Lamarck considers the two following principles as established by his observations; viz: 1. That it is in the elevation of the moon above, and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> below, the equator that we are to search for those regularly varied effects which she produces on our atmosphere. 2. That the determinable circumstances, which con- Sin ortu in quarto (namque is certissimus auctor) Pura, neque obtusis per coelum cornibus ibit; Totus et ille dies, et qui nascentur <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> illo Exactum <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> menem, pluvia ventique carebunt. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">Note</a> (B) Georg. I. 427. spire to increase or diminish the moon's influence in her different declinations, are her apogees and perigees, her conjunctions with and oppositions to the sun; and lastly, the solar solstices and equinoxes. Considering that every lunar month, or every revolution of the moon in the zodiac, may be divided into two distinct portions, each containing about fourteen days, and each giving occasion to a particular atmospheric <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, we may assume these as two circumstances of importance in meteorology, and we may call one the boreal or northern constitution, viz. that in which the moon passes through the six northern signs of the zodiac, and the other, the austral or southern constitution, viz. that in which the traverses the six southern signs. Lamarck is convinced by observation, that in these climates, during a boreal constitution, there chiefly prevail southerly, south-westerly, and westerly winds, though sometimes, in the summer, the winds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to the south-east. In general, during this constitution, the barometer exhibits only moderate elevations of the mercury; most commonly the season is rainy or moist, and the air loaded with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. And, lastly, it is particularly during this constitution that we observe the effects of storms and tempests, when the causes which occasion them become <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. On the contrary, during an austral constitution, the winds which chiefly predominate blow from the north and north-west, and in the summer north-east, and even easterly winds. In general during this constitution, the barometer exhibits considerable elevations in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of mercury, at least if the wind is not very strong; the weather is then most usually clear, cold and dry, and in the summer it is seldom (we might almost say never) during this constitution that storms are formed. These atmospheric constitutions are not, however, so permanently characterized as to render it easy to distinguish them at all times by the state of the atmosphere. The atmospheric air is a moveable fluid, and so easily displaced, that it is not surprising that in the temperate zones, where the influence of the heavenly bodies acts less strongly than between the tropics, from various causes, that counteract very often the regular influence of the moon, and tend to mask and even change its effects. The perturbations which these variable causes produce on the regular effects of the influence of the moon on the atmosphere, occasion in fact many variations in the two atmospheric constitutions which we have been describing; and this is doubtless the reason why they have been hitherto disregarded. M. Lamarck positively asserts, that these perturbations, though frequent, and sometimes very considerable, do not prevent the character of each of these constitutions from being remarked in the greatest number of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> that he finds, according to his observations, is estimated at five out of eight; that is to say, out of 48 atmospheric constitutions comprehended in the lunar year, he estimates there will be found at least 30 agreeing with the principles pointed out in his memoir; and he adds, that among the disturbing causes which modify the before-mentioned effects, several may be foreseen, and perhaps even appreciated as to their quantity of effect. He considers what is here pointed out as a fact; as an order of things which any one may prove by observation. Lamarck has also endeavoured to ascertain what <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> there may be in the periodical return of the variations in the atmosphere at the end of nineteen years; and he has found, by comparing meteorological observations, that this return is far from being so correct as is generally believed. Astronomers also know well, that the cycle of nineteen years is not exact within an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> and a half; an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> which amounts to a whole day in the course of 308 years. M. Cotte has also bestowed much attention on this subject of the moon's influence; but appears to think that our observations are not sufficiently numerous or accurate, to deduce any thing like a correct theory, and he is not disposed to go so far as M. Lamarck. M. Cotte agrees in general with Mr Luke Howard's observations on the moon's influence. (See Meteorology). He noted, during the space of 34 years and five months, (from the 1st of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1768, to the 22nd of May 1802), the ascending and descending <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the barometer in each of the syzygies and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the moon which have occurred through that period of time. He states the total sum of the elevations and depressions of the mercury at each of the phases as follows. For 34 Years. New moon. 1st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">Quart</a>. Full Moon. 2d Quart. | Sum of elevations | 218 | 296 | 199 | 290 | |------------------|-----|-----|-----|-----| | Depressions | 281 | 229 | 279 | 106 | Differences | 63 | 67 | 80 | 84 | These results, of nearly 35 years observations, confirm, as will be seen, the conclusions drawn by Mr Howard, both from his observations for one year at Plaistow, and those made for 10 years in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>'s apartments. It is to be remarked, first, That the four numbers which express the differences between the elevations and depressions are nearly in an exact proportion, since \(63 : 67 :: 80 : 84\). Secondly, That the two latter phases, viz. the full moon and last quarter, have more effect than the two first. Thirdly, He examined what phases of the moon corresponded to the greatest and least height of the mercury for each month during ten years, and obtained the following results. For 10 Years. New Moon. 1st Quart. Full Moon. 2d Quart. | Greatest elevation occurred at | 26 | 40 | 26 | 28 | | Greatest depression occurred at | 30 | 34 | 29 | 27 | Differences | 4 | 6 | 3 | 1 | The science may be therefore said to have advanced one step farther towards perfection on this occasion; and it is to be hoped that, by redoubling our diligence in multiplying observations, and combining them in various ways to obtain their results, its progress may be still accelerated. The useful purposes which may be thereby answered in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and medicine, may be properly urged to observers as the means of MOON-Eyed, among horses, when the weakness of the eye increases or decreases according to the course of the moon; so that in the wane of the moon his eyes are muddy and troubled, and at new moon they clear up. This observation is probably inaccurate. MOON-Flone, or Adularia. See ADULARIA, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MOON-Wort. See LUNARIA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Index.

MOORE

Pages 398-398
or MORE, EDWARD, an ingenious writer, was bred a linen-draper, but quitted business to join the retinue of the Muses; and he certainly had a very happy and pleasing talent for poetry. In his Trial of Selim the Persian, he complimented Lord Lyttleton in an elegant kind of panegyric, couched under the appearance of accusation: and his Fables for the Female Sex, for easy verification, poignant satire, and striking morals, approach nearer to the manner of Gay than any other of the numerous imitations of that author. He wrote also three dramatic pieces; The Gamester, a tragedy; The Foundling, and Gil Blas, comedies. The success of these was not such as they merited, the first of them having met with a cold reception, for no other apparent reason but because it too nearly touched a favourite and fashionable vice; and the second having been condemned for its supposed resemblance to Sir Richard Steele's Confucius Lovers, but to which good judges have been inclined to give it greatly the preference. Mr Moore married a lady of the name of Hamilton, daughter to Mr Hamilton table-decker to the princesses, who had herself a very poetical turn, and has been said to have assisted him in the writing of his tragedy. One specimen of her poetry, however, was handed about before their marriage, and has since appeared in print in different collections of songs, particularly in one called the Goldfinch. It was addressed to a daughter of the famous Stephen Duck; and begins with the following stanza: Would you think it, my Duck? (for the fault I must own), Your Jenny at last is quite covetous grown: Though millions if Fortune should lavishly pour, I still would be wretched if I had not More. And after half a dozen stanzas more, in which, with great ingenuity and delicacy, and yet in a manner that expresses a great affection, she concludes with the following lines: You may wonder, my girl, who this dear one can be? Whole merit can boast such a conquest as me: But you shan't know his name, tho' I told you before, It begins with an M, but I dare not say More. In the year 1753, Mr Moore commenced a weekly miscellaneous paper, entitled, The World, by Adam Fitz-Adam, in which undertaking he was affiliated to Lord Chesterfield with some Essays. This paper was collected into volumes, and Mr Moore died soon after.

MOORING

Pages 398-398

the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of confining and securing a ship in a particular station, by chains <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, which are either fastened to the adjacent shore, or to anchors in the bottom. A ship may be either moored by the head, or by the head and stern; that is to say, the may be secured by anchors before her, without any behind; or she may have anchors out, both before and behind her; or her cables may be attached to posts, rings, or moorings, which answer the same purpose. When a ship is moored by the head with her own anchors, they are disposed according to the circumstances of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where she lies and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> she is to continue therein. Thus, wherever the tide ebbs and flows, it is usual to carry one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> out towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and another towards the ebb, particularly where there is little room to range about; and the anchors are laid in the same manner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the vessel is moored head and stern in the same place. The situation of the anchors, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, is usually opposed to the reigning winds, or those which are most dangerous; so that the ship rides therein with the effort of both her cables. Thus if she rides in a bay, or road, which is exposed to a northerly <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and heavy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, the anchors passing from the opposite bows ought to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> east and west from each other: hence both the cables <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> retain the ship in her station with equal effort against the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the wind and sea.

MOORINGS

Pages 398-398

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, are usually an assemblage of anchors, chains, and bridles, laid athwart the bottom of a river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> haven, to ride the shipping contained therein. The anchors employed on this occasion have rarely more than one fluke, which is sunk in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> near low-water mark. Two anchors being fixed in this manner on the opposite side of the river, are furnished with a chain extending across from one to the other. In the middle of the chain is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> link, whose lower end terminates in a swivel, which turns round in the chain as about an axis, whenever the ship veers about with the change of the tide. To this swivel link are attached the bridles, which are short pieces of cable, well served, whose upper ends are drawn into the ship at the mooring ports, and afterwards fastened to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a> or cable bolts.
