A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of moorings of this sort are fixed in the harbours adjacent to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>-yards, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, &c.

MOORLANDS

Pages 398-399

a tract so called, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> rises gradually into small hills, which run through the midst of England in one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ridge, rising higher and higher to Scotland, and feeding forth many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> here is so foul and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, that the snows <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> almost all the year on the tops of the hills; and it is withal very rugged and barren: it, however, yields plenty of coal, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, rance-marble, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>; and some of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a> hills bear such a sweet though short grass, as is very grateful to the oxen, of which here is MOORLANDS. It is observed here, that the west <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> always brings <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and the east and south fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; that though this tract is full of bogs, it is as healthy as any other part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and that it produces the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> as the Peak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>. MOORS. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">MOROCCO</a>.

MOORS

Pages 399-399

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, those who summon the courts for the several headings; such as the lords bailiffs. Every moor has the like office with our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> of the hundred.

MOOT

Pages 399-399

a difficult <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> argued by the young <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BARRISTERS">barristers</a> and students at the inns of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, the better to qualify them for practice, and to defend the causes of their clients. This, which is called mooting, is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> exercise of the inns of court. Particular times are appointed for the arguing moot <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>: the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where this exercise is performed was anciently called moot-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and there is a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> surveyor of the moots, annually chosen by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> to appoint the moot men for the inns of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, and to keep an account of the performance of exercises. The word is formed either from the Saxon metan, gemetan, "meeting"; or from the French mot, "word."

MOPSUS

Pages 399-399

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated prophet, son of Manto and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, during the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He was consulted by Amphimachus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Colophon, who wished to know what success would attend his arms in a war which he was going to undertake. He predicted the greatest calamities; but Calchas, who had been a footslayer of the Greeks during the Trojan war, promised the greatest successes. Amphimachus followed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Calchas; but the prediction of Mopsus was fully verified. This had such an effect upon Calchas, that he died soon after. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is attributed by some to another mortification of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The two footslayers, jealous of each other's fame, came to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of their skill in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. Calchas first asked his antagonist, how many figs a neighbouring tree bore? 10,000 except one, replied Mopsus, and one single vessel can contain them all. The figs were gathered, and his conjectures were true. Mopsus now, to try his adversary, asked him how many young ones a certain pregnant fow would bring forth? Calchas confessed his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>; and Mopsus immediately said that the fow would bring forth on the morrow ten young ones, of which only one should be a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a>, all <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and that the females should all be known by their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> streaks. The morrow proved the veracity of his prediction; and Calchas died by the excess of grief which his defeat produced. Mopsus after death was ranked among the gods, and had an oracle at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, celebrated for the true and decisive answers which it gave.—Another Mopsus, son of Ampyx and Chloris, born at Titarella in Thessaly. He was the prophet and footslayer of the Argonauts, and died at his return from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> by the bite of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>. Jason erected him a monument on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shore, where afterwards the Africans built him a temple, where he gave <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>. He has often been confounded with the son of Manto, as their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a> and their names were alike. MORÆA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 6th order, Enfatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORAI

Pages 399-399

is the name given at Otaheite in the South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the burying grounds, which are also places of worship. This is a pile of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> raised pyramidically upon an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> base <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> 267 feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 87 wide. On each side is a flight of steps; those at the sides being broader than those at the ends; so that it terminated not in a square of the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> with the base, but in a ridge like the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. There were 11 of these steps to one of these morais, each of which was 4 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, so that the height of the pile was 44 feet; each step was formed of one course of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> coral stone, which was neatly squared and polished; the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> (for there was no hollow within) consisted of round pebbles, which, from the regularity of their figure, seemed to have been wrought. The foundation was of rock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which were also squared. In the middle of the top stood an image of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> carved in wood, and near it lay the broken one of a fish carved in stone. The whole of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of one side of a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> or square 360 feet by 354, which was walled in with stone, and paved with flat stones in its whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. About 100 yards to the west of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> was another paved area or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in which were several small stages raised on wooden pillars about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet high, which are called by the Indians evatas, and seem to be a kind of altars, as upon these are placed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> of all kinds, as offerings to their gods. On some of them were seen whole hogs, and on others the skulls of above 50, beside the skulls of many dogs. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of ambition among the natives is to have a magnificent morai. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> deities (for they have them of both sexes) are worshipped by the men, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> by the women; and each have morais, to which the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> is not admitted, though they have also morais <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both.

MORAL PHILOSOPHY

Pages 444-445

To good minds, and some traces of which are found in the lowest, are seldom united with proportioned means <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> opportunities of exercising them; so that the moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the noble energies and impulses of the mind, can hardly find proper scope even in the most fortunate condition; but are much depressed in some, and almost entirely restrained in the generality, by the numerous clogs of an indigent, sickly, or embarrased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Were such mighty powers, such godlike affections, planted in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> to be folded up in the narrow womb of our present existence, never to be produced into a more perfect life, nor to expatiate in the ample <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>? Let it be considered, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that no profession, no enjoyment, within the round of mortal things, is commensurate to the desires, or adequate to the capacities, of the mind. The most exalted condition has its abatements; the happiest conjuncture of fortune leaves many wishes behind; and, after the highest gratifications, the mind is carried forward in pursuit of new ones without end. Add to all, the fond desire of immortality, the secret dread of non-existence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> for perfection, joined to the improbability or the impossibility of attaining it here; and then judge whether this elaborate structure, this magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of inward powers and organs, does not plainly point out an hereafter, and intimate eternity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>? Does <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> give the finishing touches to the lesser and ignoble instances of her skill, and raise every other creature to the maturity and perfection of his being; and shall she leave her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> workmanship unfinished? Does she carry the vegetative and animal life in man to their full vigour and highest destination; and shall he suffer his intellectual, his moral, his divine life, to fade away, and be for ever extinguished? Would such abortions in the moral world be congruous to that perfection of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and goodness which upholds and adorns the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>? We must therefore conclude from this detail, that the present state, even at its best, is only the womb of man's being, in which the noblest principles of his nature are in a manner fettered, or secluded from a correspondent sphere of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; and therefore destined for a future and unbounded state, where they shall emancipate themselves, and exert the fulness of their strength. The most accomplished mortal, in this low and dark apartment of nature, is only the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of what he shall be when he takes his ethereal flight, and puts on immortality. Without a reference to that state, man were a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>, a rude unfinished embryo, a monster in nature. But this being once supposed, he still maintains his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the masterpiece of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; his latent powers are all suitable to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> and progression of nature; his noble aspirations, and the pains of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, are his efforts towards a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> birth, the pangs of his delivery into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and perfection; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his discharge from gaol, his separation from his fellow prisoners, and introduction into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of those heroic spirits who are gone before him, and of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eternal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">Parent</a>. The fetters of his mortal coil being loosed, and his prison walls broken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be bare and open on every side to the admission of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and virtue, and their fair attendant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>; every vital and intellectual spring will evolve itself with a divine elasticity in the free <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of heaven. He will then peep at the universe and its glorious Author through a dark grate or a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> medium, nor receive the reflections of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> through the frail openings of sensible organs: but will be all eye, all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, all ethereal and divine feeling*. Let one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, however, of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> be attended to: That as in the womb we receive our original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, form, and the essential, stamina of our being, which we carry along with us into the light, and which greatly affect the succeeding periods of our life; so our temper and condition in the future life will depend on the conduct we have observed, and the character we have formed, in the present life. We are here in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> what we shall be at full length hereafter. The first rude sketch or outlines of reason and virtue must be drawn at present, to be afterwards enlarged to the future and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. This, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> duly attended to, must prove not only an immortal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, but an admirable incentive to virtue. For he who faithfully and ardently follows the light of knowledge, and incendie, and pants after higher improvements in virtue, will be wonderfully animated and inflamed in that pursuit by a full conviction that the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> does not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> with life—that his struggles, arising from the weakness of nature and the strength of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, will be turned into triumphs—that his career in the track of wisdom and goodness will be both swifter and smoother—and those generous arduous with which he glows towards heaven, i.e. the perfection and immortality of virtue, will find their adequate object and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> in a sphere proportionably enlarged, incorruptible, immortal. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, what an inexplicable damp must it be to the good man, to dread the total extinction of that light and virtue, without which life, nay, immortality itself, were not worth a figgle with? Many writers draw their proofs of the immortality of the soul, and of a future state of rewards and punishments, from the unequal distribution of these here. It cannot be dissembled that wicked men often escape the outward <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to their crimes, and do not feel the inward that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> their demerit seems to require, partly from the callowness induced upon their nature by the habits of vice, and partly from the dissipation of their minds abroad by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or business—and sometimes good men do not reap all the natural and genuine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their virtue, through the many unforeseen or unavoidable calamities in which they are involved. To the smallest reflection, however, it is obvious, that the natural tendency of virtue is to produce happiness; that if it were universally practised, it would, in fact, produce the greatest sum of happiness of which human nature is capable; and that this tendency is defeated only by numerous individuals, who, forsaking the laws of virtue, injure and oppress those who steadily adhere to them. But the natural tendency of virtue is the result of that constitution of things which was established by God at the creation of the world. This being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, we must either conclude, that there will be a future state, in which all the moral obliquities of the present shall be made straight; or else admit, that the designs of infinite wisdom, goodness, and power, can be finally defeated by the perverse conduct of human weaknesses.—But this last supposition is so extravagantly absurd, Motives to Virtue. That the reality of a future state, the only other possible alternative, may be pronounced to have the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of perfect demonstration. Virtue has present rewards, and vice present punishments annexed to it; such rewards and punishments as make virtue, in most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> that happen, far more eligible than vice; but, in the infinite variety of human contingencies, it may sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> out, that the inflexible practice of virtue shall deprive a man of considerable advantages to himself, his family, or friends, which he might <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by a well-timed piece of roguery; suppose by betraying his trust, voting against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, selling his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or any other crime where the security against discovery shall heighten the temptation. Or, it may happen, that a strict adherence to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, to the cause of liberty and virtue, shall expose him, or his family, to the loss of everything, nay, to poverty, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, death itself, or to torments far more intolerable. Now what shall secure a man's virtue in circumstances of such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>? What shall enforce the obligations of conscience against the allurements of so many interests, the dread of so many and so terrible evils, and the almost unformidable aversion of human nature to excessive pain! The conflict is the greater, when the circumstances of the crime are such as easily admit a variety of alleviations from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, natural affection, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to one's family or friends, perhaps in indigence: these will give it even the air of virtue. Add to all, that the crime may be thought to have few bad consequences,—may be easily concealed,—or imagined possible to be retrieved in a good measure by future good conduct. It is obvious to which side most men will lean in such a case; and how much need there is of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> in the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, from the consideration of a God, of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and of an immortal state of retribution, to keep the mind firm and uncorrupted in those or like instances of singular trial or distress. But without supposing such peculiar instances, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of a governing Mind, and a persuasion that virtue is not only befriended by him here, but will be crowned by him hereafter with rewards suitable to its nature, vast in themselves, and immortal in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, must be not only a mighty support and incentive to the practice of virtue, but a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against vice. The thoughts of an Almighty Judge, and of an impartial future reckoning, are often alarming, inexplicably so, even to the floutest offenders. On the other hand, how supporting must it be to the good man, to think that he acts under the eye of his friend, as well as judge! How improving, to consider the present state as connected with a future one, and every relation in which he stands as a school of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> for his affections; every trial as the exercise of some virtue; and the virtuous deeds which result from both, as introductory to higher scenes of action and enjoyment! Finally, how transporting is it to view death as his discharge from the warfare of mortality, and a triumphant entry into a state of freedom, security, and perfection, in which knowledge and wisdom shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> upon him from every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; where each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> shall have its proper object: and his virtue, which was often damped or defeated here, shall be enthroned in undisturbed and eternal empire? On reviewing this short system of morals, and the advantages which support and enforce it, and comparing it with both the Christian scheme, what light and vigour do they borrow from thence! How clearly and fully does Christianity lay open the connexions of our nature, both material and immaterial, and future as well as present! What an ample and beautiful detail does it present of the duties we owe to God, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and ourselves, promulgated in the most simple, intelligible, and popular manner; divested of every partiality of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and adapted to the general state of mankind! With what bright and alluring examples does it illustrate and recommend the practice of those duties: and with what mighty sanctions does it enforce that practice! How strongly does it describe the corruptions of our nature; the deviations of our life from the rule of duty, and the causes of both! How marvellous and benevolent a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> does it unfold, by which those corruptions may be remedied, and our nature restored from its deviations to transcendent heights of virtue and piety! Finally, what a fair and comprehensive prospect does it give us of the administration of God, of which it represents the present state only as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and a period of warfare and trial! How solemn and unbounded are the scenes which it opens beyond it! the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead, the general judgment, the equal distribution of rewards and punishments to the good and the bad; and the full completion of divine wisdom and goodness in the final establishment of order, perfection, and happiness! How glorious then is that scheme of religion, and how worthy of affection as well as of admiration, which, by making such discoveries, and affording such affluences, has disclosed the unfading fruits and triumphs of virtue, and secured its interests beyond the power of time and chance. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">MORAL Sense</a>, that whereby we perceive what is good, virtuous, and beautiful, in actions, manners, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. See MORAL <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. MORALITY. See MORAL Philosophy. MORANT-Point, the most easterly point or promontory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Jamaica, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 75° 36'. N. Lat. 17° 56'.

MORASS

Pages 445-445

a marsh, fen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> low moist ground, which receives the waters from above without having any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to carry them off again. Somner derives the word from the Saxon merfe, "lake;" Salmasius from mare, "a collection of waters;" others from the German marath, "a muddy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>;" and others from marafe, of maricetum, à maricis, i.e. rufes. See Draining, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, there is a particular kind of morasses called moles, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-moles, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people dig their peat or turf for firing. See Moss.

MORAT

Pages 445-446
or Murten, a considerable town of Switzerland, Switzerland, capital of a bailiwick of the same name, belonging to the cantons of Bern and Friburg. It is seated on the lake Morat, on the road from Avenche to Bern, 10 miles west of Bern and 10 miles north-east of Friburg. The lake is about six miles long and two broad, and the country about it pleasant and well cultivated. The lakes of Morat and Neufchatel are parallel to each other, but the latter is more elevated, discharging itself by means of the river Broye into the lake of Neufchatel. According to M. de Luc, the former is 15 French feet above the level of Neufchatel lake; and both these lakes, as well as that of Biene, seem formerly to have extended considerably beyond their present limits, and from the position of the country appear to have been once united. Formerly the large fish named *lilurus glanis*, or the salath, frequented these lakes, but has not been caught in them for a long time past. The environs of this town and lake were carefully examined by Mr Coxe, during his residence in Switzerland, who made several excursions across the lake to a ridge of hills situated between it and Neufchatel. Here are many delightful prospects; particularly one from the top of Mount Vuilly, which, he says, is perhaps the only central spot from which the eye can at once comprehend the vast amphitheatre formed on one side by the Jura stretching from the environs of Geneva as far as Baille, and, on the other, by that stupendous chain of snowy Alps which extend from the frontiers of Italy to the confines of Germany, and is lost at each extremity in the horizon. Morat is celebrated for the obstinate defence it made against Charles the Bold, duke of Burgundy, and for the battle which afterwards followed on the 22d of June 1476, where the duke was defeated, and his army almost entirely destroyed*. Not far from the town, and adjoining to the high road, there still remains a monument of this victory. It is a square building, filled with the bones of Burgundian soldiers who were slain at the siege and in the battle; the number of which appears to have been very considerable. There are several inscriptions in the Latin and German languages commemorating the victory.

MORATA

Pages 446-446

*<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a> Fulvia*, an Italian lady, distinguished for her learning, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, in 1526. Her father, after teaching the belles lettres in several cities of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, was made preceptor to the two young princes of Ferrara, the sons of Alphonso I. The uncommon abilities he discovered in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> determined him to give her all the advantages of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Meanwhile the princes of Ferrara studying polite literature, it was judged expedient that she should have a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in the same pursuit; and Morata being called, she was heard by the astonished courtiers to declaim in Latin, to speak Greek, and to explain the paradoxes of Cicero. Her father dying, she was obliged to return home to take upon her the management of family affairs, and the education of her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> and three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>; both which she executed with the greatest diligence and success. In the meantime Andrew Grunthler, a young German physician, had married her, and with him she went to Germany, taking her brother along with her, whom she instructed in the Latin and Greek tongues; and after staying a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Augsburg, went to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHWEINFURT">Schweinfurt</a> in Franconia, where her husband was born: but they had not been there <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before that town was unhappily besieged and burnt; however, escaping the flames, they fled in the utmost distress to Hammelburg. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> they were also obliged to quit, and were reduced to the last extremities, when the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> Palatine invited Grunthler to be professor of physic at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>. He entered on his new office in 1554; but they no sooner began to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> the sweets of repose, than a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, occasioned by the distresses and hardships they had suffered, seized upon Morata, who died in 1555, in the 29th year of her <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and her husband and brother did not long survive her. She composed several works, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which were burnt with the town of Schweinfurt; the remainder, which consist of orations, dialogues, letters, and translations, were collected and published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of *Olympiae Fulviae Moratae, faminae doctissime, et <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> divinæ, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> omnia quæ hactenus inveneri potuerint; quibus Caëli secundi curiosis epistolæ ac orationes accerrent*.

MORAVIA

Pages 446-446

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, which rises in Bulgaria, runs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> through <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a> by Niša, and falls into the Danube at Semondria, to the eastward of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>. **Moravia**, a marquisate of Germany, derives the name of *Mahern*, as it is called by the Germans, and of *Morawa*, as it is called by the natives, from the river of that name, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Glatz, and passes through the middle of it. It is bounded to the south by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, to the north by Glatz and Silezia, to the west by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and to the east by Silezia and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>; being about 120 miles in length and 100 in breadth. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is overrun with woods and mountains, where the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but much wholesomer than in the low grounds, which are full of bogs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. The mountains, in general, are barren; but the more champaign parts tolerably fertile, yielding corn, with plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, good saffron, and pasture. Nor is it altogether destitute of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and garden stuff. Moravia also abounds in horses, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, sheep, and goats. In the woods and about the lakes there is plenty of wild fowl, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, venison, bees, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, hares, foxes, wolves, beavers, &c. This country affords marble, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and vitriol, with mineral waters, and warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is imported. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, Morawa, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Morau, are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, abound with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, crayfish, barbels, eels, perch, and many other sorts of fish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the inhabitants is a dialect of the Slavonic, differing little from the Bohemian; but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and citizens speak German and French. Moravia was anciently inhabited by the Quadi, who were driven out by the Slavni. Its kings, who were once powerful and independent, afterwards became dependent on, and tributary to, the German emperors and kings. At last, in the year 908, the Moravian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was parcelled out among the Germans, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, and Hungarians. In 1086, that part of it properly called Moravia was declared a marquisate by the German <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> Henry IV. and united with Bohemia, to whose dukes and kings it hath ever since been subject. Though it is not very populous, it contains about 42 greater or walled <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 17 smaller or open towns, and 198 market towns, besides villages, &c. The

MORDAUNT

Pages 446-447
Charles, earl of Peterborough, a celebrated commander both by sea and land, was the son of John Lord Mordaunt Viscount Avalon, and was born about the year 1638. In 1675 he succeeded his father in his honours and estate. While young he served under the admirals Torrington and Narborough in the Mediterranean against the Algerines; and in 1680 embarked for Africa with the earl of Plymouth, and distinguished himself at Tangier when it was besieged by the Moors. In the reign of James II. he voted against the repeal of the test act; and disliking the measures of the court, obtained leave to go to Holland to accept the command of a Dutch squadron in the West Indies. He afterwards accompanied the prince of Orange into this kingdom; and upon his advancement to the throne, was sworn of the privy-council, made one of the lords of the bedchamber to his majesty, also first commissioner of the treasury, and advanced to the dignity of earl of Monmouth. But in November 1690 he was dismissed from his post in the treasury. On the death of his uncle Henry earl of Peterborough in 1697, he succeeded to that title; and, upon the accession of Queen Anne, was invested with the commission of captain-general and governor of Jamaica. In 1705 he was sworn of the privy-council; and the same year declared general and commander in chief of the forces sent to Spain, and joint admiral of the fleet with Sir Cloudley Shovel, of which the year following he had the sole command. His taking Barcelona with a handful of men, and afterwards relieving it when greatly distressed by the enemy; his driving out of Spain the duke of Anjou, and the French army, which consisted of 25,000 men, though his own troops never amounted to 10,000; his gaining possession of Catalonia, of the kingdoms of Valencia, Arragon, and the isle of Majorca, with part of Murcia and Castile, and thereby giving the earl of Galway an opportunity of advancing to Madrid without a blow; are astonishing instances of his bravery and conduct. For these important services his lordship was declared general in Spain by Charles III. afterwards emperor of Germany; and on his return to England he received the thanks of the house of lords. His lordship was afterwards employed in several embassies to foreign courts, installed knight of the Garter, and made governor of Minorca. In the reign of George I. he was general of all the marine forces in Great Britain, in which post he was continued by King George II. He died in his passage to Lisbon, where he was going for the recovery of his health, in 1735. His lordship was distinguished by various shining qualities: for, to the greatest personal courage and resolution, he added all the arts and address of a general; a lively and penetrating genius; and a great extent of knowledge upon almost every subject of importance within the compass of ancient and modern literature; hence his familiar letters, inserted among those of his friend Mr Pope, are an ornament to that excellent collection.

MORDELLA

Pages 447-447

a genus of insects of the coleoptera order. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORE

Pages 447-449

Sir Thomas, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, the son of Sir John More, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, one of the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, was born in the year 1482, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">Milk</a>-street <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He was first sent to a school at St Anthony's in Threadneedle Street; and afterward introduced into the family of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Moreton, who in 1497 sent him to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. During his residence at the university he constantly attended the lectures of Linacre and Grocinus, on the Greek and Latin languages. Having in the space of about two years made considerable proficiency in academical learning, he came to New Inn in London, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; whence, after some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn, of which his father was a member. Notwithstanding his application to the law, however, being now about 23 years old, he was so bigotted to monkish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, that he wore a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> shirt next his skin, frequently fasted, and often slept on a bare plank. In the year 1533, being then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he distingued himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> for granting a subsidy and three fifteenths for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Henry VII.'s eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, Margaret, to the king of Scotland. The motion was rejected; and the king was so highly offended at this opposition from a beardless boy, that he revenged himself on Mr More's father, by sending him, on a frivolous pretence, to the Tower, and obliging him to pay 100l. for his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Being now called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he was appointed law reader at Furnival's inn, which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he held about three years; but about this time he also read a public lecture in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Lawrence, Old Jewry, upon St Austin's treatise De Civitate Dei, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. He had indeed formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of becoming a Franciscan friar, but was dissuaded from it; and, by the advice of Dr Colet, married Jane, the eldest daughter of John <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLT">Colt</a>, Esq., of Newhall in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. In 1538 he was appointed judge of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London, was made a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, and became very eminent at the bar. In 1546 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> in the retinue of Bishop Tonstall, and Dr Knight, who were sent by King Henry VIII. to renew the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the archduke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. On his return, Cardinal Wolsey would have engaged Mr More in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and offered him a pension, which he refused. Nevertheless, it was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he accepted the place of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the requests, was created a knight, admitted of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and in 1520 made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the exchequer. About this time he built a house on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, at Chelsea, and married a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife. This wife, whose name was Middleton, and a widow, was old, ill tempered, and covetous; nevertheless Erasmus says, he was as fond of her as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she were a young maid. In the 14th year of Henry VIII. Sir Thomas More was made speaker of the house of commons; in which capacity he had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to oppose the then powerful minister, Wolsey, in his demand of an oppressive subsidy; notwithstanding which, it was not long before he was made chancellor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, and was treated by the king with singular familiarity. The king having once dined with Sir Thomas at Chelsea, walked with him near an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> in the garden, with his arm round his neck. After he was gone, Mr Roper, Sir Thomas's son-in-law, observed how happy he was to be so familiarly treated by the king: to which Sir Thomas replied, "I thank our lord, son Roper, I find his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> my very good lord indeed, and believe he doth as singularly favour me as any subject within this realm: howbeit, I must tell thee, I have no cause to be proud thereof; for if my head would win him a castle in France, it would not fail to go off." From this anecdote it appears, that Sir Thomas knew his grace to be a villain. In 1526 he was sent with Cardinal Wolsey and others, on a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> embassy to France, and in 1529 with Bishop Tonstall to Cambrai. The king, it seems, was so well satisfied with his services on these occasions, that in the following year, Wolsey being disgraced, he made him chancellor; which seems the more extraordinary, when we are told that Sir Thomas had repeatedly declared his disapprobation of the king's divorce, on which the great defender of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> was so positively bent. Having executed the office of chancellor about three years, with equal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and integrity, he resigned the seals in 1533, probably to avoid the danger of his refusing to confirm the king's divorce. He now retired to his house at Chelsea; dismissed many of his servants; sent his children with their respective families to their own houses (for hitherto, he had, it seems, maintained all his children, with their families, in his own house, in the true style of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>); and spent his time in study and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>: but the capricious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> would not suffer him to enjoy his tranquillity. Though now reduced to a private station, and even to indigence, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the legality of the king's marriage with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Boleyn was deemed of so much importance, that various means were tried to procure his approbation; but all persuasion proving ineffectual, he was, with some others, attainted in the house of lords of misprision of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, for encouraging <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Barton, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in her treasonable practices. His innocence in this affair appeared so clearly, that they were obliged to strike his name out of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. He was then accused of other crimes, but with the same effect; till, refusing to take the oath enjoined by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of supremacy, he was committed to the Tower, and, after 15 months imprisonment, was tried at the bar of the king's bench for high treason, in denying the king's supremacy. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> rested on the sole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of Rich the solicitor general, whom Sir Thomas, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, sufficiently discredited; nevertheless the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> brought him in guilty, and he was condemned to suffer as a traitor. The merciful Harry, however, indulged him with simple decollation; and he was accordingly beheaded on Tower hill, on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1535. His body, which was first interred in the Tower, was begged by his daughter Margaret, and deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of the church at Chelsea, where a monument, with an inscription written by himself, had been some time before erected. This monument with the inscription is still to be seen in that church. The same daughter, Margaret, also procured his head after it had remained 14 days upon London <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and placed it in a vault belonging to the Roper family, under a chapel adjoining to St Dunstan's church in Canterbury. Sir Thomas More was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of some learning, and an upright judge; a very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, yet cheerful, and even affectedly witty. witty (A). He wanted not sagacity, where religion was out of the question; but in that his faculties were so enveloped, as to render him a weak and credulous enthusiast. He left one son and three daughters; of whom Margaret, the eldest, was very remarkable for her knowledge of the Greek and Latin languages. She married a Mr Roper of Wellhall in Kent, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> Sir Thomas More was published by Mr Hearne at Oxford in 1716. Mrs Roper died in 1544; and was buried in the vault of St Dunstan's in Canterbury, with her father's head in her arms. Sir Thomas was the author of various works, though his Utopia is the only performance that has survived in the esteem of the world; owing to the rest being chiefly of a polemic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: his answer to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> has only gained him the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of having the best knack of any man in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, at calling bad names in good Latin. His English works were collected and published by order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, in 1557; his Latin, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, in 1563, and at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, in 1566.

MOREA

Pages 449-449

formerly called the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, to which it is joined by the isthmus of Corinth. Its form resembles a mulberry <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and its name is derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mulberry trees which it produces. It is about 180 miles in length, and 130 in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> fertile, except in the middle, where it is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and is watered by a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. It is divided into three provinces; Scania, Belvedera, and Brazzo-di-Maina. It was taken from the Turks by the Venetians in 1687; but they lost it again in 1715. The sangiac of the Morea resides at Modon. See GREECE and PELOPONNESUS.

MOREFA

Pages 449-449

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Myfa, in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was occupied by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a>, formerly at the head of a band of robbers, but afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Abrettenus, and enriched with possessions, first by Antony, and then by Cæsar.

MOREL

Pages 449-449

the name of several celebrated printers to the kings of France, who, like the Stephens, were also men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning. Frederic Morel, who was interpreter in the Greek and Latin tongues, as well as printer to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, was heir to Valcozan, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> he had married.—He was born in Champagne, and he died in an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1583. His sons and grandsons trode in his steps; they distinguished themselves in literature, and maintained also the reputation which he had acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. The edition of St Gregory of Nyssa, by his son <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> Morel, is held in great estimation by the learned. Morel, Frederic, son of the preceding, and still more celebrated than his father, was professor and interpreter to the king, and printer in ordinary for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, Latin, and French languages. He was so devoted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, that when he was told his wife was at the point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he would not stir till he had finished the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which he had begun. Before it was finished, he was informed that she was actually dead: I am sorry for it (replied he coldly), she was an excellent woman. This printer acquired great reputation from the works which he published, which were very numerous and beautifully executed. From the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> in the king's library, he published several treatises of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, Theodore, St Cyril; and he accompanied them with a translation. His edition of the works of Oecumenius and Aretas, in 2 vols. folio, is much esteemed. In short, after distinguishing himself by his knowledge in the languages, he died <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 27, 1630, at the age of 78. His sons and grandsons followed the same profession. Morel, William, regius professor of Greek, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the king's printing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Paris, died 1564. He composed a Dictionnaire Grec-Latin Francois, which was published in quarto in 1622, and some other works which indicate very extensive learning. His editions of the Greek authors are exceedingly beautiful. This great scholar, who was of a different family from the preceding, had a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> named John, who died in prison (where he had been confined for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>) at the age of 20, and whose body was dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, and burnt Feb. 27, 1559. They were of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Tillieul, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MORTAIN">Mortain</a> in Normandy.

MORESQUE

Pages 449-449

Moresk, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Morisco, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, carving, &c. done after the manner of the Moors; consisting of several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> pieces and compartments promiscuously intermingled, not containing any perfect <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or other animal, but a wild resemblance of birds, beasts, trees, &c. There are also called arabesques, and are particularly used in embroideries, damask <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, &c. Moresque Dances, vulgarly called Morrice dances, are those altogether in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Moors, as farabands, chacons, &c. and are usually performed with castanets, tambours, &c. There are few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> places in England where the morrice dance is not known. It was probably introduced about, or a little before, the reign of Henry VIII. and is a dance of young men in their shirts, with bells at their feet, and ribbands of various colours tied round their arms and flung across their shoulders. MORGAGNA. See FATA.

MORGAGNI

Pages 449-450

John Baptist, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine, first professor of anatomy in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, and member of several of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of learned men in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, was born in the year 1682, at Forli, a town in the district of La Romagna in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. His (A) This last disposition, we are told, he could not restrain even at his execution. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> being come, he ascended the scaffold, which seemed so weak that it was ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; whereupon, "I pray (said he) see me safe up, and for my coming <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> let me shift for myself." His prayers being ended, he turned to the executioner, and with a cheerful countenance said, "Pluck up thy spirits, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and be not afraid to do thy office; my neck is very short, take heed therefore thou strike not awry for saving thy honesty." Then laying his head upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, he bade him stay until he had put aside his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, saying, "That had never committed any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>." of his physician, and that of professor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, with a pension of £200 per annum. The Praeudium Botanicum, which he published in 1669, procured him so much reputation, that the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> invited him to the professorship of botany in 1669; which he accepted, and acquitted himself in it with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ability. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1683, aged 63. He published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>, in 2 vols. folio; with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, Plantarum Historia Oxoniensis Universalis. The first part of this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has not been printed; and it is not known what has become of it.

MORGES

Pages 48-48

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some trade, and situated on the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, five miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 42'. N. Lat. 46° 29'.

MORGO

Pages 48-48

anciently **Amorgos**, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, which produces wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and corn. It is well cultivated, and the inhabitants are affable, and generally of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The best parts belong to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. The greatest inconvenience in this island is the want of wood. It is 30 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26° 15'. N. Lat. 36° 30'.

MORIAH

Pages 48-48

one of the eminences of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; on which <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> went to offer his son, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> wanted to build the temple, which was afterwards executed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>: The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of Araunah; originally narrow, so scarce to contain the temple, but enlarged by means of ramparts; and surrounded with a triple wall, so as to add <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength to the temple, (Josephus). It may be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, to which it was joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> and gallery, (Id.)

MORILLES

Pages 48-48

a kind of mushroom, about the size of a walnut, pierced with holes like a honeycomb, and said to be good for creating an appetite. It is often used in sauces and ragouts.

MORINA

Pages 48-48

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDRIA">andria</a> clas*; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, *Aggregate*. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**.

MORINDA

Pages 48-48

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the *pentandra clas*, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, *Aggregate*. See **<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>**.

MORINORUM CASTELLUM

Pages 48-48

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>*, simply *Castellum* (Antonine); situated on an eminence, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on its top, in the territory of the Morini. Now *Mont Cofel*, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>.

MORISON

Pages 48-66

ROBERT**, physician and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, was born at Aberdeen in 1620, bred at the university there, and taught <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it; but having a strong inclination to botany, made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in that science. The civil wars obliged him to leave his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; which, however, he did not do till he had first signalized his zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and his courage, in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the inhabitants of Aberdeen and the Presbyterian troops on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of Aberdeen, in which he received a dangerous wound on the head. As soon as he was cured of it, he went into France; and fixing at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he applied assiduously to botany and anatomy. He was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, who gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>. He exercised the office till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and afterwards went over to England in 1660. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., to whom the duke of Orleans had presented him at Blois, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of... veal it from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the king's resentment, he opened a hole in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and after he had whispered there that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDAS">Midas</a> had the ears of an ass, he covered the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as before, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had buried his words in the ground. On that place, as the poets mention, grew a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of reeds, which when agitated by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> uttered the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> that had been buried beneath, and published to the world that Midas had the ears of an ass. Some explain the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of the ears of Midas, by the supposition that he kept a number of informers and spies, who were continually employed in gathering every seditious word that might drop from the mouths of his subjects. Midas, according to Strabo, died of drinking bull's hot blood. This he did, as Plutarch mentions, to free himself from the numerous ill <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> which continually tormented him. Midas, according to some, was son of Cybele. He built a town which he called Ancyra.

MORISONIA

Pages 450-450

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONADELPHIA">monadelphia</a> class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 25th order, Putaminæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORLACHIA

Pages 450-452

a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. The inhabitants are called Morlacks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Morlacchi; they inhabit the pleasant valleys of Koter, along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Kerha, Cettina, Narenta, and among the inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Dalmatia. The inhabitants are by some said to be of Walachian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, as is indicated by their name; Morlachia being a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of Mauro <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Walachia: and the Walachians are said to be descendants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman colonies planted in these countries. This, however, is denied by the Abbé Fortis, who published a volume of travels into that country. He informs us, that the origin of the Morlacchi is involved in the darkness of barbarous ages, together with that of many other nations, resembling them too much in customs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that they may be taken for one people, dispersed in the vast tracts from the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the Frozen ocean. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the name, the Abbé observes, that the Morlacchi generally call themselves, in their own language, Vlachi; a national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, of which no vestige is found in the records of Dalmatia till the 13th century. It signifies powerful men, or men of authority; and the denomination of Moro Vlachi, corruptly Morlacchi, as they are now called, may perhaps point out the original of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. This word may possibly signify the conquerors that came from the sea; moor, in all the dialects of the Slavonian language, signifying the sea. With regard to the character of these people, we are informed that they are much injured by their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> neighbours. The inhabitants of the sea <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Dalmatia tell many frightful stories of their avarice and cruelty; but these, in our author's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, are all either of an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any have happened in latter times, they ought rather to be ascribed to the corruption of a few individuals, than to the bad disposition of the nation in general; and though thievish tricks are frequent among them, he informs us, that a stranger may travel securely through their country, where he is faithfully escorted, and hospitably treated. As to the Morlacchi themselves, they are represented as open and sincere to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they would be taken for simpletons in any other country; and by means of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> they have been so often duped by the Italians, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of an Italian and the faith of a dog, are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> among the Morlacchi. They are very hospitable to strangers; and their hospitality is equally conspicuous among the rich and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Morlachia. The rich prepares a roasted lamb or sheep, and the poor with equal cordiality offers whatever he has; nor is this generosity confined to strangers, but generally extends itself to all who are in want. When a Morlack is on a journey, and comes to lodge at a friend's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the family, or the new married <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>, if there happen to be one, receives and kisses him when he alights from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or at the door of the house: but a foreigner is rarely favoured with these <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> civilities; on the contrary, the women, if they are young, hide themselves, and keep out of his way. The Morlacchi in general have little notion of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy, and readily consume in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> as much as would be sufficient for several months, whenever any occasion of merriment presents itself. A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the holiday of the saint protector of the family, the arrival of relations or friends, or any other joyful incident, consumes of course all that there is to eat and to drink in the house. Yet the Morlack is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> economist in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his wearing apparel; for rather than spoil his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, he takes it off, let it <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> ever so hard, and goes bareheaded in the storm. In the same manner he treats his shoes, if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is dirty and they are not very old. Nothing but an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPOTENCE">impotence</a> hinders a Morlack from being punctual; and if he cannot repay the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he borrowed at the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he carries a small present to his creditor, and requests a longer term. Friendship is lasting among the Morlacchi. They have even made it a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> point, and tie the sacred bond at the foot of the altar. The Slavonian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> contains a particular benediction for the solemn union of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> or two female friends in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>. The male friends thus united are called Pobratimi, and the female Pojefreme, which means half-brothers and half-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>.
