From those consecrated friendships among the Morlacchi and other nations of the same origin, it should seem that the sworn brothers arose; a denomination frequent enough among the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between these and the Pobratimi of Morlachia consists not only in the want of the ritual <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the union itself. For, among the Morlacchi, the sole view is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and advantage; but such a brotherhood among the Italians is generally commenced by bad men, to enable them the more to hurt and disturb <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. But as the friendships of the Morlacchi are strong and sacred, so their quarrels are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> unextinguishable. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from father to son; and the mothers fail not to put their children in mind of their duty to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> their father if he has had the misfortune to be killed, and to show them often the bloody shirt and arms of the dead. And so deeply is revenge rooted in the minds of this nation, that all the missionaries in the world would not be able to eradicate it. A Morlack is naturally inclined to do good to his fellow creatures, and is full of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the smallest benefit; but implacable if injured or insulted. A Morlack who has killed another of a powerful family, is commonly obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself by flight; and Malacchi, and to keep out of the way for several years. If during that time he has been fortunate enough to escape the search of his pursuers, and has got a small sum of money, he endeavours to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> and peace; and, that he may treat about the conditions in person, he asks and obtains a safe conduct, which is faithfully maintained, though only verbally granted. Then he finds mediators; and, on the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the relations of the two hostile families are assembled, and the criminal is introduced, dragging himself along on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, the mufket, piftol, or cutlass, with which he committed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, hung about his neck; and while he continues in that humble posture, one or more of the relations recites a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on the dead, which sometimes rekindles the flames of revenge, and puts the poor prostrate in no small danger. The Morlack, whether they happen to be of the Roman or of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, have very singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> about <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of their teachers daily augments this monstrous evil. They are as firmly persuaded of the reality of witches, fairies, enchantments, nocturnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a>, and fortifies, as if they had seen a thousand examples of them. Nor do they make the least doubt about the existence of vampires: and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them, as in Transylvania, the sucking the blood of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>. Therefore, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> dies suspected of becoming a vampire, or vu-kodlik, as they call it, they cut his hams, and prick his whole body with pins; pretending, that after this operation he cannot walk about. There are even instances of Morlacchi, who, imagining that they may possibly thirst for children's blood after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, entreat their heirs, and sometimes oblige them to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, to treat them as vampires when they die. A most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> reigns in Morlachia, as it generally does in other parts, between the Latin and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, which their respective priests fail not to foment, and tell a thousand little scandalous stories of each other. The churches of the Latins are poor, but not very dirty; those of the Greeks are equally poor, and shamefully ill kept. Our author has seen the curate of a Morlack village sitting on the ground in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, to hear the confession of women on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> by his side: a strange posture indeed! but a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the innocent manners of those good people, who have the most profound veneration for their spiritual pastors, and a total dependence upon them; who, on their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, frequently make use of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, and correct the bodies of their offending flock with the cudgel. Innocence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of pastoral ages, are still preferred among the Morlacchi, or at least many traces of them remain in the places farthest distant from our settlements. Pure cordiality of sentiment is not there restrained by other regards, and displays itself without any distinction of circumstances. A young handsome Morlack girl, who meets a man of her district on the road, kisses him affectionately, without the least imputation of impropriety; and M. Fortis has seen all the women and girls, all the young men and old, kissing one another as they came into the churchyard on a holiday; so that they looked as if they all belonged to one family. He often observed the same thing on the road, and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the maritime <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the Morlacchi came to sell their Morlacchi commodities. The dress of the unmarried women is the most complex and whimsical, in respect to the ornaments of the head; for when married they are not allowed to wear anything else but a handkerchief, either <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or coloured tied about it. The girls use a scarlet cap, to which they commonly hang a veil falling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the shoulders, as a mark of their virginity. The better sort adorn their caps with strings of silver coins, among which are frequently seen very ancient and valuable ones; they have moreover <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> rings of very curious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and small silver chains with the figures of half moons fastened to the ends of them. But the poor are forced to content themselves with plain caps; or if they have any ornaments, they consist only of small exotic shells, round glass beads, or bits of tin. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> merit of these caps, which constitute the good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> as well as vanity of the Morlack young ladies, is to attract and fix the eyes of all who are near them by the multitude of ornaments, and the noise they make on the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of their heads. Both old and young women wear about their necks <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> strings of round glass beads, of various size and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; and many rings of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, tin, or silver, on their fingers. Their bracelets are of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> covered with wrought tin or silver; and they embroider their stomachers, or adorn them with beads or shells. But the use of stays is unknown, nor do they put whalebone or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in the stomacher. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> woollen girdle surrounds their petticoat, which is commonly decked with shells, and of blue colour, and therefore called modrina. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> as well as petticoat, is of a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGE">serge</a>; and both reach near to the ankle: the gown is bordered with scarlet, and called fadak. They use no modrina in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and only wear the fadak without sleeves over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> petticoat or shift. The girls always wear <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> stockings; and their shoes are like those of the men, called opanke. The sole is of undressed ox hide, and the upper part of sheep's skin thongs knotted, which they call apute; and these they fasten above the ankles, something like the ancient cothurnus. The unmarried women, even of the richest families, are not permitted to wear any other sort of shoes; though after marriage, they may, if they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, lay aside the opanke, and use the Turkish slippers. The girls keep their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> tressed under their caps, but when married they let it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> dishevelled on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; sometimes they tie it under the chin; and always have medals, beads, or bored coins, in the Tartar or American <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> twisted amongst it. Nothing is more common among the Morlacchi than marriages concluded between the old people of the respective families, especially when the parties live at a great distance, and neither see nor know each other; and the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of these alliances is the ambition of being related to a numerous and powerful family, famous for having produced valiant men. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> is very rare; nor does the father of the maid inquire much into the circumstances of the family that asks her. Sometimes a daughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> is given in marriage to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> or tenant, as was usual in patriarchal times; so little are the women regarded in this country. But on these occasions, the Morlacchi girls enjoy the privilege of refusal. For he who acts by proxy, having obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, is obliged to go and bring the bridegroom: and, if on seeing each other, the young people are reciprocally content, the marriage is concluded, but not otherwise. In some parts it is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the bride to go to see the house and family of the proposed husband, before she gives a definitive answer; and if the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or persons are disagreeable to her, she is at liberty to annul the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>. The bride is conducted to a church, veiled, and surrounded by the friends of the bridegroom, or svati, as they are called, on horseback; and the sacred ceremony is performed amidst the noise of muskets, pistols, barbaric shouts and acclamations, which continue till the return to her father's house or to that of her husband, if not far off. The first day's entertainment is sometimes made at the bride's house, but generally at the bridegroom's, whither the svati hasten immediately after the nuptial benediction; and at the same time three or four men run on foot to tell the good news; the first who gets to the house has a kind of a towel embroidered at the ends, as a premium. The domachin, or head of the house, comes out to meet his daughter-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and a child is handed to her, before she alights, to care for it; and if there happen to be none in the house, the child is borrowed from one of the neighbours. When she alights, she kneels down, and kisses the threshold.—Then the mother-in-law, or in her place some other female relation, presents a corn sieve, full of different kinds of grain, nuts, almonds, and other small fruit, which the bride scatters upon the svati, by handfuls, behind her back. The bride does not sit at the great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> the first day, but has one apart for herself, the two diversi, and the flaeboe. The bridegroom sits at table with the svati; but in all that day, consecrated to the matrimonial union, he must neither unloosen nor cut any thing whatever. The knum carves his meat, and cuts his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. It is the domachin's business to give the toast; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>-fvati is the first who pledges him. Generally the bukkara, a very large wooden cup, goes round, first to the saint protector of the family; next to the prosperity of the holy faith; and sometimes to a name the most sublime and venerable. The most extravagant abundance reigns at these feasts; and each of the svati contributes, by sending a share of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. The dinner begins with fruit and cheese; and the soup comes last, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> contrary to our custom. All sorts of domestic fowls, kid, lamb, and sometimes venison, are heaped in prodigal quantities upon their tables. These nuptial feasts, called sfdrave by the ancient Huns, are by the Morlacchi called sfdravize, from whence the Italian word sfdravizzzo is undoubtedly derived. They continue three, six, eight, or more days, according to the ability or prodigal disposition of the family where they are held. The new married wife gets no inconsiderable profit in these days of joy; and it usually amounts to much more than all the portion she brings with her, which often consists of nothing but her own clothes and perhaps a cow; nay, it happens sometimes that the parents, instead of giving money with their daughter, get something from the bridegroom by way of price. The bride carries <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> every morning, to wash the hands of her guests as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the feasting lasts; and each of them throws a small piece of money into the basin after performing that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, which is a very rare one among them, excepting on such occasions. The Morlacchi pass their youth in the woods, attending their flocks and herds; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of quiet and leisure they often become dextrous in carving with a simple <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>: they make wooden cups, and whistles adorned with fanciful bas-reliefs, which are not void of merit, and at least show the genius of the people.

MORNAY

Pages 452-453

PHILIPPE DE, seigneur du Plessis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARLY">Marly</a>, was born at Buhy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Eilhuy in Upper Normandy in France, in 1549, and was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. What was then thought a prodigy in a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, he made a rapid progress in the belles lettres, in the learned languages, and in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. He was at first destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but the principles of Calvinism, which he had imbibed from his mother, effectively excluded him from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments to which he was entitled by his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, abilities, and birth. After the horrible massacre of St Bartholomew, Philippe de Mornay made the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Germany, England, and the Low Countries; and he was equally improved and delighted by his travels. Mornay afterwards joined the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Navarre, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> leader of the Protestant party, and so well known since by the name of Henry IV. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> sent Mornay, who employed his whole abilities, both as a soldier and a writer, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Protestant cause, to conduct a negociation with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of England; and left him wholly to his own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> in the management of that business. He was successful in almost every negociation, because he conducted it like an able politician, and not with a spirit of intrigue. He tenderly loved Henry IV, and spoke to him on all occasions as to a friend. When he was wounded at Aunale, he wrote to him in these words: "Sire, You have <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough acted the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Alexander, it is now time you should <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> that of Caesar. It is our duty to die for your majesty, &c. It is glorious for you, Sire, that I dare venture to tell you it is your duty to live for us." This faithful subject did everything in his power to raise Henry to the throne. But when he deserted the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, he reproached him in the bitterest manner, and retired from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Henry still loved him; and was extremely affected with an insult which he received in 1597 from one Saint Phal, who <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> him with a cudgel, and left him for dead. Mornay demanded <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> from the king, who gave him the following answer, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> as well of his spirit as of his goodness of heart. "Monsieur Duplefis, I am exceedingly offended at the insult you have received; and I sympathize with you both as your sovereign and your friend. In the former capacity, I shall do justice to you and to myself; and had I sustained only the character of your friend, there are few perhaps who would have drawn their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or sacrificed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> more cheerfully in your cause. Be satisfied, then, that I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> act the part of a king, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and a friend," &c. Mornay's knowledge, probity, and valour, made him the foul of the Protestant party, and procured him the contemptuous appellation of the Pope of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>. He defended their doctrines both by speech and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. One of his books on the Iniquity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">Mass</a>, having stirred up all the Catholic divines, he refused to make any reply to their censures and criticisms except in a public conference. This was accordingly appointed to be held A.D. 1600, at Fountainbleau, where the court then was. The two champions were, Du Perron bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVREUX">Evreux</a>, and Mornay. After a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many arguments and replies on both sides, the victory was adjudged to Du Perron. He had boasted that he would point out to the satisfaction of every one five hundred errors in his adversary's book, and he partly kept his word. The Calvinists did not fail to claim the victory on this occasion, and they still continue to do so. This conference, instead of putting an end to the differences, was productive of new quarrels among the controversialists, and of much profane <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTINES">libertines</a>. A Huguenot minister, who was present at the conference, observed with great concern to a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the same party, "The bishop of Evreux has already driven Mornay from several strong holds." "No <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> (replied the folder), provided he does not drive him from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>." This was an important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the river <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, of which Duplessis was governor. Hither he retired, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> being constantly occupied in defending the Huguenots, and in making himself formidable to the Catholics. When <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII. was making preparations against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, Duplessis wrote him a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, dissuading him from such a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>. After employing the most plausible arguments, he concludes in the following manner: "To make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the subject, is an indication of weakness in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Authority consists in the quiet submission of the people, and is established by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and justice of the governor. Force of arms ought never to be employed except in repelling a foreign enemy. The late king would have sent the new ministers of state to learn the first elements of politics, who like unskilful surgeons would apply violent remedies to every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and advise a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to cut off an arm when his finger aches." These remonstrances produced no other effect than the loss of the government of Saumur, of which he was deprived by Louis XIII. in 1621. He died two years after, November 11, 1623, aged 74, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARONY">barony</a> de la Foret-sur-Seure in Poitou. The Protestant cause never had an abler supporter, or one who did it more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> by his virtues and abilities. Censeur des courtisans, mais à la cour aimé; Fier ennemi de Rome, et de Rome estimé.—Henriade. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his works: 1. Un Traité de l'Eucharistie, 1604, in folio. 2. Un Traité de la vérité de la <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> Chrétienne, 8vo. 3. A book entitled La Mystère d'Iniquité, 4to. 4. Un discours sur le droit pretendu par ceux de la maison de Guise, 8vo. 5. Curious and interesting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> from the year 1572 to 1629, 4 vols. 4to. valuable. 6. Letters; which are written with great spirit and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> des Liques has given us his life in quarto; a book more interesting for the matter than the manner.

MORNE-GAROU

Pages 453-453

a very remarkable volcanic mountain on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Vincent's in the West Indies. It was visited by Mr James Anderson surgeon in the year 1764. See ST VINCENTS.

MORNING

Pages 453-453

the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> rising. The astronomers reckon morning, mane, from the time of midnight to that of mid-day. Thus an eclipse is said to begin at 11 o'clock in the morning, &c. Morning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>, is the planet Venus, when a little to the westward of the sun; that is, when she rises a little before. In this situation she is called by the Greeks Phosphorus; by the Latins Lucifer, &c.

MOROC

Pages 453-453
or MAROC, a beautiful bird of Abyssinia, described by Mr Bruce, who thinks its name is derived from mar, "honey," though he says that he never heard it was further concerned in the honey than destroying bees. It seems to pursue those insects out of enmity or diversion as well as for food, leaving great numbers dead on the ground, besides those which it devours for food. The moroc resembles the cuckoo in size and shape, but differs in other respects. Its mouth is very wide, the opening reaching almost to its eyes; the inside of the mouth and throat yellow, the tongue sharp-pointed, and capable of being drawn almost half its length out of the mouth beyond the point of its beak, and is very flexible. The head and neck are brown, without any mixture of other colours: there are likewise a number of very small and scarcely visible hairs at the root of the beak. This seems to be the bird mentioned by Sparman under the name of cuculus indicator, which (he says) has the singular property of discovering the nests of wild bees, and leading travellers by a certain cry to the place where the treasure is deposited. According to Sparman's account, it makes known these discoveries by the same cry to foxes as well as to the human species; but Jerome Lobo, who mentions the Abyssinian bird, takes no notice of the foxes, though he mentions its singing melodiously when it arrives at the place where the honey is deposited. Both these accounts are severely criticised by Mr Bruce, who says, that honey is so abundant on every hillock and every tree, that a bird possessing this faculty could be of no use to man or to any other animal in that country, and that having never heard of such a bird in Abyssinia, he considers the account of it as a fiction.

MOROCCO

Pages 453-465

an empire of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, comprehending Situation a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, is bound and bounded on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>; on the east by daries, the river Mulvya, which separates it from Algiers; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Mediterranean; and on the south by Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather by the river <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SUS">Sus</a>, which divides it from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Tafilet. Its greatest length is from the north-east to the south-west, amounting to above 590 miles; its breadth is not above 260 where broadest, and in the narrowest places it is not above half that breadth. The ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Morocco has been already History given under the article MAURITANIA. It <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> under the dominion of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> upwards of 400 years. On the decline of that empire it fell under the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, who held it till about the year 600, when the Goths were driven out by the Vandals, the Vandals by the Greeks, and they in their turn by the Saracens, who conquered not only this empire, but may say the whole continent of Africa; at least their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, one way or other, is to be found in all parts of it. The Saracen empire did not continue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> united under one head, and many princes set up for themselves in Africa as well as elsewhere, through whose dissensions the Almoravides were at length raised to the sovereignty, as related under the article Algiers, No. 2. Yulef, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> monarch of that line, built the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Morocco, conquered the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and the Moorish dominions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; all which were lost by his grandson Abbu Halli, who was defeated and killed by the Spaniards. On this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> passed to the Mohedians, or Almohedes, with whom it had not continued above three generations, when Mohammed the son of Al Manfur lost the famous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Sierra Morena, in which 200,000 Moors were slain, and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which Alphonso X. retook a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many of the Moorish conquests immediately after. Mohammed died soon after this disgrace, and left several sons, between whom a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> ensued, during which the viceroys of Fez, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, and Tremefen, found means to establish themselves as independent princes. At length one of the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> blood of Tremefen having defeated the Almohedes, made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the kingdoms of Morocco and Fez, and entailed them on his own family. In a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, this family was expelled by the Merini, the Merini by the Oatazes, and these by the Sharifs of Hafcen, who have kept the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> ever since. Nothing can be conceived more unjust and despotic than the government of Morocco, and nothing more degenerate than the character of the people. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is allowed to have not only an uncontrollable power over the lives and fortunes of his subjects, but in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> over their consciences, in as much as he is the only person who, as the successor of the prophet, has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to interpret the Koran; and appoints all the judges under him, of whom those of Morocco and Fez are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, whose business it is to explain and dispense all matters relating to their religion; and who, being his creatures and dependents, dare not steer otherwise than as he directs. Whenever therefore the laws are enacted by him, and proclaimed by his governors in all the provinces, as is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> done, that none may plead <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, they are everywhere received with an implicit and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> submission. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the subjects are bred up with a notion, that those who die in the execution of his command are entitled to an immediate admittance into paradise, and those who have the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to die by his hand to a still greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in it. After this we need not wonder at finding so much cruelty, oppression, and tyranny on the one side, and so much submission, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, and misery on the other. This latter, however, extends no farther than the Moors: for as to the mountaineers, the subjection and tribute they pay to those tyrants was always involuntary; and as for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, their zeal and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> is owing merely to the great sway and power which they have gained in the government, on various accounts. They were first introduced, or rather their importation increased, by the policy of Muley Ishmael, a late emperor, at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when there was a great decrease of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in the empire, occasioned in some degree by the enormous cruelties exercised by its former sovereigns, who have been known not unfrequently, through a slight disgust, to abandon a whole town or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. In the character of Muley Ishmael were found the most singular inconsistencies; for it is certain, that although a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, yet in other respects, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> to repair the mischief which he committed, he left nothing undone for the encouragement of population.—He introduced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> colonies of negroes from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>; built <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> for them, many of which are still remaining, affiged them portions of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and encouraged their increase by every possible means. He soon initiated them in the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; and had his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> been followed, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> by this time would have been populous, and probably flourishing. As the negroes are of a more lively, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and enterprising disposition than the Moors, they might soon have been taught the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; and their singular ingenuity might have been directed to other useful purposes. It is true, Muley Ishmael, when he adopted this plan, had more objects in view than that of merely peopling his dominions. He <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> plainly that his own subjects were of too capricious a disposition to form foldiers calculated for his tyrannical purposes. They had uniformly manifested an inclination to change their sovereigns, though more from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of variety than to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the government, or restrain the abuses of tyranny. Muley Ishmael had discernment enough to see, that by forming an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of slaves, whose sole dependence should rest upon their master, he could easily train them in such a manner as to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> in the strictest conformity to his wishes. He soon learnt that the great object with the negroes was plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of plunder; in these he liberally indulged them, and the plan fully answered his expectations. Though, however, Muley Ishmael had no great merit in introducing subjects for the purposes of tyranny, yet the good effects of this new colonization were very generally experienced. By intermarrying among themselves, and intermixing among the Moors (for the Moors <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> keep negro women as concubines, though they seldom marry them), a new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people started up, who became useful subjects as the native inhabitants, and brought the empire into a much more flourishing state than it had ever been in since their great revolution. Sidi Mahomet, his grandson and successor, had different views, and was actuated by different motives. From his inordinate avarice, he ceased to act towards his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> troops in the generous manner which had distinguished his predecessor Muley Ishmael; and they soon showed themselves discontented with his conduct. They offered to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his eldest son Muley <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, on the throne; but this prince, not unmindful of the duty which he owed his father and sovereign, declined their offer. They next applied to Muley Yazid, who at first accepted of the affiance they tendered, but in a short time relinquished the plan. Sidi Mahomet, disgusted with this conduct of the negroes, determined to curb their growing power, by disbanding a considerable part of these troops, and banishing them to distant parts of the empire. A most flagrant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of despotism, which renders the emperors more formidable to their subjects, is their of the emperors making themselves their sole heirs, and, in virtue of that, perors, feigning upon all their effects, and making only such provision for their families as they think proper; and often, on some frivolous pretence, leaving them destitute of any, according to the liking or dislike they bear to the deceased; so that, upon the whole, they are the only makers, judges, and interpreters, and in many instances likewise the executioners, of their own laws, which have no other limits than their own arbitrary will. The titles which the emperors of Morocco assume, are those of Most glorious, mighty, and noble emperor of Africa; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Fez and Morocco, Taflet, Sus, Dorka, and all the Algarbe, and its territories in Africa; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> Sharif (or, as others write it, Xarif), that is, successor or vicegerent, of the great Prophet Mohammed, &c. The judges or magistrates who act immediately under the emperor are either spiritual or temporal, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>. The mufti and the cadis are judges of all religious and civil affairs; and the bashaws, governors, alcaldes, and other military officers, of those that concern the state or the army: all of them the most obsequious creatures and slaves of their prince, and no less the rapacious tyrants of his subjects, and from whom neither <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> nor favour can be obtained but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> dint of money and extortionate bribery, from the highest to the lowest. Neither can it indeed be otherwise in such an arbitrary government, where the highest posts must not only be bought of the prince at a most extravagant price, and kept only by as exorbitant a tribute, which is yearly paid to him, but where no one is sure to continue longer than he can bribe some of the courtiers to insinuate to the monarch that he pays to the utmost of his power and much beyond what was expected from him. There are instances of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> elevating at once a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> folder to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a>, or making him a confidential friend; the following <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> he would perhaps imprison him, or reduce him again to the station of a private folder. Yet such is the disposition of these people, that they have an unbounded thirst for rank and power with all their uncertainties; and what is more extraordinary, when they have obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> station, they seldom fail to afford their sovereign a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> for ill treating them, by abusing in some way or other their trust. From what has been said, it may be reasonably concluded that the revenue arising to the emperor from the last-mentioned source, that of bribery, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTORTION">extortion</a>, and confiscation, must be very considerable, though there is no possibility to make any other conjecture of its real amount than that it must be an immense one. Another considerable branch is the piratical trade, which brings the greater income into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, as he is not at any expense either for fitting out of corsair vessels, or maintaining their men; and yet has the tenth of all the cargo and of all the captives; besides which, he appropriates to himself all the rest of them, by paying the captors 50 crowns per head, by which means he engrosses all the slaves to his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and advantage. This article is indeed a very considerable addition to his revenue, not only as he sells their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> at a very high rate, but likewise as he has the profit of all their labour, without allowing them any other maintenance than a little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, or any other assistance when sick, than what medicines a Spanish convent, which he tolerates there, gives them gratis; and which, nevertheless, is forced to pay him an annual present for that toleration, besides furnishing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> with medicines, and the slaves with lodging and diet when they are not able to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Another branch of his revenue consists in the tenth part of all cattle, corn, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, wax, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and other products of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which is exacted of the Arabs and Berbers, as well as of the natives; and these are levied, or rather farmed, by the bashaws, governors, alcaldes, &c., with all possible severity. The Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> likewise pay an income or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, the former of six crowns per head on all males from 15 years and upwards, besides other arbitrary imposts, fines, &c. That on the Christians, for the liberty of trading in his dominions, rises and falls according to their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> they drive; but which, whatever it may bring yearly into his coffers, is yet detrimental to trade in general, seeing it discourages great numbers from settling there, notwithstanding the artful invitations which the emperors and their ministers make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to invite them to it; for, besides those arbitrary exactions, there is still another great hardship attending them, viz. that they cannot leave the country without forfeiting all their debts and effects to the crown. The duties on all imports and exports is another branch of his income, the amount of which, it is said, does not exceed 165,000l. per annum. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of the empire of Morocco is in general sufficiently temperate, healthy, and not so hot as its situation might <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to suppose. The chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which form Atlas, on the eastern side, defends it from the east winds, that would scorch up the earth were they frequent. The summit of these mountains is always covered with snow; and their abundant descending streams spread verdure through the neighbourhood, make the winter more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and temper the heats of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the west side, which extends along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> from north to south, also refreshes the land with regular breezes, that seldom vary according to their seasons. At a distance from the sea, within land, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is so great, that the rivulets become dry in summer; but as in hot countries dews are plentiful, the nights are there always cool. The rains are tolerably regular in winter; and are even abundant, though the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is not loaded with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> as in northern latitudes. Those rains which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by intervals are favourable to the earth, and increase its fecundity. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> the country is covered with verdure, and enamelled with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. Barley is cut in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, but the wheat <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. All fruits are early in this climate; and in forward years the vintage is over in the beginning of September. Though in general there is more uniformity and less <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in hot than in northern climates, the first are nevertheless exposed to the intemperance of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>: too heavy rains often impede the harvest; and drought has still greater inconveniences, for it endures the propagation of locusts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of Morocco is exceedingly fertile. It is soil, and most so in the inland provinces. On the western coast it is in general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and stony, and is better adapted to the vine and olive than the culture of wheat. They annually burn, before the September rains, the stubble, which is left rather long; and this and the dung of cattle, every day turned to pasture, form the sole manure the land receives. The soil requires but little labour, and the ploughing is so light that the furrows are scarcely five inches deep; for which reason, in some provinces, wooden ploughshares are used for cheapness. The empire of Morocco might supply itself with all productions, as well from the abundance and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of its products, as from the few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> wants of the Moors occasioned by climate or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Its wealth consists in the fruitfulness of its soil: its corn, fruits, fruits, flocks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, and wax, would not only supply its necessities, but yield a superflux, which might become an object of immense trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> with other nations. Such numerous exports might return an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, were its government fixed and secure, and did subjects enjoy the fruits of their labour and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in safety. The increase of corn in Morocco is often as sixty to one, and thirty is held to be but an indifferent harvest. The Moors, naturally indolent, take little care of the culture of their fruits. Oranges, lemons, and thick-skinned fruits, the trees of which require little nurture, grow in the open fields; and there are very large plantations of them found, which they take the trouble to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in order to increase their product. Their vines, which yield excellent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, are planted as far as the 33rd degree, as in the southern provinces of France, and are equally vigorous. But at Morocco, where they yield a large and delicious grape, they are supported by vine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> five and six feet above ground; and as they are obliged to be watered, the little wine made there is seldom preserved. Figs are very good in some parts of the empire, but toward the south they are scarcely ripe before they are full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>; the heats and night dews may, perhaps, contribute to this speedy decay. Melons, for the same reason, are rarely eatable; they have but a moment of maturity; which passes so rapidly that it is with difficulty seized. Water melons are everywhere reared, and in some provinces are excellent. Apricots, apples, and pears, are in tolerable plenty in the neighbourhood of Fez and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEQUINEZ">Mequinez</a>, where water is less scarce and the climate more temperate. But in the plain, which extends along the western coast, these delicate fruits are very indifferent, have lost juice or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and the peaches there do not <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>. The tree called the prickly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, or the Barbary fig, is plentifully found in the empire of Morocco; and is planted round vineyards and gardens, because its thick and thorny leaves, which are wonderfully prolific, form impenetrable hedges. From these leaves a fruit is produced, covered with a thorny skin, that must be taken off with care. This fruit is mild, and full of very hard, small kernels. The olive is everywhere found along the coast, but particularly to the south. In the province of Suz, between the 25th and 30th degrees, the inhabitants have an almond harvest, which varies little because of the mildness of the climate; but the fruit is small, for which reason they take little care of the trees, and they degenerate with time. The palm tree is common in the southern provinces of Morocco; but dates ripen there with difficulty, and few are good except in the province of Suz and toward Taflet. On the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALLEE">Sallee</a> and Mamora there are forests of oak, which produce acorns near two inches long. They taste like chestnuts, and are eaten raw and roasted. Salt abounds in the empire, and in some places on the coast requires only the trouble of gathering. Independent of the salt pits formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the soft water, there are pits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in the country whence great quantities are obtained. It is carried even as far as Tombut, whence it passes to the interior parts of Africa. The Moors cultivate their lands only in proportion to their wants; hence two-thirds of the empire at least <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> waste. Here the doum, that is, the fan or wild palm tree, grows in abundance; and from which those people, when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> renders them industrious, find great advantage. The shepherds, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>-drivers, camel drivers, and travellers, gather the leaves, of which they make mats, fringes, baskets, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, boarsis or large wallets to carry corn, twine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, girths, and covers for their pack saddles. This plant, with which also they heat their ovens, produces a mild and resinous fruit that ripens in September and October. It is in form like the raisin, contains a kernel, and is astringent and very proper to temper and counteract the effects of the watery and laxative fruits, of which these people in summer make an immoderate use. Unacquainted with the sources of wealth of which their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were possessed, the Moors pretend there are <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in the empire, which the emperors will not permit to be worked, lest their subjects should thus find means to shake off their yoke. It is not improbable but that the mountains of Atlas may contain unexplored <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>; but there is no good <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that they have ever yielded gold and silver. There are known <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> mines in the south; but the working of them has been found too expensive, that the natives would rather use imported iron, notwithstanding the heavy duty it pays, by which its price is doubled. There are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> mines in the neighbourhood of Santa Cruz, which are not only sufficient for the small consumption of the empire, where copper is little used, but are also an object of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>, and would become much more so were the duties less immoderate. Neither the elephant nor the rhinoceros is to be found either in this or the other states of Barbary; but the deserts abound with lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, and monstrous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>. The Barbary horses were formerly very valuable, and thought equal to the Arabian. Though the breed is now said to be decayed, yet some very fine ones are occasionally imported into England. Camels and dromedaries, asses, mules, and kumrabs (a most serviceable creature, begot by an ass upon a cow), are their beasts of burden. Their cows are but small, and barren of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. Their sheep yield but indifferent fleeces, but are very large, as are their goats. Bears, porcupines, foxes, apes, hares, rabbits, ferrets, weasels, moles, chameleons, and all kinds of reptiles, are found here. Partridges and quails, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, hawks, and all kinds of wild fowl, are frequent on the coast. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mountains form the chain which goes under the name of Mount Atlas, and runs the whole length of Barbary from east to west, passing through Morocco, and abutting upon that ocean which separates the eastern from the western continent, and is from this mountain called the Atlantic Ocean. See Atlas. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides the Malva or Muluya above mentioned, which rises in the deserts, and running from south to north divides Morocco from the kingdom of Algiers, are the Suz, Ommirabib, Rabbata, Larache, Darodt, Sebon, Gueron, and Tensift, which rise in Mount Atlas, and fall into the Atlantic ocean. The traffic of the empire by land is either with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>-Inlandia or Negroland: to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> they send <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a>, consisting of several thousand camels, horses, and mules, twice every year, partly for traffic, and partly on a religious account; for numbers of pilgrims take that opportunity of paying their devotions to their great prophet. The goods they carry to the east are woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, manufactures, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a>, and ostrich feathers; and they bring back from thence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, muslins, and drugs. By their caravans to Negroland, they fend salt, silk, and woollen manufactures, and bring back gold and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> in return, but chiefly negroes. The caravans always go strong enough to defend themselves against the wild Arabs in the deserts of Africa and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; though, notwithstanding all their vigilance, some of the stragglers and baggage often fall into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>: they are also forced to load one-half of their camels with water, to prevent their perishing with drought and thirst in those inhospitable deserts. And there is still a more dangerous enemy, which is the sand itself: when the winds rise, the caravan is perfectly blinded with dust; and there have been instances both in Africa and Asia, where whole caravans, and even armies, have been buried alive in the sands. The natives have hardly any trading vessels, but are seldom without some corsairs. These, and European merchant ships, bring them whatever they want from abroad; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen cloth, stuffs, iron wrought and unwrought, arms, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, lead, and the like: for which they take in return, copper, wax, hides, Morocco leather, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> (which is very fine), gums, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, dates, almonds, and other fruits. The duties paid by the English in the ports of Morocco are but half those paid by other Europeans. It is a general observation, that no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is fond of trading with these states, not only on account of their capricious despotism, but the villany of their individuals, both natives and Jews, many of whom take all opportunities of cheating, and when detected are seldom punished. The land forces of the emperor of Morocco consist principally of black troops, and some few <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; amounting altogether to an army of about 36,000 men upon the establishment, two-thirds of which are cavalry. This establishment, however, upon occasion, admits of a considerable increase, as every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is supposed to be a soldier, and when called upon is obliged to act in that capacity. About 6000 of the standing forces form the emperor's body <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and are always kept near his person; the remainder are quartered in the different towns of the empire, and are under the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the bashaws of the provinces. They are all clothed by the emperor, and receive a trifling pay; but their chief dependence is on plunder, which they have frequent opportunities of acquiring. The black troops are naturally of a very fiery disposition, capable of enduring great fatigue, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, thirst, and every difficulty to which a military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is exposed. They appear well calculated for skirmishing parties, or for the purpose of harassing an enemy; but were they obliged to undergo a regular attack, from their total want of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> they would soon be routed. In all their manoeuvres they have no notion whatever of order and regularity, but have altogether more the appearance of a rabble than of an army. The emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> consists of about 15 small frigates, a few xebecs, and between 20 and 30 row-galleys. The whole is commanded by one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>; but as these vessels are principally used for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>, they seldom unite in a fleet. The number of the seamen in service is computed at 6000. The coins of this empire are a fluce, a blanquil, and ducat. The fluce is a small copper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, 20 whereof make a blanquil, of the value of twopence <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. The blanquil is of silver, and the ducat of gold, not unlike that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and worth about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings. Both these pieces are liable to be clipped and filed by the Jews, that the Moors always carry scales in their pockets to weigh them; and when they are found to be much diminished in their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, they are recoined by the Jews, who are matters of the mint, by which they <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a considerable profit; as they do also by exchanging the light pieces for those that are full weight. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a> accounts are kept in ounces, 10 of which make a ducat; but in payments to the government, it is said they reckon 17 one-half for a ducat. With respect to religion, the inhabitants of Morocco are Mohammedans, of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Ali; and have a chief or high-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who is also the supreme civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and the last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> in all causes ecclesiastical and civil. They have a great veneration for their hermits, and for idiots and madmen; as well as for those who by their tricks have got the reputation of wizzard: all whom they look upon as inspired persons, and not only honour as saints while they live, but build tombs and chapels over them when dead; which places are not only religiously visited by their devotees far and near, but are esteemed inviolable sanctuaries for all sorts of criminals except in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. Notwithstanding the natives are zealous Mohammedans, they allow foreigners the free and open profession of their religion, and their very slaves have their priests and chapels in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city; though it must be owned that the Christian slaves are here treated with the utmost cruelty. Here, as in all other Mohammedan countries, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a> and their comments upon it are their only written laws; and though in some instances their cadi and other civil magistrates are controlled by the arbitrary determinations of their princes, bashaws, generals, and military officers, yet the latter have generally a very great deference and regard for their laws. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>, theft, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, are commonly punished with death: and their punishments for other crimes, particularly those against the state, are very cruel; as impaling, dragging the prisoner through the streets at a mule's heels till all his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is torn off, throwing him from a high tower upon iron hooks. The inhabitants of the empire of Morocco, known by the name of Moors, are a mixture of Arabian and of the African nations formed into tribes; with the origin of Morocco, of whom we are but imperfectly acquainted. These tribes, each strangers to the other, and ever divided by traditional hatred or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, seldom mingle. It seems probable that most of the caits who occupy the provinces of Morocco have been repulsed from the eastern to the western Africa, during those different revolutions by which this part of the world has been agitated; that they have followed the standard of their chiefs, whose names they have preserved; and that by these they, as well as the countries they inhabit, are distinguished. At present these tribes are called cabilles or cabiles, from the Arabic word kabilea; and they are so numerous, that it is impossible to have a knowledge of them all. The native subjects of the empire of Morocco may be divided into two principal classes; the Brebes and the Moors. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the name, and the origin of the people, of the first class, are equally unknown. Like the Moors, at the time of the invasion by the Arabs, they may have adopted the Mahometan religion, which is consonant to their manners and principal usages; but they are an ignorant people, and observe none of the precepts of that religion, but the aversion it enjoins against other modes of worship. Confining to the mountains, the Brebes preserve great animosity against the Moors, whom they confound with the Arabs, and consider as usurpers.—They thus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> in their retreats a ferocity of mind, and a strength of body, which makes them more fit for war and every kind of labour than the Moors of the plains in general are. The independence they boast of gives even a greater degree of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> to their countenance. The prejudices of their religion make them submit to the authority of the emperors of Morocco; but they throw off the yoke at their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and retire into the mountains, where it is difficult to attack or overcome them. The Brebes have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of their own, and never marry but among each other. They have tribes or castes among them who are exceedingly powerful both by their number and courage. The Moors of the plains may be distinguished into those who lead a pastoral life, and those who inhabit the cities. The former live in tents; and that they may allow their ground a year's rest, they annually change the place of their encampments, and go in search of fresh pasturage; but they cannot take this step without acquainting their governor. Like the ancient Arabs, they are entirely devoted to a pastoral life: their encampments, which they call douchars, are composed of several tents, and form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>; or they are ranged in two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, and their flocks, when they return from pasture, occupy the centre. The tents of the Moors, viewed in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, are of a conical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; they are from 8 to 10 feet high, and from 20 to 25 feet long; like those of high antiquity, they resemble a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> reversed. They are made of cloth composed of goats and camels' <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and the leaves of the wild palm, by which they are rendered impervious to water; but at a distance their black <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> gives them a very disagreeable look. The Moors, when encamped, live in the greatest simplicity, and exhibit a faithful <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the inhabitants of the earth in the first ages of the world. The nature of their education, the temperature of the climate, and the rigour of the government, diminish the wants of the people, who find in their plains, in the milk and wool of their flocks, every thing necessary for food and clothing. Polygamy is allowed among them; a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> so far from being injurious to a people who have few wants, that it is a great convenience in the economy of those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, because the women are intrusted with the whole care of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> management. In their half-closed tents, they are employed in milking the cows for daily use; and when the milk abounds, in making <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, in picking their corn, their barley, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, which they do daily in a mill composed of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> about 18 inches in diameter, the uppermost having a handle, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on an axis fixed in the under one: they make bread likewise every day, which they bake between two earthen plates, and often upon the ground after it has been heated by fire. Their ordinary food is the coofcoofoo; which is a paste made with their meal in the form of small grains like Italian pasta. This coofcoofoo is dressed in the vapour of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> soup, in a hollow <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> perforated with many small holes in the bottom, and the dish is enclosed in a kettle where meat is boiled; the coofcoofoo, which is in the hollow dish, grows gradually soft by the vapour of the broth, with which it is from time to time moistened. This simple food is very nourishing, and even agreeable when one has got the better of the prejudices which every nation entertains for its own customs. The common people eat it with milk or butter indifferently; but those of higher rank, such as the governors of provinces and lieutenants, who live in the centre of the encampments, add to it some succulent broth, made with a mixture of mutton, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, pigeons, or hedgehogs, and then pour on it a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fresh butter. The women in their tents spin wool, and weave it into cloth on looms suspended the whole length of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. Each piece is about five ells long, and one and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; it is neither dressed nor dyed, and it has no seam; they wash it when it is dirty; and as it is the only <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of the Moors, they wear it night and day. It is called haick, and is the true <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the ancient draperies. The Moors of the plain wear nothing but their dres, &c., woollen stuff; they have neither shirts nor drawers. Linen among these people is a luxury known only to those of the court or the city. The whole wardrobe of a country Moor in easy circumstances consists in a haick for winter, another for summer, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, a hood, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of flippers. The common people both in the country and in towns wear a kind of tunic of woollen cloth, white, gray, or striped, which reaches to the middle of the leg, with great sleeves and a hood; it resembles the habit of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHUSIANS">Carthusians</a>. The women's dres in the country is likewise confined to a haick, which covers the neck and the shoulders, and is fastened with a silver clasp. The ornaments they are fondest of are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> rings, which are either in the form of rings or crescents, made of silver, bracelets, and rings for the small of the leg; they wear these trinkets at their most ordinary occupations; less out of vanity than because they are unacquainted with the use of caskets or cabinets for keeping them. They also wear necklaces made of coloured glass beads or cloves strung on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> of silk. The Moors consider their wives less in the light of companions than in that of slaves destined to labour. Except in the business of tillage, they are employed in every servile operation; nay, in some of the poorer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> a woman is often seen yoked in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> along with a mule, an ass, or some other animal. When the Moors remove their douchars, all the men seat themselves in a circle on the ground; and with their elbows resting on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the time in conversation, while the women strike the tents, fold them up into bundles, and place them on the backs of their camels or oxen. The old women are then each loaded with a parcel, and the young carry the children on their shoulders. shoulders suspended in a cloth girt round their bodies. In the more southern parts the women are likewise employed in the care of the horses: the husband, who in these climates is always a depot, ifuses his orders, and seems only made to be obeyed. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> ceremonies of the Moors that live in tents pretty much resemble those of the same people that live in the cities. In the douchars they are generally most brilliant and gay; the strangers that pass along are invited, and made to contribute to the feast; but this is done more from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> than from any mercenary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>. The tribes of the plain generally avoid mixing by marriage with one another: the prejudices that divide these people are commonly perpetuated; or, if they are partially healed, they never fail to revive upon trifling occasions, such as a strayed camel, or the preference of a pasture or a well. Marriages have sometimes taken place among them, that, so far from cementing their differences, have occasioned the most tragical scenes. Husbands have been known to murder their wives, and women their husbands, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> national quarrels. Parents are not encumbered with their children, however numerous they may be, for they are very early employed in domestic affairs; they tend the flocks, they gather wood, and they assist in ploughing and reaping. In the evening, when they return from the field, all the children of the douchar assemble in a common tent, where the iman, who himself can hardly spell, makes them read a few sentences from the Koran written on boards, and instructs them in their religion by the light of a fire made of straw, of bushes, and cow dung dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. As the heat is very great in the inland parts of the country, children of both sexes go quite naked till the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of nine or ten. The douchars dispersed over the plains are always in the neighbourhood of some rivulet or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and they are a kind of inns for the reception of travellers. There is generally a tent erected for their use, if they have not brought one along with them, where they are accommodated with poultry, milk, and eggs, and with whatever is necessary for their horses. Instead of wood for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, they have the cow dung, which, when mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, makes a very brisk fire. A guard is always set on the tents of travellers, especially if they are Europeans, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of their wealth might tempt the avidity of the Moors, who are naturally inclined to thieving.
