MOSCOW

Pages 485-488

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the empire of Russia, deriving its name from the river Moskva, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Moikva, on which the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is situated. It was from this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> that the czars of old took the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of dukes of Moscow. The province is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the duchies of Tver, Rostov, Sudal, and Wladimir; on the south by Rezan, from which it is separated by the river Oca; on the east by the principality of Chachine, and the same river Oca parting it from Nizh-Novgorod; and on the west by the duchies of Rzeka, Bielar and Smolensko. It extends about 200 miles in length, and about 100 in breadth; and is watered by the Moikva, Oca, and Cifma, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Wolga: nevertheless, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is not very fertile. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, however, though sharp, is salubrious; and this consideration, with the advantage of its being situated in the midst of the best provinces in the empire, induced the czars to make it their chief residence. In the western <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Moscow is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> forest, from whence flows the celebrated river Dnieper, or Borysthenes, which, traversing the duchy of Smolensko, winds in a serpentine course to Ukraine, Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. Moscow, the capital of the above province, and till the beginning of the last century the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of all Russia, is situated in a spacious plain on the banks of the river Moikva. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 37° 31' N. Lat. 55° 45'. The Russian antiquaries differ considerably in their opinions concerning the first foundation of Moscow; the following relation, Mr Coxe says, is generally esteemed by the best authors the most probable account. Kiev was the metropolis, when George son of Vladimir Monomakh ascended in 1154 the Russian throne. That monarch, being insulted in a progress through his dominions by a rich and powerful nobleman named Stephen Kuteikho, put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and confiscated his domains, which consisted of the lands now occupied by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Moscow and the adjacent territory. Pleaded with the situation of the ground lying at the confluence of the Moikva and Neglina, he laid the foundation of a new town, which he called Moikva from the river of that name. Upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a> of George, the new town was not neglected by his son Andrew, who transferred the seat of empire from Kiev to Vladimir; but it fell into such decay under his immediate successors, that when Daniel, son of Alexander Nevski, received, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire, the duchy of Muscovy as his portion, and fixed his residence upon the confluence of the Moikva and Neglina, he may be said to have newly founded the town. The spot now occupied by the Kremlin was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> overgrown with a thick wood and a morass, in the midst whereof was a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> containing a single wooden hut. Upon this part Daniel constructed churches and monasteries, and various buildings, and enclosed it with wooden fortifications: he first assumed the title of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Moscow; and was so attached to this situation, that when in 1392 he succeeded his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Andrew Alexandrovitch in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> duchy of Vladimir, he did not remove his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to Vladimir, but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his residence at Moscow, which then became the capital of the Russian dominions. His successors followed his example; among whom his son Ivan considerably enlarged the new metropolis, and in 1367 his grandson Demetrius Ivanovitch Doniski surrounded the Kremlin with a brick wall. These new fortifications, however, were not strong enough to prevent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a> in 1382, from taking the town after a short siege. Being soon evacuated by that desultory conqueror, it again came into the possession of the Russians; but was frequently invaded and occupied by the Tartars, who in the 14th and 15th centuries overrun the greatest part of Russia, and who even maintained a garrison in Moscow until they were finally expelled by Ivan Vasilievitch I. To him Moscow is indebted for its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> splendour, and under him it became the principal and most considerable city of the Russian empire. Moscow continued the metropolis of Russia until the beginning of the 18th century, when, to the great dissatisfaction of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, but with great advantage probably to the state, the seat of empire was transferred to Petersburgh. Notwithstanding the predilection which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> conceived for Petersburgh, in which all the succeeding sovereigns excepting Peter the II. have fixed their residence, Moscow, according to Mr Coxe, is still the most populous city of the Russian empire. Here the chief <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> who do not belong to the court reside; they here support a large <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of retainers; they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to gratify their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for a ruder and more expensive magnificence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> style of feudal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>; and are not, as at Petersburgh, eclipsed by the superior splendour of the court. Moscow is represented as the largest town in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; its circumference within the rampart, which encloses the suburbs, being exactly 39 versts or 26 miles; but it is built in so straggling and disjointed a manner, that its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> corresponds to its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. Some Russian authors rate its inhabitants at 500,000 souls, a number evidently exaggerated. According to a computation, which Mr Coxe says may be depended upon, Moscow contains within the ramparts 250,000 souls, and in the adjacent villages 50,000. The streets of Moscow are in general exceedingly long and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; some of them are paved; others, particularly those in the suburbs, are formed with trunks of trees, or are boarded with planks like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of a room; wretched hovels are blended with large palaces; cottages of one story stand next to the most superb and lately manions. Many brick structures are covered with wooden tops; some of the wooden houses are painted; others have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> doors and roofs. Numerous churches present themselves in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, built in a peculiar style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; some with domes of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, others of tin, gilt or painted green, and many roofed with wood. In a word, some parts of this vast city have the look of a sequestered <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a populous town; some of a contemptible village, others of a great capital. Moscow may be considered as a town built upon the Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, but gradually becoming more and more European, and exhibiting in its present state a motley mixture of discordant architecture. It is distributed into the following divisions. 1. The Kremlin. This stands in the central and highest part of the city; is of a triangular form, and about two miles in circumference; and is surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and brick; which were constructed in the year 1491, under the reign of Ivan Vasilievitch I. It contains the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the czars, several churches, two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, the patriarchal palace, the arsenal now in ruins, and one private <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which belonged to Boris Godunof before he was raised to the throne. 2. Khitaigorod, or the Chinese town, is enclosed on one side by that wall of the Kremlin which runs from the Moskva to the Neglina; and on the other side by a brick wall of inferior height. It is much larger than the Kremlin, and contains the university, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>-house and many other public buildings, and all the tradesmen's shops. The edifices are mostly stuccoed or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> washed, and it has the only street in Moscow in which the houses stand <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to one another without any intervals between them. 3. The Bielgorod, or White Town, which runs quite round the two preceding divisions, is supposed to derive its name from a white wall with which it was formerly enclosed, and of which some remains are still to be seen. 4. Semlainogorod, which environs all the three other quarters, takes its denomination from a circular rampart of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with which it is encompassed. These two last mentioned divisions exhibit a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of churches, convents, palaces, brick and wooden houses, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> hovels, in no degree superior to peasants' cottages. 5. The Sloboda, or suburbs, form a vast exterior circle round all the parts already described, and are invested with a low rampart and ditch. These suburbs contain, beside buildings of all kinds and denominations, corn fields, much open pasture, and some small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, which give rise to the Neglina. The river Moskva, from which the city takes its name, flows through it in a winding channel; but excepting in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is only navigable for rafts. It receives the Yauza in the Semlainogorod, and the Neglina at the western extremity of the Kremlin; the beds of both these last-mentioned rivulets are in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> little better than dry channels. The places of divine worship at Moscow are exceedingly numerous; including chapels, they amount to above 1000; there are 484 public churches, of which 199 are of brick; and the others of wood; the former are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> stuccoed or white-washed, the latter painted of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The most ancient churches of Moscow are generally <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings, with a cupola and four small domes, some whereof are of copper or iron girt; others of tin, either plain or painted green. Their cupolas and domes are for the most part ornamented with crosses entwined with thin chains or wires. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Holy Trinity, sometimes called the church of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, which stands in the Khitaigorod, close to the gate leading into the Kremlin, has a kind of high steeple and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten domes: it was built in the reign of Ivan Vasilievitch II. The inside of the churches is mostly composed of three parts; that called by the Greeks "nave," by the Russians "trapeza;" the body; and the sanctuary or shrine. Over the door of each church is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of the saint to whom it is dedicated, to which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people pay their homage as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> along, by taking off their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, crossing themselves, and occasionally touching the ground with their heads. The bells, which form an inconsiderable part of public worship in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as the length or shortness of their peals ascends the greater or lesser sanctity of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, are hung in belfries detached from the church: they do not swing like our bells; but are fixed immovably to the beams, and are rung by a rope tied to the clapper and pulled sidewise. Some of these bells are of a stupendous size; one in the tower of St Ivan's church weighs 3557 Russian pounds, or 127,836 English pounds. It has always been esteemed a meritorious <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to present a church with bells; and the piety of the donor has been measured by their magnitude. According to this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of estimation, Boris Godunof, who gave a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> of 288,000 pounds to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Moscow, was the most pious sovereign of Russia, until he was surpassed by the empress <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, at whose expense a bell was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> weighing 432,000 pounds, and which exceeded in bigness every bell in the known world. The height of this enormous bell is 19 feet, its circumference at the bottom 21 yards 11 inches; its greatest thickness 23 inches. The beam to which this vast machine was fastened being accidentally burnt, the bell fell <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and a fragment was broken off towards the bottom, which left an aperture large enough to admit two persons abreast without stooping. The palace, inhabited by the ancient czars, stands at the extremity of the Kremlin. Part of this palace is old, and remains in the same state in which it was built under Ivan Vasilievitch I. The remainder has been successively added at different intervals, without any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and in various styles of architecture, which has produced a motley pile of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, remarkable for nothing but the incongruity of the several structures. The top is thickly set with numerous little gilded spires and globes; and a large portion of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> is decorated with the arms of of all the provinces which compose the Russian empire. The apartments are in general exceedingly small, excepting one single room called the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> chamber, in which the ancient czars used to give audience to foreign ambassadors, and which has been repeatedly described by several English travellers who visited Moscow before the imperial residence was transferred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>. The room is large and vaulted, and has in the centre an enormous pillar of stone which supports the ceiling. In this palace Peter the Great came into the world, in the year 1672. In that part called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> are deposited the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, jewels, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> robes, used at the coronation of the sovereign, besides several curiosities relative to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the country. Of the great number of churches contained in this city, two in particular, namely, that of St Michael and that of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">Assumption</a> of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, are remarkable; the one for being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the sovereigns of Russia were formerly interred, and the other where they are crowned. These edifices, which are situated in the Kremlin, are both in the same style of architecture; and their exterior form, though modelled according to the ancient style of the country, is not absolutely inelegant. In the cathedral of St Michael, which contains the tombs of the Russian sovereigns, the bodies are not, as with us, deposited in vaults, or beneath the pavement, but are entombed in raised sepulchres, mostly of brick, in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, and about two feet in height. When Mr Coxe visited the cathedral, the most ancient were covered with palls of red cloth, others of red velvet, and that of Peter II. with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> tissue, bordered with silver fringe and ermine. Each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> has at its lower extremity a small silver plate, upon which is engraved the name of the deceased sovereign, and the era of his death. The cathedral of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, which has long been appropriated to the coronation of the Russian sovereigns, is the most splendid and magnificent in Moscow. The screen is in many parts covered with plates of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> silver and gold richly worked. From the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> hangs an enormous chandelier of maffy silver, weighing 2940 pounds: it was made in England, and was a present from Morosof, prime minister and favourite of Alexey Michaelowitch. The sacred utensils and episcopal vestments are extraordinarily rich, but the taste of the workmanship is in general rude, and by no means equal to the materials. Many of the paintings which cover the inside walls are of a colossal size: some are very ancient, and were executed so early as in the latter end of the 15th century. It contains, amongst the rest a head of the Virgin, supposed to have been delineated by St Luke, and greatly celebrated in this country for its sanctity and the power of working <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> is almost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; its head is ornamented with a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and body are gilded, which gives it a most grotesque appearance. It is placed in the screen, and enclosed within a large silver covering, which is only taken off on great festivals, or for the curiosity of strangers. In this cathedral are deposited the remains of the Russian patriarchs. The place in the Khitaigorod, where the public archives are deposited, is a strong brick building, containing several vaulted apartments with iron floors. These archives, consisting of a numerous collection of state papers, were crowded into boxes and thrown aside like common lumber, until the empress Catherine ordered them to be revised and arranged. In conformity to this mandate, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a> has disposed them in chronological order with such perfect regularity, that any single <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a> may be inspected with little trouble. They are enclosed in separate cabinets with glass doors: those relative to Russia are all classified according to the several provinces which they concern; and over each cabinet is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the name of the province to which it is appropriated. In the same manner the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> relative to foreign kingdoms are placed in separate divisions under the respective titles of Poland, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, England, France, Germany, &c. The university of Moscow, all situated in the Khitaigorod, was founded, at the instance of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Shuvalov, by the empress <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, for 600 students; who are clothed, boarded, and instructed, at the expense of the crown. Besides this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, there are two gymnasia or seminaries for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of youth, endowed also by Elizabeth; in which are taught, by twenty-three professors, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, classics, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, the Greek, Latin, Russian, German, French, Italian, and Tartar languages; history, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, architecture, fortification, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, music, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Moscow is the centre of the inland <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Russia, and particularly connects the trade between Europe and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. The only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to this city is formed by the Moskva, which falling into the Occa near Columna, communicates by means of that river with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>. But as the Moskva is only navigable in spring upon the melting of the snows, the principal merchandise is conveyed to and from Moscow upon sledges in winter. The whole of the retail trade is carried on in the Khitaigorod; where according to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> common in Russia, as well as in most kingdoms of the East, all the shops are collected together in one spot. The place is like a kind of fair, consisting of many rows of low brick buildings; the intervals between them resembling alleys. These shops or booths occupy a considerable space; they do not, as with us, make part of the houses inhabited by the tradesmen, but are quite detached from their dwellings, which for the most part are at some distance in another quarter of the town. The tradesman comes to his shop in the morning, remains there all day, and returns home to his family in the afternoon. Every trade has its separate department; and they who sell the same goods have booths adjoining to each other. Furs and skins form the most considerable article of commerce in Moscow; and the shops which vend these commodities occupy several streets. Amongst the curiosities of Moscow, the market for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of houses is not the least remarkable. It is held in a large open space in one of the suburbs; and exhibits a great variety of ready made houses, thickly strewed upon the ground. The purchaser who wants a dwelling, repairs to this spot, mentions the number of rooms he requires, examines the different timbers, which are regularly numbered, and bargains for that which suits him. The house is sometimes paid for on the spot, and taken away by the purchaser; or sometimes the vender contracts to transport and erect it upon the place where it is designed to stand. It may appear incredible to assert, that a dwelling may be thus bought, bought, removed, raised and inhabited, within the space of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; but we shall conceive it practicable by considering that these ready-made houses are in general merely collections of trunks of trees tenoned and mortised at each extremity into one another, so that nothing more is required than the labour of transporting and adjusting them. But this summary mode of building is not always peculiar to the meaner hovels; as wooden structures of very large dimensions and handsome appearance are occasionally formed in Russia with an expedition almost inconceivable to the inhabitants of other countries. A remarkable instance of this dispatch was displayed the last time the empress came to Moscow. Her majesty proposed to reside in the mansion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Galitzin, which is esteemed the completest edifice in this city; but as it was not sufficiently spacious for her reception, a temporary addition of wood, larger than the original house, was begun and finished within the space of six weeks. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>-like fabric was so handsome and commodious, that the materials which were taken down at her majesty's departure, were to be re-constructed as a kind of imperial villa upon an eminence near the city. Mr Coxe mentions an admirable <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> in this city for preventing riots, or for stopping the concourse of people in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of fires, which are very frequent and violent in those parts, where the houses are mostly of wood, and the streets are laid with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. At the entrance of each street there is a chevaux-de-frise gate, one end whereof turns upon a pivot, and the other rolls upon a wheel; near it is a sentry box in which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is occasionally stationed. In times of riot or fire the sentinel shuts the gate, and all passage is immediately stopped. Among the public institutions of Moscow, the most remarkable is the Foundling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, endowed in 1764 by the empress Catherine, and supported by voluntary contributions and legacies, and other charitable gifts. In order to encourage donations, her majesty granted to all benefactors some valuable privileges, and a certain degree of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in proportion to the extent of their liberality. Among the principal contributors must be mentioned a private merchant named Dimidoff, a person of great wealth, who has expended in favour of this <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> above 100,000. The hospital, which is situated in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> part of the town upon a gentle ascent near the river Moskva, is an immense pile of building of a quadrangular shape, part of which was only finished when Mr Coxe (whose account we are transcribing) was at Moscow. It contained, at that time, three thousand foundlings; and, when the whole is completed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> receive eight thousand. The children are brought to the porter's lodge, and admitted without any recommendation. The rooms are lofty and large; the dormitories, which are separate from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> rooms, are very airy, and the beds are not crowded: each foundling, even each infant, has a separate <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. The children remain two years in the nursery, when they are admitted into the lowest class; the boys and girls continue together until they are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which time they are separated. They all learn to read, write, and calf accounts. The boys are taught to knit; they occasionally card <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and work in the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The girls learn to knit, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, and all kinds of needlework; they spin and weave <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>; they are employed in cookery, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAKING">baking</a>, and housework of all sorts. At the age of fourteen the foundlings enter into the first class; when they have the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of choosing any particular branch of trade; and for this purpose there are different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of manufactures established in the hospital, of which the principal are <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stockings, ribbons, lace, gloves, buttons, and cabinet work. A separate room is appropriated to each trade. Some boys and girls are instructed in the French and German languages, and a few boys in the Latin tongue; others learn music, drawing, and dancing. Moscow was taken and plundered by the French in 1812.

MOSELLE

Pages 488-488

a river of Germany, which rises in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Voges in Lorraine, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a>. MOSELLE is also the name of a department of France, which includes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lorraine.

MOSES

Pages 488-490

the son of Amram and Jochebed, was born in the year 1571 before Christ. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, perceiving that the Hebrews were become a formidable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, issued forth an edict commanding all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> children to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. To avoid this cruel edict, Jochebed, the mother of Moses, having concealed her son for three months, at length made an ark <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of bulrushes, daubed it with pitch, laid the child in it, and exposed him on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Thermuthis the king's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who happened to be walking by the river's side, perceived the floating cradle, commanded it to be brought to her, and struck with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the child, determined to preserve his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In three years afterwards the princess adopted him for her own son, called his name Moses, and caused him be diligently instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians. But his father and mother, to whom he was restored by a fortunate accident, were at still greater pains to teach him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of his fathers. Many things are related by historians concerning the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Moses's life, which are not to be found in the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. According to Josephus and Eusebius, he made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on the Ethiopians, and completely defeated them. They add, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> Saba, in which the enemy had been forced to take refuge, was betrayed into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by the king's daughter, who became deeply enamoured of him, when she beheld from the top of the walls his valorous exploits at the head of the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. But as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this expedition is more than doubtful, we shall therefore confine ourselves to the narrative of sacred writ, which commences at the fortieth year of Moses's life. He then left the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Pharaoh, and went to visit his countrymen the Hebrews, who groaned under the ill usage and oppression of their unfeeling masters. Having perceived an Egyptian smiting a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, he slew the Egyptian, and buried him in the sand. But he was obliged, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, to fly into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Midian, where he married Zipporah, daughter of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> Jethro, by whom he had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. Here he lived 40 years; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his employment was to tend the flocks of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Having one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> led his flock toward Mount Horeb, God appeared to him in the midst of a bush which burned with fire but was not consumed, and commanded him to go and deliver his brethren from their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. Moses at first refused to go; but was at length prevailed on by two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>. racles which the Almighty wrought for his conviction. Upon his return to Egypt, he, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, went to the court of Pharaoh, and told him that God commanded him to let the Hebrews go to offer sacrifices in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. But the impious monarch disdained this command, and caused the labour of the Israelites to be doubled. The messengers of the Almighty again returned to the king, and wrought a miracle in his sight, that they might move his heart, and induce him to let the people depart. Aaron having <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his miraculous rod, it was immediately converted into a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>; but the same thing being performed by the magicians, the king's heart was hardened more and more; and his obstinacy at last drew down the judgments of the Almighty on his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which was afflicted with ten dreadful plagues. The first was the changing of the waters of the Nile and of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> into blood, so that the Egyptians died of thirst. In consequence of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, the land was covered with innumerable swarms of frogs, which entered even into Pharaoh's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. By the third plague, the dust was converted into <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>, which cruelly tormented both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. The fourth plague was a multitude of destructive flies which spread throughout Egypt, and infected the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The fifth was a sudden pestilence, which destroyed all the cattle of the Egyptians, without injuring those of the Israelites. The sixth produced numberless ulcers and fiery boils upon man and upon beast. The seventh was a dreadful storm of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which destroyed every thing that was in the field, whether man or beast, and spared only the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel dwelt. By the eighth plague swarms of locusts were brought into the country, which devoured every green <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, the fruit of the trees and the produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. By the ninth plague thick darkness covered all the land of Egypt, except the dwellings of the children of Israel. The tenth and last plague was the death of the firstborn in Egypt, who were all in one night cut off by the destroying angel, from the firstborn of the king to the firstborn of the slaves and of the cattle. This dreadful calamity moved the heart of the hardened Pharaoh, and he at length consented to allow the people of Israel to depart from his kingdom. Profane authors who have spoken of Moses, seem to have been in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> acquainted with these mighty wonders. That he performed miracles, must have been allowed by many, by whom he was considered as a famous magician; and he could scarcely appear in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to men who did not acknowledge him for the messenger of the Almighty. Both Diodorus and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> mention the distressful state to which Egypt was reduced by these terrible calamities. The Hebrews, amounting to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 600,000 men, without reckoning women and children, left Egypt on the 15th day of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Nisan, which, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this deliverance, was thenceforth reckoned the first month of their year. Scarcely had they reached the shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> when Pharaoh with a powerful army fell out in pursuit of them. On this occasion Moses stretched forth his rod upon the sea; and the waters thereof being divided, remained suspended on both sides till the Hebrews passed through dry-footed.—The Egyptians determined to follow the same course; but God caused a violent <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to blow, which brought back the waters to their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and the whole army of Pharaoh perished in the waves. After the miraculous passage of the Red sea, the army proceeded towards Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>, and arrived at Marah, where the waters were bitter; but Moses, by casting a tree into them, rendered them fit for drinking. Their tenth encampment was at Rephidim, where Moses drew <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the rock in Horeb, by smiting it with his rod. Here likewise Amalek attacked Israel. While Joshua fought against the Amalekites, Moses stood on the top of a hill, and lifted up his hands; in consequence of which the Israelites prevailed, and cut their enemies in pieces. They at length arrived at the foot of Mount Sinai on the third day of the ninth month after their departure from Egypt. Moses having ascended several times into the mount, received the law from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of God himself in the midst of thunders and lightnings, and concluded the famous covenant betwixt the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> and the children of Israel. When he descended from Sinai, he found that the people had fallen into the idolatrous worship of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> calf. The messenger of God, shocked at such ingratitude, broke in pieces the tables of the law which he carried in his hands, and put 23,000 of the transgressors to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. He afterwards reascended into the mountain, and there obtained new tables of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on which the law was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>. When Moses descended, his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> shone so that the Israelites dared not to come nigh unto him, and he was obliged to cover it with a veil. The Israelites were here employed in constructing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> according to a pattern shown them by God. It was erected and consecrated at the foot of the Mount Sinai on the first day of the first month of the second year after their departure from Egypt; and it served the Israelites instead of a temple till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, who built a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the God of his fathers after a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> shown him by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. Moses having dedicated the tabernacle, he consecrated Aaron and his sons to be its ministers, and appointed the Levites to its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He likewise gave various commandments concerning the worship of God and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Jews. This was a theocracy in the full <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the word. God himself governed them immediately by means of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Moses, whom he had chosen to be the interpreter of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the people; and he required all the honours belonging to their king to be paid unto himself. He dwelt in his tabernacle, which was situated in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, like a monarch in his palace. He gave answers to those who consulted him, and himself denounced punishments against the transgressors of his laws. This properly was the time of the theocracy, taken in its full extent; for God was not only considered as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> who was the object of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, but as the sovereign to whom the honours of supreme majesty were paid. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> was nearly the same under Joshua; who, being filled with the spirit of Moses, undertook nothing without consulting God. Every <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, both of the leader and of the people, was regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Almighty, who rewarded their fidelity and obedience by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of miracles, victories, and successes. After Moses had regulated everything regarding the civil administration, Moses is incontestably the author of the first five books of the Old Testament, which go by the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>; and which are acknowledged to be inspired, by the Jews and by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of every persuasion. Some, however, have denied that Moses was the author of these books; and have founded their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on this, that he always speaks of himself in the third person. But this manner of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> is by no means peculiar to Moses: it occurs also in several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians; such as Xenophon, Caesar, Josephus, &c., who possessed more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> or good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> historians, whose egotism is altogether disgusting, have not like them left to posterity a spectacle of ridiculous vanity and self-conceit. After all, it is proper to observe, that profane authors have related many falsehoods and absurdities concerning Moses, and concerning the origin and the religion of the Jews, with which they were but little acquainted. Plutarch, in his book concerning Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, says that Judaeus and Hierotheus were brothers, and descended from Typhon; and that the former gave his name to the country and its inhabitants, and the latter to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city. Others say that they came from Mount Ida in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. Strabo is the only author who speaks anything like reason and truth concerning them; though he too says that they were descended from the Egyptians, and considers Moses their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> as an Egyptian priest. He acknowledges, however, that they were a people strictly <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and sincerely religious. Other authors by whom they are mentioned, seem not to have had the smallest acquaintance either with their laws or their worship. They frequently confound them with the Christians, as is the case with Juvenal, Tacitus, and Quintilian.

MOSHEIM

Pages 490-490

John Laurence, an illustrious German divine, was born in 1695, of a noble family, which might seem to open to his ambition a fair path to civil promotion; but his zeal for the interests of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, his thirst after knowledge, and particularly his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for sacred literature, induced him to consecrate his talents to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> loaded him with literary honours; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> invited him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> called him thence to Helmstadt, where he filled the academical <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; was honoured with the character of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and presided over the seminaries of learning in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wolfenbuttel and the principality of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANKENBURG">Blankenburg</a>. When a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was formed of giving an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of lustre to the universities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>, by filling it with men of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in letters, Dr Mosheim was deemed worthy to appear at the head of it, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; and here he died, in 1755, universally lamented. In depth of judgment, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of learning, in purity of taste, in the powers of eloquence, and in a laborious application to all the various branches of erudition and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he had certainly very few superiors. His Latin translation of Cudworth's Intellectual System, enriched with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> annotations, discovered a profound acquaintance with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> learning and philosophy. His illustrations of the Scriptures, his labours in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Christianity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> he <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon religion and philosophy, appear in many volumes of sacred and profane literature; and the Ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the birth of Christ to the beginning of the 18th century, is unquestionably the best that is extant. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, written in Latin, has been translated into English, and accompanied with notes and chronological tables by Archibald Maclean, D.D., and from this translator's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition, 1758, in 5 vols 8vo, this short account is taken.

MOSKITO

Pages 490-490
or Mosquito country, is situated in North America, between 85 and 88 degrees of west longitude, and between 13 and 15 degrees of north latitude; having the north sea on the north and east, Nicaragua on the south, and Honduras on the west; and indeed the Spaniards esteem it a part of the principality of Honduras, though they have no colonies in the Mosquito country. When the Spaniards first invaded this part of Mexico, they massacred the greatest part of the natives, which gave those that escaped into the inaccessible part of the country an impenetrable aversion to them; and they have always appeared ready to join any Europeans that come upon their coasts against the Spaniards, and particularly the English, who frequently come hither; and the Mosquito men being excellent marksmen, the English employ them in striking the manati fish, &c., and many of the Mosquito Indians come to Jamaica, and sail with the English in their voyages. These people are so situated between morasses and inaccessible mountains, and a coast full of rocks and shoals, that no attempts against them by the Spaniards, whom they mortally hate, could ever succeed. Nevertheless, they are a mild inoffensive people, of great morality and virtue, and will never trust a man who has once deceived them. They have so great a veneration towards the English, that they have spontaneously put themselves and their lands under the protection and dominion of the crown of England. This was first done when the duke of Albemarle was governor of Jamaica, and the king of the Moskitos received a commission from his grace, under the seal of that island; and since this time they have been steady in their alliance with the English. But in the year 1786, this country was ceded to Spain, and consequently became a Spanish province.

MOSTRA

in the Italian music, a mark at the end of a line <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> space, to show that the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the next line is in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> this note be accompanied with a sharp or flat, it is proper to place these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> along with the mostra.

MOTACILLA

Pages 493-493

the Wagtail and Warbler; a genus of birds of the order of Passeres. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOTE

Pages 493-493

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> books, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convention; as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> mote, burgh mote, twain mote, &c. Mote was also used for a fortres or castle; as mota de <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, &c. Mote also denoted a standing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to keep fish in; and sometimes a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ditch encompassing a castle or dwelling <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Mote-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>, or Mot-Bell, the bell so called, which was used by the English Saxons to call people together to the court. See Folkmote. MOTH. See Phalena, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOTHER

Pages 493-508

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation, denoting a woman who hath born a child. MOTHER-of-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a>. See Mytilus, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">MOTION</a> is now generally considered as incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, being a simple idea <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> notion received by the senses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, however, thought differently. Some of them defined it to be a passage out of one state into another; which conveys no idea to him. Motion. who is ignorant of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of motion.—The Peripatetic definition has been mentioned elsewhere and shown to be wholly unintelligible, as well as their celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of motion into four classes, belonging to the three categories, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, and where; (see <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, No 188, 189, 190.) The Cartesians, too, among the moderns, pretend to define motion, by calling it a passage or removal of one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, out of the neighbourhood of those parts to which it is immediately contiguous, into the neighbourhood of others. Borelli defines motion to be the successive passage of a body from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place. Others say that it is the application of a body to different parts of infinite and immovable space; and a late writer* of uncommon acuteness has given as a definition of motion—change of place. We have elsewhere offered our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of every possible attempt to define motion: but as the author of the last quoted definition has endeavoured to obviate such objections as ours, candour requires that he be heard for himself. "It is said (he observes) by some, that change implies motion, and therefore cannot be a part of its definition, being the very thing defined. To this I answer, We are speaking of the sensible idea of motion, as it appears to our sight; now changes do appear to our view, and to all our senses, which give us no idea of motion. Changes in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, flavour, smell, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>, softness, pain, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; in these, and many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, changes do not produce ideas like that produced by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> rolling or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> falling. We may perhaps ultimately trace them to motion, but to insensible motions; to motions which arise only in reflection, and constitute no part of the actual idea of change. We can therefore conceive of change, without conceiving at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of motion.—Change is a generic idea, including many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; motion, as a sensible idea, is a species of that genus. Change is therefore a necessary part of the definition of motion; it marks the genus of the thing defined. Motion is a change; but as there are many species of change, which of those species is motion? The answer is, It is a change of place. This marks the species; and distinguishes it from change of colour, of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>." This is the ablest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of an attempt to define motion that we have ever seen; and at first view the definition itself appears to be perfect. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of definers, "confiders a definition† as a speech declaring what a thing is. Every thing essential to the thing defined, and nothing more, must be contained in the definition. Now the essence of a thing consists of these two parts: first, what is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to it with other things of the same kind; and secondly, what distinguishes it from other things of the same kind. The first is called the genus of the thing; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, its specific <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. The definition, therefore, consists of these two parts." In obedience to this rule, the definition under consideration seems to consist of the genus, signified by the word change; and of the specific difference, denoted by the words of place. But does the speech change of place really declare what motion is? We cannot admit that it does; as, in our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, a change of place is the effect of motion, and not motion itself. Suppose a lover of dialectic undertaking to define the stroke by which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his neighbour wounded with a bludgeon; what should we think of his art were he to call it a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTUSION">contusion</a> on the head? He might say that contusion is a general term, as contusions may be produced on the arms, on the legs, and on various parts of the body; and as there are many species of contusion, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he were asked which of those species was the stroke to be defined, he might answer, "a contusion on the head." Here would be apparently the genus and specific difference; the former denoted by contusion, and the latter by the words on the head. But would this be a definition of a stroke? No, surely: a contusion on the head may be the effect of a stroke; but it can no more be the stroke itself, than a blow can be a bludgeon, or a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> wound the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. Equally evident it is, that a change of place cannot be motion; because every body must have been actually moved before we can discern, or even conceive, a change of its place. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of changing the place would perhaps come nearer to a definition of motion; but so far would it be from "a speech declaring what motion is," that we are confident a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had never by any of his senses perceived a body in actual motion, would acquire no ideas whatever from the words "act of changing place." He might have experienced changes in heat, cold, smell, and sound; but he could not possibly combine the ideas of such changes with the signification of the word place, were he even capable of understanding that word, which to us appears to be more than doubtful. (See Metaphysics, No 40, 41.) The distinctions of motion into different kinds have been no less various, and no less insignificant, than the divisions of motion into Peripatetic division of motion into four classes, yet consider themselves as either <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> or relative. Thus we are told, that "absolute motion is the change of absolute place, and that its celerity must be measured by the quantity of absolute space which the moving body runs through in a given time." "Relative motion, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, is a mutation of the relative or vulgar place of the moving body, and has its celerity estimated by the quantity of relative space run through." Now it is obvious, that this distinction conveys no ideas without a farther explanation of the terms by which it is expressed; but that explanation is impossible to be given. Thus, before we can understand what absolute motion is, we must understand what is meant by absolute place. But absolute place is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; for all place is relative, and consists in the positions of different bodies with regard to one another. Were a globe in the regions of empty space to be put in motion by Almighty Power, and all the rest of the corporeal world to be soon afterwards annihilated, the motion would undoubtedly continue unchanged; and yet, according to this distinction, it would be at first relative, and afterwards absolute. That the beginning of such a motion would be perceptible, and the remainder of it imperceptible, is readily granted; but on this account to consider it as of two kinds, is as absurd as to suppose the motion of the minute hand of a clock to be affected by our looking at it. Leaving therefore these unintelligible distinctions, respecting motion, we now come to consider a question full of a very abstruse nature, but much agitated among philosophers, viz., viz. What is the original source of motion in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>? Is it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to matter? or are we to ascribe it to the immediate and continual agency of some immaterial being? The former has been strenuously argued by the Cartesians, and the latter by the Newtonians. The arguments of the former, founded upon the chimerical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of vortices and the original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of matter, were evidently inconclusive; and the hypothesis of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, who asserted that it was naturally incapable of motion, appeared more probable. To account for the quantity of motion in the universe, therefore, it became necessary to have recourse either to the Deity, or to some subordinate spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>; and this became the more necessary, as the doctrine of an absolute <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> in the celestial spaces, that is, throughout the incomparably greatest part of the creation, was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> maxims of the system. As it was absolutely denied that matter existed in these spaces, and it was plain that the celestial bodies affected one another at immense distances, the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> and repulsion were naturally called in as the sources of motion by their impulse upon inert and sluggish matter. These being admitted, a speculation ensued concerning their nature. Spiritual, it was confessed, they were; but whether they were to be accounted the immediate <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the divine Spirit himself, or that of some subordinate and inferior spirit, was a matter of no little dispute. Sir Isaac Newton, towards the latter part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, began to relax somewhat of the rigidity of his former doctrine; and allowed that a very subtle medium, which he called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, might be the cause of attraction and repulsion, and thus of the whole phenomena of nature. Since his time the multitude of discoveries in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, the familiarity of that fluid to fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, with the vast influence it has on every part of the creation with which we are acquainted, have rendered it very probable that the ether mentioned by Sir Isaac is no other than the element of fire, "the most subtle and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> of all bodies, which seems to pervade and expand itself throughout the whole universe." Electrical experiments show that this mighty agent is everywhere present, ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> forth into action, if not restrained and governed with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. Being always restless and in motion, it actuates and enlivens the whole visible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; is equally fitted to produce and to destroy; distinguishes the various stages of nature, and keeps up the perpetual round of generations and corruptions, pregnant with forms which it constantly sends forth and absorbs. So quick in its motions, so subtle and penetrating in its nature, so extensive in its effects, it leaveth no other than the vegetative <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> or vital spirit of the world. "The animal spirit in man is the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and motion. To suppose sense in the corporeal world would be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and unwarranted; but locomotive faculties are evident in all its parts. The Pythagoreans, Platonists, and Stoics, held the world to be an animal; though some of them have chosen to consider it as a vegetable. However, the phenomena do plainly show, that there is a spirit that moves, and a mind or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a> that presides. This providence, Plutarch <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, was thought to be in regard to the world what the soul is in regard to man. The order and course of things, and the experiments we daily make, show that there is a mind which governs and actuates this mundane system as the proper and real agent and cause; and that the inferior instrumental cause is pure ether, fire, or the substance of light, which is applied and determined by an infinite mind in the macrocosm or universe, with unlimited power, and according to stated rules, as it is in the microcosm with limited power and skill by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind. We have no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> either from experiment or reason of any other agent or efficient cause than the mind or spirit. When, therefore, we speak of corporeal agents, or corporeal causes, this is to be understood in a different, subordinate, and improper sense; and such an agent we know light or elementary fire to be." That this elementary fire, absorbed and fixed in all Experiment-bodies, may be the cause of the universal principle of gravity, is made sufficiently evident by numberless experiments. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a> having calcined in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> glass some regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, found that the impurities had gained one-tenth in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, though the regulus, during the whole time of the operation, sent up a thick <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, and thereby lost a considerable part of its own substance. It is vain to allege that any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matter floating in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, or that the air itself, may have been hurried into the mass by the action of the fire, and that by this additional matter the weight was increased; for it is known experimentally, that if a quantity of metal be even hermetically secured within a vessel of glass to keep off the air and all foreign matter, and the vessel be placed for some time in a strong fire, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> exhibit the same effect. "I have seen the operation performed (says Mr Jones) on two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a> filings, hermetically sealed up in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> flask, which in two hours gained 55 grains, or that is nearly one 17th. Had it remained longer in the fire, it might probably have gained something more; as, in one of Mr Boyle's experiments, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> filings were found to have gained a fourth." Of accounting for these effects there are but two possible ways: 1. If the quantity of matter be the same, or, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of calcination, be somewhat less, after being exposed to the action of the fire, while the gravity of the whole is become greater; then does it follow, that gravity is not according to the quantity of matter, and of course is not one of its properties. 2. If there be an increase of the mass, it can be imputed to nothing but the matter of light or fire entangled in its passage through the substance, and so fixed in its pores, or combined with its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> parts, as to gravitate together with it. Yet it is certain, from the phenomenon of light darting from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, that this elementary fire does not gravitate till it is fixed in metal, or some other solid substance.—Here then we have a fluid which gravitates, if it gravitate at all, in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> and not in others. So that whichever way forever the experiment be interpreted, we are forced to conclude that elementary or solar fire may be the cause of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>." That it is likewise in many cases the cause of repulsion, is known to every one who has seen it <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FUSE">fuse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, and convert <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> into elastic vapour. But there is a fact recorded by Mr Jones, which seems to evince that the same fluid, which as it issues from the sun exhibits itself in the form of light and heat, is in other circumstances converted into a very fine air, Motion or cold ether, which rushes very forcibly towards the body of that luminary. "As a sequel to what has been observed (says he) concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> of solid substances with the particles of fire, give me leave to subjoin an experiment of M. de Stair. He tells us, that upon heating <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> in a glass, whence the air was exhausted by the rays of the sun collected in a burning glass, the vessel in which the said red lead was contained burst in pieces with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> noise. Now, as all explosions in general must be ascribed either to an admixture of the air into a rarefied space, or to what is called the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of it; and as air was not admitted upon this occasion, it must have been <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> within the vessel; and certainly was so, because Dr Hales has made it appear that this substance, like crude tartar and many others, will yield a considerable quantity of air in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. What went into the metal therefore as fire, came out of it again as air; which in a manner forces upon us conclusions of ineffinable value in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and such as may carry us very far into the most sublime part of it." One of the conclusions which the ingenious author thinks thus forced upon us, is, that the motion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> round the sun, as well as round their own axes, is to be attributed to the continual agency of this fluid, under its two forms of elementary fire and pure air. As fire and light, we know that it runs with inconceivable rapidity from the body of the sun, and penetrates every corporeal substance, exerting itself sometimes with such force as nothing with which we are acquainted is able to resist. If it be indeed a fact, that this elementary fire, or principle of light and heat, afterwards cools, and becomes pure air, there cannot be a doubt, but that under such a form it will return with great force, though surely in a somewhat different <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, towards the sun, forming a vortex, in which the planets are included, and by which they must of course be carried round the centre. Mr Jones does not suppose that the air into which the principle of light and heat is converted, is of so gross a nature as our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. He rather considers it as cool ether, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as he represents light to be ether heated: but he maintains, that this ether, in its aerial form, though not fit for human respiration, is a better pabulum of fire than the air which we breathe. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> is exceedingly plausible; and the author supports it by many experiments. He has not, indeed, convinced us that the solar light is convertible or convertible into pure air; but he has, by just reasoning from undoubted facts, proved that the whole expanse of heaven, as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> wander, is filled not only with light, which is indeed obvious to the senses, but also with a fluid, which, whatever it may be called, supplies the place of the air in feeding the fire of these ignited bodies. That the motion of the heavenly bodies should result from the perpetual agency of such a medium, appears to us a much more rational hypothesis, than that which makes them act upon each other at immense distances through empty space. But the hypothesis is by no means so complete a solution of the phenomena as some of its fond admirers pretend to think it. This fluid, whether called ether, heat, light, or air, is still material; and the question returns upon him who imagines that it is sufficient to account for gravitation, repulsion, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a>, &c. "What moves the fluid itself, or makes the parts of which it is composed cohere together?" However widely it may be extended, it is incapable of positive infinity; and therefore may be divided into parts separated from each other; so that it must be held together by a foreign force, as well as a ball of lead, or a piece of wax.
