The followers of Ali, dissatisfied with this name, substitute that of Adlia, which means "afforters of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>," literally "Judiciaries;" a denomination which they have assumed in consequence of a doctrinal point they advance in opposition to the Sonnite faith. A small Arabic treatise, entitled Theological Fragments concerning the Sects and Religions of the World, has the following passage: "These sectaries who pretend that God acts only on principles of justice, conformable to human reason, are called Adlia or Judiciaries. God cannot (say they) command an impracticable worship, nor ordain impossible actions, nor enjoin men to perform what is beyond their ability; but wherever he requires obedience, will bestow the power to obey. He removes the cause of evil, he allows us to reason, and imposes only what is easy, not what is difficult; he makes no man responsible for the actions of another, nor punishes him for that in which he has no part; he imputes not as a crime what himself has created in man; nor does he require him to avoid what <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> has decreed.—This would be injustice and tyranny, of which God is incapable, from the perfection of his being." To this doctrine, which diametrically opposes the system of the Sonnites, the Motoualis add certain ceremonies which increase their mutual aversion. They curse Omar and Moaouia as rebels and usurpers; and celebrate Ali and Hosain as saints and martyrs. They begin their ablutions at the elbow, instead of the end of the finger, as is customary with the Turks; they think themselves defiled by the touch of strangers; and, contrary to the general practice of the East, neither eat nor drink out of a vessel which has been used by a person not of their sect, nor will they even fit with such at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. These doctrines and customs, by separating the Motoualis from their neighbours, have rendered them a distinct <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. It is said they have long existed as a nation in this country, though their name has never been mentioned by any European writer before the 18th century; it is not even to be found in the maps of D'Anville: La Roque, who left their country not a hundred years ago, gives them the name of Amédians. Be this as it may, in later times their wars, robberies, successes, and various changes of fortune, have rendered them of consequence in Syria. Till about the middle of this century, they only possessed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BALBEC">Balbec</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and a few places in the valley, and Anti-Lebanon, which seems to have been their original country. Motoualis, country. At that period we find them under a like government with the Druzes, that is to say, under a number of Shaiks, with one principal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the family of Harfouch. After the year 1750 they established themselves among the heights of Bekaa, and got footing in Lebanon, where they obtained lands belonging to the Maronites, almost as far as Beharrai. They even incumbered them so much by their ravages, as to oblige the emir Yousef to attack them with open force and expel them; but on the other side, they advanced along the river even to the neighbourhood of Sour (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>). In this situation, Shaik Daher had the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, in 1760, to attach them to his party. The pachas of Saide and Damascus claimed tributes, which they had neglected paying, and complained of several robberies committed on their subjects by the Motoualis; they were desirous of chastising them; but this vengeance was neither certain nor easy. Daher interposed; and by becoming security for the tribute, and promising to prevent any depredations, acquired allies who were able, as it is said, to arm 10,000 horsemen, all resolute and formidable troops. Shortly after they took possession of Sour, and made this village their principal sea port. In 1771 they were of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to Ali Bey and Daher against the Ottomans. But Emir Yousef having in their absence armed the Druzes, ravaged their country. He was besieging the castle of Djezin, when the Motoualis, returning from Damascus, received intelligence of this invasion. At the relation of the barbarities committed by the Druzes, an advanced corps, of only 500 men, were so enraged, that they immediately rushed forward against the enemy, determined to perish in taking vengeance. But the surprise and confusion they occasioned, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> which reigned between the two factions of Manfour and Yousef, so much favoured this desperate attack, that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, consisting of 25,000 men, was completely overthrown. In the following year, the affairs of Daher taking a favourable turn, the zeal of the Motoualis cooled towards him, and they finally abandoned him in the catastrophe in which he lost his life. But they have suffered for their imprudence under the administration of the pacha who succeeded him. Since the year 1777, Djezzar, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a> and Saide, has incessantly laboured to destroy them. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> forced them in 1784 to a reconciliation with the Druzes, and to enter into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the emir Yousef. Though reduced to less than 700 armed men, they did more in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> than 15,000 or 20,000 Druzes and Maronites assembled at Dair-el-Kamar. They alone took the strong fortresses of Mar-Djebaa, and put to the sword 50 or 60 Epirots who defended it. But the misunderstanding which prevailed among the chiefs of the Druzes having rendered abortive all their operations, the pacha has obtained possession of the whole valley, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Balbec itself. At this period not more than 500 families of the Motoualis remained, who took refuge in Anti-Lebanon, and the Lebanon of the Maronites; and, driven as they now are from their native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, it is probable they will be totally annihilated, and even their very name become extinct.

MOUFET

Pages 508-509

THOMAS, a celebrated English physician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and practised medicine with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. Towards the latter end of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> life he retired to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and died about the year 1600. This physician is known by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which was begun by Edward Wotton, and printed at London in 1634, folio, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Theatrum Insectorum. A translation of it into English was published at London in 1658, folio. Martin Lister gives a very unfavourable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of this book: "As Mouset (says he) made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of Wotton, Gesner, &c., an excellent work might have been expected from him; and yet his Theatrum is full of confusion, and he has made a very bad use of the materials with which these authors have furnished him. He is ignorant of the subject of which he treats, and his manner of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> is altogether barbarous. Besides this, he is extremely arrogant, to say no worse; for though he has copied Aldrovandus in innumerable places, he never once mentions his name." But Ray thinks that Lister, by expressing himself in this manner, has not done <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to Mouset; and he maintains that the latter has rendered an essential <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the republic of letters.

MOUG-DEN

Pages 509-509
or CHEN-YANG; a city of Chinese Tartary, and capital of the country of the Mantchews or Eastern Tartars. These people have been at great pains to ornament it with several public edifices, and to provide it with magazines of arms and storehouses. They consider it as the principal place of their nation; and since China has been under their dominion, they have established the same tribunals here as at Peking, excepting that called Liou-pou; these tribunals are composed of Tartars only; their determination is final; and in all their acts they use the Tartar characters and language. The city is built on an eminence; a number of rivers add much to the fertility of the surrounding country. It may be considered as a double city, of which one is enclosed within the other: the interior contains the emperor's palace, hotels of the principal mandarins, sovereign courts, and the different tribunals; the exterior is inhabited by the common people, tradesmen, and all those who by their employments or professions are not obliged to lodge in the interior. The latter is almost a league in circumference; and the walls which enclose both are more than three leagues round; these walls were entirely rebuilt in 1631, and repaired several times under the reign of Kang-hi.

MOULD

Pages 509-510
or MOULD, in the mechanic arts, &c., a cavity artificially cut, with a design to give its form or impression to some softer matter applied therein. Moulds are implements of great use in sculpture, foundry, &c. The workmen employed in melting the mineral or metallic ore dug out of mines, have their several moulds to receive the melted metal as it comes out of the furnace; but these are different according to the diversity of metals and works. In gold mines, they have moulds for ingots; in silver mines, for bars; in copper and lead mines, for pigs or falcons; in tin mines, for pigs and ingots; and in iron mines, for sows, chimney backs, anvils, caldrons, pots, and other large utensils and merchandises of iron; which are here cast, as it were, at first hand. Moulds of founders of large works, as statues, bells, guns, and other brazen works, are of wax, supported within-side by what we call a core, and covered without-side with a cape or case. It is in the space which the wax took up, which is afterwards melted away to leave it free, that the liquid metal runs, and the work is formed; being carried thither through a great number of little canals, which cover the whole mould. See Foundery. Moulds of moneyers are frames full of sand, wherein the plates of metal are cast that are to serve for the striking of species of gold and silver. See Coining. A sort of concave moulds made of clay, having within them the figures and inscriptions of ancient Roman coins, are found in many parts of England, and supposed to have been used for the casting of money. Mr Baker having been favoured with a sight of some of these moulds found in Shropshire, bearing the same types and inscriptions with some of the Roman coins, gave an account of them to the Royal Society. They were found in digging of sand, at a place called Ryton in Shropshire, about a mile from the great Watling-street road. They are all of the size of the Roman denarius, and of little more than the thickness of our halfpenny. They are made of a smooth pot or brick clay, which seems to have been first well cleansed from dirt and sand, and well beaten or kneaded, to render it fit for taking a fair impression. There were a great many of them found together, and there are of them not unfrequently found in Yorkshire; but they do not seem to have been met with in any other kingdom, except that some have been said to be once found at Lyons. They have been sometimes found in great numbers joined together side by side, on one flat piece of clay, as if intended for the casting of a great number of coins at once; and both these, and all the others that have been found, seem to have been of the emperor Severus. They are sometimes found impressed on both sides, and some have the head of Severus on one side and some well-known reverse of his on the other. They seem plainly to have been intended for the coinage of money, though it is not easy to say in what manner they can have been employed for that purpose, especially those which have impressions on both sides, unless it may be supposed that they coined two pieces at the same time by the help of three moulds, of which this was to be the middle one. If by disposing these into some sort of iron frame or case, as our letter-founders do the brass moulds for casting their types, the melted metal could be easily poured into them, it would certainly be a very easy method of coining, as such moulds require little time or expense to make, and therefore might be supplied with new ones as often as they happen to break. These moulds seem to have been burnt or baked sufficiently to make them hard; but not so as to render them porous like our bricks, whereby they would have lost their smooth and even surface, which in these is plainly so close, that whatever metal should be formed in them would have no appearance like the sand-holes by which counterfeit coins and metals are usually detected. Moulds of founders of small works are like the frames of coiners: it is in these frames, which are likewise filled with sand, that their several works are fashioned; into which, when the two frames of which the mould is composed, are rejoined, the melted brass is run. Moulds of letter-founders are partly of steel and partly of wood. The wood, properly speaking, serves only to cover the real mould which is within, and to prevent Moulds prevent the workman, who holds it in his hand, from being incommoded by the heat of the melted metal. Only one letter or type can be formed at once in each mould. See LETTER FOUNDRY. Moulds, in the manufacture of paper, are little frames composed of several brafs or iron wires, fastened together by another wire till finer. Each mould is of the bigness of the sheet of paper to be made, and has a rim or ledge of wood to which the wires are fastened. These moulds are more usually called frames or forms. See PAPER-Making. Moulds, with furnace and crucible makers, are made of wood, of the same form with the crucibles; that is, in form of a truncated cone: they have handles of wood to hold and turn them with, when being covered with the earth, the workman has a mind to round or flatten his vessel. Moulds for leaden bullets are little iron pincers, each of whose branches terminates in a hemispherical concave, which when shut form an entire sphere. In the lips or sides where the branches meet is a little jet or hole, through which the melted lead is conveyed. Laboratory Moulds are made of wood, for filling and driving all sorts of rockets and cartridges, &c. Glaziers Moulds. The glaziers have two kinds of moulds, both serving to cast their lead: in the one they cast the lead into long rods or canes fit to be drawn through the vice, and the grooves formed therein; this they sometimes call ingot-mould. In the other, they mould those little pieces of lead a line thick and two lines broad, fastened to the iron bars. These may be also cast in the vice. Goldsmiths Moulds. The goldsmiths use the bones of the cuttle fish to make moulds for their small works; which they do by pressing the pattern between two bones, and leaving a jet or hole to convey the metal through, after the pattern has been taken out. Mould, among masons, is a piece of hard wood or iron hollowed within side, answerable to the contours of the mouldings or cornices, &c., to be formed. This is otherwise caliber. Moulds, among plumbers, are the tables on which they cast sheets of lead. These they sometimes call simply tables. Besides which they have other real moulds, wherewith they cast pipes without soldering. See each described under PLUMBERY. Moulds, among the glass grinders, are wooden frames, wherein they make the tubes wherewith they fit their perspectives, telescopes, and other optic machines. These moulds are cylinders, of a length and diameter according to the use they are to be applied to, but always thicker at one end than the other, to facilitate the sliding. The tubes made on these moulds are of two kinds; the one simply of pasteboard and paper; the other of thin leaves of wood joined to the pasteboard. To make these tubes to draw out, only the last or innermost is formed on the mould; each tube made afterwards serving as a mould to that which is to go over it, but without taking out the mould from the first. See GRINDING. Moulds used in basket-making are very simple, consisting ordinarily of a willow or other turned or bent into an oval, circle, square, or other figure, according to the baskets, panniers, hampers, and other utensils intended. On these moulds they make, or more properly measure, all their work; and accordingly they have moulds of all sizes, shapes, &c. Mould, in ship-building, a thin flexible piece of timber, used by shipwrights as a pattern whereby to form the different curves of the timbers, and other compassing pieces in a ship's frame. There are two sorts of these, viz. the bend mould and hollow mould; the former of these determines the convexity of the timbers, and the latter their concavity on the outside, where they approach the heel, particularly towards the extremities of the vessel. The figure given to the timbers by this pattern is called their bevelling. Moulds, among tallow chandlers, are of two kinds: the first for the common dipped candles, being the vessel wherein the melted tallow is disposed, and the wick dipped. This is of wood, of a triangular form, and supported on one of its angles: so that it has an opening of near a foot a-top: the other, used in the fabric of mould candles, is of brafs, pewter, or tin.—Here each candle has its several mould. See CANDLE. Mould, among gold-beaters, a certain number of leaves of vellum or pieces of gut, cut square of a certain size, and laid over one another, between which they put the leaves of gold and silver which they beat on the marble with the hammer. See GOLD LEAF. They have four kinds of moulds; two whereof are of vellum and two of gut; the smallest of those of vellum consists of 40 or 50 leaves; the largest contains 100: for the others, each contains 500 leaves. The moulds have all their several cases, consisting of two pieces of parchment, serving to keep the leaves of the mould in their place, and prevent their being disordered in beating. Mould, in Agriculture, a general name for the soft earthy substance with which the dry land is generally covered, and in which all kinds of vegetables take root and grow. It is far from being an homogeneous substance; being composed of decayed animal and vegetable matters, along with calcareous, argillaceous, and siliceous earths, mixed together in various proportions, and with the different degrees of moisture, constituting every variety of SOIL.

MOULDINESS

Pages 510-510

is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lanugo, which is produced on the surface of animal or vegetable matters in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>; and which viewed through a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> appears like a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, out of which arise herbs and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. See MUCOR, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOULDING

Pages 510-510

any thing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in a mould, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that seems to have been so, though in reality it were cut with a chisel or the axe.

MOULDINGS

Pages 510-510

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, projections beyond the naked wall, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, wainscot, &c. the assemblage of which forms corniches, door <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and other decorations of Architecture. See that article. MOULINET is used in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, to signify a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, which being crossed with two levers, is usually applied to cranes, capstans, and other sorts of engines of the like <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to draw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, heave up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, &c. Moulinet is also a kind of turnstile <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wooden crofs, which turns horizontally upon a stake fixed in the ground; usually placed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> to keep out horses, and to oblige passengers to go and come one by one. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOULINS">moulins</a> are often set near the outworks.

MOULIN

Pages 510-511

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIER">Allier</a>, and containing about 16,000 inhabitants. The houses of the Chartreux, and that of the Visitation, are magnificent. It has a considerable trade in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, and is seated on the river Allier, in a pleasant fertile plain, almost in the middle of France, 30 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and 55 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Clermont. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 25'. N. Lat. 46° 34'.

MOULTING

Pages 511-511
or Molting, the falling off or change of hair, feathers, skins, horns, or other parts of animals, happening in some annually, in others only at certain stages of life. The generality of animals moult in the spring. The moulting of a hawk is called mewing. The moulting of a deer is the quitting of his horns in February or March. The moulting of a serpent is the putting off his skin. See EXUVIA.

MOULTON

Pages 511-511

South, on the same stream, 182 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. This, as well as the former, was anciently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> demesne. It sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the reign of Edward I. consists of a mayor, 18 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, a recorder, town clerk, and 2 ferjeants at mace. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are ferges, shalloons, and felts; and a considerable market for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>.

MOUND

Pages 511-511

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> globe with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> upon it, such as our kings are usually drawn with, holding it in their left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, as they do the sceptre in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>.

MOUNT

Pages 511-511

an elevation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, called also mountain. See MOUNTAIN. MOUNT Edgecumbe, a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> peak, at the entrance of Cook's strait, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NEW_ZEALAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, on the west side. Its height is supposed not to be much inferior to that of the Peak of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOUNT_SORREL">MOUNT <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SORREL">Sorrel</a>, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTERSHIRE">Leicestershire</a>, so named from a high mount <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock adjoining to the town, of a dusky <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or borrel-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, extremely hard. Of rough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> hewn out of this rock the town is built. It has a market on Mondays. It was noted formerly for its castle, and is seated on the river Stour, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. It is 20 miles south-east by south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, and 105 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west by north of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 9'. N. Lat. 52° 45'. MOUNTS of Piety, certain funds or establishments in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> out on some small security. There were also mounts of piety in England, raised by contribution for the benefit of people ruined by the extortions of the Jews.

MOUNTAIN

Pages 511-514

a considerable eminence of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, elevated above the surrounding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>: It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> full of inequalities, cavities more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less exposed, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> uncovered. For the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, see MOUNTAIN, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">Attraction</a> of MOUNTAINS. This is a late discovery, and a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of universal gravity. According to the Newtonian system, an attractive power is not only exerted between those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which constitute the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, but likewise between all comparatively smaller bodies, and even between the smallest particles of which they are composed. Agreeably to this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, a heavy body, which ought to gravitate or tend toward the centre of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> perpendicular to its surface, supposing the said surface to be perfectly even and spherical, ought likewise, though in a less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, to be attracted and tend towards a mountain placed on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface; so that a plumb line, for instance, of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, hanging in the neighbourhood of such a mountain, ought to be drawn from a perpendicular situation, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the attractive power of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of matter of which it is composed acting in a direction different from that exerted by the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of matter in the earth, and with a proportionably inferior degree of force. Though Sir Isaac Newton had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago hinted at an experiment of this kind, and had remarked, that "a mountain of an hemispherical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, three miles <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, would not, by its attraction, draw the plumb line two minutes out of the perpendicular (E):" yet no attempt to ascertain this matter by actual experiment was made till about the year 1738; when the French academicians, particularly M. Bouguer and Condamin, who were sent to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a degree under the equator, attempted to discover the attractive power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIMBORAZO">Chimborazo</a>, a mountain in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Quito. According to their observations, which were however made under circumstances by no means favourable to an accurate solution of so nice and difficult a problem, the mountain Chimborazo exerted an attraction equal to eight seconds. Though this experiment was not perhaps sufficient to prove satisfactorily even the reality of an attraction, much less the precise quantity of it; yet it does not appear that any steps had been since taken to repeat it. Through the munificence of his Britannic majesty, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> were enabled to undertake the execution of this delicate and important experiment; the astronomer royal was chosen to conduct it. After various inquiries, the mountain Schellihen, situated nearly in the centre of Scotland, was pitched upon as the most proper for the purpose that could be found in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. The observations were made by taking the meridian zenith distances of different fixed stars, near the zenith, by means of a zenith <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a> of ten feet radius; first on the south, and afterwards on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the hill, the greatest length of which extended in an east and west direction. It is evident, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the mass of matter in the hill exerted any sensible attraction, it would cause the plumb-line of the sector, through which an observer viewed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> in the meridian, to deviate from its perpendicular situation, and would attract it contrariwise at (E) By a very easy calculation it is found that such a mountain would attract the plumb line 1' 18" from the perpendicular. Mountains. the two stations, thereby doubling the effect. On the south side the plumb line would be drawn to the northward by the attractive power of the hill placed to the northward of it; and on the north side, a contrary and equal deflection of the plumb line would take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in consequence of the attraction of the hill now to the southward of it. The apparent zenith distances of the stars would be affected contrariwise; those being increased at the one station which were diminished at the other; and the correspondent quantities of the deflection of the plumb line would give the observer the sum of the contrary attractions of the hill, acting on the plumb line at the two stations; the half of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of course indicate the attractive power of the hill. The various operations requisite for this experiment lasted about four months; and from them it appears that the sum of the two contrary attractions of the mountain Schehallien, in the two temporary observations which were successively fixed half way up the hill (where the effect of its attraction would be greatest), was equal to $11''6$.—From a rough computation, founded on the known <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, and on an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> that the density of the hill is equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> density of the earth, it appears that the attraction of the hill should amount to about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of this quantity. From thence it was inferred that the density of the hill is only about half the mean density of the earth. It does not appear, however, that the mountain Schehallien has ever been a volcano, or is hollow; as it is extremely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and dense, and seemingly composed of an entire rock. The inferences drawn from these experiments may be reduced to the following: "1. It appears, that the mountain Schehallien exerts a sensible attraction; therefore, from the rules of philosophizing, we are to conclude, that every mountain, and indeed every particle of the earth, is endowed with the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, in proportion to its quantity of matter. "2. The law of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of this force, in the inverse ratio of the squares of the distances, as laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Sir Isaac Newton, is also confirmed by this experiment. For if the force of attraction of the hill had been only to that of the earth, as the matter in the hill to that of the earth, and had not been greatly increased by the near approach to its centre, the attraction thereof must have been wholly insensible. But now, by only supposing the mean density of the earth to be double to that of the hill, which seems very probable from other considerations, the attraction of the hill will be reconciled to the general law of the variation of attraction in the inverse duplicate ratio of the distances, as deduced by Sir Isaac Newton from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the heavenly bodies with the force of gravity at the surface of the earth; and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> will be preserved. "3. We may now, therefore, be allowed to admit this law, and to acknowledge, that the mean density of the earth is at least double of that at the surface; and consequently that the density of the internal parts of the earth is much greater than near the surface. Hence also, the whole quantity of matter in the earth will be at least as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> again, as if it had been all composed of matter of the same density with that at the surface; or will be about four or five times as great as if it were all composed of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.—This conclusion, Mr Maskelyne adds, is totally contrary to the hypothesis of some naturalists, who suppose the earth to be only a great hollow shell of matter, supporting itself from the property of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, with an immense vacancy in the midst of it. But were that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the attraction of mountains, and even smaller inequalities in the earth's surface would be very great, contrary to experiment, and would affect the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of the degrees of the meridian much more than we find they do; and the variation of gravity, in different latitudes, in going from the equator to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, as found by pendulums, would not be near so regular as it has been found by experiment to be. "4. As mountains are by these experiments found capable of producing sensible deflections of the plumb <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of astronomical instruments; it becomes a matter of great importance, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of degrees in the meridian, either to choose places where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> attraction of the elevated parts may be small; or where, by their situation, they may compensate or counteract the effects of each other." For measuring the heights of mountains, see <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">Barometer</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a> Mountains. See Aetna, Hecla, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a>; see also Volcano, Geology Index. Marble Mountains. Of these there are great numbers in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, from which, though immense quantities have been carried off for the multitude of great works erected by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians; yet in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of Mr Bruce, who passed by them in his journey to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, there is still a sufficient supply to build Rome, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, Corinth, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and half a dozen more of such cities. The first mountain of this kind mentioned by Mr Bruce is one opposite to Terfowey, consisting partly of green marble, partly of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> blush upon a gray ground, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> spots. Here he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a monstrous obelisk of marble very nearly square, broken at the end, and nearly 30 feet long and 19 feet in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Throughout the plain there were scattered small pieces of jasper, with green, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and red spots called in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> dioptra languinosa; and all the mountains upon that side seemed to consist of the same materials. From Mr Bruce's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of these mountains, it would appear that they are composed of serpentine, and not of calcareous marble. Written Mountain, Mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">Inscriptions</a>, or Jbel-el-Mokattab, a supposed mountain or chain of mountains, in the wilderness of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>; on which, for a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of space, the marble of which the mountain consists is interbedded with innumerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, reaching from the ground sometimes to the height of 12 or 14 feet. These were mentioned by a Greek author in the third century, and some of them have been copied by Pococke and other late travellers; but, after all, there is still a very great uncertainty even of the existence of such mountain or mountains. The vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these inscriptions, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> place in which they are found, and the length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> requisite for executing the task, have induced a notion by no means unnatural, that they are the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the Israelites during their forty years wandering in the wilderness. Others are of opinion that they contain nothing of any importance, Mountains, importance, but consist merely of the names of travellers and the dates of their journeys. M. Niebuhr, who visited this country during his travels in the east, made every attempt in his power, though without success, to obtain a sight of this celebrated mountain. On applying to some Greeks at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, they all declared that they knew nothing of the written mountain; they, however, directed him to an Arabian sheik, who had passed all his lifetime in travelling between Suez and Mount Sinai; but he knew no more of it than the former. Understanding, however, that a considerable reward would be given to any person who would conduct them thither, this Arab directed them to another; who pretended not only to know that mountain, but all others upon which there were any inscriptions throughout the desert. On inquiring particularly, however, our travellers found that he was not to be depended upon; so that they were obliged to have recourse to a fourth sheik, who by his conversation convinced them that he had seen mountains with inscriptions in unknown characters upon them. It does not appear, however, that this person was very capable, more than the rest, of leading them to the place they so much wished for; though he conducted them to some rocks upon which there were inscriptions in unknown characters. They are most numerous in a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> between two mountains named Om-er-riffein; and, says M. Niebuhr, "the pretended Jibel-el-Mokatteb may possibly be in its neighbourhood." Some of these inscriptions were copied by our author; but he does not look upon them to be of any consequence. "They seem (says he) to have been executed at idle hours by travellers, who were satisfied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the unpolished rock with any pointed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, adding to their names and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of their journeys some rude figures, which bespeak the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a people but little skilled in the arts. When such inscriptions are executed with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of transmitting to posterity the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of such events as might afford instructive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>, greater care is generally taken in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the inscriptions are engraven with more regularity." When M. Niebuhr arrived at last at the mountain to which the sheik had promised to conduct him, he did not find any inscriptions; but on climbing up to the top, he found out an Egyptian cemetery, the stones of which were covered with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> stones are from five to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet in length, some standing on end and others lying flat; and "the more carefully they are examined (says he), the more certainly do they appear to be sepulchral stones, having epitaphs <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on them. In the middle of these stones is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, of which only the walls now remain; and within it are likewise a great many of the sepulchral stones. At one end of the building seems to have been a small chamber, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> still remains. It is supported upon square pillars; and these, as well as the walls of the chamber, are covered with hieroglyphic inscriptions. Through the whole building are various busts executed in the manner of the ancient Egyptians. The sepulchral stones and the busts are of hard and fine grained sandstone," M. Niebuhr is of opinion that this cemetery was not the work of the Egyptians themselves, but of some colony which came from Egypt, and had adopted the manners and customs of the people. He supposes that it might have been built by the Arabs, who had conquered Egypt under the shepherd kings, and adopted the Egyptian manners during their residence there. As it must have belonged to an opulent <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, however, he owns that there is a great difficulty in accounting for the existence of such a city in the midst of a desert. The translator of Volney's travels attributes these inscriptions to the pilgrims who visit Mount Sinai. But to this, as well as to every other conjecture, there is this objection, that whether the inscriptions be well executed or not, whether they contain matters of importance or not, they ought to have been written in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which somebody could understand; but from the copies that have been taken of them by Dr. Pococke and others, it does not appear that they could be explained either by him or any other person. When Dr. Clayton, bishop of Clogher, visited this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world about the year 1723, he expressed the greatest desire to have the matter concerning this written mountain or mountains ascertained, and even made an offer of 500l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> to any literary person who would undertake the journey and endeavour to decipher the inscriptions; but no such person has appeared, and the existence of the mountains is testified only by the superior of a convent at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, who gave that mentioned in the beginning of this article. Until that part of the world, therefore, become more accessible to travellers, there is but little hope that we can come to any certainty in the matter. M. Niebuhr plainly, from his own accounts, had not influence enough with the Arabs to show him almost anything, as they refused to conduct him even to the summit of Mount Sinai. White Mountains. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEW_HAMPSHIRE">New <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>. Mountains of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>, a chain of mountains in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, extending between Abyssinia and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOMOTAPA">Monomotapa</a>, and so called from their great height. Mountains of the Lions, also in Africa, divide <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIGRITIA">Nigritia</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and extend as far as Ethiopia. They were styled by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> the mountains of God, on account of their being greatly subject to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. Mountain of Forty Days; a mountain of Judea, situated in the plain of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a> to the north of that city. According to the abbé Mariti's description, the summit of it is covered neither with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, turf, nor earth; it consists of a solid mass of white marble, the surface of which is become <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> by the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>. "The path by which you ascend to it (says our author) fills one with terror, as it rises with a winding course between two abysses, which the eye <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> feebly behold. This path is at first pretty broad, but it at length becomes so confined, that one can with difficulty place both feet upon it at the same time. When we had ascended a little higher, we found an Arab stretched out on the path, who made us pay a certain toll for our passage. Here the traveller requires courage. One of the parapets of the path being broke, we clung to the part which remained until we had reached a small grotto, situated very commodiously, as it gave us an opportunity of recovering our breath. When we had rested ourselves a little, we pursued our course, which became still more dangerous. Suspended almost from the rock, and having before our eyes all the horror of Mountain, the precipice, we could advance only by dragging one foot after the other; so that had the smallest fragments given way under us, we should have been hurried to the bottom of this frightful <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a>. "This mountain is one of the highest in the province, and one of its most sacred places. It takes its name from the rigorous fast which Christ observed here after having triumphed over the vanities of the world and the power of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of this miracle, a chapel was formerly constructed on the summit of the mountain. It may be seen from the plain, but we could not approach it, as the path was almost entirely destroyed. It, however, may be accessible on the other side of the mountain, which we did not visit. A great many scattered grottos are seen here; in one of which, according to Quarenius, were deposited the bodies of several anchorites, which are still entire. I have heard the same thing affeited in the country, but I could never meet with any person who had seen them. Here we enjoyed the most beautiful prospect imaginable. This part of the mountain of Forty Days overlooks the mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, the country of Gilead, the country of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMONITES">Ammonites</a>, the plains of Moab, the plain of Jericho, the river Jordan, and the whole extent of the Dead <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. It was here that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> said to the Son of God, 'All these kingdoms will I give thee, if thou wilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down and worship me.'"

MOURNING

Pages 514-515

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was expressed various ways. Amongst the Jews, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their relations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> intimate friends, grief or mourning was signified by weeping, tearing their clothes, smiting their breasts, or tearing them with their nails, pulling or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and beards, walking softly, i.e. barefoot, lying upon the ground, fasting, or eating upon the ground. They kept themselves <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> shut up in their houses, covered their faces, and abstained from all <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, even <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and saying their usual prayers. They neither dressed themselves, nor made their beds, nor shaved themselves, nor cut their nails, nor went into the bath, nor saluted any body: so that fullness seems to have been an indication of sorrow, and dirtiness of distress. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of mourning among the Jews was generally <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days; though this was lengthened or shortened according to circumstances; but 30 days were thought sufficient upon the funeral occasions. The different periods of the time of mourning required different degrees of grief, and different tokens of it. The Greeks, on the death of friends, showed their sorrow by excluding themselves from all gaiety, entertainments, games, public solemnities, the enjoyment of wine, and the delights of music. They sat in gloomy and solitary places, stripped themselves of all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> ornaments, put on a coarse <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> stuff by way of mourning, tore their hair, shaved their heads, rolled themselves in the dust and mire, sprinkled ashes on their heads, smote their breasts with their palms, tore their faces, and frequently cried out with a lamentable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and dawling tone, reiterating the interjection ο, ο, ο; hence funeral lamentations were called Ελέος. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they appeared in public during the time of mourning, they had a veil thrown over their faces and heads. During the funeral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, certain persons called Σεβαστοί, marched before, and sung melancholy strains called ορεγνυμενοι Ἰάκωβος, Ἀπόστολος, and Ἀπόστολος. These vocal mourners sung thrice during the procession round the pile and round the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. Flutes were also used to heighten the solemnity. At the funerals of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, their fellow soldiers who attended, as a testimony of their affliction, held their shields, their spears, and the rest of their armour, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>. The tokens of private grief among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were the same as those already observed as customary among the Greeks. Black or dark <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> were the colours of the mourning habits worn by the men; they were also <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to the women. The mourning of the emperors at first was black. In the time of Augustus, the women wore <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> veils, and the rest of their dress black. From the time of Domitian they wore nothing but white habits, without any ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, jewels, or pearls. The men let their hair and beards grow, and wore no wreaths of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on their heads while the days of mourning <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. The longest time of mourning was ten months: this was Numa's establishment, and took in his whole year. For a widow to marry during this time was infamous. Mourning was not used for children who died under three years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. From this age to ten they mourned as many months as the child was years old. A remarkable victory, or other happy event, occasioned the shortening of the time of mourning: The birth of a child, or the attainment of any remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> in the family, certain feasts in honour of the gods, or the consecration of a temple, had the same effect. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Cannae, the commonwealth decreed that mourning should not be worn for more than 30 days, that the loss might be forgotten as soon as possible. When public magistrates died, or persons of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, also when any remarkable calamity happened, all public meetings were intermitted, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, shops, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and all places of concourse were shut up, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> put on a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of sorrow; the senators laid aside the laticlave, and the consuls sat in a lower seat than ordinary. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> also, and was observed upon the death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after he had been sentenced to death by their judges. Prayse, or mourning women, (by the Greeks called Σεβαστοί ἐπικοινωνοί), went about the streets: this was customary MOUSE. See Mus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MOUSE-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">Ear</a>. See Hieracium, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. MOUSE-Tail. See Myosurus, Mammalia Index. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DOR">Dor</a>-MOUSE. See Myoxus, Mammalia Index. Shrew-MOUSE. See Sorex, Mammalia Index.

MOUSSELLE

Pages 515-515

the name of an East <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> tree, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> tubular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty. They are of a sweet agreeable smell, and the Gentoos are very fond of wearing them, stringing and hanging them about their necks and arms. The fruit is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cherry, of the shape and size of our white heart cherry, but the footstalk is not quite so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. This fruit has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in it, containing a bitter oily kernel. The Indians rub with this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> stung by a scorpion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bitten by a centipede, which it soon cures. The crows are very fond of the fruit.

MOUSUL

Pages 515-515
or Mosul, a large city of Turkey in Asia, and capital of a beglerbegate, stands on the west bank of the Tigris, in the latitude, according to Mr Ives's observation, of 36° 30' north. It is surrounded with stone walls, but has many of its streets lying waste. Tavernier speaks of it as a ruined place, with only two blind markets and a sorry castle; yet, he says, that it is much frequented by merchants, and that its bazaars commands 3000 men. There is a bridge of boats over the Tigris; and the city is a thoroughfare from Persia to Syria, which makes it a place of trade, and which is more augmented by a constant traffic from this place to Bagdad. The country on this side the river is sandy and barren; but on the opposite side it is exceedingly fruitful, yielding good crops of corn and fruit in abundance. Mr Ives says it was the best built city he had seen in Turkey; but had nothing in it to attract the notice of an European. It was besieged for near six months by Nadir Shah without success. Breaches were frequently made in the walls, and assaults continued for three days unsuccessfully; but the assailants were constantly repulsed, and the breaches made in the daytime repaired during the night. The besieged had unanimously resolved to die rather than to submit. The Turks declared, that should the place be forced to surrender, they were determined to put to death all their wives and daughters first, that they might not fall into the vile hands of the abhorred Persians. The place was therefore defended with uncommon bravery; even the women and children exerted themselves with the greatest alacrity. The Christians behaved in such a manner as to gain the esteem and admiration of the other inhabitants; and some of their churches being demolished, they were afterwards repaired at the expense of government. In this city there are a great many mosques, the largest and most flatly of which is ornamented on the top with green tiles. At the doors of these houses there are usually inscriptions in gilt letters, declaring the awfulness of the building, as being the house of God. One of them has a minaret which bends like those of Bagdad. Some of the most bigoted Turks say, that Mahomet saluted this minaret as he passed; on which it bent its head in reverence to the prophet, and ever after continued in that situation. The manufacture of this city is muslin (muslin), which is made very strong and pretty fine. In the year 1757, this city and the country adjacent were visited by a dreadful famine, owing to the preceding hard winter, and innumerable multitudes of locusts, by which the fruits of the earth were destroyed. When Mr Ives was there in 1758, the country was comparatively depopulated. Almost all the brute creation had been destroyed for the subsistence of man. During the famine, the people had eaten dogs, and every kind of animal which is held in abhorrence at any other time, not sparing even their own children; and the dead bodies lay in the streets for want of people to bury them. Their fruit trees were also destroyed by the frost; so that when our author was there scarcely any fruit could be had. The neighbouring mountains afford silver mines; and they would yield much quicksilver if the Turks had either the skill or inclination to work them to advantage. Lanza says, that some time ago an Englishman who travelled through this country got two or three bottles of it, which he presented to the basha as a specimen of what might be done in that way; but no farther attempt was made. Here also are some lead mines, which supply as much of that metal as furnishes them with bullets and some necessary utensils. MOU-TAN or Peony Shrub of China: also called hoa-ouang, or "the king of flowers," and peleangkin, "an hundred ounces of gold," in allusion to the excessive price given formerly by some of the virtuosi for certain species of this plant. The mou-tan seems to claim pre-eminence, not only on account of the splendour and number of its flowers, and of the sweet odour which they diffuse around, but also on account of the multitude of leaves which compose them, and of the beautiful golden spots with which they are interspersed. This plant, which is of a shrubby nature, shoots forth a number of branches, which form a top almost as large as those of the finest orange trees.

MOUTH

Pages 515-515

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, consisting of the lips, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, the inside of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, the palate, the salivary glands, the os hyoides, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-UVULA">uvula</a>, and the tonsils; which see under the article ANATOMY. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> observes, that the mouth in the several <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals is nicely adapted to the uses of such a part, and well sized and shaped for the formation of speech, the gathering and receiving of food, the catching of prey, &c. In some creatures it is wide and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, in others little and narrow; in some it is formed with a deep incisure into the head, for the better catching and holding of prey, and more easy commination of hard, large, and troublesome food; and in others with a shorter incisure, for the gathering and holding of herbaceous food. In birds it is neatly shaped for piercing the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; hard and horny, to supply the want of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; hooked, in the rapacious kind, to catch and hold their prey; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and slender in those that have their food to grope for in moribund places; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and long in those that search for it in the mud. Nor is the mouth less remarkable in insects; in some it is forcipated, to catch, hold, and tear the prey; in others aculeated, to pierce and wound animals, and suck their blood; in others, strongly rigid, with jaws and teeth, to gnaw and scrape out

MOVEABLE

Pages 508-508

in general, denotes anything capable of being moved. MOVEABLE Feasts, are such as are not always held on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the year <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>; though they be on the same day of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. See Feasts. Thus, Easter is a moveable feast, being always held on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> which falls upon or next after the first full <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> following the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. All the other moveable feasts follow Easter, i.e., they keep their distance from it; so that they are fixed with respect thereto. Such are Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Ash Wednesday, Ascension day, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENTECOST">Pentecost</a>, Trinity Sunday, &c., which see under their proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, SEPTUAGESIMA, &c. MOVEABLE Subject, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, anything that moves itself, or can be moved; in contradistinction to immovable or heritable subjects, as lands, houses, &c.

MOVEMENT

Pages 508-508
Motion, a term frequently used in the same sense with automaton. The most usual movements for keeping time are watches and clocks: the first are such as show the parts of time, and are portable in the pocket; the second, such as publish it by sounds, and are fixed as furniture. See Horology. Movement, in its popular use among us, signifies all the inner works of a watch, clock, or other engine, which move, and by that motion carry on the design of the instrument. The movement of a clock or watch is the inside, or that part which measures the time, strikes, &c., exclusive of the frame, case, dial plate, &c. The parts common to both of these movements are, the main-spring, with its appurtenances; lying in the spring box, and in the middle thereof lapping about the spring-arbor, to which one end of it is fastened. A-top of the spring-arbor is the endless screw and its wheel; but in spring-clocks, this is a ratchet-wheel with its click, that stops it. That which the main-spring draws, and round which the chain or string is wrapped, is called the fusey; this is ordinarily taper; in large works, going with weights, it is cylindrical, and called the barrel. The small teeth at the bottom of the fusey or barrel, which step it in winding up, is called the ratchet; and that which stops it when wound up, and is for that end driven up by the spring, the garde-gout. The wheels are various: the parts of a wheel are, the hoop or rim, the teeth, the cros, and the collet or piece of brass soldered on the arbor or spindle wherein the wheel is rivetted. The little wheels playing in the teeth of the larger are called pinions; and their teeth, which are 4, 5, 6, 8, &c., are called levers; the ends of the spindle are called pivots; and the guttered wheel, with iron spikes at bottom, wherein the line of ordinary clocks runs, the pulley. We need not say anything of the hand, screws, wedges, stops, &c. See Wheel, Fusey, &c. Perpetual Movement. See Perpetual Motion.

MOWEE

Pages 515-516

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, discovered by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook, is 162 miles in circumference. A low isthmus divides it into two circular peninsulas, of which the eastern is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the size of the western. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in both rise to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height, and may be seen at the distance of more than 30 leagues. The northern shores, like those of Owhyhee, afford no foundations, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> presents the same appearance of verdure and fertility. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is computed at about 65,000. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 175° 56' N. Lat. 20° 53'.

MOXA

Pages 516-516
or Mugwort of China, is a soft lanuginous substance, prepared in Japan from the young leaves of a species of Artemisia, by beating them together when thoroughly dried, and rubbing them between the hands till only the fine fibres are left. The down on the leaves of mullein, cotton, hemp, &c., answers the same purpose. In the Eastern countries it is used by burning it on the skin; a little cone of the moxa is laid upon the part, previously moistened, and set on fire at the top; it burns down with a temperate glowing heat, and produces a dark coloured spot, the exfoliation of which is promoted by applying a little garlic; the ulcer is left to discharge, or is soon healed, according to the intention in using the moxa. MOYRA. See Moira.

MOZAMBIQUE

Pages 484-485

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, lying south of Quiluba, and taking its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, which is situated on an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, at the mouth of a river of the same name, in 15 deg. S. Lat. The island is 30 miles in circumference, and very populous, though the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is said to be very hot, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in general dry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and barren; yet they have most of the tropical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, hogs, and sheep. There is a kind of fowl here, both the feathers and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of which are black, inasmuch that, when they are boiled, the broth looks like <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>; and yet their flesh is very delicate and good food. The town of Mozambique is regularly fortified, and has a good harbour, defended by a citadel, with several churches and monasteries. The Portuguese shipping to and from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> touch here for refreshments. As the island abounds in cattle, the Portuguese slaughter and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> up a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of beef, which they afterwards send to the Brazils, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sell to the European shipping. They also also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> European goods with the natives for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, elephants <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and slaves. There is another town called Mongala, situated also on an island, and garnished by the Portuguese, being their chief <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> for European goods. The gold they receive from the natives is found near the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or in the sands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>; no gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, or at least very few, being at present wrought in Africa.

MUCILAGE

Pages 516-516

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, is in general any viscid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> glutinous liquor. Mucilage also imports the liquor which principally serves to moisten the ligaments and cartilages of the articulations, and is supplied by the mucilaginous glands.

MUCK

Pages 516-516
or RUNNING A MUCK, is a practice that has prevailed time immemorial in Batavia. To run a muck, in the original sense of the word, is to get intoxicated with opium, and then rush into the street with a drawn weapon, and kill any one that comes in the way, till the party is himself either killed or taken prisoner. If the officer take one of these amocks or mohawks (as they have been called by an easy corruption) alive, he has a considerable reward; and the unhappy wretch is always broken alive on the wheel: but such is the fury of their desperation, that three out of four are necessarily destroyed in attempting to secure them. MUD-IGUANA. See Muræna, Ichthyology Index.

MUCOR

Pages 516-516

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of the order of fungi, belonging to the cryptogamia clasps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MUCUS

Pages 516-516

a mucilaginous liquor secreted by certain glands, and serving to lubricate many of the internal cavities of the body. In its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state it is generally limpid and colourless; but, from certain causes, assumes a thick consistence and a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> like pus. For the distinguishing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> between pus and mucus, see <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, No 2769.

MUFFLE

Pages 516-516

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a vessel employed in some metallurgic operations. In <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it represents an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vault, the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which is closed by a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, and the lower part or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of which is a rectangular plane. It is a little oven that is placed horizontally in a flay and enamelling furnaces, so that its open side corresponds with the door of the fireplace of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>. Under this arched oven small cupels or crucibles are placed; and the substances contained are thus exposed to intense <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> without contact of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or ashes.

MUFTI

Pages 516-516

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> order, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> of the Muftulman <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The authority of the mufti is very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> in the Ottoman empire; for even the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> himself, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he would preserve any appearance of religion, cannot, without hearing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, put any person to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, or so much as inflict any corporal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. In all actions, especially criminal ones, his opinion is required, by giving him a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is stated under feigned names; which he subscribes with the words, He shall, or shall not, be punished. Such outward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> is paid to the mufti, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior himself rises up to him, and advances <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> steps to meet him when he comes into his presence. He alone has the honour of kissing the sultan's left shoulder, whilst the prime vizier kisses only the hem of his garment.
