An epigram of Callimachus gives the attributes of the Muses in as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. Calliope the deeds of heroes sings; Great Clio sweeps to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> the strings; Euterpe teaches mimes their silent show; Melpomene presides o'er scenes of wo; Terpsichore the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>'s soft pow'r displays; And Erato gives hymns the gods to praise; Polyhymnia's skill inspires melodious strains; Urania wife, the starry course explains; And gay Thalia's glass <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out where folly reigns. This epigram does not, however, exactly correspond with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of other poets, or of the ancient painters, in characterizing the attributes of the Muses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had numberless ingenious and fanciful ideas concerning the muses, which we have not room to recite. —"It seems (says the abbé Barthélemy) as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the first poets, enchanted with the beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, occasion of Analys, were led to invoke the nymphs of the woods, hills, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, and fountains; and that yielding to the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for allegory, they gave them names relative to the influence (A) It has been said, that when the citizens of Sicyon directed three skilful statuaries to make each of them <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the three Muses, they were all so well executed, that they did not know which to choose, but erected all the nine, and that Hesiod and Homer only gave them names. Muses might be supposed to have over the productions of the mind. At first three Muses only were admitted, Melicte, Mneme, and Aeide; that is to say, the meditation or reflection necessary to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; memory, which records illustrious deeds; and song, which accompanies their recital. In proportion as improvement was made in the art of verification, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and effects were personified, the number of the Muses increased, and the names they now received referred to the charms of poetry, its celestial origin, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the pleasure and gaiety it inspires, the song and dance which add to it new charms, and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with which it is crowned. Afterwards were associated with them the Graces, whose employment it is to embellish poetry, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> who is so frequently its object. These ideas took birth in a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in Thrace, where <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, and their disciples, suddenly appeared in the midst of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. The Muses were honoured there on the Pierian mount; and extending their dominion, successively took their stations on Pindus, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, and all those solitary places where the painters of nature, surrounded by the most pleasing images, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> the divine glow of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, make the Muses the soul of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in our system; from whence the imaginary music of the spheres.

MUSEUM

Pages 527-544

a name which originally signified a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, which took up at least one-fourth of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> was called the museum, on account of its being set apart for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the sciences. Here were lodged and entertained the men of learning; who were divided into many companies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> colleges, according to the sciences of which they were the professors; and to each of these houses or colleges was allotted a handsome revenue. The foundation of this establishment is attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a>, who here placed his library. Hence the word museum is now applied to any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> set apart as a repository for things that have an immediate relation to the arts. The museum at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, called the Ashmolean museum, is a noble pile of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, erected at the expense of the university, at the west end of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, at which side it has a magnificent portal, sustained by pillars of the Corinthian order. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, which is to the street, extends about 60 feet, where there is this inscription over the entrance in gilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, Museum Ashmoleanum, schola naturalis historiae, officina chymica. It was begun in 1679, and finished in 1683, when a valuable collection of curiosities was presented to the university by Elias Ashmole, Esq. which were the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> repented there: several accessions have been since made to the museum; among which are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, and other Egyptian antiquities, an entire mummy, Roman antiquities, altars, medals, lamps, &c., and a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities. For an account of the British museum, see <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">LONDON</a>, No. 146. MUSHROOM. See FUNGI, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. To try the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a>:—Take an onion, and strip the outer skin, and boil it with your mushrooms; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the onion become blue or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, there are certainly dangerous ones amongst them; if it remain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, they are good. MUSIC; The art of combining sounds in a manner agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> may be either simultaneous or successive: in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it constitutes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; in the last, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>. But though the same sounds, or intervals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, which give <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> when heard in succession, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not always produce the same effect in harmony; yet the principles which constitute the simpler and more perfect kinds of harmony, are almost, if not entirely, the same with those of melody. By perfect harmony, we do not here <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that plenitude, those complex modifications of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONIC">harmonic</a> sound, which are admired in practice; but that harmony which is called perfect by theorists and artists; that harmony which results from the coalescence of simultaneous sounds produced by vibrations in the proportions of thirds, fifths, and octaves, or their duplicates. The principles upon which these various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of sound are founded, and by which they are regulated, constitute a science, which is not only extensive but profound, when we would investigate the principles from whence these happy modifications of sound result, and by which they are determined; or when we would explore the sensations, whether mental or corporeal, with which they affect us. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> definitions of music are not proportioned in their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to our present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of that art; but M. Rousseau betrays a temerity highly inconsistent with the philosophical character, when from thence he infers, that their ideas were vague and undetermined. Every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> susceptible of refinement and delicacy in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> or sentiment, must be conscious that there is a music in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> as well as in sound; and that the ideas of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>, of harmony and symmetry, are, if we may <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, equally constituent of visible as of audible music. Those illustrious minds, whose comprehensive prospects in every science where taste and propriety prevail took in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> at a single glance, would behold with contempt and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> those narrow and microscopic views of which alone their successors in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> have discovered themselves capacious. With these definitions, however, we are less concerned, as they bear no proportion to the ideas which are now entertained of music. Nor can we follow M. Rousseau, from whatever venerable sources his authority may be derived, in adopting his Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> for the word music. The established derivation from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">Musa</a> could only be questioned by a paradoxical genius. That music had been practised in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> before it was known as an art in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, is indeed a fact which cannot be questioned; but it does not thence follow that the Greeks had borrowed the name as well as the art from Egypt. If the art of music be so natural to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that vocal melody is practised wherever articulate sounds are used, there can be little reason for deducing the idea of music from the whistling of winds through the reeds that grew on the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. And indeed, when we reflect with how easy a transition we may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from the accents of speaking to diatonic sounds; when we observe how early children adapt the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of their amusements to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> and melody, however rude; when we consider how early and universally these practices take place—there is no avoiding the conclusion, that the idea of music is connoted to man, and implied in the original principles of his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. We have already said, that the principles on which it is founded, and the rules by which it is conducted, constitute a science. The same maxims when applied to practice form an art; hence its first and most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> and practical music. Speculative music is, if we may be permitted to use the expression, the knowledge of the nature and use of those materials which compose it, or, in other words, of all the different relations between the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low, between the harsh and the sweet, between the swift and the slow, between the strong and the weak, of which sounds are susceptible; relations which, comprehending all the possible combinations of music and sound, seem likewise to comprehend all the causes of the impressions which their succession can make upon the ear and upon the soul. Practical music is the art of applying and reducing to practice those principles which result from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of agreeable sounds, whether simultaneous or successive; or, in other words, to conduct and arrange sounds according to the proportions resulting from consonance, from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and succession, in such a manner as to produce upon the ear the effect which the composer intends. This is the art which we call <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>*. With respect to the actual production of sounds by voices or instruments, which is called execution, this department is merely <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> and operative; which, only presupposing the powers of founding the intervals true, of exactly proportioning their degrees of duration, of elevating or depressing sounds according to those gradations which are prescribed by the tone, and to the value required by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, demands no other knowledge but a familiar acquaintance with the characters used in music, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of expressing them with promptitude and facility. Speculative music is likewise divided into two departments; viz. the knowledge of the proportions of sounds or their intervals, and that of their relative durations; that is to say, of measure and of time. The first is what among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> seems to have been called harmonical music. It shows in what the nature of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> or melody consists; and discovers what is consonant or discordant, agreeable or disagreeable, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODULATION">modulation</a>. It discovers, in a word, the effects which sounds produce on the ear by their nature, by their force, and by their intervals; which is equally applicable to their consonance and their succession. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> has been called rhythmical, because it treats of sounds with regard to their time and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. It contains the explication of their continuance, of their proportions, of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, whether <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> or short, quick or slow, of the different modes of succession and the parts into which they are divided, that to these the succession of sounds may be conformed. Practical music is likewise divided into two departments, which correspond to the two preceding. That which answers to harmonical music, and which the ancients called melopee, teaches the rules for combining and varying the intervals, whether consonant or dissonant, in an agreeable and harmonious manner. The second, which answers to the rhythmical music, and which they called rhythmopoea, contains the rules for applying the different modes of time, for understanding the feet by which verses were scanned, and the diversities of measure; in a word, for the practice of the rhythmus. Music is at present divided more simply into melody and harmony; for since the introduction of harmony, the proportion between the length and shortness of sounds, or even that between the distance of returning cadences, are of less <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> amongst us. For it often happens in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages, that the verses assume their measures from the musical air, and almost entirely lose the smallest share of proportion and quantity which in themselves they possess. By melody the successions of sound are regulated in such a manner as to produce pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>. See MELODY. Harmony consists in uniting to each of the sounds, in a regular succession, two or more different sounds, which simultaneously striking the ear soothe it by their concurrence. See HARMONY. Music, according to Rousseau, may be, and perhaps likewise ought to be, divided into the physical and the imitative. The first is limited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> mechanism of sounds, and reaches no farther than the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, without carrying its impressions to the heart, and can produce nothing but corporeal sensations more or less agreeable. Such is the music of songs, of hymns, of all the airs which only consist in combinations of melodious sounds, and in general all music which is merely harmonious. It may, however, be questioned, whether every sound, even to the most simple, is not either by nature or by early and confirmed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, imitative. If we may trust our own feelings, there is no such thing in nature as music which gives mechanical pleasure alone. For if so, it must give such pleasure as we receive from tastes, from odours, or from other grateful titillations; but we absolutely deny that there are any musical sensations or pleasures, in the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> analogous to these. Let any piece of music be resolved into its elementary parts and their proportions, it will then easily appear from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is no more than the vehicle of such perceptions, and that mind alone can be susceptible of them. It may indeed happen, from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the performers and the complication of the harmony, that meaning and sentiment may be lost in the multiplicity of sounds; but this, though it may be harmony, loses the name of music. The second department of this division, by lively and accentuated inflections, and by sounds which may be said to speak, expresses all the passions, paints every possible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, reflects every object, subjects the whole of nature to its skilful imitations, and impresses even on the heart and soul of man sentiments proper to affect them in the most sensible manner. This, continues nues he, which is the genuine lyric and theatrical music, was what gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> charms and energy to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; this is what, in our days, we exert ourselves in applying to the drama, and what our fingers execute on the stage. It is in this music alone, and not in harmonies or the refection of nature, that we must expect to find accounts of those prodigious effects which it formerly produced. But, with M. Rousseau's permission, all music which is not in some degree characterized by these pathetic and imitative powers, deserves no better name than that of a musical jargon, and can only be effectuated by such a complication and intricacy of harmony, as may confound, but cannot entertain the audience. This character, therefore, ought to be added as essential to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of music; and it must be attributed to our neglect of this alone, whilst our whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is bestowed on harmony and execution, that the best performances of our artists and composers are heard with little's indifference and obduracy, nor ever can conciliate any admirers, but such as are induced, by pedantry and affectation, to pretend what they do not feel. Still may the curse of indifference and inattention pursue and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> up the souls of every composer or performer, who pretends to regale our ears with this musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGERDEMAIN">legerdemain</a>, till the grin of scorn, or the hiss of infamy, teach them to correct this depravity of taste, and entertain us with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of nature! Whilst moral effects are sought in the natural effects of sound alone, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCRUTINY">scrutiny</a> will be vain, and disputes will be maintained without being understood: but sounds as representatives of objects, whether by nature or association, introduce new scenes to the fancy and new feelings to the heart; not from their <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL_POWERS">mechanical powers</a>, but from the connection established by the Author of our frame between sounds and the object which either by natural resemblance or unavoidable association they are made to represent. It would seem that music was one of those arts which were first discovered; and that vocal was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to instrumental music, if in the earliest ages there was any music which could be said to be purely instrumental. For it is more than probable, that music was originally formed to be the vehicle of poetry; and of consequence, though the voice might be supported and accompanied by instruments, yet music was never intended for instruments alone. We are told by ancient authors, that all the laws, whether <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> or divine, exhortations to virtue, the knowledge of the characters and actions of gods and heroes, the lives and achievements of illustrious men, were written in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and sung publicly by a quire to the sound of instruments; and it appears from the Scriptures, that such from the earliest times was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> among the Israelites. Nor was it possible to find means more efficacious for impressing on the mind of man the principles of morals, and inspiring the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of virtue. Perhaps, however, this was not the result of a premeditated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; but inspired by sublime sentiments and elevation of thought, which in accents that were suited and proportioned to their celestial nature endeavoured to find a language worthy of themselves and expressive of their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. It merits attention, that the ancients were duly sensible of the value and importance of this divine art, not only as a symbol of that universal order and symmetry which prevails through the whole frame of material and intelligent nature, but as productive of the most momentous effects both in moral and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who disagreed almost in every other maxim of politics, are unanimous in their approbation of music, as an efficacious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in the formation of the public character and in conducting the state; and it was the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that whilst the gymnastic exercises rendered the constitution robust and hardy, music humanized the character, and softened those habits of roughness and ferocity by which men might otherwise have degenerated into savages. The gradations by which voices were exerted and tuned, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of one instrument succeeded to another, or by which the principles of music were collected and methodized in such a manner as to give it the form of an art and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of a science, are topics so fruitful of conjecture and so void of certainty, that we must leave them to employ minds more speculative and inventions more prolific than ours, or transfer them to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of music as a more proper place for such disquisitions. For the amusement of the curious, Rousseau in his Musical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, Plates C and N, has transferred some fragments of Grecian, Persian, American, Chinese, and Swiss music, with which performers may entertain themselves at leisure. When they have tried the pieces, it is imagined they will be less languidly fond than that author of ascribing the power of music to its <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with the national accents where it is composed. This may doubtless have its influence; but there are other causes more permanent and less arbitrary to which it owes its most powerful and universal charms. The music now most generally celebrated and practiced is that of the Italians, or their successful imitators. The English, from the invasion of the Saxons, to that more late though lucid era in which they imbibed the art and copied the manner of the Italians, had a music which neither pleased the soul nor charmed the ear. The primitive music of the French deserves no higher <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. Of all the barbarous nations, the Scots and Irish seem to have perfected the most affecting original music. The first consists of a melody characterized by tenderness: it melts the soul to a pleasing pensive languor. The other is the native expression of grief and melancholy. Taffoni informs us, that in his time a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> from Scotland had imported into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> a lamentable kind of music from his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and that he himself had composed pieces in the same spirit. From this expressive though laconic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, we learn that the character of our national music was even then established; yet so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> is our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and credulity, that we ascribe the best and most impassioned airs which are extant among us to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Rizzio; as if an Italian lutanist, who had lived for a short time in Scotland, could, at once, as it were by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, have imbibed a spirit and composed in a manner so different from his own. It is yet more surprising that Geminiani should have entertained and published the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, upon the miserable authority of popular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> alone; for the fact is authenticated by no better credentials. The primitive music of the Scots may be divided into the martial, the pastoral, and the festive. The first consists either either in marches, which were played before the chieftains, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the battles which they fought, or in lamentations for the catastrophes of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the extinction of families. These wild effusions of natural melody preserve several of the rules preferable for composition. The strains, though rude and untutored, are frequently terrible or mournful in a very high degree. The port or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> is sometimes in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, sometimes in treble time; regular in its measures, and exact in the distance between its returning cadences; most frequently, though not always, loud and brisk. The pi-broch, or imitation of battles, is wild, and abrupt in its transitions from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> to interval and from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> to key; various and destitute in its movements; frequently <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> in the return of its cadences; and in short, through the whole, seems inspired with such fury and enthusiasm, that the hearer is irresistibly infected with all the rage of precipitate courage, notwithstanding the rudeness of the accents by which it is kindled. To this the pastoral forms a striking <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>. Its accents are plaintive, yet soothing; its harmony generally flat; its modulations natural and agreeable; its rhythm simple and regular; its returning cadences at equal distance; its transitions from one concinnous interval to another, at least for the most part; its movements flow, and may be either in common or treble time. It scarcely admits of any other harmony than that of a simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>. A greater number of parts would cover the air, and destroy the melody. To this we shall add what has been said upon the same subject by Dr Franklin. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">Writing</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> K———, he proceeds thus: "Give me leave, on this occasion, to extend a little the sense of your position, 'That melody and harmony are separately agreeable, and in union delightful;' and to give it as my opinion, that the reason why the Scotch tunes have lived so long, and will probably live for ever (if they escape being stifled in modern affected ornament), is merely this, that they are really compositions of melody and harmony united, or rather that their melody is harmony. I mean, the simple tunes sung by a single voice. As this will appear paradoxical, I must explain my meaning. In common acceptation, indeed, only an agreeable succession of sounds is called melody; and only the coexistence of agreeable sounds harmony. But since the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is capable of retaining for some moments a perfect idea of the pitch of a past sound, so as to compare it with the pitch of a succeeding sound, and judge truly of their agreement or disagreement, there may and does arise from thence a sense of a harmony between the present and past sounds, equally pleasing with that between two present sounds." Now the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the old Scotch tunes is this, that almost every succeeding emphatic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> is a third, a fifth, an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a>, or in short some note that is in concord with the preceding note. Thirds are chiefly used, which are very pleasing concords. I use the word emphatical, to distinguish those notes which have a stress laid on them in fingering the tune, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> connecting notes that serve merely, like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> in common speech, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACK">tack</a> the whole together. "That we have a most perfect idea of a sound <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> past, I might <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to all acquainted with music, who know how easy it is to repeat a sound in the same pitch with one just heard. In tuning an instrument, a good ear can as easily determine that two strings are in unison by sounding them separately, as by sounding them together; their disagreement is also as easily, I believe I may say more easily and better distinguished when sounded separately; for when sounded together, though you know by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> that one is higher than the other, you cannot tell which it is. I have ascribed to memory the ability of comparing the pitch of a present tone with that of one past. But if there should be, as possibly there may be, something in the ear similar to what we find in the eye, that ability would not be entirely owing to memory. Possibly the vibrations given to the auditory nerves by a particular sound may actually continue for some time after the cause of these vibrations is past, and the agreement or disagreement of a subsequent sound become by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with them more discernible. For the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> made on the visual nerves by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> object will continue for 20 or 30 seconds." After some experiments to prove the permanency of visible impressions, he continues thus: "Farther, when we consider by whom these ancient tunes were composed, and how they were first performed, we shall see that such harmonical succession of sounds was natural, and even necessary in their construction. They were composed by the minstrels of those days, to be played on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a> accompanied by the voice. The harp was strung with wire, which gives a sound of long continuance; and had no contrivance like that of the modern harpsichord, by which the sound of the preceding note can be stopt the moment a succeeding note begins. To avoid actual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, it was therefore necessary that the succeeding emphatic note should be a chord with the preceding, as their sounds must exist at the same time. Hence arose that beauty in those tunes that has so long pleased, and will please forever, though men scarce know why. That they were originally composed for the harp, and of the most simple kind, I mean a harp without any half-notes but those in the natural <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, and with no more than two octaves of strings, from C to C, I conjecture from another circumstance; which is, that not one of these tunes really ancient, has a single <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> half-note in it; and that in tunes where it is most convenient for the voice to use the middle notes of the harp, and place the key in F, there the B, which if used should be a B flat, is always omitted, by passing over it with a third. The connoisseurs in modern music will say I have no taste; but I cannot help adding, that I believe our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, in having a good song, distinctly articulated, sung to one of those tunes, and accompanied by the harp, felt more real pleasure than is communicated by the generality of modern operas, exclusive of that arising from the scenery and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>. Most tunes of late composition, not having this natural harmony united with their melody, have recourse to the artificial harmony of a bass, and other accompanying parts. This support, in my opinion, the old tunes do not need, and are rather confused than aided by it. Whoever has heard James Oswald play them on his violincello, will be less inclined to dispute this with me. I have more than once seen tears of pleasure in the eyes of his auditors; and yet I think, even his playing those tunes would would please more if he gave them less modern ornament." As these observations are for the most part true, and always ingenious, we need no other apology for quoting them at length. It is only proper to remark, that the transition in Scots music by consonant intervals, does not seem, as Dr Franklin imagines, to arise from the nature of the instruments upon which they played. It is more than probable, that the ancient British harp was not strung with wire, but with the same materials as the Welsh harps at present. These strings have not the same permanency of tone as metal; so that the sound of a preceding emphatic note must have expired before the subsequent accented note could be introduced. Besides, they who are acquainted with the manoeuvre of the Irish harp, know well that there is a method of discontinuing sounds no less easy and effectual than upon the harpsichord. When the performer finds it proper to interrupt a note, he has no more to do but return his finger gently upon the string immediately struck, which effectually stops its vibration. That <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Scots music which we have distinguished by the name of fiddle seems now limited to reels and country-dances. These may be either in common or treble time. They most frequently consist of two strains: each of these contains eight or twelve bars. They are truly rhythmical; but the mirth which they excite seems rather to be inspired by the vivacity of the movement, than either by the force or variety of the melody. They possess a manoeuvre and expression peculiar to themselves, which it is impossible to describe, and which can only be exhibited by good performers. Having thus far pursued the general idea of music, we shall, after the history, give a more particular detail of the science. **HISTORY OF MUSIC.** Music is capable of so infinite a variety, so greatly does the most simple differ from the most complex, and so multiplied are the degrees between these two extremes, that in no <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> could the incidents respecting that fascinating art have been few or uninteresting. But, that accounts of these incidents should have been handed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to us, scanty and imperfect, is no <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of surprise, when we recollect that the history of music is the history only of sounds, of which writing is a very inadequate medium; and that men would long employ themselves in the pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of cultivating music before they possessed either the ability or the inclination to record their exertions. No accurate traces, therefore, of the actual state of music, in the earlier ages of the world, can be discerned. Our ideas on the subject have no foundation firmer than conjecture and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>. It is probable, that among all barbarous nations some degree of similarity is discernible in the style of their music. Neither will much <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> appear during the first dawns of civilization. But in the more advanced periods of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, when the powers of the human mind are permitted without obstacle to exert their native <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and tendency to invention, and are at the same time affected by the infinite variety of circumstances and situations which before had no existence, and which in one case accelerate, and in another retard; then that similarity, once so indistinguishable, gives place to the endless diversity of which the subject is capable. The practice of music being universal in all ages and all nations, it would be absurd to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the invention of the art to any one man. It must have suffered a regular progression, through infancy, childhood, and youth, before it could arrive at maturity. The first attempts must have been rude and artless. Perhaps the first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> was a reed of the lake. No <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> has been able to produce proofs of antiquity so indisputable as the Egyptians. It would be vain, therefore, to attempt tracing music higher than the history of Egypt. By comparing the accounts of Diodorus Siculus and of Plato, there is reason to suppose, that in very ancient times the study of music in Egypt was confined to the priesthood, who used it only on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and solemn occasions; that, as well as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, it was circumscribed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; that it was esteemed sacred, and forbidden to be employed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> or common occasions; and that innovation in it was prohibited: But what the style or relative excellence of this very ancient music was, there are no traces by which we can form an accurate judgment. After the reigns of the Pharaohs, the Egyptians fell by turns under the dominion of the Ethiopians, the Persians, the Greeks, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. By such revolutions, the manners and amusements of the people, as well as their form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, must have been changed. In the age of the Ptolemies, the musical games and contests instituted by those monarchs were of Greek origin, and the musicians who performed were chiefly Greek. The most ancient monuments of human art and industry, at present extant at Rome, are the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">obelisks</a> brought thither from Egypt, two of which are said to have been erected by Sesostris at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>, about 400 years before the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>. These were by the order of Augustus brought to Rome after the conquest of Egypt. One of them called *guglia rossa*, or the broken pillar, which during the sacking of the city in 1527 was thrown down and broken, still lies in the Campus Martius. On it is seen the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a musi-An Egyptian instrument of two strings, and with a neck. It resembles much the calafrone still used in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. This curious relic of antiquity is mentioned, because it affords better <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> than, on the subject of ancient music, is usually to be met with, that the Egyptians, at so very early a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of their history, had advanced to a considerable degree of excellence in the cultivation of the arts. By means of its neck, this instrument was capable, with only two strings, of producing a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of notes. These two strings, if tuned fourths to each other, would furnish that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of sounds called by the ancients *heptachord*, which which consists of a conjunct tetrachord as B, C, D, E; E, F, G, A; if tuned fifths, they would produce an octave, or two disjunct tetrachords. The calafione is tuned in this last manner. The annals of no nation other than Egypt, for many ages after the period of the obelisk at Heliopolis, exhibit the vestige of any contrivance to shorten strings during performance by a neck or finger-board. Father Montfaucon observes, that after examining 500 ancient lyres, harps, and citharas, he could discover no such thing. Egypt indeed seems to have been the source of human intelligence, and the favorite residence of genius and invention. From that celebrated country did the Greeks derive their knowledge of the first elements of those arts and sciences in which they afterwards so eminently excelled. From Greece again did the Romans borrow their attainments in the same pursuits. And from the records of those different nations have the moderns been enabled to accomplish so wonderful an improvement in literature. The Hermes or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> of the Egyptians, surnamed Trifmegistus, or thrice illustrious, who was, according to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, the secretary of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, is celebrated as the inventor of music. It has already been observed, that no person ought strictly to be called the inventor of an art which seems to be natural to, and coeval with, the human species; but the Egyptian Mercury is without doubt entitled to the praise of having made striking improvements in music, as well as of having advanced in various respects the civilization of the people, whose government was chiefly committed to his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. The account given by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a> of the manner in which he accidentally invented the lyre, is at once entertaining and probable. "The Nile (says Apollodorus), after having overflowed the whole country of Egypt, when it returned within its natural bounds, left on the shore a great number of dead animals of various kinds, and among the rest a tortoise; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of which being dried and wafted by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, nothing remained within the shell but nerves and cartilages, and these being braced and contracted by the drying <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> became sonorous. Mercury, walking along the banks of the Nile, happened to strike his foot against this shell; and was so pleased with the sound produced, that the idea of a lyre started into his imagination. He constructed the instrument in the form of a tortoise, and strung it with the dried sinews of dead animals." How beautiful to conceive the energetic powers of the human mind in the early ages of the world, exploring the yet undiscovered capabilities of nature, and directed to the inexhaustible store by the finger of God in the form of accident! The monaulos, or single flute, called by the Egyptians photinx, was probably one of the most ancient instruments used either by them or any other nation. From various remains of ancient sculpture, it appears to have been shaped like a bull's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, and was at first, it may be supposed, no other than the horn itself. Before the invention of flutes, as no other instrument except those of percussion were known, music must have been little more than metrical. When the art of refining and lengthening sounds was first discovered, the power of music over mankind, from the agreeable surpise occasioned by soft and extended notes, was probably irresistible. At a time when all the rest of the world was involved in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> ignorance, the Egyptians were possessed of musical instruments capable of much variety and expression.—Of this the astonishing remains of the city Thebes still subsisting afford ample evidence. In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from Mr Bruce, ingrossed in Dr Burney's history of Music, there is given a particular description of the Theban harp, an instrument of extensive compass, and exquisite elegance of form. It is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> harp accompanied with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> taken from the ruins of an Egyptian ancient sepulchre at Thebes, supposed by Mr Bruce to be that of the father of Sesostris. On the subject of this harp, Mr Bruce makes the following striking observation. It overturns all the accounts of the earliest state of ancient music and instruments in Egypt, and is altogether, in its form, ornaments, and compass, an incontrovertible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>, stronger than a thousand Greek quotations, that <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, drawing, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, and music, were at the greatest perfection when this harp was made; and that what we think in Egypt was the invention of arts was only the beginning of the era of their restoration." Indeed, when the beauty and powers of this harp, along with the very great antiquity of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> which represents it, are considered, such an opinion as that which Mr Bruce hints at, does not seem to be devoid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>. It cannot be doubted that during the reigns of the Ptolemies, who were voluptuous princes, music must have been much cultivated and encouraged. The father of Cleopatra, who was the last of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of kings, derived his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of auletes, or flute-player, from his excessive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the flute. Like Nero, he used to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a> himself in the dress of a tibicen, and exhibit his performance in the public musical contests. Some authors, particularly Am. Marcellinus and M. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAU">Pau</a>, refuse to the Egyptians, at any period of their history, any musical genius, or any excellence in the art; but the arguments used to support this opinion seem to be inconclusive, and the evidences of the opposite decision appear to be incontrovertible. The sacred Scriptures afford almost the only mate-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> trials from which any knowledge of Hebrew music can be drawn. In the rapid sketch, therefore, of ancient music which we mean to exhibit, a very few observations are all which can properly be given to that department of our subject. Moses, who led the Israelites out of Egypt, was educated by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in all the literature and elegant arts cultivated in that country. It is probable, therefore, that the taste and style of Egyptian music would be infused in some degree into that of the Hebrews. Music appears to have been interwoven through the whole tissue of religious <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. The priesthood seem to have been musicians hereditarily and by office. The prophets appear to have accompanied their inspired effusions with music; and every prophet, like the present improvisatori of Italy, seems to have been accompanied by a musical instrument. Music, vocal and instrumental, constituted a great part of the funeral ceremonies of the Jews. The pomp and expense used on these occasions advanced by degrees to an excessive extent. The number of flute-players in the processions amounted sometimes to several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, hundreds, and the attendance of the guests <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> frequently for 30 days.* The Hebrew language abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>, and has so few <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>, that in the original <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> they had no characters. It must, therefore, have been harsh and unfavourable to music. Their instruments of music were chiefly those of percussion; so that, both on account of the language and the instruments, the music must have been coarse and noisy. The vast numbers of performers too, whom it was the taste of the Hebrews to collect together, could with such a language and such instruments produce nothing but clamour and jargon. According to Josephus, there were 200,000 musicians at the dedication of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple. Such are the circumstances from which only an idea of Hebrew music can be formed; for the Jews, neither ancient nor modern, have ever had any characters peculiar to music; and the melodies used in their religious ceremonies have at all times been entirely traditional. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, with the Phoenician colony which he led into Greece, imported at the same time various arts into that country. By the assistance of his Phoenician artificers, that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> discovered <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in Thrace and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> at Thebes. At Thebes that metal is still termed cadmia. Of these materials, and of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, they formed to themselves armour and instruments of war. These they struck against each other during their dances at sacrifices, by which they first obtained the idea of music. Such is the account given of the origin of that species of music in Greece produced by instruments of percussion. The invention of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> instruments in Greece is attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>; and to the Grecian Mercury is assigned, by the poets and historians of that country, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of many discoveries probably due to the Egyptian Hermes, particularly the invention of stringed instruments. The lyre of the Egyptian Mercury had only three strings; that of the Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; the last was perhaps no more than an improvement on the other. When the Greeks deified a prince or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of their own country, they usually assigned him an Egyptian name, and with the name bestowed on their new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> all the actions, attributes, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of the original. The Grecian lyre, although said to have been invented by Mercury, was cultivated principally by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, who first played upon it with method, and accompanied it with the voice. The celebrated contest between him and Marfyas is mentioned by various authors; in which, by conjoining the voice with his lyre (a combination never before attempted), his music was declared superior to the flute of Marfyas. The progress of the lyre, according to Diodorus Siculus, the Grecian is the following. "The muses added to the Grecian lyre the string called mefe; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a> that of Iichanos; and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a> and Thamyras those strings which are named hypate and parhypate." It has been already mentioned, that the lyre invented by the Egyptian Mercury had but three strings. By putting these circumstances together, we may perhaps acquire some knowledge of the progress of music, or at least of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of its scale in the highest antiquity. Mefe, in the Greek music, is the fourth found of the second tetrachord of the great system, and first tetrachord invented by the ancients, answering to our A, on the fifth line in the base. If this sound then was added to the former three, it proves that the most ancient tetrachord was that from E in the base to A; and that the three original strings in the Mercurian and Apollonian lyre were tuned E, F, G, which the Greeks call hypate meson, parhypate meson, and meson diatonicos: The addition, therefore, of mefe to these, completed the first and most ancient tetrachord E, F, G, A. The string Iichanos again being added to these, and answering to our D on the third line in the base, extended the compass downwards, and gave the ancient lyre a regular series of five sounds. The two strings hypate and parhypate, corresponding with our B and C in the base, completed the heptachord or seven sounds b, c, d, e, f, g, a; a compass which received no addition till after the days of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a>. It might perhaps be expected, that in a history of Greek music something ought to be said concerning the muses, Apollo, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and the other gods and demi-gods, who in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> of that country appear to have promoted and improved the art. But such a discussion would be too diffusive, and involve too much foreign matter for the plan we have chosen to adopt. We cannot avoid, however, making a few observations on the poems of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, in so far as connected with our subject. It has been imagined, with much appearance of probability, that the occupation of the first poets and musicians of Greece resembled that of the Celtic and German <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BARDS">bards</a> and the feasts of the first of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>. They sang their poems in the streets of the cities and in the palaces of princes in Greece. They were treated with high respect, and regarded as inspired persons. Such was the employment of Homer. His poems, so justly celebrated, exhibit the most authentic picture that can be found in the annals of antiquity, although perhaps somewhat highly coloured, of the times of which he wrote and in which he lived. Music is always named throughout the Iliad and Odyssey with rapture; but as in these poems no mention is made of instrumental music unaccompanied with poetry and singing, a considerable share no doubt of the poet's praises is to be attributed to the poetry. The instruments most frequently named are the lyre, the flute, and the syrinx. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a> appears not to have been known at the siege of Troy, although it had come to be in use in the days of Homer himself. From the time of Homer till that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAPPHO">Sappho</a>, there is almost a total blank in literature. Only a few fragments remain of the works of those poets and musicians whose names are preserved as having flourished between those periods (A). During the century which elapsed between the days of Sappho and those of Anacreon, no literary productions are preserved entire. (A) <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> lived so near to Homer, that it has been disputed which of them is the most ancient. It is now, we believe, universally admitted, that the palm of antiquity is due to Homer; but we consider them as having both flourished in the same era. From Anacreon to Pindar there is another chain of near a century. Subsequent to this time, the works still extant of the three great tragic poets, Æschylus, Sophocles, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EURIPIDES">Euripides</a>, together with those of Plato, Aristotle, Aristothenes, Euclid, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, Callimachus, Polybius, and many others, produced all within a space less than 300 years, distinguishing this illustrious and uncommon period as that in which the whole powers of genius seem to have been exerted to illuminate and instruct mankind in future ages. Then it was that eloquence, poetry, music, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, history, painting, sculpture, like the spontaneous blossoms of nature, flourished without the appearance of labour or of art. The poets, as well epic as lyric and elegiac, were all likewise musicians; so strictly connected were music and poetry for many ages. It would afford amusement to collect the biographical anecdotes of these favourites of genius, and to assign to each the respective improvements made by him in music and poetry; but our limits do not admit of so extensive a disquisition; for which, therefore, reference must be made to the editors and commentators of these authors, and to the voluminous histories of music lately published. The invention of notation and musical characters marked a distinguished era in the progress of music. There are a diversity of accounts respecting the person to whom the honour of that invention is due; but the evidences seem to preponderate in favour of Terpander, a celebrated poet and musician, whose genius music is much indebted. He flourished about the 27th Olympiad, or 671 years before Christ. Before that valuable discovery, music being entirely traditional, must have depended much on the memory and taste of the performer. There is an incident mentioned in the accounts handed down to us of the Olympic games, which may serve in some degree to mark the character of music at the time in which it happened. Lucian relates that a young flute-player named Harmonides, at his first public appearance in these games, began a solo with so violent a blast, on purpose to surprise and elevate the audience, that he breathed his last breath into his flute, and died on the spot. When to this anecdote, wonderful to us, and almost incredible, is added that circumstance, that the trumpet-players at these public exhibitions expressed an excess of joy when they found their exertions had neither rent their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> nor burst their blood-vessels, some idea may be formed of the noisy and vociferous style of music which then prevailed; and from such facts only can any opinion be obtained of the actual state of ancient music. In whatever manner the flute was played on, there is no doubt that it was long in Greece an instrument of high favour, and that the flute-players were held in much estimation. The flute used by Ifmenias, a celebrated Theban musician, cost at Corinth three talents, or £81. 5s. If, says Xenophon, a bad flute-player would pass for a good one, he must, like the great flute-players, expend <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums on rich furniture, and appear in public with a great retinue of servants. The ancients, it appears, were not less extravagant in gratifying the ministers of their pleasures than ourselves. Amebebas, a harper, was paid an Attic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, or £93. 1s. per day for his performance (B). It is proper to add, that the celebrated musicians of Greece who performed in public were of both sexes; and that the beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMIA">Lamia</a>, who was taken captive by Demetrius, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> engagement in which he vanquished Ptolemy Soter, and who herself captivated her conqueror, was a public performer, as well as were many other elevated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> spirits, who are recorded by ancient authors in terms of admiration, and of whom, did our limits here admit of biography, we would treat with pleasure. The philosophers of Greece, whose capacious minds grasped every other object of human intelligence, were not inattentive to the theory of music, or the philosophy of sound. This department of science became the source of various sects, and of much diversity of opinion.—The founders of the most distinguished sects were <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> and Aristothenes. Like every other people, the Romans, from their Roman first origin as a nation, were possessed of a species of music which might be distinguished as their own. It appears to have been rude and coarse, and probably was a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the music in use among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a> and other tribes around them in Italy; but as soon as they began to open a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Greece, from that country, with their arts and philosophy, they borrowed also their music and musical instruments. No account, therefore, of Roman music is to be expected that would not be a repetition of what has been said on the subject of the music of Greece. The excessive vanity of Nero with respect to music, displayed in his public contentions for superiority with the most celebrated professors of the art in Greece and Rome, is known to every one conversant in the history of Rome. The solicitude with which that detestable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> attended to his voice is curious, and will throw some light on the practices of singers in ancient times. He was in use to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on his back, with a thin plate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> on his stomach. He took frequent emetics and cathartics, obtained from all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and such meats as were held to be prejudicial to singing. Apprehensive of injuring his voice, he at length desisted from haranguing the soldiery and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>; and after his return from Greece established an officer (Phonacius) to regulate his tones in speaking. Most nations have consented in introducing music into their religious ceremonies. That art was early admitted into the rites of the Egyptians and Hebrews; and that it constituted a considerable part of the Grecian and Roman religious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, appears from the writings of many ancient authors. The same pleasing art soon obtained an introduction into the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, as the Acts of the Apostles discover in many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>. There remain no specimens of the music employed in the worship of the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; but probably it was at first the same with that used in the Pagan rites of the Greeks and Romans. The practice (B) Rofcius gained 500 sesterzia, or £436l. 9s. 2d. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. practice of chanting the psalms was introduced into the western churches by St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>, about 350 years after Christ. In the year 600, the method of chanting was improved by St Gregory the Great. The Ambrosian chant contained four modes. In the Gregorian the number was doubled. So early as the age of Constantine the Great, prior to either of the periods last mentioned, when the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> first obtained the countenance of power, instrumental music came to be introduced into the service of the church. In England, according to Bishop Stillington, music was employed in the church service, first by St Augustine, and afterwards much improved by St Dunstan, who was himself an eminent musician, and who is said to have first furnished the English churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> with the organ. The organ, the most majestic of all instruments, seems to have been an improvement of the hydraulicon or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> organ of the Greeks. The first organ seen in France was sent from Constantinople in 757, as a present to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Pepin from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine Copronymus VI. In Italy, Germany, and England, that instrument became frequent during the 10th century. During the dark ages no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of genius or taste in any department of science seems to have been produced in any part of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and except in Italy, where the cultivation of music was rather more the object of attention, that art was neglected equally with all others. There has always been observed a correspondence in every country between the progress of music and the cultivation of other arts and sciences. In the middle ages, therefore, when the most fertile provinces of Europe were occupied by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, Huns, Vandals, and other barbarous tribes, whose language was as harsh as their manners were savage, little perfection and no improvement of music is to be looked for. Literature, arts, and refinements, were encouraged more early at the courts of the Roman pontiffs than in any other country; and owing to that circumstance it is, that the scale, the counterpoint, the best melodies, the dramas religious and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a>, the chief graces and elegancies of modern music, have derived their origin from Italy. In modern times, Italy has been to the rest of Europe what ancient Greece was to Rome. The Italians have aided the civilization of their conquerors, and enlightened the minds of those whose superior prowess had enslaved them. Having mentioned counterpoint, it would be improper not to make one or two observations on an invention which is supposed to have been the source of great innovation in the practice of music. Counterpoint, or music in parts, seems to be an invention purely modern. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> harmony meant in the language of antiquity what is now understood by melody. Guido, a monk of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, is, in the general opinion, supposed to have entertained the first idea of counterpoint about the year 1022: an art which, since his time, has experienced gradual and imperceptible improvements, far exceeding the powers or comprehension of any one individual. The term counterpoint, or contra punctum, denotes its own etymology and import. Musical notation was at one time performed by small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; and the present <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> is only an improvement of that practice. Counterpoint, therefore, denotes the notation of harmony or music in parts, by points opposite to each other. The improvements of this important acquisition to the art of music kept pace at first with those of the organ; an instrument admirably adapted to harmony. And both the one and the other were till the 13th century employed chiefly in sacred music. It was at this period that sacred music began to be cultivated. Before the invention of characters for time, music in parts must have consisted entirely of simple counterpoint, or note against note, as is still practised in psalmody. But the happy discovery of a time-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> extended infinitely the powers of combined sounds. The ancients had no other resource to denote time and movement in music except two characters (—), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a long and a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>. But time is of such importance in music, that it can impart meaning and energy to the repetition of the same sound. Without it variety of tones has no effect with respect to gravity and acuteness. The invention of the time-table is attributed by almost all the writers on music of the last and present century to John de Muris, who flourished about the year 1330. But in a manuscript of John de Muris himself, bequeathed to the Vatican library by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, that honour seems to be yielded to Magister Franco, who appears to have been alive as late as at least 1083. John de Muris, however, who there is some cause to believe was an Englishman, though not the inventor of the cantus mensurabilis, did certainly by his numerous writings greatly improve it. His tract on the Art of Counterpoint is the most clear and useful <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on the subject of which those times can boast. In the 11th century, during the first crusade, Europe began to emerge from the barbarous stupidity and ignorance which had long overwhelmed it. While its inhabitants were exercising in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> every species of rapine and pious cruelty, art, ingenuity, and reason, insensibly civilized and softened their minds. Then it was that the poets and songsters, known by the name of Troubadours, who first appeared in Provence, instituted a new profession; which obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Poitou, and many other princes and barons, who had themselves cultivated music and poetry with success. At the courts of their munificent patrons the troubadours were treated with respect. The ladies, whose charms they celebrated, gave them the most generous and flattering reception. The success of some inspired others with hopes, and excited exertions in the exercise of their art; impelling them towards perfection with a rapidity which the united force alone of emulation and emolument could occasion. These founders of modern versification, constructing their songs on plans of their own, classical authority, either through ignorance or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, was entirely disregarded. It does not appear, however, during the cultivation and favour of Provençal literature, that any one troubadour so far outstripped the rest as to become a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of imitation. The progress of taste must ever be impeded by the ignorance and caprice of those who cultivate an art without science or principles. During almost two centuries after the arrangement of the scale attributed to Guido, and the invention of the time-table ascribed to Franco, no remains of secular music can be discovered, except those of the troubadours or Provencal poets. In the simple tunes of these bards no time indeed is marked, and but little variety of notation appears: It is not difficult, however, to discover in them the germs of the future melodies, as well as the poetry of France and Italy. Had the poetry and music of the troubadours been treated of in an agreeable manner by the writers who have chosen that subject, it would have been discovered to be worthy of attention; the poetry, as interesting to literature; the melody to which it was sung, as curious to the musical historian. Almost every species of Italian poetry is derived from the Provencals. Air, the most captivating part of secular vocal music, seems to have had the same origin. The most ancient strains that have been spared by time, are such as were set to the songs of the troubadours. The Provencal language began to be in favour with poets about the end of the 13th century. In the 14th it became the general vehicle, not only of poetry, but of prose, to all who were ignorant of Latin. And these were not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> only. At this period viols, or performers on the vielle or viol, juglars or flute-players, musiciors or players on other instruments, and comedians or comedians, abounded all over Europe. This swarm of poet-musicians, who were formerly comprehended in France under the general title of jongleurs, travelled from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to province, singing their verses at the courts of princes. They were rewarded with clothes, horses, arms, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Jongleurs or musicians were employed often to sing the verses of troubadours, who themselves happened to be deficient in voice or ignorant of music. The term troubadour, therefore, implies poetry as well as music. The jongleurs, menestriers, strollers, or minstrels, were frequently musicians, without any pretensions to poetry. These last have been common at all times; but the troubadour or bard has distinguished a particular profession, either in ancient or modern times, only during the early dawns of literature. In the 13th century the songs were on various subjects; moral, merry, amorous: and at that time melody seems to have been little more than plain song or chanting. The notes were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and written on four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> only like those of the Roman church in the cliff C, and without any marks for time. The movement and embellishments of the air depended on the abilities of the finger.
