At length he was confounded with the supreme God; and all the titles, attributes, operations, perfections, and ensigns of the Most High were ascribed to him. Sometimes he is called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMIDA">Amida</a>, and represented with the head of a dog, and worshipped as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of mankind. He sometimes appears as a princely personage, issuing from the mouth of a fish. At other times, he wears a lunette on his head, in which are seen cities, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, towers, trees, in short, all that the world contains. These transformations are evidently the children of allegorical or hieroglyphical emblems, and form an exact counterpart to the symbolical worship of the Egyptians. The enormous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of mythological traditions which have in a manner deluged the vast continent of India, would fill many volumes: We have selected the preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as a specimen only, by which our readers may be qualified to judge of the rest. If they find themselves disposed to indulge their curiosity at greater length, we must refer them to Thévenot's and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>'s Travels, to Mons. Anquetil in his Zond Avesta, Halhed's Introduction to his Translation of the Code of Gentoo Laws, Col. Dow's History of Hindostan, Grofe's Voyage to the East Indies, Asiatic Researches, vol. i. and ii. The mythology of the Persians is, if possible, still Persian more extravagant than that of the Hindoos. It supposes the world to have been repeatedly destroyed, and repeopled by creatures of different formation, who were successively annihilated or banished for their disobedience to the supreme Being. The monstrous griffin Sinergh tells the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> Caherman that he had already lived to see the earth seven times filled with creatures, and seven times a perfect void: that before the creation of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, this globe was inhabited by a race of beings called Peri and Dives, whose characters formed a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a>. The Peri are described as beautiful and benevolent; the Dives as deformed, malevolent, and mischievous, differing from infernal demons only in this, that they are not as yet confined to the pit of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. They are forever ranging over the world, to scatter <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> and misery among the sons of men. The Peri nearly resemble the fairies of Europe: and perhaps the Dives gave birth to the giants and magicians of the middle ages. The Peri and Dives wage incessant wars; and when the Dives make any of the Peri prisoners, they shut them up in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> cages, and hang them on the highest trees, to expose them to public view, and to the fury of every chilling blast. When the Peri are in danger of being overpowered by their foes, they solicit the assistance of some mortal hero; which produces a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of mythological adventures, highly ornamental to the strains of the Persian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BARDS">bards</a>, and which, at the same time, furnishes an inexhaustible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of the most diversified machinery. One of the most celebrated adventurers in the mythology of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> is Tadmuras, one of their most ancient monarchs. This prince performs a variety of exploits, while he endeavours to recover the fairy Merjan. He attacks the Dive Demruth in his own cave; where having vanquished the giant or demon, he finds vast piles of hoarded wealth: these he carries off with the fair captive. The battles, labours, and adventures of Roftan, another Persian worthy, who lived many ages after the former, are celebrated by the Persian bards with the same extravagance of hyperbole with which the labours of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> have been sung by the poets of Greece and Rome. The adventures of the Persian heroes breathe all the wildness of achievement recorded of the knights-birth-place of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>. The doctrine of enchantments, and transformations, &c., exhibited in both, is a characteristic symptom of one common original. Persia is the genuine classic ground of eastern mythology, and the source of the ideas of chivalry and romance; from which they were propagated to the regions of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a>, and indeed to the remotest corners of Europe towards the west. Perhaps our readers may be of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, when we offer it as a conjecture, that the tales of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of the Peri and Dives originated from a vague tradition concerning good and bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>: nor is it, in our opinion, improbable, that the fable of the wars between the gods and giants, so famous in the mythology of Greece and Italy, was imported into the former of these countries from the same quarter. For a more particular account of the Persian mythology, our readers may consult Dr Hyde. Hyde Relig. vet. Peri. Medor. &c. D'Herbelot's Bibl. Orient. and Mr Richardson's introduction to his Persian and Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>. The mythology of the Chaldeans, like that of the other nations of the east, commences at a period myriads of years prior to the era of the Mosaic creation. Their cosmogony, exhibited by Berosus, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Belus, and deeply versed in the antiquities of his country, is a piece of mythology of the most extravagant nature. It has been copied by Eusebius (Chron. lib. i. p. 5.) it is likewise to be found in Syncellus, copied from Alexander Polyhistor. According to this historian, there were at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> written records preserved with the greatest care, comprehending a period of fifteen myriads of years. Those writings likewise contained a history of the heavens and the sea, of the earth, and of the origin of mankind. "In the beginning (says Berosus, copying from Oannes, of whom we shall give a brief account below) there was nothing but darkness and an abyss of water, wherein resided most hideous beings produced from a twofold principle. Men appeared with two wings; some with two and some with four faces. They had one body, but two heads; the one of a man, the other of a woman. Other human figures were to be seen, furnished with the legs and horns of goats. Some had the feet of horses behind, but before were fashioned like men, resembling hippocentaurs." The remaining part of this mythology is much of the same complexion; indeed so extravagant, that we imagine our readers will readily enough dispense with our translating the sequel. "Of all these (says the author) were preserved delineations in the temple of Belus at Babylon. The person who was supposed to preside over them was called Oannes. This word, in the Chaldean language, is Thalath, which the Greeks call Θαλάθος, but it more properly imports the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. Matters being in this situation, their god (says Eusebius), the god (says Syncellus) came and cut the woman asunder; and out of one half of her he formed the earth, and out of the other he made the heavens; and, at the same time, he destroyed the monsters of the abyss." This whole mythology is an allegorical history copied from hieroglyphical representations, the real purport of which could not be deciphered by the author. Such, in general, were the consequences of the hieroglyphical style of writing. Oannes, the great civilizer and legislator of the Chaldeans, according to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>, who copied from Berosus, was an amphibious animal of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> appearance. He was endowed with reason and a very uncommon acuteness of parts. His whole body resembled a fish. Under the head of a fish he had also another head, and feet below similar to those of a man, which were subjoined to the tail of the fish. His <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and language were articulate and perfectly intelligible, and there was a figure of him still extant in the days of Berosus. He made his appearance in the Erythrean or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> sea, where it borders upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>. This monstrous being conversed with men by day; but at night he plunged into the sea, and remained concealed in the water till next morning. He taught the Babylonians the use of letters, and the knowledge of all the arts and sciences. He instructed them in the method of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> houses, constructing temples, and all other edifices. He taught them to compile laws and religious ceremonies, and explained to them the principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. In a word he communicated to them every thing necessary, useful, and ornamental; and so universal were his instructions, that not one single article had ever been added to them since the time they were first communicated. Heliadius is of opinion that this strange personage, whoever he was, came to be represented under the figure of a fish, not because he was actually believed to be such, but because he was clothed with the skin of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. By this account our readers will see that the Babylonian Oannes is the exact counterpart of the Fohi of the Chinefe, and the Thoth or the Mercury of Trismegistus of the Egyptians. It is likewise apparent that the idea of the monster compounded of the man and the fish has originated from some hieroglyphic of that form grafted upon the appearance of man. Some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> mythologists have been of opinion, that Oannes was actually Noah the great preacher of righteousness; who, as some think, settled in Shinar or Chaldea after the deluge, and who, in consequence of his connexion with that event, might be properly represented under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the Man of the Sea. The nativity of Venus, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and The nat- love, is another piece of mythology famous among the Babylonians and Assyrians. An <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, say they, of a prodigious size, dropt from heaven into the river <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. Some doves settled upon this egg, after that the fishes had rolled it to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. In a short time this egg produced Venus, who was afterwards called Dea <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, the Syrian goddess. In consequence of this tradition (says Hyginus), pigeons and fishes became sacred to this goddess among the Syrians, who always abstained from eating the one or the other. Of this imaginary being we have a very exact and entertaining history in the treatise De Dea Syria, generally ascribed to Lucian. In this mythological tradition our readers will probably discover an allusion to the celebrated Mundane egg; and at the same time the story of the fishes will lead them to anticipate the connexion between the sea and the moon. This same deity was the Atargatis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASCALON">Ascalon</a>, described by Diodorus the Sicilian; the one half of her body a woman and the other a fish. This was no doubt a hieroglyphic figure of the moon, importing the influence of that planet upon the sea and the fex. The oriental name of this deity evidently <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to the moon; for it is compounded of two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> words (ב), which import "the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> of heaven." The fable of Semiramis is nearly connected with the preceding one. Diodorus Siculus has preserved of Semiramis the mythological history of this deity, which he and all the writers of antiquity have confounded with the Babylonian princesses of the same name. That historian informs us, that the word Semiramis, in the Syrian dialect, signifies "a wild pigeon;" but we apprehend that this term was a name or epithet of the moon. (b) Adar or Hadar, "magnificus;" and Gad, "exercitus turmi." moon, as it is compounded of two words (c) of an import naturally applicable to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> planet. It was a general practice among the Orientals to denominate their sacred animals from that deity to which they were consecrated. Hence the moon being called Semiramis, and the pigeon being sacred to her divinity, the latter was called by the name of the former. As the bounds prefcribed this article render it impossible for us to do <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to this interesting piece of mythology, we must beg leave to refer our readers for farther information to Diod. Sic. lib. ii. Hyginus Poet. Aitron. Fab. 197. Pharnutus de Nat. Deor. Ovid. Metam. lib. iv. Athen. in Apol. Izetzes, Chil. ix. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 275. Seld. de Diis Syr. Syrii. ii. p. 183. We should now proceed to the mythology of the Arabians, the far greatest part of which is, however, buried in the abyss of ages; though, when, we reflect on the genius and character of that people, we must be convinced that they too, as well as the other nations of the east, abounded in fabulous relations and romantic compositions. The natives of that country have always been enthusiastically addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, of which fable is the essence. Wherever the Mules have erected their throne, fables and miracles have always appeared in their train. In the Koran we meet with frequent allusions to well-known traditionary fables. These had been transmitted from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> to generation by the bards and rhapsodists for the entertainment of the vulgar. In Arabia, from the earliest ages, it has always been one of the favourite entertainments of the common people, to assemble in the serene evenings around their tents, or on the platforms with which their houses are generally covered, or in large halls erected for the purpose, in order to amuse themselves with traditional narrations of the most distinguished actions of their most remote <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Oriental imagery always embellished their romantic details. The glow of fancy, the love of the marvellous, the propensity towards the hyperbolical and the vast, which constitute the essence of oriental <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, must ever have drawn the relation aside into the devious regions of fiction and fairy land. The religion of Mahomet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the original fabric of idolatry and mythology together. The Arabian fables current in modern times are borrowed or imitated from Persian compositions; Persia being still the grand nursery of romance in the east. In Egypt we find idolatry, theology, and mythology, almost inseparably blended together. The inhabitants of this region, too, as well as of others in the vicinity of the centre of population, adhered for several centuries to the worship of the true God. At last, however, conscious of their own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a>, imperfection, and total unfitness to approach an infinitely perfect Being, distant, as they imagined, and invisible, they began to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> about for some beings more exalted, and more perfect than themselves, by whose mediation they might prefer their prayers to the supreme Majesty of heaven. The luminaries of heaven, which they imagined were animated bodies, naturally presented themselves. These were splendid and glorious beings. They were thought to partake of the divine nature: they were revered as the satraps, prefects, and representatives of the supreme Lord of the universe. They were visible, they were beneficent; they dwelt nearer to the gods, they were near at hand and always accessible. These were, of course, employed as mediators and intercessors between the supreme Divinity and his humble subjects of this lower world. Thus employed, they might claim a subordinate share of worship, which was accordingly assigned them. In process of time, however, that worship, which was originally addressed to the supreme Creator by the mediation of the heavenly bodies, was in a great measure forgotten, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> of mankind ultimately terminated on those illustrious creatures. To this circumstance, we think, we may ascribe the origin of that species of idolatry called Zabijm, Origin of or the worship of the host of heaven, which overpread Zabijm, the world early and almost universally. In Egypt this mode of worship was adopted in all its most absurd and most enthusiastic forms; and at the same time the most heterogeneous mythology appeared in its train. The mythology of the ancient Egyptians was so various and multiform, so complicated and so mysterious, that it would require many volumes even to give a superficial account of its origin and progress, not only in its mother country, but even in many other parts of the eastern and western world. Besides, the idolatry and mythology of that wonderful country are so closely connected and so inseparably blended together, that it is impossible to describe the latter without at the same time developing the former. We hope, therefore, our readers will not be disappointed, if, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this nature, we touch only upon some of the leading or most interesting articles of this complicated subject. The Egyptians confounded the revolutions of the reign of heavenly bodies with the reigns of their most early gods and monarchs. Hence the incredible number of years in demigods, &c., in Egypt, according to them, filled the Egyptian throne successively in the most early periods of time. To these, according to their system, succeeded twelve demigods, who likewise reigned an amazing number of years. These imaginary reigns were no other than the periodical revolutions of the heavenly bodies preserved in their almanacks, which might be carried back, and actually were carried back, at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Hence the fabulous antiquity of that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. The imaginary exploits and adventures of these gods and demigods furnished an inexhaustible fund of mythological romances. To the demigods succeeded the kings of the cynic cycle, personages equally chimerical with the former. The import of this epithet is greatly perplexed critics and etymologists. We apprehend it is an oriental word importing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, elevation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. This appellation intimated, that the monarchs of that cycle, admitting that they actually existed, were more powerful and more highly revered than their successors. After the princes of the cynic cycle comes another race, denominated Nekyes, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> likewise implying royal, splendid, glorious. These cycles (c) Shem or Sem, "a sign," and ramah, "high." cycles figure high in the mythological annals of the Egyptians, and have furnished materials for a variety of learned and ingenious disquisitions. The wars and adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, Oris, Typhon, and other allegorical personages who figure in the Egyptian rubric; the wanderings of Isis, the sister and wife of Osiris; the transformation of the gods into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of animals; their birth, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, peregrinations, and exploits;—compose a body of mythological fictions so various, so complicated, so ridiculous, and often so apparently absurd, that all attempts to develop and explain them have hitherto proved unfruitful. All, or the greatest part, of those extravagant fables, are the offspring of hieroglyphical or allegorical emblems devised by the priests and sages of that nation, with a view to conceal the mysteries of their religion from that class of men whom they stigmatized with the name of the uninstructed rabble. The worship of brute animals and of certain vegetables, universal among the Egyptians, was another exuberant source of mythological adventures. The Egyptian priests, many of whom were likewise profound philosophers, observed, or pretended to observe, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> between the qualities of certain animals and vegetables, and those of some of their subordinate divinities. Such animals and vegetables they adopted, and consecrated to the deities to whom they were supposed to bear this analogical resemblance; and in process of time they considered them as the visible emblems of those divinities to which they were consecrated. By these the vulgar addressed their archetypes: in the same manner, as in other countries, pictures and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> were employed for the very same purpose. The mob, in process of time, forgetting the emblematical character of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> and vegetables, addressed their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> immediately to them; and of course these became the ultimate objects of vulgar adoration. After that these objects, animate or inanimate, were consecrated as the visible symbols of the deities, it soon became fashionable to make use of their figures to represent those deities to which they were consecrated. This practice was the natural consequence of the hieroglyphical style which universally prevailed among the ancient Egyptians. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a> was represented under the figure of a ram, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APIS">Apis</a>, under that of a cow, Osiris of a bull, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a> of a goat, Thoth or Mercury of an ibis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUBASTIS">Bubastis</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> of a cat, &c. It was likewise a common practice among those deluded people to dignify these objects, by giving them the names of those deities which they represented. By this mode of dignifying these sacred emblems, the veneration of the rabble was considerably enhanced, and the ardour of their devotion inflamed in proportion. From these two sources, we think, are derived the fabulous transformation of the gods, so generally celebrated in the Egyptian mythology, and from it imported into Greece and Italy. In consequence of this practice, their mythological system was rendered at once enormous and unintelligible. Their Thoth, or Mercury Trismegistus, was, in our opinion, the inventor of this unhappy system. This personage, according to the Egyptians, was the original author of letters, geometry, astronomy, music, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; in a word, of all the elegant and useful arts, and of all the branches of science and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He it was who first discovered the analogy between the divine affections, influences, appearances, operations, and the corresponding properties, qualities, and instincts of certain animals, and the propriety of dedicating particular kinds of vegetables to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of particular deities. The priests, whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to expound the mysteries of that allegorical hieroglyphical religion, (see Mysteries), gradually lost all knowledge of the primary import of the symbolical characters. To supply this defect, and at the same time to veil their own ignorance, the facerdotal intruders had recourse to fable and fiction. They heaped fable upon fable, till their religion became an accumulated chaos of mythological absurdities. Two of the most learned and most acute of the ancient philosophers have attempted a rational explication of the latent import of the Egyptian mythology; but both have failed in the attempt; nor have the moderns, who have laboured in the same department, performed their part with much better success. Instead, therefore, of prosecuting this inexplicable subject, which would swell this article beyond all proportion, we must beg leave to refer those who are desirous of further information to the following authors, where they will find enough to gratify their curiosity, if not to inform their judgment: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, lib. ii. Diodorus Siculus, lib. i. Plut. Isis et <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPHIR">Ophir</a>; Jamblichus de Myth. Egypt. Horapollo Hieroglyp. Egypt. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MACROBI">Macrobi</a>. Sat. cap. 23. among the ancients; and among the moderns, Kircher's Oedip. Voss. de Orig. et Prog. Idol. Mr Bryant's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a> of Anc. Mythol. Monf. Gebelin Monde Prim.; and above all, to the learned Jablonski's Panth. Egyptorum. The elements of Phoenician mythology have been preferred by Eusebius, Præp. Evang. lib. init. In mythology, the large extract which that learned father hath copied from Philo Biblius's translation of Sanchoniathon's History of Phœnicia, we are furnished with several articles of mythology. Some of these throw considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of the sacred history; and all of them are strictly connected with the mythology of the Greeks and Romans. There we have preferred a brief but entertaining detail of the fabulous adventures of Uranus, Cronus, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAGON">Dagon</a>, Thoth or Mercury, probably the same with the Egyptian hero of that name. Here we find Muth or Pluto, Æpheceus or Vulcan, Æfeulapius, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a>, Poedon or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, &c. Astarte, or Venus <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-URANIA">Urania</a>, makes a conspicuous figure in the catalogue of Phœnician worthies; Pallas or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> is planted on the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>; in a word, all the branches of the family of the Titans, who in after ages figured in the rubric of the Greeks, are brought upon the stage, and their exploits and adventures briefly detailed. By comparing this fragment with the mythology of the Atlantidae and that of the Cretans preferred by Diodorus the Sicilian, lib. v. we think there is good reason to conclude, that the family of the Titans, and Phœnician branches of which seem to have been both the authors and objects of a great part of the Grecian idolatry, originally emigrated from Phœnicia. This conjecture will receive additional strength, when it is considered, that almost all their names recorded in the fabulous records of Greece, may be easily traced up to a Phœnician Phoenician original. We agree with Herodotus, that a considerable part of the idolatry of Greece may have been borrowed from the Egyptians; at the same time, we imagine it highly probable, that the idolatry of the Egyptians and Phoenicians was, in its original <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, nearly the same. Both systems were Sabatini, or the worship of the host of heaven. The Pelagi, according to Herodotus, learned the names of the gods from the Egyptians; but in this conjecture he is certainly warped by his partiality for that people. Had those names been imported from Egypt, they would no doubt have bestrayed their Egyptian original; whereas, every etymologist will be convinced that every one is of Phoenician <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. The adventures of Jupiter, Juno, Mercury, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, Diana, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, Minerva or Pallas, Venus, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>, Proserpine, Pluto, Neptune, and the other descendants and coadjutors of the ambitious family of the Titans, furnish by far the greatest part of the mythology of Greece. They left Phoenicia, we think, about the age of Moses; they settled in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, a large and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; from this region they made their way into Greece, which, according to the most authentic accounts, was at that time inhabited by a race of savages. The arts and inventions which they communicated to the natives; the mysteries of religion which they inculcated; the laws, customs, polity, and good order, which they established; in short, the blessings of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and civilization, which they everywhere disseminated, in process of time inspired the unpolished inhabitants with a kind of divine admiration. Those ambitious mortals improved this admiration into divine homage and adoration. The greater part of that worship, which had been formerly addressed to the luminaries of heaven, was now transferred to those illustrious personages. They claimed and obtained divine honours from the deluded rabble of enthusiastic Greeks. Hence sprung an inexhaustible fund of the most inconsistent and irreconcilable fictions. The foibles and frailties of the deified mortals were transmitted to posterity, incorporated as it were with the pompous attributes of supreme divinity. Hence the heterogeneous mixture of the mighty and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> which chequers the characters of the heroes of the Iliad and Odyssey. The Greeks adopted the oriental fables; the import of which they did not understand. These they accommodated to heroes and illustrious personages, who had figured in their own country in the earliest periods. The labours of Hercules originated in Egypt, and evidently relate to the annual progress of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, though the vain-glorious Greeks accommodated them to a hero of their own, the reputed son of Jupiter and Alcmene. The expedition of Osiris they borrowed from the Egyptians, and transferred to their Bacchus, the son of Jupiter and Semele the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>. The transformation and wanderings of Io are evidently transcribed from the Egyptian romance of the travels of Isis in quest of the body of Osiris, or of the Phoenician Ashtaroth, drawn from Sanchoniathon. Io or Iah is in reality the Egyptian name of the moon, and Ashtaroth was the name of the same planet among the Phoenicians. Both these fables are allegorical representations of the anomalies of the lunar planet, or perhaps of the progress of the worship of that planet in different parts of the world. The fable of the conflagration occasioned by Phaeton is clearly of oriental extraction, and alludes to an excessive drought which in the early periods of time scorched Ethiopia and the adjacent countries. The fabulous adventures of Perseus are said to have happened in the same regions, and are allegorical representations of the influence of the solar luminary; for the original Perseus was the sun. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> of Proserpine and the wanderings of Ceres; the Eleusinian mysteries; the orgia or sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of Bacchus; the rites and worship of the Cabiri—were imported from Egypt and Phoenicia; but strangely garbled and disfigured by the hierophants of Greece. The gantomachia, or war between the gods and the giants, and all the fabulous events and varieties of that war, form an exact counterpart to the battles of the Peri and Dives, celebrated in the romantic annals of Persia. A considerable part of the mythology of the Greeks sprang from their ignorance of the oriental languages, ignorant of which they disdained to apply themselves to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of oriental languages spoken by people whom, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of their heart, they stigmatized with the epithet of barbarians. This aversion to every foreign dialect was highly detrimental to their progress in the sciences. The same neglect or aversion has, we imagine, proved an irreparable injury to the republic of letters in all succeeding ages. The poets, or strolling bards, laid hold on those oriental legends, which they sophisticked with their own additions and improvements, in order to accommodate them to the popular taste. These wonderful tales figured in their rhapsodical compositions, and were greedily swallowed down by the credulous vulgar. Those fictions, as they rolled down, were constantly augmented with fresh materials, till in process of time their original import was either forgotten or buried in impenetrable darkness. A multitude of these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a> has collected in his Theogonia, or Generation of the Gods, which unhappily became the religious creed of the illiterate part of the Greeks. Indeed fable was so closely interwoven with the religion of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> volatile people, that it seems to have contaminated not only their religious and moral, but even their political tenets. The far-famed oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a> was copied from that of Ammon at Thebes in Egypt: The oracle of Dodona. Apollo at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> was an emanation from the same source: The celebrated Apollo Pythius of the Greeks was no other than Ob or Aub of the Egyptians, who denominated the basilisk or royal snake Oub Cai, because it was held sacred to the sun. Ob or Aub is still retained in the Coptic dialect, and is one of the many names or epithets of that luminary. In short, the groundwork of the Grecian mythology is to be traced in the east. Only a small part of it was fabricated in the country; and what was imported pure and genuine was miserably sophisticked by the hands through which it passed, in order to give it a Grecian air, and to accommodate its style to the Grecian taste. To enlarge upon this topic would be altogether superfluous, as our learned readers must be well acquainted with it already, and the unlearned may without much trouble or expense furnish themselves with books upon that subject. The Roman mythology was borrowed from the Greeks, Greece. Greeks. That people had addicted themselves for many centuries to the arts of war and civil polity. Science and philosophy were either neglected or unknown. At last they conquered Greece, the native land of science, and then "Grecia capta ferum victorem cepit arte et intuitu agresti Latio." This being the case, their mythology was, upon the whole, a transcript from that of Greece. They had indeed gleaned a few fables from the Pelasgi and Hetruscans, which, however, are of so little consequence, that they are scarce worth the trouble of transcribing. The mythology of the Celtic nations is in a good measure lost. There may possibly still remain some vestiges of the Druidical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> in the remotest parts of the Highlands and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Scotland; and perhaps in the uncivilized places of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. These, we presume, would afford our readers but little entertainment, and still less instruction. Instead therefore of giving a detail of those uninteresting articles, we shall beg leave to refer our readers to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a>'s Poems, and Col. Valency's Collections of Irish Antiquities, for satisfaction on that subject. The mythology of the northern nations, i.e., of the Norwegians, Danes, Swedes, Icelanders, &c., is uncommonly curious and entertaining. The Edda and Voluppa contain a complete collection of fables which have not the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with those of the Greeks and Romans. They are wholly of an oriental complexion, and seem almost congenial with the tales of the Persians above described. The Edda was compiled in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> in the 13th century. It is a kind of system of the Scandinavian mythology; and has been reckoned, and we believe justly, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the Voluppa, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> of the northern nations. Odin or Othin, or Woden or Waden, was the supreme divinity of those people. His exploits and adventures furnish the far greatest part of their mythological creed. That hero is supposed to have emigrated from the east; but from what country or at what period is not certainly known. His achievements are magnified beyond all credibility. He is represented as the god of battles, and as slaughtering thousands at a blow. His <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is called Valhalla; it is situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Midgard, where, according to the fable, the souls of heroes who had bravely fallen in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> enjoy supreme felicity. They spend the day in mimic hunting matches, or imaginary combats. At night they assemble in the palace of Valhalla, where they feast on the most delicious viands, drested and served up by the Valkyries, virgins adorned with celestial charms, and flushed with the bloom of everlasting youth. They solace themselves with drinking <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAD">mead</a> out of the skulls of enemies whom they killed in their days of nature. Mead, it seems, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a> of the Scandinavian heroes. Sleepner, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> of Odin, is celebrated along with his master. Hela, the hell of the Scandinavians, affords a variety of fables equally shocking and heterogeneous. Loki, the evil genius or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> of the northern people, nearly resembles the Typhon of the Egyptians. Signa or Sinna is the comfort of Loki; from this name the English word sin is derived. The giants Weymur, Ferbantor, Belrophor, and Hellunda, perform a variety of exploits, and are exhibited in the most frightful attitudes. One would be tempted to imagine, that they perform the exact counterpart of the giants of the Greek and Roman mythologists. Instead of glancing at these ridiculous and uninteresting fables, which is all that the limits preferred us would permit, we shall take the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to lay before our readers a brief account of the contents of the Voluppa, which is indeed the text of the Scandinavian mythology. The word Voluppa imports, "the prophesy of Vola or Fola." This was, perhaps, a general name for the prophetic ladies of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, as Sibyl was appropriated to women endowed with the like <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> in the south. Certain it is, that the ancients generally connected madness with the prophetic faculty. Of this we have two celebrated examples: the one in Lycophron's Alexandra, and the other in the Sibyl of the Roman poet. The word vola signifies "mad or foolish;" whence the English words fool, foolish, folly. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPA">Spa</a>, the latter part of the composition, signifies "to prophesy," and is still current among the common people in Scotland, in the word Spoe, which has nearly the same signification. The Voluppa consists of between 200 and 300 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The prophetess having imposed silence on all intelligent beings, declares that she is about to reveal the works of the Father of nature, the actions and operations of the gods, which no mortal ever knew before herself. She then begins with a description of the chaos; and then proceeds to the formation of the world, the creation of the different species of its inhabitants, giants, men, and dwarfs. She then explains the employments of the fairies or deities, whom the northern people call normers; the functions of the deities, their most memorable adventures, their disputes with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOKE">Loke</a>, and the vengeance that ensued. She at last concludes with a long and indeed animated description of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> state of the universe, and its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> by a general conflagration. In this catastrophe, Odin and all the rabble of the Pagan divinities, are to be confounded in the general ruin, no more to appear on the stage of the universe. Out of the ruins of the former world, according to the Voluppa, a new one shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up, arrayed in all the bloom of celestial beauty. Such is the doctrine exhibited in the fabulous Voluppa. So congenial are some of the details therein delivered, especially those relating to the final dissolution of the present system, and the succession of a new heaven and a new earth, that we find ourselves strongly inclined to suspect, that the original fabricator of the work was a semi-pagan writer, much of the same complexion with the authors of the Sibylline oracles, and of some other apocryphal pieces which appeared in the world during the first ages of Christianity. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the only mythological countries must be <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. The other parts of that large continent were originally inhabited by savages, most of them as remote from religion as from civilization. The two vast empires of Mexico and Peru had existed about 450 years only before the Spanish invasion. In neither of them was the use of letters understood; and of course the ancient opinions of the natives relating to the origin of the universe, the changes which succeeded, and every other monument of antiquity, were obliterated and lost. Clavigero has indeed enumerated a vast canaille of sanguinary gods worshipped by the Mexicans; Mexicans; but produces nothing either entertaining or interesting with respect to their mythology. The information to be derived from any other quarter is little to be depended upon. It passes through the hands of bigotted missionaries or other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, who were so deeply tinctured with fanaticism, that they viewed every <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, every sentiment, every custom, every religious opinion and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of those half-civilized people, through a false medium. They often imagined they discovered resemblances and analogies between the rites of those savages and the dogmas of Christianity, which nowhere existed but in their own heated imagination. The only remarkable piece of mythology in the annals of the Peruvians, is the pretended extraction of Manco Capac the first Inca of Peru, and of Mama Ocolla his consort. These two illustrious personages appeared first on the banks of the lake Titicaca. They were persons of a majestic stature, and clothed in decent garments. They declared themselves to be the children of the Sun, sent by their benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, who beheld with pity the miseries of the human race, to instruct and to reclaim them. Thus we find these two legislators availed themselves of a pretence which had often been employed in more civilized regions to the very same purposes. The idolatry of Peru was gentle and beneificent, that of Mexico gloomy and fan- guinary. Hence we may see, that every mode of superstition, where a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> is not concerned, borrows its complexion from the characters of its professors. In the course of this article, our readers will observe, that we have not much enlarged upon the mythology of the Greeks and Romans; that subject we imagine to be so universally known by the learned, and so little valued by the vulgar, that a minute discussion of it would be altogether superfluous. Besides, we hope it will be remembered, that the narrowness of the limits prescribed us would scarce admit of a more copious detail. We would flatter ourselves, that in the course of our disquisition, we have thrown out a few reflections and observations, which may perhaps prove more acceptable to both descriptions of readers.

MYTILUS

Pages 653-653

the Mussel, a genus of animals, belonging to the order of vermes testacea. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">CONCHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MYTTOTON

Pages 653-653

a coarse kind of food, used by the labouring people among the Greeks, and sometimes among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It was made of garlic, onions, eggs, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and reckoned very wholesome.

MYUS

Pages 653-653

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the twelve <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>; seated on the Meander, at the distance of 30 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In Strabo's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was incorporated with the Milesians, on account of the paucity of inhabitants, from its being formerly overwhelmed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>: for which reason the Ionians configned its suffrage and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> ceremonies to the people of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> allotted this town to Themistocles, in order to furnish his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with meat: Magneia was to support him in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and Lamplacus in wine. The town now lies in ruins.

MYXINE

Pages 653-654

the Hag; a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes intestina. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. N. N, A liquid consonant, and the 13th <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Greek, Latin, English, &c. alphabets. The n is a nasal consonant: its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is that of a d, passed through the nose; so that when the nose is stopped by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, it is usual to pronounce d for n. M. Abbé de Dangeau observes, that in the French, the n is frequently a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> nasal vowel, without any thing of the consonant in it. He calls it the Slavonic vowel. The Hebrews call their n <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a>, which signifies child, as being supposed the offspring of m; partly on account of the resemblance of sound, and partly on that of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. Thus from the m, by omitting the last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, is formed n; and thus from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> N, by omitting the first column, is formed the Greek minuscule ν. Hence for biennies, &c. the Latins frequently <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> bimnas, &c. and the same people convert the Greek ν, at the end of a word, into an m, as Φαρμακον, pharmacum, &c. See M. N before p, b, and m, the Latins change into m, and frequently into l and r; as in in-ludo, illudo; irrigo, irrigo, &c.: in which they agree with the Hebrews, who, in lieu of nun, frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a>: and the Greeks do the same; as when for Manlius, they write Μαλλιος, &c. The Greeks also, before x, y, z, v, changed the ν into γ: in which they were followed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>: who, for Angulus, wrote Aggulus; for anceps, agceps, &c. The Latins retrench the n from Greek <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a> ending ing in av; as Λων, Leo; Δρακον, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a>; on the contrary, the Greeks add it to the Latin ones ending in o; as Κατον, Neron, Cato, Nero. N, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, was a numeral letter, signifying 900; according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in Baronius, N, quoque nongentos numero defignat habendos. And when a line was struck over it, N, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> thousand. Among the ancient lawyers, N.L. stood for non liquet, i.e. the cause is not clear enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> upon. N, or No, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, &c., is used as an abbreviation of numero, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

NAARDA

Pages 654-654

NEARDA, Neerda, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nehordea, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town situated on the confines of Mesopotamia and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>; populous, and with a rich and extensive territory, not easily to be attacked by an enemy, being surrounded on all sides by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and strong walls (Jofephus). In the lower <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> the Jews had a celebrated school there.

NAAS

Pages 654-654

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILDARE">Kildare</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>. It is the shire town of that county, and alternately with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHY">Athy</a> the assizes town. It is distant above 15 miles south-west from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, in N. Lat. 53° 10' W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 50'. It gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of viscount to the family of Burke. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was anciently the residence of the kings of Leinster: the name signifies "the place of elders," for here the states of that province assembled during the 6th, 7th, and 8th centuries, after the Naasfeighan of Carmen had been anathematized by the Christian clergy. On the arrival of the English it was fortified; many castles were erected, the ruins of which are partly visible; and parliaments were held there. At the foot of the mount <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rath are the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> founded in 1484, for eremites of the order of St Augustin. In the 12th century the baron of Naas founded a priory dedicated to St John the Baptist, for Augustinian regular canons. In the centre of this town the family of Euflae erected a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> for Dominican friars, dedicated to St Euflachius; and it appears that their possessions in Naas were granted them in the year 1355. This place was a strong hold during the civil wars.

NABATENE

Pages 654-654
or Regio Nabatæorum, according to Jerome, comprised all the country lying between the Euphrates and the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red sea, and thus contained Arabia Deserta, with a part of the Petraea: so called from Nabaioth, the first born of Ishmael. According to Diodorus, it was situated between Syria and Egypt. The people Nabataei (i.e. Maccabees, Diodorus Siculus): inhabiting a desert and barren country: they lived by plundering their neighbours, according to Diodorus. Nabatheus the epithet.

NABIS

Pages 654-654
tyrant of Sparta, reigned about 204 B.C.; and is reported to have exceeded all other tyrants so far, that, upon comparison, he left the epithets of gracious and merciful to Dionysus and Phalaris. He is said to have contrived an instrument of torture in the form of a statue of a beautiful woman, whose rich drapery concealed a number of iron spikes in her bosom and arms. When any one therefore opposed his demands, he would say, "If I have not talents enough to prevail with you, perhaps my woman Apega may persuade you." The statue then appeared; which Nabis taking by the hand, led up to the person, who, being embraced by it, was thus tortured into compliance. To render his tyranny less unpopular, Nabis made an alliance with Flaminius the Roman general, and pursued with the most inveterate enmity the war which he had undertaken against the Achaeans. He besieged Gythium, and defeated Philopoemen in a naval battle. His triumph was short, the general of the Achaeans soon repaired his losses, and Nabis was defeated in an engagement, and killed as he attempted to save his life by flight, about 194 years before the Christian era.

NABLOUS

Pages 654-654

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, anciently celebrated under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, likewise called Nablous, is situated near to Sichem on the ruins of the Niepolis of the Greeks, and is the residence of a sheik, who is subordinate to the pasha of Damascus, from whom he farms the tribute of the province.

NABLUM

Pages 654-654

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Nebel, was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music among the Jews. It had strings like the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, and was played upon by both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Its form was that of a Greek A. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and Vulgate, it is called nobulum, psalterion, lyra; and sometimes cithara.

NABO

Pages 654-654
or Nebo, in Mythology, a deity of the Babylonians, who possessed the next rank to Bel. It is mentioned by Isaiah, chap. xlviii. Vossius apprehends that Nabo was the moon, and Bel the sun: but Grotius supposes that Nabo was some celebrated prophet of the country; which opinion is confirmed by the etymology of the name, signifying, according to Jerome, "one that presides over prophecy."

NABOB

Pages 654-654

properly NAVAB, the plural of Noib, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>. As used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, it is the same as NAZIM. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> also given to the wives and daughters of princes, as well as to the princes themselves.

NABONASSAR

Pages 654-654

first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Chaldeans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Babylonians; memorable for the Jewish era which bears his name, which is generally fixed in 3257, beginning on Wednesday, February 26th, in the 3967th of the Julian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, 747 years before Christ. The Babylonians revolting from the Medes, who had overthrown the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, did, under Nabonassar, found a dominion, which was much increased under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>. It is probable, that this Nabonassar is that Baladan in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of Kings, xx. 12. father of Merodach, who sent ambassadors to Hezekiah. See 2 Chron. xxxii.

NABOPOLASSAR

Pages 654-654
king of Babylon: he joined with Ashyages the Mede, to destroy the empire of Assyria; which having accomplished, they founded the two empires of the Medes under Ashyages, and the Chaldeans under Nabopolassar, 627 B.C.

NABUCHADNEZZAR

Pages 654-655
or Nabuchodonosor II. king of Assyria, son of Nabopolassar, and styled the Great, was associated by his father in the empire, 607 B.C. and the following year he took Jehoiakim king of Judah prisoner, and proposed to carry him and his subjects in captivity into Babylon; but upon his submission, and promising to hold his kingdom under Nabuchodonosor, he was permitted to remain at Jerusalem. In 603 B.C. Jehoiakim attempted to shake off the Assyrian yoke, but without success; and this revolt brought on the general captivity. Nabuchadnezzar having subdued the Ethiopians, Arabians, Idumæans, Philistines, Syrians, Persians, Medes, Syrians, NÆVIUS, Cneius, a famous poet of Campania, was bred a soldier; but quitted the profession of arms, in order to apply himself to poetry, which he prosecuted with great diligence. He composed a history in verse, and a great number of comedies; but it is said that his first performance of this kind so displeased Metellus on account of the satirical strokes it contained, that he procured his being banished from the city: on which he retired to Utica in Africa, where he at length died, 202 B.C. We have only some fragments left of his works. There was another Nævius, a famous augur in the reign of Tarquin, who, to convince the king and the Romans of his preternatural power, cut a flint with a razor, and turned the ridicule of the populace to admiration. Tarquin rewarded his merit by erecting him a statue in the comitium, which was still in being in the age of Augustus. The razor and flint were buried near it under an altar, and it was usual among the Romans to make witnesses in civil causes swear near it. This miraculous event of cutting a flint with a razor, though believed by some writers, is treated as fabulous and improbable by Cicero, who himself had been augur. NÆVUS, a mole on the skin, generally called a mother's mark; also the tumour known by the name of a wen. All preternatural tumours on the skin, in the form of a wart or tubercle, are called excrescences; by the Greeks they are called acrothymia; and when they are born with a person, they are called nœvi materni, or marks from the mother. See Tumours, Surgery Index.

NAGERA

Pages 655-655
or NAGARA, a town of Spain, in Old Castile, and the territory of Rioja, with the title of a duchy and fortresses; famous for a battle fought in its neighbourhood in 1369. It is situated in a fertile country, on a brook called Nafrilla. W. Long. 2. 20. N. Lat. 42. 45.

NAGRACUT

Pages 655-655

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul, with a rich temple to which the Indians go in pilgrimage. It is seated on the river Ravi. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78. 10. N. Lat. 33. 12.

NAHUM

Pages 655-655
or the Prophecy of NAHUM, a canonical book of the Old Testament. Nahum, the seventh of the 12 lesser prophets, was a native of Elkochai, a little village of Galilee. The subject of his prophecy is the destruction of Nineveh, which he describes in the most lively and pathetic manner; his style is bold and figurative, and cannot be exceeded by the most perfect masters of oratory. This prophecy was verified at the siege of that city by Assyrians, in the year of the world 3378, 622 years before Christ.

NAIADES

Pages 655-655

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, certain inferior deities who presided over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and fountains. The Naiades generally inhabited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and resorted to the woods <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> meadows near the stream over which they presided. They are represented as young and beautiful virgins, often leaning upon an urn, from which flows a stream of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIGLE">Aigle</a> was the fairest of the Naiades, according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. Their name seems to be derived from naios, "to flow." They were held in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and often sacrifices of goats and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> were offered to them, with libations of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Sometimes they received only offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, fruit, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>.

NAIANT

Pages 655-655

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> fishes, when borne in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> posture, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>.

NAIAS

Pages 655-655

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dicotyledons; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NAIL

Pages 655-656

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length, containing the 16th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a yard. NAILING of Cannon. When circumstances make it necessary to abandon cannon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> when the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> are seized, and it is not however possible to take them away, it is proper to nail them up; in order to render them useless; which is done by driving a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nail or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> spike into the vent of a piece of artillery, to render it unserviceable. There are various contrivances to force the nail out, as also sundry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> invented for that purpose, but they have never been found of general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; so that the best method is to drill a new vent. One Gasper Vimercalus was the first who invented the nailing of cannon. He was a native of Bremen, and made use of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> first in nailing up the artillery of Sigismund Malatesta.

NAILS

Pages 655-655

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c., small spikes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, &c., which being driven into wood, serve to bind several pieces together, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to fasten something upon them. Nails were made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hebrews for cancelling bonds; and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed by striking them through the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. This seems to be alluded to in Scripture, where God is said by our crucified Saviour to have "blotted out the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-writing of ordinances that was against us, and to have taken it out of the way, nailing it to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>," Col. ii. 14. For the cause and ceremony of driving the annual nail, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLAVUS">clavus</a> annalis, among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, see ANNALIS Clavus.

NAIM

Pages 656-656
or NAIRN, situated at the bottom of Mount Hermon on the north side, was anciently a city of the tribe of Issachar, in the province of Galilee. It was near the gates of this city that our Saviour restored to life the only son of a widow, and where he inspired Mary Magdalen to come and mourn for her sins at his feet. These circumstances alone make this place worthy of notice; for at present Naim is only a hamlet inhabited by Christians, Mahometans, and Hebrews, where there is not a single monument to attract the curiosity of the traveller.

NAIRES

Pages 656-656

NAHERS, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> NAYERS, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a name which is given by the Malabarians to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, who form a very numerous class or tribe, out of which the sovereigns of Malabar choose their body <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>.

NAIRN

Pages 656-656

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Scotland, comprehending the western <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Murray. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Murray frith, on the west and south by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, and on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a>. The length is about 18 miles, and the breadth about 14. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate and salubrious, and the winter remarkably mild. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rough and mountainous; yet there are some fruitful valleys which produce good crops of oats and barley; but in general the country is much better adapted for pasture. Here are also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> woods of fir, and other trees, that afford shelter to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, of which there is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty. The most remarkable firths <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> valleys in this county are Strathnairn, on the river of that name, in the south-west part of the shire; and on the south-east side, Strathrin, on both sides of Findhorn river. Nairn is well watered with streams, rivulets, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> abounding with fish. In the southern part there is a small lake, called Moy. The greater part of the shire is peopled by the Frasers, a warlike Highland clan, whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Lovat, lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> on the scaffold for having been concerned in the rebellion of 1745. Here are a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages; but no <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> except Nairn, supposed to be the Tugis of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, situated at the mouth of the river which bears the same name; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough, which gave the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of lord to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, forfeited in the rebellion of 1715. The harbour, which opened in the Murray frith, is now choked up with sand; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of the town is too inconsiderable to deserve notice. About four miles from Nairn stands the castle of Calder on the river of that name, belonging to a branch of the family of Campbell; and five miles to the north-west of Nairn, stands Fort George, built by order of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Arderfer, a small isthmus upon the Murray frith. The following is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the parishes of this county, according to the Statistical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. | <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">Parish</a> | Population in 1755 | Population in 1790-1798 | |----------|-------------------|------------------------| | Ardclach | 1163 | 1186 | | Auldearn | 1951 | 1406 | | Calder | 882 | 1062 | | Nairn | 1698 | 2400 | | | 5694 | | | Increase | 360 | | Population in 1801, including part of some other Parishes. | Parish | Population | |----------|------------| | Ardclach | 1256 | | Auldearn | 1401 | | Calder | 1179 | | Croy (Nairn <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>) | 562 | | Moy do. | 34 | | Nairn town | 2215 | | Urquhart (do.) | 1610 |

NAISSANT

Pages 656-656

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is applied to any animal issuing out of the midst of some ordinary, and showing only his head, shoulders, fore feet, and legs, with the tip of his tail; the rest of his body being hid in the shield, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon it: in which it differs from issuant, which denotes a living creature arising out of the bottom of any ordinary or charge.

NAISSUS

Pages 656-656

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Dardania, a district of Moesia Superior, said to be the birthplace of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, which seems probable from his often residing at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Naissani, the

NAKIB

Pages 656-657

in the oriental dignities, the name of an officer who is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the cadiliskier, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as he may be called, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior. His office is to carry the standard of Mahomet.

NAKOUS

Pages 657-657

an Egyptian musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, made like two plates of briss, and of all sizes, from two inches to a foot in diameter; they hold them by strings fastened to their middles, and strike them together so as to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They are used in the Coptic churches and in the Mahometan processions.

NAME

Pages 657-658

denotes a word whereby men have agreed to express some idea; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> which serves to denote or signify a thing or subject spoken of. See Word. This the grammarians usually call a noun, nomen, though their noun is not of quite so much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> as our name. See Noun. Seneca, lib. ii. de Beneficiis, observes, that there are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of things which have no name; and which, therefore, we are forced to call by other borrowed names. Ingens est (says he) rerum copia sine nomine, quae cum propriis appellatibibus signare non possumus, alienis accommodatis utimur: which may show why, in the course of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, we frequently give <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> senses to the same word. Names are distinguished into proper and appellative. Proper NAMES, are those which represent some individual thing or person, so as to distinguish it from all other things of the same <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, which represents a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Appellative or General NAMES, are those which signify <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; or which are common to several individuals of the same species; as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, animal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, oak, &c. Proper names are either called Christian, as being given at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; or furnaces: The first imposed for distinction of persons, answering to the Roman praenomen; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, for the distinction of families, answering to the nomen of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and the patronymic of the Greeks. Originally every person had but one name; as among the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, &c. among the Egyptians, Butiris; among the Chaldees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINUS">Ninus</a>; the Medes, Abyagor; the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>; the Romans, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>; the Gauls, Divitiacus; the Germans, Ariovitus; the Britons, Corbelan; the English, Hengist, &c. And thus of other nations, except the savages of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, whom Pliny and Marcellinus represent as anonymi, "nameless." The Jews gave the name at the circumcision, viz. eight days after the birth: the Romans, to females the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to males the ninth; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they held a feast, called nominalia. Since Christianity has obtained, most nations have followed the Jews, baptizing and giving the name on the eighth day after the birth; except our English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, who, till of late, baptized and gave the name on the birth day.
