Guaimarius, not being in a condition to oppose the invaders by force, was preparing to pay them a large sum of money, which they demanded, when the Normans proposed to attack them; and, having got arms and horses from the prince, they engaged the infidels with such fury and bravery, that they entirely defeated them, and obliged them to fly to their ships. By this complete victory Guaimarius was filled with such admiration of the valour of these strangers, that he entreated them to remain in his country; offering them lands, and the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> employments; but not being able to prevail with them to stay in Italy, or even accept of his presents; at their departure he sent some ambassadors with them to Normandy, in vessels loaded with exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, rich furniture for horses, &c., in order to allure the valiant Normans to leave their own country. This kind invitation encouraged a Norman chief, named Ofmond Drengot, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in Italy about the year 1015; having killed another <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>, which obliged him to leave his own country, in order to avoid the resentment of his sovereign, Robert duke of Normandy. In the meantime, the city of Bari had revolted from the Greeks, and chosen one Mello for their leader, whose wife and children happened soon after to fall into the hands of their enemies, and were sent prisoners to Constantinople. No sooner, therefore, did Mello hear of the arrival of these adventurers, than he engaged them to assist him; and having drawn together a considerable army, defeated the Greeks with great slaughter, and obliged them to abandon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. In this engagement the Normans distinguished themselves by their bravery; and the news of their success soon brought from Normandy an innumerable multitude of their countrymen, with their wives and children. By this reinforcement, Mello gained two other victories, took a great many towns, and obliged the Greeks to abandon a large territory; but, in 1019, they were utterly defeated, and everything recovered by the Greeks. The Greek but are at general, Bajanus, continued to go on with such surprising success, that he almost entirely re-established the affairs of his countrymen in Italy, and made a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the western part of Puglia, which he called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITANATA">Capitanata</a>, and which to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> retains the name of Capitanata. His great progress at last alarmed the emperors of Germany; and, in 1027, Pandulphus prince of Capua made himself master of Naples; but was obliged, three years afterwards, to leave it, by the Normans, who built the city of Areva, which was now erected into a county. In consequence of this piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, great numbers of Norman adventurers migrated into Italy; among whom were William, Drogo, and Umbert, three of the sons of Tancred duke of Hautville; from whose posterity those princes were descended, who first conquered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Sicily from the Saracens, and formed the present kingdom of Naples. In 1040, the Greek emperor Michael Paleologus, in order to secure the affection of his fickle subjects, undertook the conquest of Italy from the Saracens, and for that purpose sent a general named Michael Maniacus into Sicily. This commander, hearing of the great reputation of the Normans, sent to Guaimarius, prince of Salerno, entreating him to grant him some of those warriors. His request was most willingly hearkened to by the prince of Salerno, who, to encourage the Normans to engage in the expedition, promised them some additional rewards besides the emperor's pay. William, Drogo, and Umbert, accordingly marched from Salerno with 300 of their countrymen; and, passing over into Sicily, distinguished themselves most remarkably in the conquest of that island. Maniacus acknowledged, that the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of Messina was chiefly owing to their valour; and William with his Normans gained a complete victory over the Saracens before <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, where he killed the governor of the city in single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. Maniacus made himself master of Syracuse, and almost entirely reduced the whole island; but, being accused of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, was next year carried prisoner to Constantinople. His successor Doceanus, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of no abilities, quickly lost the whole island except Messina, and treated his Norman auxiliaries with the utmost contempt. He would not allow them any share of the booty; and even caused one Ardoine, a noble Lombard, and associate and interpreter of the Normans, to be whipped round the camp, because he refused to part with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> of a Saracen whom he had slain in single combat. The consequences of this tyrannical behaviour were very fatal to the Greeks. Greeks. Ardoïn soon after obtained leave to return to Italy under a pretence of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a>, and all the Normans embarked at night along with him; but instead of going to Rome, Ardoïn went immediately to Averla, where he persuaded Count Rainulphus, sovereign of that province, to join with him in the design he had formed of attacking the Greek provinces in Italy, which he showed him would be an easy conquest, as the inhabitants submitted with great reluctance to the Greeks, and the provinces were at that time almost entirely defenceless. Rainulphus approved of the scheme, and raised 300 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, whom he sent under 12 officers to join the other Normans under the sons of Tancred; and made an agreement with Ardoïn, that the conquests should be equally divided among the chief leaders. Their first enterprise was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Melphis, one of the strongest cities in Puglia, which presently surrendered; and they increased its fortifications so much, that it thenceforth became impregnable. Soon after this they made themselves masters of Venosa, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASCOLI">Ascoli</a>, and Lavello, with very little opposition. Doceanus, alarmed with the rapidity of their conquests, immediately left Sicily, and marched with his army into Puglia, where he attacked the invaders near the river Oliviento; but after a fierce engagement, he was obliged to retire with considerable loss. The Greeks were soon after defeated a second time at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANNE">Canne</a>; and in a third engagement, which happened near the river Ofanto, the army of Doceanus was entirely routed, and he himself obliged to fly to Bari. On this bad success Doceanus was ordered to return to his command in Sicily, and another general was sent with an army into Puglia. This new commander, however, had no better success than his predecessor; for his army was entirely defeated in an engagement with the Normans, and he himself taken prisoner. Atenuphilus, brother to one of the princes of Benevento on whom the Normans had conferred the chief command, set at liberty the captive general without consulting them, on receiving from him a considerable sum of money. With this the Normans were so much displeased that they deprived Atenuphilus of his command, and bestowed it on Argyrus son to the late Mello, who had escaped from Constantinople, and now assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of duke and prince of Italy. Before this time also Maniacus, whom we have formerly mentioned, had returned to Italy; and to strike the greater terror into the revolted cities, had executed a number of people of all ages and sexes with great inhumanity. Soon after this Maniacus openly rebelled against the Greek emperor Constantinus, and prevailed upon his own army to proclaim him emperor, beginning hostilities immediately against the Greek cities. Argyrus at the same time took Giovenazzo and besieged Trani, and soon after besieged Maniacus himself in Tarento; but he, being afraid of falling into the hands of the Normans, fled to Otranto, and from thence to Bulgaria, where, being entirely defeated by one of the emperor's generals, he was taken prisoner, and had his head struck off. The Normans having now conquered the greatest part of Puglia, proceeded to make a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of their conquest, in which, after each commander had got his proper share, the city of Melphis was left <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all, and appropriated as a place for assembling to consult about the most important affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Argyrus alone was neglected in this division; but he, having gained the favour of the emperor by expelling the rebel Maniacus from Italy, was by him created duke of Bari, on purpose to check the power of the Normans, with the title of prince and duke of Puglia. The Normans, however, were too powerful to be much awed by Argyrus, and behaved with great influence to the neighbouring princes; but as they could not be expelled by force, and were confirmed in their conquests by Henry II., emperor of Germany in 1047, the Greek emperor attempted to get rid of them, by sending Argyrus with large sums of money to bribe them to enter into his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> against the Persians. But they, perceiving the snare, replied that they were resolved not to leave Italy unless they were expelled by force: upon which Argyrus made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the same money in bribing the Puglians to assassinate these invaders. This brought Great numbers on a massacre, in which greater numbers of Normans perished than had fallen in all the late wars. Argyrus massacred, attempted to take advantage of the confusion produced by this massacre, but was defeated; after which he had recourse to Pope Leo, beseeching him to deliver Italy from these cruel tyrants: but this scheme proved still more unsuccessful than the others had been; for the pope himself was defeated and taken prisoner; and, in consequence of the respect showed him by the Normans, granted them, as a fief of the holy see, all the conquests they had made or should make in Calabria in all their conquests, and Sicily. Soon after this, the Norman power became extremely formidable; the famous Robert Guiscard ascended the throne in 1056. He made great progress in the conquest of Calabria, and reduced most of the cities which held out for the Greeks in these parts. About the same time the counts of Capua were expelled from their territory; and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> Desiderius mentions his having seen the children of Landulphus V. the last count, going about as vagabonds, and begging for their support. The pope alarmed by these conquests, excommunicated the Normans in wholesale, pretending that they had seized some of the territories belonging to the church; but by the pretended submission of Robert, he not only was persuaded to take off the sentence of excommunication, but to invest him with the provinces of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily. After this, he continued the war against the Greeks with great success. In 1071, in conjunction with his brother Roger, he conquered the island of Sicily, and quelled the title of count, referring to himself only the half of Palermo, Messina, and the valley of Demona. The like success attended his arms against Salerno in 1074; but after this, having unadvisedly taken some places from the pope, he again fell under the sentence of excommunication; yet he was reconciled to him in 1080, and received a second time the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of all his dominions. The next year he undertook an expedition against the Greeks; and though the emperor was assisted by a Venetian fleet, Robert made himself master of the island of Corfu, reduced Durazzo, and great part of Romania; insomuch that by the success of his arms, and his near approach to Constantinople, he struck an universal terror among the Greeks. But while Robert was thus extending his conquests, he was alarmed. alarmed by the news of a formidable rebellion in Italy, and that the emperor Henry had taken the city of Rome, and closely shut up the pope in the castle of St. Angelo. Robert, therefore, leaving the command of the army to his son Boemund, returned to Italy, where he immediately dispersed the rebels, and released the pope, while his son gained a considerable victory over the Greeks. After this Robert made great preparations for another expedition into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, in order to second his son Boemund. Alexius Comnenus, who was about this time declared emperor by the Greek army, being assisted by the Venetian fleet, endeavoured to oppose his passage; but was entirely defeated, with the loss of a great many galleys. But a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FINAL">final</a> stop was now put to his enterprises by his death, which happened in the island of Corfu in 1285. Though the power of the Normans was thus thoroughly established in Italy and Sicily, and though the prince of Benevento was in 1130 invested by the pope with the title of king of Sicily, yet by reason of the civil dissensions which took place among themselves, and the general confusion which reigned in Italy in those ages, they were obliged, notwithstanding all their valour, to submit to the emperor in 1195. By him the Sicilians were treated with so great cruelty, that the empress Constanza was induced to confine against him in 1197, took him prisoner, and released him only on condition of his sending off his army immediately for the Holy Land. This was complied with; but the emperor did not long survive the reconciliation, being poisoned, as was supposed, by order of the empress. In 1254 the pope claimed the kingdom as a fief devolved on the church in consequence of a sentence of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> pronounced against King Frederick at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Lyons; and, in 1263, the kingdom was, in consequence of this right, conferred on Charles count of Anjou. After much contention and bloodshed, the French thus became masters of Sicily and Naples. Their government was unsupportably tyrannical; and at the same time the haughtiness of their king so provoked the pope, that he resolved to humble him.—Charles had resolved on an expedition against Constantinople; and for this purpose had fitted out a fleet of 100 galleys, 30 large ships, 200 transports, besides many other smaller vessels, on board of which he intended to embark 10,000 horse, and a numerous army of foot. This formidable armament greatly alarmed the emperor Michael Paleologus; for which reason he entered into a negotiation with John di Procida, a noble Salernitan, lord of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Procida in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Naples, who had formed a scheme for a general revolt in the island of Sicily. John, though a nobleman, was also a physician, and had been counsellor to two former princes, and even to King Charles himself; but being stripped of his estate by the king under pretence of treason, and his wife being debauched by the French, he retired to Constanza <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Arragon, where he was created a baron of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, by her husband King Peter, and lord of Luxen, Benizzano, and Palma. As he was greatly exasperated against the French, he employed many spies both in Puglia and Sicily; and being informed that the Sicilians were totally disaffected to the French, he came to the island in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, and concerted a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> with the most powerful of the malecontents for a revolution in favour of Constanza, though she derived her right only as being the daughter of a former usurper named Manfred. Procida then set out for Constanza, where in some private conferences with the emperor, he persuaded him, that the most probable means of defeating Charles's scheme was by afflicting the Spaniards and Sicilian malecontents. Paleologus accordingly granted him a large sum of money, and on his departure sent one of his secretaries along with him, who, landing in Sicily, had a conference with the chief conspirators. John, having received letters from them, disguised himself in the habit of a Franciscan, and went to Suriano in the neighbourhood of Rome. As he well knew the enmity which subsisted between the pope and King Charles, he disclosed his design to his holiness; who readily entered into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, wrote to Peter to hasten his armament, promising him the investiture of the island as soon as he had taken possession of it; and, by refusing the assistance he had promised to Charles, obliged him for the present to delay his expedition. In the beginning of the year 1280, Procida returned to Arragon, and by showing the letters from the pope and Sicilian barons, prevailed on Peter to embark in his design, by assuring him of the assistance of Paleologus. This king of Arragon accordingly prepared a formidable fleet under pretence of invading Africa, and is even said to have received 20,000 ducats from Charles, in order to assist him in his preparations. But while John went on thus successfully with his scheme, all his measures were in danger of being broken by the death of Pope Nicholas. The new pope, Martin IV. was entirely in the interest of Charles, on whom, in 1281, he conferred the senatorial <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of Rome. Procida, however, still resolved to prosecute his scheme; and, leaving Italy, had another conference with the conspirators in Sicily; after which, he again went to Constanza, and obtained from Paleologus 30,000 ounces of gold, with which he immediately returned to Arragon. The death of Nicholas had damped the ardour of Peter; but, being urged with great earnestness by John, he again renewed his preparations; which alarmed the pope and the king of France. In consequence of this they sent a message to him, desiring to know against what Saracens he designed to employ his armament. In this particular Peter refused to satisfy them; upon which they earnestly counselled Charles to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against an invasion: but he neglected their advice, being wholly intent on his eastern expedition, and encouraged by a revolt which had happened in Greece; and to facilitate his expedition, he prevailed on the pope to excommunicate the Greeks, on pretence that they had broken some of the articles of union concluded at the council of Lyons a few years before. Peter in the meantime continued his preparations with great diligence, intending to put to sea the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Procida had returned to Palermo, to wait for a favourable opportunity of putting his design in execution, which was soon afforded him by the French. On Easter Monday, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 30, 1282, the chief conspirators had assembled at Palermo; and, after dinner, both the Palermits and French went in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> to the church of Monreale, about three miles without the city. While they were sporting sporting in the fields, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> happened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by with her train, who being observed by one Drochetus, a Frenchman, he ran to her, and began to use her in a rude manner, under pretence of searching for concealed arms. A young Sicilian, exasperated at this affront, stabbed him with his own sword; and a tumult ensuing, 200 French were immediately murdered. The enraged populace then ran to the city, crying out, "Let the French die, let the French die;" and without distinction of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, slaughtered all of that nation they could find, even such as had fled to the churches. The conspirators then left Palermo, and excited the inhabitants to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> the French all over the island, excepting in Messina, which city at first refused to be concerned in the revolt. But, being invited by the Palermians to throw off the French yoke, a few weeks after, the citizens in a tumultuous manner destroyed some of the French; and pulling down the arms of King Charles, and erecting those of the city, chose one Baldwin for their governor, who saved the remaining French from the fury of the populace, and allowed them to transport themselves, with their wives and children to Italy. Eight thousand persons are said to have been murdered on this occasion. Immediately after this massacre, the Sicilians offered their allegiance to the king of Arragon; who accepted of the invitation, and landed with his forces at Trapani. From thence he went to Palermo, where he was crowned king of Sicily with great solemnity, and Charles left the island with precipitation. The day after he landed his army in Italy, the Arragonian fleet arrived, took 29 of his galleys, and the next day burnt 80 transports in presence of his army. Soon after this Charles sent an embassy to Peter, accusing him of perfidy, in invading his dominions in time of peace; and, according to some, challenged him at the same time to decide the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> by single combat. Others say that the challenge was given by Peter. Certain it is, however, that a challenge was given, and to appearance accepted; but Peter determined to employ much more effectual means in support of his pretensions than trifling to a duel; and therefore pushed on his operations most vigorously, while his adversary trifled away his time; and thus he at last became master of the contested kingdom; which, however, he did not long enjoy, dying about the end of the year 1285. By his will, Peter left the kingdom of Arragon to his eldest son Alphonso, and Sicily to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> James his other son, who was also to succeed to the kingdom of Arragon in case Alphonso should die without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue. Accordingly, Don James was solemnly crowned at Palermo the 2d of February 1286. In 1295, however, he deserted them, and tamely resigned up his right to Charles, son to him above mentioned, in a manner perhaps unparalleled. On his resignation the Sicilians conferred the crown upon his brother Don Frederic; after which the war continued with great violence till the year 1303, when a peace was concluded, and the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily formally disjoined; Frederic being allowed to keep the latter, under the name of Trinacria; and Charles being confirmed in the possession of the former, which he quietly enjoyed till his death in 1309. Naples continued to be governed by its own kings till the beginning of the 16th century, when the kings of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> contended for the sovereignty of this country. Frederic, at that time king of Naples, resigned the sovereignty to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII., on being created duke of Anjou, and receiving an annual pension of 30,000 ducats. But, in 1504, the French were entirely defeated by the Spaniards, and obliged to evacuate the kingdom; and the following year Louis renounced all pretensions to the crown, which from this time hath remained almost constantly in the hands of the Spaniards. The government of the Spaniards proved no less oppressive to the Neapolitans than that of others had been. The kings of Spain set no bounds to their exactions, and of consequence the people were loaded with all manner of taxes; even the most indispensible necessaries of life not being exempted. In 1647, a new tax was laid on fruit; which the people looked upon as the most grievous oppression, the chief part of their subsistence, during the summer months, being fruit, which in the kingdom of Naples is very plentiful and delicious. The edict for collecting the new duty was no sooner published, than the people began to murmur in a tumultuous manner; and when the viceroy came abroad, they surrounded his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, bawling out to have their grievances redressed. They were encouraged in their sedition, by the news that the citizens of Palermo had actually revolted on account of the imposition of new duties. The viceroy, therefore, apprehensive of greater disorders, began to think of taking off the tax; but those who farmed the tax having bribed some of his favourites, he was by their means persuaded not to abolish it. The indignation of the people, who had suspected his intention, was now greatly increased, especially as they were privately excited by several malecontents. The farmers of the revenue, and all those concerned in raising the taxes, had incurred the hatred and detestation of the people, particularly of Tommaso Aniello, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Maffianielo of Amalfi, a fisherman, whose wife, having been discovered in smuggling a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, was imprisoned, and condemned to pay a fine of 100 ducats. Maffianielo, a few years before, had come to Naples from Amalfi, where his father had been a fisherman. At this time he was about 24 years of age, and the father of four children. He was of a middle stature, and an agreeable aspect; was distinguished for his boldness, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and integrity; and had a great influence with his companions, by whom he was beloved and esteemed. As he was obliged even to sell his furniture to pay the heavy fine, he had conceived an implacable hatred against the farmers of the taxes, and was also moved with compassion for the miserable state of the city and kingdom. He therefore formed a design, with some of his companions, to raise a tumult in the market place on the festival day of the Carmelites, usually celebrated about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, when between 500 and 600 youths entertain the people by a mock fight; one half of them, in the character of Turks, defending a wooden castle, which is attacked and stormed by the other half in the character of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Maffianielo being appointed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of one of these parties, and one Pione, who was privy to his design, commanding the other, for several weeks before before the festival they were very diligent in reviewing and training their followers, who were armed with sticks and reeds; but a small and unforeseen accident tempted them to begin their enterprise without waiting for the festival. On the 7th of July a dispute happening in the market-place betwixt the tax-gatherers and some gardeners of Pozzuolo who had brought some figs into the city, whether the buyer or seller should pay the duty; after the tumult had continued several hours, Maffianello, who was present with his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, excited the mob to pillage the office built in the market for receiving the duty, and to drive away the officers with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. The elect of the people, who, by deciding against the gardeners, had increased the tumult, ran to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and informed the viceroy, who most imprudently neglected all means of putting a stop to the commotion. Maffianello, in the mean time, being joined by great numbers of people, ordered his young troop to set fire to all the offices for the taxes through the city; which command being executed with despatch, he then conducted them directly to the palace, where the viceroy, instead of ordering his Spanish and German guards to disperse them, encouraged their insolence by timidly granting their demands. As they rushed into the palace in a furious manner, he escaped by a private door, and endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself in the Café del Ovo; but being overtaken by the rioters in the streets, he was trampled upon by them, and pulled by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and whiskers. However, by throwing some handfuls of gold among them, he again escaped, and took sanctuary in a convent of Minims, where, being joined by the archbishop of Naples, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Filomarini, and several nobles, by their advice he signed a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILLET">billet</a>, by which he abolished all taxes upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. As a means to quell the tumult, he likewise desired the cardinal to offer Maffianello a pension of 2400 crowns, who generously rejected the bribe; and declared, that if the viceroy would keep his word, he would find them obedient subjects. It was now expected that the tumult would cease; but Maffianello, upon his return to the market-place, being joined by several malecontents, among whom were Genuino and one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERONNE">Peronne</a>, who had formerly been a captain of the Sbirri, he was advised by them to order the houses of those concerned in raising the tax to be burned; which were accordingly in a few days reduced to ashes, with all their rich furniture. Maffianello being now <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> master of the whole city, and being joined by great numbers of people of desperate fortunes, he required the viceroy, who had retired to the Café Nuovo, to abolish all the taxes, and to deliver up the writ of exemption granted by Charles V. This new demand greatly embarrassed the viceroy; but to appease the people, he drew up a false <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> in letters of gold, and sent it to them by their favourite the duke of Matalone, who had before been in confinement. The fraud, however, being discovered, the duke was pulled from his horse and maltreated by the mob, and at length committed as a prisoner to Peronne. This accident, to the great joy of the viceroy, enraged the people against the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, several of whom they killed, burnt the houses of others, and threatened to extirpate them all. Maffianello, in the mean time, tarried and half naked, commanded his followers, who were now well armed, and reckoned about 100,000 men, with a most absolute sway. He ate and slept little, gave his orders with great precision and judgment, appeared full of moderation, without ambition and interested views. But the duke of Matalone having procured his liberty by bribing Peronne, the viceroy imitated his example, and secretly corrupted Genuino to betray his chief. A conspiracy was accordingly formed against Maffianello by Matalone and Peronne; the duke, who was equally exasperated against the viceroy, proposing, that after his death his brother D. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> should head the rebels. Maffianello in the mean time, by means of the cardinal archbishop, was negotiating a general peace and accommodation; but while both parties were assembling in the convent of the Carmelites, the banditti hired by Matalone made an unsuccessful attempt upon Maffianello's life. His followers immediately killed 150 of them. Peronne and D. Joseph being discovered to be concerned in the conspiracy, were likewise put to death, and the duke with great difficulty escaped. Maffianello by this conspiracy was rendered more suspicious and severe. He began to abuse his power by putting several persons to death upon slight pretences; and, to force the viceroy to an accommodation, he cut off all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the castles, which were unprovided with provision and ammunition.—The viceroy likewise being afraid lest the French should take advantage of the commotion, earnestly desired to agree to a treaty; which was accordingly concluded on the fifth day of the insurrection, by the mediation of the cardinal archbishop. By the treaty it was stipulated, that all duties imposed since the time of Charles V. should be abolished; that the writ of exemption granted by that viceroy emperor should be delivered to the people; that for the future no new taxes should be imposed; that the vote of the elect of the people should be equal to the votes of the nobility; that an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of oblivion should be granted for all that was past; and that the people should continue in arms under Maffianello till the ratification of the treaty by the king. By this treaty, no less than 10,000 persons who fattened upon the blood of the public were ruined.—The people when it was solemnly published, manifested an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> joy, believing they had now recovered all their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges. Maffianello, at the desire of the viceroy, went to the palace to visit him, accompanied by the archbishop, who was obliged to threaten him with excommunication, before he would consent to lay aside his rags and assume a magnificent dress. He was received by the duke with the greatest demonstrations of respect and friendship, while the duchess entertained his wife, and presented her with a robe of cloth of silver, and some jewels.—The viceroy, to preserve some shadow of authority, appointed him captain-general; and at his departure Maffianello made him a present of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> chain of great value, which with great difficulty he prevailed upon to accept; but yielded at length to the entreaties of the cardinal. Next day, in consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> granted him by the viceroy, he began to exercise all the functions of sovereign authority; and having caused a scaffold to be erected in one of the streets, and several veral gibbets, he judged all crimes, whether civil or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, in the last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>; and ordered the guilty to be immediately put to death, which was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> he inflicted on all offences. Though he neglected all forms of law, and even frequently judged by physiognomy, yet he is said not to have overlooked any criminal, or punished any innocent person. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and prosperity were of very short continuance; for his mind becoming distracted and delirious for two or three days, he committed a great many mad and extravagant actions; and on the 18th of July he was affianced with the consent of the viceroy. The tumult did not end with the death of Maffaniello: on the contrary, the people now expelled the Spaniards from most of the cities throughout the kingdom; and this general insurrection being the subject of discourse at Rome, the duke of Guise, who happened then to be at the pope's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, took the opportunity, at the instigation of his holiness, to offer his service to the Neapolitans against the Spaniards. The duke was prompted by his ambition to engage in this enterprise, especially as he himself had borne distant pretensions to the crown. The Spaniards in the meantime made a vigorous attack on the city; but were repulsed by the people, who now formally renounced their allegiance to them. In a short time, however, their city being surprised by the new viceroy, the count d'Oniate, and the duke of Guise himself taken prisoner, the people returned to their allegiance; and thus all the attempts of the French on Naples were frustrated. From that time the Spaniards continued in peaceable possession of the kingdom till the year 1707, when it was taken from them by Prince Eugene. It was formally ceded to the emperor by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RASTADT">Rastadt</a> in 1713; but was recovered by the Spaniards in 1734, and the king of Spain's eldest son is now king of Naples and Sicily. For a particular account of these revolutions, see the articles SPAIN and SICILY. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Naples is extremely hot, especially in July, August, and September. In winter there is seldom any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> or snow, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>.—On account of its fertility, it is justly termed an earthly paradise; for it abounds with all sorts of grain, the finest fruit and garden productions of every kind, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and wine, in the greatest plenty and perfection. It affords also saffron, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, vitriol, sulphur, rock crystal, marble, and several sorts of minerals, together with fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. The horses of this country are famous, and the flocks and herds very numerous. Besides these products, of which a considerable part is exported, there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of linens, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, and glassware. Waistcoats, caps, stockings, and gloves, are also made of the hair or filaments of a shell fish, which are warmer than those of wool, and of a beautiful glossy green. In this kingdom likewise is found that called the Phrygian stone, or pietra fungifera, which, being laid in a damp shady place, will yield <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a>, sometimes of a very large size, especially if the stone is sprinkled with hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. See AGARICUS. As to the mountains of this country, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are the Apennines, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> it from south to north; and Mount Vesuvius, which, as is well known, is a noted volcano, five Italian miles from Naples. The side of this mountain next the sea yields wine, particularly the two famed wines called Vino Greco and La-chryme Christi. One of the greatest inconveniences to which this kingdom is exposed is earthquakes, which the eruptions of Mount Vesuvius contribute, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, to prevent. Another inconvenience, which, however, is common to it with other hot countries, is the great number of reptiles and insects, of which some are very poisonous. With respect to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, it is on a very bad footing here. The number of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and monasteries is astonishing. It is said, the clergy and convents possess two thirds of the whole kingdom: nay, some maintain, that were the kingdom divided into five parts, four would be found in the hands of the church. Notwithstanding this power and influence of the clergy, they have not been able hitherto to get the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> established here. In the year 1731, measures were taken for lessening the number of convents; and lately the order of Jesuits hath been suppressed. The papal bulls cannot be made public without the king's permission; nor are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> compelled to kneel in the churches, or at meeting the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a> they can very easily procure <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> meat. In the year 1740, the Jews were allowed to settle in the kingdom during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of 50 years, and several privileges were granted them during that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which, the grant was supposed to be renewed, unless they were expressly ordered to quit the country. The revenue of the kingdom is generally computed at 3,000,000 crowns: but, as Mr Addison observes, there is no country in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> which pays greater taxes, and where, at the same time, the public is left the better for them, most of them going to the enriching of the private persons to whom they are mortgaged. The military force of this kingdom is said to consist of about 30,000 men, of which the Swiss regiments are the best. As to the marine, it consists only of a few galleys. The only order here is that of St Januarius, which was instituted by Don Carlos in the year 1738. The king of Naples, or of the two Sicilies, is an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> monarch. The high colleges are, the council of state, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, the Sicily council, the council of war, &c. This kingdom is a papal fief; and the king, in acknowledgement of the pope's feudal right, sends him every year a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> palfrey, and a purse of 600 ducats. The title of the king's eldest son is prince of Calabria. The number both of the high and low nobility in the kingdom of Naples is very great. "I am assured (says Dr Moore) * View of that the king of Naples counts among his subjects <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, &c. 100 persons with the title of prince, and a still greater in Italy, with that of duke. Six or seven of these have estates which produce from 10 to 12 or 13,000l. a-year; a considerable number have fortunes of about half that value; and the annual revenue of many is not above 1000l. or 2000l. The inferior orders of the nobility are much poorer. Many counts and marquises have not above 300l. or 400l. a-year of paternal estate; many have still less; and not a few enjoy the title without any estate whatever. These nobles, however, are excessively fond of splendour and show, which appears in the brilliancy of their equipages, the number of their attendants, the richness of their dress, and the grandeur grandeur of their titles. The finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> are painted, gilt, varnished, and lined, in a richer and more beautiful manner than has yet become fashionable either in England or in France. They are often drawn by six and sometimes by eight horses. Before the carriage, it is the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> to have two running footmen, and behind three or four servants in the richest liveries. The ladies and gentlemen within the coaches glitter in all the brilliancy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, and jewels.—This finery is not confined to the persons within and without the coaches; it is extended to the horses, whose heads, manes, and tails, are ornamented with the rarest plumage, and set off with ribbons and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>.” We shall mention a circumstance from which an idea may be formed of the grandeur of a Neapolitan palace, and the number of domestics which some of the nobility retain. “I dined (continues our author) at the prince Iacci’s, where we passed through 12 or 13 large rooms before we arrived at the dining room. There were 36 persons at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> served by the prince’s domestics, and each guest had a footman behind his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, while other domestics belonging to the prince remained in the adjacent rooms and in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. No estate in England could support such a number of servants, paid and fed as English servants are; but in Naples the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> are very moderate indeed, and the greater number of men servants, belonging to the first families, give their attendance through the day only, and find beds and provisions for themselves. It must be remembered also, that few of the nobles give any entertainments; and those who do not are said to live very sparingly; so that the whole of their revenue, whatever it may be, is expended on articles of show.” In the kingdom of Naples, the hereditary jurisdiction of the nobles over their vassals subsists in the full rigour of the feudal government. The peasants therefore are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; and it depends entirely on the personal character of the master, whether their poverty be not the least of their grievances. As this power is too often abused, the importance of the nobility depends in a great measure on the favour of the king, who, under pretence of any offence, can confine them to their estates, or imprison them at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. Unless this prince were to very impolitic as to disgust all the nobility at once, and so unite the whole body against him, he has little to fear from their resentment. Even in case of such an union, as the nobles have lost the affection of their vassals, what could they do in opposition to a standing army of 30,000 men, entirely devoted to the crown? The government of Naples, therefore, is in fact a despotic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, though something like the form of a feudal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> in its ancient purity is still kept up by the biennial summons of the general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>. This convention, which consists of the nobility and commons, is called together every two years, to deliberate on the customary free gift to the crown. The inhabitants of this country have at all times borne but an indifferent character among other nations. “From the few hints dropped by the classic authors, we collect that the ancient Neapolitans were a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of epicures, of a soft indolent turn, adverse from martial exercises, passionately fond of theatrical amusements and music, expert in all the refined arts that administer to the caprices of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, extravagant in their expressions and gestures, and dupes to various sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. If we make allowance for a quantity of northern blood which has joined the original Grecian stream, and imparted a roughness not yet worn off by the mildness of the climate, we shall find the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Neapolitans very like the ancient.—Provisions being here plentiful and cheap, the lower class of people <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> but little. Their delight is to bask in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and do nothing. Persons of a middle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> frequent places of public resort; and very few of any rank attend to their proper business with the zeal and activity we are wont to meet with in the professional men of colder countries. Gluttony is a predominant vice, while instances of ebriety are comparatively rare. In the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> sex, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for finery is almost superior to every other; and, though chastity is not the characteristic virtue of the country, Mr Swinburne doubts* whether a Neapolitan woman would not <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> times out of ten prefer a present to a lover. That furious jealousy for which the nation was once so remarkable, is now greatly abated. The breach of the conjugal vow sometimes occasions quarrels and affections among people of an inferior station; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, affections are often perpetrated from much less cogent motives. Of these vices, many are doublets owing to that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> and opprobrium under which they groan, and to a radical defect in the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; though the kingdom is divided into 12 provinces or jurisdictions. Such was the former state of Naples. But being seized by the emperor of France, he affirmed, “the Neapolitan dynasty has ceased to reign: its existence is incompatible with the repose of Europe, and the honour of our crown.” By virtue of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> which passed in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of March 1866, the emperor <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a> conferred the kingdom of Naples on his brother Joseph, now king of Spain, and his legitimate heirs male, referring to that prince the rights afforded to him by the constitutions of the empire, in providing always that the crown of France and that of Naples shall never be united upon the same head. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MURAT">Murat</a> succeeded Joseph as king of Naples. Naples, anciently Porthenope, afterwards Neapolis, the capital of the kingdom of that name in Italy, lies in the province called Terra di Lavoro, which is the richest and best inhabited of the whole kingdom, and comprehends a part of the ancient Campania Felix or the Happy. This city is fabled to owe its foundation to a Syren, and to have received its ancient name from its supernatural founders. Whatever be its origin, it is the first for neatness, and the second for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, of all the cities in Italy. It was formerly a place of strength; but its walls at present being of no real defence, its safety depends of course upon the force of its armies. It is most advantageously situated, having a delicious country on one side, and a noble bay of the Mediterranean on the other, with an excellent harbour. The circumference, including the suburbs, is said not to be less than 18 Italian miles, and the number of the inhabitants therein little less than 400,000. The houses are of stone, flat roofed, and generally lofty and uniform; but many of them have balconies, with lattice windows. The streets are well paved; but they are not lighted at night, and in the daytime are figured, in many places, by stalls, on which provisions are exposed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. Here are a great number of fine churches, NAPLES Churches, convents, fountains, and palaces of the nobility, many of whom constantly reside here. It is usual to walk on the tops of the houses in the evenings, to breathe the sweet cool <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, after a hot sultry day. The climate here is so mild and warm, even in the winter, that plenty of green peas, artichokes, asparagus, and other vegetables, may be had so early as the beginning of the new year, and even all the winter. This city swarms with monks and nuns of all sorts, to such a degree, that there are no less than 19 convents of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a> alone, 18 of the Franciscans, 8 of the Augustines, and an equal proportion of the rest. The magnificence of many of the churches exceeds imagination. In a cloister of the Carthusian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFIX">crucifix</a>, said to be done by Michael Angelo, of inimitable workmanship. To repel hostile attempts by sea, which from its situation, maritime powers might be tempted to make, Naples has, to the west, the Castel del Ovo, a confused pile of ancient buildings, and some modern batteries. The rock upon which this fortress stands was originally called <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, then Lucullanum; and was considered as a place of strength so early as the year 475. Along the line of the shore towards the east are some batteries on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of land, the bastions of the arsenal, and above it the lofty wall of the Castel Nuovo. This last fortress has been the usual refuge of the sovereigns and viceroys in all civil wars and tumults; for which reason they have long fixed their residence near its walls. A blockhouse and batteries defend the mouth of the harbour, and at the eastern extremity of the town is the Torrione de Carmine, better known by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> it made in Massimiliano's rebellion than by its extent or military strength. The castle of St Elmo commands Naples in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and is in reality calculated rather to annoy and awe the citizens than to defend them from foreign invaders. The city is indeed far from being secure against a bombardment; for the sea is so deep, that a large vessel may come up to the very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> in defiance of the blockhouse and batteries, &c. Pictures, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and antiquities, are not so common in Naples as might be expected in so great and ancient a city, many of the most valuable pieces having been sent to Spain by the viceroys. The bay is one of the finest in the world, being almost of a round figure, about 30 miles in diameter, and three parts of it sheltered with a noble circuit of woods and mountains. The city stands in the bosom of this bay, in as pleasant a situation, perhaps, as is in the world. Mr Keyler says, they reckon about 18,000 donne libere, or courtezans, in the city; and Dr Moore computes the number of lascarons or blackguards at above 30,000. The greater part of these wretches have no dwelling houses, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> every night under porticos, piazzas, or any kind of shelter they can find. Those of them who have wives and children, live in the suburbs of Naples near Peufilippo, in huts, or in caverns or chambers dug out of that mountain. They are generally represented as a lazy, licentious, and turbulent set of people, as indeed by far the greater part of the rabble are, who prefer begging or robbing, or running errands, to any fixed and permanent employment. Yet there are in Naples some flourishing manufactures, particularly of silk stockings, soap, snuff-boxes of tortoise shells and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> of Mount Vesuvius, tables, and ornamental furniture of marble. The city is supplied with a vast quantity of water, by means of a very costly aqueduct, from the foot of Mount Vesuvius. Mr Additon says, it is incredible how great a multitude of retainers to the law there are in Naples, who find continual employment from the fiery temper of the inhabitants. There are five piazzas or squares in the city, appropriated to the nobility, viz. those called Capuana, Nilo, Montagna, Porto, and Porta Nova. Of all the palaces, that of the king is not only the most magnificent, but also in the best style of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, though Gothic, is a very grand splendid edifice. It is here that the head and blood of St Januarius, the tutelary saint of Naples, are kept, the latter in two glass or crystal vials. The pretended liquefaction of the dried blood, as soon as brought near the head of the saint, is a thing well known; Mr Additon says, it is one of the most bungling tricks he ever <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>. The harbour is spacious, and kept in good repair. It is fortified with a mole, which runs about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> into the sea, and at the extremity has a high lanthorn to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> ships safely into the harbour. Luxury here is restrained by severe sumptuary laws, and the women are more closely confined than in any other city of Italy. Here is an university and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> of wits, the one called Gli Ardenti, and the other Gli Ottogi. The nunnery for ladies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is said to be the largest in the whole world, containing no less than 3,500 nuns, besides servants. The Mount of Piety, or the office for advancing money to the poor, on pledges, at a low interest, or without any, has an income of upwards of 50,000 ducats. The arsenal is said to contain arms for 50,000 men. The walls of the city consist of hard <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> stones, called piperno. Instead of ice, vast quantities of snow are used for cooling their liquors, not so much as water being drank without it; so that, it is said, a scarcity of it would as soon occasion a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> as a dearth of corn or provisions. Certain persons, who <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> the monopoly of it from the government, supply the city all the year round from a mountain about 18 miles off, at so much the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. In the beginning of 1799, it was taken by a body of French troops under General Championet. The streets of this city were lighted for the first time on the 16th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, 1806. Naples stands 110 miles south-east from Rome, 164 north-east from Palermo in Sicily, 217 south-east from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and 305 from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. E. Long. 14° 20'. N. Lat. 40° 55'.

NARBO

Pages 673-673

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Volcae Tectosages, called also Narbo Martius, from the Legio Martia, the colony led thither 59 years before the consulate of Caesar, (Velleius); increased with a colony of the Dacamani <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenth legion by Caesar. An ancient trading town on the Atax, which discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> through the Locus Rubrefus, or Rubrenis. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">Capital</a> of Gallia Narbonensis; furnished Colonia Julia Paterna, from Julius Caesar, the father of Augustus by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a>. Now called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>.

NARBONNE

Pages 673-673

is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of Aude, with an archbishop's see, and is particularly famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. It is seated on a canal cut from the river Aude, which being but three miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, vessels come up it laden with merchandise, which renders

NARCISSUS

Pages 674-674

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 6th order, Spouhaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NARCOTICS

Pages 674-674

in Medicine, soporiferous drugs, which bring on a stupefaction. Among narcotics the most eminent are those usually prepared for medicinal uses from the poppy, especially opium; as also all those prepared from mandragoras, hyoscyamus, stramonium and datura. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NARDO

Pages 674-674

a pretty populous town in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in the Terra d'<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> and a bishop's see. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 27. N. Lat. 43. 28. In this little <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> are 8000 inhabitants. The steeple of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is built in a very uncommon but showy style of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. Luca Giordano and Solimena have adorned the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> with some agreeable paintings. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Balzo estate. The Aquavivas were the next possessors: they are thought to have come from the Marca di <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>. In 1401, in consideration of their relationship to Pope Boniface IX, Laudiflaus erected their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATRI">Atri</a> into a dukedom, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> till then seldom granted to any but princes of the blood <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>. Claudius Aquaviva, a famous general of the Jesuits, who died in 1615, was of this family.

NARDUS

Pages 674-674

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. This plant was highly valued by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, both as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> and medicine. The unguentum nardinum, was used at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and feasts as a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>. Its value is evident from that passage of Scripture, where our Saviour's head was anointed with a box of it, with which Judas found fault. From a passage in Horace, it appears that this ointment was so valuable among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, that as much as could be contained in a small box of precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was considered as a fort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessel of wine, and a proper quota for a guest to contribute at an entertainment, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>: Nardo <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-VINA">vina</a> merere, Nardi parvus onyx efficiet cadum.

NAREA

Pages 674-674

the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the empire of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> still governed by its own princes, who have the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Beneros. Its territory was formerly more extensive than at present, the Galla having almost quite surrounded it, especially on the south-east and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the west is the most unknown <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>; the kingdom itself stands like a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the middle of a plain, being a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and mountainous country. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, rising in the fourth and fifth degrees of north latitude, spread themselves over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> part of the country, and fill it with marshes all the way from south by east to north <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> north-west. These marshes are bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, of which those nearest the marshes are overgrown with coffee trees, the largest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the only ones, which grow in this country. The kingdom of Narea Proper is interspersed with small, unwholesome, but very fertile valleys. The mountainous country of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a> adjoins immediately to Narea, and is said to be governed by a separate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; but the Galla having settled themselves in all the flat ground to the very edge of the marshes, have in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Abyssinia for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> past. The Nareans who inhabit the mountainous country have the lightest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of any people in Abyssinia; but those who inhabit the borders of the marshes are perfectly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and have the features and woolly heads of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>; but the mountaineers of Narea, and much more those of Caffa, are fair complexioned, more so than even the Neapolitans or Sicilians. It is said that snow has been seen to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> on some of the mountains of Caffa; but Mr Bruce imagines this to be a mistake, and thinks that it must have been <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>. Narea abounds with cattle, grain, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, both in the high and low country. The medium of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, which they sell by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of trade are coarse cotton cloths, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, beads, and incense, which are carried from this country to the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>, and the parts of the African continent towards the Atlantic. The people are exceedingly brave; and though they have been driven out of the low country by multitudes of Galla, they now bid them defiance, and drive them from their frontiers whenever they come too near. The Narean prisoners taken in these skirmishes are sold to the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> at Gondar; and at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, the women are more esteemed than those of any other part of the world. Both sexes have a cheerful kind disposition, and attach themselves inviolably to their masters, if properly treated. The people of Narea and Caffa speak a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> peculiar to themselves.

NARRATION

Pages 674-682

NARRATION, in oratory, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a recital <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rehearsal of a fact as it happened, or as it is supposed to have happened. See ORATORY, No. 26. Concerning NARRATION and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">DESCRIPTION</a> we have the following rules and observations in the Elements of Criticism. 1. The first rule is, That in history the reflections ought to be chaste and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>; for while the mind is intent upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, it is little disposed to the operation of the imagination. Strada's Belgic history is full of poetical images, which being discordant with the subject, are unpleasing; and they have a still worse effect by giving an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of fiction to a genuine history. Such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> ought to be scattered with a sparing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, even in epic poetry; and at no rate are they proper till the reader be warmed, and by an enlivened imagination be prepared to relish them: in that state of mind, they are agreeable; but while we are fedate and attentive to an historical chain of facts, we reject with disdain every fiction. 2. Vida, following Horace, recommends a modest commencement of an epic poem; giving for a reason that the writer ought to husband his fire. Besides bold thoughts and figures are never relished till the mind be heated and thoroughly engaged, which is not the reader's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> at the commencement. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> introduces not a single simile in the first book of the Iliad, nor in the first book of the Odyssey. On the other hand, Shakespeare begins one of his plays with a sentiment too bold for the most heated imagination: <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>. Hung be the heav'ns with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, yield <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to night! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">Comets</a>, importing change of times and states, Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky, And with them scourge the bad revolving stars, That have consented unto Henry's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>! Henry the Fifth, too famous to live <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>! England ne'er lost a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of so much worth. First <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> Henry VI. The passage with which Strada begins his history, is too poetical for a subject of that kind; and at any rate too <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> for the beginning of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> performance. 3. A third rule or observation is, That where the subject is intended for entertainment solely, not for instruction, a thing ought to be described as it appears, not as it is in reality. In running, for example, the impulse upon the ground is proportioned in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the celerity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; though in appearance it is otherwise, for a person in swift motion seems to skim the ground, and scarcely to touch it. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, describes quick running according to appearance; and raises an image far more lively than by adhering scrupulously to truth: Hos super adventit Volfsa de gente Camilla, Agmen agens equitum, et florentes <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> catervas, Bellatrix: non illa colo calathifive Minervae Foeminea assuetas manus; sed praetia virgo Dura pati curfique pedum praevertere ventos. Illa vel intactae fegentis per summa volaret <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>, nec teneras curfu laefisset aristas: Vel mare per medium, fluctu suspensa tumenti, Ferret iter, celere nec tingeret sequore plantas. Aeneid, vii. 803. In narration as well as in description, objects narration ought to be painted so accurately as to form in the mind of the reader distinct and lively images. Every useless circumstance ought indeed to be suppressed, because every such circumstance loads the narration; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a circumstance be necessary, however slight, it cannot be described too minutely. The force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> consists in raising complete images, which have the effect to transport the reader as by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> into the very <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the important <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and to convert him as it were into a spectator, beholding every thing that passes. The narrative in an epic poem ought to rival a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in the liveliness and accuracy of its representations: no circumstance must be omitted that tends to make a complete image; because an imperfect image as well as any other imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and uninteresting. We shall illustrate this rule by several examples, giving the first place to a beautiful passage from Virgil: Qualis populea moerens Philomela sub umbra Amicus queritur foetus, quos durus arator Observans nido implumis detraxit. Georg. lib. iv. 511. The poplar, ploughman, and unfledged young, though not essential in the description, tend to make a complete image, and upon that account are an embellishment. Again: Hic viridem Æneas frondenti ex ilice metam Constituit, signum nautis. Æneid, v. 129. Horace addressing to Fortune: Te pauper ambit sollicita prece Ruris <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONUS">colonus</a>: te dominam æquoris, Quicumque Bithynia lacessit Carpathium pelagus carinâ. Carm. lib. i. ode 35. — Illum ex moenibus hosticiis Matrona bellantis tyranni Prolificiens, et adulta virgo, Subspiret: Eheu, ne rudis agminum. Sponfus lacelat regius afternum Tæctu leonem, quem cruenta Per medias rapit ira cedes. Carm. lib. iii. ode 2. Shakespeare says, "You may as well go about to turn the fun to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a> by fanning in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s feather." The peacock's feather, not to mention the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the object, completes the image: an accurate image cannot be formed of that fanciful operation, without conceiving a particular feather; and one is at a loss when this is neglected in the description. Again, "The rogues flighted me into the river with as little remorse, as they would have drown'd a bitch's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> puppies, fifteen i' th' litter." Old Lady. You would not be a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>? <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. No, not for all the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> under heaven. Old Lady. 'Tis strange: a threepence bow'd would hire me, old as I am, to queen it. Henry VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> ii. sc. 5.
