In the following passage, the action, with all its material Narration. al circumstances, is represented so much to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that it would scarce appear more distinct to a real spectator; and it is the manner of description that contributes greatly to the sublimity of the passage— He spoke; and, to confirm his words, out flew Millions of flaming swords, drawn from the thighs Of mighty cherubim; the sudden blaze Far round illumining <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>; highly they rag'd Against the Highest, and fierce with grasped arms, Clash'd on their sounding shields the din of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Hurling defiance toward the vault of heav'n. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, book i. The following passage from Shakespeare falls not much short of that now mentioned in particularity of description: O you hard hearts! ye cruel men of Rome! Knew you not Pompey? Many a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and oft Have you climb'd up to walls and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, To towers and windows, yea, to chimney tops, Your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> in your arms, and there have sat The live-long day with patient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> To see great Pompey <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the streets of Rome; And when you <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his chariot but appear, Have you not made an universal shout, That Tyber trembled underneath his banks, To hear the replication of your sounds, Made in his concave shore? Julius Caesar, act i. sc. i. The following passage is scarcely inferior to either of those mentioned: "Far before the rest, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a> comes: bright in the smiles of youth, fair as the first beams of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. His long <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> waves on his back: his dark brow is half beneath his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> hangs loose on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>'s side; and his spear glitters as he moves. I fled from his terrible eye, king of high Temora." Fingal. The Henriade of Voltaire errs greatly against the foregoing rule: every incident is touched in a summary way, without ever descending to circumstances. This manner is good in a general history, the purpose of which is to record important transactions: but in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> it is cold and uninteresting; because it is impracticable to form distinct images of persons or things represented in a manner so superficial. It is observed above, that every useless circumstance ought to be suppressed. The crowding such circumstances is, on the one hand, not less to be avoided than the conciseness for which Voltaire is blamed, on the other. In the Æneid, Barce, the nurse of Sichæus, whom we never hear of before nor after, is introduced for a purpose not more important than to call <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> to her sister Dido: and that it might not be thought unjust in Dido, even in this trivial circumstance, to prefer her husband's nurse before her own, the poet takes care to inform his reader, that Dido's nurse was dead. To this may be opposed a beautiful passage in the same book, where, after Dido's last speech, the poet, without detaining his readers by describing the manner of her death, hastens to the lamentation of her attendants: Dixerat: atque illam media inter talia ferro Collapsam alpicium comites, ensenique cuoro Spumantem, sparfafaque manus. It clamor <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTA">alta</a> Atria; concussam bacchatur fama per urbem; Lamentis gemituque, et femineo ululatu Tecta fremunt, resonat magnis plangoribus æther. Lib. iv. 663. As an appendix to the foregoing rule, may be added the following observation. That to make a sudden and strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, some single circumstance, happily selected, has more power than the most laboured description. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, mentioning to his lady some voices he heard while he was murdering the King, says, There's one did laugh in's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and one cry'd <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>! They wak'd each other; and I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and heard them: But they did say their prayers, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> them Again to sleep. Lady. There are two lodg'd together. Macbeth. One cry'd, God bless us! and, Amen! the other; As they had seem me with these hangman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, Listening their fear. I could not say, Amen, When they did say, God bless us. Lady. Consider it not so deeply. Macbeth. But wherefore could not I pronounce Amen! I had most need of blessing, and Amen Stuck in my throat. Lady. These deeds must not be thought After these ways; so, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make us mad. Macbeth. Methought, I heard a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> cry, Sleep no more! Macbeth doth murder sleep, &c. Act ii. sc. 2. Describing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry: I saw young Harry, with his beaver on, His cuisses on his thighs, gallantly arm'd, Rise from the ground like feather'd <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; And vaulted with such ease into his seat, As if an angel dropt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, To turn and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> a fiery Pegasus, And witch the world with noble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>. First Part Henry IV. act iii. sc. 3. King Henry. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a>, if thou think'st on Heaven's bliss, Hold up thy hand, make signal of thy hope, He dies, and makes no sign! <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Part Henry VI. act iii. sc. 3. The same author, speaking ludicrously of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> debilitated with diseases, says, "Half of them dare not shake the snow from off their capslocks, lest they shake themselves to pieces." "I have seen the walls of Balclutha, but they were desolate. The flames had refounded in the halls: and the voice of the people is heard no more. The stream of Clutha was removed from its place by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the walls. The thistle shook there its lonely head: the moss whittled to the wind. The fox looked out from the windows: and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> grass of the wall waved round..." Narration round his head. Defolate is the dwelling of Morna: silence is in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of her fathers.” To draw a character is the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> stroke of description. In this Tacitus excels; his portraits are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and lively, not a feature wanting or misplaced. Shakespeare, however, exceeds Tacitus in liveliness; some characteristic circumstance being generally invented or laid hold of, which paints more to the life than many words. The following instances will explain our meaning, and at the same time prove our observation to be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>. Why should a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose blood is warm within, Sit like his grandfire cut in alabaster? Sleep when he <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a>, and creep into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, By being peevish? I tell thee what, Antonio, (I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> thee, and it is my love that speaks), There are a sort of men, whose visages Do cream and mantle like a standing pond; And do a wilful stillness entertain, With purpose to be dress'd in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, gravity, profound conceit; As who should say, I am Sir Oracle, And when I ope my lips, let no dog bark! O my Antonio! I do know of those, That therefore only are reputed wise, For saying nothing. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, act i. sc. 1. Again: “Gratiano speaks an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nothing, more than any man in all Venice: his reasons are two grains of wheat hid in two bushels of chaff; you shall seek all day ere you find them; and when you have them, they are not worth the search.” Ibid. In the following passage a character is completed by a single stroke: Shallow. O the mad days that I have spent; and to see how many of mine old acquaintance are dead. Silence. We shall all follow, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>. Shallow. Certain, 'tis certain, very sure, very sure; Death (as the Psalmist <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>) is certain to all: all shall die. How a good yoke of bullocks at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> fair? Slender. Truly cousin, I was not there. Shallow. Death is certain. Is old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> of your town living yet? Silence. Dead, Sir. Shallow. Dead! see, see: he drew a good bow: and dead. He <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> a fine shot. How a score of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a> now? Silence. Thereafter as they be. A score of good ewes may be worth ten pounds. Shallow. And is old Double dead? Second part Henry IV, act iii. sc. 2. Describing a jealous husband: “Neither press, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, well, vault, but he hath an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of such places, and goes to them by his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. There is no hiding you in the house.” Merry Wives of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, act iv. sc. 3. Congreve has an imitative stroke of this kind in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of Love for Love: Ben <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">Legend</a>. Well, father, and how do all at home? how does <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Dick, and brother Val. Vol. XIV. Part II. Sir Sampson. Dick's dead, as you say. Act iii. sc. 6. Falstaff speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Pistol: “He's no swaggerer, hoffest; a tame cheater i'faith; you may froak him as gently as a puppy greyhound; he will not swagger with a Barbary hen, if her feathers turn back in any show of resistance.” Second part Henry IV, act ii. sc. 4. Offian, among his other excellencies, is eminently successful in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; and he never fails to delight his reader with the beautiful attitudes of his heroes. Take the following instance: “O Oscar! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the strong in arm; but spare the feeble hand. Be thou a stream of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> against the foes of thy people; but like the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">gale</a> that moves the grass to those who ask thine aid.—So, Tremor lived; such Trathal was; and such has Fingal been. My arm was the support of the injured; and the weak reft behind the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> of my <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>.” “We heard the voice of joy on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and we thought that the mighty Cathmor came. Cathmor the friend of strangers! the brother of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-haired Cairbar! But their souls were not the same; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of heaven was on the bosom of Cathmor. His towers rose on the banks of Atha: <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> paths led to his halls: seven chiefs stood on these paths, and called the stranger to the feast. But Cathmor dwelt in the wood to avoid the voice of praise.” “Dermid and Oscar were one: they reaped the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> together. Their friendship was strong as their steel; and death walked between them to the field. They rush on the foe like two rocks falling from the brow of Ardvon. Their swords are stained with the blood of the valiant: warriors faint at their name. Who is equal to Oscar but Dermid? who to Dermid but Oscar?” “Son of Comhal, replied the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the strength of Morni's arm has failed: I attempted to draw the sword of my youth, but it remains in its place: I throw the spear, but it falls short of the mark: and I feel the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of my shield. We decay like the grass of the mountain, and our strength returns no more. I have a son, O Fingal! his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> has delighted in the actions of Morni's youth; but his sword has not been fitted against the foe, neither has his fame begun. I come with him to battle, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his arm. His renown will be a fun to my soul, in the dark <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of my departure. O that the name of Morni were forgot among the people! that the heroes would only say, Behold the father of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>!” Some writers, through <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of imagination, fall into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; some are guilty of downright absurdities; and some even rave like madmen. Against such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> errors one cannot be more effectually warned than by collecting instances; and the first shall be of a contradiction, the most venial of all. Virgil speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, Vol. XIV. Part II. Again: When first young Maro, in his boundless mind, A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> t'outlast immortal Rome <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>'d. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Criticism, 30. The following examples are of absurdities: "Alii pulsis e tormento catenis discerpti sectique, dimidiatum corpore pugnabant fibi superfluites, ac per- emptae partis ultores." Strada, Dec. ii. 2. Il pover huomo, che non sen' era accorto, Andava combatendo, ed era morto. Berni. He fled, but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, left his life behind. Iliad, xi. 443. Full through his neck the weighty falchion sped: Along the pavement roll'd the muttering head. Odyssey, xxii. 365. The last article is of raving like one mad. Cleopatra speaking to the aspic, Welcome, thou kind deceiver, Thou best of thieves; who, with an easy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, Dost open life, and unperceived by us Ev'n steal us from ourselves; discharging so Death's dreadful office, better than himself; Touching our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> so gently into slumber, That Death stands by, deceiv'd by his own image, And thinks himself but sleep. Dryden, All for Love, act v. Having discussed what observations occurred upon the thoughts or things expressed, we proceed to what more peculiarly concerns the language or verbal drefs. As words are intimately connected with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> they represent, the emotions raised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> ought to be concordant. An elevated subject requires an elevated style; what is familiar, ought to be familiarly expressed: a subject that is serious and important, ought to be clothed in plain nervous language: a description, on the other hand, addressed to the imagination, is susceptible of the highest ornaments that founding words and figurative <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> can bestow upon it. We shall give a few examples of the foregoing rules. A poet of any genius is not apt to dress a high subject in low words; and yet blemishes of that kind are found even in classical works. Horace, observing that men are satisfied with themselves, but seldom with their condition, introduces <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> indulging to each his own choice: Jam faciam quod vultis; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERIS">eris</a> tu, qui modo miles, Mercator; tu, consultus modo, rusticus: hinc vos, Vos hinc, mutatis discedit partibus, eia, Quid? statis? nolint. atei licet effe beatis. Quid causae est, merito quin illis Jupiter ambas Iratus buccas inflat, neque se fore posthac Tam facilem dicat, votis ut praebat aurem? Sat. i. 16. Jupiter in wrath puffing up both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, is a low and ludicrous expression, far from suitable to the gravity and importance of the subject: every one must feel the discordance. The following couplet, sinking far below the subject, is no less ludicrous: Not one looks backward, onward still he goes, Yet ne'er looks forward farther than his nose. Essay on Man, ep. iv. 223. On the other hand, to raise the expression above the tone of the subject, is a fault than which none is more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Take the following instances: Ocean le plus fidèle à servir ses deffins, Ne fous le ciel brûlant des plus noirs Africains. Bajazet, act iii. sc. 8. Les ombres par trois fois ont obscurci les cieux Depuis que le sommeil n'est entré dans vos yeux; Et le jour a trois fois chassé la nuit obscure Depuis que votre corps languit sans nourriture. Phaedra, act i. sc. 3. Affueris. Ce mortel, qui montra tant de zèle pour moi, Vit-il encore? Asaph.—Il voit l'aître qui vous éclaire. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>, act ii. sc. 3. Oui, c'est Agamemnon, c'est ton roi qui teveille; Viens, reconnais la voix qui frappe ton oreille. Iphigenie. No jocund <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> drinks to-day, But the great cannon to the clouds shall tell; And the king's rowse the heav'n shall bruit again, Respeaking earthly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>, act i. sc. 2.
