Southerne, Fate of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>, act iii. In the Funeral Orations of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are raised far above the tone of the subject; "L'Ocean etonné de se voir traversé tant de fois, en des appareils si <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, et pour des causes si différentes, &c." Pag. 6. "Grande reine, je satisfais à vos plus tendres désirs, quand je célèbre ce monarque; et son cœur qui n'a jamais vécu que pour lui, s'éveille, tout poudre qu'il est, et devient sensible, même sous ce drap mortuaire, au nom d'un époux si cher." Pag. 32. The following passage, intended, one would imagine, as a receipt to boil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is altogether <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> by the laboured elevation of the diction: A maffy cauldron of stupendous frame They brought, and plac'd it o'er the rising <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>: Then heap the lighted wood; the flame divides Beneath the vase, and climbs around the sides: In its wide womb they pour the rushing stream: The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water bubbles to the brim. Iliad, xviii. 405. In a passage at the beginning of the 4th book of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>, one feels a sudden bound upward without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, which accords not with the subject: "Calypso," My waking thought admits no balmy rest, Nor the sweet bliss of soft oblivion share; But watchful woe distracts my aching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, My heart the subject of corroding care: From haunts of men with wandering steps and flow I solitary steal, and soothe my pensive woe. Here every substantive is faithfully attended by some tumid epithet. We proceed to a second remark, not less important than the former. No person of reflection but must be sensible, that an incident makes a stronger impression on an eye witness, than when heard at second hand. Writers of genius, sensible that the eye is the best avenue to the heart, represent everything as passing in our sight; and, from readers or hearers, transform us as it were into spectators: a skilful writer conceals himself, and presents his personages: in a word, everything becomes dramatic as much as possible. Plutarch, de gloria Atheniensium, observes, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> makes his reader a spectator, and inspires him with the same passions as if he were an eye witness. In the fine arts, it is a rule to put the capital objects in the strongest point of view; and even to present them oftener than once, where it can be done. In history <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and in the best light: an equestrian statue is placed in a centre of streets, that it may be seen from many places at once. In no <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is there greater opportunity for this rule than in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>: Sequitur pulcherrimus Astur, Astur equo fidens et vericoloribus armis. Full many a lady I've ey'd with best regard, and many a time Th' <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of their tongues hath into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> Brought my too diligent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>: for several virtues Have I lik'd several women: never any With so full foul, but some defect in her Did quarrel with the noblest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> she ow'd, And put it to the foil. But you, O you, So perfect, and so peerless, are created Of every creature's best. Orlando.—Whate'er you are That, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> inaccessible, Under the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of melancholy boughs, Loe and neglect the creeping hours of time; If ever you have look'd on better days; If ever been where bells have knoll'd to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; If ever sat at any good man's feast; If ever from your eyelids wip'd a tear, And known what 'tis to pity, and be pity'd; Let gentleness my strong enforcement be, In the which hope I blush, and hide my sword. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> sen. True is it that we have seen better days; And have with holy <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> been knoll'd to church; And sat at good men's feasts; and wip'd our eyes Of drops that sacred pity had engender'd; And therefore fit you down in gentleness, And take upon command what help we have, That to your wanting may be ministr'd. As you like it. With thee conversing I forget all time; All seasons and their change, all please alike. Sweet Sweet is the breath of morn, her rising sweet, With <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> of earliest birds; pleasant the fun When first on this delightful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> he spreads His orient beams on herbs, tree, fruit, and flow'r Glittering with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>; fragrant the fertile <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> After soft show'rs; and sweet the coming on Of grateful ev'n'ning mild, the silent night With this her solemn <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, and this fair <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, And these the gems of heav'n, her starry train: But neither breath of morn, when she ascends With charm of earliest birds, nor rising sun On this delightful land, nor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, fruit, flow'r, Glittering with dew, nor fragrance after show'rs, Nor grateful ev'n'ning mild, nor silent night, With this her solemn bird, nor walk by moon, Or glittering <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> light, without thee is sweet. Paradise Lost, book iv. l. 634. "What <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> ye, that ye <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this proverb, The fathers have eaten four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and the children's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are set on edge? As I live, faith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion to use this proverb in Israel. If a man keep my judgments to deal truly, he is just, he shall surely live. But if he be a robber, a shedder of blood: if he have eaten upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and defiled his neighbour's wife: if he have oppressed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and needy, have spoiled by violence, have not restored the pledge, have lifted up his eyes to idols, have given forth upon usury, and have taken increase: shall he live? he shall not live: he shall surely die; and his blood shall be upon him. Now, lo, if he beget a son, that feeth all his father's sins, and confedereth, and doth not such like; that hath not eaten upon the mountains, hath not lifted up his eyes to idols, nor defiled his neighbour's wife, hath not oppressed any, nor withheld the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> to the hungry, and covered the naked with a garment: that hath not received usury nor increase, that hath executed my judgments, and walked in my statutes: he shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live. The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. Have I any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> that the wicked should die, faith the Lord God; and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> xvii. A concise comprehensive style is a great ornament in narration; and a superfluity of unnecessary words, not less than of circumstances, a great nuisance. A judicious selection of the striking circumstances, clothed in a nervous style, is delightful. In this style, Tacitus excels all writers, ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. Instances are numberless: take the following specimen: "Crebra hinc praedia, et læpium in modum latrocinii: per falsum, per paludes; ut cuique fors aut virtus: te-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a>, proviso, ob iram, ob prædam, jusfla, et aliquando ignaris ducibus." Annal. lib. xii. § 39. After Tacitus, Ossian in that respect justly merits the place of distinction. One cannot go wrong for examples in any part of the book. If a concise or nervous style by a beauty, tautology must be a blemish; and yet writers, fettered by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, are not sufficiently careful to avoid this slovenly practice: they may be pitied, but they cannot be justified. Take for a specimen the following instances, from the best poet, for verification at least, that England has to boast of: High on his helm celestial lightnings play, His beamy shield emits a living ray; Th' unweary'd blaze incessant streams supplies, Like the red star that fires the autumnal skies. Iliad. 5. Strength and omnipotence invest thy throne. Ibid. 576. So silent fountains, from a rock's tall head, In fable streams soft trickling waters fled. Ibid. ix. 19. His clanging armour rung. Ibid. xii. 94. Fear on their cheek, and horror in their eye. Ibid. xv. 4. The blaze of armour flash'd against the day. Ibid. xvii. 736. As when the piercing blasts of Boreas blow. Ibid. xix. 380. And like the moon, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> resplendent shield Blaz'd with long rays, and gleam'd athwart the field. Ibid. xix. 402. No—could our swiftness o'er the winds prevail, Or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the pinions of the western gale; All were in vain— Ibid. xix. 604. The humid sweat from every pore descends. Ibid. xxiii. 829. We <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> this article with a curious inquiry. An object, however ugly to the sight, is far from being so when represented by colours or by words. What is the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>? With respect to painting, the cause is obvious: a good picture, whatever the subject be, is agreeable by the pleasure we take in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>; and this pleasure overbalancing the disagreeableness of the subject, makes the picture upon the whole agreeable. With respect to the description of an ugly object, the cause follows. To connect individuals in the social state, no particular contributes more than language, by the power it possesses of an expeditious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of thought, and a lively representation of transactions. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> hath not been satisfied to recommend language by its utility merely: independent of utility, it is made susceptible of many beauties, which are directly felt, without any intervening reflection. And this unfolds the mystery; for the pleasure of language is so great, as in a lively description to overbalance the disagreeableness of the image raised by it. This, however, is no encouragement to choose a disagreeable subject; for the pleasure is incomparably greater where the subject and the description are both of them agreeable. The following description is upon the whole agreeable, though the subject described is in itself dismal: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> times the space that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> day and night To mortal men, he with his horrid crew... Lay vanquished, rolling in the fiery <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, Confound though immortal! but his doom Refer'd him to more wrath; for now the thought Both of lost <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and lasting pain Torments him: round he throws his baleful eyes That witness'd huge affliction and dismay, Mix'd with obdurate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and steadfast hate. At once as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> ken he views The dismal situation waste and wild: A dungeon horrible, on all sides round As one great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> flamed; yet from those flames No light, but rather darkness visible Serv'd only to discover sights of woe, Regions of sorrow, doleful shades, where peace And rest can never dwell, hope never comes That comes to all; but torture without end Still urges, and a fiery deluge, fed With ever-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sulphur unconsum'd! Such place eternal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> had prepar'd For those rebellious. *Paradise Lost*, book i. 50. An unmanly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits in time of danger is not an agreeable sight; and yet a fine description or representation of it will be relished: *K. Richard*. What must the king do now? must he submit? The king shall do it: must he be depos'd? The king shall be contented: must he lose The name of king? o' God's name let it go: I'll give my jewels for a set of beads; My gorgeous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, for a hermitage; My gay apparel, for an almsman's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>; My figur'd goblets, for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of wood; My sceptre, for a palmer's walking-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>; My subjects, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of carved saints; And my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for a little grave; A little, little grave,—an obscure grave. Or I'll be buried in the king's high way; Some way of common <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a>, where subjects feet May hourly trample on their sovereign's head; For on my heart they tread now, whilst I live; And, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a>'d once, why not upon my head? *Richard II*, act iii. sc. 6. Objects that strike terror in a spectator, have in poetry and painting a fine effect. The picture, by raising a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of terror, agitates the mind; and in that condition every beauty makes a deep impression. May not <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> heighten the pleasure, by opposing our present security to the danger of encountering the object represented. The other shape, If shape it might be call'd that shape had none Diffinguishable in member, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, or limb; Or substance might be call'd that shadow seem'd, For each seem'd either; black it flood as night, Fierce as ten furies, terrible as hell, And shook a dreadful dart. *Par. Lost*, book ii. 666. Now storming fury rose, And clamour such as heard in heaven till now Was never: arms on armour clashing bray'd Horrible <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, and the madding <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> Of brazen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> rage; dire was the noise Of conflict; overhead the dismal hills Of fiery darts in flaming valleys flew, And flying vaulted either hoit with fire. So under fiery cope together rush'd Both battles main, with ruinous assault And unextinguishable rage: all heaven Refounded, and had earth been then, all earth Had to her centre hook. *Ibid.*, book vi. 207. *Ghoth.* But that I am forbid To tell the secrets of my prison-house, I could a tale unfold, whose lightest word Would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> up thy soul, freeze thy young blood, Make thy two eyes, like stars start from their spheres, Thy knotty and combined locks to part, And each particular hair to stand on end, Like quills upon the fretful porcupine: But this eternal blazon must not be To ears of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> and blood. *Hamlet*, act i. sc. 8. *Gratiano*. Poor Desdemona! I'm glad thy father's dead: Thy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was mortal to him; and pure grief Shore his old thread in twain. Did he live now, This fight would make him do a desperate turn: Yea, curse his better angel from his side, And fall to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>. *Othello*, act v. sc. 8. Objects of horror must be excepted from the foregoing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>; for no description, however lively, is sufficient to overbalance the disgust raised even by the idea of such objects. Every thing horrible ought therefore to be avoided in a description. *NARSES*, the eunuch who rivalled <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a> in heroism under the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, emerged from obscurity A.D. 538. From the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the palace, and the administration of the private revenue, he was suddenly exalted to the head of an army. He is ranked among the few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> who have rescued that unhappy name from the contempt and hatred of mankind. A feeble <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> body concealed the soul of a statesman and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>. His youth had been employed in the management of the loom and distaff, in the cares of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and the service of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>; but, while his hands were busy, he secretly exercised the faculties of a vigorous and discerning mind. A stranger to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, he studied in the palace to dissemble, to flatter, and to persuade; and as soon as he approached the person of the emperor, Justinian lifted with surplice and pleasure to the manly counsels of his chamberlain and private <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>. The talents of Narsete were tried and improved in frequent embassies; he led an army into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, acquired a practical knowledge of the war and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and presumed to strive with the genius of Belisarius. Twelve years after his return, the eunuch was chosen to achieve the conquest which had been left imperfect by the first of the Roman generals. Instead of being dazzled by vanity or emulation, he ferociously declared, that unless he were armed with an adequate force, he would never consent to risk his own <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and that of his sovereign. Justinian granted to the favourite what he might have denied to the hero: the Gothic war was rekindled from its ashes, and the preparations were not unworthy of the ancient majesty of the empire. Narsete defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, the Franks, and the Alamanni; Alamanni; the Italian cities opened their gates to the conqueror; he entered the capital in triumph; and having established the seat of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 15 years to govern Italy under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXARCH">Exarch</a>. His virtues, we are told, were stained with avairce; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> reign he accumulated a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver which surpassed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of a private fortune. His government was oppressive or unpopular; and the general discontent was expressed with freedom by the deputies of Rome. Before the throne of Justinian they boldly declared, that their Gothic servitude had been more tolerable than the despotism of a Greek eunuch; and that unless their tyranny were instantly removed, they would consult their own happiness in the choice of a master. Thus was his disgrace the effect of the people's disaffection; and his death, though in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was unseasonable and premature, since his genius alone could have repaired the last and fatal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of his life. He died about the year 567, and, as some say, at the advanced age of 95; but this does not appear very probable. See Gibbon's Rom. Hist. vol. iv. 4to edit. p. 194, 298, &c.

NARVA

Pages 682-682

a strong town of the Russian empire, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, with a castle and a harbour. It was taken by the Muscovites from the Danes in 1558, by the Swedes in 1581, and they defeated the Muscovites near it in 1700; but it was retaken by the Russians in 1704 by storm, and the inhabitants sent to Astrakhan. It is situated on the river Narva, 95 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WIBURG">Wiburg</a>, and 172 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° O. N. Lat. 59° 3'.

NASSAU-DILLENBOURG

Pages 682-682

a principality of Germany, situated near the former. It has not much arable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but plenty of wood, good quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, some silver and vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, with store of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, for the working and smelting of which there are many forges and founderies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and by these, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of their iron, the inhabitants chiefly subsist. Calvinism is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the principality, which contains five <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and two boroughs, and belongs entirely to William V. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> of the United Provinces, whose father succeeded to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it in 1739 on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Prince Christian, and to the rest in 1743 on the death of Prince William Hyacinth of Siegen. The prince, on account of this principality also and Dietz, has a seat and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes, at the diets of the empire and circle. His assentment in the matricula, for Nassau-Dillenbourg, is 102 florins monthly; and to the chamber judicatory, 59 rixdollars six and half kruitzers, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. His revenue from this principality is computed at above 130,000 florins.

NASSAU-HADAMOR

Pages 682-682

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Germany, which, till the year 1711, had princes of its own; but now belongs wholly to William V. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>.

NASSAU-SIEGEN

Pages 682-682

a small principality of Germany in the Westerwalde, is in general a mountainous woody <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with some arable and pasture ground, and a good breed of cattle. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are chiefly those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, having an iron mine in the neighbourhood of Siegen. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> John the Younger, in 1626, embraced the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and endeavoured to introduce it into the country; but the principality, upon the extinction of the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>-Siegen in 1743, falling to the line of Nassau-Dietz, and therein to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> of the United Provinces, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> were delivered from their apprehensions of Popish tyranny and bigotry. The prince, on account of these territories, has a seat and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> at the diets of the empire and circle in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes. His assentment in the matricula for Nassau-Siegen is 773 florins monthly; and towards the maintenance of the chamber judicatory, 50 rixdollars, six kruitzers and a half, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. The revenue of this principality is estimated at 100,000 rixdollars.

NATES

Pages 682-682

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> expressing those two fleshy exterior parts of the body, vulgarly called the buttocks. See ANATOMY. NATES Cerebri, are two circular protuberances of the brain, situated on the back side of the medulla oblongata, near the cerebellum.

NATION

Pages 682-687

a collective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, used for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people inhabiting a certain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, confined within fixed limits, and under the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. NATIONAL DEBT: the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> owing by government. Our limits permit us to give but a very general sketch of this subject: However, as it is of considerable importance to every inhabitant of these kingdoms, we shall endeavour to give as clear and comprehensive a view of it as the bounds necessarily prescribed us <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit. In order to this, it may not be improper to refer back to the times that have gone before us, that we may the better discover the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of public revenues, the manner of their expenditure, and the causes of public debt. In that rude state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> which precedes the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and the improvements of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, when those expensive luxuries which commerce and manufactures can alone introduce, are altogether unknown; the person who possesses a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> revenue can spend <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enjoy that revenue in no other way than by maintaining nearly as many people as it can maintain. Among our feudal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> during which estates used to continue in the same family, sufficiently demonstrates the general disposition of people to live within their income. Though the rustic hospitality constantly exercised by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> landholders may not to us in the present times seem consistent with that order which we are apt to consider as inseparably connected with good economy, yet we must certainly allow them to have been at least so far frugal as not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> to have spent their whole income. Some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this money, perhaps, they spent in purchasing the few objects of vanity and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> with which the circumstances of the times could furnish them: but some part of it they seem commonly to have hoarded. They could not well indeed do any thing else but hoard whatever money they saved. To trade was disgraceful to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>; and to lend money at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, which at that time was considered as usury and prohibited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, would have been still more fo. The same disposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> and to hoard prevailed in the sovereign as well as in the subjects. Among nations to whom commerce and manufactures are little known, the sovereign is in a situation which naturally disposes him to the parsimony requisite for accumulation. In that situation the expense even of a sovereign cannot be directed by that vanity which delights in the gaudy finery of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the times affords but few of the trinkets in which that finery consists. Standing armies are not then necessary; so that the expense even of a sovereign, like that of any other great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, can be employed in scarce anything but bounty to his tenants and hospitality to his retainers. But bounty and hospitality very seldom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to extravagance: though vanity almost always does. All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sovereigns of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> accordingly had treasuries. Every Tartar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> in the present times is said to have one. In a commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with every sort of expensive luxury, the sovereign, in the same manner as almost all the great proprietors in his dominions, naturally spends a great part of his revenue in purchasing those luxuries. His own and the neighbouring countries supply him abundantly with all the costly trinkets which compose the splendid but insignificant pageantry of a court. His ordinary expense becomes equal to his ordinary revenue, and it is well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it does not frequently exceed it. The amassing of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> can no longer be expected: and when extraordinary exigencies require extraordinary expenses, he must necessarily call upon his subjects for an extraordinary aid. The late <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> and his father are the only great princes of Europe who, since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Henry IV. of France in 1610, are supposed to have amassed any considerable treasure. The parsimony which leads to accumulation has become almost as rare in republican as in monarchical governments. The Italian republics, the United Provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, are all in debt. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> is the single republic in Europe which has amassed any considerable treasure. The other Swiss republics have not. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for some sort of pageantry, for splendid buildings at least and other public ornaments, frequently prevails as much in the apparently sober <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a little republic as in the dissipated court of the greatest king. The want of parsimony in time of peace imposes the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of contracting debt in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. When war comes, there is no money in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> but what is necessary for carrying on the ordinary expense of the peace establishment. In war an establishment of three or four times that expense becomes necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the state, and consequently a revenue three or four times greater than the peace revenue. Supposing that the sovereign should have what he fears ever has, the immediate means of augmenting his revenue in proportion to the augmentation of his expense; yet still the produce of the taxes, from which this increase of revenue must be drawn, will not begin to come into the treasury till perhaps ten or twelve months after they are imposed. But the moment in which war begins, or rather the moment in which it appears likely to begin, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> must be augmented, the fleets must be fitted out, the garrisoned <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> must be put into a posture of defence: that army, that fleet, those garrisoned towns, must be furnished with arms, ammunition, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. An immediate and great expense must be incurred in that moment of immediate danger, which will not wait for the gradual and slow returns of the new taxes. In this exigency government can have no other resources but in borrowing. The same commercial state of society which, by the operation of moral causes, brings government in this manner into the necessity of borrowing, produces in the subjects both an ability and an inclination to lend. If it commonly brings along with it the necessity of borrowing, it likewise brings along with it the facility of doing so. A country abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and manufacturers, necessarily abounds with a set of people through whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> not only their own capitals, but the capitals of all those who either lend them money or trust them with goods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> as frequently or more frequently than the revenue of a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who without trade or business lives upon his income, passes through his hands. The revenue of such a man can regularly pass through his hands only once in a year. But the whole amount of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of a merchant who deals in a trade of which the returns are very quick may sometimes pass through his hands two, three, or four times in a year. A country abounding with merchants and manufacturers, therefore, necessarily abounds with a set of people, who have it at all times in their power to advance, if they choose to do so, a very large sum of money to government. Hence the ability in the subjects of a commercial state to lend. The progress of the enormous debts which at present oppress, and will in the long-run probably ruin, all the great nations of Europe, has been pretty uniform. In England, after the Revolution, when new connexions with Europe introduced a new system of foreign politics, the expenses of the nation not only in settling the new establishment, but in maintaining long wars, as principals, on the continent, for the security of the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, reducing the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, settling the Spanish succession, supporting the house of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, maintaining the liberties of the Germanic body, and other purposes, increased to an unusual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>: insomuch that it was not thought advisable to raise all the expenses of any one year by taxes to be levied within that year, lest the unaccustomed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of them should create murmurs among the people. It was therefore the policy of the times to anticipate the revenues of their posterity, by borrowing immense sums for the current <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the state, and to lay no more taxes upon the subject than would suffice to pay the annual interest of the sums so borrowed; by this means converting the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> debt into a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, transferable from one man to another at any time and in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. This system indeed seems to have had its origin in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, A.D. 1344; which government then owed about 60,000l. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; and being unable to pay it, formed the principal into an aggregate sum, called metaphorically a mount or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, the shares whereof were transferable like our stocks, with interest at 5 per cent. the prices varying according to the exigencies of the state. National state. This laid the foundation of what is called the national debt; for a few long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> created in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, will hardly deserve that name. Nations, like private men, have generally begun to borrow upon what may be called personal credit, without affixing or mortgaging any particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the payment of the debt; and when this resource has failed them, they have gone on to borrow upon assignments or mortgages of particular funds. What is called the unfunded debt of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is contracted in the former of those two ways. It consists partly in a debt which bears, or is supposed to bear, no interest; and which resembles the debts that a private man contracts upon account; and partly in a debt which bears interest, and which resembles what a private man contracts upon his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> or promissory <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. The debts which are due either for extraordinary services, or for services neither paid for nor paid at the time when they are performed; part of the extraordinary expenses of the army, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, and ordnance, the arrears of subsidies to foreign princes, those of seamen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, &c., usually constitute a debt of the first kind. Navy and exchequer bills, which are issued sometimes in payment of a part of such debts and sometimes for other purposes, constitute a debt of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind; exchequer bills <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> interest from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which they are issued, and navy bills six months after they are issued. The bank of England, either by voluntarily discounting those bills at their current value, or by agreeing with government for certain considerations to circulate exchequer bills, that is, to receive them at par, paying the interest which happens to be due upon them, keeps up their value, and facilitates their circulation, and thereby frequently enables government to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a very large debt of this kind. During the great recoinage in King William's time, when the bank of England thought proper to put a stop to its usual transactions, exchequer bills and tallies are said to have sold from 25 to 60 per cent, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a> owing partly, no doubt, to the supposed infallibility of the new government established by the Revolution, but partly too to the want of the support of the bank of England. When this resource is exhausted, and it becomes necessary, in order to raise money, to assign or mortgage some particular branch of the public revenue for the payment of the debt, government has upon different occasions done this in two different ways. Sometimes it has made this assignment or mortgage for a short <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time only, a year or a few years, for example; and sometimes for perpetuity. In the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the fund was supposed sufficient to pay within the limited time both principal and interest of the money borrowed: In the other, it was supposed sufficient to pay the interest only, or a perpetual annuity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the interest; government being at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to redeem at any time this annuity upon paying back the principal sum borrowed. When money was raised in the one way, it was said to be raised by anticipation; when in the other, by perpetual funding, or, more shortly, by funding. In the reign of King William, when the debt began to be amassed, and during a great part of that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, before we had become so familiar as we are now with the practice of perpetual funding, the greater part of the new taxes were imposed but for a short period of time (for four, five, six, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years only), and a great part of the grants of every year consisted in loans upon anticipation of the produce of those taxes. The produce being frequently insufficient for paying within the limited term the principal and interest of the money borrowed, deficiencies arose; to make good which it became necessary to prolong the term. On the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1697, the funded and unfunded debts amounted to £21,515,742l. 13s. 8½d.; at the same time, in 1714, they were £33,681,076l. 5s. 6½d. In 1755, before the breaking out of the war, they amounted to £72,289,673l.; and on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1763, at the conclusion of the peace, they had accumulated to £122,603,336l. 8s. 2½d. of funded debt, and of unfunded £13,027,589l. 2s. 2½d. more. In 1775, they were very nearly 130 millions; and the last American war added upwards of 120 millions more to that enormous sum: to pay the interest of which, and the charges of management, amounting annually to nearly eight millions and a half, the extraordinary revenues elsewhere enumerated * (excepting only the land-tax and annual malt tax) are in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> mortgaged and made perpetual by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Perpetual we say; but still redeemable by the same authority that imposed them; which, if it at any time can pay off the capital, will abolish those taxes which are raised to discharge the interest. By this means, then, the quantity of property in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is greatly increased in idea compared with former times; yet, if we coolly consider it, not at all increased in reality. We may boast of large fortunes, and quantities of money in the funds. But where does this money exist? It exists only in name, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in public <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in parliamentary security: and that is undoubtedly sufficient for the creditors of the public to rely on. But then what is the pledge which the public faith has pawned for the security of these debts? The land, the trade, and the personal industry of the subject; from which the money must arise that supplies the several taxes. In these, therefore, and these only, the property of the public creditors does really and intrinsically exist; and of course the land, the trade, and the personal industry of individuals, are diminished in their true value <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much as they are pledged to answer. If A's income amounts to 100l. per annum; and he is so far indebted to B, that he pays him 50l. per annum for his interest; one half of the value of A's property is transferred to B the creditor. The creditor's property exists in the demand which he has upon the debtor, and nowhere else; and the debtor is only a trustee to his creditor for one half of the value of his income. In short, the property of a creditor of the public consists in a certain portion of the national taxes; by how much therefore he is the richer, by so much the nation, which pays these taxes, is the poorer. The only advantage that can result to a nation from public debts, is the increase of circulation, by multiplying the call of the kingdom, and creating a new species of currency, assignable at any time and in any quantity; always therefore ready to be employed in any beneficial undertaking, by means of this its transferable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and yet producing some profit even when when it lies idle and unemployed. A certain proportion of debt seems to be highly useful to a trading people; but what that proportion is, it is not for us to determine. This much is indubitably certain, that the present magnitude of our national encumbrances very far exceeds all calculations of commercial benefit, and is productive of the greatest inconveniences. For, first, The enormous taxes that are raised upon the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the payment of the interest of this debt, are a hurt both to trade and manufactures, by raising the price as well of the artificer's subsistence as of the raw material, and of course, in a much greater proportion, the price of the commodity itself. Nay, the very increase of paper circulation itself, when extended beyond what is requisite for commerce or foreign <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tendency to increase the price of provisions as well as of all other merchandise. For as its effect is to multiply the cash of the kingdom, and this to such an extent that much must remain unemployed, that cash (which is the universal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the respective values of all other commodities) must necessarily sink in its own value, and every thing grow comparatively dearer. Secondly, If part of this debt be owing to foreigners, either they draw out of the kingdom annually a considerable quantity of specie for the interest; or else it is made an argument to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them unreasonable privileges in order to induce them to reside here. Thirdly, If the whole be owing to subjects only, it is then charging the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and industrious subject, who pays his share of the taxes to maintain the indolent and idle creditor who receives them. Lastly, and principally, It weakens the internal strength of a state, by anticipating those resources which should be reserved to defend it in case of necessity. The interest we now pay for our debts would undoubtedly be sufficient to maintain the most vigorous war that any national motives could possibly require. If indeed our ancestors in King William's time had annually paid, so long as their exigencies lasted, a far less sum than we now annually raise upon their accounts, they would not in time of war have borne so great burdens as they have bequeathed to and fettered upon their posterity in time of peace; and might have been eased the instant the exigence was over. On the whole, then, the national debt is undoubtedly a subject of vast importance, and as such it has been always considered; for much has been said and written upon it, and many schemes have been proposed at various times and by various persons for gradually removing it, it being considered by the most judicious as a most pernicious encumbrance to a commercial country. Some, we are aware, think it of vast utility; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is too eccentric, and in our estimation too feebly supported, to be convincing. The public debt is indubitably a great grievance; and every lover of his country must surely wish to see it removed: the period, however, when this blessing shall take place, if indeed it ever arrive, must at least be very distant. We refer such as wish for farther information on this interesting topic to those who have treated of it at full length, as Smith in his Wealth of Nations, and Sir John Sinclair in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Revenue. The writings of Dr Price likewise deserve considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, especially as one of his plans for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the debt has in fact been adopted, and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> established, by the legislature: His three plans may be found in a pamphlet by William Morgan, entitled, A Review of Dr Price's Writings on the Subject of the Finances of this Kingdom. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATAL">Natal</a> Day, the day of a person's birth. The word nativity is chiefly used in speaking of the saints; as, the nativity of St John the Baptist, &c. But when we say the Nativity, it is understood of that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, or the feast of Christmas. Nativity, nativitas, in ancient law books, signifies <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> or servitude. Nativity, in Astrology, the theme or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the heavens, and particularly of the twelve houses, at the moment when a person was born; called also the horoscope. Calculating the nativity, or by calculation seeking to know how long the queen should live, &c. was made felony, an. 23 Eliz. c. 2. Nativo habendo, in Law, a writ directed to the heir, for a lord who claimed inheritance in any villain, when a villain was run away from him, for the apprehending and restoring him to the lord. Natrix, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">Natural History</a>, a name given by some old writers to the natrix. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name of the Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, being the most westerly part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Asia, and consisting of a large <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, which extends from the river <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> as far as the Archipelago, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Marmora, the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLIPOLI">Gallipoli</a> and of Constantinople, which separate it from Europe on the west. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea, and on the south by the Mediterranean. Natrix, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-snake, called also torquata, from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> about its neck. See Ophiology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Natrum, or Natron, the nitre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, one of the fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>. See Soda, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. It is found in great abundance in many parts of Asia, where the natives <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> it up from the surface of the ground, and call it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The earliest account we have of it is in the Scriptures, where we find that the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> called nitre in those times would ferment with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, and possessed a detergent quality, so that it was used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> and in washing. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> compares the stinging of songs with a heavy heart, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> of vinegar and nitre: and Jeremiah says, that if the finder wash himself with nitre, his sin is not cleansed off. These are properties that perfectly agree with this salt, but not at all with our <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, which is the nitre of the moderns. Natterjack, a species of Rana, which see, Reptology Index. Natural, in general, something that relates to nature. See Nature. Natural children, are those born out of lawful wedlock. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">Bastard</a>. Natural Functions, are those actions whereby the aliments are changed and assimilated so as to become a part of the body. Natural, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is used where animals, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. are blazoned with the colours they naturally have, though different from the common colours. of heraldry: and this is to prevent their armories being accused of falsity, when blazoned with the names of colours unknown in heraldry. **NATURAL Note**, in Music, is used in opposition to flat and sharp notes, which are called *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> notes*. See NOTE, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">SCALE</a>, &c. Natural is also used for something coming immediately out of the hands of nature: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to *factitious* or artificial, which signifies something wrought by art. See ARTIFICIAL. Bishop Wilkins observes, that there appears a world of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between natural and artificial things, when viewed with microscopes. The first ever appear adorned with all imaginable elegance and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; the latter, though the most curious in their kind, infinitely rude and unhewn: the finest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> appears a rough <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and the most accurate engraving or embossment, as if done with a mattock or a trowel. **NATURAL Beauty**, or the beauty of natural objects, is that quality or those qualities in the works of nature, or more properly of God, which are calculated to excite pleasing sensations in the minds of all such persons of true taste as attentively observe them. It will not, we trust, be deemed improper or impertinent, therefore, to introduce a few observations on this subject, previous to our treating of natural history.—To many, it is hoped, it will appear to be a very proper introduction to that important article. "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> to beauty, which, when cultivated and improved, we term taste, is universally diffused through the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> species;" and it is most uniform with respect to those objects, which being out of our power, are not liable to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from accident, caprice, or fashion. The verdant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, the shady <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, the variegated landscape, the boundless ocean, and the starry firmament, are contemplated with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by every attentive beholder. But the emotions of different spectators, though similar in kind, differ widely in degree; and to relish with full delight the enchanting scenes of nature, the mind must be uncorrupted by avarice, sensuality, or ambition; quick in her sensibilities; elevated in her sentiments; and devout in her affections. He who possesses such exalted powers of perception and enjoyment, may almost say, with the poet, I care not, Fortune! what you me deny; You cannot rob me of free Nature's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; You cannot shut the windows of the sky, Through which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> shows her bright'ning <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>; You cannot bar my constant feet to trace The woods and lawns, by living stream, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>: Let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> my nerves and finer fibres brace, And I their toys to the great children leave: Of fancy, reason, virtue, nought can me bereave. "Perhaps such ardent enthusiasm may not be compatible with the necessary toils and active offices which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> has assigned to the generality of men. But there are none to whom some portion of it may not prove advantageous: and if it were cherished by each individual, in that degree which is consistent with the indispensable duties of his station, the felicity of human life would be considerably augmented. From this source, the refined and vivid pleasures of the imagination are almost entirely derived: and the elegant arts owe their choicest beauties to a taste for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of nature. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> are express imitations of visible objects; and where would be the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, if divested of the imagery and embellishments which the borrow from rural scenes? Painters, statuaries, and poets, therefore, are always ambitious to acknowledge themselves the pupils of nature; and as their skill increases, they grow more and more delighted with every view of the animal and vegetable world. But the pleasure resulting from admiration is transient; and to cultivate taste, without regard to its influence on the passions and affections, 'is to rear a tree for its blossoms, which is capable of yielding the richest and most valuable fruit.' Physical and moral beauty bear so intimate a relation to each other, that they may be considered as different gradations in the scale of excellence; and the knowledge and relish of the former should be deemed only a step to the nobler and more permanent enjoyments of the latter. "Whoever has visited the Leasowes, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, must have felt the force and propriety of an inscription which meets the eye at the entrance into those delightful grounds. Would you then taste the tranquil <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>? Be sure your bosoms be serene: Devoid of hate, devoid of strife, Devoid of all that poisons life: And much it 'vails you, in their place, To graft the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. "Now such scenes contribute powerfully to inspire that serenity which is necessary to enjoy and to heighten their beauties. By a secret contagion, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> catches the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> which she contemplates; and the frame within assimilates itself to that which is without. For, Who can forbear to smile with Nature? Can The stormy passions in the bosom roll, While every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-GALE">gale</a> is peace, and every grove Is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>? "In this state of sweet composure, we become susceptible of virtuous impressions, from almost every surrounding object. The patient ox is viewed with generous complacency; the guileless sheep with pity; and the playful lamb raises emotions of tenderness and love. We rejoice with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, in his liberty and exemption from toil, while he ranges at large through enamelled pastures; and the frolics of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLT">colt</a> would afford unmixed delight, did we not recollect the bondage which he is soon to undergo. We are charmed with the song of birds, soothed with the buzz of insects, and pleased with the sportive motions of fishes, because these are expressions of enjoyment; and we exult in the felicity of the whole animated <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Thus an equal and extensive benevolence is called forth into exertion; and having felt a common interest in the gratifications of inferior beings, we shall be no longer indifferent to their sufferings, or become wantonly instrumental in producing them. "It seems to be the intention of Providence, that the lower order of animals should be subservient to the comfort, convenience, and sustenance of man. But his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of dominion extends no farther; and if this right be exercised with mildness, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the subjects of his power will be no less benefitted." ed than himself. For various species of living creatures are annually multiplied by human art, improved in their perceptive powers by human culture, and plentifully fed by human industry. The relation, therefore, is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> between such animals and man; and he may supply his own wants by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their labour, the produce of their bodies, and even the sacrifice of their lives, whilst he co-operates with all-gracious Heaven in promoting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, the great end of existence. "But though it be true, that partial evil, with respect to different orders of sensitive beings, may be universal good; and that it is a wise and benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of nature, to make destruction itself, within certain limitations, the cause of an increase of life and enjoyment; yet a generous person will extend his compassionate regards to every individual that suffers for his sake: and whilst he sighs Even for the kid or lamb that parts its life Beneath the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, he will naturally be solicitous to mitigate pain, both in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and degree, by the gentlest modes of inflicting it. "We are inclined to believe, however, that this sense of humanity would soon be obliterated, and that the heart would grow callous to every soft <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, were it not for the benignant influence of the smiling face of nature. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Lauzun, when imprisoned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the castle of Pignerol, amused himself during a long period of time with catching flies, and delivering them to be devoured by a rapacious spider. Such an entertainment was equally singular and cruel; and inconsistent, we believe, with his former character, and his subsequent turn of mind. But his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">cell</a> had no window, and received only a glimmering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from an aperture in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. In less unfavourable circumstances, may we not presume, that instead of sporting with misery, he would have released the agonizing flies, and bid them enjoy that freedom of which he himself was bereaved? "But the taste for natural beauty is subservient to higher purposes than those which have been enumerated; and the cultivation of it not only refines and humanizes, but dignifies and exalts the affections. It elevates them to the admiration and love of that Being who is the author of all that is fair, sublime, and good in the creation. Scepticism and irreligion are hardly compatible with the sensibility of heart which arises from a just and lively relish of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, harmony, and order subsisting in the world around us; and emotions of piety must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up spontaneously in the bosom that is in unison with all animated nature. Actuated by this divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, man finds a fane in every grove; and, glowing with devout fervour, he joins his song to the universal chorus, or mutes the praise of the Almighty, in more expressive silence. Thus they "Whom Nature's works can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, with God himself Hold <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>: grow familiar, day by day, With his conceptions; <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; And form to his the relish of their souls." On the whole, then, it certainly appears, that the advantages resulting from a taste for natural beauties are great and important: it is equally certain, that as it is useful, so it is a continual source of real enjoyment; for a more rational pleasure cannot possibly occupy the attention or captivate the affections of mankind, than that which arises from a due consideration of the works of nature. Pleasure, we know, is a necessary ingredient in human life, in order in some measure to counterbalance the pains, the evils, and little-neffes, which are at times perhaps unavoidable, and in order to render life tolerable. It is the part then of the moralist, and it has been frequently his business, to point out and recommend such pleasures as are highly gratifying, and are yet perfectly innocent. The Spectator, whose works will be admired as long as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in which they are written is understood, recommends strongly and elegantly the pleasure of a garden; and a later writer, of no common degree of merit, and of very considerable fame, has an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on the same subject, from which we shall select a few observations, and so conclude the article. "Not he alone (says this elegant writer) is to be esteemed a benefactor to mankind, who makes a useful discovery; but he also who can point out and recommend an innocent pleasure. Of this kind are the pleasures arising from the observation of nature; and they are highly agreeable to every taste uncorrupted by vicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. Rural scenes of almost every kind are delightful to the mind of man. But the misfortune is, that the greater part are hurried on in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of life with too great rapidity to be able to give attention to that which solicits no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The darkest habitation in the dirtiest street of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, where money can be earned, has greater charms with many than the groves of Hagley. "The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of refined pleasure, the elegant Epicurus, fixed the seat of his enjoyment in a garden. He was of opinion, that a tranquil spot, furnished with the united sweets of art and nature, was the best adapted to delicate repose. And even the feverish philosophers of antiquity were wont to discourse in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of a spreading tree, in some cultivated plantation. It is obvious, on intuition, that nature often intended solely to please the eye in her vegetable productions. She decorates the floweret that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> beneath our feet in all the perfections of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> beauty. She has clothed the garden with a constant succession of various hues. Even the leaves of the tree undergo a pleasing vicissitude. The fresh verdure which they exhibit in the spring, the various shades which they assume in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and ruffet tinge of autumn, and the nakedness of winter, afford a constant pleasure to a lively imagination. From the snowdrop to the moss rose the flower garden displays an infinite variety of shape and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The taste of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIST">florist</a> has been ridiculed as trifling; yet surely without reason. Did nature bring forth the tulip and the lily, the rose and the honeysuckle, to be neglected by the haughty pretender to superior reason? To omit a single social duty for the cultivation of a polyanthus were ridiculous as well as criminal; but to pass by the beauties lavished before us, without observing them, is no less ingratitude than stupidity. A bad heart finds little amusement but in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the active world, where scope is given for the indulgence of malignant..."

Hence, taking the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of known animals at 23,000, that of vegetables at 50,000 and that of minerals 267, the whole number of known species of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> objects <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 73,267. II. Though the classification of natural bodies is of the highest importance towards making us acquainted studying with unknown species, and distinguishing them from those which we already know; this alone is not sufficient to form a naturalist. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object should be to learn the habits, manners, and uses of the objects which he is studying; and he may perhaps be assisted in this object by the following observations. 1. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the natural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal kingdom</a>, it is necessary to ascertain both the distinctive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of each individual animal, and its peculiar habits, properties and uses. The naturalist first learns that the sheep, for instance, is in the class <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, being one of those animals that suckle their young; in the order pecora, because it is hoofed, and has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in the upper jaw; and that it is distinguished from other animals of the same order, by its having several blunt wedge-like incisive fore-teeth in the lower jaw only, hollow reclined horns, and no tusks. This information would satisfy many, who call themselves naturalists; but it is far from being all that is required; the philosophical investigator of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> inquires into its habits; as its food, its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of gestation, its season of lambing, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> most suited to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and vigour. He endeavours to learn what produces the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>, whether climate, food, or some peculiarity in the breed; and is anxious to ascertain what variety is most disposed to fatten, and what food effects this speedily; with many other very useful particulars. The information of the first kind is of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, and even necessary in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; but that of the latter is most useful. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a traveller discovers an animal possessing any useful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, or producing any useful drug, if he have not the first kind of information, he gives so confused and inaccurate a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it, that others, mistaking the animal, discredit the author's account, and the world loses the benefit of his discovery. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, or the natural history of the vegetable kingdom, in the usual acceptation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, implies and only (c) This number, drawn from the article Botany, compared with the three first volumes of Widenow's edition of the Species Plantarum, and with Peroon's edition of the Systema Vegetabilium, of Linné, is certainly very far below the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Many years ago, the number of known species was reckoned at above twenty thousand, and there is reason to believe that it exceeds fifty thousand. Objects and only the knowledge of the distinctive characters of utility of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and he who knows the greatest number, and is most accurate in determining the different species, is accounted the best botanist. This however constitutes but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the science; there is another distinct department, which may properly be termed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of botany, which is both more interesting and more useful. This includes the knowledge of the structure, or the anatomy of plants; and the knowledge of the uses, or functions of their various parts, as of the leaves, the bark, the pith, the roots, the juices, &c.; which is called the physiology of plants. It includes also an acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and climate adapted to different vegetables, their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of propagation, and the various uses to which their several parts or productions may be applied.
