Botany, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, which may be called practical botany, is subservient, and absolutely necessary to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the philosophy of botany; for no one that is unacquainted with the classification of plants can either convey to others his own information, or himself receive the benefit of that of others, respecting either the structure and economy or the habits and the uses of such plants, as may have been investigated. If medical virtues are discovered in any vegetable production; without the accuracy of the practical botanist, to ascertain and describe the particular plant which affords it, the discovery is often lost; or perhaps, what is worse, the virtues are attributed to a different plant, and it is only by repeated failures, and in some cases after much mischief, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> is detected. It is evident that the same may happen to the agriculturist, the dyer, or any other artizan, who has discovered in the vegetable kingdom the means of improving his art, but has not botanical knowledge sufficient to give an accurate character of the plant, to which he is indebted for his discovery. 3. In Mineralogy, or the natural history of the mineral kingdom, almost half the students are of that class, who content themselves with collecting, and being able to arrange systematically the minerals they meet with. But in this department of natural history, as well as the other two, which we have considered, something more than arrangement is required. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who can analyze, and separate the component parts of mineral productions; who knows the art of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a>, and who knows a priori the probable site of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, or a mine, and can tell the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a stratum of coal, or of marble, that we may call a mineralogist. The natural history of the mineral kingdom includes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">geology</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a> upon which are founded the different theories of the formation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It includes the knowledge of those facts, upon which the art of mining, and the art of separating and purifying <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, is founded; and its object is to teach likewise the properties of those metals, as well as of the earths, and other mineral productions, when separated and in their simple state. With respect to the utility of the study of natural history, we have unavoidably given many instances of it, in considering the object of the science. We need therefore add but few others. The grazier knows the advantage of attending to the habits and distinctive marks of our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals. It is natural history, though not often studied scientifically, that teaches him what variety of sheep to prefer; by what means to obtain a variety of cows, remarkable for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; how to choose the flock to the best adapted to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and what is the best food for them during winter. Much benefit is likely to accrue from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> lately paid to the cultivation of what are termed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> grasses. Instead of sowing his hay feeds indiscriminately, the grazier may select only such grasses as are, by observation, found to be most suited to his soil and cattle. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>'s knowledge of the proper succession of crops, the best times for sowing them, when to weed, and with what to manure, as well as how to destroy both weeds and insects, is the knowledge of a naturalist; and surely he who is scientifically acquainted with the growth of plants, knowing what part the soil acts in vegetation, and what is the aliment most required by them, will have great advantage over the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> empirical farmer, who has no better reason for what he does, than that his father did the same before him. By studying the natural history of insects, we learn the habits of such as are noxious and injurious, and thence derive the means of destroying them. The mineralogist has often enriched individual proprietors of land, and benefited his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, by the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; he is enabled to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the planners of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> by warning them of obstructions; and his knowledge has aided the physician in ascertaining the virtues of minerals, and of mineral waters. In the arts, a knowledge of natural history prevents confusion, and those innumerable errors that must be committed, when the natural productions which are employed cannot be accurately discriminated from others. It is to the naturalist that we are many times indebted for the introduction of foreign animals and foreign plants into our own country. Wheat, oats, barley, and other vegetables, which are now become necessary to our existence, were not originally of British growth. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>, now so general and so useful, was first introduced into this country by Gerard, a noted botanist, and was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> cultivated in his garden as a rarity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit tree, the farinaceous palms, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, have all been transported by naturalists of the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to regions where they never grew before. Besides the above, and many similar instances of advantage to be derived from studying the different branches of natural history, these two incalculable benefits necessarily arise to the student himself, from attending to the whole, or any part of the science; namely, a power of abstracting the mind, and reasoning methodically; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of contemplating the Creator in his works*. Our limits do not permit us to enter further into the fertile topic of the utility and advantages of natural history. Its utility, in a moral and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> point of view, has been ably illustrated by Mr Ray, in his "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> of God;" by Mr Bingley, in the introduction. Mode of preserving specimens. Art of preserving objects of natural history, to teach the mode of preserving specimens. This art, called by the French Taxidermie, is exceedingly curious, and would well deserve a much fuller consideration than we can here allot to it. We shall confine our attention on this subject entirely to the animal kingdom, and even here we must be very <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>. The art of preparing and mounting the skins of animals appears to be pretty old; but it made no great progress before the 17th century, when Reaumur made some attempts to preserve the specimens from the attacks of insects. In the Journal de Physique for 1773, there is a memoir addressed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by M. Kuckhan, on the methods of preparing birds, which is very curious, but is liable to many objections. In the same volume is a memoir by Mauduit, principally respecting the means of preserving animal specimens from the attacks of insects. His preservatives are of a poisonous nature; and, of course, their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is dangerous, while they do not appear to have been attended with the expected success. The arsenical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> of Beccero, much celebrated about the same time, is liable to similar objections. The latest, and probably the best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on this subject, is that published a few years ago by M. Nicolas; and from this the following observations are derived. Instruments employed. The instruments employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of specimens are much the same as those used by anatomists in their ordinary directions, consisting of small knives or scalpels, forceps or pincers of various forms, probes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, and pins or wires. Preservatives against insects. The preservatives employed by M. Nicolas to protect the specimens from insects, are principally of two kinds: 1. Sulphur, which he applies to the skins by means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUMIGATION">fumigation</a>, thus impregnating them with fulphurous acid; 2. A liquor for macerating the skins, another liquor for rubbing over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and a pomatum for anointing the inside of the skin. The first liquor is prepared by steeping a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> and a half of powdered oak bark, and four ounces of powdered <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, in twenty English pints of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, for two days, taking care to shake the mixture from time to time. The pomatum is prepared of a pound of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> soap, half a pound of caustic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, four ounces of powdered alum, two English pints of water, four ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a>, and the same of camphire. The soap, cut into small pieces, is put into an earthen pipkin, over a moderate fire; the water poured over it; and when the whole is formed into a sort of soft paste, the alum and then the oil are added; the whole well stirred together, removed from the fire, and when it is nearly cold the camphire is added; being before <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> rubbed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> with a little spirit of wine. The pomatum, thus prepared, must be kept in glass vessels, well stopp'd; and, when used, is to be lowered with water to the consistence of thin cream, and laid on the skins by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. The liquor employed for preserving the fur is prepared by infusing an ounce of white soap shred very small, two ounces of camphire broken into very small pieces, the same of colocynth or bitter-apple grofsly powdered, in two English pints of spirit of wine, for four or five days, shaking the vessel from time to time, after which the liquor is to be filtered through blotting-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. M. Nicolas has given directions for preparing and preserving specimens of all the various classes of animals. We shall, as far as our limits permit, briefly follow him through each. In skinning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, he proposes to make an incision along the middle of the back, from the haunches to the shoulders, except in those animals whose skin is quadruped, very thick and hard, or is set with spines, in which the opening must be made at the belly in the usual manner. In detaching the skin from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, we must occasionally employ the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and as we proceed, must insert tow between the skin and flesh, to prevent foiling the fur. When the whole body is detached, and the skin drawn down as far as the ankles, the nose, and the tip of the tail, the whole body is to be cut away except the head and extremities, which are left to give a better form and support to the specimen. All the fleshy and fatty parts, the brain, and the eyes, however, must be cut away, and nothing left but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, the spaces between which and the skin must be stuffed with tow cut fine, and a little soft clay must be put within the orbits, in order to fix the artificial eyes. Before stuffing, the skin is to be steeped for several days, from five to fifteen, according to the size of the animal, in the liquor first described, and after steeping, the inside is to be well anointed with the pomatum. When the legs and head are stuffed, the cavity of the skull filled with very dry moss, and the eyes fixed, wires are to be passed through the inside of the body, the extremities, and the head and tail, in the following manner. Three <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wires of a moderate size, well annealed, at least twice as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the animal, are to be twisted together for nearly half the length, and while one wire is left straight, the other two are to be bent at each end, so as to form a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. When the skin is turned, ready for stuffing, these wires are to be placed within it in such a manner as that the straight wire shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the head and tail, and the crossing wires through the extremities, coming out at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of each foot; and in this way after the cavity is filled up with tow, and the open part neatly stitched, the specimen may be fixed on a board in its natural position. Nothing remains now but to impregnate the fur with the bitter liquor last described, which is done by means of a sponge, with which the whole outside is to be well washed, then covered with folds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and dried in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>. The art of preserving birds is perhaps the most curious part of the present subject, and is that to which the most attention has been given. M. Nicolas has explained at some length the mode recommended by M. Kuckhan in the Journal de Physique; that by Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LATHAM">Latham</a>, in the Naturalist's and Traveller's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">Companion</a>; that of Mauduit, inserted in the fifth number of the Encyclopédie Methodique; and that of Dufresne, adopted by M. Daudin, and inserted in his Traité d'Ornithologie; after which he details his own. He describes three methods of preparing birds, according as we can procure fresh-killed specimens, whole dried skins brought from abroad, or detached parts of several Mode of several individuals of the same species. We shall here preserving confine ourselves to the first of these, as being best specimens, adapted to the generality of our readers. When a fresh-killed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> is procured, it is to be placed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, upon its back, with the tail turned towards the operator, who, after having separated with his fingers the feathers which cover the belly towards the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left, is to make with a scalpel, a longitudinal incision through the skin, from the point of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>-bone to about the middle of the belly. The edges of the skin are now to be raised with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of flat pincers, on each side, carefully separating the flesh as occasion may require, by the knife, and inserting a little cotton from time to time, to prevent foiling the feathers. In this way the skin is to be detached from the shoulders and neck, and as much as possible of the body laid bare, after which a pretty strong thread is to be passed through the nostrils, and tied under the lower mandible, leaving the ends of the thread when tied together, at least twice as long as the neck. Now, holding the bird by the thread, with the back turned towards him, the operator is to hold together the feathers on the two edges of the incision as well as those that cover the breast, and pushing the head of the bird inwards with his thumb so as to form the neck into an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, is to cut off near the body, detach from it the gullet and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> pipe, and all the fleshy parts, both of the neck and head, by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the skin as far back as possible towards the beak, and cutting off the neck-bones <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the head; he is to empty the skull with a little iron <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in the form of an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-pick, and clean it properly with cotton. He is now to wrap cotton or tow about the head and neck, and to separate the rest of the skin, leaving the pinions and bones of the wings, and legs, and the tail, as directed for quadrupeds. After this has been done, the skin is to be turned out like a glove, with all its feathers turned inwards, all the natural openings of the bird, as well as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>-holes, &c., made in killing the bird, are to be stitched up with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> and fine thread; then the whole skin as well as the bones, are to be washed with a strong infusion of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAN">tan</a> with a little alum, by means of a pencil-brush, and the skin inclosed in a covered vessel that it may not dry too hastily. In ten or twelve hours time we may wash the skin and bones again with the astringent liquor. Twice washing in this manner will be sufficient for very small birds, but those of a middling size will require maceration in the first liquor employed for quadrupeds during two days, and four or five days for those of larger size. The skins being well impregnated with the astringent liquor, are to be smeared with the soapy pomatum, have artificial eyes fixed in the orbits by means of wax, and stuffed and mounted much in the same manner as quadrupeds, except that the wires employed for this purpose are rather differently bended. Great nicety is required in fixing the different parts of a bird in its natural position, and in arranging the feathers smoothly and evenly. M. Nicolas directs thin plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, to be placed so as to secure the wings in the proper position till the whole is completely arranged. To preserve the feet and legs of birds, he anoints them with linseed oil mixed with camphire, and applied a little warm. The last operation consists in enveloping the bird with bandages of muslin or fine linen, pinned round the neck, breast, body, and rump, as well as to secure the feathers in their places during drying, as to allow of their being drenched with the bitter liquor to preserve them from the attacks of insects. The different orders of insects require different modes of preparation. The following is a summary of our author's mode of preserving each kind. For the coleoptera and hemiptera.—One of these insects, as soon as caught, is to be carefully wrapped in very fine paper, with the ends of the paper curled round to prevent the animal from moving; and this roll of paper, including the insect, is to be put into a little box of pasteboard till the insect-hunter returns home. Each insect is then to be held between the thumb and forefinger of the left hand, the wings to be raised by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>, and held open with the middle finger, while the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> of the animal is slit open from the back, and the entrails abstracted by means of an iron wire, and the cavity as well as the edges of the wound are to be washed with the bitter spirituous liquor described in No. 36, by means of a very fine pencil. Then a small cotton plug impregnated with oil of petroleum is to be stuffed into the cavity, with the point of a wire, till the cavity is sufficiently full, when the wings are to be suffered to return to their natural situation, and the insect is ready for mounting. For mounting these insects, M. Nicolas employs little squares of card, through the middle and across which he passes a small iron wire well annealed, and about the size of a harpsichord string. A very fine needle is now to be passed through the animal, as near as possible to the centre; and after having covered the upright iron wire with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> coating of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a>-water, he passes it through the hole made by the needle, and fixes the animal in such a manner that its feet may rest upon the card. For the lepidoptera.—He recommends them to be put, when caught, into a triangular piece of paper, and afterwards into a pasteboard box of the same form, opening with a hinge. For mounting these insects it is sufficient to perforate their bodies with a fine needle, armed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> thread impregnated with the bitter spirituous liquor, making the needle enter by the head and come out at the end of the belly, and then cutting the thread with scissors. The insect thus prepared is mounted by means of a card, as directed for the coleoptera, and a piece of wood about an inch long, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and a proper thickness, is placed below the wings on each side very near the body, and the wings are kept down by means of plates of lead. In the preparation of specimen of fisher, M. Nicolas prefers the method of Mauduit to that given by Dr Lettsom in the Naturalist's and Traveller's Companion; but as Mauduit's method requires much skill and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, he recommends the following, especially for the flat kinds of fish. He makes a longitudinal incision with scissors along the belly of the fish from the anus to the lower mandible, and then gradually and carefully separates the skin from the flesh with the assistance of the blade and flat handle of a scalpel, till he has laid bare one side of the animal. He then passes to the other side, proceeding in the same manner to detach the skin from that part, after which he separates the head from the body with a pair pair of scissors, and clears away the fleshy parts attached to the head. He now detaches the skin from the back as far as the anus, and then laying the fish on the table, he passes the flat handle of the scalpel below the skin that covers the tail and neighbouring parts, in order to separate it completely. This done, he pushes the tail inwards, and with the assistance of the scalpel and drawing the skin very gently, he detaches this as near as possible to the end of the tail, which he then separates with scissors, thus leaving the skin with nothing attached to it but the head and extremity of the tail. In only remains now to clear away the ears and eyes, and properly clean the head. The skin is now steeped for some days in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a> liquor, then laid on a table, and when the head is properly arranged, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the body of the fish made of soft clay, mixed with fine sand, is placed within the skin, which is made to fit neatly over it, is then bound with little bandages of linen, and suffered to dry. When the clay is quite dry and hard, and the skin has acquired so much firmness as to retain its proper form, it is to be gently beaten all over to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the clay, so that it may be withdrawn through the opening. When this is done, the whole inside of the skin and head is to be smeared by means of a pencil brush with the soap pomatum. After which it is to be entirely filled with cut tow, and the opening stitched up as neatly as possible. Then artificial eyes are to be placed in the orbits by means of soft wax, and the whole body is to be covered with a coat of white <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> prepared by dissolving four ounces of clear turpentine, three ounces of sandarac, and one ounce of mastic in tears, with eight ounces of oil of turpentine, and four ounces of spirit of wine, in a bottle placed in a water bath. In preparing specimens of reptiles,—after what has been said above, little direction will be required. The skin is to be stript backwards as far as the head, which is to be cut off and cleaned as in other specimens; after which the skin is to be macerated, anointed within with pomatum, stuffed and varnished as before. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRUSTACEA">crustacea</a>, including <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, lobsters, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>-fish, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-urchins, require but little preparation. In crabs the shell, and in lobsters the tail, is to be separated from the rest of the body; as much as possible of the meat is to be picked out from the body and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> claws; the whole interior is to be smeared with the soap pomatum, and after having united the parts, the whole is to be suffered to dry. The star-fish and urchins, if taken alive, should be killed by plunging them in spirit of wine, and afterwards drying them in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or in an oven moderately heated. As to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> the only mode of preserving the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>, or those with naked bodies, is to keep them in spirits; and of the testacea or shell-fish, the only part thought worth preserving is the shell; for the preparation of which, see <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a>. The above is but an imperfect <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of M. Nicolas's "Methode de preparer et conserver les Animaux de toutes les classes," which is illustrated by plates, and is well deserving the attention of collectors of specimens. There is also an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on this subject by Dufrene, under Zoödiermie, in the Nouveau Dictionnaire d'Histoire Naturelle. It will be expected that in this introductory article on natural history, we should say something of its rise and progress. Much of our observations on this subject have been anticipated in preceding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> on particular branches of natural history, so that little remains for us to do in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> than to give a general sketch of the early history of this branch of physics. We have reason to believe that the works of nature Jews have formed the favourite study among the ingenious and writers, inquisitive from the earliest ages of the world. From the continual allusions to the Creator's works, and the beautiful metaphors drawn from them, which abound in the inspired writings of the Jewish prophets and poets, especially those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a>, Isaiah, Daniel and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, we know that these sages were well acquainted with natural history, as far at least as observation extended. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, as we are told, was acquainted with all vegetables, "from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> of Lebanon to the hyssop that springeth out of the wall;" and probably if wise a man was well acquainted with the other kingdoms of nature. Some writers have gone so far as to assert that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a> learned natural history from the writings of Solomon, though on what data they ground this assertion, we are at a loss to determine. The principal writers on natural history among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, whose writings have come down to us, are Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Pliny the elder. Of the first Aristotle, we may remark with Haller, that his writings on this subject exhibit a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> chain of physical and anatomical facts, which for the most part appear to have been the result of accurate observation. He relied less than any of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> naturalists on uncertain and fabulous report; he industriously collected and examined natural bodies, and appears to have himself dissected many animals, especially fishes, or at least to have been present at their dissection. There are even to be found in his writings, references by letters to figures which he employed to illustrate his observations. Theophrastus wrote chiefly on the natural history of plants and fossils, on winds, and on fire. His works have been edited by Hainius, but, except in plants, they do not contain much that is worthy of our observation more than what is to be found in the writings of Aristotle. The natural history of Pliny is a valuable repository of ancient knowledge, which, notwithstanding all its errors and extravagances, we may venture to call after the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> of his nephew, a comprehensive and learned work, little less various than nature herself. The author, in the dedication of his work to Vespasian, sensible of the defects with which it abounds, apologizes for them, from the consideration that the path which he took had been in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> untrodden, and held forth to the traveller few enticements; while some parts of his subject had been so often handled, that readers were become cloyed with them: that it was an arduous task to give what is old an appearance of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>; to add <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and authority to what is new; to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> a lustre upon subjects that have been obscured by time; to render acceptable what is become trite and disgusting; to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to doubtful relations; and, in a word, to reprovet every thing according to nature, and with all its natural properties. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> must be acknowledged to be <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and noble, and when we consider that the work was composed in the midst of important engagements, engagements, and chiefly at broken periods stolen from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, we shall not wonder that it was imperfectly executed. The ancients had no idea of methodical or systematic distinctions. As they were acquainted with but few bodies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the moderns, and attended only to those which were useful to man; they distinguished them only by their usual properties, their native country, their habitations, and the useful purposes to which they might be applied. From the few productions which they described, they were not led to perceive the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of searching among them for distinctive marks or relations, which may prevent their being confounded with each other. They doubtless believed that their descriptions were sufficient, and that the names which they imposed would descend with their customs to posterity, without being affected by the disorders and alterations that have changed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of countries and the seat of empires. But the revolutions that have desolated the fairest regions of the globe, by inflating or displacing their inhabitants, or by confounding them with one another, and altering their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, have frequently almost extinguished the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> of science. After many ages of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and barbarity, we find in the few works of the ancient naturalists, which have escaped the ravages of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the devastations of civil <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, little more than uncertainty and obscurity, with respect to those species which they have described. Notwithstanding the labours of numerous commentators, we do not certainly know what species of plant is the *cienta* employed by the Greeks for the execution of criminals, and which terminated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. We cannot be sure that the animals, which we find best characterized in the ancient writings, bore the names which we <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them; nor are we more certain with respect to the ancient nomenclature of minerals. As long as studious men cultivated the sciences only through the medium of the writings of the ancients, and attempted nothing beyond the interpretation of these, *natural history*, like every other branch of physics, remained obscure and confused, and fiction or imagination took the place of facts; but when they perceived the advantage of studying nature herself, and interrogating her by observation, methods were created, and distinctive characters for the species introduced. This fortunate revolution took place in the 16th century. Caesalpinus first attempted to reduce vegetables to classes, and distinguish them into tribes according to their form.—Gesner, besides the fine hints that he first gave of the constant relation between the structure of the seed and that of the other parts of plants, was the first who attempted any systematic and methodical arrangement of animals. In the 17th century, Morison, Ray, and Rivinus, improved on the hints of Caesalpinus respecting the classification of vegetables; and Aldrovandus, Rhedi, and Swammerdam upon those of Gesner respecting animals; and in a short time this first impulse given to the art of arranging and distinguishing natural bodies by constant characters, was communicated to all those who were employed in the study of nature. Tournefort, profiting by all the attempts towards method and system in the classification of vegetables that had been made before him, advanced a considerable step in botany, by his beautiful method of distinguishing plants according to the form of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, which he published towards the end of the 17th century. The same year of the 18th century (1707) gave birth to two men who have advanced the science of Buffon's natural history far beyond any of their predecessors. We need scarcely mention the names of Linné and Buffon. The Swedish naturalist extended his enlarged views through every branch of natural history; he arranged in his *Systema Naturae* and *Systema Vegetabilium* all the productions of nature, and distinguished them by characters that were precise and simple; he created a new language for expressing with brevity all these characters, and thus presented to the view, as in a compendious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, all the properties of bodies. Buffon, proceeding in a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, treated more copiously the most important parts of natural history, and of the animals that are most nearly allied to man, in a work which the fire of his genius and the brilliancy of his style have rendered a universal favourite. The rival of Aristotle and Pliny, whose genius he seems to have combined in the greatness of his views and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and altogether one of the first writers of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he inspired a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for the study of nature in numbers, who without his works would never have engaged in such a study, and communicated to his countrymen that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which has ever since survived him. After what has been given in the particular treatises on natural history in this Encyclopedia, both as to the progress of the science, and the principal works on each department of it, since the time of Linné and Buffon; it is unnecessary for us to trace its progress beyond that period. The advances made within these few years are immense, our stock of information is prodigiously increased, and the modes of study greatly improved and facilitated. The labours of Cuvier, Geoffroy, Lacépéde, Dumont, Dumeril, Lamarck, Duvernois, Sonnini, Bloch, Spallanzani, Esper, Jussieu, Wildenow, Werner, Patrin, St Fond, Brochant, Brongniart, Klaproth, Fourcroy, Vauquelin, Shaw, Latham, Bancroft, Cateby, Ellis, Smith, Withering, Woodville, Kirwan, Playfair, Thomson, Jameston, &c., with the assistance to be derived from the *Annales de Muséum National*, the *Naturalist's Miscellany*, the *Linnean Transactions*, and the splendid plates of Merian, Schreber, Curtis, Sowerby, Sotheby, &c., afford ample proofs of the industry and success with which this delightful field has been cultivated, and of the rich <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> that has been derived from the united efforts of so many men of genius and talents. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">NATURAL Philosophy</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> defined to be that branch of knowledge which considers the powers and properties of natural bodies, and their mutual actions on one another. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral philosophy</a> is the mind of man; its inquiries and researches are into the intellectual world. Natural philosophy, on the other hand, is only concerned with the material part of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. The Moralist's business is to inquire into the nature of virtue, the causes and effects of vice; to propose remedies for it, and to point out the mode of attaining <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, which only can be the result of virtuous conduct. The Naturalist, on the contrary, has nothing to do with spirit; his business is solely about body or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; and he ought to have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and accurate knowledge of all material substances, together with their affections and properties; and if possible, he is to investigate the reasons of such and such appearances.—Indeed, the first and principal part of this science is, to collect all the manifest and sensible appearances of things, and reduce them into a body of natural history. Philosophy has often been said, and is even now very generally thought, to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> an inquiry into all the causes of things; but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> informs us, that though we are acquainted with a good number of effects, we can trace but few of their causes; so that philosophy itself will really be found to be in general but a collection of facts. Still, however, it differs from natural history in its appropriated sense; the business of which is only to observe the appearances of natural bodies separately, and from these appearances to classify them with other bodies: natural philosophy goes farther, and recites the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of two or more bodies of the same or different kinds upon one another; and though it can neither investigate nor point out the causes of those effects, whatever they are, yet, from mathematical reasoning combined with experience, it can be demonstrated, that in such circumstances such effects must always take place. There are evidently two ways of making observations on the material world: the first is, when we view things nearly as they happen to occur, without any design or intervention of our own; in which way, indeed, no great improvements can be expected in the art, because chance having the direction, only exhibits occasional or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> properties. The other method is, when, after a thorough acquaintance with bodies, we apply them to other bodies equally known, diligently attending to the result, and observing whether any thing new arises. Such seems to be in general the nature of our article; nor is it our intention to be much more particular at present. We must therefore refer our readers respectively to those parts of the subject, respecting which they wish for more satisfaction and minuter details. The ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> definitions of the word philosophy, together with its origin, as well as the manner of philosophizing in former times as well as at present, with the gradual improvement of science, particularly natural, we shall introduce, we think, more properly, under the words PHILOSOPHY and PHYSICS. We need only add, under the present article, what however is well known, that natural philosophy was till lately divided only into four parts, commonly called the four branches, viz. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>; 2. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a>; 3. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>; and, 4. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>; and these again are subdivided into various parts. Modern discoveries have added, however, two more parts to the number, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>. It is remarkable, that in the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> these two latter branches are never taken notice of in lecturing on natural philosophy, the old <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> being still retained, without any mention of these two important articles. The reason may be, that they are only subject to experiment, and not yet reduced to mathematical reasoning; which is the method of teaching philosophy in one of those celebrated seminaries. Of these branches of this extensive science, it is not our intention to take even a general view in this place. We must therefore refer our readers to each particular article, where they will find them treated at considerable length.

NATURALISATION

Pages 701-701

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of naturalizing an alien, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> putting him into the condition of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>-born subject, and entitling him to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges thereof. But none can be naturalized unless they have received the sacrament within one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> before the bringing in of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>, and taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> and supremacy in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. A person who is naturalized may have lands by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, as heir at law, as well as obtain them by purchase; but he is disabled from being a member of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> or parliament; or from holding offices, 7 Jac. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2. 12 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">Will</a>. III. cap. 2. All children born out of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s dominions, whose fathers were or are subjects of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their birth, are adjudged to be natural born subjects of this realm, except children of parents attainted of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, or that are in the actual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> at enmity with us, 4 Geo. II. cap. 21. Every foreign scaman, who in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> serves two years on board an English ship, is ipso facto naturalized, 13 Geo. II. cap. 3. And all foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Jews, upon their residing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in any of the British colonies, without being absent above two months at a time, or serving two years in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity there, are upon taking the oaths naturalized to all intents and purposes, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been born in this kingdom; and therefore are admissible to all such privileges, and no other, as Protestants or Jews born in this kingdom are entitled to. See ALIEN and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENIZEN">DENIZEN</a>. In France before the Revolution, naturalization was the king's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>; in England it is only done by act of parliament. In the former of those places, before their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was overturned, Swiss, Savoyards, and Scots, did not require naturalization, being reputed regnicoles, or natives.

NATURALS

Pages 701-701

among physicians, whatever naturally belongs to an animal, in opposition to non-naturals. See NON-NATURALS.

NATURE

Pages 701-702

according to Mr Boyle, has eight different significations; it being used, 1. For the author of nature, whom the schoolmen call Natura Naturans, being the same with God. 2. By the nature of a thing, we sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> its essence; that is, the attributes which make it what it is, whether the thing be corporeal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not; as when we attempt to define the nature of a fluid, of a triangle, &c. 3. Sometimes we confound that which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has by nature with what accrues to him by birth; as when we say, that such a man is noble by nature. 4. Sometimes we take nature for an internal principle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; as when we say, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> by nature falls to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Sometimes we understand by nature, the established course of things. 6. Sometimes we take nature for an aggregate of powers belonging to a body, especially a living one; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> physicians say, that nature is strong, weak, or spent; or that, in such or such diseases, nature left to herself <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> perform the cure. 7. Sometimes we <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> nature for the universe, or whole system of the corporeal works of God; as when it is said of a phoenix, or chimera, that there is no such thing in nature. 8. Sometimes too, and that most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a>, we express by the word nature, a kind of semi-deity, or other strange kind of being. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, says the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, I were to propose a notion of nature, less ambiguous than these already mentioned, and with regard to which many axioms relating to that word may be conveniently understood, I should first distinguish between the universal and the particular nature of things. Universal nature I would define to be the aggregate of the bodies that make up the world in its present state, considered as a principle, by virtue whereof they <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> and suffer, according to the laws of motion prescribed by the Author of all things. And this makes way for the other subordinate notion; since the particular nature of an individual consists in the general nature applied to a distinct portion of the universe; or, which is the same thing, it is a particular assemblage of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> properties of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, motion, &c. Kingdoms of Nature. See Kingdoms. Conduct or Operations of Nature. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>.

NAUCRARI

Pages 703-703

among the Athenians, was the name given to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates of the *demos*, "boroughs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> townships," called *navergaei*; because each was obliged, besides two horsemen, to furnish out one ship for the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

NAUCRATES

Pages 703-703

a Greek poet, who was employed by Artcmisia to write a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> upon Mausolus.—An orator who endeavoured to alienate the cities of Lycia from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Brutus.

NAUCRATIS

Pages 703-703

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> on the left side of the Canopic mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. It was celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and no ship was permitted to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> at any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but was obliged to sail directly to the city, there to deposit its cargo. It gave birth to Athenaeus.

NAUCRATITES NOMOS

Pages 703-703

in *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>* (Pliny); a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the Delta, so called from that town Naucratis; though <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> comprises it under the Nomos Saites.

NAUCYDES

Pages 703-703

a statuary who lived about four centuries before the Christian era.

NAULUM

Pages 806-806

in Roman antiquity, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> put into the mouth of a person deceased to enable him to pay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> the ferryman for his passage. It was to be of the current <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> of the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; so that from this money the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the person’s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> may be known. The sum for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> men was a farthing, but the rich in general were very liberal to Charon, as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of coins often found in the neighbourhood of Rome on opening the graves of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. Charon was looked upon as a very morose and obstinate old fellow, who would not carry over any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> without his fare: and hence the proverbial <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> in Juvenal, Furor eft poft omnia perdere naulum. A similar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the Greeks: The money put into the mouth of the deceased was by them called Δανάειον.

NAUMACHIA

Pages 806-809

in antiquity, a show <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spectacle among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, representing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fight. These mock sea fights are supposed to have originated at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, when the Romans first instructed their men in the knowledge of naval affairs. Afterwards they were intended to entertain the populace, as well as to improve the seamen. They were often, like other shows, exhibited at the expense of individuals, to increase their popularity. In these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> they sometimes strove to excel each other in swiftness; and sometimes engaged in a warlike manner. The naumachiae of Claudius indeed was a most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> diversion. The combatants used to destroy each other to amuse a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> and a cruel mob. As they passed before him, they used this melancholy greeting, "Ave Imperator, moriatur te salutant." The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> replied, "Avete vos." This they understood as an answer of kindness, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of their lives; but they soon discovered that it proceeded from wanton cruelty, and barbarous insensibility. In the time of the emperor Domitian, such a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vessels engaged as would have nearly formed two regular fleets for a real fight, and the channel of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> was equal in magnitude to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> river. The emperor Heliogabalus is reported to have filled the channel where the vessels were to ride with wine instead of water. Tritons and sea monsters were frequently exhibited during the engagement. Suetonius and Dio Cassius inform us, that at one of these sea fights of Domitian a violent shower fell; the emperor, however, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the end of the engagement, often changing his clothes, nor would he suffer any one to depart; and as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> continued for several hours, many were seized with distempers, and some even died, Suet. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 4. Dio. lib. lxvii. Naumachiae were also places fitted up for these shows, a fort of circi or amphitheatres, with seats and porticoes, &c. There were several of them at Rome; three built by Augustus, one by Claudius, another by Domitian, and another by Nero; which served for the reverse of his medals. Claudius used the lake Fucinus as a naumachia.

NAUMBURG

Pages 809-809

a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Saxe-Naumburg, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALA">Sala</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 20'. N. Lat. 51° 12'.

NAUPACTUS

Pages 809-809
or NAUPACTUM, in Ancient Geography, a city of Aetolia, at the mouth of the Evenus. The word is derived from ναῦς and ἀναγράφειν, because it was there that the Heraclidae built the first ship which carried them to Peloponnesus. It first belonged to the Locri Ozolae, and afterwards fell into the hands of the Athenians, who gave it to the Messenians, who had been driven from Peloponnesus by the Lacedaemonians. It became the property of the Lacedaemonians after the battle of Egoptomos, and it was restored to the Locri. Philip of Macedon afterwards took it, and gave it to the Aetolians; from which circumstance it has generally been called one of the chief cities of their country. E. Long. 22° 20'. N. Lat. 38° 0'. There was on the shore a temple of Neptune, and near it a cave filled with offerings, and dedicated to Venus, where widows resorted to request new husbands of the goddess. Pausan. lib. x. p. 898.

NAUPLIA

Pages 809-809

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. It was the naval station of the Argives. The fountain Canathos was in its neighbourhood.

NAUPLIUS

Pages 809-809

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a son of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> and Amyone, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Euboea. He was the father of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALAMEDES">Palamedes</a>, who was so unjustly sacrificed to the artifice and resentment of Ulysses by the Greeks at the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Palamedes highly enraged Nauplius; and to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the injustice of the Grecian princes, he endeavoured to debauch their wives, and ruin their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. When the Greeks returned from the Trojan war, Nauplius was pleased to see them distressed in a storm on the coasts of Euboea; and to make their disaster still more universal, he lighted fires on such places as were surrounded with the most dangerous rocks, that the fleet might be shipwrecked upon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. This had the desired effect; but Nauplius was so disappointed when he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Ulysses and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a> escape from the general distress, that he threw himself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. According to some mythologists there were two persons of this name: one a native of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, who went to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> with Jason. He was son of Neptune and Amyone.—The other was king of Euboea, and lived about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Trojan war. He was, as some observe, son of Clytonas, one of the descendants of Nauplius the Argonaut. The Argonaut was remarkable for his knowledge of sea affairs and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He built the town of Nauplia, and sold Auge <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Aleus to King Teuthras, to screen her from her father's resentment.

NAUPORTUS

Pages 809-809
or NAUPORTUM, in Ancient Geography, a town on a cognominal river, towards its source, in Pannonia Superior. The reason of the name, according to Pliny, is that the ship Argo, after coming up the Danube, the Save, and the Laubach, was thence carried on men's shoulders over the Alps into the Adriatic. The river Nauportus rises in the Alps, near Longaticum, at the distance of six miles from the town Nauportum; which was a colony of the Taurisci, a people on the confines of Noricum. Now Upper Laubach in Carinthia, on the river Laubach. E. Long. 14° 40'. N. Lat. 46° 28'.

NAUSCOPY

Pages 809-809

the art of discovering the approach of ships <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> at a considerable distance. This pretended art was discovered by M. Bottineau, employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of France, from the year 1782 to 1784; the account of it is as follows: "This knowledge is not derived either from the undulation of the waves, or from the subtlety of sight, or from any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; but merely from observation of the horizon, which discovers signs indicating the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> of ships or of land. "On the approximation of a ship toward the land, or towards another ship, there appears in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a> of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, visible to everyone without any painful <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. It is not by any kind of accident that this meteor appears under these circumstances; on the contrary, it is the necessary result of the approximation of one vessel towards another, or towards the land. The existence of the meteor, and the knowledge of its different modifications, are what constitute the certainty and the precision of my informations. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> I am asked, how it is possible that the approach of a ship towards land should give birth to any meteor whatsoever in the atmosphere, and what connexion there can be between two objects at such a distance from each other? I reply, that I am not obliged to give an account of the hows and the wherefores; that it is sufficient for me to have discovered the fact, without being obliged to account for its principle." The writer concludes, by desiring to be called on for experimental proofs, and by promising in future a complete treatise of Nauscopy, with maps, plates, &c.

NAUSEA

Pages 809-810
or SICKNESS; a retching or propensity and endeavour to vomit, arising from something which irritates the stomach.

NAUTILUS

Pages 810-810

a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes testacea. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NAVAL

Pages 702-702

something relating to a ship; whence, NAVAL <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. See SHIP-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>. NAVAL <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>, in antiquity, a fortification, consisting of a ditch and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a wall built in the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, and extended from one point of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to another. This was sometimes defended with towers, and beautified with gates, through which they issued forth to attack their enemies. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> hath left us a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Grecian fortifications of this sort, in the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, beginning at ver. 436. Iliad ii. Then, to secure the naval camp and powers, They rais'd embattled walls with lofty towers: From space to space were ample gates around, For passing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>; and a trench profound, Of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and deep in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> below Strong piles infix'd stood adverse to the foe. POPE'S Transl. Towards the sea, or within it, they fixed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pales of wood, like those in their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> harbours: before these the vessels of burden were placed in such order as that they might be instead of a wall, and give protection to those within; in which manner Nicias is reported by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> to have encamped himself; but this seems only to have been practised when the enemy was thought superior in strength, and raised great apprehensions of danger in them. When their fortifications were thought strong enough to defend them from the assaults of enemies, it was frequent to drag their ships to shore, which the Greeks called navas, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> fulvocere. Around the ships the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> disposed their tents, as appears everywhere in Homer: but this seems only to have been practised in winter, when their enemy's fleet was laid up and could not assault them; or in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> sieges, and when they lay in no danger from their enemies by sea; as in the Trojan war, where the defenders of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> never once attempted to encounter the Grecians in a sea-fight. The adjacent places were usually filled with inns and stews, well stocked with females, that prostituted themselves to the mariners, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and artificers of all sorts, who flocked thither in great numbers; this, however, appears to have happened only in times of peace. NAVAL <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Romans, a crown adorned with figures of prows of ships, conferred on persons who in sea engagements first boarded the enemy's vessel. See CROWN. NAVAL Engagement. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TACTICS">Tactics</a>, Naval. NAVAL Stores, comprehend all those particulars made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, not only in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, but in every other kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> for shipping, pitch, tar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, cordage, sail cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, ordnance, and fire arms of every sort, ship chandlery wares, &c. NAVAL Tactics, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> operations of fleets. See Tactics, Naval.

NAVAN

Pages 702-702

a borough town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a>; situated about 23 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, on the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>. It consists of two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> streets, which intersect each other at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>.—The tholse, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> town <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was formerly in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute, and walled in by Hugh de Lacy. An <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> for regular canons, dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, was erected here; but whether antecedent to the end of the 12th century is not certain: about that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, however, it was either founded or re-edified by Joceline de Angulo or Nangle. In the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> ground are the remains of many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> tombs. A barrack for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> is now built on the site of the abbey.

NAVARRA

Pages 702-703

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Navarre, erected soon after the invasion of the Moors; and is otherwise called Upper Navarre, to distinguish it from Lower Navarre belonging to the French. It is bounded on the south and east by Arragon, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Pyrenees, and on the west by Old Castile and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>; extending from south to north about 80 miles, from east to west about 75. It abounds in sheep and cattle; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> of all kinds, as boars, flags, and roebucks; and in wild fowl, horses, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>; yielding also some grain, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and a variety of minerals, medicinal waters, and hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. Some of the ancient chiefs of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> were called Sobrarbores, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, as it is supposed, which prevailed among some of those free nations, of choosing and swearing their Navarre, their princes under some particular tree. The name of the province is supposed to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of *Nava Errea*, signifying, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Vaforones, its ancient inhabitants, "a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of valleys." For the particulars of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, see the article Spain. **Navarre, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>**, an officer of eminence in the 16th century, and particularly celebrated for his dexterity in the directing and springing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. He was a native of Biscay, and of low <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. According to Paul Jove, who affirms that he had an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from his own mouth, he was first a sailor; but being disgusted with that employment, he sought his fortune in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, when poverty compelled him to become footman to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of Arragon. He afterwards enlisted himself a soldier in the Hougline <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; and having served there for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, went to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> again, and distinguished himself by his courage. The reputation of his valour having reached the ears of Gonzalo de Cordova, this general employed him in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>. Having contributed greatly to the taking of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> by very opportunely springing a mine, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> rewarded him for this signal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> with the earldom of Alveto, situated in that kingdom, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of Navarre. Having the command of a naval expedition against the Moors in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, he was at first very successful, and took possession of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and some other places; but being afterwards shipwrecked on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Gerbes, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heats and the Moorish cavalry destroyed a part of his army. Our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> was equally unfortunate in Italy: He was made prisoner at the famous <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> in 1512, and languished in France for the space of two years. When finding that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Spain, who had been prejudiced against him by his courtiers, would do nothing towards his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>, he went into the service of Francis I, who gave him the command of 20 companies of infantry, consisting of Gascons, Biscayans, and the inhabitants of the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. He distinguished himself in several successful expeditions, until the year 1522, when having been sent to the relief of the Genoese, he was taken by the Imperialists. They conducted him to Naples, where he remained a prisoner for three years in the Castel del Ovo. From this confinement he was released by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, and afterwards fought at the siege of Naples under Lauric in 1528: but being again made prisoner at the unfortunate retreat from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AVERSA">Aversa</a>, he was conducted a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time to the Castel del Ovo. Here the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, having by order of the emperor, caused several persons of the Angevine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> to be beheaded, our hero would undoubtedly have suffered the same fate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the governor, seeing his distressed situation, and feeling for the misfortunes of so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, had not saved him the shame of this last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> by allowing him to die a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Others pretend that he was strangled in his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, having arrived at a very advanced <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Paul Jove and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Thomasini have written his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.
