"And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene." We find no particular place in the prophets in which it is said that the Messiah should be called a Nazarene; and St Matthew only quotes the prophets in general. Perhaps he would intimate, that the consecration of the Nazarites, and the great purity of which they made profession, was a type and a sort of prophecy of those of our Saviour, or else that the name נזיר Nazir or Nazarite given to the patriarch Joseph, Gen. xlii. 26. Deut. xxxiii. 16. was a prophecy which was to be fulfilled in the person of Jesus Christ, of whom Joseph was a figure. Lastly, St Jerome was of opinion, that St Matthew here alludes to that passage of Isaiah xi. 1. and lx. 21. "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a branch (in Hebrew Nezer) shall grow out of his roots." This branch or Nezer, and this rod, are certainly intended to denote Jesus Christ, by the general consent of all the fathers and interpreters. When the word Nazarean is put for the heretics known by this name, it denotes Christians converted from Judaism, whose chief error consisted in defending the necessity or expediency of the works of the law, and who obstinately adhered to the practice of the Jewish ceremonies. The name of Nazarenes at first had nothing odious in it, and it was often given to the first Christians. The fathers frequently mention the gospel of the Nazarenes, which differs nothing from that of St Matthew, which was either in Hebrew or Syriac, for the use of the first converts, but was afterwards corrupted by the Ebionites. These Nazareans preserved this first gospel in its primitive purity. Some of them were still in being in the time of St Jerome, who does not reproach them with any error. They were very zealous observers of the law of Moses, but held the traditions of the Pharisees in very great contempt. Nazarite, when put to signify those under the ancient law who made a vow of observing a more than ordinary degree of purity (Numb. ubi cit.), denotes a man or woman who engage themselves by a vow to abstain from wine and all intoxicating liquors, to let their hair grow without cutting or shaving, not to enter into any house that was polluted by having a dead corpse in it, nor to be present at any funeral. And if by chance any one should have died in their presence, they began again the whole ceremony of their consecration and Nazariteship. This ceremony generally lasted eight days, sometimes a month, and sometimes their whole lives. When the time of their Nazariteship... Nazarite ship was accomplished, the priest brought the person to the door of the temple, who there offered to the Lord a he lamb for a burnt-offering, a he lamb for an expiatory sacrifice, and a ram for a peace-offering. They offered likewise loaves and cakes, with wine neccesary for the libations. After all this was sacrificed and offered to the Lord, the priest or some other shaved the head of the Nazarite at the door of the tabernacle, and burnt his hair, throwing it upon the fire of the altar. Then the priest put into the hand of the Nazarite the shoulder of the ram roasted, with a loaf and a cake, which the Nazarite returning into the hands of the priest, he offered them to the Lord, lifting them up in the presence of the Nazarite. And from this time he might again drink wine, his Nazariteship being now accomplished. As to those that were perpetual Nazarites, as were Samson and John the Baptist, it appears that they were consecrated to their Nazariteship by their parents, and continued all their lives in this state without drinking wine or cutting their hair. Those that made a vow of Nazariteship out of Palestine, and could not come to the temple when their vow was expired, contented themselves with observing the abstinence required by the law, and after that cutting their hair in the place where they were: as to the offerings and sacrifices prescribed by Moses, which were to be offered at the temple by themselves, or by others for them, they deferred this till they could have a convenient opportunity. Hence it was, that St Paul being at Corinth, and having made the vow of a Nazarite, he had his hair cut off at Cenchrea, and put off fulfilling the rest of his vow till he should arrive at Jerusalem, Acts xviii., 18. When a person found that he was not in a condition to make a vow of Nazariteship, or had not leisure to perform the ceremonies belonging to it, he contented himself by contributing to the expense of the sacrifice and offerings of those that had made and fulfilled this vow; and by this means he became a partaker in the merit of such Nazariteship. When St Paul came to Jerusalem, in the year of Christ 58, the apostle St James the Less, with the other brethren, said to him, Acts xxi. 23, 24, that to quiet the minds of the converted Jews, who had been informed that he everywhere preached up the entire abolition of the law of Moses, he ought to join himself to four of the faithful who had a vow of Nazariteship upon them, and contribute to the charge of the ceremony at the shaving of their heads; by which the new converts would perceive that he continued to keep the law, and that what they had heard of him was not true. The Hebrew word Nazir, or Nazarite, which is made use of to express a man exalted to great dignity, as it is said of the patriarch Joseph, Gen. xlii. 26, and Deut. xxiii. 16, "that he was separated from his brethren," as it is in our translation; or as the Vulgate and others understand the Hebrew, "that he was a Nazarite among his brethren," is variously understood. Some think that the Hebrew word נזיר, Nazir, in these places, signifies one who is crowned, chosen, separated, or distinguished; the word כתר, Nazir, signifies a crown. The Septuagint translate this word a chief, or him that is honoured. Calmet thinks that this was a term of dignity in the courts of eastern princes, and that at this day in the court of Persia the word Nazir signifies the superintendent-general of the king's household, the chief officer of the crown, the high steward of his family, treasurers, and revenues; and that in this sense Joseph was the Nazir of the court of Pharaoh. Le Clerc translates the Nazir, a prince, and calls Joseph "the prince of his brethren," in the two places already quoted. Mr Pool declares in favour of this last translation. See Joseph, Chardin, Chrysost. St Jerome, &c. NAZIANZEN See GREGORY Nazianzen.

NAZIM

Pages 813-813

the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, viceroy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governor of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in Hindoostan; the same as Subahdar, or Nabob.

NEALED

Pages 813-813

among seamen, is used when the founding is deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the shore; as also when the shore is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, clayey, oozy, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> foul and rocky ground.

NEALING

Pages 813-813
or rather Annealing, a term used for the preparing of several matters, by heating or baking them in the oven, or the like. NEALING of glass, is the baking of glass, to dry, harden, and give it the due consistence, after it has been blown, and fashioned into the proper works.—This is usually performed in a kind of a tower called the leer, built over the melting furnace. See Glass. Nealing of glass is also used for the art of staining glass with metallic colours. "One fine use of silver (says Mr Boyle) was only discovered since the art of annealing upon glass came to be practised. For prepared silver, or even the crude metal, being burnt on a glass plate, will tinge it of a fine yellow or golden colour. And there are several mineral earths, and other coarse matters, of use in this art, which by means of fire impart transparent colours to glass, and sometimes very different ones from those of the bodies themselves. NEALING of steel, is the heating it in the fire to a blood-red heat, and then taking it out, and letting it cool gently of itself. This is done to make it softer, in order to engrave and punch upon it. See Tempering and Engraving. NEALING is also used for the art or act of burning or baking earthen or other ware in an oven. The miners at Mendip, when they meet with a rock they cannot cut through, anneal it by laying on wood and coal, and contriving the fire so that they quit the mine before the operation begins, it being dangerous to enter it again before it be quite cleared of the smoke. NEALING of tile is used in ancient statutes for the burning of tile. The word is formed of the Saxon onelan, accendere, to light, burn. NEAP or NEEP TIDES, are those tides which happen when the moon is in the middle of the second and fourth quarters. The neap tides are low tides, in respect of their opposites the spring tides. As the highest of the spring tides is three days after the full or change, so the lowest of the neap is four days before the full or change. On which occasion the seamen say that it is deep neap. NEAPED. When a ship wants water, so that she cannot get out of the harbour, off the ground, or out of the dock, the seamen say she is neaped, or beneaped.

NEAPOLIS

Pages 813-814

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, in the Nomos Panopolitanus, between Thebes to the south, and Panopolis to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, on the east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; otherwise called Caerne. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Neapolis second Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>, situated near the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> on the south side.—A third of Campania, an ancient town and a colony from Cumae. (See Velleius, Pliny, Strabo;) accounted a Greek city, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stickler for Greek usages. (See Livy, Tacitus.) Its hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> were in nothing inferior to those of Baiae, according to Strabo; at two miles distance from it stands the monument of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, held in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> veneration by learned posterity. The Younger Pliny relates, that Virgil's birth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> was more religiously observed by Silius Italicus than his own, especially at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, where he referred to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> as to a temple. The city is washed by the river Sebethus. Virgil feigns the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Sebethis to preside over the stream. Now Naples, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of that name. See Naples. A fourth, Neapolis of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, near the Meander. (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>.)—A fifth, an inland town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRENAICA">Cyrenaica</a>, situated between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMAIS">Ptolemais</a> and Arsinoe, (Ptolemy;) and to be distinguished from the Caenopolis, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Neapolis, on the east border of the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, (id.) A sixth of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, (Strabo;) which belonged first to the Ephesians, but afterwards to the Samians, who exchanged Marathrum, a more distant city, for a nearer.—A seventh, Napolis of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> Adjecta, situated at the distance of 12 miles to the east of Philippi, (Antonine.)—An eighth, Neapolis of Pisdia, on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALATIA">Galatia</a>, situated between Amblada and Pappa, (Ptolemy.)—A ninth of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, the ancient Sichem, which see; so called upon its restoration by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">Coin</a>, Pliny, Josephus.)—A tenth of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, situated on the south-west side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 30 miles to the north of Metalla; now called Neapoli.—An eleventh, of the Regio Syrtica, called also Lepcis.—A twelfth, of Zeugitana on the Mediterranean, to the east of Cyprea, and south of the Promontorium Mercurii.

NEBEL

Pages 814-814
or NABLUM, a musical instrument among the Jews. See Nablum.

NEBIO

Pages 814-814
or Nebbio, a ruined city of Italy, on the north side of the island of Corsica, with a bishop's see, whose bishop resides at San Fiorenzo, from which it is a mile distant.

NEBO

Pages 814-814

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Abarim, and their highest top, whither Moses was ordered to ascend to take a view of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, and there die. Situated in the land of Moab over against <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>: with a cognominal town at its foot (Ilaiah) belonging to the Reubenites, which afterwards returned to the Moabites; in Jerome's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> desolate; eight miles to the south of Heshbon.

NEBULY

Pages 814-814
or Nebulee, in Heraldry, is when a coat is charged with several little figures, in form of words running within one another, or when the outline of a bordure, ordinary, &c. is indented or waved.

NECESSITY

Pages 815-816

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, as it implies a defect of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, excuses from the guilt of crimes. See CRIME. Compulsion and inevitable necessity are a constraint upon the will, whereby a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is urged to do that which his judgment disapproves; and which, it is to be presumed, his will (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> left to itself) would reject. As punishments are therefore only inflicted for the abuse of that free will which God has given to man, it is highly <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and equitable that a man should be excused for those acts which are done through unavoidable force and compulsion. 1. Of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, is the obligation of civil subjection, whereby the inferior is constrained by the superior to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> contrary to what his own reason and inclination would suggest: as when a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> establishes iniquity by a law, and commands the subject to do an act contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> found morality. How far this excuse will be admitted in furo conscientiae, or whether the inferior in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is not bound to obey the divine rather than the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> law, it is not our business to decide; though, among the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it is believed the question will hardly bear a doubt. But, however that may be, obedience to the laws in being is undoubtedly a sufficient extenuation of civil guilt before the municipal tribunal. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> who burnt Latimer and Ridley, in the bigotted days of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, was not liable to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> for executing so horrid an office; being justified by the commands of that magistracy which endeavoured to restore <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a>, under the holy auspices of its merciless sifter, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">Persecution</a>. As to persons in private relations, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> case where constraint of a superior is allowed as an excuse for criminal misconduct, is with regard to the matrimonial subjection of the wife to her husband: for neither a son nor a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> are excused from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of any crime, whether <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> or otherwise, by the command or coercion of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; though in some cases the command or authority of the husband, either express or implied, will privilege the wife from punishment, even from capital offences. And therefore, if a woman commit theft, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGLARY">burglary</a>, or other civil offences against the law of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, by the coercion of her husband, or even in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, which the law construes a coercion, she is not guilty of any crime; being considered as acting by compulsion, and not of her own will. This doctrine is at least 1000 years old in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, being to be found among the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Ina the West Saxon. And it appears, that among the northern nations on the continent, this privilege extended to any woman transgressing in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with a man, and to any servant that committed a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> offence with a freeman: the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> or freeman only was punished, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> or slave dismissed; procul dubio quod alterum libertas, alterum necessitas impellere. But (besides that, in our law, which is a stranger to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, no impunity is given to servants, who are as much free agents as their masters) even with regard to wives, this rule admits of an exception in crimes that are mala in se, and prohibited by the law of nature; as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, and the like: not only because these are of a deeper dye, but also, since in a state of nature no one is in subjection to another, it would be unreasonable to screen an offender from the punishment due to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> crimes, by the refinements and subdivisions of civil society. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> also (the highest crime which a member of society can, as such, be guilty of), no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> in coverture shall excuse the wife; no presumption of the husband's coercion shall extenuate her guilt: as well because of the odiousness and dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the crime itself, as because the husband, having broken through the most sacred tie of social <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> by rebellion against the state, has no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to that obedience from a wife, which he himself as a subject has forgotten to pay. In inferior misdemeanours also, we may remark another exception, that a wife may be indicted and set in the pillory with her husband, for keeping a brothel: for this is an offence touching the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in which the wife has a principal share; and is also such an offence as the law presumes to be generally conducted by the intrigues of the female <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. And in all cases where the wife offends alone, without the company or coercion of her husband, she is responsible for her offence as much as any female. 2. Another <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of compulsion or necessity is what our law calls durefs per minus; or threats and menaces, which induce a fear of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or other bodily harm, and which take away for that reason the guilt of many crimes and misdemeanors, at least before the human tribunal. But then that fear which compels a man to do an unwarrantable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> ought to be just and well grounded; such, "qui cadere posset in virum confusum, non timidum et meticulo sum," as Bracton expresses it in the words of the civil law. Therefore in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> or rebellion, a man may be justified in doing many treasonable acts by compulsion of the enemy or rebels, which would admit of no excuse in the time of peace. This, however, seems only, or at least principally, to hold as to positive crimes, so created by the laws of society, and which therefore society may excuse; but not as to natural offences, so declared by the law of God, wherein human magistrates are only the executioners of divine punishment. And therefore though a man be violently assaulted, and hath no other possible means of escaping death but by killing an innocent person, this fear and force shall not acquit him of murder; for he ought rather to die himself than escape by the murder of an innocent. But in such a case he is permitted to kill the assailant; for there the law of nature, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-<a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> its primary canon, have made him his own protector. 3. There is a third species of necessity, which may be distinguished from the actual compulsion of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force or fear; being the result of reason and reflection, which act upon and constrain a man's will, and oblige him to do an action which without such obligation would be criminal. And that is, when a man has his choice of two evils set before him, and being under a necessity of choosing one, he chooses the least pernicious Necesity, pernicious of the two. Here the will cannot be said freely to exert itself, being rather <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>; or, if active, it is rather in rejecting the greater evil than in choosing the less. Of this sort is that necessity, where a man by the commandment of the law is bound to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> another for any capital offence, or to disperse a riot, and resistance is made to his authority: it is here justifiable, and even necessary, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a>, to wound, or perhaps to kill the offenders, rather than permit the murderer to escape, or the riot to continue. For the preservation of the peace of the kingdom, and the apprehending of notorious malefactors, are of the utmost consequence to the public; and therefore excuse the felony, which the killing would otherwise amount to. 4. There is yet another case of necessity, which has occasioned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> speculation among the writers upon general law; viz. whether a man in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> want of food or clothing may justify stealing either, to relieve his present necessities. And this both Grotius and Puffendorf, together with many other of the foreign jurists, hold in the affirmative; maintaining by many ingenious, humane, and plausible reasons, that in such cases the community of goods, by a kind of tacit concession of society, is revived. And some even of our lawyers have held the same; though it seems to be an unwarranted doctrine, borrowed from the notions of some civilians; at least it is now antiquated, the law of England admitting no such excuse at present. And this its doctrine is agreeable not only to the sentiments of many of the wisest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, particularly Cicero, who holds, That si quis cuicum inconveniens verendum est, potius quam de alterius commodis detractandum est; but also to the Jewish law, as certified by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> himself: "If a thief steal to satisfy his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> when he is hungry, he shall restore sevenfold, and shall give all the substance of his house;" which was the ordinary punishment for theft in that kingdom. And this is founded upon the highest reason: for men's properties would be under a strange insecurity, if liable to be invaded according to the wants of others; of which wants no man can possibly be an adequate judge but the party himself who pleads them. In England especially, there would be a peculiar impropriety in admitting so dubious an abuse: for by the laws such sufficient provision is made for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> by the power of the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, that it is impossible that the most needy stranger should ever be reduced to the necessity of thieving to support nature. The case of a stranger is, by the way, the strongest instance put to Baron Puffendorf, and whereon he builds his principal arguments: which, however they may hold upon the continent, where the parsimonious industry of the natives orders every one to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> or starve, yet must lose all their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and efficacy in England, where <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> is reduced to a system, and interwoven in our very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. Therefore our laws ought by no means to be taxed with being unmerciful, for denying this privilege to the necessitous; especially when we consider, that the king, on the representation of his ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, hath a power to soften the law, and to extend mercy in cases of peculiar hardship. An advantage which is wanting in many states, particularly those which are democratical; and these have in its stead introduced and adopted, in the body of the law itself, a multitude of circumstances tending to alleviate its rigour. But the founders of our constitution thought it better to vest in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the power of pardoning particular objects of compassion, than to countenance and establish theft by one general undistinguishing law.

NECHO

Pages 816-816
king of Egypt, began his reign 690 B.C., and was killed eight years after by Sabaco, king of Ethiopia. Pianmiticus his son succeeded him, and was the father, as Herodotus informs us, of Necho II, who reigned in the 616 B.C. This Necho II, is celebrated in history for attempting, though in vain, to cut a canal from the Nile to the Arabian gulf. He carried his arms as far as the Euphrates, and conquered the city of Carchemish. This prince is not only known in Scripture under the name of Necho, but also in profane history. He no sooner succeeded to the crown than he raised great land armies, and fitted out vast fleets, as well upon the Mediterranean as upon the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red sea: he gave battle to the Syrians near the city of Migdol; routed them, and made himself master of the city of Cadytis. The learned, however, are not agreed about this city Cadytis. Some will have it to be Cades in Arabia Petraea, others Jerusalem; and others say it is the city of Cedes, or Kedesh, in Galilee, in the tribe of Naphtali. The Scriptures acquaint us with the whole expedition of Necho in all its particulars, 2 Kings xxiii. 29, &c. and 2 Chr. xxxv. 25, 27, &c. In the year of the world 3394, this prince having drawn out his army into the field to make war with the Assyrians or Babylonians, and to take the city of Carchemish, otherwise called Circumcision, upon the Euphrates, Josiah king of Judah, who was a tributary to the king of Babylon, marched to oppose his passage. Necho, who had no designs against him, sent to tell him, "What have I to do with you, king of Judah? It is not against you that I am come forth, but against another people, against whom the Lord has commanded me to make war. Leave off therefore to set yourself against me, for fear the Lord should punish you for your resistance." But Josiah would not hearken to the remonstrances of Necho, but gave him battle at Megiddo, where he received the wound of which he died. The people of Jerusalem set up Jehoahaz for king of Judah, and Necho soon passed forwards, without making any longer stay in Judea. But at his return from his expedition, which was very successful, he halted at Riblah in Syria; and sending for Jehoahaz king of the Jews, he deposed him, loaded him with chains, and sent him into Egypt. Then coming to Jerusalem, he set up Eliakim, or Jehoiakim, in his place, and exacted the payment of 100 talents of silver and one talent of gold from the country. Jeremiah (xlv. 2) acquaints us that the city of Carchemish was taken from Necho by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah; so that Necho did not enjoy his conquest above four years. Josephus adds, that the king of Babylon pursuing his victory, brought under his dominion all the country which is between the Euphrates and Egypt, excepting Judea. Thus Necho was again reduced within the limits of his own country.

NECROLOGY

Pages 816-817

necrologium, formed of νεκρός, "dead," and λόγος, "discourse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enumeration," a book anciently kept in churches and monasteries, wherein were registered the benefactors of the same, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their deaths, and the days of their commemoration; as also the deaths of the priors, abbots, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, canons, &c. This was otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> and obituary.

NECROMANCY

Pages 817-820

the art of revealing future events by a pretended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the dead. This superstitious and impious imposture appears to have had its origin at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and to have been thence propagated in every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> with the manners of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> has made us acquainted. The conquests of Sesostris might introduce it into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; the Israelites would naturally borrow it from the people among whom they sojourned 400 years; and it would easily find its way into Phoenicia, from the vicinity of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. From the Egyptians and Phoenicians it was adopted, with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of paganism, by the Greeks; and it was imported into Rome with Grecian literature and Grecian manners. It was not however confined to the pagan nations of antiquity: it spread itself through all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> nations of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and took such deep root as to be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> retained even after those nations were converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Of its early antiquity we have complete <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in the writings of Moses, where it is severely condemned as an abomination to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> *; and though it appears to have been even then spread into Phoenicia, we might yet conclude its birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to have been Egypt, because, at their exodus, the Israelites were corrupted only by Egyptian superstitions, and because necromancy seems to be one of those abominations which the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> represents his countrymen as having brought with them from Egypt, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to practise till they were carried captives into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> from sacred we proceed to consult profane authors, we shall find them not only affirming Egypt to have been the birthplace of necromancy, but in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> accounting for the origin of so impious a delusion. † Lib i. § 2. From Diodorus the Sicilian † we learn, that the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> the ferryman of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, of Styx, Cocytus, the Elysian Fields, Tartarus, the judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHADAMANTHUS">Rhadamanthus</a>, &c, with the whole scenery of the infernal regions, were imported from Egypt into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians, and indeed all the people of the east, made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of caves for burying places, which were well suited to the solemn shades of the surviving friends, and proper receptacles for those who were never more to behold the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. In Egypt, many of these subterraneous cavities being dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rock, still remain, and command the admiration of travellers; and near to the pyramids in particular there are some apartments of a wonderful fabric, which though they extend in length 4400 feet, and are about 30 feet in depth, appear to have been, if not entirely dug, at least reduced to form by the chisel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pickaxe of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. From the practice of burying in such caverns sprung the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the infernal mansions were situated somewhither near the centre of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which by the Egyptians was believed to be not very distant from its surface ‡. In these dreary mansions, it was very easy for such adepts as the priests of Egypt to fabricate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a>, Tartarus, the Elysian Fields, and all those scenes which were displayed before the initiated (see <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>), and by them described to the million of the people. As it was in those dark abodes that necromancy was practised, it would be no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for such magicians as withstood Moses to impose so far upon the credulous vulgar, as to make them believe, that in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their invocations they actually <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the ghosts of their friends ascend out of the earth. It appears from the book of Exodus, that the Israelitish women were, even in the wilderness, well acquainted with the use of the mirror, which was therefore undoubtedly known to the Egyptians. But a mirror of a particular form and properly illuminated at the instant required, might easily be made to reflect, in a cavern from which all other light was carefully excluded, the image of the deceased, who was called upon by the necromancer; and we can readily conceive, that with respect to the question to be proposed, a person might be concealed, prepared to give such ambiguous answers as would satisfy the inquirer, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the oracle. The terrified imaginations of the spectators would aid the delusion, and make a very slight resemblance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for the ghost or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of their departed friend; or the necromancer might assign plausible reasons why a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a>, after having dwelt for some time in the infernal regions, should lose something of its resemblance to the body which it animated. Such juggling tricks, though performed by artists less accomplished than Jannes and Jambres, have gained credit among people much more enlightened than the Egyptians can possibly have been when the science of necromancy was invented by their priests. That the Israelites, notwithstanding the prohibition of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, continued to practise the rites of necromancy, is apparent from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>'s transaction with the witch of Endor (see <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>). From the same transaction, it is likewise apparent that the witches of Israel, and therefore in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the necromancers of Egypt, pretended to evoke the ghosts of the dead by a demon or familiar spirit, which they had at their command to employ upon every emergency. This demon was called OB; and therefore Saul desires his servants to find him a woman who was mistress of an OB (A). (A) The original, or radical, signification of this word occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> xxxii. ver. 19.; where Elihu compares his belly to new bottles, which he calls oboth, the plural of ob. But as bottles were then made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, new bottles filled with wine and ready to burst, as Elihu describes them, would of course be of a form nearly globular. Necromancy—It is probable that those wretched impostors had in their pay some persons who occasionally acted the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the demon, and when the execution of the plot required their agency, emitted, by means of a cavity dug for that purpose, a low hollow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> from below the ground. Hence we find Isaiah, in his denunciations against Ariel*, saying, "Thou shalt be brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and shalt speak out of the ground; and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be as of one that hath a familiar spirit (an ob) out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust." But though the Egyptian priests were undoubtedly the inventors of the whole mystery of necromancy, and though it was from them imported into Greece by the Sellii or priests of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>, it does not appear that the Grecian necromancers pretended to be masters of ob or familiar spirits. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOPSUS">Mopsus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, Eumolpus, &c., who either travelled into Egypt in quest of knowledge, or were actually natives of that country, instructed the early Greeks in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> science: but whatever might be the practice of these apostles themselves, their disciples professed to do all the feats of magic by performing certain rites, by offering certain sacrifices, by muttering a certain form of words, by charms, spells, and exorcisms. By these they pretended to evoke the dead as certainly as the Egyptians and Jews did by their familiar spirits. By a small display of critical learning this might be easily proved from the popular story of Orpheus and Eurydice, which certainly was founded on one of these necromantic deceptions exhibited in a cave near Dodona, where the priests had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HADES">hades</a> or infernal manufactory, in humble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of those with which the first of them were well acquainted in Egypt. It is indeed evident, without the aid of criticism: no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of any letters is ignorant, that whatever superstitions of this kind prevailed among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were borrowed from the Greeks. But we all know that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> makes one of his shepherds, by means of certain herbs, poisons, and seances' charms, raise up ghosts from the bottoms of their graves; and Lucan has fabricated a story of this kind, which may be considered as an exact <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the witch of Endor. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a> he makes young Pompey travel by night to a Thessalian encampment, and anxiously inquire of her the issue of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> necromancer, by a tedious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of charms and incantations, conjures up the ghost of a soldier who had been lately slain. The phantom, after a long preamble, denounces a prediction much of the same kind with that which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel received from Samuel at Endor; and though we have elsewhere shown, that nothing but the spirit of God could have foreseen the inevitable destruction of Saul, his sons, and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> (fee MAGIC), it was very easy for any man of tolerable sagacity to foresee the defeat of Pompey's raw and undisciplined troops by the hardy veterans of the victorious Caesar. It would be endless to enumerate all the fallacious evocations of ghosts, and the ambiguous responses returned by those pretended spirits, of which we have accounts from the poets and historians of the celebrated nations of antiquity. We shall therefore proceed to mention a few which occur in the fabulous history of more modern nations, and then leave the subject to the meditation of our readers. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>'s Northern Antiquities, we have the following account of a necromantic exploit, between which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the ancient heroes into hell, it is impossible not to remark a striking similitude. "Odin the sovereign of man arises. He saddles his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> Sleipner; he mounts, and is conveyed to the subterranean abode of Hela. The dog which guards the gates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> meets him. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and his jaws are stained with blood. He opens his voracious mouth to bite, and barks a long time at the father of magic. Odin pursues his way; and the infernal cavern resounds and trembles under his horse's hoofs. At length he reaches the deep abode of death, and stops near the eastern gate, where stands the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the prophetess. He sings with a voice adapted to call up the dead; he looks towards the world; he engraves Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> on her tomb; he utters mysterious words; and he demands an answer, until the prophetess is constrained to arise and thus utter the words of the dead.—'Who is this unknown that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to disturb my repose, and drag me from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, in which I have been dead so long, all covered with snow, and moistened with the rains?' &c. The Gaelic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> pretended to be masters of the same secret. This is evident from the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, not uncommon among the Scotch Highlanders so lately as in the beginning of the 18th century. By a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> excellently versed in the antiquities of that people, and a steady friend to the writer of this article, we have been informed, that not many years ago some of the Highlanders relied implicitly upon certain oracular responses, called in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> taghairm. This word seems to be compounded of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a>, which in some parts of the Highlands is still used to denote a spirit or ghost, and ghaire, which signifies calling upon or invoking. Taghairm, therefore, in its original import, is necromancy in the most proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of that word. There were different kinds of taghairm, of which one was very lately practised in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>. The diviner covered himself with a cow's hide, and repaired at night to some deep-founding cave, whither the person who consulted lar. Hence it may be inferred that the original import of ob was round or globular: but b and p being labials, are often changed into each other; and therefore, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> ob is derived the Greek όψ, oculus, oculata, video, and the Latin opis, a name under which the earth was worshipped. Upis was a name of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>: the father of one of the Dianas was likewise Upis; but this Upis was undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between upis and opis is nothing; hence we are led to believe, that as they are all derived from ob, this word was employed by the early idolaters of Egypt to denote the first and greatest of Pagan gods, the sun. If so, those wretches who pretended to be mistresses of ob, were exactly the same kind of impostors with the Pythoneses of the Greeks. Necromancy fulted him followed soon after without any attendants. At the mouth of the cave he proposed aloud the questions of which he wanted solutions; and the man within pronounced the responses in a tone of voice similar to that with which the old or pretended demons of antiquity, gave from beneath the ground their oracular answers. That in the latter days of tughairm, the Gaelic diviners pretended to evoke ghosts, and from them to extort solutions of difficulties proposed, we have no positive evidence; but that such was the original pretence there can be little doubt, when we reflect either upon the place where this species of divination was practised, or upon the import of the word by which it was denominated. As we have been led to mention tughairm, we shall beg leave to make a few observations on another species of it, called tughairm an uisce, or "tughairm by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>." This too was last practised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Skye, by a man of the name of McCuidhean, whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had long been famous for the art. He lived near a beautiful cascade on a small river; and when consulted on any matter of consequence, he covered his whole body with a cow's hide, that necessary implement of Highland divination, and placed himself between the water of the cascade and the rock over which it flowed. Then another man with a heavy pole gave repeated strokes to the water, and the diviner behind it crying out now and then in Gaelic, "Is this a flock of sheep?" This operation was continued till McCuidhean was perceived to be frantic or furious, when he was considered as in a condition to answer the most important questions. He was frequently consulted about futurity; and though he could not, in the proper sense of the word, be called a necromancer, his responses were listened to as proceeding from something more than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>. A degree of frenzy, either real or affected, seems to have accompanied the predictions of certain kinds of diviners in all ages; and we cannot help remarking the similarity between the madness of McCuidhean and that of the Sibyl in the fifth book of the Aeneid; though we cannot suppose the one to have been borrowed from the other. At, Phæbi nondum patiens, immannis in antro Bacchatur vates, magnum, si peccore poscit Exeunte Deum: tanto magis ille fatigat Os rabidum, fera corda domans, singulique premendo. Struggling in vain, impatient of her load, And laboring underneath the ponderous god; The more she strove to shake him from her breast, With more and far superior force he press'd. Dryden. That all these pretences, whether ancient or modern, to the power of divination by means of familiar spirits, or by the art of necromancy, were groundless as well as impious, it would be affronting the understandings of our readers to offer any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Under the article Magic we have said enough on the subject, and perhaps more than enough, to those who know that demons, if they have any existence, and the departed spirits of good and bad men, are all under the control of Him who governs the intellectual as well as material world by fixed and equal laws.—These details of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, however, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be useless, if, by showing how <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and wretched a creature man becomes when left to his own inventions, they shall make any one grateful for the benefits of good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the blessings of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECROPOLIS">Necropolis</a>, a suburb of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in Egypt. It signifies "the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">City</a> of the Dead;" wherein there were <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, gardens, and superstitious tombs. Here Cleopatra is said to have applied the apic to her breast, to prevent being led in triumph by Augustus, who endeavoured to save her. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECROSIS">Necrosis</a>, visceris, in Medicine, a complete mortification of any part; called also sideratio and sphacelus. Nectanebus, or Nectanabis, a king of Egypt, who defended his country against the Persians. His grandson of the same name made an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGESILAUS">Agesilaus</a> king of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, and with his assistance he quelled a rebellion of his subjects. Some time after he was joined by the Sidonians, Phenicians, and inhabitants of Cyprus, who had revolted from the king of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. This powerful confederacy was soon attacked by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> the king of Persia, who marched at the head of his troops. Nectanebus, to defend his frontiers against so dangerous an enemy, levied 20,000 mercenary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in Greece, the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and 60,000 were furnished in Egypt. This numerous body was not equal to the Persian forces, and Nectanebus, defeated in a battle, gave up all hopes of resistance, and fled into Ethiopia, where he found a safe <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Egypt became from that time tributary to the king of Persia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECTAR">Nectar</a>, among ancient poets, the drink of the fabulous deities of the heathens; in contradistinction from their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> food, which was called ambrosia. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NECTARINE">Nectarine</a>, a fruit differing in nothing from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> peach, of which it is a species, but in having a smoother rind and a firmer pulp. See Persica. Nectarium, from nectar, the fabled "drink of the gods;" defined by Linnaeus to be a part of the corolla, or appendage to the petals, appropriated for containing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, a species of vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> under a fluid form, that oozes from the plant, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of bees and other insects. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, which seems to consider the nectarium as necessary a part of the corolla as the petals, it is certain that all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are not provided with this appendage, neither indeed is it essential to fructification. There is, besides, a manifest impropriety in terming the nectarium a part of the corolla. Linnaeus might, Milne, with equal propriety, have termed it a part or appendage of the stamens, calyx, or pointal, as the appearance in question is confined to no particular part of the flower, but is as various in point of situation as of form. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> nectarium is exceedingly vague; and, if any determinate meaning can be affixed to it, is expressive of all the singularities which are observed in the different parts of flowers. The tube, or lower part of flowers with one petal, Linnaeus considers as a true nectarium, because it is generally found to contain the sweet liquor formerly mentioned. This liquor Pontedera compares to that called amnios in pregnant animals, which enters the fertile or impregnated seeds; but that this is not at least Nectarium, least its sole use, is evident from this circumstance, that the honey or liquor in question is to be found in flowers where there are either no seeds, or those which, from the want of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs, cannot be impregnated. Thus the male flowers of nettle and willow, the female flowers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side laurel and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bryony, the male and female flowers of clutia, kiggelaria, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, all abound with the honey or nectar alluded to. Vaillant was of opinion, that the nectarium was an essential part of the corolla; for which reason he distinguished the singular appearances in fennel flower and columbine by the name of petals: the coloured leaves which are now termed the petals he designates the flower cup. That the nectarium, however, is frequently distinct from the petals, is evident both from the well known examples just mentioned, as likewise from the flowers of monkshood, hellebore, hyopyrum, fennel flower of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, barrenwort, gras of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, chocolate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, cherleria, and sauvagesia. These general observations being premised, we proceed to take a nearer and more particular view of the principal diversities, both in form and situation, of this striking appendage to the flower. 1. In many flowers the nectarium is shaped like a spur or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and that either in flowers of one petal, as valerian, water milfoil (utricularia), butterwort, and calvesfoot; or in such as have more than one, as larkspur, violet, fumitory, balsam, and orchis. 2. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, the nectarium is properly a part of the corolla, as lying within the substance of the petals: ranunculus, lily, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> imperial, water <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, mouse tail, ananas or pine apple, dog's-tooth violet, piperidge bush, vallifloria, hermannia, uvularia, and swertia. 3. The nectarium is frequently placed in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> or row within the petals, though entirely unconnected with their substance. In this situation it often resembles a cup, as in narcissus. A nectarium of this kind is said by Linnaeus to crown the corolla. The following are examples: daffodil, sea daffodil, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPION">campion</a>, vicious campion, swallow-wort, stapelia, cynanchum, nepenthes, cherleria, balsam-tree, African spirea, witch-hazel, olax, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>-flower. 4. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>-cress, buckler, mustard, Barbadoes cherry, and monotropa, the nectarium is situated upon or makes part of the calyx. 5. The nectarium in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> flower-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> is seated upon the antherae or tops of the stamens; whence the name edenanthera, or glandular anthera, which has been given to this genus of plants. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> it is placed upon the filaments; bean-caper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, fraxinella, marvel of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-flower, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-wort, roella, and commelina. 6. In hyacinth, flowering-ruth, stock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> flower, and rocket, the nectarium is placed upon the seed-bud. 7. In honey-flower, orpine, buckwheat, collinsonia, latrea, navelwort, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, clutia, kiggelaria, sea-side laurel, and African spirea, it is attached to the common receptacle. Lastly, in ginger, nettle, dyer's weed, heart-feed, coffea, turmeric, grewia, bastard-orpine, vanellae, threew-tree, and willow, the nectarium is of a very singular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and cannot properly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under any of the foregoing heads. In discriminating the genera, the nectarium often furnishes an essential character. Plants which have the nectarium distinct from the petals, that is, not lodged within their substance, are Nectarium affirmed by Linnaeus to be generally poisonous. The following are adduced as examples: monkshood, heliophore, columbine, fennel-flower, gras of Parnassus, barren-wort, oleander, marvel of Peru, bean-caper, succulent swallow-wort, fraxinella, and honey-flower.

NECULA

Pages 820-820

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mullein. The Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> both used the stalks of a peculiar kind of mullein, called thyrallis by Nicander, for the making of wicks of lamps. We have a kind of mullein called lychnites, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-wick mullein, from the λυχνίτης of Dioscorides; but it is not certain that ours is the same plant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used the stalks of many different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> for the wicks of their candles and lamps. The rush, stripped of its bark, was as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> with them as with us for that purpose; and they also used the nettle, this mullein, and many other plants, whose stalks were composed of tough filaments, for the same purpose; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them out like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and when dry <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> them in melted resin, and other such inflammable substances. When thus prepared, they are readily inflammable, like our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a>; and this mullein, having stalks more <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and more firm than all the others, was used to make those lights with which they set fire to the funeral pile, for consuming the ashes of their dead friends.

NECYDALIS

Pages 820-820

a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEEDHAM

Pages 820-824

JOHN TUBERVILLE, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> the 10th of September in the year 1713. His parents were descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble families. His father, who had once possessed a considerable patrimony at Hilton, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Monmouth, was of the younger and Catholic branch of the Needham family: the head of the elder and Protestant branch was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kilmory, created viscount in the year 1625. The father of Mr. Needham died young, and left but a small fortune to his four children. His eldest son, who is the subject of this article, prosecuted his studies under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> clergy of the English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>, where he took orders, taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> for several years, gave eminent proofs of sagacity and genius, and surpassed all the other professors of that seminary in the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In 1740, he was engaged by his superiors in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the English mission, and was intrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the school erected at Twyford, near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the Roman Catholic youth. In 1744, he was appointed professor of philosophy in the English college at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, where, on account of his bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he remained only 15 months. After his return, he passed several years at London and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, which were principally employed in microscopical observations, and in other branches of experimental philosophy. The results of these observations and experiments were published in the Philosophical Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of London in 1749, and in a volume in 1750 at Paris in 1750; and an account of them was also given by M. de Buffon, in the first volumes of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. There was an intimate connexion between this illustrious French naturalist and Mr Needham: they made their experiments and observations together; Needham, together though the results and systems which they deduced from the same objects and operations were totally different. Mr Needham was admitted to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the Royal Society of London in the year 1747, and in the Antiquarian Society some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after. From the year 1751 to 1767 he was chiefly employed in finishing the education of several English and Irish noblemen, by attending them as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in their travels through France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and other countries. He then retired from this wandering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the English seminary at Paris, and in 1768 was chosen by the Royal Academy of Sciences in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> a corresponding member. When the regency of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in order to the revival of philosophy and literature in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, formed the project of an Imperial academy, which was preceded by the erection of a small literary society to prepare the way for its execution, Mr Needham was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Cobentzel and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Neny, and was appointed successively <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of both these foundations. He held this place, together with some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments in the Low Countries, until his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1781. "His piety, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and purity of manners (we follow the expressions of the abbé Mann) were eminent; his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the doctrines and duties of Christianity was inviolable. His zealous opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> infidels was indefatigable, and even passionate. His probity was untainted. He was incapable of every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of duplicity; his beneficence was universal, and his unsuspicious candour rendered him often a dupe to perfidy." These and other good qualities the panegyrist attributes to his deceased friend; and the learned authors of the Monthly Review, to whom Mr Needham was known, admit the justness of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. He was undoubtedly (say they), both an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a worthy citizen; but though his death be a real loss to the literary world, yet he died seafarably for himself; for had he lived to see <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II. and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> making so free with the paint, patches, and trinkets of the mother <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, confiscating her lands, abolishing her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, suppressing her holidays, introducing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> into her worship, erecting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> conductors to disperse the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of the Vatican, and achieving many other things in this style of improvement, it would have vexed full fore his feeling heart. For this honest man was narrow even to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and bigotry in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> system; and we never knew a man in whom there was such an unaccountable mixture of implicit <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and philosophical curiosity as in Mr Needham. He was a keen and judicious observer of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, had a peculiar dexterity in confirming his observations by experiments, and he was always occupied (sometimes indeed with too much fancy and precipitation) in generalizing facts, and reducing them to his system. "His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> (says Abbé Mann) was neither remarkable for fecundity nor method: his writings are rather the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of a subject expressed with energy, and thrown upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in a hurry, than finished treatises." His works are well known both in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and in France. Needham, a town in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, 73 miles from London, stands on the Orwell, 9 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Huntingdonshire. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>**, a very common little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> utensil made of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, pointed at one end, and pierced at the other, used in sewing, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">Needles</a> make a very considerable article in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, though there is scarce any commodity cheaper, the consumption of them being almost incredible. The sizes are from No. 1, the largest, to No. 25, the smallest. In the manufacture of needles, German and Hungarian steel is of most repute. In the making of them, the first thing is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the steel through a coal fire, and under a hammer, to bring it out of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> into a cylindrical one. This done, it is drawn through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hole of a wire-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and returned into the fire, and drawn through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hole of the iron smaller than the first; and thus successively from hole to hole, till it has acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fineness required for that species of needles; observing every time it is to be drawn, that it be greased over with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, to render it more manageable. The steel thus reduced to a fine wire, is cut in pieces of the length of the needles intended. These pieces are flattened at one end on the anvil, in order to form the head and eye: they are then put into the fire to soften them farther; and thence taken out and pierced at each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of the flat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> on the anvil, by force of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a> on of well-tempered steel, and laid on a leader <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> to bring out, with another punch on, the little piece of steel remaining in the eye. The corners are then filed off the square of the heads, and a little cavity filed on each side of the flat of the head; this done, the point is formed with a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and the whole filed over: they are then laid to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow iron, crooked at one end, in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> fire; and when taken out thence, are thrown into a basin of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to harden. On this operation a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> depends; too much heat burns them, and too little leaves them soft; the medium is learned by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. When they are thus hardened, they are laid in an iron shovel, on a fire more or less brisk in proportion to the thickness of the needles; taking care to move them from time to time. This serves to temper them, and take off their brittleness; great care here too must be taken of the degree of heat. They are then straightened one after another with the hammer, the coldness of the water used in hardening them, having twisted the greatest part of them. The next <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is the polishing them. To do this, they take 12,000 or 15,000 needles, and range them in little heaps against each other on a piece of new buckram sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERY">emery</a> dust. The needles thus disposed, emery dust is thrown over them, which is again sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives; at last the whole is made up into a roll, well bound at both ends. This roll is then laid on a polishing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and over it a thick plank loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which two men <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> backwards and forwards a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and a half, or two days, successively; by which means the roll thus continually agitated by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the plank over it, the needles withinside being rubbed against each other with oil and emery, are infinitely polished. After polishing they are taken out, and the filth washed off them with hot water and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>: they are then wiped in hot bran, a little moistened, placed with the needles in a round box, suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, which is kept stirring till the bran and needles be dry. The needles thus wiped in two or three different brans, are taken out and put in wooden vessels, to have the good separated from those whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or eyes have been broken either in polishing or wiping; the points are then all turned the same way, and finished with an emery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> turned with a wheel. This operation finishes them, and there remains nothing but to make them into packets of 250 each.
