It was taken by the Prussians in 1741, who augmented the fortifications af- ter the peace in 1742, and built a citadel to which they gave the name of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is situated on a river of the same name, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17. 35. N. Lat. 50. 32.

NEIUS MONS

Pages 831-831

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, at the foot of which stood <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITHACA">Ithaca</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of that name, (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>).

NELSON

Pages 831-834

The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> Viscount, one of the most celebrated naval commanders, was the son of the reverend Edmund Nelson, and was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNHAM">Burnham</a> Thorpe, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, where his father was rector, in the year 1758. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the school of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Walsham; but we are unacquainted with the particulars relative to his childhood, and whether the progress he made in his studies was in any respect ex- traordinary. It is certain, however, that he discovered a strong predilection for the naval profession at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and having quitted school at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twelve years, went on board the Raifonable of 64 guns, commanded by his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Maurice Suckling. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April 1773, a voyage of discovery to the north pole was undertaken by the honourable Constantine John Phipps, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Mulgrave, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an application by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> to Lord <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>; and although the instructions which were issued, prohibited all boys from being received on board, yet the enterprising spirit of Horatio Nelson earnestly solicited to be appointed coxswain to Captain Lutwidge, rather than submit to be left behind; and his unfettered spirit so forcibly struck the captain, that his wish was complied with. When the ship returned to England in the month of October 1773, Mr Nelson having received information that a squadron was fitting out for the East Indies, em- ployed all his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to be appointed to one of the ships. It was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he was placed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>- forte of 20 guns, commanded by the celebrated Captain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a>, and stationed in the fore-top to keep watch, but soon after removed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-deck. He obtained the professional order of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> on the 8th of April, 1777, and received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> the next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of the Lowestoffe of 32 guns, Captain William Locker, in which ship he arrived at Jamaica; but feeling that his glowing mind was cir- cumscribed in so small a frigate, he requested the com- mand of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHOONER">schooner</a>, which acted as tender to the Lowestoffe, thus availing himself of the opportunity of becoming an experienced pilot for every intricate pas- sage through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, situated on the northern side of Hispaniola. When Sir <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Parker arrived at Jamaica in the year 1778, Lieutenant Nelson was nominated by that gallant <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> to be the third of his own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> ship, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> he soon became the first. In this ship his services terminated in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a lieutenant. On the 11th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, 1779, he obtained the rank of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>-captain; and during the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years he had been in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he not only became an able officer by his constant <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his duty, and his keen observation, but also laid the foundation of being a pilot of distinguished eminence. The first ship to which he was appointed after being made a post <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>- <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TAIN">tain</a>, was the Hinchingbroke. On the arrival of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> d'Estaing at Hispaniola, as an attack upon Jamaica was immediately apprehended, Captain Nelson was intrusted with the command of the batteries of Port Royal, with the concurring approbation of the British admiral and general. In the month of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1780, it was re- solved on to reduce Fort Juan, on the river St John, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, when Captain Nelson was made choice of to command the naval department, and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> was committed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Polson. In accomplishing the object of this arduous and interesting undertaking, Nelson's usual intrepidity was again ex- hibited. Having quitted the ship under his command, he superintended the transporting of the troops in boats, 300 miles up a river, which none but Spaniards had ever navigated since the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the buccaneers. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and vigorous exertions were represented by Major Polson to General Dalling in their true colours, nor was his gallantry passed over by that officer in silence. After storming an out-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> belonging to the enemy, he constructed batteries, and fought the Spaniards; and it is to his conduct in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Fort Juan that the success of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> has been justly and chiefly ascribed. He was next appointed to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a>, at that time stationed at Jamaica; on his arrival at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> every medical affluence was given him which his situation required; but as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on the decline, he deemed it expedient to return to England in his majesty's ship Lion, the honourable William Cornwallis commander, to whose unremitting care and attention he owed the preservation of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He obtained the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a> in the month of August 1781, which put his delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to the severest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, as he was stationed during the whole of the ensuing winter in the north seas. He sailed from Quebec in the month of October, 1782, with a convoy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, where he had an opportunity of joining the fleet under Sir Samuel Hood; and in the month following he sailed with him to the West Indies, where he was honourably employed until the termination of hostilities. He soon after received orders to repair to England, being directed to attend in his way, his royal highness <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> William Henry on his visit to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a>. When he reached England, the Albemarle was paid off at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a> on the 31st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, 1783. During the autumn of that year he paid a visit to France, where he continued till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the ensuing year, when he received the command of the Boreas frigate of 28 guns, and his destination was the Leeward Islands, where he continued until June 1787, and was then ordered to repair to England. In the month of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> the same year he was married to the amiable and accomplished widow of Dr Neibit, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a>. When the Boreas frigate was paid off at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEERNESS">Sheerness</a> on the 30th November, 1787, he retired to the parsonage-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Burnham Thorpe, which had been conferred upon him by his father for a place of residence, there to enjoy the consolations which result from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> felicity. He again came forward on the 30th of January 1793, to shine forth more conspicuous as a naval officer than he had ever done before, at which time he received the command of the Agamemnon of 64 guns, being soon placed under the orders of that truly great and illustrious character, Lord Hood, who at that period was destined to command in the Mediterranean. The unlimited confidence reposed in him by this noble and gallant admiral, is an incontestable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> estimation in which his courage and naval abilities were held. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> his superior designed to attack batteries, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cut ships out of the harbours in which they were moored; if troops were to be landed in perilous situations, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difficulty to be explored, the great Nelson took the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> on every such occasion, seconded by the brave officers and crew belonging to the Agamemnon, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTIA">Bastia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALVI">Calvi</a>, witnessed his gallant and intrepid deportment, of which Lord Hood did not fail to make honourable mention. At the siege of Calvi Captain Nelson lost the sight of his right eye, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of the enemy having struck that of which he had the command, and driven some particles of sand against his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> with irresistible impetuosity. When Lord Hood left his station in the Mediterranean in the month of October, 1794, the command devolved on Admiral Hotham, who honoured our <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> with an equal share of his confidence and esteem. On the 13th and 14th of March, and 13th of July 1795, he again rendered himself conspicuous in the actions which then took place with the French fleet; and soon after he was chosen by Admiral Hotham to cooperate with General De Vins, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, in which service he continued so long as Hotham retained the command, who was superceded by Sir John Jervis. This officer so much applauded the conduct of Captain Nelson, that he received the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of wearing a pendant of distinction; and in the month of May he was removed from the Agamemnon to the Captain of 74 guns. On the 11th of August he had a captain appointed under him. From April to October 1795, Commodore Nelson was continually employed in the most <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and arduous service, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, the taking of Porto Ferrajo, with the island of Caprea, and finally in the evacuation of Bastia. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1796 he hoisted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> pendant on board La Minerve, frigate, and was dispatched with that ship, and La Blanche, to Porto Ferrajo, to bring the naval stores left there to Gibraltar, which the fleet was in much want of. While on this service in the night of the 17th December, he fell in with two Spanish frigates, one of which he immediately attacked, and ordered the Blanche to bear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to engage the other. About half past ten the commodore brought his ship to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which continued without interruption till half past one, when the Spanish frigate of 40 guns, 28 of which were 18 pounders, struck to La Minerve. After various other active and important services during the three preceding months, Sir Horatio Nelson, in April 1797, hoisted his flag on board the Captain of 74 guns as rear-admiral of the blue, and in the end of May he shifted his flag from the Captain to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>, when he was appointed to the command of the inner squadron at the blockade of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>. While on this service he exhibited another remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his undaunted personal courage. In the attack on the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-boats in July, he was boarded in his barge, which had only the usual complement of 10 men, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COCKSWAIN">cockswain</a>. The commander of the Spanish gun-boats, in a barge with 30 men and officers, made a desperate attack on the admiral and his brave companions. The conflict remained long doubtful, but after 18 of the Spaniards were killed, and almost the whole of the remainder wounded, the rear-admiral and his brave crew succeeded in carrying this superior force. On the 15th of July the same year, Admiral Nelson was detached with a small squadron to attack the town of Santa Cruz in the island of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENERIFFE">Teneriffe</a>. A thousand men, including <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, were landed in the course of a dark night, made themselves masters of the town, and retained possession of it for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hours; but finding it impossible to storm the citadel, they prepared for their retreat, which the Spaniards allowed them to make unmolested, agreeable to the stipulations which had been entered into. In this unfortunate attack the brave Nelson lost his arm by a cannon shot. But a more splendid <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of the life of our hero is now opening. On the 13th of April 1798 he was detached tached from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> St Vincent's fleet, in pursuit of the French to the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, with 12 sail of the line and one 50 gun ship, while the enemy's fleet consisted of 13 sail of the line and four frigates, protected by the batteries on the shore, and several gun-boats. This memorable action commenced at sunset, and terminated gloriously for the honour of our hero and that of the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. Nine sail of the line fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the conqueror, two were burnt, and two effected their escape. The brave Nelson was wounded in the action, believing himself to have been shot through the head; but after his wound was examined by the surgeon, it was happily found not to be mortal, a circumstance which diffused the most lively satisfaction throughout the whole fleet. To the honour of this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> it ought to be mentioned, that even under the conviction of approaching <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, he prepared for the interesting change with calmness and fortitude, desired his chaplain to recommend him to Lady Nelson, appointed the brave Hardy to the rank of post-captain and to the command of a ship, and took an affectionate leave of Captain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a>. The French admiral's ship, L'Orient, was blown up during the action. From the mainmast of this ship Captain Hallowell ordered a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> to be constructed, which was presented to Admiral Nelson, and gratefully accepted by the hero, as a token of affectionate regard. For some months he had it placed upright in his cabin; but in consequence of the entreaties of an old <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, the admiral was at length prevailed on to allow it to be removed. Our readers <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be surprised that Lord Nelson should now be regarded as the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the empire, and the support of her national <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. It is to his gallantry and naval skill that we are indebted for the victory of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, and the annihilation of that formidable northern confederacy which menaced the prosperity, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, the very existence of the rest of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. One of the most important services which Lord Nelson performed, was the pursuit of the combined fleets of France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> to the West Indies. This fleet had sailed from Cadiz on the 10th of April, and it was at first conjectured that Egypt was the place of their destination. In consequence of this conjecture, Lord Nelson sailed in pursuit of the enemy for the coast of Egypt; and, having missed his object, after reconnoitring that coast, he passed the straits of Gibraltar, and anchored in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAGOS">Lagos</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on the 12th of May; soon after which he sailed for the West Indies with ten ships of the line; arrived off Barbados on the 4th of June; and having touched at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOBAGO">Tobago</a>, Trinidad, and Grenada, at the latter of which places he was informed that the combined fleet had been seen on the 6th off <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINICA">Dominica</a>; he reached Antigua on the 12th, where he received information that the enemy had been seen on the 8th standing to the northward. Lord Nelson, without the loss of a moment, continued the pursuit of the enemy on their return to Europe, where they arrived about the end of July; and after taking in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> at Gibraltar, and reconnoitring the harbour of Cadiz; he returned to England, where he arrived in the Victory, on the 18th of August, after having been engaged for nearly four months in one of the most arduous, and, at the same time, one of the most important and beneficial, although, in its immediate object, unsuccessful enterprises, for which his life was distinguished. His lordship had now been absent from England more than two years, on the Mediterranean station. The concluding scene of this extraordinary man's naval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, kindles emotions of admiration and regret; and at once excites both transport and extreme of sorrow. Perhaps no action, in point of splendour and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, can equal that which deprived his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of one of the greatest heroes it ever produced, Britons appear to be sensible of its vast importance; yet it is not improbable that posterity will consider it as still more splendid, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and admiration not being damped by the poignant recollection that they personally <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the man by whose loss it was accomplished. When Lord Nelson perceived that, in consequence of his manoeuvres, he had reduced the enemy to the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of engaging him, he exclaimed in the presence of Captain Hardy and the other officers who surrounded him on the quarter deck; "Now they cannot escape us; I think we shall at least make sure of twenty of them.—I shall probably lose a leg, but that will be purchasing a victory cheaply." But alas! amidst the inexplicable satisfaction and delight, which a victory so splendid could not fail to inspire, he has left us to lament that it was purchased by the loss of a life so incomparably valuable. His lordship's flag ship fell on board the Redoubtable, by which means he was exposed to the fire of the musketry from the tops; and the insignia of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, it is supposed, flung him out to the aims of the enemy, which in the issue were too fatally successful. His secretary was cut in two by his side with a chain shot, and soon after a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> grazed his lordship's shoulder, entered his left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, and passed through his lungs. He lived about three hours after this tragic event, during which he remained perfectly collected, and he displayed the same heroic magnanimity in the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which had so eminently distinguished him through the whole of his career. His last words to Captain Hardy were, "I know I am dying, I could have wished to survive to breathe my last upon British ground, but the will of God be done!" In a few moments he expired. His last signal ought not, and will not be forgotten, which was by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELEGRAPH">telegraph</a>,— "That England expected every man would do his duty." He spoke in raptures concerning the event of the day only a short time before his dissolution, and sent word to Admiral Collingwood, desiring that he would make his affectionate farewell to all his brother seamen throughout the fleet. In this manner died, in the 47th year of his age, the greatest commander that perhaps ever adorned the British navy, leaving behind him a name dear to Great Britain, and an example of heroism which will inspire his companions in arms to emulate his virtues, that they too may live in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of a grateful posterity. His singular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of attack on this memorable occasion was communicated by his lordship to all his captains, who unanimously gave it as their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it could not possibly fail of success, being concerted with such consummate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; and they even pledged their lives for the favourable result of it. His titles were, Viscount Nelson, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Bronté.—The united <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> voted him a pension of 300l. a year, to continue during his own life and his two next heirs; the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> made him a present of 10,000l.; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signor gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> aigrette worth 4000l.; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Russia gave him a diamond box worth 2500l.; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> made him presents to the amount of 500l. together with the dukedom of Bronté, and an estate of 300l. per annum. Thus all Europe conspired to testify the estimation in which they held this distinguished hero; and the numerous monuments which have been, and still are erected to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> throughout the British empire, will continue lasting evidences of the esteem in which he was held by his grateful country. Parliament also voted a sum for the purchase of an estate for his heirs, and his majesty conferred the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl on his immediate successor. Nor were his talents wholly confined to the knowledge of naval <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a>, for it is known that as a senator he was highly respectable, although he enjoyed few opportunities of coming forward in that capacity. When he did, his speeches were heard by their lordships with respect, and the most profound attention. The few specimens we have of his abilities as a politician, afford no <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proof that if he had devoted as much of his time to those studies as he did to his peculiar profession, he would have made a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>.

NEMAUSIS

Pages 834-834
or NEMAUSUM, in Ancient Geography, the capital of the Arecomici in Gallia Narbonensis; a colony, (Coin), with the surname of Augustus, (Inscription). In it stands a Roman amphitheatre, which is still almost entire. Now Nîmes in Languedoc. NEMEA (Strabo, Livy); a river of Achaea, running between Sicyon and Corinth, the common boundary of both territories, and falling into the Corinthian bay.

NEMEA

Pages 834-834

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, situated between Cleone and Philus in Argolis; whether town, district, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other thing, uncertain; there a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> stood in which the Argives celebrated the Nemean games, and there happened all the fabulous circumstances of the Nemean lion. The district Nemea is called Bembinadia, (Pliny); a village, Bembina, standing near Nemea, (Strabo). Stephanus places Nemea in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>; though not in Elis, but on its borders; Pliny, erroneously, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. In the adjoining mountain is still shown the den of the lion, distant 15 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Nemea, (Paulianas); in which stands a considerable temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Nemeus and Cleoneus, from the vicinity of these two places. This place gave name to the Nemean games, celebrated every third year.

NEMEAN GAMES

Pages 834-834

so called from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEMEA">Nemea</a>, a village between the cities of Cleone and Philus, where they were celebrated every third year. The exercises were chariot-races, and all the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENTATHLON">Pentathlon</a>. These games were instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Opheltes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Archemorus the son of Euphletes and Creusa, who was nursed by Hypsipyle; who leaving him in a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> while she went to show the besiegers of Thebes a fountain, at her return found him dead, and a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> twined about his neck; whence the fountain, before called Langia, was named Archemorus; and the captains, to comfort Hypsipyle, instituted these games. Others ascribe their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, after his victory over the Nemean lion. Others allow, that they were instituted first in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Archemorus; but interrupted, and revived again by Hercules. The victors were crowned with parsley, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> used at funerals, and feigned to have sprung from Archemorus's blood. The Argives presided at these games.

NEMESIANUS

Pages 834-834

AURELIUS OLYMPIUS, a Latin poet who was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and flourished about the year 281, under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARUS">Carus</a>, and his sons Carinus and Numerian: the last of which emperors was so fond of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, that he contested the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with Nemesianus, who had written a poem upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs. We have still remaining a poem of our author called Cyngegeticon, and four elegies: they were published by Paulus Manutius in 1538; by Barthelet in 1613; at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1653; with the notes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> Vitius. Giraldi hath preserved a fragment of Nemesianus, which was communicated to him by Sanazarus, to whom we are obliged for our poet's works: for having found them written in Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, he procured them to be put into the Roman, and then sent them to Paulus Manutius. Although this poem hath acquired some reputation, it is greatly inferior to those of Oppian and Gratian upon the same subject; yet Nemesianus's style is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> enough, and has some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of elegance. The world was so much possessed with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his poem in the eighth century, that it was read among the classics in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, as appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the celebrated Hincmar bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, to his nephew Hincmar of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAON">Laon</a>.

NEMESIS

Pages 834-834

in Pagan worship, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Neceffity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of Oceanus and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOX">Nox</a>, had the care of revenging the crimes which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> left unpunished. She was also called Adryphaea, because Adraustus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> first raised an altar to her; and Rhomophia, from her having a magnificent temple at Rhamnus in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. She had likewise a temple at Rome in the Capitol. She is represented with a stern countenance, holding a whip in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scales in the other.

NEMESIUS

Pages 834-835

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> who embraced Christianity, and was made bishop of Emesa in Phoenicia, where he had his birth; he flourished in the beginning of the fifth century. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of his extant, entitled De Natura Hominis, in which he refutes the fatality of the Stoics and the errors of the Manichaeans, the Apollinarists, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>; but he espouses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRE_EXISTENCE">pre-existence</a> of souls (A). This treatise was translated by Valla, and printed in 1535. Another version was afterwards made of it by Ellebodius, and printed in 1665; it is also inserted in the Bibliotheca Patrum, in Greek and Latin. Lastly, another edition was published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1671, folio, with a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, wherein the editor endeavours to prove, from a passage in this book, that (A) It is much more probable that he and Origen both brought their opinion with them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, than that either of them borrowed it from the other. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III, Chap. IV. the circulation of the blood was known to Nemesius; which, however, was since shown to be a mistake by Dr Freind, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Physic.

NEMINE CONTRADICENTE

Pages 835-835

"none contradicting it;" a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> when anything is carried without opposition.

NEMOURS

Pages 835-835

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, in the Gatinois, formerly with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a>. It is seated on the river Loing, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 45. N. Lat. 48. 15.

NENAGH

Pages 835-835

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> and fair town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIPPERARY">Tipperary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, 75 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It is situated on a branch of the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a> which runs into Lough-Derg. Here stand the ruins of an old castle called Nenagh-round. Also those of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> founded in the year 1200, for canons following the rule of St Augustin. It was dedicated to St John the Baptist, and was usually called Teachon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St John's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the reign of Henry III. a friary for conventual Franciscans was also founded here, and esteemed the richest foundation of that order in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Here is a barrack for two troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. This town was burnt on St Stephen's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, 1348, by the Irish. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> held here are four.

NENIA

Pages 835-835
or NENA, in the ancient poetry, a kind of funeral song sung to the music of flutes at the obsequies of the dead. Authors represent them as sorry compositions, sung by hired women mourners called Preface. The first rise of these Nenia is ascribed to the physicians. In the heathen antiquity, the goddess of tears and funerals was called Nenia; whom some suppose to have given that name to the funeral song, and others to have taken her name from it.

NEOCESARIA

Pages 835-835

(Pliny), a town of Pontus on the south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the left side of the Lycus. About the year 342, when Leontius and Sallustius were consuls, it was entirely ruined by a dreadful earthquake, no edifice having withstood the violence of the shock, except the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and the bishop's habitation, who was saved, with the clergy and some other pious persons, while the rest of the inhabitants were buried in its ruins.

NEOMAGUS

Pages 835-835

(<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); a town of Gallia Narbonensis, on the confines of the Tricassini. Now Nyons in Dauphine.

NEOMENIA

Pages 835-835
or Noumenia, a festival of the ancient Greeks, at the beginning of every lunar month, which, as the name imports, was observed upon the day of the new moon, in honour of all the gods, but especially Apollo, who was called Neomenios, because the sun is the fountain of light; and whatever distinction of times and seasons may be taken from other planets, yet they are all owing to him as the original of those borrowed rays by which they shine. The games and public entertainments at these festivals were made by the rich, to whose tables the poor flocked in great numbers. The Athenians at these times offered solemn prayers and sacrifices for the prosperity of their country during the ensuing month. See Games. The Jews had also their neomenia, or feast of the new moon, on which peculiar sacrifices were appointed: and on this day they had a sort of family entertainment and rejoicing. The most celebrated neomenia of all others was that at the beginning of the civil year, or first day of the month Tifiri, on which no fervile labour was performed: they then offered particular burnt sacrifices, and sounded the trumpets of the temple. The modern Jews keep the neomenia only as a feast of devotion, which any one may observe or not as he pleases.

NEOPHYTES

Pages 835-835

"new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>;" a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to those heathens who had newly embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; such persons being considered as regenerated, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> born anew by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> neophytes has been also used for new priests, or those <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> admitted into orders, and sometimes for the novices in monasteries. It is still applied to the converts made by the missionaries among the infidels.

NEPAL

Pages 835-835

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATNA">Patna</a>, at the distance of about 12 days journey. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are both narrow and dangerous, but in the plains they are allowed to be good. Some parts of it are obnoxious to a putrid fever, of which those who are seized with it die in a few days; but the people in the plains are not obnoxious to it. The plain is about 200 miles in circumference, and the only entrance to it is by the mountains. It contains three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities; Cat'hamandu, having about 18,000 houses; Lelit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATTAN">Pattan</a> contains 24,000; and B'hatgan 12,000 families. Besides these there are many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are Timi and Cipoli. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the inhabitants, like that of most other countries in a state little removed from barbarism, abounds with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of absurd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> and ceremonies, which it would be superfluous to enumerate; but many of them adopt that of the Brahmins, the moral <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which, in many respects, must be allowed to be excellent. The temple of Baghero in the city of Lelit Pattan, is said to be superior to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, on account of the immense quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and jewels which it contains; and the waters of a river about three miles from Cat'hamandu are considered as holy, to which people of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> are conveyed in the prospect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This kingdom is believed to be of very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, as its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and independence have been preserved from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial; yet the dissensions of its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> completely ruined it not many years ago, who could not agree about the choice of a proper successor on the death of their sovereign.

NEPELIUM

Pages 836-836

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the meloecea clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPENTHES

Pages 835-835

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gynandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking among those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPETA

Pages 835-836

CATMINT, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nep, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPHEW

Pages 836-836

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> relative to uncle and aunt, signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sister's son; who, according to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is in the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>, but according to the canon in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>.

NEPHRITIC

Pages 836-836

something that relates to the kidneys. See Kidney. Nephritic Wood, (lignum nephriticum), a wood of a very dense and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture, and of a fine grain, brought to us from New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in small blocks, in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, and covered with its bark. This wood is said to be a good diuretic; and we are told it is used among the Indians in all diseases of the kidneys and bladder, and in suppression of urine, from whatever cause. It is also recommended in fevers, and in obstructions of the visera. The way of taking it among the Indians is only an infusion in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. These uses are not however properly ascertained. See Guilandina, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Nephritic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>. See Nephrite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jade, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index. Nephritics, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines proper for diseases of the kidneys. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> Index. Nephritis, or inflammation of the kidneys. See Medicine Index.

NEPOS

Pages 836-836

Cornelius, a celebrated Latin biographer, who flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Julius Caesar, and lived, according to St Jerome, to the fifth year of Augustus. He was an Italian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> Cattullus, and born at Holfilia, a small town in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, in Cilalpine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. Aufonius, however, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it that he was born in the Gauls; and in that they may both be in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, provided that under the name of Gaul is comprehended Gallia Cilalpina, which is in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEANDER">Leander</a> Alberti thinks Nepos's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was Verona; and he is sure that he was either born in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> neighbourhood. For the rest, Cicero and Atticus were friends of our author; who wrote the lives of the Greek historians, as he himself attests in that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a>, speaking of Philistus. What he says, also, in the lives of Cato and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, proves that he had also written the lives of the Latin captains and historians. He wrote some other excellent works which are lost. All that we have left of his at present is, "The Lives of the illustrious Greek and Roman Captains;" which were a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time ascribed to AEmilius Probus, who published them, as it is said, under his own name, to infuse himself thereby into the favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius; but, in the course of time, the fraud has been discovered, although several learned persons have confounded the two authors. This piece has been translated into French by the Sieur de Claveret, with a dedication to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Longueville, in 1663; and again by M. le Gras, then of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of the Oratory at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1729, 12mo. We have an excellent translation of it into English, by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, which has gone through several editions.

NEPTUNE

Pages 836-837

in Pagan worship, the god of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Vesta <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ops, and the Neptune, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Pluto. He assisted Jupiter in his expeditions; on which that god, when he arrived at the supreme power, assigned him the sea and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> for his empire. He was, however, expelled from heaven with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> for conspiring against Jupiter, when they were both employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAOMEDON">Laomedon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; but that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> dismissing Neptune without a reward, he sent a sea monster to lay waste the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on which he was obliged to expose his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Hecate. He is said to have been the first inventor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> and chariot <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACING">racing</a>; on which account <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> king of Pontus threw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> drawn by four horses into the sea in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this god; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> instituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> at his festival, during which all other horses left working, and the mules were adorned with wreaths of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. In a contest with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> he produced a horse by striking the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>; and on another occasion, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of skill with Minerva and Vulcan, produced a bull, whence that animal was sacrificed to him. His favourite wife was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>, whom he <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> courted in vain, till sending a dolphin to intercede for him, he met with success; on which he rewarded the dolphin by placing him among the stars. He had also two other wives, one of whom was called Salacia from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the other Venilia from the ebbing and flowing of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. He had likewise many concubines, by whom he had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children. He is represented with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, with a garment of an azure or sea green; holding his trident in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and seated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> shell drawn by sea horses; attended by the sea gods Palemon, Glaucus, and Phorcys, and the sea goddesses Thetis, Melita, and Panopæa, and a long train of tritons and sea nymphs. This deity was known in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> by the name of Canobus or Cunopus, and was worshipped as the numen aquarum or spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of certain vases or pitchers, with which the Egyptians filtrated the water of their sacred river, in order to purify and render it fit for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. From the mouth of each of these vases, which were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, arose the head and sometimes the head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or woman. Such are the emblems which still remain of the Egyptian Neptune or Canobus; and it was by this emblem that the tutelar god of Egypt vanquished the god of Chaldea in the ridiculous manner mentioned by Ruffinus in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. "The Chaldeans (says he) who adored the fire, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 26, carried their god into various countries that he might try his strength in contests with other gods. He vanquished, as we may easily conceive, the images made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and wood, &c. by reducing them to ashes; and thus the worship of fire was everywhere established. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Canobus, unwilling, as became him, to admit the superiority of strange gods, contrived to make his god vanquish the god of Chaldea in a pitched <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The vases which were worshipped as the emblems of Canobus being used for filtering the waters of the Nile, were of course perforated on all sides with very small holes. This faithful priest having stopped all the holes in one of these..." these with wax, and painted the vase of different colours for a reason which the reader <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit to be a good one, filled it up with water, and fitted to its mouth the head of an idol. This emblem of Canobus was then placed in a small fire brought by the Chaldeans as the emblem of their god; and thus the gods of Egypt and Chaldea were forced into battle. The contest, however, was of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> melting the wax made way for the water to run out, which quickly extinguished the fire; and thus Canobus vanquished the god of the Chaldeans." Ridiculous as this story is, it is perfectly suitable to the genius of Paganism, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> artifices of the Pagan priesthood; but we suspect that the historian laboured under one mistake, and substituted the Chaldeans instead of the Persians. See Polytheism.

NEREIDS

Pages 837-837

in the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> nymphs, daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a> and Doris.—The Nereids were esteemed very handsome; inasmuch that Caephe, the wife of Cepheus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ethiopia, having triumphed over all the beauties of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and daring to vie with the Nereids, they were so enraged that they sent a prodigious sea monster into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and, to appease them, she was commanded by the oracle to expose her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a>, bound to a rock, to be devoured by the monster. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments, the Nereids are represented riding upon sea horses; sometimes with an entire <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form, and at other times with the tail of a fish.

NEREIS

Pages 837-837

a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEREUS

Pages 837-837

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a marine deity, was son of Oceanus and Thetis. He settled in the Aegean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was considered as a prophet, and had the power of assuming what form he pleased. He married his sister Doris, by whom he had 50 daughters called the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>, who constantly attended on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and when he went abroad surrounded his chariot.

NERIUM

Pages 837-837

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 30th order, Contortae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">Dyeing</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NERO

Pages 837-838

Claudius Domitius Caesar, a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Domitius Ahenobarbus and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Germanicus. He was adopted by the emperor Claudius, A.D. 50, and four years after he succeeded him on the throne. In the beginning of his reign he showed several marks of the greatest kindness and condescension, affability, complaisance, and popularity. The object of his administration seemed to be the good of his people; and when he was desired to sign his name to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of malcontents that were to be executed, he exclaimed, Would to heaven I could not write! He hated flattery; and when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had liberally commended the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, he desired them to keep their praises till he deserved them. These promising virtues soon, however, proved to be <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>: Nero soon displayed the real propensities of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He delivered himself from the sway of his mother, and at last ordered her to be murdered. This unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of barbarity might astonish some, but Nero had his devoted adherents; and when he declared that he had taken away his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself from ruin, the senate applauded his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and the people signified their approbation. Many of his courtiers shared her unhappy fate; and Nero sacrificed to his fury <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> caprice all such as obstructed his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or diverted his inclination. In the night he generally went from his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> to visit the meanest taverns, and all the scenes of debauchery which Rome contained. In this nocturnal riot he was fond of insulting the people in the streets; and his attempts to offer violence to the wife of a Roman senator nearly cost him his life. He also turned <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, and openly appeared on the Roman stage in the meanest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. In his attempts to excel in music, and to conquer the disadvantages of a hoarse disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, he moderated his meals, and often palled the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> without eating. The Olympic games attracted his notice: he went into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and presented himself a candidate for the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He was defeated in wrestling; but the flattery of the spectators adjudged him the victory, and he returned to Rome with all the splendour and pomp of an eastern conqueror, drawn in the chariot of Augustus, and attended by a band of musicians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>, and stage dancers from every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the empire. These private and public amusements of the emperor were indeed innocent; his character only was injured, and not the lives of the people. His conduct, however, soon became more abominable: he disguised himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a woman, and was publicly married to one of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>. This violence to nature and decency was soon exchanged for another: Nero refused his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and celebrated his nuptials with one of his meanest catamites: and it was on this occasion that one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> observed that the world would have been happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Nero's father had had such a wife. But his cruelty was now displayed in a still higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, for he sacrificed to his wantonness his wife Ophelia Poppea, and the celebrated writers Seneca, Lucan, Petronius, &c. Nor did the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> escape his barbarity. He had heard of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; and as he wished to renew that dismal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, he caused Rome to be set on fire in different places. The conflagration became soon universal, and during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> successive days the fire <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. All was desolation: nothing was heard but the lamentations of mothers whose children had perished in the flames, the groans of the dying, and the continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of palaces and buildings. Nero was the only one who enjoyed the general consternation. He placed himself on the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower, and he sang on his lyre the destruction of Troy, a dreadful scene which his barbarity had realized before his eyes. He attempted to avert the public odium from his head by a pretended commiseration of the miseries of his subjects. He began to repair the streets and public buildings at his own expense. He built himself a celebrated palace, which he called his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It was liberally adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and with everything rare and exquisite. It contained spacious fields, artificial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, woods, gardens, orchards, and whatever exhibited a beautiful scene. The entrance of this edifice could admit a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> colossus of the emperor 120 feet high; the galleries were each a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the whole was covered with gold. gold. The roofs of the dining halls represented the firmament, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; and continually turned round night and day, showering <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> all sorts of perfumes and sweet waters. When this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> edifice, which, according to Pliny, extended all round the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, was finished, Nero said, that now he could lodge like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. His profusion was not less remarkable in all his other actions. When he went a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, his nets were of gold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. He never appeared twice in the same garment; and when he took a voyage, there were thousands of servants to take care of his wardrobe. This continuation of debauchery and extravagance at last roused the people. Many conspiracies were formed against him; but they were generally discovered, and such as were accused suffered the severest punishments. The most dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against Nero's life was that of Piso, from which he was saved by the confession of a slave. The conspiracy of Galba proved more successful, who, when he was informed that his plot was known to Nero, declared himself emperor. The unpopularity of Nero favoured his cause; he was acknowledged by all the Roman empire, and the senate condemned the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> to be dragged naked through the streets of Rome, and whipped to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and afterwards to be thrown down from the Tarpeian rock like the meanest malefactor. This, however, was not executed; for Nero prevented it by a voluntary death. He killed himself, A.D. 68, in the 32d year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, after a reign of 13 years and eight months. Rome was filled with acclamations on the occasion; and the citizens, more strongly to indicate their joy, wore caps, such as were generally used by slaves who had received their freedom. Their vengeance was not only exercised against the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the deceased monster, but many of his friends were the object of the public resentment; and many were crushed to pieces in such a violent manner, that one of the senators, amid the universal joy, said that he was afraid they should soon have cause to wish for Nero. The tyrant, as he expired, requested that his head might not be cut off from his body, and exposed to the influence of the populace, but that the whole might be burned on the funeral pile. His request was granted by one of Galba's freedmen, and his obsequies were performed with the usual ceremonies. Though his death seemed to be the source of general gladness, yet many of his favourites lamented his fall, and were grieved to see that their pleasures and amusements were dropped by the death of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of debauchery and extravagance. Even the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a> sent ambassadors to Rome, to console with the Romans, and to beg that they would honour and revere the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Nero. His statues were also crowned with garlands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; and many imagined that he was not dead, but that he would soon make his appearance and take vengeance on his enemies. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to observe, in finishing the character of this tyrannical monster, that the name of Nero is even now used emphatically to express a barbarous and unfeeling oppressor. Pliny calls him the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy and fury of mankind; and so indeed he has been called by all writers, who exhibit Nero as a pattern of the most execrable barbarity and unpardonable wantonness. The same Pliny furnishes us with this singular anecdote of him: "Nero had ordered himself to be painted under the figure of a colossus, upon cloth or canvas, 120 feet in height." He adds, "that this preposterous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, when it was finished, met with its fate from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which consumed it, and involved likewise the most beautiful part of the gardens where it was placed in the conflagration."

NERVA

Pages 838-838

COCELIUS, a Roman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> after Domitian, who was the last of the 12 Caesars. He was a native of Narnia in Umbria; his family, however, was originally of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius says he was born on the 17th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, in the 18th year of Tiberius's reign, and of the Christian era the 32d. Nero in the 12th year of his reign made him praetor, and erected a statue for him in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> on account of his poems (for he was one of the best poets of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>), some of which were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to him. He was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> in 71 with Vespasian, and in 90 with Domitian. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> authors uniformly celebrate him as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of a most mild and humane temper, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> moderation and generosity, who looked on his office as emperor, not as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was for his own advantage, but for that of his people; and whilst he reigned, which was however but for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he made the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his subjects his only end and pursuit. He narrowly escaped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> under Domitian; was naturally of a weak and timorous disposition; and, as some say, addicted to excessive drinking. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> unanimously chose him emperor; and they had no cause to repent of their choice, for he was constantly attentive to what could make them happy; he was generous, merciful, and disinterested. An instance of his great lenity appears in his pardoning Calpurnius Crassus who conspired against him. In short, he omitted nothing that might contribute to the restoring of the empire to its former lustre: recalling those who had been banished for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and redressing all grievances that came to his knowledge. He however found his strength failing, and that it would be impossible for him to finish his designs, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he adopted Trajan. After his death, which happened in the year 98, he was ranked among the gods. He was the first Roman emperor of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>.

NERVES

Pages 838-838

in Anatomy, certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> glistering cords, proceeding from the brain and spinal marrow, and dividing into very small branches, which are sent off throughout all parts of the body; and which are found to be the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. NERVOUS FLUID. See ANATOMY Index.

NESSUS

Pages 838-838

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated Centaur, son of Ixion and a Cloud. He offered violence to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEJANIRA">Dejanira</a>, whom <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> had intrusted to his care, with orders to carry her across the river Evenus. Hercules <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the distress of his wife from the opposite shore of the river, and immediately he let fly one of his poisoned arrows, which struck the Centaur to the heart. Nessus, as he expired, gave the tunic he then wore to Dejanira, assuring her that from the poisoned blood which had flowed from his wounds, it had received the power of calling a husband away from unlawful loves. Dejanira received it with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and this mournful present caused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hercules.—A river which separates Thrace from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>. It is also called Neftir, Neftor, and Neftus.

NESTOR

Pages 839-839

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a son of Neleus and Chloris, nephew to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELIAS">Pelias</a> and grandson to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. He had eleven brothers, who were all killed with his father by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. His tender <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> detained him at home, and was the cause of his preservation. The conqueror spared his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and placed him upon the throne of Pylos. He married Eurydice the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Clymenus; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, Anaxibia the daughter of Atreus. He soon distinguished himself in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; and was present at the nuptials of Perithous, when a bloody engagement took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the Lapithae and Centaurs. As <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pylos and Messenia he led his subjects to the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, where he distinguished himself among the rest of the Grecian chiefs, by eloquence, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> displays his character as the most perfect of all his heroes; and Agamemnon exclaims, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had 20 generals like Nestor, he should soon see the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> reduced to ashes. After the Trojan war Nestor retired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, where he enjoyed in the bosom of his family the peace and tranquility which were due to his wisdom and to his age. The manner and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> are unknown: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are all agreed that he lived three generations of men; which length of time is supposed to be 300 years, though more probably only 90 years, allowing 30 years for each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>.
