From that circumstance, therefore, it was usual among the Greeks and the Latins, when they wished a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and happy life to their friends, to wish them to see the years of Nestor. He had many children; two daughters, Pheidice and Polycaste; and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sons, Perseus, Stratius, Aretus, Echephron, Pitilatus, Antilochus, and Thrafymedes. Nestor was one of the Argonauts, according to Valerius Flaccus, v. §80, &c.—A poet of Lycaonia in the age of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus. He was father to Pifander, who under the emperor Alexander wrote some fabulous stories—One of the body guards of Alexander. Nestor, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> name is not known, was a native of Russia, and the earliest historian of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. He was born in 1056 at Bielozero; and in the 19th year of his age he assumed the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> in the convent of Petcherski at Kiof, and took the name of Nestor. He there made a considerable proficiency in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>: but seems to have formed his style and manner rather from the Byzantine historians, Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Synecus, than from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> classics. The time of Nestor’s death is not ascertained; but he is supposed to have lived to an advanced age, and to have died about the year 1115. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, to which he has prefixed an introduction, which after a short sketch of the early state of the world, taken from the Byzantine writers, contains a geographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Russia and the adjacent regions; an account of the Slavonian nations, their manners, their emigrations from the banks of the Danube, their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>, and settlement in the several countries wherein their descendants are now established. He then enters upon a chronological <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of the Russian annals, from the year 858 to about 1113. His style is simple and unadorned, such as suits a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> recorder of facts; but his chronological exactness, though it renders his narrative dry and tedious, contributes to ascertain the era and authenticity of the events which he relates. It is remarkable (says Mr. Coxe, from whom we have taken this narrative), that an author of such importance, whose name frequently occurs in the early Russian books, should have remained in obscurity above 600 years; and been scarcely known to his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> countrymen, the origin and actions of whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> he records with such circumstantial exactness. A copy of his Chronicle was given in 1668 by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Radziwil to the library of Konigsburg, where it lay unnoticed till <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great, in his passage through that town, ordered a transcript of it to be sent to Petersburg. But it still was not known as the performance of Nestor: for when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a> in 1732 published the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a German translation, he mentioned it as the work of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> Theodosius of Kiof; an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> which arose from the following circumstance: The ingenious editor not being at that time sufficiently acquainted with the Slavonian tongue, employed an interpreter, who, by mistaking a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, supposed it to have been written by a person whose name was Theodorus. This ridiculous blunder was soon circulated and copied by many foreign writers, even long after it had been candidly acknowledged and corrected by Muller.

NESTORIANS

Pages 839-840

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, still said to be subsisting in some parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; whose distinguishing tenet is, that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> is not the mother of God. They take their name from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NESTORIUS">Nestorius</a> bishop of Constantinople, whose doctrines were spread with much zeal through <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> promoters of the Nestorian cause was Barhumas, created bishop of Nisibis, A.D. 435. Such was his zeal and success, that the Nestorians, who still remain in Chaldea, Persia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and the adjacent countries, consider him alone as their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> and founder. By him Phrozes the Persian monarch was persuaded to expel those Christians who adopted the opinions of the Greeks, and to admit the Nestorians in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, putting them in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seat of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authority in Persia, the see of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, which the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of the Nestorians has always filled even <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to our <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.—Barhumas also erected a school at Nisibis, from which proceeded those Nestorian doctors who in the fifth and sixth centuries spread abroad their tenets through Egypt, Syria, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. He differed considerably from Nestorius, holding that there are two persons in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, as well as that the Virgin was not his mother, as God, but only as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The abettors of this doctrine refuse the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Nestorians; alleging that it had been handed down from the earliest times of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the tenth century, the Nestorians in Chaldea, whence they are sometimes called Chaldeans, extended their spiritual conquests beyond Mount Imaus, and introduced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> into Tartary properly so called, and especially into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Karit, bordering on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of China. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of that country, whom the Nestorians converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, assumed, according to the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, the name of John after his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, to which he added Nestorians, added the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">Presbyter</a>, from a principle of Nestorius' <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; whence it is said his successors were each of them called Presbyter John until the time of Gengis Khan. But Moheim observes, that the famous Presbyter John did not begin to reign in that part of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> before the conclusion of the 11th century. The Nestorians formed so considerable a body of Christians, that the missionaries of Rome were industrious in their endeavours to reduce them under the papal yoke. Innocent IV. in 1246, and Nicolas IV. in 1278, used their utmost efforts for this purpose, but without success. Till the time of Pope Julius III., the Nestorians acknowledged but one patriarch, who resided first at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, and afterwards at Mosul; but a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> arising among them, in 1551 the patriarchate became divided, at least for a time, and a new patriarch was consecrated by that pope, whose successors fixed their residence in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> in the mountainous part of Persia, where they still continue, distinguished by the name of Simeon; and so far down as the last century, these patriarchs persevered in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the church of Rome, but seem at present to have withdrawn themselves from it. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Nestorian pontiffs, who form the opposite party, and look with a hostile eye on this little patriarch, have since the year 1559 been distinguished by the general denomination of Elias, and reside constantly in the city of Mosul. Their spiritual dominion is very extensive, takes in a great part of Asia, and comprehends also within its circuit the Arabian Nestorians, and also the Christians of St Thomas, who dwell along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar. It is observed, to the lasting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Nestorians, that all the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> established in the East, they have been the most careful and successful in avoiding a multitude of superstitious opinions and practices that have infected the Greek and Latin churches. About the middle of the 17th century, the Romish missionaries gained over to their communion a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Nestorians, whom they formed into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> church; the patriarchs or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of which reside in the city of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMIDA">Amida</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a>, and all assume the denomination of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. Nevertheless the Nestorians in general persevere to our own times in their refusal to enter into the communion of the Romish church, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties and alluring offers that have been made by the pope's legate to conquer their inflexible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>.

NESTORIUS

Pages 840-841

from whom the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Nestorian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> derive their name, was born in Germanica a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Antioch, where he was likewise baptized; and soon after his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> he withdrew himself to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in the suburbs of that city. Upon his being admitted to the order of priesthood, he quickly acquired so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by the eloquence of his preaching, and the regularity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius he was deemed a fit person to fill the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> see in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and was accordingly consecrated bishop of Constantinople in the year 429. In one of his first sermons after his promotion, he publicly declared his intention to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon heretics; and with that intolerant spirit which has so often disgraced the preachers of the mild <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, he called upon the emperor to free the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from heretics, promising to give him heaven as a reward for his zeal. To this spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> he added one, that, though Nestorius' carnal, he possibly judged of equal force:—" Join with me (laid he) in war against them, and I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> assist you against the Persians." Although the wiser and better <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his audience were amazed to see a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, before he had tasted (as the historian expresses himself) the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of his city, declare that he would persecute all who were not of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; yet the majority of the people approved of this discourse, and encouraged him to execute his purpose. Accordingly, five days after his consecration, he attempted to demolish the church in which the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> secretly held their assemblies; and he succeeded so far in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, that these people, growing desperate, set it on fire themselves, and consumed with it some of the neighbouring houses. This fire excited great commotions in the city, and Nestorius was ever afterwards called an incendiary. From the Arians he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> against the Novatians, but was stopped in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> by the interposition of the emperor. He then let loose his fury upon those Christians of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Lydia, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, who celebrated the feast of Easter upon the 14th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; and for this unimportant deviation from the Catholic practice, many of those people were murdered by his agents both at Miletum and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>.—One cannot be sorry that such a relentless persecutor should himself be afterwards condemned as a heretic, for holding an opinion which no man who speaks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thinks with philosophic accuracy will now venture to controvert. This obnoxious tenet which produced a schism in the church, and was condemned by a general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, was nothing more than that "the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> cannot with propriety be called the mother of God." The people being accustomed to hear this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, were much inflamed against their bishop, imagining that he had revived the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of Paulus Samosetanus and Photinus, who taught that Jesus Christ was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> man. The monks declared openly against him, and, with some of the most considerable men of Constantinople, separated themselves from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. Several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> wrote to him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> persuasions to acknowledge that Mary was the mother of God; and when he would not comply, they procured his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> in the council of Ephesus, which deprived him of his see. He then retired to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monastery at Antioch, whence he was taken four years afterwards by the emperor's order, and banished in 435 to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">Tarsus</a>. That city being taken and destroyed by the Barbarians, he was removed to Panopolis, a city of Thebais; where he was not suffered to remain <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but was compelled to go from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, till, being in one of his journeys mortally bruised by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> relieved him from the fury of his persecutors. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we examine such of his writings as remain, we shall find that he was very unjustly condemned. It appears that he rejected the errors of Ebion, Paulus Samosetanus, and Photinus; that he maintained in express terms, that the divine Word was united to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in Jesus Christ in the most strict and intimate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> possible; that these two natures, in this state of union, make but one Christ and one person; that the properties of the Divine and human natures may both be attributed to this person; and that Jesus Christ may be said to have been born of a virgin, to have suffered and and died; but he never would admit that God could be said to have been born, to have suffered, or to have died.—When we consider that every person partakes of the substance of his mother, and that it is this which constitutes the parental and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> relation between them, it is indeed surprising that the expression "Mother of God" should ever have been admitted into the Christian church, or that any man who understands the meaning of the words should condemn Nestorius for not having used them.

NESTUS

Pages 841-841
or Nessus, a river which separates Thrace from Macedonia. It falls into the Ægean sea near the island Thasos. It is sometimes called Neus and Nefius.

NET

Pages 841-842

a device for catching fish and fowl. See the article FISHERY. The taking fowls by nets is the readiest and most advantageous of all others, where numbers are to be taken. The making the nets is very easy, and what every true sportsman ought to be able to do for himself. All the necessary tools are wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, of which there should be several of different sizes, some round and others flat; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of round pointed and flat scissors; and a wheel to <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> off the thread. The pack-thread is to be of different strength and thicknesses, according to the sort of birds to be taken; and the general size of the meshes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not for very small birds, is two inches from point to point. The nets should neither be made too deep nor too <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, for they are then difficult to manage; and they must be verged on each side with twisted thread. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the thread is too bright and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and is therefore in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> to be altered. The most usual colour is the rufset; which is to be obtained by plunging the net, after it is made, into a tanner's pit, and letting it <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there till it be sufficiently tinged: this is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the net, since it preserves the thread as well as alters the colour. The green colour is given by chopping some green wheat and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> it in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then soaking the net in this green tincture. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour is given in the same manner with the decoction of celandine; which gives a pale straw-colour, which is the colour of stubble in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> nets are to be used on ploughed lands, the green on grassy grounds, and the yellow on stubble lands. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a>-NET, among fowlers, a net generally used for taking such small birds as play in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stoop either to prey, gig, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like; as larks, linnets, buntings, &c. The time of the year for using this net is from August to November; and the best time is very early in the morning: and it is to be observed, that the milder the air, and the brighter the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is, the better will be the sport, and of longer continuance. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where this net should be laid, ought to be plain champaign, either on short stubbles, green leas, or flat meadows, near corn fields, and somewhat remote from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages: you must be sure to let your net lie <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the ground, that the birds creep not out and make their escape.—The net is made of a fine packthread with a small mesh, not exceeding half an inch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; it must be three fathoms long, and but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: it must be verged about with a small but strong <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>; and the two ends extended upon two small long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, suitable to the breadth of the net, with four stakes, tail-strings, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>.—This net is composed of two, which must be exactly alike; and are to be laid opposite to one another, so even and close, that when they are drawn and pulled over, the sides must meet and touch each other. You must stake this net <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with strong stakes, very stiff on their lines, so that you may with a nimble touch <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> them to and fro at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; then fasten your drawing-cord or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-lines (of which there must be a dozen at least, and each two yards long) to the upper end of the foremost stakes; and so extend them of such a straightness, that with a little strength they may rise up in the nets and cast them over. Your nets being thus laid, place your gigs, or playing-wantons, about 20 or 30 paces beyond, and as much on this side your nets: the gigs must be fastened to the tops of long poles, and turned into the wind, so as they may play to make a noise therein. These gigs are a sort of toys made of long goose-feathers, like shuttle-cocks, and with little small tunnels of wood running in broad and flat swan-quills, made round like a small hoop; and so, with longer strings fastened to a pole, will, with any small wind or air, move after such a manner, that birds will come in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flocks to play about them. When you have placed your gigs, then place your stake; which is a small stake of wood, to prick down into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, having in it a mortice-hole, in which a small and slender piece of wood, about two feet long, is fastened, so as it may move up and down at pleasure: and fasten to this longer stick a small line, which, running through a hole in the stick above-mentioned, and so coming up to the place where you are to fit, you may, by drawing the line up and down with your <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, raise up the longer stick as you see occasion. Fasten a live lark, or such like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, to this longer stick, which, with the line making it to stir up and down by your pulling, will entice the birds to come to your net. There is another stake, or enticement, to draw on these birds, called a looking-glass; which is a round stake of wood, as big as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s arm, made very sharp at the end, to thrust it into the ground: they make it very hollow in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, above five fingers deep; into which hollow they place a three-square piece of wood about a foot long, and each two inches broad, lying upon the top of the stake, and going with a foot into the hollowness: which foot must have a great knob at the top, and another at the bottom, with a deep flendernels between; to which flendernels you are to fasten a small packthread, which, running through a hole in the side of the stake, must come up to the place where you fit. The three-square piece of wood which lies on the top of the stake, must be of such a poise and evenness, and the foot of the socket so smooth and round, that it may whirl and turn round upon the least touch; winding the packthread so many times about it, which being suddenly drawn, and as suddenly let go, will keep the engine in a constant rotatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>: then fasten with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a> on the uppermost flat squares of the three-square piece, about 20 small pieces of looking-glass, and paint all the square wood between them of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and lively <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; which, in the the continual motion, will give such a reflection, that the birds will play about to admiration until they are taken. Both this and the other stake are to be placed in the middle between the two nets, about two or three feet distance from each other; so that in the falling of the nets, the cords may not touch or annoy them: neither must they stand one before or after another; the glass being kept in a continual motion, and the bird very often fluttering. Having placed your nets in this manner, as also your gigs and stakes, go to the further end of your long drawing lines and stake lines; and having placed yourself, lay the main drawing line across your thigh, and, with your left, pull the stake line to show the birds; and when you perceive them to play near and about your nets and stakes, then pull the net over with both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with a quick but not too hasty motion; for otherwise your sport will be spoiled. See Plate CCCLXIX, where A shows the bodies of the main net, and how they ought to be laid. B, the tail lines, or the hinder lines, staked to the ground. C, the fore lines staked also to the ground. D, the bird stake. E, the looking glass stake. G, the line which draws the bird stake. H, the line that draws the glass stake. I, the drawing double lines of the nets, which pulls them over. K, the stakes which stake down the four nether <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the nets and the two tail lines. L, the stakes that stake down the fore lines. M, the single line, with the wooden <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> to pull the net over with. N, the stake that stakes down the single line, and where the man should sit; and O, the gig. Net, Neat, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, something pure, and unadulterated with any foreign mixture. Thus wines are said to be net when not falsified or balderdashed; and coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, &c. are net when the filth and ordure are separated from them. See Neat. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> is said to be net when it has no stains or flaws; a crystal, when transparent throughout. Net is also used for what remains after the tare has been taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of any merchandise, i.e., when it is weighed clear of all package. See Tare. Thus we say, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> weighs 450 pounds; the tare is 50 pounds, and there remain net 400 pounds. Net Produce, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express what any commodity has yielded, all tare and charges deducted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> sometimes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the Italian words netto proceduto, for net produce.

NETHERLANDS

Pages 842-843

anciently called Belgia, but since denominated Low Countries <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Netherlands, from their low situation, are situated between 2° and 7° of east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 50° and 53° 30' of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude: and are bounded by the German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the north, Germany on the east, by Lorraine and France on the south, and by another <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of France and the British seas on the west; extending near 300 miles in length from north to south, and 200 miles in breadth from east to west. They consist of 17 provinces; 10 of which are called the Austrian and French Netherlands, and the other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> the United Provinces. The greatest part of the Netherlands was conquered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and that part which lies towards <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in their subjection till the decline of that empire; after which the Franks became masters of it; and under the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, it was part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. Towards the end of the 15th century Maximilian of Austria, son of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand II, acquired, by marrying the only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, the duchies of Brabant, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIMBURG">Limburg</a>, and Luxembourg; the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, Burgundy, Hainault, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Zeeland, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>; and the lordship of Friesland. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Austria, son to Maximilian and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, married Jane the daughter of Ferdinand <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Arragon and of Isabella <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Castile; by which means their son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> inherited not only almost all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> countries then lately discovered in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, but also those noble provinces of the Netherlands, and was chosen emperor under the name of Charles V. Towards the latter end of the 1527, he added to his dominions the temporalities of the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> on both sides of the Yssel; and Henry of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, being disturbed through <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the duke of Guelderland, and tired with the continued rebellion of his own subjects, surrendered to the emperor the temporalities of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, which was confirmed by the pope, and the states of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In 1536, Charles V bought of Charles of Egmond the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Guelderland and of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> should die without issue. The same year the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a> took the oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and submitted to Charles V. and in 1543 he put a garrison into the city of Cambrai, and built a citadel there. Having thus united the 17 provinces, as it were in one body, he ordered that they should continue for ever under the same prince, without being ever separated or dismembered; for which purpose he published in November 1549, with the consent and at the request of the states of all the provinces, a perpetual and irrevocable edict or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by which it was enacted, that in order to keep all those provinces together under one and the same prince, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of representation, with regard to the succession of a prince or princes, should take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for ever both in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and collateral line, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> laws of some provinces to the contrary. Charles had even a mind to incorporate these provinces with the Germanic body, and to make of them a circle of the empire, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the circle of Burgundy, in order thereby to engage the princes of the empire to concern themselves for the preservation of those provinces. But the Netherlands, always jealous of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, did not seem to like that incorporation; and when they were demanded to pay their share towards the expenses of the empire, they refused it: whereupon the princes of Germany refused, in their turn, to take any part in the wars in Flanders, and looked upon those provinces as by no means belonging to the Germanic body. Philip of Austria and his son Charles, who were born in the Netherlands, had for these provinces that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> affection which men <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to have for their native country; and, knowing how jealous the inhabitants were of their liberty, and of the privileges granted to them by their former princes, they took great care to preserve them and suffered willingly that the states, who were the guardians of the people's liberty and privileges, should should in a manner share the supreme authority with them. Philip II., son to the emperor Charles V., had not the same affection for the Netherlands, nor those generous sentiments which his father had endeavoured to inspire him with. Being born in Spain of a Portuguese woman, he had no regard but for his native country; and, when he removed out of the Netherlands, he left them to the weak <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a woman, to the proud and haughty spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Grenville, and to the wild ambition of some lords of these provinces, who availing themselves of the imprudent conduct and continual blunders of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Spain, found their private <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the disturbances they could not fail to produce. Philip II., also, instead of the mild and moderate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> which his predecessors had successfully employed on many occasions, as best suiting the genius and temper of the people, had recourse to the most violent and cruel proceedings; which, far from curing the evil, served only to exacerbate it more and render it incurable. The Spaniards, whom he sent thither, being born and educated in an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarchy, jealous of the liberties and envious of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the people, broke through all their privileges, and used them almost after the same manner as they had done the inhabitants of their new and ill-gotten dominions in America. This treatment occasioned a general insurrection. The counts <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOORN">Hoorn</a>, Egmont, and the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, appeared at the head of it, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>'s reformation gaining ground about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the Netherlands, his disciples joined the malecontents: whereupon King Philip introduced a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in order to suppress them, and many thousands were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, besides those that perished by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; for these persecutions and encroachments had occasioned a civil war, in which several battles were fought. The counts Hoorn and Egmont were taken and beheaded: but the prince of Orange, retiring into Holland, with the affluence of England and France, preferred Holland and some of the adjacent provinces, which entered into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> for their mutual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> at Utrecht in 1579, and they have ever since been styled the United Provinces; but the other provinces were reduced to the obedience of Spain by the duke of Alva and other Spanish generals. However, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> privileges were in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> restored; every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was allowed its great council or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, whose concurrence was required to the making of laws, and raising <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for the government, though these assemblies were too often obliged to follow the dictates of the court. The emperor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II., endeavoured to deprive them even of the form of their free <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and he might very probably have succeeded, had he not attempted at the same time a reformation of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The Austrian Netherlands are wholly Catholic, and so bigotted to the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, that though they had tamely submitted to many encroachments of the archducal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on their civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, no sooner did the monarch encroach upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the holy mother church than they resisted his authority, and claimed all their ancient privileges <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. The same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and worship made them very lately contribute to expel from their territories the French whom they had invited to relieve them from the Austrian yoke. Thus her religious bigotry for once saved a free people from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rod of despotism on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the cruelties of frantic democracies on the other. The provinces under the government of France were, till the late revolution, under the same severe arbitrary dominion as the other subjects of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and they now <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> the same miseries with the rest of the republic. The Spaniards continued possessed of almost eight of these provinces, until the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, general of the allies, gained the memorable victory of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAMILLIES">Ramillies</a>. After which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and great part of these provinces, acknowledged Charles VI. (afterwards emperor) their sovereign; and his daughter, the late empress queen, remained possessed of them till the war that followed the death of her father, when the French made an entire conquest of them, except part of the province of Luxemburg; but they were restored by the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle in 1748, and the French retained only Artois, the Cambresis, part of Flanders, part of Hainault, and part of Luxemburg, of which they have had the dominion now upwards of eighty years. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally fruitful, but differs in the several parts. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> also differs in the several provinces; in those towards the south it does not differ much from that of England, though the seasons are more regular. In the northern provinces the winter is generally very sharp, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> sultry hot; but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and excessive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> seldom continue above five or six weeks. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is reckoned very wholesome, but is subject to thick fogs in winter, through the moistness of the country, which would be very noxious, were it not for the dry easterly winds, which, blowing off a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continent for two or three months in the year, clear the air, and occasion very sharp frosts in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> and February; during which, the ports, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> shut up. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country is low and flat; for, except some small hills and a few rising grounds in Utrecht and Guelderland, and in the parts lying towards Germany, there is no hill to be seen in the whole 17 provinces. This is the reason why they have been called the Low Countries. French Flanders abounds in grain, vegetables, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and cattle, but is in want of wood. For the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the events which took place in the Netherlands during the French revolution, by which they were united to France, see FRANCE. For the Dutch Netherlands, see UNITED PROVINCES.

Pages 843-843

among the Jews, the poverty of the Gibeonites, who were condemned by Joshua to be hewers of wood and drawers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God.

NETOPION

Pages 843-843

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a very fragrant and costly ointment, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the finest spicery ingredients. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, in his Treatise of the Diseases of Women, frequently prescribes the netopion in diseases of the uterus; and in other places he speaks of its being poured into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> as a remedy for deafness; these compositions, by their attenuating qualities, dividing the viscous and thick humours. The word netopion is also sometimes used to express the unguentum Egyptianum, and sometimes simply for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of almonds.

NETTINGS

Pages 843-844

in a ship, a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> made of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> seized together with rope yarn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twine, and fixed Nettings fixed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> and in the tops; they are sometimes stretched upon the ledges from the wafte trees to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> trees, from the top of the forecastle to the poop, and sometimes are laid in the wafte of a ship to serve instead of gratings. NETTLE.
