There are numerous hot fountains in different parts of the valley, and also on the sides of the mountains: but the most remarkable is that called the chaldeira, situated in the eastern part of the valley, on a small eminence by the side of a river, on which is a basin about 30 feet diameter, where the water continually boils with prodigious fury. A few yards distant from it is a cavern in the side of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, in which the water boils in a dreadful manner, throwing out a thick, muddy, unctuous water, several yards from its mouth with a hideous noise. In the middle of the river are several places where the water boils up so hot, that a person cannot dip his finger into it without being scalded; also along its banks are several apertures, out of which the steam rises to a considerable height, so hot that there is no approaching it with one's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>: in other places, a person would think that 100 smiths bellows were blowing altogether, and sulphureous steams issuing out in thousands of places; so that native sulphur is found in every chink, and the ground covered with it like hoar <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>; even the bushes that happen to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> near these places are covered with pure brimstone, condensing from the steam that issues out of the ground, which in many places is covered over with a substance like burnt <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>. In these small caverns from which the steam issues, the people often boil their vams. Near these boiling fountains are several mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; two in particular, whose waters have a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, of an acid taste, and bitter to the tongue. About half a mile to the westward, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the river side, are several hot springs, which are used by sick people with great success. Alto, on the side of a hill west of St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, are many others, with three <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a> houses, which are most commonly used. These waters are very warm, although not boiling hot; but at the same place issue several streams of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> mineral water, by which they are tempered, according to every one's liking. About a mile south of this place, and over a low ridge of hills, lies a fine lake about two leagues in circumference, and very deep, the water thick, and of a greenish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. At the north end is a plain piece of ground, where the sulphureous steams issue out in many places, attended with a surprising blowing noise. Our author could observe strong springs in the lake, but could not determine whether they were hot or cold; this lake seems to have no visible evacuation. The other springs immediately form a considerable river, called Ribeira Quente, which runs a course about two or three leagues, through a deep rent in the mountains, on each side of which are several places where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> issues out. It discharges itself into the sea on the south side, near which are some places where the water boils up at some distance in the sea. This wonderful place had been taken little notice of until very lately: so little curiosity had the gentlemen of the island, that scarcely any of them had seen it, until of late some persons, afflicted with very virulent disorders, were persuaded to try its waters, and found immediate relief from them. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it has become more and more frequented; several persons who had lost the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> by the gouty have been cured; and also others who were troubled with eruptions on their bodies. A clergyman, who was greatly afflicted with the gout, tried the said waters, and was in a short time perfectly cured, and has had no return of it since. When Mr Maffon was there, several old gentlemen, who were quite worn out with the said disorder, were using the waters, and had received incredible benefit from them; in particular, an old <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> about 60 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, who had been tormented with that disorder more than 20 years, and often confined to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> for six months together: he had used these waters for about three weeks, had quite recovered the use of his limbs, and walked about in the greatest spirits imaginable. A friar also who had been troubled with the said disorder about 12 years and reduced to a cripple, by using them a short time was quite well, and went a-hunting every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. There are several other hot springs in the island, particularly at Ribeira Grande; but they do not possess the same virtues, at least not in so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The east and west part of the island rises into high mountains; but the middle is low, interspersed with round conic hills, all of which have very recent marks of fire; all the parts below the surface consisting of melted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> lying very hollow. Most of the mountains to the westward have their tops hollowed out like a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNCH">punch</a> bowl, and contain wa- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the Milanese, a country of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, bounded on the west by Savoy, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, and Montferrat; by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> on the north; by the territories of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, the duchies of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, Parma, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a> on the east; and by the territories of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> on the south. It is 150 miles long, and 78 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Anciently this duchy, containing the north part of the old Liguria, was called Insubria, from its inhabitants the Insubres; who were conquered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, as these were by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>; who in their turn were subdued by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>. Dieder, the last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Lombards, was taken prisoner by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, who put an end to the Longobardic empire, and appointed governors of Milan. These governors being at a distance from their masters, soon began to assume an independency, which brought a dreadful calamity on the country; for, in 1152, the capital itself was levelled with the ground by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic Barbarossa, who committed great devastations otherwise throughout the duchy. Under this emperor lived one Galvian, a nobleman who was defended from Otho a Milanese. Galvian, along with William <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Montferrat, served in the crusade, when Godfrey of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a> took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; he killed in single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> the Saracen general, whom he stripped of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>, which was adorned with the image of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> swallowing a youth; and this ever afterwards was the badge of that family. His grandson Galvian, having opposed the emperor, was taken prisoner, and carried in irons into Germany, from whence he made his escape, and returning to Milan, died in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of his country. From him descended another Otho, at the time that Otho IV. was emperor of Germany, and who soon distinguished himself by the accomplishments both of his mind and body. When he grew up, he was received into the family of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Octavian Ubaldini at Rome. This prelate, who was himself aspiring at the popedom, was in a short time greatly taken with the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and accomplishments of young Otho and predicted his future greatness. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, one Torriano, or Torriano, a Milanese nobleman of unbounded ambition, was attempting to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Milan. The popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> had some time before been caballing against the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and at last, Torriano putting himself at their head, expelled the bishop, and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or banished all the nobility; by which means the popular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was fully established; and Torriano, under this pretence, ruled every thing as he pleased. He was, however, soon opposed by one Francesco Sforza, who formed a great party, pretending to deliver the city from Torriano's haughtiness and cruelty. But while the two parties were collecting their forces against each other, Cardinal Ubaldini was projecting the destruction of both, by means of his favourite Otho. This prelate had for some time borne an implacable hatred to Torriano, because he had been by him prevented from carrying out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> of St. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>'s church at Milan, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARBUNCLE">carbuncle</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a> of great value, which he pretended to reserve for adorning the papal tiara; for which reason he now determined to oppose his ambition. Ubaldini began with naming Otho archbishop of Milan; which, as the pope's legate, he had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to do. This nomination was confirmed by Pope Urban IV.; and the party of the nobility having now got a head from the pope himself, began to gather strength. Otho in the mean time employed himself in collecting troops; and had no sooner procured a show of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, than he advanced towards Lago Maggiore, and took possession of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARONA">Arona</a>, a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> near that lake: but Torriano, marching immediately against him with all his troops, obliged him to abandon the place, and leave his party to make the best terms they could with the conqueror. This was followed by the destruction of the castles of Arona, Anghiari, and Brebia: soon after which Torriano died, and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, who had sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to get himself elected podesta, or practor of Milan, for ten years. During his lifetime, however, the party of the nobility increased considerably under Otho, notwithstanding the check they had received. Philip died in 1265, having lost ground considerably in the affections of the people, though he obtained a great reputation for his courage and conduct. His successor Napi rendered himself terrible to the nobility whom he proscribed, and put to death as often as he could get them into his power. He proceeded such lengths, and acted with such fury against that unfortunate party, that Pope Clement IV., who had succeeded Urban, at last interdicted Milan, and excommunicated Napi and all his party. By this Napi began to lose his popularity, and the public disaffection towards him was much heightened by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> cruelty of his temper. But in the mean time, the party of the nobility was in the utmost distress. Otho himself and his friends, having spent all their substance, wandered about from place to place; the pope not being in a capacity of giving them any assistance. Otho, however, was not discouraged by his bad success, but found means still to keep up the spirits of his party, who now chose for their general Squarcini Burii, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of great eminence and courage, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> was married to Matthew Visconti, afterwards called Matthew the Great. At the same time they renewed their confederacy with the marquis of Montferrat, who was son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. The marquis agreed to this confederacy chiefly with a view to become master of the Milanese. The nobility now again began to make head; and having collected an army, which was joined by 600 Spanish Spanish cavalry and a body of foot, gained some advantages. But in the mean time Napi, having gathered together a superior army, suddenly attacked Otho and Burri, and defeated them. After this disaster Otho applied to the pope; from whom, however, he did not obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> he desired; and in the mean time Napi invited the emperor Rodolph into Italy, with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of being crowned at Milan. This invitation was accepted of with great readiness by Rodolph; who constituted Napi his governor and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>-general in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a>, sending to him at the same time a fine body of German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, the command of which was given to Caffoni, Napi’s nephew. On this Otho again applied to the pope (Gregory X.); but he was so far from granting him any alliance, that he is said to have entered into a scheme of assassinating him privately; but Otho escaped the danger, and in 1276 began to recover his affairs. The reason of Pope Gregory’s enmity to him was, that he and his party were thought to be Gibellines, and were opposed by great numbers of the nobility themselves; but after that pope’s death, the Milanese exiles being united under one head, soon became formidable. They now chose for their general Godfrey count of Languedo, a noble <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, and an inveterate enemy of the Torriano family. This nobleman being rich and powerful, enlisted many German and other mercenaries, at whose head he marched towards the Lago Maggiore. All the towns in that country opened their gates to him, through the interest of the Visconti family, who resided in these parts. But this success soon met with a severe check in an unfortunate engagement, wherein Godfrey was defeated and taken prisoner; after which he and 34 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> had their heads struck off, and sent from the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> piled up in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> waggon. This defeat greatly affected Otho; but having in a short time recovered himself, he again attacked his enemies, and defeated them; but, suffering his troops to grow remiss after their victory, the fugitives rallied, and entirely defeated him. The next year, however, Otho had better success, and totally defeated and took prisoner Napi himself. After this victory Caffoni was obliged to abandon Milan to his competitor, who kept possession of it till his death, which happened in 1295, in the 87th year of his age. Otho was succeeded by Matthew Visconti above mentioned; and Milan <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in subjection to that family without any very memorable occurrence till the year 1378, when, by the death of Galeazzo II., his brother Barnabo became sovereign of Milan. He was of a brave and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> disposition; but excessively profuse in his expenses, as his brother Galeazzo had also been; and to procure <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to supply his extravagancies, was obliged to oppress his subjects. Galeazzo had engaged in an enterprise against <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, and the siege of it was continued by Barnabo. It lasted for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years; and during this time is said to have cost 300 millions of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, a prodigious sum in those days, near 40 millions <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, the lowest gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> being in value somewhat more than half-a-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> English. Both the brothers were excessively fond of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. Barnabo erected a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the Adda, consisting of three stories; the lowest for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> and heavy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, the middle for horses, and the uppermost for foot passengers. He built also another bridge which was carried over houses without touching them. To accomplish these, and many other expensive schemes, he became one of the greatest tyrants imaginable, and every day produced fresh instances of his rapacity and cruelty. He instituted a chamber of inquiry, for punishing all those who had for five years before been guilty of killing boars, or even of eating them at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of another. They who could not redeem themselves by money were hanged, and above 100 wretches perished in that manner. Those who had anything to lose were stripped of all their substance, and obliged to labour at the fortifications and other public works. He obliged his subjects to maintain a great many hunting dogs, and each district was taxed a certain number. The overseers of his dogs were at the same time the instruments of his rapacity. When the dogs were <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and slender, the owners were always fined; but when the dogs were fat, the owners were also fined for suffering them to live without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. The extravagant behaviour of Barnabo soon rendered public affairs ready for a revolution, which was at last accomplished by his nephew John Galeazzo. He affected a solitary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, void of ambition, and even inclining to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; but at the same time took care to have his uncle’s <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> filled with spies, who gave him information of all that passed. He reduced his table and manner of living, pretending that he took these steps as preparations for a retirement from the world, which was soon to take place, after he had paid a religious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a>. In short, he acted his part so well, that even Barnabo, though abundantly cautious, had no suspicion of his having any designs against him; and so entirely did he conceal his ambition, that he several times made application to his uncle for his interest to procure him a quiet retreat as soon as his religious vows were performed. One of these was to pay a visit to the church of the blessed Virgin upon Mount Varzi. This was to be done with so much secrecy that all kinds of eye-witnesses were to be excluded; and it was with difficulty that Barnabo himself and two of his sons were allowed to accompany our devotee. But, in the mean time, the hypocritical Galeazzo had <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> advancing from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>; so that Barnabo and his sons were immediately seized, and the houses of those who had sided with them given up to be plundered. The booty in plate, money, and all kinds of rich furniture, was immense. The ministers of the late government were dragged from their hiding places, and put to death; and at last the citadel itself fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Galeazzo, who found in it an immense sum of money. Barnabo was carried prisoner to Trivoli, a castle of his own building, where he had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to find one person still faithful to him. This was his mistress, named Dominia Porra; who, when he was abandoned by all the world, flung herself up a voluntary prisoner in his chamber, and remained with him as long as he lived, which was only <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months after his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>. John Galeazzo was the first who took upon him the title of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Milan, and was a prince of great policy and no less ambition. He made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Florentines, became master of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> and Bologna, and entirely defeated the emperor in 1411, so that he entertained hopes of becoming master of all Lombardy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off all possibility of invading it either from France. France or Germany; but his designs were frustrated by death, which happened in 1402, in the 53rd year of his age. After his decease the Milanese government fell into the most violent distractions, so that it could not be supported, even in time of peace, without an army of 20,000 foot and as many horse. In the year 1421, however, Philip duke of Milan became master of Genoa; but though he gained great advantages in all parts of Italy, the different states still found means to counterbalance his successes, and prevent him from enslaving them: so that Milan never became the capital of any extensive empire; and in 1437 Genoa revolted, and was never afterwards reduced. Philip died in 1448, and by his death the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> line of the Visconti family was at an end. The next lawful heir was Valentina his sister, who had married the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, son to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. of France. By the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the lawful progeny of it was to succeed to the duchy of Milan in failure of the heirs male of the Visconti family; but this succession was disputed by Sforza, who had married Philip's natural daughter. It is certain, however, that the rightful succession was vested in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Orleans and the kings of France; and therefore though the Sforza family got possession of the duchy for the present, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XII. afterwards put in his claim, being a grandson to John Galeazzo. For some time he was successful; but the French behaved in such an insolent manner, that they were driven out of the Milanese by the Swiss and Maximilian Sforza. The Swiss and Milanese were in their turn expelled by Francis I. who obliged the Sforza family to relinquish the government for a pension of 30,000 ducats a-year. Francis Sforza, the son of Maximilian, however, being assisted by the emperor and the pope, regained the possession of the Milanese about the year 1521; and, eight years after, the French king, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Cambrai, gave up his claim on the duchy. But, in fact, the emperors of Germany seem to have had the fairest title to the Milanese in right of their being for a long time sovereigns of Italy. On the death of Francis Sforza, therefore, in the year 1536, the emperor Charles V. declared the Milanese to be an imperial fief, and granted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> of it to his son Philip II. king of Spain. In his family it continued till the year 1706, when the French and Spaniards were driven out by the Imperialists, and the emperor again took possession of it as a fief. It was confirmed to his house by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a> in 1714, by the quadruple alliance in 1718, and by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle in 1748. The duchy of Milan is one of the finest provinces in Italy. It is bounded on the south by the Apennine mountains, and the territory of Genoa; on the north by Switzerland; on the east by the Venetian territories, and the duchies of Mantua, Parma, and Placentia; and on the west by Savoy, Piedmont, and Montferrat; extending from north to south about 100 miles, and from east to west about 108. It is well watered by the Teggino, the Seifa, the Adda, the Po, the Oglio, the Lambro, Serio, &c., and also by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>. Of the latter, the Lago Maggiore is between 30 and 40 miles in length, and in some places six or seven miles broad. In it lie the Boromean islands, as they are called, viz. Isola Bella and Isola Madre, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of which almost exceeds imagination: art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> seem to have vied with one another in embellishing them. In each of them is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> with delicious gardens, belonging to the Boromean family. The water of the lake is clear and of a greenish colour, and abounds with fish. The hills with which it is surrounded present a most charming landscape, being planted with vines and chestnut trees, interspersed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> houses. There is a canal running from it towards Switzerland, with which the city of Milan has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>. It was anciently called Lacus Verbanius. The Lago de <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMO">Como</a>, which was called by the Latin poets Lacus Larius, but had its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name from the city near which it lies, extends itself about 30 miles northward from Como, but its greatest breadth is not above five miles. From the Lago Maggiore issues the Teggino; and from that of Como the Adda. Of the other lakes, that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUGANO">Lugano</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDA">Guarda</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>: that of Guarda was anciently called Benacus. The trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this duchy consist principally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuffs, stockings, gloves, and handkerchiefs, linen and woollen cloth, hardware, curious works of crystal, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, hyacinths, and other gems; but their exports are usually far short of their imports. As to the revenue of the duchy, it must without doubt be very considerable. It is said to have amounted to 2,000,000 of dollars while the duchy was in the hands of the Spaniards. In the year 1767, the Austrian government of Milan published a law, by which all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> which the pope or the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> had till then exercised over <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, either with regard to their effects or persons, was transferred to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> established for that purpose at Milan. By the same edict, all ecclesiastics were obliged to sell the estates which they had become possessed of since the year 1722; and no subject, whether ecclesiastic or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a>, was to go to Rome to solicit any favour, except letters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, without the consent of the said council. This duchy was subdued by the French in the year 1796, when it was regarded as a constituent part of the Cisalpine republic. When hostilities recommenced in 1799, it was again taken by the allies, but afterwards reconquered by the army of Dijon under Bonaparte, who entered the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> on the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1800. It now forms part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Italy. Milan, the capital of the duchy of that name, in Latin <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDIOLANUM">Mediolanum</a>, is a very large city, and has a wall and rampart round it, with a citadel; yet is thought to be incapable of making any great resistance. The gardens within the city take up a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ground. In the citadel is a foundry for cannon, and an arsenal furnished with arms for 12,000 men. The governor of it is quite independent of the governor general of the Milanese, who resides in the city, in a large but old and ill-contrived palace. The yearly income of the governor of Milan is said to be 200,000 guilders. The council belonging to the city is composed of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and 60 doctors of law, who are all nobles, and independent of the governor general; Milan hath experienced a great variety of fortune, having been subject sometimes to the French, sometimes to the Spaniards, and sometimes to the Germans. A great number of persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and fortune live in it, especially during the winter. The ladies in France are not allowed more <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> than those of this city; even the austerities of the monastic life are so far mitigated here, that gentlemen have not only the liberty of talking with the nuns, and of rallying and laughing at the grate, but also of joining with them in concerts of music, and of spending whole afternoons in their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The place where the beau monde take the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, either in their coaches or on foot, is the rampart between the Porta Orientale and the Porta Tosa, where it is straight and broad, and extremely pleasant, being planted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> mulberry trees, and commanding a prospect on one side of the open country, and on the other of the gardens and vineyards between the ramparts and the city. Milan, which is said to have been built by the Gauls about 200 years after the foundation of Rome, contains a great number of stately edifices, as churches, convents, palaces, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a vast pile, all of marble; and though something has been doing for near 400 years towards the outward or inward ornament thereof, it is not yet finished. Of the great number of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> about it, that of St Bartholomew, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> freed alive, with his skin hanging over his shoulders; and of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>, over the main portal, are the finest. The pillars supporting the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the church are all of marble, and the windows finely painted. This church contains a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of great value, particularly a shrine of rock crystal, in which the body of St Charles Borromeo is deposited. The other churches most worthy a stranger's notice are those of St Alexander, St Jerome, St Giovanni di Ca'arotti della Paffione, that of the Jesuits, and of St Ambrose, in which lie the bodies of the saint and of the kings Pepin and Bernard. In the Ambrosian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, founded by Frederic Borromeo, 16 professors teach gratis. In the same college is also an academy of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, and a library containing about 45,000 printed books and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>; among the last of which is a translation of Josephus's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Jews, done by Rufinus about 1200 years ago, and written on the bark of a tree; St Ambrose's works on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, finely illuminated; the orations of Gregory Nazianzen, and the works of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, in folio, with Petrarch's notes. In the museum are Leonardi da Vinci's mathematical and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> drawings, in 12 large volumes. The seminary for sciences, the college of the nobles, the Helvetian college, and the mathematical academy, are noble foundations, and stately buildings. Of the hospitals, the most remarkable are the Lazaretto, and that called the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; the latter of which receives sick persons, foundlings, and lunatics, and has six smaller hospitals depending on it, with a revenue of 100,000 rix dollars. The number of the inhabitants of this city is said to be about 250,000. It has been 40 times besieged, taken 27 times, and four times almost entirely demolished; yet it hath always recovered itself. It is said that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> is sold here only by one person, and in one place. The court of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> is held in the Dominican convent, near the church of Madonna della Gratia. The houses of entertainment, and the ordinaries here, are represented as very indifferent.—Mr Keyler says, it is not unusual for young travellers, when they go to any of the taverns in Milan, to be asked, "whether they choose a letto fornito, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> bedfellow," who continues marked till she enters the bedchamber. Milan is described as inferior to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> both in beauty and convenience, many of the streets being crooked and narrow, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> windows much more frequent than in that city; even in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> palaces, the windows are often composed promiscuously of glass and paper. Two large canals extend from hence, the one to the Tesino, and the other to the Adda; the Tesino having a communication with the Lago Maggiore, and, by a canal, with the Sefia; and the Adda issuing from the Lago di Como, and having a communication by canals with the Lombro and Scrio. In a void space in one of the streets of Milan, where stood the house of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARBER">barber</a> who had conferred with the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> his fellow citizens, is erected a pillar called Colonna Infame, with an inscription to perpetuate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the execrable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. The environs of this city are very pleasant, being adorned with beautiful seats, gardens, orchards, &c. About two Italian miles from it, at the seat of the Simonetti family, is a building, that would have been a masterpiece of its kind had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> designed it for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECHO">echo</a>. It <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> return or repeat the report of a pistol above 60 times; and any single musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> well touched will have the same effect as a great number of instruments, and produce a most surprising and delightful <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>. According to Dr Moore, "there is no place in Italy, perhaps in Europe, where strangers are received in such an easy hospitable manner as at Milan. Formerly the Milanese nobility displayed a degree of splendour and magnificence, not only in their entertainments, but in their usual style of living, unknown in any other country of Europe. They are under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> at present of living at less expense, but they still show the same obliging and hospitable disposition. This country having, not very long since, been possessed by the French, from whom it devolved to the Spaniards, and from them to the Germans, the troops of those nations have, at different periods, had their residence here, and in the course of these vicissitudes, produced a style of manners, and stamped a character on the inhabitants of this duchy, different from what prevails in any other part of Italy; and nice observers imagine they perceive in Milanese manners, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, formality, and honesty imputed to those three nations, blended with the ingenuity natural to Italians. The great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> having been burnt to the ground last year, there are no dramatic entertainments, except at a small temporary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a>, which is little frequented; but the company assemble every evening in their carriages on the ramparts, and drive about, in the same manner as at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, till it is pretty late. In Italy, the ladies have no notion of quitting their carriages at the public walks, and using their own legs as in England and France. On seeing the number of servants, and the splendour of the equipages which appear every evening at the Corso on the ramparts, one would not suspect that degree of depopulation, and diminution of wealth, which we are assured has taken place within these few years all over the Milanese; and which proceeds from the bur- denfome nature of fome late taxes, and the infolent and opprefive manner in which they are gathered."—E. Long. 9. 11. N. Lat. 45. 28.

THEORY OF NAVIGATION

Pages 710-711

The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a ship in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is well known to depend on the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> upon its sails, regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the helm. As the water is a resisting medium and the bulk of the ship very considerable, it thence follows that there is always a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resistance on her fore-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; and when this resistance becomes sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the moving force of the wind upon the sails, the ship attains her utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of velocity, and her motion is no longer accelerated. This velocity is different according to the different strength of the wind; but the stronger the wind, the greater resistance is made to the ship's passage through the water; and hence, though the wind should blow ever so strong, there is also a limit to the velocity of the ship; for the sails and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> can bear but a certain force of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and when the resistance on the fore-part becomes more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to their strength, the velocity can be no longer increased, and the rigging gives way. The direction of a ship's motion depends on the position of her sails with regard to the wind, combined with the action of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> direction of the ship is, when she runs directly before the wind, the sails are then disposed, so as to be at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> thereto. But this is not always the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, both on account of the variable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the winds, and the situation of the intended port, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of intermediate headlands or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. When the wind therefore happens not to be favourable, the sails are placed so as to make an oblique <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> both with the direction of the ship and with the wind; and the sails, together with the rudder, must be managed in such a manner, that the direction of the ship may make an acute angle with that of the wind; and the ship, making boards on different tacks, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> by this means arrive at the intended port. The reason of the ship's motion in this case is, that the water resists the side more than the fore-part, and that in the same proportion as her length exceeds her breadth. This proportion is so considerable, that the ship continually flies off where the resistance is least, and that sometimes with great swiftness. In this way of sailing, however, there is a great limitation: for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the angle made by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> with the direction of the wind be too acute, the ship cannot be kept in that position; neither is it possible for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ship to make a more acute angle with the wind than about 6 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; though small sloops, it is said, may make an angle of about 5 points with it. In all these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, however, the velocity of the ship is greatly retarded; and that not only on account of the obliquity of her motion, but by reason of what is called her <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-way. This is occasioned by the yielding of the water on the lee-side of the ship, by which means the vessel acquires a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> motion, partly in the direction of the wind, and partly in that which is necessary for attaining the desired port. It is perhaps impossible to lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> any mathematical principles on which the lee-way of a ship could be properly calculated; only we may see in general that it depends on the strength of the wind, the roughness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and the velocity of the ship. When the wind is not very strong, the resistance of the water on the lee-side bears a very great proportion to that of the current of air; and therefore it will yield but very little; however, supposing the ship to remain remain in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it is evident, that the water having once begun to yield, will continue to do so for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, even though no additional force was applied to it; but as the wind continually applies the same force as at first, the lee-way of the ship must go on constantly increasing till the resistance of the water on the lee-side balances the force applied on the other, when it will become uniform, as doth the motion of a ship failing before the wind. If the ship changes her place with any degree of velocity, then every time she moves her own length, a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water is to be put in motion, which hath not yet received any momentum, and which of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> will make a greater resistance than it can do when the ship remains in the same place. In proportion to the swiftness of the ship, then, the lee-way will be the less; but if the wind is very strong, the velocity of the ship bears but a small proportion to that of the current of air; and the same effects must follow as though the ship moved slowly, and the wind was gentle; that is, the ship must make a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of lee-way.—The same thing happens when the sea rises <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, whether the wind is strong or not; for then the whole-water of the ocean, as far as the swell reaches, has acquired a motion in a certain direction, and that to a very considerable depth. The mountainous waves will not fail to carry the ship very much out of her course; and this deviation will certainly be according to their velocity and magnitude. In all cases of a rough sea, therefore, a great deal of lee-way is made.—Another circumstance also makes a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> in the quantity of the lee-way; namely, the lightness or heaviness of the ship; it being evident, that when the ship sinks deep in the water, a much greater quantity of that element is to be put in motion before she can make any lee-way, than when she swims on the surface. As therefore it is impossible to calculate all these things with mathematical exactness, it is plain that the real course of a ship is exceedingly difficult to be found, and frequent errors must be made, which can only be corrected by celestial observations. In many places of the ocean there are currents, or places where the water, instead of remaining at rest, runs with a very considerable velocity for a great way in some particular direction, and which will certainly carry the ship greatly out of her course. This occasions an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the same nature with the lee-way; and therefore, whenever a current is perceived, its direction and velocity ought to be determined, and the proper allowances made. Another source of error in reckoning the course of a ship proceeds from the variation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a>. There are few parts of the world where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> points exactly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and in those where the variation is known, it is subject to very considerable alterations. By these means the course of the ship is mistaken; for as the sailors have no other standard to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them than the compass, if the needle, instead of pointing due north, should point north-east, a prodigious error would be occasioned during the course of the voyage, and the ship would not come near the port to which she was bound. To avoid errors of this kind, the only method is, to observe the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s amplitude and azimuth as frequently as possible, by which the variation of the compass will be perceived, and the proper allowances can then be made for errors in the course which this may have occasioned. Errors will arise in the reckoning of a ship, especially when she sails in high latitudes, from the spheroidal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; for as the polar diameter of our globe is found to be considerably shorter than the equatorial one, it thence follows, that the farther we remove from the equator, the longer are the degrees of latitude. Of consequence, if a navigator assigns any certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of miles for the length of a degree of latitude near the equator, he must vary that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> as he approaches towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, otherwise he will imagine that he hath not sailed so far as he actually hath done. It would therefore be necessary to have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> containing the length of a degree of latitude in every different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> from the equator to either pole; as without this troublesome calculation must be made at every time the navigator makes a reckoning of his course. Such a table, however, hath not yet appeared; neither indeed does it seem to be an easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to make it, on account of the difficulty of measuring the length even of one or two degrees of latitude in different parts of the world. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton first discovered this spheroidal figure of the earth; and showed, from experiments on pendulums, that the polar diameter was to the equatorial one as 229 to 230. This proportion, however, hath not been admitted by succeeding calculators. The French mathematicians, who measured a degree on the meridian in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, made the proportion between the equatorial and polar diameters to be as 1 to 0.9891. Those who measured a degree at Quito in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, made the proportion 1 to 0.99624, or 266 to 265. M. Bouguer makes the proportion to be as 179 to 178; and M. Buffon, in one part of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the earth, makes the equatorial diameter exceed the polar one by \( \frac{1}{3} \) of the whole. According to M. du Sejour, this proportion is as 321 to 320; and M. de la Place, in his Memoir upon the Figure of Spheroids, has deduced the same proportion. From these variations it appears that the point is not exactly determined, and consequently that any corrections which can be made with regard to the spheroidal figure of the earth must be very uncertain. It is of consequence to navigators in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyage to take the nearest way to their port; but this is scarcely possible to be done. The shortest distance between any two points on the surface of a sphere is measured by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of a great circle intercepted between them; and therefore it is advisable to direct the ship along a great circle of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface. But this is a matter of considerable difficulty, because there are no fixed marks by which it can be readily known whether the ship sails in the direction of a great circle or not. For this reason the sailors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> choose to direct their course by the rhumbs, or the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> of the place by the compasses. These bearings do not point out the shortest distance between places; because, on a globe, the rhumbs are spirals, and not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of great circles. However, when the places <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> directly under the equator, or exactly under the same meridian, the rhumb then coincides with the arch of a great circle, and of consequence shows the nearest way. The sailing on the arch of a great circle is called great circle sailing; and the cases of it depend all on the solution of problems in spherical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>.

TV

Pages 721-729

such that the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> TV is exactly equal to the departure: and in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> would be easily obtained. For TV is to MN as the fine PT to the fine PM; that is, as the cosine of latitude is to the radius. The latitude of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> TV is not, however, easily determined with accuracy; various methods have, therefore, been taken in order to obtain it nearly, with as little trouble as possible: first, by taking the arithmetical <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of the two latitudes for that of the mean parallel; secondly, by using the arithmetical mean of the cosines of the latitudes; thirdly, by using the geometrical mean of the cosines of the latitudes; and lastly, by employing the parallel deduced from the mean of the meridional parts of the two latitudes. The first of these methods is that which is generally used. In order to illustrate the computations in middle latitude sailing, let the triangle ABC (fig. 17) represent a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> sailing, wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> is the difference of latitude, AC the distance, BC the departure, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> BAC the course. Also, let the triangle DBC be a figure in parallel sailing, in which DC is the difference of longitude, BC the meridian distance, and the angle DCB the middle latitude. In these triangles there is, therefore, one side BC <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to both; and that triangle is to be first resolved in which two parts are given, and then the unknown parts of the other triangle <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be easily obtained. **Prob. I.** Given the latitudes and longitudes of two places, to find the course and distance between them. **Example.** Required the course and distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of May, in latitude 56° 12' N, and longitude 2° 37' W, to the Naze of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, in latitude 57° 50' N, and longitude 7° 27' E. | Latitude <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of May | 56° 12' N | |----------------------|-----------| | Latitude Naze of Norway | 57° 50' N | Difference of latitude = 1° 38' = 98' Middle latitude = 57° 1 Longitude Isle of May = 2° 37' W Longitude Naze of Norway = 7° 27' E Difference of longitude = 10° 4' = 60' **By <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a>.** Draw the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">AD</a> (fig. 18) to represent the meridian of the May; with the chord of 60° describe the arc mn, upon which lay off the chord of 32° 59', the complement of the middle latitude from m to n; from D through n draw the line DC equal to 60°; the difference of longitude, and from C draw CB perpendicular to AD; make BA equal to 98', the difference of latitude, and join AC; which applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> will <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> 343 miles, the distance sought; and the angle A being measured by means of the line of chords, will be found equal to 73° 24', the required course. **By Calculation.** To find the course (d). As the difference of latitude = 98' = 1.99123 is to the difference of longitude = 60° = 2.78164 so is the cosine of middle latitude = 57° 1' = 9.73591 to the tangent of the cosine = 73° 24' = 10.52572 To find the distance. As radius = 10.00000 is to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECANT">secant</a> of the course = 73° 24' = 10.54411 so is the difference of latitude = 98' = 1.99123 to the distance = 343 = 2.53534 **By Inspection.** To middle latitude = 57°, and 1° 51' one-fourth of the difference of longitude in a distance <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, the corresponding difference of latitude is 8.2.2. Now 2.4.5, one-fourth of the difference of latitude, and 8.2.2, taken in a departure column, are found to agree nearest in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> marked 64 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> at the bottom, which is the course; and the corresponding distance 8.5.1 multiplied by 4 gives 343 miles, the distance required. **By Gunter's Scale.** The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from 98 the difference of latitude, to 60° the difference of longitude on numbers, being laid the same way from 33°, the complement of the middle latitude on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, will reach to a certain point beyond the termination of the line on the scale. Now the extent between this point and 92° on lines, will reach from 45° to 73° 24', the course on the line of tangents. And the extent from 73° 24' the course, to 33° the complement of the middle latitude on the line of lines, being laid the same way from 60° the difference of longitude, will reach to 343 the distance on the line of numbers. The true course, therefore, from the island of May to the Naze of Norway is N 73° 24' E, ENE 3° E nearly; but as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> at the May is 25 points west, therefore, the course per compass from the May is E 8 S. **Prob. II.** Given one latitude, course, and distance failed, to find the other latitude and difference of longitude. **Example.** A ship from Brest, in latitude 48° 23' N, and longitude 4° 30' W, sailed SW 1/4 W 238 miles. Required the latitude and longitude come to? **By Construction.** With the course and distance construct the triangle ABC (fig. 17), and the difference of latitude AB being measured, will be found equal to 142 miles; hence the latitude come to is 46° 1' N, and the middle latitude 47° 12'. Prob. III. Given both latitudes and course, required the distance and difference of longitude? Example. A ship from St Antonio, in latitude 17° 0' N, and longitude 24° 25' W, sailed NW, \(\frac{3}{4}\) N, till by observation her latitude is found to be 28° 34' N. Required the distance sailed, and longitude come to? Latitude St Antonio 17° 0' N - 17° 0' N Latitude by observation 28 34 N - 28 34 N Difference of lat. 11 34 = 694 m. 45 34 Middle lat. 22 47 By Construction. Construct the triangle ABC (fig. 19.), with the given course and difference of latitude, and make the angle BCD equal to the middle latitude. Now the distance AC and difference of longitude DC being measured, will be found equal to 864 and 558 respectively. By Calculation. To find the distance. To determine the difference of longitude made good upon <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> courses, by middle latitude failing. Rule I. With the several courses and distances find the difference of latitude and departure made good, and the ship's present latitude, as in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> failing. Now enter the traverse table with the given middle latitude, and the departure in a latitude column, the corresponding distance will be the difference of longitude, of the same name with the departure. Example. A ship from Cape Clear, in latitude \(51^\circ 18'\) N, longitude \(9^\circ 46'\) W, sailed as follows:—SWbS \(34\) miles, WbN \(63\) miles, NNW \(48\) miles, and NE\(E\) \(85\) miles. Longitude of Cape Clear \(9^\circ 46'\) W Difference of longitude \(1^\circ 12'\) W Longitude come to \(10^\circ 58'\) W The above method is that always practised to find the difference of longitude made good in the course of Theorems might be investigated for computing the Mercator's errors to which the above method is liable. These corrections may, however, be avoided, by using the following method. **Rule II.** Complete the traverse table as before, to which annex five columns: the first column is to contain the several latitudes the ship is in at the end of each course and distance; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, the sums of each following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of latitude; the third, half the sums, or middle latitudes; and the fourth and fifth columns are to contain the differences of longitude. Now find the difference of longitude answering to each middle latitude and its corresponding departure, and put them in the east or west difference of longitude columns, according to the name of the departure. Then the difference of the sums of the east and west columns will be the difference of longitude made good, of the same name with the greater. **Example.** A ship from Halliford in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, in lat. $64^\circ 30' N$, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. $27^\circ 15' W$, sailed as follows: SSW $46$ miles, SW $61$ miles, SbW $59$ miles, SEbE $86$ miles, SbE½E $76$ miles.
