Latitude Halliford - $64^\circ 30' N$ Difference of latitude - $4^\circ 24' S$ Latitude in - $60^\circ 6' N$ Sum - $124^\circ 36'$ Middle latitude - $62^\circ 18'$ Now, to middle lat. $62^\circ 18'$, and departure $21.3$, the difference of long. is $46^\circ E$. Long. Halliford - $27^\circ 15' W$ Longitude in - $16^\circ 29'$ The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of comm. method, in this Ex. is $12'$. **Chap. VI. Of Mercator's Sailing.** It was observed in Middle Latitude Sailing, that the difference of longitude made upon an oblique rhumb could not be exactly determined by using the middle latitude. In Mercator's sailing, the difference of longitude is very easily found, and the several problems of sailing resolved with the utmost accuracy, by the affluence of Mercator's chart or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> tables. In Mercator's chart, the meridians are straight lines parallel to each other; and the degrees of latitude, which at the equator are equal to those of longitude, increase with the distance of the parallel from the equator. The parts of the meridian thus increased are called *meridional parts*. A table of these parts was first constructed by Mr Edward Wright, by the continual addition of the fecants of each minute of latitude. For by parallel sailing, \[ R : \text{cof. of lat.} :: \text{<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of equat.} : \text{similar part of parallel.} \] And And because the equator and meridian on the globe are equal; therefore, \[ R : \text{cof. lat.} :: \text{part of meridian} : \text{similar part of parallel}. \] Or sec. lat. \( R :: \text{part of merid.} : \text{similar part of parallel}. \) Hence, \( \frac{\text{secant latitude}}{\text{part of meridian}} = \frac{R}{\text{part of parallel}} \). But in Mercator's chart the parallels of latitude are equal, and radius is a constant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> therefore, the latitude be assumed successively equal to \( 1^\circ, 2^\circ, 3^\circ \), &c., and the corresponding parts of the enlarged meridian be represented by \( a, b, c, \) &c.; then, \[ \frac{\text{secant } 1^\circ}{\text{part of mer. } a} = \frac{\text{secant } 2^\circ}{\text{part of mer. } b} = \frac{\text{secant } 3^\circ}{\text{part of mer. } c}, \] &c. Hence secant \( 1^\circ : \text{part of mer. } a :: \text{secant } 2^\circ : \text{part of mer. } b :: \text{secant } 3^\circ : \text{part of mer. } c, \) &c. Therefore by 12th V. Euclid, Secant \( 1^\circ : \text{part of mer. } a + \text{secant } 2^\circ + \text{secant } 3^\circ, \) &c.: parts of \( a + b + \text{mer. } c, \) &c. That is, the meridional parts of any given latitude are equal to the sum of the secants of the minutes in that latitude (E). Since \( CD : LK :: R : \text{secant } LD, \) fig. 15. And in the triangle CED, \[ ED : CD :: R : \text{tangent } CED; \] Therefore, \( ED : LK :: R^2 : \text{secant } LD \times \text{tangent } CED \) \[ \frac{ED \times \text{sec. } LD}{R} \times \frac{\text{tang. } CED}{R}. \] But \( \frac{ED \times \text{secant } LD}{R} \) is the enlarged portion of the meridian answering to \( ED. \) Now the sum of all the quantities \( \frac{ED \times \text{secant } LD}{R} \) corresponding to the sum of all the ED's contained in AS, will be the meridional parts answering to the difference of latitude AS; and MN is the sum of all the corresponding portions of the equator LK. Whence \( MN = \text{mer. diff. of lat.} \times \text{tangent } \frac{CED}{R}. \) That is, the difference of longitude is equal to the meridional difference of latitude multiplied by the tangent of the course, and divided by the radius. This equation answers to a right-angled rectilineal triangle, having an angle equal to the course; the adjacent side equal to the meridional difference of latitude, and the opposite side the difference of longitude. This triangle is, therefore, similar to a triangle constructed, with the course and difference of latitude, according to the principles of plane sailing, and the homologous sides will be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a>. Hence, if, in fig. 26, the angle A represents the course, AB the difference of latitude, and if AD be made equal to the meridional difference of latitude; then DE, drawn perpendicular to AD, meeting the distance produced to E, will be the difference of longitude. It is scarcely necessary to observe, that the meridional difference of latitude is found by the same rules as the proper difference of latitude; that is, if the given latitudes be of the same name, the difference of the corresponding meridional parts will be the meridional difference of latitude; but if the latitudes are of a contrary denomination, the sum of these parts will be the meridional difference of latitude. **Prob. I.** Given the latitudes and longitudes of two places, to find the course and distance between them. Ex. Required the course and distance between Cape <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>, in latitude \( 42^\circ 52' N, \) longitude \( 9^\circ 17' W, \) and Port Praya in the island of St Jago, in latitude \( 14^\circ 54' N, \) and longitude \( 23^\circ 29' W? \) | Lat. Cape Finisterre | Mer. parts | |---------------------|-----------| | Latitude Port Praya | Mer. parts | Difference of lat. \( = 27^\circ 58' \) Mer. diff. lat. \( = 1948 \) Longitude Cape Finisterre \( = 9^\circ 17' W \) Longitude Port Praya \( = 23^\circ 29' W \) Diff. longitude \( = 14^\circ 12' = 852. \) **By Construction.** Draw the straight line AD (fig. 26.) to represent the meridian of Cape Finisterre, upon which lay off AB, AD equal to 1678, and 1948, the proper and meridional differences of latitude; from D draw DE perpendicular to AD, and equal to the difference of longitude 852, join AE, and draw BC parallel to DE; then the difference AC will measure 1831 miles, and the course BAC \( 23^\circ 37'. \) **By Calculation.** To find the course. As the meridian difference of lat. \( 1948 : 3.28959 \) is to the difference of longitude \( 852 : 2.93044 \) so is radius \( 10.00000 \) to the tangent of the course \( 23^\circ 37' : 9.64085 \) To find the distance. As radius \( 10.00000 \) is to the secant of the course \( 23^\circ 37' : 10.03798 \) so is the difference of latitude \( 1678 : 3.22479 \) to the distance \( 1831 : 3.26277 \) **By Inspection.** As the meridian difference of latitude and difference of longitude are too <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> to be found in the tables, let the tenth of each be taken; these are 194.8 and 85.2 respectively. Now these are found to agree nearest under \( 24^\circ \); and to 167.8, one-tenth of the proper difference of latitude, the distance is about 183 miles, which multiplied by 10 is 1830 miles. **By Gunter's Scale.** The extent 1948, the meridional difference of latitude, to 852, the difference of longitude on the line of numbers, will reach from \( 45^\circ \) to \( 23^\circ 37', \) the course on --- (e) This is not strictly true; for instead of taking the sum of the secants of every minute in the distance of the given parallel from the equator, the sum of the secants of every point of latitude should be taken. Practice.

WATER-FOWL

Pages 116-116

Of the vast variety of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-fowl that frequent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, it is amazing to reflect how few are known to breed here: the cause that principally urges them to leave this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, seems to be not merely the want of food, but the desire of a secure retreat. Our country is too populous for birds so shy and timid as the bulk of these are: when great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> waste, a tract of woods and fen, doubtless many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of birds (which at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> migrate) remained in security throughout the year.—Egrets, a species of heron now scarcely known in this island, were in former times in prodigious plenty; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRANE">crane</a>, that has totally forsaken this country, bred familiarly in our marshes; their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of incubation, as well as of all other cloven-footed water-fowl (the heron excepted), being on the ground, and exposed to every one. As rural economy increased in this country, these animals were more and more disturbed; at length, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of alarms, they were necessitated to seek, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, some lonely safe habitation. On the contrary, those that build <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lay in the almost inaccessible rocks that impend over the British seas, breed there still in vast numbers, having little to fear from the approach of mankind: the only disturbance they meet with in general being from the desperate attempts of some few to get their eggs. [Merged from CLOVEN-FOOTED WATER-FOWL, p.116] 15. Herons. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> heron is an uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, and visits us at uncertain seasons; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> kind and the bittern never leave us. 16. Curlews. The curlew breeds sometimes on our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; but, considering the vast flights that appear in winter, it is probable that the greater part retire to other countries: the whimbrel breeds on the Grampian hills, in the neighbourhood of Invercauld. 17. Snipes. The woodcock breeds in the moist woods of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> countries. Some snipes breed here, but the greatest part retire elsewhere: as do every other species of this genus. 18. Sandpipers. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAPWING">lapwing</a> continues here the whole year; the ruff breeds here, but retires in winter; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">Migration</a>, the redshank and sandpiper breed in this country, and reside here. All the others absent themselves during summer. 19. Plovers and oyster-catcher. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>-legged plover and sandpiper visit us only in winter; the dotterel appears in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and in autumn; yet, what is very singular, we do not find it breeds in South Britain. The oyster catcher lives with us the whole year. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> plover and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-lark breed in England. The green plover breeds on the mountains of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, and on the Grampian hills. We must here remark, that every species of the genera of curlews, woodcocks, sandpipers, and plovers, that forsakes us in the spring, retires to Sweden, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, to breed: as soon as the young can fly, they return to us again, because the frosts which set in early in those countries totally deprive them of the means of subsisting; as the dryness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the ground, in general, during our summer, prevent them from penetrating the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with their bills, in search of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, which are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> food of these birds. Mr Ekmark speaks thus of the retreat of the whole tribe of cloven-footed waterfowl out of his country (Sweden) at the approach of winter; and Mr Klein gives much the same account of those of Poland and Prussia. 20. Rails and gallinules. Every species of these two genera continues with us the whole year; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-rail excepted, which is not seen here in winter. It likewise continues in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> only during the summer months, when they are very numerous, as Mr Smith tells us in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>, p. 336. Great numbers appear in Anglesea the latter end of May; it is supposed that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over from Ireland, the passage between the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> being but small. As we have instances of these birds lighting on ships in the Channel and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, we may conjecture their winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> to be in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>.

WEB-FOOTED BIRDS

Pages 117-119

23. Auks. Breed near Fordside in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, but quit their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> in winter. They are then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in different parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which they visit, not regularly, but accidentally. 24. Auk and guillemot. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> auk <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pinguin sometimes breeds in St Kilda. The auk, the guillemot, and puffin, inhabit most of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> cliffs of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, in amazing numbers, during <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> guillemot breeds in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">Bass</a> rocks and in St Kilda, and sometimes in Llandudno rocks. We are at a loss for the breeding <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; neither can we be very certain of the winter residence of any of them, excepting of the lesser guillemot and black billed auk, which, during winter, visit in vast flocks the frith of Forth. 25. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a>. These chiefly breed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, and in some countries near the pole; but some of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> throated divers, the northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">Migration</a>, and the inner, may breed in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Scotland and its isles. 26. Terns. Every species breeds here; but leaves us in the winter. 27. Petrels. The fulmar breeds in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of St Kilda, and continues there the whole year except September and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of October: the shearwater visits the isle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> in April; breeds there; and, leaving it in August or the beginning of September, disperses over all parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. The storminch is seen at all distances from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> on the same vast watery tract; nor is ever found near the shore except by some very rare accident, unless in the breeding season. Mr Pennant found it on some little rocky isles off the north of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>. It also breeds in St Kilda. He also supposes that it nests on the Blasket isles off <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a>, and that it is the gourder of Mr Smith. 28. Mergansers. This whole genus is mentioned among the birds that fill the Lapland lakes during summer. Mr Pennant has seen the young of the red-breasted in the north of Scotland: a few of these, and perhaps of the goosanders, may breed there. 29. Ducks. Of the numerous species that form this genus, we know of few that breed here: The swan and goose, the shield duck, the eider duck, a few shovellers, garganies, and teals, and a very small portion of the wild ducks. The rest contribute to form that amazing multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-fowl that annually repair from most parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to the woods and lakes of Lapland and other arctic regions, there to perform the functions of incubation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a> in full security. They and their young quit their retreat in September, and disperse themselves over Europe. With us they make their appearance the beginning of October; circulate first round our shores; and, when compelled by severe <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, betake themselves to our lakes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. Of the web-footed fowl there are some of hardier constitutions than others: these endure the ordinary winters of the more northern countries; but when the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> reigns there with more than <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> rigour, they repair for shelter to these kingdoms: this regulates the appearance of some of the diver kind, as also of the wild swans, the swallow-tailed shield duck, and the different sorts of goosanders which then visit our coasts. Barentz found the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARNACLES">barnacles</a> with their nests in great numbers in <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol16.html#article-NOVA_ZEMBLA">Nova Zembla</a>. (Collect. Voy. Dutch East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, 8vo, 1773, p. 19.) Celsius, in his Exot. 368, also affirms, that the Dutch discovered them on the rocks of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and in Waygate straits. They, as well as the other species of wild geese, go very far north to breed, as appears from the histories of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> and Spitzbergan, by Fgele and Crantz. These birds seem to make <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> a resting place, as Herrewegh observes: few continue there to breed, but only visit that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, and after a short stay retire still further north. 30. Corvora. The corvora and shag breed on most of our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rocks; the gannet in some of the Scotch isles and on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Kerry: the two first continue on our shores the whole year. The gannet disperses itself all round the seas of Great Britain, in pursuit of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and pilchard, and even as far as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a> to prey on the sardina. But of the numerous species of fowl here enumerated, it may be observed how very few intrust themselves to us in the breeding season, and what a distant flight they make to perform the first great dictate of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. There seems to be scarcely any but what we have traced to Lapland, a country of lakes, rivers, swamps, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">alps</a>, covered with thick and gloomy forests, that afford shelter during summer to these fowls, which in winter disperse over the greatest part of Europe. In those arctic regions, by reason of the thickness of the woods, the ground remains moist and penetrable to the woodcocks, and other slender-billed fowl; and for the web-footed birds, the waters afford larvae innumerable of the tormenting gnat. The days there are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and the beautiful meteorous nights indulge them with every opportunity of collecting so minute a food: whilst mankind is very sparingly scattered over that vast northern waste. Why then should Linnaeus, the great explorer of these rude deserts, be amazed at the myriads of waterfowl that migrated with him out of Lapland? which exceeded in multitude the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>; covering, for eight whole days and nights, the surface of the river <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CALIX">Calix</a>! His partial observation as a botanist, would confine their food to the vegetable kingdom, almost denied to the Lapland waters; inattentive to a more plenteous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of insect food, which the all-bountiful Creator had spread for them in the wilderness. It may be remarked, that the lakes of mountainous rocky countries in general are destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; few or none are seen on those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; and Linnaeus makes the same observation in respect to those of Lapland; having, during his whole tour, discovered only a single specimen of a lemma triflora, or "ivy-leaved duck's meat," Flora Lap. No. 472.; a few of the feirpus lacustris, or "bulrush," No. 18.; the alopecurus geniculatus, or "flote foxtail-grass," No. 38.; and the ranunculus aquatilis, No. 234.; which are all he enumerates in his Prolegomena to that excellent performance. We shall afterwards state the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> arguments for and against the migration of swallows; but here we shall give a short <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of the arguments used by the Hon. Daines Barrington against the migration of birds in general, from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> published by him in the 62d volume of the Philosophical Transactions. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> denies that any well-attested instances can be produced of this supposed migration; which, he thinks, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there were any such periodical flight, could not possibly have escaped the frequent observation of seamen. It has indeed been asserted that birds of passage become invisible in their flight, because they rise too high in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> to be perceived, and because they choose the night for their passage. The author, however, expresses his doubts "whether any <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> was ever seen to rise to a greater height than perhaps twice that of St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>;" and he further endeavours to show, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of some of these supposed migrations (from the northern parts of Europe, for instance, to the line) is too great to be accounted for, by having recourse to the argument founded on a nocturnal passage. The author next recites, in a chronological order, all the instances that he has been able to collect, of birds having been actually seen by mariners when they were crossing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> extent of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and he endeavours to show that no stress can be laid on the few casual observations of this kind that have been produced in support of the doctrine of a regular and periodical migration. Mr Barrington afterwards proceeds to invalidate M. Adanson's celebrated observation with respect to the migration of the swallow in particular, and which has been considered by many as perfectly decisive of the present question. He endeavours to show that the four swallows which that naturalist caught, on their settling upon his ship, on the 6th of October, at about the distance of 50 leagues from the coast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, and which he supposes to have been then proceeding from Europe to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the winter in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, could not be true European swallows; or, if they were, could not have been on their return from Europe to Africa. His objections are founded principally on some proofs which he produces of M. Adanson's want of accuracy on this subject, which has led him, in the present instance, to mistake two African species of the swallow tribe, described and engraved by Brisson, for European swallows, to which they bear a general resemblance; or granting even that they were European swallows, he contends that they were fitting from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> de Verd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to the coast of Africa; "to which short flight, however, they were unequal, and accordingly fell into the sailors' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>."—We shall here only add, in opposition to the remarks of Mr Barrington, the following observations of the Rev. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a>* in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Mr Pennant on this subject. "We must not (says he) deny migration in general; Arguments because migration certainly does subsist in some places, in support as my <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> has fully informed me. Of it, the motions of these birds he has ocular demonstration, for many weeks together, both spring and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>: during which periods myriads of the swallow kind <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the Straits from north to south, and from south to north, according to the season. And these vast migrations consist not only of lirundines, but of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a>-birds, hoopoes, oro pendolos, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> thrushes, &c. &c. and also of many of our soft-billed summer birds of passage; and moreover of birds which never leave us, such as all the various sorts of hawks and kites. Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BELON">Belon</a>, 200 years ago, gives a curious account of the incredible armies of hawks and kites which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in the spring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> traversing the Thracian Bosphorus from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> to Europe. Besides the above mentioned, he remarks that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> is swelled by whole troops of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> and vultures. "Now it is no wonder that birds residing in Africa should retreat before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> as it advances, and retire to milder regions, and especially birds of prey, whose blood being heated with hot animal food, are more impatient of a fultry <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>: but then I cannot help wondering why kites and hawks, and such hardy birds as are known to defy all the severity of England, and even of Sweden and all northern Europe, should want to migrate from the south of Europe, and be dissatisfied with the winters of Andalusia. "It does not appear to me that much stress may be laid on the difficulty and hazard that birds must run in their migrations, by reason of vast oceans, cross winds, &c.; because, if we reflect, a bird may travel from England to the equator without launching out and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a>..." posing itself to boundless seas, and that by crossing the water at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> and again at Gibraltar. And I with the more confidence advance this obvious remark, because my brother has always found that some of his birds, and particularly the swallow kind, are very sparing of their pains in crossing the Mediterranean: for when arrived at Gibraltar, they do not, "rang'd in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, wedge their way, and set forth Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> caravan high over seas <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">Flying</a>, and over lands with mutual wing Easing their flight."
